content: Alex Maier (11:38): I'm going to backstep or talk differently or be devil's advocate to the only thing that I'm promoting, which is it depends. It really depends because it depends upon how you approach things. There's a lot of what I'm talking about with product marketing is directly applicable to products that are created that provide utility versus products that are created that have subjective value. So case in point, let's take a look at the Northface. I think they're easy one to pick on. So the Northface has, what is it? Their Summit series, I think it is. And there's a lot of the backend of that is a lot of that is rooted in climbing Mount Everest and having extreme conditions and needing the best of the best and truly focusing on innovation. And that's great. But if you look at where that company has gone over the last, slowly over the last decade or so, is they've moved from a staunch focus on utility and objective-based value to subjective based value, which is, does it have the right fashion trend, colorway, pattern? (12:57): How is it being envisioned in an urban environment? And I'm not here to say that that's wrong or that's bad, but the more that you do float over into that world, the less in my mind, product marketing, as we've described it so far, matters and brand absolutely then takes the cake. Now we could probably have a whole nother podcast on what does product marketing look like in a subjective based valued world. It's going to be probably something completely different. Not prepared for that because I'm sure there's a lot of like if ands or buts on that. But as we look at this, I think a good definition going back to your one of your original questions is, was product marketing. Product marketing is definitely there for supporting products that have a objective based value, meaning like, is the rubber sticky? Are the handlebars solid? Does the shock go up and down smooth? (14:01): Is the weighing jacket keeping me dry? Those things and those value points.

Alex Maier (14:19): Yeah, it totally is. I think they trade one for the other. And I do believe that that is a big miss. As you look at even like a company, I'm going to pick on Nike for a second, like the original premise of where the company started that the story has been told many times is unique tread on the bottom of a running shoe to make you run faster. Bill Bauerman and the whole University of Oregon history and legacy there. It was based upon innovation and utility. And then what came of that was this idea of irreverence and challenging the norms and supporting the underdog and where the brand has evolved to now to where when you see and you ask people, why do you wear Nike? And again, I'm not saying that that's bad, but what I define, has Nike lost shelf space with specialty retail run shops? Alex Maier (16:40): What I would do, I mean, if this was one of the takeaways from our conversation today is to say, if I'm a marketing leader in the outdoor industry, how much of my team's focus is put on supporting product adoption and sell through? And I'm not talking just e-commerce and having PDP imagery, but how much of it is focused on truly collecting those consumer insights, understanding the stories to tell and telling those stories and have an equal voice at the table. Do you have a product marketing director and a brand marketing director and are they of equal status at both informing each other's work? That would be amazing. If you don't, if you're brand marketing heavy, then you likely product marketing in your mind, just by matter of how you set up, is going to be an afterthought and you're naturally going to be driving the company in that direction. (17:30): And what'll happen is you'll start to sense some friction within your organization where merchandising teams, retail buyers, your sales team, they're going, "Oh man, struggles with products, struggle with sale through. Things are having to get put on discount and clearance." Your product creation teams are going, "Man, we keep leaving all this innovation on the cutting room floor. Why is that? Why can't we sell on this awesome new fabrics that we have? " It's because just because you build it, just because you have the product doesn't mean you understand how to bring it to market. And a big thing we talk about in SaaS is product market fit. You don't talk a lot about that. And then product market fit in the outdoor space is usually put on product creation teams to own. And if the product doesn't receive adoption, it falls back on the product team. (18:25): Marketing teams rarely are the ones that get the finger pointed at them because they're over here creating brand campaigns saying we're building an affinity for the brand and there's no owners put on them there. Whereas in tech, on our team, we have a dedicated product marketing manager and this person is tied directly to our product creation and engineering teams. They understand the pain point that they're solving. They understand how that problem was solved with our products solutions and then they go to market with it and they inform, "Hey, social teams, brand teams, community teams, we need to talk about these solutions. Here's how we would talk about these solutions. Can you guys help us here?" But you have someone who's actually advocating for that, for the product marketing.

Garmin just recently launched one. I'm forgetting one of their Phoenix line watches, but it has now the SATCOM capability and the piece was definitely chock full of emotion. Myles McCutcheon (11:56): If you are mired in a streak where you may not be payingyour best games and you may have had a few losses or something like that andyou're putting out content that screams, look at how great we are at goalscoring, look at how solid our team is and stuff like that. There's amisalignment from the product to the message. And I mean I think we do a goodjob of managing that, but I think a lot of teams do as well. And that'sprobably from just past history, knowing that sports fans are damn passionate,man. They are hardcore and they love their games and their teams and if you areslightly misaligned from your brand or what's happening, they will pick up onthat.

Cole Heilborn (12:48): I guess what you're maybe alluding to is a challenge thatmaybe we don't consider in the outdoor space if your brand is the team andtheir performance in a season or in a game. So is that brand always shiftingand from a content perspective you have to be shifting that content?

Myles McCutcheon (13:06): No, our brand itself is solid. I think it's thecommunications and how we message around it. A lot of what's content is insports is yeah, sure there's content marketing a hundred percent. There's brandmarketing, there's ticket marketing and evergreen kind of membership membermarketing and stuff like that. But your daily always on machine is there aswell. And that's where those nuances I think are really important becausethat's the stuff that gets picked up. That's the stuff that people share, retweet,quote, look at scrutinize and stuff like that. So while your brand is stillthis rock solid piece of granite, if you stray from that kind of tone of voiceor some of the communications within there a little bit even by accident,that's where I think you can step in it a bit.

Cole Heilborn (13:53): I see. Gotcha. What type of content do sports teamstypically put out? What do you guys put out that works well that maybe isdifferent than the outdoor world?

Myles McCutcheon (14:03): I think every team is slightly different based on theirpriorities, their business priorities. Where we pride ourselves is high qualitysocial first content. We are very active during games. Our social team isincredibly, incredibly strong and smart and they work really well with my team,which is the producers, the shooters, the editors and photographers and stufflike that. And it's this wonderful little synergy during a live game where weare working back and forth in communication the whole time sharing moments,highlights, clipping together, a small pack of five saves you see within a twominute penalty kill that potentially our game saving saves a goalie makes andputting that out to your audience in near real time is what a way that we kindof differentiate. We also look to help communicate the team message. So there'sinterviews with players with hockey operations. The Canucks are deeply investedwithin the community here and I think probably one of the strongest, if not thestrongest in the league and how we work with our community and community groupsand stuff like that. (15:15): So we do a lot of community work too and whether that'shighlighting some of our key beneficiaries, players going to visit sickchildren in a hospital, the organization itself helping at a food bank or puttogether some housing for those in need and stuff like that, that's other formsof content that we get out there. And lastly, all of the content marketing. Sowhen we're stepping towards the playoffs, we will have a playoff based spotthat's full of stoke and hype and make sure you don't miss it. If you can't gettickets, you better be watching on TV or upfront cheering or a season launchcampaign. It is typical to most teams. Some teams work with outside agenciesfor that kind of stuff. We tend to keep all that in-house.

Cole Heilborn (15:58): Tell me more about, so like a game is happening, what isyour team doing and how are you guys simultaneously shooting and then cuttingthat and publishing that? That seems ridiculous.

So it's fascinating to watch in the benefit of having a coupleshooters is you lessen the chance that if it's a back toback goal, you missthat, but there's times where we have to bite the bullets. content: Myles McCutcheon (21:14): Great question, and that's one we've kind of pivoted onand it's due to, in my opinion at least how the world has changed in terms oflonger form storytelling. We've opted to stay away from stuff that's longerform so to speak and focus more on the social audience, social first audiencefor a few reasons. One, you're fishing where the fish are on Twitter, onInstagram, on threads nay and stuff like Snapchat, even it's been around for awhile or TikTok as well. You're fishing where the audience is in a way that youcan grow that audience and engage with people in a new way. Longer form stuffto do well takes real effort as you know and a lot of your audience knows. Ittakes real time and it takes a team and when you look at content that may havebeen done 5, 6, 7, 8 years ago for more of a YouTube based audience, the barwasn't as high as it is now and with high level athletes and super high levelproduction companies coming in and doing essentially that same content which isbehind the scenes, which is in the room, which is long form, but to a qualitythat we couldn't imagine because they have three shooters, because they have aline producer, because they have an executive producer, because they have asound person, because they have three editors continually working to make thisstory the best it can be. (23:02): We could focus on all that. There's no way we're shootinga game. The teamwork or the size of the team to create something of the qualitythat the audience now expects in those spaces is massive and it's justsomeplace we can't play because we're talking to a broad audience and have alot of messages we have to share. You look at everybody references F1 drive tosurvive. Of course the NHL recently dipped his toes in there with the sameproduction company box to box on their face off series. LeBrons had a doc madeabout him. Steph Curry was doing stuff with Facebook four years ago. These werereally well done pieces. David Beckham documentary is Outlandishly Good, that'shis own production company. That production is not a cheap production to pulloff and that's what audiences really expect now is high quality in the roomkind of stuff. And while we can get in the room, we don't have the access thatwe necessarily want at times because frankly it's a sports team and there's alot of stuff going on and as much as we'd like to get in there, it's not in thebest interest of everybody at times to be in that room.

Chris Whitten (00:00:08): If I was a photographer, I would never want to think that I would want to give so much value to my clients beyond what they hired me for, that I'm not interchangeable or replaceable. It's not enough to just throw it on a site and then hope it all goes well. You have to really dial in your marketing systems to be top of mind. That's where I truly believe that creatives are not a commodity because there is so much like heart and soul poured out into what they do, but also at the same time, you can tell when it's not there. And so I just think just positioning yourself not to be a commodity.

content:
Chris Whitten (00:02:39): Yeah, totally. I grew up in a small town, east Texas, and I remember far back I would always steal my mom's Polaroid, and so that's kind of how I introduced myself into this crazy business. And then ended up going to school out in Savannah, Georgia at Savannah College of Art and Design and majored in photography and moved back to Texas when I graduated to Dallas specifically. And that was kind of my entrance into commercial advertising. I forget where I was, but it was one day on set and called us a chip on my shoulder. Someone was like, yeah, I think I was asking somebody that worked at an agency if they thought I would be a good agency producer. And they were like, nah, the skills don't translate. And I was like, I don't think you're right. And so in 2018 joined up with Saatchi and Saatchi and on a six month contract and was producing some, I was kind of like a content creator and produced a lot of work for an automotive client that was a partnership of the Olympics. (00:03:45): And so got to do a lot of cool stuff. Ended up going to the Korea games in 2018. Shortly thereafter in 21 I got hired by the same company full-time Versace and and came in full-time as an art producer and did that for about three years. Loved the company, red Bull, kind of saw an opportunity and took it and been there five months. And so that's kind of a long-winded way of my career. But I've sat in every position on the production side from PA all the way up to producer. And so that's my, I've seen it all talking direct with clients and just being the fly on the wall, the assistant or the PA over in the corner filling people's coffee up. So yeah, that's a little snapshot.

Cole Heilborn (00:04:35): Yeah. So why is this general topic of helping creative something that you care about? Yeah. Why is this something you like talking about?

Chris Whitten (00:04:43): Yeah, I think for everyone and if they look at their career and how they got started, someone took a chance on, there was one point where you didn't have a portfolio or you didn't have, I remember going and visiting photographers fresh out of school and I would put my little portfolio I made in art school and it was trash looking back now, but it was like that's what I would show them to assist them. And they're like, we just want to see that you're a cool person. And so I had a mentor in Dallas that kind of took me under his wing. And so I just thought that why not do that for other people and just help as best we can. And I know that I'm put on this earth to help people in whatever capacity. And so it was kind of when I, to answer the question more is I was getting, when you're on agency side, you get a bunch of outreach from photographers and directors and 75% of it's bad and it's very nonchalant, oh, just let me know if you ever want to work with me. And I was like, I don't know you and I get a thousand of those emails a week. And so I was like, instead of being a grouch, which I can sometimes be, I'm like, what's some ways that I can just try to share information of helping people get better at this? So that's kind of what preempted it all.

Cole Heilborn (00:06:10): Gotcha. So I think this kind of sets the stage for your first idea. You mentioned you get thousands of these emails a day and I got to assume a lot of people in branded positions or creative directors are in a similar, they experience something similar. There's a lot of people who reach out looking for work. My belief or I don't know if belief is too strong of a word, but my assumption would be that the perception is that creatives are commodities because there's how many photographers looking to shoot for X outdoor brands, right? But your first kind of idea here is that creatives are not commodities. Tell us more about that idea against the backdrop of what you just shared.

content: Chris Whitten (00:06:55): It's a new concept to me that when we first talked, you was like, what are your thoughts on this? And so I really had to think about it. And I think some brands, smaller ones could see, oh, these are just, there's so many people out there that shoot or direct or whatever that it's like we can just interchange 'em, whatever. But if you niche down to what it is you're shooting for automotive for example, there's very few people that are really great at automotive and especially very few in the United States that live in the lower 48. And so it's not a commodity. And I think, and I'm trying to think mindset too is as if I was a photographer, I would never want to think that that I'm interchangeable. And so I would want to give so much value to my clients beyond what they hired me for, that I'm not interchangeable or replaceable. So what I bring to the table on set or post or pre, it's like I would never want to go anywhere else. I think a practical example is a car dealership of some brands. When you go buy them, it's a royal pain in the butt. You're there for four hours. (00:08:27): I don't want to name any brands, but we just bought a car and I was there for five hours and then we went to another dealership to buy my wife's car two weeks ago and it was like we drove the car, took 15 minutes, we were like, Hey, we're going to go home and think about it. They were like, cool, see you later. Where most car they would be like Stay, want to leave. And it just feels like this thing. They're like, oh, can we get you a coffee or a water to go kind of thing. And we were like, no, we're good. Came back and we did all the paperwork just over the phone and on DocuSign and then we came and got the keys and that was it. And so that's the type of service. One of my favorite books is Unreasonable Hospitality by Will Guardia and he talks about just being unreasonable with your value and all the things you bring to the table and you can't IR replace that and that's not interchangeable. So that's kind of what I would say about that.

Chris Whitten (00:09:55): Yeah, and I think yes, I think it's also a learned thing of it's hard when this goes back to the team around you having an excellent producer or EP or someone on your team. That's why crew, as we know, that's why crews are structured the way they are. So the photographer or director can focus on that, just the creative and so that they have a team around them that's thinking of every little other thing that would bring the extra value to the client so that you keep getting hired over and over. And even if that producer or whatever is freelance, it only behooves them to make everything excellent and above par so that you do get hired again and again. And it is a learned trait. Some people have the innate ability just to the servanthood mentality, and that's really what I'm getting down to is we're just here to serve the client and the art of the creative as best we can. (00:11:07): And it comes with not just taking a great picture or a great moving image, it's above that. What's one thing that you could do on set that just is unforgettable? One example, a producer, we're sitting at lunch and it was a long shoot, it was like 15 days just on set and plus scout prep. Everything was like 25 total days that we were away from our families and it was just nonchalantly passed out. These postcards pre-stamped to everyone at the table, even the assistant, everybody. He's like, Hey, send this to someone you love. I was like, I'll never forget that because it just got to quickly, he was like, write it down, I'll mail him out. I just quickly wrote a note to my wife and then she got it. It was so cool. But that's the stuff that's like, oh, I'm going to remember that forever and that guy's forever going to, if I ever need him again, he's the first call.

Chris Whitten (00:12:23): Yeah, I do. And do you think question for you is in your experience, and I will say we can be cocky in this, like, well, I know how to do this, I'm the expert here, and so it's like, yeah, you should hire me. And so it's this cockiness that comes to set even or in the pitch and not this, and that's where it's like, oh, well I can get another guy that's just as talented that's not this cocky and doesn't have this attitude. Would you see that from your experience or

Cole Heilborn (00:13:05): The attitude that can come along with it? For sure. I try not to work with those people because it's not fun, it's not a team sport because I think we put so much emphasis of our worth in our work that it inevitably attaches your ego to what you do. And if you're not careful, you can really let that, it can push you to a good point. It can push you past that point where it becomes this kind of toxic attitude. And I dunno, I hope that we don't come across that way when we work with folks. We try not to hire folks who are like that because it's just not fun. But I think it is definitely out there for sure.

Chris Whitten (00:13:52): And so I just think just positioning yourself not to be a commodity and I think those things that we talked about will put you in that commodity category and in a sense just does a disservice to the creative field as a whole.

Cole Heilborn (00:14:11): So I feel like one piece of the equation of this idea of creatives are not commodities is it comes down to the value that the creative is actually producing. And in a time when it seems like there's a lot of flux around the ROI and the value of the assets that we produce, it then maybe makes me question, well, are we all commodities because maybe AI will take all of our jobs one day. Who knows what piece of the value, value creation is connected to this idea of creatives being a commodity or not being a commodity?

And there's a lot of photographers that can shoot that, and so looking at the multitude of websites that you could go that house these or the websites, it's like, well, you could view that as a commodity, but I think understanding that as the creator, as the photographer, your work has to sit, you have to sit outside of your work because once you place it on these sites or on your site, it's up to someone else's interpretation. So how do you stand out as a photographer or director to not be viewed as that? And I'm still struggling with not struggling, I'm still just trying to understand that concept as well. It's like, but what can you do to level up how things are viewed? And I think it comes down to, it backs into probably something we're going to talk about a little bit later is it's not enough to just throw it on a site and then hope it all goes well. You have to really dial in your marketing systems to be top of mind. That's where I truly believe that creatives are not a commodity because there is so much heart and soul poured out into what they do, (00:16:40): But also at the same time, you can tell when it's not there.

Cole Heilborn (00:16:48): Yeah. Gotcha. Tell me more about mindset and from the position of the creator, what role does mindset play in their ability to find work to succeed?

Chris Whitten (00:17:03): Yeah, I think it plays like 98% of it.

Cole Heilborn (00:17:11): Fascinating. Tell me more.

And one thing we learned in art school is not everyone's going to like it, and so we don't want to ever hear about that, but if you've been to art school or you're listening to this and you're in art school or whatever, you get ripped for stuff and it's to your face and it's by your peers and sometimes your friends and first it's a tough pill to swallow and then it hardens you for it just hardened you for the world because the is not everyone's going to like your stuff and that's okay. Some people will, some people won't. So that brings in fear, self-doubt, hesitation, all these things that compress us to not then marketing ourselves well. (00:18:06): And so if we get in our head about all these things, then it's going to just push it all down. And that's where some of the best photographers in the world, we don't even know about our directors. I say photographers a lot, just my field, even though I produce both, we don't know about because they're terrible at marketing, but I think that's the big holdback is in their head like, oh man, I don't want to do this. I'm just going to put it on this site and then I may put it on Instagram or LinkedIn or whatever and hope somebody sees it. So that is a lot of what I talk about is just mindset. Let's just do it, push it out there and let's just create a system, kind of a set it and forget it system to put work in front of people so that it's like all your fears and hesitation is right there and then you hit send and you post 30 days worth of content, whatever through a service, and then it's out and you're done and then you can go work on other things, bettering your craft, all the fun stuff.

Cole Heilborn (00:19:23): How many photographers who, this is a really overly simplistic question. I say that because I feel like sometimes I overly simplify questions on this podcast and I'm trying to do a better job.

Chris Whitten (00:19:53): I would say back to the 90 ish percent. It's like if you haven't got work in six months or 12 months or whatever, then I would just want to look at what your outreach has been, and if it's zero, then why? I don't want to bother this person. I don't want to, whatever. All the things that we start telling ourselves in our head that no one ever told you, call it putting your voice into the silence. Well, who told you that? Well, no one, I just thought it. I was like, okay, it's not true. Then the same amount of mindset we call it that it takes to tell you those negative things is the same amount that tell you the opposite. And so if we could just shift it, just whatever seems negative, shift it to positive and then do that thing, I think it just hangs a lot. (00:20:51): I mean, pretty much everybody I talk to is the same thing over and over. Well, I didn't want to bother. Oh, but all the excuses is, and if we're talking about outreach, let's just say we're talking about outreach specifically is the big bottleneck and I think it relates to mindset is like yesterday I'm in this massive project at work and I think I got three emails from people I've never met photographers, directors that are just introducing themselves and not to mention the way they word their emails is completely trash. It puts all the work on me and we can get to that later, but I just deleted them because I physically don't have time in the day. I was meetings every 30 minutes and I still haven't packed. And I was like, I hope they emailed back.

Chris Whitten (00:25:51): Yeah. I don't know if I would define it as a commodity. I see what you're saying. And back to the part of being annoying. If someone finds it annoying, then do you want to work with that person if that's what's going to really get under their skin? It's like I'm trying to work with you. And it goes back to what you're saying in the outreach too, but I understand your point and I would politely disagree, but

Cole Heilborn (00:26:29): No, that's great. I'm just curious

Let me just go through this stack. Here's a perfect one for Cole. And then it's like, that requires me to do work now, so now I'm working for you. (00:30:17): And it just brought me back to this moment that I was with my dad at a car show in Houston and we saw an Acura IEX for the first time on the turntable. Some language would be like if you want a meet in-person meeting and give this big block of time. I had a photographer I was talking to and she lived two hours outside of Seattle and one of this client that she wanted to meet up with was in Seattle, and I was like, give her a week that you're going to be in Seattle and this week is wide open for you to go meet coffee with her. And she's like, but I don't live in Seattle. I was like, but the day she picked, you're going to be in Seattle. And so she ended up booking a meeting just because she just made herself available. And so that's not necessarily language, it's like strategy. Find a way to honor that person, whether it's work or something. Being at Saatchi, Saatchi has a big client base. I only worked on a vehicle brand, so it was hard for somebody if they didn't really know or didn't do a ton of research, they could mention a brand that I wasn't on, but I still was like, doesn't matter, they tried. It's hard to sometimes know exactly if I only touch one brand or if I'm on multiple brands, stuff like that. (00:33:42): I think even I don't view this as creepy, some other people may, but LinkedIn or whatever, find out what college they went to and just find a tidbit of, oh, I saw that Michigan beat, blah, blah blah in football this week. So outside as a company, our really big thing, our goal, our vision is just getting more people outside. And we've done so much research about how people are just spending so much time on their screens and not enough time outside actually enjoying that time outside. And it seems counterintuitive that would be using online and internet platforms to try and get people to actually spend less time online, but we're trying to figure out how to tap into this new technology and use that as a way to encourage people to get outside. I think the thing, people are always really resistant to change, especially when it comes to technology. I'll use the example for myself personally of when smartphones first came out, which really dates me, but back in the day when they first came out for many years, it was just like, why do I even need that? But over the years, we've seen how that has just become such a central part of our lives, and I think the vision here with Web3 and trying to just embrace this technology early and just be early adapters and figure out how we can use this in a positive way is really what the aim of the outer verse is. It's really, I think, going to continue to just change and evolve. And so the challenge we're facing right now is everyone wants to know the exact specifics of what we're doing with it, and we're still figuring it out in a lot of ways, but we know that there's all this opportunity, for instance, attaching move to earn utility to our apps and things like that. So if you look at Gaia and t TR Forks, there's ways that eventually we're hoping to tie in NFTs and blockchain technology to be able to say, oh, we can see that you got outside, you went for a trail run, you went for a bike ride, et cetera. So we're trying to figure out how to best use this technology to make it something that gives people positive reward for that outside time.

content: Ariel Macrae (16:39): Yeah. So it's complicated for people who are not crypto educated, and I count myself in that it's a really complex thing out. So that was crucial for us because you'll see a lot of the negative feedback or connotations about NFTs and blockchains and things of that nature are that it's really bad for the environment. (17:47): And traditional blockchain is blockchain like crypto and Ethereum. They use so much energy because every time they have to verify a purchase or verify someone's chain, it's running it through so many systems and using just tons and tons of energy to process. Whereas Solana is super low energy. So the comparison we like to make from the info that they've shared with us is that one Solana transaction is basically the equivalent of doing two Google searches on your computer, which all of us do so many on a daily basis. The reality of these things that we do frequently that are energy users like that, a lot of people don't even consider it, but NFTs blockchain, they just have this kind of bad reputation of being bad for the environment. And so we're kind of trying to not necessarily prove people wrong, but just give them the information that this is not that and it is energy efficient and it is, we're moving in the direction of just trying to continually be conscious and sustainable.

content: Chris King (19:52): Yeah, so I mean I can break it down pretty down to the request really when I got here, we have what some may look at is a decent sized photo budget and content budget. We do not have the content and photo budgets of our competitors these days of where we want to be at. And that's part of growing. And so I think the challenge for me right off the bat is how do I take this budget and really exceed the current expectations of the content strategy that we're had? And I think that that's a real challenge and I think it's been a challenge for others before me here. And what I had to offer here is that one, I try not to do it a lot, but I was able to shoot content if we needed quick things. (21:00): We're not the outdoor industry company that's going to trade somebody gear for work. I really, it's important to me having been on the other side that people and contractors who work for or working for four and feel that it's a fair rate because I need these people to come back and I want to make sure that we just really set a standard there. And I think before I got here, there was a bit of a lack in production knowledge, and I don't think it was the end goal of like, Hey, we need this content to be great. It's just that I think having that Rolodex really helped me a lot and I just have some awesome friends that have become important to me for sure. But what was going on is that with the small photo budget, the team here would shoot really, really good content, but the budget didn't run very far. (21:56): And one thing about or that a lot of people don't know is that we've got an insane amount of products in the 300 range and all the way down to boxers and all the way up to $700 Gore-Tex shells. And with a 20 capsule unit photo budget would be no problem. You could really focus on experiences and you could make sure all those things were captured. But what the problem was was that how do we get all of these items shot in outdoor locations with the budget that we had and those images were really helping the e-comm, our website really looked great. And so we had become dependent on those outdoor images to sell items. And so we kind of had a few different options. And what the change I've been doing is that after figuring out that, hey, we can't, it's impossible to shoot all these items in different scenes, is that how can we create a better studio photography experience to showcase these items and then use the photo budget that we have to really showcase experience and then our top of line items and really show the brand versus showing the ins and outs of every single piece that we make. (23:16): And that was kind of the first deal was fix the content capture. And so that's what we've definitely been working on the past year.

I don't know from the production side when you were doing that, how would you experience that with clients?

content: Chris King (23:57): Totally. I mean I think, man, you can make such amazing content these days with little amounts of money. Where extra money comes in is once you have the piece of equipment and you have the talent behind the camera, now you're just building a support system. We have our ambassador team that we often use as our models for athletes or for showing people in athletic environments. And then sometimes we have to use professional models. And when you build, the more amount of people on set is the more money. And so around the DP or around the photographer, you can have stylist, you can have hair and makeup, you can have assistance and you can rent expensive equipment. You can rent crazy stabilizers and cable cans. And as you know, that train never ends, right? Do we want to have nice cinema lenses? And then the money just goes higher and higher and higher and all of a sudden you can get to 10 or $15,000 a day on a set really, really fast. (25:10): And there's nothing more fun than having a large budget and being able to take a chef's knife and improve the little things around the DP or the photographer and also give them the comfort that they have the support, which whenever I had that support and I was shooting, it's like you can totally zone out and not even have to worry how the models look or have to worry, worry about dumping cards or have to worry that stuff is set up and ready to go. And that is when you have that kind of comforting feel like that, I think you can really do your best work. And so what I tried to do was make sure that I could now use my talents on set and be on set. I'm technically, I'm a salaried employee, so we're not paying a day rate for me, but knowing what a photographer and videographer usually needed, I wanted to be that assistant in the back and maybe we hire another assistant also that's also helping. (26:07): And I was just trying to trim the fat as much as possible and knowing that we could start at a base level because there were low expectations when I got here, we could just start ground bottom and really focus on a good location and making sure that the clothes were representing the use case that they were in. And so as simple as it sounds, making sure rain jackets were shot in the rain, simple stuff like that. And using the amazing space we have around here in the Pacific Northwest and not traveling a ton allowed me to kind of fine tune these shoots, though they're still expensive. The end of a three day shoot with a small crew was still, and models and ambassadors is still costing 20 to 30 grand at the end of the day, usually around 10,000 bucks a day. And so that sounds like an insane amount of money, but to shoot the amount of items that we were shooting and the experiences that we were trying to do, when you're competing with the North faces and the Patagonia and those people, that isn't the top. And so that was really the challenge coming in here and something that I think we did a really good job at and the internal marketing team here at or is awesome and people just want to see the brand flourish, which is great. And it's been a huge support since I've been here.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:30): So it sounds like in order to figure out how to stretch the dollars and figure out where they should best be allocated, did you first start by designing the entire strategy and figuring out what's important or what can we do or what can be shot on a studio? How did you walk me through that strategy side of it?

Chris King (27:53): Yeah, I remember we were a couple of weeks in and it was late, it was July. And so spring 22 had not been shot yet and we need to have spring summer deliverables by usually October 1st because we launched in March and it was a bad fire season, so there was smoke everywhere in the Pacific Northwest. And I remember working with a colleague of mine and saying, all right, show me the budget. Let's see the Excel sheet. And I could immediately tell right off the bat that there was large amounts of money being spent on things that weren't necessary. And it's a really tough position to be in as a new head of marketing is that there are a lot of vendors that work with the company for a long time, and I've been on the other side of this myself that usually when your connect, that's a marketing at a company leaves, oftentimes they bring their people in. (29:01): And now I'm on the other side of that having to have conversations with photographers and videographers that we plain and simple to capture the content that we need. We can't afford you. And as much as I think your photography is amazing, we need to do five shoots this summer, not one. And we can't blow our entire budget on one or two photo shoots. We had to spread it out as much as we could. And so figuring out, okay, now where can we go? What's cheap for us to get to? Where do we need to go? And at that time, climbing was a big part of the seasonal capture that we were doing. So I remember the first shoot we went on was to Smith Rock down in Bend and it kind of gave me an idea of what the expectations were because everyone down there had been on a photo shoot with or before, a lot of our ambassadors were there, people were helping that were part of or, and it really kind let me know that the productions that or was used to was 10 to 15 people going around an outdoor location and definitely more of a, it's hard. (30:08): It's hard that many people to get the contents herding cats. And it definitely let me know that we needed to downsize as much as possible and again, spread the money around as much as we could. We needed to have four person teams without a huge travel or send gear to people that were in those locations to make sure that we could get a variety of content. And so it was a really fast moment and there were some definite wins that summer, but it was also crazy. You're just drinking from the fire hose trying to fix all the things that the people above you expect. So yeah, just kind looking at the spreadsheet and starting there,

Because I'm assuming because you can't afford it all.

content: Chris King (31:24): Yes. So I think from a priority perspective when I'm designing a shoot is that I start with our crew first and really at, or we like to use a variety of content creators so that the content isn't all the same, which is also a challenge in itself too. And thankfully again, got some good connects as I just noticed as I was perusing your podcast, a few people that have been on here before we work with and I think like, okay, we got our team, we have, can we afford to have video as well as photo? And we start with that team and who needs assistance? Do we need an assistant for both photo and video? Can we have one assistant for both? Can I come and help with that stuff? And then from there we got to pick the location. And so we are really trying to figure out as a brand where we want to show up in our imagery and we're Pacific Northwest through and through, but we also want to expand. (32:30): And so I think we're going to shoot most of our stuff up in the Pacific Northwest, but we're also going to venture to other places too because we want to make sure that in order for us to expand to the east coast, we need to have some east coast imagery. Maybe it's not all of it, but there has to be some, right? And looking at the full season, where is that large travel budget going to come in and what can we do at home? And so going back to the individual, shoot, something that's very important to me, which I think is maybe not for others because we've all been on shoots where we're sleeping at janky motels with four to a room. I want to make sure that everyone has a great place to sleep and sometimes their own bedroom if possible, or a great bunk situation and that everyone is well fed. (33:20): And again, there's an experience beyond the shoe. I've just learned that if we're in a beautiful place and we don't have to worry about going to get not a great sleep at the end of the night and not have a, not a party per se, but just a fun, relax time to get regenerated for the next day, I want to make sure that's a great situation.

Chris King (31:24): So I think I tend to spend more on the travel side of it than others do, but that's important to me for my crew and making sure that there, like I said, there's a great experience in there. So we'll do the travel and then from there we get to figure out the talent situation and are we bringing ambassadors on the shoot? Do we need models? Build that out. And then usually with the extra that's left is okay, what extra gear can we bring with us to take the production to the next level? (34:17): What do we need to rent? Are we going to rent some nicer cinema lenses? Are we going to rent stabilizers? Are we going to rent rain machines? Are we going to rent a 12 by 12 scrimm to really set up a beautiful setting that isn't blown out by the sun? Just that little stuff that adds up really quick when you're on a one week shoot. And so that's kind of how I look at it. And oftentimes, hey, we might just be on a trail and trying to hit the best light and we don't have any extra grip and that's it, but we have to still get that content. And some shoots I have more budget than others, but yeah, that's kind of the formula that I go with.

Cole Heilborn (34:54): Gotcha. What about, similar question but from a different perspective now. What about for brands who maybe don't have as much production experience as yourself, and maybe it sounds like you're kind of playing, you are a producer, you are playing producer for these shoots, for brands where they aren't familiar with producing something and let's say they're bringing in a producer to help them bring a shoot together. How do they decide of all the different shoots that they could pick from and work on throughout the year, maybe they want to do a product piece, they want to do a story piece, maybe they want to create a bunch of social contents and they're looking at bringing in a producer and a team to shoot all of that. How do they decide from that brand level what's worth investing in?

Chris King (35:42): Huge. I think that it's tough if you don't have the general background in which of those tools can be the most valuable. I remember earlier on in my career, I was trying to be the DP and the producer at the same time, and I remember the first time that I paid for a producer to come on a shoot and my mind was completely blown because all of a sudden I didn't have to coach models, I didn't have to talk with, we were doing a casino shoot, I didn't have to work with the people at the casino, I just could focus on what I was doing. And from then on, it became an absolute no brainer for me. And so having a good producer can be expensive, but the value rings through. It's kind of like you get a great photographer and nothing against the people that create content whatsoever. (36:42): I think you can get a good photographer and that person can run a whole shoot no problem. But for those larger scale shoots, a producer really makes that person shine. It's kind of putting nice speakers on your really nice area. And so I think if that experience isn't, there's a lot of really good companies up here in the Pacific Northwest that do produce shoots. We were using a production company up here that was before I was here, gosh, I can't remember the name, but they were helping put all these shoots together because there really wasn't a great internal person to help with that. And it is an expense for sure, but I think it helps get your shoot off the ground level and then the people, the internal people the company can focus on, alright, here's what this gear needs to look like and what are the assets that we need and we can just focus on that part where the producer can kind of wrangle everything else.

Cole Heilborn (37:38): Yeah, interesting. So what about now feels like the right time to invest in some of that story focused stuff?

content: Chris King (37:48): So in order to get to the place where we could start pushing the brand awareness and pushing outdoor research instead of just marketing single pieces of apparel, the product had to be in a great place. And so as I mentioned before, the product really needs to be in a great place. For those that don't know in larger apparel brands, or at least here, it takes about three years from an inception of a product design prototypes, building the fit and really getting the product shot from a marketing perspective and then going into a retail location takes about three years or about that time ago, brought in a new team on the product side who's just been crushing it and really bringing the clothing to a very respectable place where I think in the past or is very much or has been technical before or technical or function before fashion. (38:57): And that left us with pieces that would protect you in the outdoors no matter what. And again, there's only a select amount of people that need apparel like that and how could we keep that same mentality but also design pieces that someone who'd never, that was hiking for the first time or wanted a great down jacket or soft shell or raincoat to wear to and from the office, how could you apply that design towards that group as well? Because again, if you're growing a brand at the place you want it to be, we have to sell beyond the niche customer group. And so the clothing and the clothing design has really gotten to a place where people felt comfortable now pushing the brand because of what we had to offer. And not only is our stuff extremely well made and designed, it's starting to just look really awesome. (39:58): That was the first step of that process. The second step once we had that is that making sure that our internal, our seasonal photography and our seasonal content capture to use on web and social media and for any out of home stuff was also on point as well. And I think then at that space, and once I kind of had a good formula going there, air came the harder question because I think I know the production world really well and I know how to get a product from holding it in my hand to up on the website. I know that formula great, but now it's the request came in from our president of, okay, let's go build this brand and let's let people know who we are. And so we are going to get going on a brand awareness campaign in the start of October, kind of when it gets a little colder. We do have a ton of winter outerwear that we're pushing in a big way this year, but that now it's time to start testing some other platforms beyond just Facebook and Instagram.

content:
Cole Heilborn (41:10): Yeah, interesting. I was reading a statistic and it said since 2018 to 2021, the amount of video watched per person per week has almost doubled from about nine hours a week to now 18 hours per week. I'm just curious to hear your reaction.

Chris King (41:31): I mean, yeah, it makes sense, right? We were at home a lot and I think, gosh, I know that we definitely increased our video watching that was for sure. And whether that was watching more movies and shows on Netflix or using YouTube as a tool to work on home projects, we never took part in content has become more than just kind of a veg out situation. And a great example of that is on our YouTube channel, we have a ton of tutorial videos that we've produced in the past and everything from, Hey, here's how to put skins on your skis all the way, how to rig your climbing gear, what goes in your back country backpack, stuff that the team before I got here was working on. And man, the viewership of those videos is, I could tell you some of the stats on that is crazy, like 40 to 60 hours per week on these three minute videos is just you see people that wanted to go outside and wanted to learn new things. And I think from a content strategy, yes, of course we were maybe watching six seasons of Peaky Blinders in a week, but I think also there was this education piece that's always been there, but I think it came in because a lot of people started doing new things. When COVID started, the outdoor spaces exploded. You couldn't, with the supply chain and the amount of people joining the sport, you couldn't find a bike for a few years there. (43:16): And I think people wanted to know how to do things. They wanted to exceed their talent levels. And you saw just this explosion of camping and hiking and mountain biking and backcountry skiing. And fortunately for us, we are in a great place for that and noticed that our certain pieces of our content started to just increase. But that's the name of the game these days.

content:
Cole Heilborn (43:40): So if content, if video consumption has doubled, I mean, I guess a simple assumption would be that brands output of video has doubled. And then would that also mean, am I wrong to believe that then budgets have also doubled?

Chris King (44:06): We are trying to be very conservative right now because, and I doubt we're the only one, we're kind of wondering if this push to the outdoors is going to last. And I think the really good thing about COVID is that on one side there was a major mental health explosion about not being able to ever really leave your job because you were just at home all the time and living the at-home life. And it's, it was hard to turn it off there for a while. But the other side of it is that you had this like, okay, maybe I'll get up early, maybe my list of responsibilities, maybe I don't need eight hours to get that done during the day. (44:55): I think for a long time in offices, the two o'clock to five o'clock hour was spent surfing social media sometimes. And if you read, you can read a lot of studies that tell you that time of the day is your least productive. And I think you saw, at least I know for myself, a lot of people get outside during that time. It was the safe place to go. And so from a content perspective, we needed more content, we needed more video showcasing our products so people would know what to buy. We needed more storytelling, we needed more internal video that talked about our product technologies, more tutorial videos, and we've really been trying to do our best there. But no, the budget has kind of stayed the same because we really want to make sure that we've definitely fruited off of this outdoor push, but we want to make sure that this keeps going. And I think if you were a logical person, people are going back to work and we may be looking at a recession here in the coming years, the writing's on the wall, and we want to make sure that we can still put out what we're doing in kind of a frugal way, but also make sure that the partners that we're working with we're being fair with all of them and also keeping the quality of that content in a good place rather than trying to create more content where the quality lapses a little bit.

Cole Heilborn (46:25): Yeah. Gotcha. I'm just kind of going through some rapid fire questions. So podcasts, we're obviously in a podcast format. I'm curious, how do you see podcasts in the future of content strategy? I mean, just chatting with a lot of marketing folks through this medium, it definitely seems like something that brands are interested in producing or being a part of in a sponsor format, something like that. What do you think happening?

Chris King (47:00): Again, two paths. You produce your own internal podcasts, some brands are doing that and then, or you can sponsor a podcast. And I think coming from a production world, not a podcast world, producing a podcast is no easy job and not a job that someone who's already doing production can go and just handle, right? It's like, I think in the early days of social media, there were not social media people. It was, Hey, can you manage our Facebook or something like that. And now we have dedicated social media people. And so I think right now for us, an internal podcast is probably out of the question. And I think what it would take us to grow that as you know, got to put in that time and really make sure that you have a niche. One of the reasons why I like your podcast a lot is I really want to know what other people in the industry are doing and how they're getting through challenging problems. And I think you have a great niche in that. I think we could probably come up with something, but it would be tough. So we're actually going to try sponsoring a few podcasts this season as a bit of a test and see if there is an ROI on that. And we are doing this brand awareness campaign and we want to add a couple of different mediums to it. And I'm really curious, and I think, have you worked with sponsors on your podcast before?

Cole Heilborn (48:34): Short answer, no. It's something that we have entertained, but I think the value that we provide that we could provide to a potential sponsor is very niche and very limited just because our audience size is very niche and very focused. So it's something that, I've had a few conversations with brands, but we've never run an ad to this point. Not to say that we wouldn't be against it, but I think we just got to find the right fit for our show.

Chris King (49:06): Exactly. And I definitely wonder the same things myself, and I think the easiest form of advertising is having a call to action with an easy route to a purchase. And I think if you're in the niche of the podcast and you are about what that podcast host is talking about and they recommend a product in a non-car salesman way, you can have success there. But I don't think it's ever going to trump the success that a paid social ad is going to, only because you can click and purchase where a podcast, you have to stop listening, find a purchase portal and go from there. I mean, that's a great customer to have right there because usually that's going to probably be a repeat purchase customer. But it's an interesting space and I'm really curious to see what comes back from that personally.

Cole Heilborn (50:03): So when you think about metrics, data seems to be everything as we inform our content and the types of content that we produce. I know this is kind of a general question, but what sort of metrics are you looking at that helps inform your content strategy decisions?

content: Dax Myers (03:38): Yeah, absolutely. So Mountain Flow, we've been around since 2016, and we started in the ski wax space, really recognizing the imperative really to make a cleaner ski wax. So much of the consumables in the ski and bike industries are made with really nasty, gnarly chemicals. And so that was kind of the original impetus for mountain Flow and really just kind of leapt used that to really kind of get to a point of reach a performance threshold while completely redesigning how ski wax is made. So we use plant-based formula. It's biodegradable, it's non-toxic, no petroleum ever. And then we've taken that same ethos to all of the bike lines. And we are a certified B Corp. We actually just recer it this year. And so we put thought into every single aspect of production, and that includes the product itself, but it also includes the packaging. (04:47): And so we use post-consumer plastic in just about every single thing we put out. And then we also use our bike wash, for example, utilizes, it's a cardboard kind of hybrid container. And the way that it works is it's a thinner plastic reservoir wrapped in cardboard that uses 70% less plastic than a traditional plastic bottle. And so realistically, we kind of have our toes dipped in multiple spaces right now. And again, this is all based on recognizing the gaps in the bike and ski industry, consumables world, and seeing if we can do it better. And so we're in the process right now of launching recycled aluminum ski poles, which a hundred percent out of the realm of consumables, but it's something that isn't really being done right now in the industry. And the initial measurements are showing that recycled aluminum utilizes about 95% less carbon emissions than a virgin aluminum ski pole. (05:49): And so really trying to use the sustainability narrative to, I guess, let me rephrase that. We're focusing mostly on quality. We want to create quality goods because you can be as sustainable as you want, and if your products don't work, then nobody is going to care. And so we're walking that line. And from a marketing perspective, we definitely lean performance first, sustainability second. We would much rather somebody be like, wow, this chain loop is incredible. And then find out later that, so yeah, that's kind of the long and short of mountain flow. No, petroleum is kind of like the overarching ethos through every single product. And then, yeah, plant-based biodegradable.

And what they did is they looked at race venues, and so they looked at Alpine race and Nordic race venues and really high concentration of fluorinated wax usage in those types of venues. content: Dax Myers (14:01): Well, it's ultimately awareness. We mentioned that ski lube, or excuse me, ski wax and bike lube are commodities in the space. There's a pretty low chance that you're going to store hop looking for a specific brand. Granted, that is a little bit less true in the ski wax world, especially if you're on the race side of things. But when it comes to bike lube, I mean 13 to 17 bucks a bottle, you're just going to get whatever's closest, whatever's most convenient. And so creating an awareness and really kind of focusing on that top of funnel awareness is kind of where we've really focused. And you mentioned this, we do have a good story, which definitely is an asset for us and really helps with the narrative storytelling when it comes to cultivating that awareness. But it's a challenge, especially when there are multiple steps to maintaining and even achieving awareness. (15:11): And ultimately, the first question, without doubt, whether I'm at an event or at a trade show, first question that I'm asked is, does it work? And usually it's like, yeah, bring your bike over, we'll loop it up for you. Tell us, let us know what you think. I run the info account, the howdy@mountainflow.com, and I handle just any inquiry that comes in and anybody that reaches out, I send, reach out to me directly if you have any questions. I'm genuinely curious to know your thoughts. And so we have a lot, especially with how things have been changing, especially with the millennials coming of age, there's a ton of studies out there that say that especially in the millennial space, we're more likely to support brands that sort of take a stand on things. And so we have had people that have come up to the tent or reached out via email and say things like, I saw that you had me there. (16:12): Why don't you tell me about your products? And so that's certainly a hook, but it's not really the hook. And so realistically, to kind of continue the phishing analogy with a hook, you've got the trouble hook that's like three different, I guess hooks. We're really employing even more than that. We have five to six different awareness campaigns because ultimately we just want people to know about us. And then after you create that initial awareness, we have that really strong narrative that we can sort of, I don't want to say fall back on, but then we can utilize as people kind of move through the funnel there,

Dax Myers (17:13): Well, I think that the story really is huge there, but it's not just any sort of generic brand story in my mind. People are willing, once they're aware of not only mountain flow, but once they're also aware of the harmful effects of some of the other petroleum based products out there, that's ultimately what's driving the need to maybe jump to a few stores to find something that's not as kind of gnarly. But again, if the product doesn't work,

Yeah, so I was thinking about, as we were talking about this episode, and I was doing some prep for it, I was doing some research on commodities and just trying to understand the general landscape. And there's a lot of articles that popped up about how do you market a commodity? There are also so many different ways to differentiate a pair of skis, whether it's just true blue branding or the mechanics of the ski itself. If it's the pair of skis that I want, I'll drive across the country for a bike. And I guess it's pretty easy to something if it tastes good versus yeah, it's going on your bike, you wipe your hands off afterwards, and then you just really, I don't really think about it even working for Mountainville, throw some wax on and just go for a ride. So, which I guess really sort of segues into just creating as broad of an awareness funnel that we can, and that's ultimately how we're going to shift the paradigm is creating that awareness that the stuff is gnarly, it's nasty. There have been incremental changes. We go from short chain fluorocarbons and ski wax, which they're, it's still a fluorinated wax, but instead of breaking down, never, it'll break down at some point. (25:44): And so there have been a lot of things, FIS has really led the charge on banning fluorinated waxes. But again, they actually just moved the goalposts back again this year just because they don't have a solid sort of testing methodology. And they were getting false positives when they would test people's skis. And so I think it's the third or fourth year that that's happened. And ultimately, when it comes to just the general conversation, it's been great because it's been centering people's, it's been creating awareness on a topic that ultimately just has kind of been overlooked for a long time. But when you put things on just like an honor system, you have some people that are going to take that step based on this level of awareness that they just gained. And then you have some people that are just going to do what they've always done. (26:38): And it's great that more people are coming over to the side of recognizing that we're not just nothing that we do exist in a bubble. Everything kind of has a ripple effect in ramifications, whether it be environmental or really anything. And so I think that that's the biggest hurdle in this space is getting there. But when it comes to articulating the narrative, one thing that's kind of nice, at least from a marketing standpoint is there are really no rules. And I think that that's evidenced switching over out of the ski and bike industries, but still very much so a commodity that's evidenced in the gold standard case study, at least in my mind, in liquid death. And as far as creating a conversation, I mean, that brand can do no wrong, and some of the stuff that they do might be totally off the wall to me. But I mean, here I am talking about it.

content:
Dax Myers (28:35): Well, for us using Liquid Death as a case study, they lean in really hard to the punk and metal scene. And that aesthetic just is 100% their brand identity, and it really works for us. So our founder, Peter Arlene, incredibly articulate and just really well-spoken guy, but also just maintains an air of just goofiness. He's just a really solid, but really just like goofy, lanky guy. We've leaned in really hard to just some previous, in my opinion, it just really kind of leans into Peter's personality. And so we've been working really hard on humor and we've released, granted, we're not going anywhere nearly as viral as liquid death. It seems like everything they put on Instagram goes bananas these days. But one campaign that we had recent localized success for us was we've created a persona for Peter. He is wearing cutoff jean shorts, cowboy boots, like a flannel cutoff shirt. We've got some shots of him putting on leather work gloves. And kind of like the whole point of the story though is he rides his bike over to the gas pump and pulls out the pump and then holds it over his drive train. And the thought being, you wouldn't put gas on your drive train, why would you put petroleum products on your bike? (30:19): And so really leaning into the soft, humorous side of things to get across those more. It's not necessarily life and death, but it's certainly a more serious message than the feel of the video would. It's not serious. We're not coming out with PSAs and whatnot. I mean, we are, but we try to be funny.

Cole Heilborn (30:42): Yeah. And how has that been received?

Dax Myers (30:44): That's been really well received. As I mentioned, we haven't gone viral or anything like that, but in our sphere we've received a lot of positive impact. And so we have some really fun stuff in the mix. Really excited to just continue to articulate that story utilizing this persona, creating just a level of brand recognition around Peter and the caricature that we've created for him. And then using that to leapfrog our message across to people.

Cole Heilborn (31:20): Is a lot of the awareness that you guys are trying to drum up, is that through these types of short, creative, funny videos, or what are some other avenues that you're also exploring?

Dax Myers (31:33): So on the more serious side of things, we have a white paper in the works because ultimately we want to get as granular as possible. And given our short format attention span world that we live in right now, we Instagram, TikTok, art, really the venues for that. And so one thing, it's been a slow process, but putting together just a white paper that would be ultimately articulated on LinkedIn or something like that. We also, Peter travels around to, we do panel discussions. We're working with the, it's the, I want to get it right, it's the O Rec office, so it's the Office of Recreation for Colorado. So they have been doing a thing, it's like a tour, and they go around to different rural communities and there, there's new money coming in, and they talk about how we can just strengthen these communities through the lens of the outdoor industry. (32:32): And so as a local business owner in a rural mountain town, that fits in well. And so Peter is able to go and participate in these panel discussions, and that's getting the word out in a really genuine, less humorous way. And so ultimately for us, we just want to have our basis covered. We want everything. We want to be funny. If we had a post that went viral, that would be incredible. I think that's, especially in the social side of thing, that's what we're all striving for, but maintaining kind of like a duality there that we are a serious brand, that we are tackling a serious problem and our products work. I dunno how many times I'm going to say that, but

Cole Heilborn (33:22): So do you feel like if you can get the products in hand, get it in people's hands, they can test it out, they can prove that it works. content:
Cole Heilborn (01:53): So I was doing a little bit of internet stalking before this conversation and I was looking up Lander and it looks like it's right kind of in the northwest corner ish of Wyoming. And I noticed that you wrote a poem about Lander and the climbing, local climbing crags, it sounds like, but it's got kind of a cowboy edge to it. What's the history of the area?

Kris Hampton (02:20): Well, I mean, people have been climbing here for a long time. It really gained its popularity as a climbing town through Todd Skinner, who was one of the most famous climbers in the world in the 1990s. And his sister was a prospector or was living as a prospector here for a time while writing a book and saw these cliffs and called Todd, who was living in a teepee and over in South Dakota, and he came over to take a look at the cliffs and called back to South Dakota and said, pack all the stuff, bring it over here. And ironically, Todd is from Pinedale, Wyoming, just across the wind rivers from Lander, and he started developing and talking about the climbing here and Todd and Paul Piana and Amy Skinner and some of that crew used all these cowboy terms to name the roots and these western themed crags. And I just used the names that they had written, that they had named things to write this poem as something to give to the community after the first few times I came here.

Cole Heilborn (03:34): Did you settle in Lander because of the climbing opportunity?

Kris Hampton (03:39): No, not exactly. I met a woman here on my second trip now my wife and she grew up here, so eventually we found our way back here.

Cole Heilborn (03:50): Gotcha. Awesome. Well, Chris, I'd love if you could give us a quick introduction, a little bit of your background. You host a bunch of different podcasts, you're also a climbing coach and you've found a world where you can bring those two together. Could you give us a little background on what you do?

content:
Kris Hampton (04:08): Yeah, so actually it's interesting you just mentioned a way to bring those two worlds together. I sort of feel like that's been a lot of my life. I was a rapper, started rapping in the 1990s, early nineties, and eventually wrapped about rock climbing after I'd found climbing just sort of as a joke. But that led me to traveling and performing at all these festivals, and that's how I ended up here in Lander, Wyoming. And I eventually started a climbing coaching business. I've been doing that for a little over 10 years now, I think, and that I had all this audio background from rapping and I thought, well, gosh, I should just record all these conversations that I'm having. I've got all the equipment, I've got the know-how, let's make a podcast. And so I did. And that's the Power Company podcast, and I think we're about 270 episodes deep on that podcast. (05:09): And that sort of just became an obsession. And now I host the Power Company podcast, the Breaking Beta podcast, which is about the science of climbing. Hip hop taught me everything with my friend Devin Dabney, which is a storytelling podcast rooted in hip hop, and now I'm working on Built Outdoors for the Plug Tone Audio Network, which is a network I co-founded with my friends Devin Dabney and Emily Holland and Built Outdoors tells the story of outdoor entrepreneurs and is just a way to celebrate the small business owners in the outdoors while also telling great stories.

Cole Heilborn (05:55): On any given week, how many episodes are you typically recording? Amongst all of 'em?

Kris Hampton (06:01): I haven't the slightest idea. There are weeks where I put out four or five episodes across the different podcasts. There are weeks where I might record 10 episodes. That's probably the max. Like I said, it's an addiction and some weeks I just don't do it at all because I need the mental break.

Cole Heilborn (06:22): That's ridiculous. 10 episodes in a week, I feel like

Kris Hampton (06:27): It's an addiction.

Cole Heilborn (06:29): Are you the type of person who leaves a podcast interview feeling recharged and stoked for the next one, or do you need a day in between to kind of recharge?

content:
Kris Hampton (06:39): That's a great question. It depends on the Power Company podcast in particular. I mix it up between talking, training and really digging into some of the social issues and cultural issues within climbing. So while they do recharge some of my buckets, a lot of times they'll leave me emotionally drained, mentally drained, so I can't do a bunch of those type of episodes. But if I am splitting it up between let's talk the details of training or the science of training, let's have a conversation about deeper social issues, those things sort of come out of different buckets for me so I can fit a lot of those things into any given day.

Cole Heilborn (07:34): What's your background with climbing? How did you fall into that?

Kris Hampton (07:38): Well, actually I was a troublemaker when I was a kid, and I discovered around 16 or so that I was really good at stealing cars and stealing car stereos, but I was not very good at not getting caught. So I ended up going to jail when I was 18. And while locked up, I realized I needed a whole new set of friends, a whole new environment. I needed to just start over somewhere new. And I had gone to a climbing gym one time and having a background as a gymnast and as a skateboarder, I just sort of took to climbing and I really enjoyed that one time. So when I got out, I went straight to the climbing gym and I bought a month membership and I was in there every day for that month, and the manager was like, why don't you just vacuum the floors or something and then you don't have to buy another membership, you're here every day. Anyway, as soon as I get here, that was the last gym membership I ever bought and I've been climbing ever since.

Cole Heilborn (08:46): Wow. And the coaching business, how did that get started? When did you realize that you wanted to be able to share that experience with others?

content:
Kris Hampton (08:57): Well, I was training myself. I wanted to see how good I could become at climbing, and there wasn't a lot of information out there on how to improve at climbing, so it was a big experiment. And I started a blog called Power Company Climbing back in the days when blogs were cool, and I trained a few friends and I mentioned on the blog once that I had trained a few friends and then I got inundated with requests, so I wrote a bunch of training programs That Winter realized the way I was doing it was unsustainable. And shortly after, tried to find a way, worked on an app that we now use to train people through and just figured out a better way to communicate and a way to sort of take climbing training to a bigger platform. And as soon as I released that to the public and opened myself up for business pretty immediately, I knew I had to quit my full-time job as a mural painter. So I gave them my two weeks almost immediately, and now that's my full-time job and I have a bunch of coaches that work with me and my office manager, and it's just, for me, it's a great way to reach the community and help people become not just better at climbing, but become better climbers, better humans, and be more resilient throughout their real lives.

Cole Heilborn (10:36): So I've always been curious, you think about the trajectory of becoming good at anything, and if 10 is perfect and zero is a beginner, when you're working with folks and maybe you aren't working with folks who are brand new, but from that zero to one or zero to two spot in learning a new skill, what is something that new climbers always struggle with that they probably don't anticipate being the thing being the crux that they're dealing with currently?
