content:
Kris Hampton (11:07): I do work with new climbers and expert level climbers, and I think climbing is such an interesting sport that sort of scales itself. The experts are dealing with the same sort of struggle that the relatively new climbers are just at a different difficulty level. So I think really the thing that sort of permeates the entire sport from beginner all the way to the top levels are just doubts and doubts about exploration. We sort of come in with expectations of how something is supposed to feel when it doesn't feel that way. We end up with all these doubts and we're not willing to explore anymore, and we just get on ourselves. So encouraging both beginners and experts to continue exploring, I think is exploring their movement and their own confidence levels I think is really the biggest thing all the way across the board.

Cole Heilborn (12:12): Interesting. So that confidence component to never stop exploring, never stop discovering a new route or new holds

Kris Hampton (12:19): Or new ways to move, new ways to fit yourself between holds. Creativity is such a big part of just about any eSport climbing in particular, I think for me feels very creative and I try to encourage people not to lose that.

Cole Heilborn (12:41): So you're 230 some episodes deep in your podcast. You started in, did you say 2016?

Kris Hampton (12:48): Gosh, I honestly don't know. Dates are probably my weakest area of anything. I'm terrible at dates. If I can't connect it to a big momentous event in my life, like graduating from high school or having my first daughter, then I can't tell you the date.

Cole Heilborn (13:09): Fair enough. Was this before or after having your daughter? Did you start your podcast

Kris Hampton (13:13): After?

Cole Heilborn (13:14): Okay,

Kris Hampton (13:15): After my first daughter who's now 25, she'll be 25 in three days.

content:
Cole Heilborn (13:21): Okay. Well, congrat, happy birthday, happy early birthday. So 2016, I think I read that somewhere. That's a considerable amount of time to be in the podcast world, especially as podcasting in the last two years or three years has really become popular and mainstream. I feel like you've been doing this well Beyond me, well beyond many people. What have you noticed? What differences do you notice about the podcast landscape from then to now?

Kris Hampton (13:52): Well, it's definitely gotten more crowded, and I don't say that as a bad thing. I think as it's grown, just like anything else, I saw this with hip hop when I was really into hip hop. I saw it become easier for people to make things, and that's certainly happened in the podcast world. It's much easier now to make a podcast, put a podcast out there, and I think that's led to it's splitting off into there are some really, really bad podcasts because anybody can make one and the price of entry is pretty low. But then there are also some really creative, really great podcasts out there, and it's really hard for me to keep up. I want to really badly. I want to listen to everything good that's out there, but it's so hard to keep up. What I do find, however, inspires me to keep growing, to keep improving at podcasting and to keep being able to tell better stories.

Cole Heilborn (14:57): Interesting. You bring that up because that's kind of at the heart of where I'm hoping we can take this conversation. And I was trying to think about, so we had a conversation before this about you and your business and everything that you do, and the thing that I took away from our conversation was this idea of focus and there's so much that you can be doing as a podcaster and there's only so much time, you only have so much bandwidth. And so it sounds like what you're saying is that finding that focus has been really important. And I'm curious how focus has changed the idea of focus has maybe changed over time as you've been podcasting?

content:
Kris Hampton (15:36): Yeah, I think for me specifically, initially podcasting was all about getting training information out there, and then once I realized I had people's ear and that I could tell them more important things than just how to make your fingers stronger, then I leaned a little more toward the idea of telling the stories that aren't necessarily being told in climbing and hearing from the voices that we aren't hearing from. So that's been a big part of this for me. And now I'm just leaning more toward how can I tell stories in a bigger, more memorable way. So for me, that's how it's changed and how I've changed my focus. But this is my main marketing tool. The Power Company podcast is my main marketing tool for sure. So I also have to make sure that I'm marketing my business in the process. So there's definitely a balance there between telling other people's stories and also telling our own story.

Cole Heilborn (17:02): Yeah. How much of your time is spent actually podcasting versus being a coach?

Kris Hampton (17:12): That shifted quite a bit over the years. It started out I was doing one episode a month or something, so very small percentage of my time was spent podcasting. Now because podcasting is what I'm really excited about and learning to tell better stories is what I'm excited about. I would say I spend probably 70 to 75% of my time working on podcasts and podcast ideas.

Cole Heilborn (17:42): Interesting. And the marketing side of it all, how much does the podcast play the marketing of your coaching business?

content:
Kris Hampton (17:52): It's huge. I don't spend a lot of time directly pointing people towards the products that we make, and we have a lot, the reason I can spend 70 to 75% of my time making podcasts because we have a lot of passive offerings for climbers, eBooks, and training plans through our apps and things like that and products that we sell. And I don't spend a lot of time pushing people in that direction. But what I do through the podcast is put my expertise out there as a climber, as a climbing coach, as someone who's spent a lot of time reading books, listening to other podcasts, talking with coaches across a variety of different sports, reading research into training across a bunch of different sports and trying to synthesize all that into how can we be better climbers. So for me, putting my expertise out there front and center brings people into this company and by taking stands on the podcast on things that I believe in and trying to tell stories that I believe in, I know that I'm getting a certain type of customer who isn't going to be something dramatically different from the type of person that we want to work with.

Cole Heilborn (19:21): Yeah, interesting. So I feel like if I go onto LinkedIn at any point during the week, I will see a post somewhere about how there's some clickbaity title that says you need to create a podcast because it will become your number one marketing tool, which I don't necessarily disagree with. However, I'm curious if you've been doing it for this long, when did you realize that the podcast was giving you more value than you were putting into it? When did you start making a profit essentially off of your podcast and the time and the energy invested?

content:
Kris Hampton (19:59): It actually happened pretty quickly for me, but I think that's largely because of the timing of getting into it early before there were many climbing podcasts and then putting out a consistent product for over several years. So I earned the trust of the climbing community through this podcast. I think that you're totally right with these Click Beatty titles, and it sort of felt like at the time if you build it, they will come scenario like, oh, I just made a podcast and people bought in and now they're coming to my website. But as the podcast landscape gets more and more crowded and there are more and more podcasts out there that put out three or four episodes and then never show up again, it's getting harder and harder to earn people's trust. So I don't think it's the case that you can just build it and they will come. I think you really have to put the work in, be consistent care about the product that you are putting out there into the airwaves, and then maybe you can earn the trust of people.

Cole Heilborn (21:19): Yeah. Yeah. It's that trust that's the variable in all of it. How do you build that? How do you foster it, and how long do you have to keep plugging away at it before you slowly start to build that bridge?

Kris Hampton (21:37): Yeah, I wish I knew the answers to any of those questions. For me, it's just keep doing it. I don't do anything that I don't want to do. I'm not going to make a podcast just as a marketing tool if I don't want to have these conversations. It's going to show in the conversation that I don't want to be there. So for me, if I'm going to do something, it's something I'm going to be excited about that I can keep doing. And I think that's how you build the trust. You are excited about it, you continue doing it even when there are five listeners and you just steadily build that.

Cole Heilborn (22:21): How do you think about the marketing of your podcast and the marketing of your business?

content: Kris Hampton (22:28): That's definitely changed too. Initially, I didn't have to worry about it. I was one of the few blogs talking about training for climbing. I was one of the few podcasts out there talking about climbing, and I think I had a better audio product than several of the other podcasts because I was doing all of my interviews in person and I had a background with audio, so I understood it a little. And now as it gets more and more crowded as it's harder and harder to reach people in a landscape where they have literally hundreds and hundreds of options to choose from, I have to be a little more thoughtful. And I've sort of narrowed it down to three principles that I try to always follow. And number one is be authentic. And that just means, like I just said, if I'm not excited about it, don't do it. I have to think it's cool. I have to think it's exciting, I have to feel good about it, I have to believe in it. And then number two is keep trying new things, but do it with healthy skepticism. (23:43): When new things come out, I'm old and crusty and I'm like, I'm not doing that. That's ridiculous. But I'm willing to try and see how it feels to me, see how it works. And I go in with a lot of skepticism. I don't just buy in immediately because it's the thing everyone's talking about. And last is a quote that I take from a strength coach named Dan John, and we use this quote in my training business often, and that's the goal, is to keep the goal the goal. And that simply means whatever my original goal is when I set out to make the thing to market the thing, I make sure that remains the goal. If my goal, let's say in climbing, the goal is to climb better, but very often people get sidetracked and in their training, they want to make their fingers stronger, and all of a sudden their whole goal is, I want to make my fingers stronger. And they forget that the goal initially was to become a better climber. And I think with making things like making a podcast, my goal is to tell good stories and get voices out there that aren't being heard. But if I'm worried about how my reels translate on Instagram, I start paying more attention to the likes I'm getting or how many views my reel gets, and now all of a sudden I'm putting all my energy toward how do I get more views on this reel? And I've lost what the actual goal is.

content:
Cole Heilborn (25:18): Interesting. Dan John, is that the individual who came up with that idea?

Kris Hampton (25:24): Yeah, he's this common sense, no bullshit strength coach, world famous strength coach who he's just brilliant. He can really pare things down into their essence and just give you a sentence that smacks you in the face.

Cole Heilborn (25:47): That's such a simple idea. But I'm even thinking about myself and goals that I have or goals that I set years ago. And I'm now wondering, huh, maybe have I lost track of that original goal? Have I replaced it with something else? And I got to imagine in today's world, it's even that much easier to do where there's always a new tool, there's always a new bandwagon to jump on, or there's TikTok blows up, and now we're all supposed to be using that.

Kris Hampton (26:18): It's so hard to not get distracted from what your original goal is. It's a thing I have to constantly ask myself. I have to remind myself every single day, this is why I'm doing this. This is the goal of this thing. Don't get distracted down these rabbit holes because I love rabbit holes, Cole, I love going down rabbit holes and learning new things, but I've only got so much room and so much growth potential. I have to focus on the things that are my actual goals.

Cole Heilborn (26:55): Do you have a story? Do you have an example of where you've distracted yourself and you've had to course correct?

Kris Hampton (27:01): Yeah. I mean, certainly with climbing it happens very easily because I love training. I love the minutia of getting stronger, of improving at something. And if left to my own devices, I could very easily just disappear into the gym and never come back out. So for myself, if I don't remind myself I need to go out and actually climb things and try the thing that started this whole process, if I don't do that, I'll stay in the gym and just keep trying to get stronger fingers. I think that's super common. And for me, that's definitely the case. I love going into the gym. I would choose to go into the gym over climbing outside a lot of days if I didn't remind myself to go out there.

content:
Kris Hampton (29:09): And I think we also have to allow that to shift. My goal with Power Company climbing originally was to build this business that could be sustainable while helping other people become better climbers. And I've done that to a level that I'm happy with. I could have continued trying to build it. Let's grow bigger, bigger, bigger, bigger, because that's what we're supposed to do. That's what we've always heard. But once I realized, oh, I've reached my goal here, I'm happy with where this business is, and it's at a place where passively I can mostly passively, I can let it run. (30:05): And then I asked myself, what do I want to do now? And because I'm like, I was waking up thinking about the podcast and thinking about who can I interview and how many can I fit in this month? And I thought, wow, let's change the goal a little bit. I'll keep some attention over here on power company climbing, and I'll make sure that I'm not forgetting about my clients, but I also want to start telling better stories, more important stories. And so now my goals have shifted. I think that's an important thing as well. Notice when you've reached your goal and you don't have to keep hammering on it, and then you can set other goals if that's what you're psyched to do.

Cole Heilborn (30:50): Was that tough to not continue to press the gas pedal a hundred percent on the coaching business? I mean, you could have kept going bigger and better, right?

content:
Kris Hampton (31:01): Yeah. I see some other training businesses doing something similar where it's like, how can we get more people in the door? And I could have gone that route, that could have become my focus. So it was hard. Here I am building this business as one of the first people in the industry to do it, and now there are other businesses that are growing bigger in different directions, and I could have easily gone that same direction had I let myself get trapped in the idea of I need to grow a bigger business. But the goal was to put a quality product out there to help people become better climbers. And I realized that one-on-one coaching isn't the most effective way to do that, and I'm doing it far more effectively through telling stories. So ultimately I'm still attacking that original goal by sort of shifting the goal, if that makes any sense. But yeah, definitely hard to do reassess and question my assumptions.

Cole Heilborn (32:17): So I'm noticing some interesting parallels, and I'm curious if this sticks for you or if I'm just way off here. So at the beginning of this conversation, you mentioned that one of the reasons why you really enjoy the coaching is that you get to help climbers build confidence and help them realize their confidence. I'm also noticing that there's a lot of things, maybe a lot of messages or philosophies that we're told in business or in the world of podcasting that we have to be doing or we should be doing. And it sounds like you're very confident knowing what you want to do and knowing what you don't want to do and not being swayed by whatever the latest trend or the latest fad is. I'm curious if there's a connection between your own confidence when it comes to climbing and how you choose to run your business and how you make decisions about how to run your business.

content:
Kris Hampton (34:19): Yeah. I don't know that I'm very good at this. I try lots of things. Like I said, I do think if we're just looking for nuts and bolts, ways to grow these things, having guests on who really believe in the mission and who aren't just a self-serving guest who's like, oh, I did this thing. I want to tell people about it. But if they really believe in what you are doing, they're far more likely to tell everyone else about it too. So I think getting guests who share your vision and share your mission is really important. For me, honestly, the big name guests haven't been as important. I can have the top climbers on my podcast, but they don't mean as much to me. They don't bring as many people in as some of the people who most climbers have never heard of, but they also share this mission, share this vision, and they're willing to tell everybody they know about it. So I think that's a really important and maybe counterintuitive thing. (35:38): Also, I think consistency goes so far, and I think a lot of people will bail when it doesn't seem to be working after the first four or five or even 10 episodes. And it really took off for me after I had 30, 40, 50 episodes. That's when it really started to grow. And I treat my audience like my friends essentially. I think that's a great way to market your product. I really believe in this hundred true fans or thousand true fans idea where I'm not terribly interested in putting my podcast in front of a million people. I would much rather really tell the stories that my thousand true fans really want to hear, because I know those true fans are going to tell all of their friends who also share this same vision. So I think for me, those things are far more important than How good is your Instagram reel or are you putting it on Twitter or TikTok?

Cole Heilborn (36:54): Yeah. What's your take on social media and how it plays a role in your podcast? There's always a new tool to be using.

content:
Kris Hampton (37:02): Yeah, it's so tricky. I love social media. I really do. I think it like anything else, it's got its upsides and its downsides. The one thing I will say is I think it's easier to fall victim to the downsides as social media proliferates everything we do. And because new tools are constantly coming out, it's hard to keep up with. It's hard to create a quality social media post when it's like, oh, I have to make it for YouTube. I have to have it on Twitter. I have to make a TikTok, I have to have a reel. I need a post in my feed. And I'm sure there are 10 others that I'm missing here because I'm just too old to even understand. So I think it's a tricky place that you should approach with some skepticism, but I do think it's valuable, and I love the idea that I can put something out there that can resonate with someone else and they can immediately share it to their friends. And that's what I'm looking for. I don't give a damn how many people like it or how many people view it, as long as the true fans out there that it resonates with them and that they can then share it with their people.

Cole Heilborn (38:28): I feel like that's a bold statement to make. If you're not concerned about the response, you're not concerned about the likes. That seems so counterintuitive.

Kris Hampton (38:38): It does, and I think it comes down to the fact that I can't control what that algorithm is, so I really just want to reach the people that I care about and that I know care about the thing that I'm making as opposed to being the next popular thing. I look into these things pretty heavily. Like I said, I love going down rabbit holes, and when reels were first becoming popular, I would look at other people's reels and think, Jesus, how did they, that's got 20,000 views? How is that even possible? And so I started looking into the algorithm and looking into what this data means. And at the time, what I found was that anytime a reel passes someone's screen, whether they watch it or not, it counted as a view. I've recently read that it has to be watched for three seconds now, which is maybe why there are lots of people saying, my reels aren't being the algorithms holding me down because they aren't being viewed like they were. Well, maybe they just changed what a view means. And so 20,000 times that it passes someone's screen is not important to me. I would rather have my a hundred people who are paying attention actually watch the thing and get something out of it. And that view count doesn't tell me if that's happening or not.

Cole Heilborn (40:13): Right. 20,000 views at three seconds. A piece doesn't account for much versus a hundred people listening to an hour long conversation.

Kris Hampton (40:22): Right? Totally. So keep the goal of goal. It's the goal is to have people listen, get something important out of it, not to gain more likes or more views.

content:
Cole Heilborn (40:36): So there's this book that I have read, and it's called Zig Wait, Zig Then Zag or Zig or Zag, I can't remember. It's sitting on the bookshelf behind me, the premise. It's a branding book and it's all about how to position yourself, how to think about where you sit in the marketplace. It's a really great book. I highly recommend it, but the entire idea is that when everyone is zigging, you should be zagging, basically do the opposite of what everyone else is doing. And I feel like, I think I've said this before, but Warren Buffet always says, do the opposite of what everyone else is doing. If everyone's buying, then you should be selling vice versa. And that might be too simplistic of a view on some of these matters. But I'm curious now that podcasting has become the thing to do, should we all stop podcasting and find the next thing?

Kris Hampton (41:32): I wish everyone else would stop podcasting because I'd be the only one left. But no, I don't think so. I think we just reexamine our assumptions about what podcasting means. For me personally, I'm leaning away from the Straight Up Interview podcast and more into how can I use sound design and music and narration to tell better stories. It doesn't mean I don't love the interview podcast, I still do, but I'm exploring all these other things because now there are, I mean, millions of interview podcasts out there and what's going to make mine special. I've spent a lot of time trying to be a better interviewer and trying to keep this conversation moving in a natural way. And I think I've maxed that out for myself, so I'm going in other directions. So I don't know if it's always a full on Zig when everyone else is zagging, but I do think that's a good idea to think about where can I go next? Everyone else has gotten to my level, where can I go? That's interesting and unique.

Cole Heilborn (42:53): Can you share more about where you're hoping to go? You mentioned that you're trying to do more narrative or story-based podcasts. Is that the next thing on your horizon?

content:
Kris Hampton (43:05): Yeah, that's what I'm working on. That's what I'm working on right now. And I've leaned into it a little bit with Hip hop Taught me everything. And the Built Outdoors series that we've just started is very much a sound rich sound designed and highly edited and produced podcasts that's very inspired by things like Radio Lab and this American Life and radio in general. I think we've almost taken this reductionist approach to podcasting where it started with these highly produced, this American life that was the big one for a lot of years. And we've gotten away from that in a reductionist sort of way, a minimalist sort of way, which I really love, and I think is a necessary evolution, so to speak. It seems like a backwards, a devolution, I guess, but I do think it's a necessary thing to really boil something down to its individual parts and then you can build it back up. So now that I've become what I think is a good interviewer, I want to expand that and be able to color those interviews with music and with sound and really weave a good story together as opposed to just a good conversation. So on our plug Tone Outdoors channel, I'm experimenting with a lot of that, and that's where I put out the cowboy poem you mentioned, and I'm just really making some art projects that I'm putting out there and seeing what sticks.

Cole Heilborn (44:56): What's your take on video podcasting? YouTube has obviously been pushing that pretty hard. I don't know much about it, but it sounds like Spotify also is making that part of their offering now. What role does that play in the future of podcasting?

And at first I thought there's no reason for a video podcast where it's just talking heads and you're seeing people talk to each other. But then recently, oh, I can't think of the name of it. Recently, a new podcast hosted by Brandon Jenkins, who's a hip hop writer, came out and it's a video podcast that's, he talks to people, it's like a talk show in this beautiful set, and they have several cameras going, and it's released on Spotify as a video podcast. And I really wanted to listen to it, but I found myself watching the video even though it's just people talking. So I have to imagine that it's going to be a big part of the future, and I just don't know where it's going yet. I would love to see there are some reels out there that are sort of acting out what's being talked about in the podcast or animated versions of what's being talked about, and I would love to see whole stories done that way. I know that's a lot of work, but I suspect it's coming.

Cole Heilborn (46:45): That would be wild. That would be so cool. I guess this is a question for the audience. If anyone feels like responding or curious, I mean, I'm looking at Chris right now. He's looking at me instead of just hearing our voices. Would you prefer to see our faces while we're chatting? I don't know. It's an interesting question, but I find myself, if the content is good enough, I would much rather watch a video. I feel like I'm picking up more on those minor social cues from the host or the guest.

I know your voice. You're this guy. And that happens a lot. And I'll have people recognize my voice and then say, oh, how did that project go that I heard you talk about last week? But there's definitely something to seeing someone's face that makes you feel like you know them in some way. And I do think that's a really important aspect of this true fans theory is bringing them into your world a little bit, and maybe video does a better job of that.

Cole Heilborn (48:06): Well, I almost wonder, this just hit me, I think about pre COVID, how conferences and going to conferences, thought leadership events, meetings were super popular. And I feel like I have some similar connection to that individual. And I wonder if this is just the next form or another form of that same type of experience. If this was in a video format,

Kris Hampton (48:40): Yeah, it could be. What you just said led me to thinking about pre COVID. Anytime I was talking to a client, it was pretty much just on the phone. Very rarely did I use Skype or whatever video platforms were available out there. But since they've been improved, I much prefer to get on a video call with someone. I like the idea of being able to see people's faces and see their mannerisms and see their reactions. It's just a nicer experience. So I think I'm talking myself into a video podcast here.

Cole Heilborn (49:21): Maybe we need to start one. If you want to add another one to your quiver of podcasts.

Kris Hampton (49:27): Cole, I want to add 15 or 20 more into my quiver. Like I said, it's totally an addiction.

Kris Hampton (50:03): And you found that thing that fires you up so important. Something you asked a little earlier, it's sort of all coming back around now. When I'm coaching climbers, one of the most important parts of coaching them is modeling my coaching philosophies for them. Not just telling them, but acting it out, making mistakes myself, exploring myself. And I think that's a big part of what I'm doing with podcasts is this constant desire to grow and to learn and to try new things and to fail at things, to put things out there into the public that's just an art project that no one else likes but me, I'm totally okay doing that because it's modeling what I want people to get out of it all. And that's this willingness to explore the things that they're excited about.

Cole Heilborn (51:12): Is it possible, coming back to this idea of focus, is it possible for you to take that philosophy and make that philosophy your focus? I think sometimes we think of focus as being, I'm going to focus on hitting this sales goal for the year, but what if you could focus on an idea rather than an outcome? Is that harder to do?

Kris Hampton (51:33): I do think it's harder to do, but I think that's the essence of the goal is to keep the goal, the goal, really boil it down to your, why am I doing this? Why do I want to do this? Why am I excited about it? And keep that thing as your goal, as your focus. So for me, my focus is never, I want to get more listeners to my podcast. I want to make a specific thing. I want to make a better podcast. I want to be this philosophy that I keep preaching.

content:
Cole Heilborn (52:11): There was an interview with, I believe it was Bill Gates, I don't remember how long ago, but he was asked if you could have, there's any attribute or any skill that you could be better at, what would it be? And if I think about that question, there's a lot of things that I wish I was better at, but his answer was, I wish that I had more focus. And I feel like coming from someone of that caliber, it hits me in a different way thinking, well, bill Gates wishes he had more focus. I feel like if anyone has focus, it's someone like him, but I wonder what's truly possible if we're able to focus entirely on what we should be focusing on. And I think there's a difference there, and this gets back to that keep the goal of the goal idea, but if you could truly find what we need to all be focusing on and then just drive towards that, I wonder what the outcome could be.

Kris Hampton (53:10): Yeah, I think it will certainly make it easier to avoid the pitfalls of social media and the doubts that come along with putting something out there that no one is listening to or paying attention to so that you can continue trying. We've heard so many stories from artists, from writers, from athletes about, I wrote this thing and it got rejected a hundred times and then someone bought it and now it's a New York Times bestseller. We hear those stories constantly, and for every one of those stories, there are hundreds of people who got rejected once or twice and stopped submitting, didn't achieve their sports goal once or twice and stop trying to reach it. So I do think if we can find what it is, we should be focusing on whatever our goal is and we can keep that the goal. We avoid a lot of those pitfalls. I have to believe that, or I wouldn't be trying to do it myself.

content:
Cole Heilborn (54:26): So as you were just speaking there, I'm thinking about a camera lens and how it focuses and to the eye. When you're focused on a subject, it looks like it. Certain range of that depth is within focus, but in reality, only one point on that z axis is actually in focus. Everything else is slightly off. And the farther you get from that focus point, it becomes more softer and softer. And I'm thinking about what are the things that we think we need to focus on versus the things that we really need to focus on? And I'm picturing this camera lens analogy where there's a lot of things that are just slightly out of focus or are kind of soft, but we think are things that we need to be focusing on. But in reality, there's only, we can only focus on one thing. I guess that's my question. Can we only focus on one thing or one point at a time, or can we be focusing on a variety of things?

Kris Hampton (55:26): Well, I love that analogy. I think priority is a singular thing. I don't think there's a such thing as priorities, and I sort of feel that way about focus as well. I think you can move your focus around just like you can with a camera lens, but at any given time, your focus should be on one thing, and you absolutely should have other things that are in soft focus that are in the background, that are simmering because you're going to burn out if you're focused only on one thing forever. So I think it's a singular, I don't think you have many things in focus. I think you focus on the one thing while these other things are soft and you can move that focus to tell whatever story it is you want to, just like you would with a camera. If you're pulling focus to tell a story in a certain way, I think we can do the same thing in our lives.

Cole Heilborn (56:35): Well, you've given me a lot more to think about. This has been an insightful conversation.

Kris Hampton (56:40): Me too. I love working my way through this stuff and I love having conversations where the person I'm talking to is willing to work through these things instead of just having the click bait headline answer.

content:
David Meredith (00:02:00): Sure. Well, FSA, it is an acronym. It stands for Full Speed Ahead. We're a component company for bicycles. We are the third largest bicycle component company in the world. Next Tora and Shimano, we make everything including drivetrain for road bikes, hbar stems, wheels, headsets, most famous for our headsets. They seem to come on every single bike imaginable and whether you know it or not, because we tend to OEM and private label a lot of that stuff too. We've been around for the better part of 25 years, almost 30 years. The parent company industries is out of Taiwan, and then we have our European office, which is outside of Milan, Italy, and our US office is here in Muckle, teel, and we've been here in Muckle, teel for maybe 12 to 15 years. I forget. We started off in Woodenville, so we've always been northwest fresh, if you will, and the American office here is the seat for all things Mountain. So our Italian office handles road and road Engineering, and then we handle mountain and Mountain engineering as well as mountain marketing and product development.

Cole Heilborn (00:03:36): Got hence your title of dirt marketing.

David Meredith (00:03:40): Exactly. So that covers all mountain bike, and then I do lots in the gravel and cyclocross markets as well.

Cole Heilborn (00:03:49): Gotcha. Okay. What do you personally enjoy riding these days? Are you taken to the gravel fad?

David Meredith (00:03:58): Actually, I am. I've took that really hard because it reminds me of being in high school and the mountain bikes that we rode in high school back in the nineties and eighties and nineties. It's basically a gravel bike now with better wheels and better brakes. So it was exciting to do that. My first gravel bike was an OED boundary, and then I traded that in for a evil shammy Hagar, which got me into a lot of trouble because it rode like a mountain bike. So I was on legit downhill trails on that bike. But now I'm in the process of getting a custom built sage titanium, and I am really excited about that one because it's my geometry, so it's going to be fun.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:04:51): So I know you have quite the history of being in and out of the industry. I'd love if you could kind of summarize your journey to where you are today. I know you started out racing, you at one point had started your own bike company. Could you kind of fill us in on some of the details?

David Meredith (00:05:10): Sure, I'll try and keep it kind of brief. I tend to tell long round about stories. Let's see. I kind of got bit by the bug in high school in the early nineties. So I ran track and I was the third fastest one 10 high hurdler in California, and mountain biking was a cross training tool for running. But I got hit by a car and it took out my chances of going to the Olympics for running. And so I just dove into cycling because I could do that, and it didn't mess my knees up too much, and I had friends that were like, Hey, you need to start racing. Okay, cool. So I started racing and I was really good at it. So basically I raced cross country throughout all of California and high school. Moved to Colorado in 93 when I turned 18, upgraded to pro and then had my ass handed to me in the cross country races. So I picked up downhill racing and turned out I was really good at that. So I raced downhill from 93 until 2003 on the Nobo circuit and a couple of World Cup invitationals. (00:06:29): I raced for Yeti, I raced for intenses, a couple other private brands as a privateer, but for the most, and then for Turner Bikes started a team with him. But in 2002, I graduated from the University of Idaho and wanted to work more inside the industry. I had been kind of a sales rep outside kind of a guy, got a job working for Marzo as a OEM, sales and marketing for them, left them after I finished grad school. I was working with 'em while I was in grad school, finished them. Then kind of got back out of the bike industry and pursued my career in journalism. Worked for a newspaper back in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, the Coeur d'Alene Press us while also kind of working for a group called the Superheroes, which was a mountain bike free ride media team. So we were making videos and I was doing sales and marketing for them for North America that got defunct after a while. (00:07:49): For whatever reason. I don't remember what happened. And I had met my wife, my then girlfriend, and she said, Hey, I'm moving to New Mexico. So I said, great.

content: David Meredith (00:05:10): So we moved to New Mexico and I end up opening up a shop, which turned out to be the only downhill free ride bike shop in all of New Mexico, one of four of its kind. I think in the country. There was Speed Goat, there was Mojo Wheels, there was Fluid Ride, and I forget, there was another one somewhere. But our primary focus was downhill gravity, teaching classes, mechanic classes, writing classes, stuff like that. That evolved into a clothing line. The clothing line couldn't get enough funding that evolved into a bicycle line, which I know I'm truncating a lot of this, but I met a friend of mine who was the dyno test engineer for Harley Davidson, helped with the Vro project. (00:08:59): He basically connected the dots on the geometry charts that I was building for bikes. And he was like, Hey, I had another friend of mine whose son I was sponsoring with my shop who was a former triathlete and a mountain bike racer, and he said, Hey, let's make bikes. So we're like, oh, well, okay, bleep, let's make some bikes. So we dove into that. The bike brand was called One Ghost Industries named after my dog Ghost. I was the one, he was the ghost and the industries was the bike, and he was named after the Ghost Dog, which is the spiritual protector of the Samurai. That's a whole separate story. But Ghost was, he inspired me to start this. And so from 2006 till 2014, basically it was myself and my business partner, Rory. We designed, built, assembled, sold, marketed our own bikes using my suspension design, and we sold them all over the world. (00:10:10): And I had a World Cup team with one racer, art Babcock, who was, he still is, he races Baja 500 and Baja 100 now in the Ironman category. So in 2014, we shelved the brands. By 2014, we had multiple brands that we were running. We had one Ghost Industries, which was the mountain brand. We had stop cycles, sustainable transportation, zero pollution, which were basically what gravel bikes are now. So I was doing mountain bikes designed for drop bars, essentially.

content: David Meredith (00:05:10): I called them Cross Mutters because they were for commuting, but they were Cyclo Cross and they were do everything, big, fat tire clearance, drop bars, all the fun stuff. And then I had a component group called Candy Components, which was handlebars stems, headsets, pedals. (00:11:14): So I sold off the IP for the component group and kept the IP for the two bike brands, shelved it, and went to work for Marzo again, a second time because I knew the product, I knew the brand, but this time they were owned by Tenneco. And so worked with them, brought them kind of back into the limelight, if you will, because by 2014 they were not necessarily as viable, but I was able to help bring them back up to online. I ran for them for North America and was able to get them to the point where Tenneco wanted to sell the brand. I brought them to the table for Shimano, for Fox, for a few other companies that were looking to buy them. As we know, Fox ended up purchasing them. When that purchase went through, everyone was going to get laid off, and I knew this, and they gave us six, eight months. (00:12:22): So I didn't wait around, but I ended up getting an offer to go and work for Crank Brothers. So I joined the team at Crank Brothers as their global sports marketing director and worked with them and from 2015 until 2017, and that was an amazing run. I have nothing but love for those guys. I had always used the pedals. I actually OEMed their product. But in 2016, we had our first son, Josiah, and my travel schedule was close to 200 days a year, global travel. So trying to do that with a newborn was just a non-start, and I had an hour and a half commute each way. I had to work in the office, didn't have provisions for working remotely, and so it was just mutually part of the way. So I was like, Hey, I can't do this anymore. They're like, okay, no worries. (00:13:33): So I left them, ended up working a little closer to home for specialized of all places, came on with them to help build out their retail stores. So I was the global service director for their retail chain. As you know, they now have specialized retail and they creating retail stores across the world.

And that's what we did. (00:14:43): So I did that for about a year and decided, Hey, this is just taking too much of my time still. I really want to spend these years with my son, the very important bonding years. When he was Little Ghost my dog, he was getting older. I really wanted to spend time with him. I had him since he was six months old, and he had literally been by my side the entire time for 14 years. So 2017 I left, or 2018 I left specialized to just be a stay-at-home dad, do freelance work, and took care of my son. My dog passed away at that time, which I was lucky enough to be able to be there with him and did that and went back to school actually in 2019 for nursing. And because I already had a master's degree, I already had an EMT certification, I was able to fast track my way into a master's of nursing. (00:15:59): So I started that, and then the pandemic rumblings were hitting in late 2019, beginning 2020, finished my semester in 2019, semester, started up in 2020 again, and started taking a really hard look at what was happening around the world and was like, I got a really bad feeling about this. So my wife and me were like, yeah, let's just ride this out and see what happens. And sure enough, the pandemic happened and life came to a halt for everybody, as we all know, by June, may I forget, maybe may I end up taking a job with InCycle Bicycles as their digital marketing director, taking on the role of helping them build and design their website and maintain an online presence because now everyone's switching to online. So creating an experience through their website, through digital integration and activations. So that was pretty fun.

(00:17:29): So I started looking around, spoke to a friend of mine here at FSA, and he's like, Hey, let's see what happens. And then after a while, and this is now by 2021, I got an offer to come on board and was like, yeah, let's, heck yeah, let's take this. This is great. Worked remotely for a year for 2021, partly because the office here was closed only essential warehouse as needed. And then because I was in California at the time, so just worked remotely until just June of this year, we moved up here and we've been here ever since, and it's been great.

Cole Heilborn (00:18:20): Wow. Yeah, that's quite the journey. There's a lot of stops in there. That sounded like a fun time.

David Meredith (00:18:27): Yeah. The cool thing about all of that that I love going back to is Ghost. He was the greatest trail dog I've ever known. content: David Meredith (01:00:49): It is, as Michael Franti puts it, stay human. And that's a mantra. Don't forget not just where you came from. That's a living sentient creature just like a human. And people don't want to compare themselves to a roach, but I just did. As consumers are getting smarter and smarter, they're listening less and less to what the brands say about themselves. Instead, they're doing their own research. They're going on online, looking up blogs, trying to find these micro influencers or these massive influencers about what do they have to say about certain experiences that they're having with certain products. So I think the main catalyst to this evolution is the consumers getting smarter and they're kind of blocking out some of the noise of what traditional marketing channels kind of produce.

So it speaks to that resident element of them understanding the impact and the benefit of bringing visitation to their backyard, but then also to that point, that connection of what that benefit means for the residents and their emotional belonging and engagement in all things marketing and kind of success, if you will, when you're promoting a destination. So they're they're just starting to field this out. And I think they're doing a bunch, I think it's over a year that they're going to be doing these different surveys and kind of really assessing within different communities so that These can then kind of opt in, if you will, and see how they're progressing and on that scale, which again to your point, I think it invites more participation from the local community and those stakeholders who might be a little bit more vocal for the means of you know visitation.

I can't tell you how many times it's happened where I'll be interviewing someone, they'll be telling me about, you know, moments in their life, how they were feeling, and I'll realize, I'll start to connect the dots for them. I'll be like, so was it because of this that you felt this way? And pe sometimes people don't realize the way their life connects. But the interview is kind of like sitting down for therapy, honestly. And your job is kind of like a therapist. Your job is to help them connect the dots, but then your job is to give them space to reflect on those ideas. your job as the interviewer is to restrain the conversation, but also give the conversation rope. Let them let them run with the let them run themselves. Sometimes people go off tangent. And tangents are great because you never know what you find. But sometimes people go way off tangent. And you need to you need to be in a spot where you can communicate to the other person and say, hey, we've only had limited time. I really want to make sure we get through these particular beats of your story, these notes. can we redirect and talk about this? and sometimes you have to just sometimes you have to stop people and say, Hey, for the sake of time, I love where this is going. I'd love to have this conversation later. But Do we make sure we cover these details first? So you have to balance the creative liberty, but you have to restrain where people go as well.

I just think that's the best way to make a better product, regardless of what your product is, to have feedback from your customers. and I find that like to in today's media landscape, like is it's starting to fade away, but a little too slowly for my liking, is people care more about numbers, you know. I don't think of our audience as numbers, I think of them as a community. And it doesn't really matter if there's a hundred people or a hundred million people in our subscribership, we're gonna just make the same kick ass magazine for the hundred people that we would for a hundred million and listen to their feedbacks and you know, as we I guess the other thing, man, is like as we as we scale and we grow, and we've grown significantly in the last six months in particular, we're investing more in our community. like ways in which they can reach out to us. You know, our customer service team has tripled in size in the last year, not because we have any problems with customer service, but because we want to be able to answer people's emails. We want to be able to talk to them. You know, I reach out to people directly from my own email. Like we're not trying to hide I just think that if you had these niche media companies, which is really what Outdoor is, is like niche media, if they started caring more about their readers you'd have a lot more successful media companies out there that were putting out really good specific media and not this like broad strokes top ten list crap that's just going for numbers and display ad impressions.

Shut down seventy-nine, came back in two thousand. shut down again in like twenty eleven, twenty twelve. in twenty nineteen, I was told it was for sale. Kim Stravers, who is a copy editor for my book and a copy editor at Powder Magazine, is our copy editor. And we still have that same crew today. And I think at a time of, you know, a lot of instability for readers on like where they were gonna get the media they wanted, they saw a big format magazine and a dude that was saying, like, hey, this is what it is, this is what it isn't, and we're, you know, not really gonna change the format. We'll change the story approach, obviously, as the times change, but we won't change the size or the respect and it resonated with people. I think you can always stare at your iPhone for so long before you start to go crazy and and we're kind of proving that method. Can you kinda describe what is that challenge that a lot of media companies are seeing, both outdoor and non outdoor?

Mike Rogge (10:31): Yeah, so I think you have to look at the ownership structure and the incentives they have. you know, I I certainly poke fun of venture capital, but I have friends that are in venture capital. I have friends that have taken venture money, it's worked out great. some of our readers are venture capitalists in New York or in the Bay. but the thing about venture capital is like they're essentially putting a bet on your company. That you're going to give a four, five, six, God, maybe even a 10 or 15x return if you really found a unicorn. And that model works really well for, say, like a tech company, but not really well for a media company. It basically like it doesn't place the value on the individual reader. it places the value on tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions of readers and consumers and what they represent and will they buy more from you? What's their lifetime value to the company, like things like that. It's like, dude, I've never cared about assistant statistic, which is the average revenue per customer. I don't I don't care what the lifetime value, quote unquote, is like one of our readers might pull me off of a boat that's sinking one day. You I mean, who knows? Like might rescue me. Like I mean, you just don't you can't, I'm never gonna r measure the value of a people off of revenue. because people are obviously worth so much more than that. but I think that's the problem with media right now is they're trying to find ways they can squeeze more revenue out, whether it's social media, you know, influencing campaigns that they can use to try to get people to buy stuff or affiliate links or top ten lists because they're clickworthy. One of my favorite things that is happening right now with the New York Post is they're getting real clickbaity with their headlines, which is it's the New York Post, it's supposed to. people are in the comments being like, Hey, I saved you the click. So it's like, is Kate Middleton still alive? And someone in the comments is like, She is. I saved you the click and ruined their display out or whatever. And it's just I love that people are getting smart to it, but part of the reason why media companies fail, I think, is because they don't give their readers the promise of their editorial mission. Sports Illustrated being a great example. Sports Illustrated has been everything except what people want to be, which is a weekly collection of really great sports feature writing or columnists. That's what people really want is like high quality stuff every week from Sports Illustrated. And they're willing to pay for it. But I think that there's just other ways of monetizing media that have proven to be kind of broken. And I don't know. I would if I have to rely on my community. Or six ad partners who are probably pining for their next job in the next year or two. I'm gonna put my faith in tens of thousands of people versus six people. There's just better, better odds. And so yeah.

And you know, it media kind of there's two kind of approaches to it. And one of them is that like you're sort of like A kitten in a box and you'll fucking grab onto anything to try to get out of it, you know, is like the best metaphor I can come up with. That's like how most media companies run. Or it's like, you know, us where you're just like, cool, we're we could lose all of our ad partners and it would not change a thing about the magazine. I can't do that. If I tried to do something like that, an issue of Mountain Gazette or like endorse the political candidate, which like we're very firmly no politics in the magazine, like blatantly about like who to vote for or anything like that, dude, our readers would let us know by canceling their subscriptions. Diana Ralston (19:46): I think part of the challenge was keeping it concise. So it was definitely an opportunity for me to listen more and talk less. (20:23): So that was actually a great experience. And so we really do try to embrace that in all aspects. So making sure that what we were saying felt authentic and good to all of us because again, like I said, we didn't want to run the risk of becoming this super. We're not corporate, we're not buttoned up, we're pretty, we're all of us are pretty casual. We're pretty no bullshit type of people. And so we wanted to make sure that that was coming through, but making us all take ourselves a little bit more seriously. I think you and I spoke again about our bios on the website are true, they're true who we are, they're true to who we are and what we like, but they are much more casual and fun than a typical funder might be looking for. They want to know how many years have you been in the nonprofit realm? What is your specific experience? And we do have that as well. And so making sure that we were telling both sides of that story was part of the process as well.

Cole Heilborn (21:43): Yeah. You mentioned that part of what motivated all of this was that you realized the nonprofit was growing up. I guess why was that important? Where is it going and how does this kind of set the stage for where you'd like to go?

content:
Diana Ralston (21:59): Well, I have a personal mission of making Canata a household name, and that's kind of been mine from the get go where even if you don't know anything about us, but the name, so in my head it's candidate is a household name synonymous with doing good so people know, Hey, this is a vetted nonprofit and I can feel good knowing that my dollar 90 cents on the dollar is going to go directly back into programs at this organization. So that is sort of a personal goal of mine, but the growing up is kind of hard, but it's also exciting. We realize, wow, we have you rattled off those stats from the website and we're also forward looking. We don't really often take time to look back and see what we've accomplished, but we've done a lot and it's exciting and it's humbling and we want to do more. (22:58): All of us are hardwired to do more and dig in, and we don't want to lose the grassroots nature of our approach to things. For example, we're trying to embark on a pretty big project within Navajo Nation and people on our team have great experience building programs and building authentic relationships with corporations or other nonprofits from the ground up. And again, relying on that people power and the sentiment that we all have the ability and the desire to get back and do good.

Cole Heilborn (23:54): So take me back to trying to become a household name. That's a pretty awesome goal. I love that. And as you mentioned, I was trying to think of what are the nonprofits that I can think of that I would label as a household name? And the only one I can come up with right now is Charity Water. I'm curious, obviously as someone you probably could rattle off a whole bunch, what are some that you have your eye on?

So I guess the desire to be a household name is really like, wow, if everybody knew candidate and associated with doing good, that's amazing. That means our programs have reached every corner of the US and they've impacted children in positive ways and they've impacted the environment in positive ways. So it's definitely a lofty goal. And we talk about, Hey, how do we actually achieve that? And I think it's really aggressively scaling our programs, but finding partners that are aligned and that have the same type of DNA that we do. So hands on want to really get in there, want to listen to the community. I think listening and responding to community needs is something that we've done all along. So again, with these really broad program areas, if we find out and hear back from leaders of a community that they don't need bikes or skateboards, they need something else to get their kids outside, we're not opposed to saying, great, let's dig in. (25:28): How can we help? How can we figure this out? And I think that that's a unique approach as in terms of a nonprofit, and we have maybe, again, because of the craft beer roots and the makeup of our current board of directors, we're entrepreneurial in spirit. And that is exciting because nothing's ever stagnant. We don't have to say no, as long as there's an identifiable problem and we think we have a solution or an opportunity to partner with other organizations to bring a solution to that community, that's exciting. And that's the way we approach everything.

Cole Heilborn (26:02): Yeah, man, I can feel the energy from a few states away. content: Diana Ralston (26:32): I think the fear always when things are growing is that you're going to lose the initial culture that people wanted to be part of, that they love the excitement, the passion, the spirit. Like I said, the no nonsense, let's all have an equal role and equal say in this, that's the fear. You get too big and you can't keep those things. We are right now, it's all women led organization. There's five women on the team. We are looking to scale this year with gig workers. So instead of adding full-time staff, we're going to train people that can help implement programs for us and they would be on a per gig basis. And I think that that is, we'll see how it goes. I mean, again, it's a pilot program, but I think by having gig workers that get to experience our culture on a part-time basis, then they go out in the world and they become ambassadors for candid, and they're spreading the gospel. (27:28): Hey, have you heard about candidate? We currently have athletes that are our treads and trails ambassadors, and we have a ton of musicians, as I mentioned, that are tunes ambassadors. And so they're all out there spreading the word and helping turn people on to candid and who we are and what we do. And I think that that's a smart way to grow. I hope at least that's what I'm telling myself that I think having those gig workers and then they get a little taste of our culture and they help bring more people that are aligned people to our world, and then it just grows. And it's not a new concept, but that thought of doing good feels good, and it's creating good in the world, it snowballs. And I think that once people come and experience a candidate event and volunteer, whether it's at a river cleanup or an instrument donation or a skateboard build, they see that it's genuine and we're authentic and we're passionate about it, and it's infectious. So that's the hope.

Diana Ralston (29:10): Yeah, I think it is important, and you don't want to swing too far one direction or the other, but with this proven track record now in seven years of impacts under our Belt, it's time to start telling that story more loudly, I guess, and be unapologetic about it. Diana Ralston (30:49): Yeah, yeah. I think even like we said initially a couple of years ago, if you looked at the website, it really didn't even talk about, Hey, only one in five kids is getting the daily recommended amount of exercise. We didn't identify the problems. It was more like, Hey, this is fun. Come build some bikes. And that has shifted the way we think about the work that we're doing has shifted, and therefore a natural result of that is we talk about it differently. But I think just having the confidence to know that the work you're doing makes a difference and that you feel good about that is maybe new for our organization to feel free to talk about it in those terms. And even, like I mentioned, our bios talking, Sarah Levitt has years of experience working in Haiti, and that doesn't come across in her current bio. So it's like, Hey, not only are there good fun things happening, there are women behind the scenes that have really impressive resumes and experience. And highlighting that a little bit more I think has helped us be positioned or be viewed as more of a serious nonprofit organization by those family foundations and big funders. So I think trying to marry the two and having a good balance between the fun, playful, and the, Hey, we're making serious change and impact in the world is important.

Cole Heilborn (32:21): Yeah. Where did that hesitation, do you feel like it came from? Did it come from a certain place? And I guess how have you worked through that?

Diana Ralston (32:30): I think initially it was myself and probably Sarah Levitt who had worked in traditional buttoned up nonprofits. We really felt strongly that we liked this entrepreneurial take some risks and tried to do things differently. We wanted to make sure that stayed intact, and maybe as a result we made things sound more playful and less serious than they actually were. So I think again, seven years of stats and thank you letters from people or just anecdotal stories that have been shared with us as a result of our work made us realize, Hey, we're not actually telling the complete story and we need to start doing that.

content:
Diana Ralston (34:37): I do think that as the type of organization that we are, we're not for every single funder. And that's okay because we want to have partnerships that everybody feels good about and that everyone has skin in the game and has a clear goal. So candidate isn't going to be for every single organization, every single family foundation or funder or donor, but I think not only having relationships with corporate partners or family foundations, et cetera, that really get who we are at our core, that we're hardwired to rally people to help us and to do good, and that there needs to be some trust there and finding funders that will trust just on our track record, but not having had a relationship with us. That's not always easy. Some people really just want to say, I'm going to give to the Red Cross. That's it, period. And that's fine. But we really like starting from the ground up and building these relationships with corporate partners and with foundations, and we have done a fairly good job of it. And I feel like the future is pretty bright in terms of attracting new donors and new funders.

But then beyond that, also realizing that you're not there to help everyone, you're there to help maybe a specific few groups of people, and that's okay. Is that what you're saying?

content:
Diana Ralston (36:30): Yeah. I think that if somebody was out there wanting to start their own nonprofit, really the advice I would give them is pick one mission and stick to it and a more narrow programmatic offerings that we have. It works for us and we like it, but it has been a stumbling block along the way. People would say, I don't understand what you do. You do this, this, this, and this. It could almost be four separate nonprofits. And again, for me and for the team that we have right now, that works really well, but it's not for everyone. And a singular focus is much easier elevator pitch than trying to explain all of the various things that candidate does.

Cole Heilborn (37:11): Why do you think that is? Why are most nonprofits set up in a way where they focus in on one specific thing, just getting musical instruments to kids? Where does that come from?

Diana Ralston (37:22): I don't know. That's an interesting question. I think just historically, that's the way nonprofits have been structured. They do one thing and they focus in on it, and that's all that they do. And so people know, if I want to support cancer research or breast cancer research, I'm going to give to the Susan b Koman Foundation. So I like the flexibility. I like that there are very few things that we can have to say no to because our program areas, environment, arts and music, the outdoors, those are broad and the needs are great, and we have the ability to respond to the needs through these various program areas.

Cole Heilborn (38:08): Yeah, no, that's well said. So as you look towards the future, other than if making candidate a household name is kind of the end goal, if there is an end, what are some of the next steps along the way for you?

So Martin Magnusson, who founded the brand, moved to Hestra in the early 30s. And there there was no ski basin around. There was nothing on the ski side. And so he started looking for opportunity and had made some gloves on his own for his personal farming and personal use. But he looked around and and the lumberjack and the the forestry industry is really big in southern Sweden at this time. And so he saw a need and he worked with them to source materials locally, which we still do. It's super important to us, finding organic materials like wool, leather that. meet the needs of the lumberjacks who he had befriended and wanted to create a product for. So Scandinavian winters are exceedingly harsh. He needed something super warm. You know lumberjacks need dexterity and they put their gloves through the ringer. And so something that was warm, had dexterity and was super durable and would give them protection. So we do the same things today. It's on a much more granular level, right? It's it's the very nitty-gritty brass tacks. So case in point, our backcountry aligned. So we have the Ergo Grip Active, which is a very lightweight, windproof glove with our Ergo Grip technology, which gives you really good dexterity. So that's for a high, high output day. When you're going on a long tour, when it's maybe warmer weather, or you're doing something that's super steep and you're gonna work up really high body temperature, that's what that glove is for. But we we realize that some people, some days you're you're not going on a full-blown uphill, steep tour. You're going on a longer, more casual tour. And so we step that up with the Ergo Grip Incline, which has a little bit more insulation, but some of those still dexterity qualities that you want. And then you can set that up even more. Say it's a storm day and you're backcountry touring, you still want that dexterity. Well this glove, the coular, army leather coular is what we call it. It's waterproof. It's got the dexterity and it's got a little bit of insulation. And so you get more granular as you go. And a lot of that is just born of experience. So Jonas Magnuson, who is a big part of our sport division, is an avid skier and Anton Magnusson, our CEO, both will go out and they're out enough and all of us know this like if you have a little bit of gear you want a lot of gear and so we're always looking for something to fill that crack of okay today didn't go quite as planned my gear maybe was too heavy was too light I need to modify this or that and so we can tinker with a glove and create one iteration difference right so if you find yourself in a different situation you're able to have a glove for that and the goal for us is to have something for any situation out there and then to build some modularity. So we have overmits and we have liners that help kind of iterate that process for you as a user. And so that's the goal is to keep iterating, right? Like there's always something that's changing, there's always something that's different. There's always a hole to be filled.

content:
Alex Sherbinow (11:22): So the old town sportsman line was really born from a couple of different things. One being that we are at our core, the users of our product. There's not a weekend that I get that I'm not on the water doing something, hunting, paddling, fishing, I mean, you name it, that's who we are. So a lot of these crazy ideas come from people in Old Town who are saying, Hey, what if we tried this and we might throw a hundred ideas at the wall and only one sticks. But a lot of that comes from us knowing what products we can build and the things that would make life easier for our own use. The other piece of it is that we can listen and talk with our consumers, especially in the digital world now, to kind of see what they're asking for, what product innovations they would like to see, what makes life on saltwater or what makes life on freshwater better in a river. (12:29): So we went out and designed a full line of sportsman boats and designed it specifically to have a boat for anyone, whether you're throwing a solo canoe on your back and you going to float the river and camp on the banks or get offshore and go five miles on Lake Michigan to catch a salmon. We specifically designed and identified key features that are going to be important to those and shared it across the entire line of boats. So for example, every boat that you can stand in has premium floor decks, so it's comfortable all day multiple rod holders because these are things that you're going to design for fishing, just overall characteristics that are going to be important no matter who you are. And then designed hus for kayaks that are going to be more specific to the water type that you're going into. So seven boats, three ways to travel, one consumer at the end of the day,

Cole Heilborn (13:32): And the different propulsion methods that you guys have developed are pretty slick as well. Can you explain those?

content:
Alex Sherbinow (13:39): Yeah. So of course you always have your traditional paddle kayaks in your paddle solo canoes. What is really unique is our pedal drive system, which if you haven't ever been in a pedal drive kayak, it will change your life instantly because you can go three miles an hour, literally give no effort. You pedal it like a bike, you're sitting high up on a lawn chair style seat, super comfortable, sit on top kayaks, and those kind of allow fishermen to get to a spot and back or someone who's camping and going to the boundary waters cover that ground quicker. And then we have our powered models, which are really what caught the consumer's eye. This year we released an autopilot kayak that actually has a GPS enabled motor in it, so it's controlled by remote control. For those anglers out there who are familiar with iPilot has a full iPilot system. So you can sit back and on your remote control or even Bluetooth on your phone, drive your boat and kind of just hang out. It's lazy man's kayaking, if you will.

Cole Heilborn (14:56): You've taken all the work out of it.

Alex Sherbinow (14:59): And the really cool part of that is that we recognize, especially for anglers, that it's incredibly difficult in a kayak to fish a spot or fish a river and imagine a fly angler in a river where there's current pushing 'em around. You only have two seconds to get your fly or your line in that exact spot that you're trying to catch a fish, and that is not efficient for any angler. So with this GPS enabled motor, you can actually spot lock and it will virtually anchor you where you're at. It'll fight the current for you. It'll fight the wind and waves and allow you to be more efficient while you're on the water fishing.

Cole Heilborn (15:43): What's the maximum speed? How fast of a current could you be in and it'll hold you?

Alex Sherbinow (17:00): Yeah, so because a lot of this technology is largely targeting toward the kayak angler, I mean, like I said, if you're trying to camp, if you're trying to just recreationally paddle, there's a boat in this line for you. But a lot of the technology, the rod holders and accessory tracks are targeted toward the angler. When we launched this, it was at Bassmaster Classic in 2020. The resounding voice of the consumer was what took you so long? They were super excited. We actually won the ICAST best of show category. And the consumer, generally speaking, especially the anglers, we're just excited that their voices were heard. Sometimes I think that gets lost in the era we live in where you can communicate with brands, you can send them direct messages and comment on Facebook posts, and you literally are at the fingertips of a brand at any given moment. Feedback has to be accounted for in real time, and you have to be quick to react and agile because if you aren't someone in a competitive world will, (18:30): We had the benefit of working with our counterparts that en coded to speed up timelines a little bit. And our consumer, just like I said, generally, we're super, super excited to have their voices heard and just have a product that's actually tailored to them and their experience.

Things like the Facebook Pixel give you direct insights as to what your consumer's engaging with and what your consumers are talking about, what they like, what they don't like. And you can see engagement rates. That's one thing, but I think there is a piece that metrics today just don't measure, and that's how people engage with the brand. And what I mean is the tone of voice in a text message, things can get lost when you jump on a phone call, all of a sudden you're getting a whole new perspective. So we as a brand are going out outside of the traditional social media, outside of looking at Google Analytics and talking with our consumer. And I say that with a grain of salt because we are in a socially distanced world, but we still find ways to engage with people at kayak tournaments where you can socially distance or before COVID at events. There's literally people there that you can have 35, 40 minute conversations with and they feel value in being heard. So I think sometimes we get caught up in technology even, (23:35): And you can take a step back and think about what your grandparents did at trade shows. Trade shows started for a reason. So it's a approach to really understand the consumer.

Cole Heilborn (23:49): It's funny you said social media. We are stepping away from the traditional use of social media and going back to the trade show format, which I feel like that's the traditional format and social media is this new thing, and now you're like, I don't even know.

(06:17): And one of our founders, John Heli, who's sort of the patriarch of the heli family right now, and he basically decided that to hell with waiting on the commodities market to be opportune for him and his family to grow and sell wool. So he basically formulated with the help of some partners and a way to control that process and take his own wool, which by the way is his life's work has been making his family's wool genetically off the charts. I mean, the wool itself is just incredible quality. It's got a tremendous amount of crimp and loft. I mean, these sheep have to survive with that fleece from in temperatures ranging from 90 degrees in the summer to minus 40 in the winter. So you can imagine what the conditions require of those animals, and then that same fiber is put into our products, obviously. (07:22): But anyway, so he worked on the genetics and he worked on this business idea and it basically was the perfect fusion of those two ideas of his to start a brand like Duckworth where he has a way to showcase this incredible American wool while also accounting for the fact that the commodities market doesn't always play in favor of the hardworking individuals that are going out every single morning and coming in late every single night to make that product possible. So it's a really amazing brand from that specific standpoint to compound on that. I think a lot of competitors within the space, a lot of competitors within the world of wool, they have sources for their wool that come from 10 different countries in three different continents, and all of our wool comes right from our ranch. I mean, what you see is what you get, and that is what makes us so special and has created such a fan following. And then to compound on that even further, we have a hundred percent American made supply chain where we oversee every step of the process. So we're not just saying, Hey, take this wall. We'll see you in a couple months. Hopefully it all works out. I mean, we're on a day-to-day call with every person at every stage of this process to make sure that we're getting the quality and the consistency and just the performance that again, is growing us into a fan favorite for a lot of people within the outdoor space.

I mean, it's something that I just don't have to think about. Because you can really, as a consumer, as someone who's reading these witnessing scenes from these stories, put yourselves in this almost total other universe. It's something unlike you've ever seen. The first time I went on Sheep Trail, which I think of the two is it's one of the most amazing outdoor experiences I've had in my entire life. We work two times a year, sheep Trail, one in the summer and one in the early fall. And basically we operate on a mixture of public and private lands and we bring these sheep six days through the mountains to bring them to summer grazing pastures.
