content: Mike Somerby (12:38): Yeah, it's around 10,000 sheep and it's pretty impressive to see an operation of this scale moving through the mountains. And there's so many elements to the story that it's almost like out of a movie. So we have sheep herders who live with the sheep almost 365 days a year, and they're out there in the field with these animals, protecting them, making sure they're getting water, making sure they're getting plenty of food, making sure the landscape is protected. We can't have sheep running through a creek bed or what have you. And we got to make sure that we're respecting the lands on which we rely obviously. But also on top of that, there's guard dogs, 125 to 150 pound dogs that are there to protect them. They're sheep dogs that are highly intelligent, that are basically the right arm of these sheep herders and the ranchers. (13:39): But yeah, it's about six days in which at least in the summertime, these sheep are moving up and over the mountains and going through some of the most amazing back country wildflower fields, mountaintops almost. It's funny because being out there with the ranchers, this is something that they've seen their whole lives. This is something they know really intimately. And for me, I mean my jaw must've been dragging on the trail the entire time. I was just like, I couldn't believe what I was seeing. It was something borderline spiritual in a way. And I actually asked the ranchers, or at least Evan and humans have had a relationship, an agricultural relationship with sheep for, I mean thousands and thousands of years now. And this is something that you can find in some of the most ancient stories on paper, on stone, what have you. And I asked them, is this something that you feel like you're sort of carrying a torch? (14:43): He said, absolutely. So it's a really incredible moment, and we do like to think of it as the last odyssey of North American agriculture. When you're working six days in a row, 50 lateral miles, thousands of vertical feet with that many animals, it's a pretty intense voyage to be sure, and a lot can go wrong, and it's definitely because of the expertise of those individuals that nothing does.

(15:48): People want to know what's under the hood, and people want to know what you're all about, who the players are, what you stand for, what you believe in, and the level of this animal husbandry, this stewardship for the land and this just epic Montana moment that is sort of frozen in time are things that people really resonate with. That other story I mentioned, which is shear and shred just as essential, it's not as sexy because it takes a lot of hard work to shear 10,000 sheep of their fleece. As you can probably imagine, it's giving a multi hundred pound animal a haircut on 10,000 times over, but all the same. I mean, that's where a lot of the magic happens too, because that's where our ranchers and other partners of the business take literally every single fleece and then grade it for quality. Someone referred to him recently as the Mick Jagger of wool, which I think is pretty awesome, but he's got it, and it's something that he just knows the back of his hand. So yeah, when he picks up that piece of wool, he can tell you, but we have computers there just to double check, and those computers will dictate our entire product line in a sense, because it tells us how much we have to make X and how much we have to make this and that. (19:09): And that's a really cool piece of it too, is we are not going to force a product to happen. This is spun gold. It's a finite quality, it's rare. You're not going to find this everywhere. And there's certain products of ours that are just by nature of the beast and by nature of how wool grows are always going to be a commodity because there's just simply never enough wool to keep up with the demand. So it's really exciting to actually have a couple products like that that are always going to have this very rare nature to them as a result of that wool production. But anyway, yeah, shear and shred is a great time. It's kind of like a party and a celebration in a lot of ways too. We share the sheep, we have some food, we break some bread, share some drinks and stories, and then the next day we go over to a local ski hill there in Dillon. I'm talking one chairlift, two seats per chair and go shred.

And actually kudos to every brand getting involved or at least taking this stand, but transparency is something that's going to be here to stay, especially in garment making with a customer base as environmentally and eco minded as the outdoor space has, you can't really get away with behind the scenes doing something really bad for the planet. And so a lot of companies have actually opened up their doors and said, this is what's going on. This is where we source our wool. This is where we clean it, this is where we spin it. (22:14): And you'll find that those do for every piece of good that does, showing people that here's how we do it, it does really make you think because there's a laundry list of countries and beyond bringing technical know-how and knowledge and a piece of our American heritage back, the wool industry was basically on the ropes and at least in this country, and Duckworth really thought that that was behind some of the ethos of the brand is that's a real shame. I mean, so we're really working hard to bring some of that technical knowledge back to the states because it is, again, it's a big piece of Montana's heritage, but it's also a piece of this nation's heritage. But I like to think of it just as importantly as when you do have that many countries involved, and I'm sure there are good people behind every single one of those stories as well, but when you do have that many countries involved, what ends up happening is you're adding about 10,000 or so miles worth of emissions to the supply chain per garment. And so that really adds up. And from a sustainability side of the equation, I think being so local while yet still trying to grow so big is something that is really important to me. And I personally probably would've had a hard time working for a company in this space that didn't practice that.

And honestly, I almost, I could have collapsed right there so I can understand how it was a bit of a undertaking 16 hours on my feet at one day, 16 hours worth of hiking. So that was a lot. So I get why that can be difficult, but we're on a mission to, even though we're working from the office in Bozeman to eat, sleep, and breathe this brand and put ourselves as close as possible to understanding every single inch of this process. (27:02): So getting the story out there has meant hiring on a really crack media team to on the fly, do some really incredible stuff and be really flexible to us.

content: Mike Somerby (24:46): It's involved really holistically looking at the way we do our advertisements, our media buys, our social pushes, what have you, and see what sort of pieces are resonating with each individual. And like you mentioned, we did have this really super niche, super hardcore group of fans and that's great. And though we did need to expand and we are actively looking to, and it's really just trying to tell the pieces of the story that can bring people together versus put distance between two individuals. Since I've moved to Montana, I think it's really interesting that no matter what side of the political spectrum you're on, for example, everyone cares about the landscape here. There's individuals on both sides who are making money exploiting certain pieces of the landscape, and that's present every state, every country, and it's too bad. (28:21): But they're someone who, again, they're both looking at this place for its natural wonder and people are inspired by it every single day. So getting at the meat of that basic inspiration of why do we get outdoors? Why do we want to spend time in the trees? Whether it's for hunting a bull elk that you plan to harvest and eat for the year, or just simply to go take a walk with the dog. I mean, I think that those two parties can overlap. And we did have sort of a following in this more hardcore Montana based market, but we're finding that quality product is quality product. And if you can get in front of the right people with the same interest, general basic urge to get outside and participate and be well protected while they're out there, you're going to be able to build a fan base that is diverse and varied and it doesn't matter what they, their activity of choice in the wilderness is, or the back country, they, they're going to find common ground over just simple quality. And I mean realistically, what you want to have at the end of the day is someone not thinking about their duckworth when they're out skiing or ice fishing or whatever you want it to be just in the background so that they can just get out and really be thoughtlessly getting into the flow.

And then similarly Shopify, which is the platform we use. That's great. We can definitely see that. And similarly on Instagram, you can see in your analytics, you can see certain cities growing. You can see various geo geolocations getting a bit larger in terms of reaching a critical mass. And it used to be when I started that it was Hyper Rocky Mountain Hyper West. On both of those accounts, our Shopify and our Instagram. And what I can see is that larger metropolitan and micropolitan areas around the country are really starting to get behind some of the ethos. (32:37): And I think again, that's part of the storytelling. There's just something for everyone. I mean, if you're in Montana, if you're in Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Nebraska, what have you, any of the Rocky Mountain Saints, I don't know how much Nebraska really is, but you can kind of find a relatability though when you're in Connecticut or you're in Arizona or you're in, I guess Arizona is mountainous, so that's a bad example, but you get what I'm saying. If you're in sort of a market that isn't necessarily one that's traditionally been for us, it's something where people look at and they're like, wow, that looks like a really cool piece of brand identity I want to get involved with. So you can definitely see based on those location metrics that there's definitely a growing desire. And I mean a lot of places, just as we've seen this past winter on the east, get pummeled with snow and cold weather too. So you don't need to be out skiing or facing Montana Sub-Zero weather to need something quality on you, and that's starting to really take shape.

content:
Cole Heilborn (33:51): How would you define a loyal customer? When has a customer reached loyalty status?

Mike Somerby (33:59): I think for us, loyalty can be defined in two ways. If you were looking at it from a very black and white budget sheet sort of direction, you could say that probably once someone makes three purchases, that's just about when you could really say, this is a very loyal customer, but I don't want to steer anyone wrong because I think that you could buy Duckworth once in your whole life and if you love it and if you wear it every day, and if you're telling folks about how much this product has really saved your skin in various situations, that's a loyal product or a loyal customer to me, and that's just as valuable. Someone again, could have just bought a t-shirt and a hat, but if they're on Instagram and they're sharing us to their story or they're sharing our posts to their friends, to me that's a loyal customer that's really hard to track. (35:00): And probably my finance manager wouldn't like me hearing that or wouldn't like to hear me saying that that is what a loyal customer is, though I think he would understand that that in the same way is just as important as someone who's going to make a bunch of buys. Our product too is very durable. So a lot of instances it will take a while to wear out, and so if you're buying once and you get everything that you need, it can last you a long, long time. On that note, just a little tangent, a piece of synthetic, a piece of plastic, you bend it back and forth about 3000 times, it snaps in half. If you had a fiber of synthetic material, if you did the same thing with a fiber of our wool, it would take about 20,000 iterations to snap in half. So it's more than six times as durable from that standing. (35:54): So again, it's kind of funny, I was talking to a buddy the other day who is a photographer and he does a lot of what he calls torture testing products for various companies. He worked with a brand here in Bozeman that he wore their pants for apparently 470 days in a row. He acknowledged there's brands out there where durability is part of everything. And so I just bought a pair of Carhartts because I want to have pants that are going to last me a long time. So if you buy Duckworth one time and it lasts you many, many, many seasons, but you're out there just telling folks at the ski lounge or just in your own neighborhood or even people in your own home that this stuff is awesome, that's a loyal customer to me. And that's really a credit to, in a minor way our storytelling, but in a major way the quality of our wool and the quality of our production that you just can't find anywhere else

content: Mike Somerby (37:29): And definitely we do. I mean, as a marketer, I acknowledge those hard facts. I acknowledge the data. If you're a VIP, if you're a great customer of ours, you're going to be getting exclusive deals, you're going to get early access, you're going to get all of the things that come with being that loyal customer that has contributed from a data perspective to our bottom line in a meaningful way. And we like to, obviously this is a family operation. This is a really down to earth operation. This is an operation based in a state where people are still very friendly to strangers in the street. And if they do see a stranger, they might try to make that a friend with the right circumstances. I used to live in New York City, are you going to talk to someone on the subway? Probably not. (38:22): And where I'm getting at that it's part of our philosophy obviously to try to be friendly and try to be neighborly and bring those qualities into the brand and into how we approach those loyal customers, those friends of the brand. We are also working with a company right now to build out a more wide loyalty program where you can earn points and you can apply those points to purchases or where you refer a friend or you bring in X new customers for us that work for us and work for our brand. You're going to be rewarded with points, you're going to be rewarded with cashback options that are just going to make it worth your while because yeah, those are absolutely true. I mean, that's why I have punch cards to a couple of local Bozeman coffee shops and breweries. It's definitely a phenomenon that's here to stay. I don't know when loyalty was necessarily seized upon as an opportunity, but I can tell you it's definitely not going anywhere anytime soon. And it's something that as we definitely move into the DTC space even further, as we move away from third party wholesalers taking care of our business for us after they receive a delivery of whatever they've ordered, we're going to want to take ownership and get to know our customers better and make sure that they feel very happy and very taken care of.

Cole Heilborn (39:58): Do you feel like that's crucial as you're making this transition away from wholesale?

Mike Somerby (40:05): Yeah, I definitely do. I think any brand in the direct to consumer base model rather should look at this loyalty and referral program as something pretty essential to bring into their mix. It's the way that, and I'm sure you've seen some of the information that the pandemic basically sped things up by a factor of, I mean, I've seen everything from two to 10 years in terms of the progress made in terms of the switch, the consumer mindset switch. It's kind of an arms race because of that in a lot of ways. I mean, everyone's competing for the same set of eyeballs on the same exact screen. It's not walking through a store, and it's like you kind of have someone's undivided attention when they're standing in front of your display. So I think adding on everything that makes sense for your brand aligns with your values. I can't think of any brand that wouldn't benefit or it would be against their values to have some sort of loyalty program, but I think it'd be pretty essential. We've gone to virtual whiteboards for collaboration, and really what we're doing is we're sort of withdrawing from our corporate culture a little bit, but fortunately our bank account's really, really, really big. So we're able to do that. But we've had virtual happy hours, virtual gifting. We've done a really good job at converting to work from home, and fortunately we're slowly starting to come back into the office in small percentages depending on location. In some offices, we're up to 25%. Some offices we're up to 50%, and in the next four months we'll get up quick and then we'll be super flexible depending on people's different situations. content:
Cole Heilborn (00:08:36): So when did you pick up the camera first though?

Chase White (00:08:41): That's a long one. I mean, I studied photography in high school and then studied photography in college as well, so I sharpened my teeth in a traditional dark room setting. And then nowadays, I'm not the tweed cap influencer film photographer, but I definitely keep a few cameras on deck at all times. But it's honestly been a lifelong thing since high school.

Cole Heilborn (00:09:16): I feel like the contract creative sounds like an idyllic, this is where we added

Chase White (00:09:23): Idyllic, maybe

Cole Heilborn (00:09:24): Idyllic. Yeah, I feel like the contract creative just seems like this perfect life balance where you can do whatever you want, you only get to work on things you enjoy, and there's definitely some of those pros to it. Paint us a picture of some of the good things that come along with being a contract creative and some of the things that maybe other folks don't realize or isn't talked about.

content: Chase White (00:09:48): Totally. Yeah, no, it's really cool. And honestly cool. I'm super excited to be talking about this with you on the podcast because it's something that I personally haven't been able to find anyone talking about anywhere else. It's certainly, I think it goes under the radar a lot because I wish I knew what the actual status for you, but today the percentage of creatives who are contractors is just staggering. So it affects a lot of people both on the brand side, in the agency world and on the actual contractor side. So it's a cool thing to bring more light to, but I think the obvious ones are the flexibility that you get when you are a contract creative. You can choose when you want to work, you can choose what you want to work on, you can choose what mediums you want to focus on. And it's not to say you can't really do that in an agency. (00:10:44): I think you can on some level, but it doesn't give you that full autonomy that being a true contractor in your own right does. But that said, there's ups and downs to everything. And being a contract creative I think is no different. The biggest one that stands out is the consistency of your income, depending on your standing in life, wherever you're at, it's not for everybody. And I'm in no way recommending it as this great thing that everyone should try to do because that uncertainty of your biz dev funnel, it's a real thing and it's always happening. No matter the best shooters in the world, same thing happens to them. So it's all relative in that sense. But you're also doing everything right. You're the accounting department, you're the sales department, you are the put out fires department, you, you're a producer, you're a director, you're everything, and you can kind of develop small teams, but then you start getting into that agency world. So it's a unique thing, not for the faint of heart, but if it is right for you, it's incredibly rewarding.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:12:09): So maybe before we go deeper, let's define contract creative. Do you see that as being one person? You mentioned as you start to work with more and more people, you start to bleed into that agency definition. To you, what is a contract creative?

Chase White (00:12:26): I think a contract creative personally is somebody who for the most part, most part, works autonomously. There are people that I have fantastic relationships with that I'll team up with on projects, but it's not a fixed team of people that we collectively are always bringing each other in on every project. The majority of my work is just myself, and I think it's an interesting idea to kind of erupt. Why is that? Why would you prefer to work by yourself? And some people just like to work fast. I like to work fast. If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together. And I like working fast, man.

Cole Heilborn (00:13:10): One question that I hear pop up a lot is why work with a contract creative? I feel like the creative industry is at a really interesting place now where a lot of brands are bringing creatives in-house to develop their own internal teams. Agencies are doing a hybrid of a lot, bringing in contractors, building out their own internal teams. I guess first, why would anyone want to work with someone like yourself?

content: Chase White (00:13:42): I think, well, personally I get a lot of flexibility from my position. I think from a brand or an agency side, you also adopt a lot of flexibility in working with somebody like that. You can pop in and hire them when you want to hire them, and then you can pop out and touch base in a couple months or whatever. You don't have to maintain that constant overhead of having that person on full staff. And today's day and age, I think there's a lot of resources that previous generations didn't have to support yourself with. Things like healthcare solutions, insurance, whatever, a lot of things like that that are now more available to a contractor to hold that lifestyle in a healthy way. But I think it just provides flexibility for everybody. And then it's like as a brand, as an outdoor brand in 2021, you're not always working on the same thing. (00:14:47): It's not just the same project over and over again. You may be a brand that's working on a mountain biking shoot this day and then next week you're working on something that's a fly fishing shoot. And the reality is an in-house person working for your brand full-time may not be the right person to work on both of those. And so I think it gives you an added ability of having some really nice sort of passionate specificity in who you're putting on what projects so that you're really kind of getting somebody on them who understands all the nuances of them and is proficient and knows all the kind of details and storylines that can happen in any given project like that. So I think you get a lot of flexibility on both ends.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:15:34): Yeah. How important is that, that specificity, when you hire someone like yourself, you're an avid fly fisher if a fly fishing company brings you in, you obviously know that world and you can make sure it's real and it's authentic and everything that you're capturing is legit. Someone who maybe isn't as in tune with that is brought in. Maybe they don't capture those authentic moments like you would, but how important is that? Can that person who doesn't know the depth of that sport or that focus, can they learn those things and then output a product that's just as good or still capture that same level of authenticity?

Chase White (00:16:15): Yeah, I think it's a great question and such a cool sort of idea to mull around because I think while it's, in no way do I mean this as a hundred percent rule, I think there are definitely exceptions, but I think if you're just take for example, if you're a climbing company and you hire somebody who's never climbed before, and granted I'm dealing in extremes here, but just to make a point, somebody who doesn't climb, they don't know all those moments to one, anticipate them coming down the pipeline, oh, I got to be right here. When that person tops out on the route for that big emotional reaction, I've got to be there. And knowing even tactically where that person, where they're going to fall if they take a whip or whatever, things like that that are like, there's a lot that goes into outdoor adventures that a lot of people don't think about. (00:17:12): We're not always dealing with some friendly fake hike. There's a lot of real tactfully stuff. Just the other day I was on a shoot where we're rafting down a whitewater river for a fly fishing shoot and it's like you can't just put anyone in that position. And if you do, I think you're bound to not only not nail it, but you're going to miss some key opportunities. So just like with the climbing example, I think you're really just going to ensure the best results if you get somebody who's personally passionate about that outdoor pursuit who happens to also be a strong creative.

Cole Heilborn (00:17:51): So to go a little further into that, this is something I've thought a lot about and in fact some of the conversations we've had on the show, actually it hasn't come out yet with an agency. We talked a lot about how does an agency make sure that they're creating authentic content. I think what you're describing here is authenticity and they have an entire process built out to, if they don't know what makes the sport or the activity, what are those authentic moments? They have an entire process, this process that they use to figure that out. I dunno, just curious to hear your reaction to something like that because I think there are people who realize, oh, I don't know how to do this, but I have ways that I know I'm going to figure out how to do it and what are the important things to capture.

Chase White (00:18:40): Totally. And that's true too. And make no mistake about it, I don't only work in fly fishing. I mean, while I'm passionate about that, I think it makes it a nice niche for myself to be able to work on stuff that I particularly understand well. But there are oftentimes where I'm out doing a shoot where we're ski touring or we're mountain biking or other things, I would say that other group that catchall makes up for about half of my work. And I think as a contract creative, it's really tough in today's market to be able to just do one sport as you're, you just won't be able to really pay your bills if you just do one thing. You have to be able to diversify.

Cole Heilborn (00:19:30): Sure.

Chase White (00:19:31): But as for your question as an agency process on adopting and injecting credibility into their shoots, I think that's fine. I don't think that would've the same power as having somebody behind the lens or somebody producing who really does know it, but I'm sure it works in plenty of cases to get the job done.

Cole Heilborn (00:19:59): Yeah. Do you have an example of maybe a project that you took on where you weren't as familiar with the inner workings of the space and what was the outcome of that?

I don't have that fire to really nail it. And that's a crazy thing to say publicly as somebody who likes having a full pipeline of work. But that's just the truth. Chase White (00:22:09): It does. It does big time because I think not all work is equal and not every dollar is equal. I particularly enjoy, I would rather make $1 doing something I love than to make $5 doing something that I find kind of dry and exhausting. I can't help. The moment that really gets me is take a big shoot. If I'm doing that in something that I'm not passionate about, people don't understand how much time goes into post-production and that's a lot of time where I'm going to be sitting there married to my computer, just going through it, making selects out of, on any given shoot, I can shoot upwards of anywhere from 2000 to 20,000 images. Culling that down takes a lot of time. And if you're trying to cu down something that you're just really not passionate about, it's tough, man. It's real tough.

Cole Heilborn (00:23:11): So is that your responsibility or the client's responsibility?

Chase White (00:23:18): I think that's the contractor's responsibility you have every right in the world to accept a job or not accept a job. And I think if you do accept a job and you are not going to bring your A game dude, that's on you. And I think you do owe your clients better than to mail something in.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:23:39): Something that I heard recently was a way to think about how you take on work. I think there's a bunch of different kind of formulas out there that people have put together that help you think through should I say yes to this job? One of them that I've always kind of looked at and used historically is time. What is it? The budget, the connections and the creative opportunity. And if you can hit two of those three, then that's a pretty solid choice. Another one that I heard recently that I feel like I'm going to add in addition to that filter is unless you can knock the project out of a park, you shouldn't take it. Which that got me really thinking. I was like, shoot, how many projects have I taken on that maybe I shouldn't have? And did we do the client the best job that we should have done or could have done? And it gets tricky, I feel like when you deal with your own personal passion for a project because you're like, well, I'm in business, I just need to do a good job all the time. But inevitably that personal level of interest I feel like greatly influences the quality of work that we're able to do.

Chase White (00:24:50): And I would take that a step further and just for the sake of exploring it, how would you apply that? If you're a really new shooter and you're trying to get experience by that theory, you shouldn't take any work, right?

Cole Heilborn (00:25:05): A hundred percent. And yeah, you should never push yourself. You should never take something that's outside your comfort zone.

Chase White (00:25:13): And I think there's ways you can caveat your work and you can build an understanding with whatever marketing manager that you're working with and say, look, hey, this isn't something I've done before. I think I can do a really good job. Here's what I can ask of you that I think you can help support me in this. Here's how we can in the best way possible, get the results you're looking for without, while caveating it, Hey, I don't know. I haven't done this exactly before. I don't know that we're going to knock this out of the park, but here's what I'm willing to do. And you could even structure it with some sort of creative compensation where it's like, I think we're going to do a really good job, but in the event that we don't and you truly aren't satisfied with the results, we can just keep it at the deposit or something like that. But if you really like it and you want to use all of these assets, then we will go through the full amount. I think things like that, you can get creative and structure it, so it's like there's a bit of a safety net for people.

Cole Heilborn (00:26:17): Yeah, interesting. Flipping it around a little bit for the marketing manager or the individual in the agency who's looking at hiring a contractor for a project, what are things that they should consider? What are things that they should prioritize?

Chase White (00:26:34): As somebody who's had brands before, and I've worked on all three sides of this gun, I've worked on the brand side, I've worked on the agency side, and I've worked on the contractor side. I think the number one thing that somebody should be looking for when they're hiring a contract creative is just a high level of creative integrity. (00:27:00): Is the level of work that they're putting out something that you think that they're personally proud of? Does it have a good amount of polish to it? Does it have punch to it? Are they proficient with the medium? Truly right? Do they have great control over their medium that they're going to be employing on your project? But I think creative integrity just as a notion is what I would look for first. Is this person executing at a really high level that I need on my project? I think that's a starting point, but as we've said before already, the second thing I go to is are they proficient in the actual task at hand of are they passionate about whatever it is we're doing? I think those are two really good starting points.

Cole Heilborn (00:27:58): How important is, I don't know, things that come after that, just basic business skills, communication skills, the ability to think strategically because I mean what you said there I feel like could be a client's biggest concern is they're super creative, but if they can't communicate and if they're not strategic, then they might just make something that they like and it doesn't actually help me.

Chase White (00:28:27): Yeah, no, I mean I think you nailed it there. That's one of the risks you take on as a brand by working with a contract creative that you wouldn't get with an agency. Like an agency is going to charge you, I don't know, 10 to 20 times as much as an individual contractor might, but they have a pretty solid fail safe program, a huge team of people that in the event that things fall apart, they're going to probably pick those up and put it back together. There's going to be a lot more sort of sifts for all these ideas to go through. So I think to your point, finding somebody that's going to work on your project that has that business acumen that can be an entrepreneur in themselves and be empathetic with your business, can they put the business hat on and think, how is my work going to affect the bottom line of this company? (00:29:29): How is my work going to make this marketing manager's life easier? How am I going to make them look good? What results are they trying to drive for their boss in supporting the business as a business person, not just as a shooter or a designer or a producer? Thinking of it with the business head on I think is a huge one. And if you can find all of those things to together, I think you're going to get better results than you would get with an agency and you're going to get it much quicker and you're going to get much cheaper.

Cole Heilborn (00:30:09): Why will it be better? Because in one hand, you're comparing a well organized machine that's capable of knocking out big campaigns with tons of resources. On the other hand, you've got potentially a scrappy individual who knows their niche really well, who's highly creative, but it's just one person.

My response to that would be that I think you're going to get a certain level of creative intimacy that comes from hiring a single person who's going to own that part of your project with you. Things move quicker. It's not like every email has to go through 20 people and then they have to deliberate how they're going to respond and all kinds of stuff. Like one person with a good creative, you can just shoot 'em a text and be like, Hey, what do you think about this? I think collaboratively. But then there's this sort of gene se quo when you get somebody who really matches up with your brand well and they're just kind of this really powerful lean extension from you, there's a really nice sort of intimacy that shows in the creative. And I think that's what a lot of we're looking for is this authenticity and this intimacy, these really understanding these minute details and how they transpire for the business. So there is something there that I think a small lean person can achieve that an agency is just too big and slow for.

Cole Heilborn (00:32:10): Yeah, and I guess all of this just kind of, there's no one size fits all. I feel like in some instances the agency is better. In some instances the contract creative is better. If you could distill down when is the agency better suited, when is the contract creative better suited? What are those differences? Why bring in one versus the other?

Chase White (00:32:34): Totally candidly, and I am truly approaching this without how it's going to affect me or whatever, answering that truthfully, the reality is a brand should employ an agency when there's a really large amount of work to be done and it has to be done properly and it has to be done on time. There is no flexibility. If you're talking about a big blockbuster brand, just pick any one brand. If you're looking at a Lululemon for example, a sort of a big athletic kind of company or something like that, I think if I were that person, I would not hire an individual contract creative to just go run this. You have huge, probably quarterly campaigns that are going out that the amount of revenue tied to those campaigns is hard to comprehend and things have to be done and they have to be done on time. You have thousands and thousands of employees dependent on this. That's a situation where I'm like, you need the safety net of a huge team working on this and you should pay for that.

Cole Heilborn (00:33:57): And on the flip side,

Chase White (00:34:01): On the side, I think brands that are more niche, I think brands that have more flexibility in their timing of the deliverables. If this person doesn't have a dedicated producer, this person doesn't have a dedicated assistant, this person doesn't have all this stuff, the factors have to line up pretty well for a one man show to really make sure they nail it quickly on time, all this kind of things. So I think that typically smaller companies that are going to benefit from the financial flexibility of using somebody who can operate on leaner terms and somebody who has more flexibility with their timing, with their product, with their campaigns, things like that. That said, I work with plenty of very large brand names in the outdoor industry and we make it work just fine, but it's not typically not like million dollar campaigns that should go to a big agency.

(00:41:57): And I think that there's things that you can do in that regard that you're just being a good human and overdelivering. Carie Behe (01:40): Yeah, sure. So I started with Cotopaxi in the fall. I've been with them for about almost six months now, which is wild to think how fast it's gone so far. But the go-to-market marketing manager is a new role for Co Epoxy. It's a relatively small marketing team. And so this is a new position that really essentially is trying to build process from start to finish on go to market. And really what that means is from ideation of product and concept to all the way to the product sitting on the store shelf, I'm responsible for developing the process, identifying the stage gates and milestones, writing the campaign briefs, and then working really closely with our stakeholders across all different departments on the team, sales, product, merchandising, our design team, our creative team is probably the biggest team I work with. And then seeing that all the way through to execution on co epoxy.com in our retail stores and then with wholesale partners.

Cole Heilborn (02:42): And it sounds like that role is pretty fresh. It it's an expanding role that's been added as you guys have been growing.

Carie Behe (02:49): Yeah, it's a brand new role and I have been saying this phrase with the team, they're probably sick of me saying it as like I'm flying the plane while building it. Plane is up in the air. There's not really a wing on it. I'm not sure if the tires are on it right now, but we're flying it in real time and I'm figuring it out. So I'm really taking 2021 as a Guinea pig type of year to develop processes as I've learned from past roles and test and learn and see how it will work in terms of all the campaigns that we're launching, the collaborations that this brand launches. We do a lot of collaborations with other partners. And so feeling how we can do all of these things at once and work on things simultaneously, understanding that there is a much longer calendar to do campaigns with.

Carie Behe (03:44): Yeah, so Epoxy is an almost 7-year-old brand born, a digitally native brand in the outdoor industry. And it was founded by really incredible entrepreneur named Davis Smith. And his goal with this brand is really to help fight and alleviate poverty and really wanting to develop a brand in the outdoor industry that gives back. And there's so many brands in the industry that give back, but I think what sets Epoxy apart with that is not only is it a certified B corporation, but that it is giving the stake in the ground for Cotopaxi is really to alleviate poverty.

Speaker 3 (04:24): Whereas

Carie Behe (04:24): So many other brands in the industry, their stake in the ground and giving back is environmentalism. Sustainability is to help get more people outside and protect the places that we're all playing in. But Cotopaxi is a little bit different from that regard, and I think most people that know who Ko Epoxy is recognizes the brand through the Fun Llama logo that we have. We have a llama as a mascot for the brand. And I think in the very early days, there were actually two llamas that the brand owned and Davis and some of the initial founders would take the llamas on campus around different universities in Utah to attract attention and start talking about how the brand was being built. And I would say the other side of what the brand is founded on is trying to find ways to sustainably manufacture and resource all of the materials that we're using. (05:18): Fair Trade's, very important. Everything that we're doing in our factories from how workers are treated, what is being sourced, we give creative control to our factory workers that sew a certain collection of our packs. They're called Del dea. And these packs are all one of a kind, they're sourced from remnant factory scraps. So they are entirely unique. And what's cool is these remnant factory scraps would've otherwise gone to waste. So we're trying to find a second life for things that otherwise would have been put into a landfill. So from a product perspective, the product is very vibrant and bright, fun colors unique and sets itself apart when you see it in the store.

And Cotopaxi has five nonprofit partners now, longer term grantee partners that we're establishing a relationship with that we will give grant money over a longer period of time, multiple years and wanting to grow and help fund projects that they're working on. So an example of one of our longer term grantee partners is Mercy Corps. They're based in Portland really helping provide relief, especially in the past year with COVID of providing relief in areas in the Americas that were just hit so hard, providing relief in terms of food, shelter support, providing relief in terms of education access. So people, children that weren't able to go to school any longer, finding ways to help them digitally access and continue their education during the pandemic. (08:09): There was a lot of really great local support that Cotopaxi did last year in the Utah community itself in Salt Lake partnering with the Utah Jazz and creating a t-shirt for that. And then at the same time, just giving back to the local community to help support with COVID Reliefs with everything that was happening with COVID last year. And the Pandemic Cotopaxi really, it had its most successful year of giving in the company's history, which was really exciting. And one of the things that our director of Impact has said, and she's quoted Bill Gates saying that 25 years of human development were undone in 25 weeks. I mean just what has happened in the past year because of this pandemic. And I think that's just been such another great component of this brand of why we give back. And this year especially being able to still, despite everything that happened, how businesses were hit hard in a variety of ways for Cotopaxi to have its most successful year of giving to date was really powerful. And then this year we decided this would be a fun component with Hoka to encourage people in a COVID responsible way. We know we're still in the middle of a pandemic, but more people are getting comfortable getting outside, but that you are finding a few friends that you potentially in your quarantine bubble that you can go and do these challenges within your community. (14:35): And so that will be a part of the collaboration as well. So very, from a marketing perspective, it's a very holistic campaign. You have everything rolling out on a website, it's coming to life in REI retail stores. content: Carie Behe (16:32): Yeah, the story is, I kind of laugh at it now, like you said, it's a different path. I didn't grow up in an outdoorsy family, grew up with a dad who likes to go hunting and fishing and set up his tree stand at five in the morning in the middle of the woods in central Pennsylvania. And I wanted nothing to do with that. And the dead of winter, the thought of going out and doing that just wasn't registering with me for some reason. And my mom and her side of the family was just so traditional sports, football, basketball, and that's what I grew up doing. I always joke that my mom was not a fun person to be around on Sundays when the Steelers were losing. So I grew up near Pittsburgh and that was kind of my childhood, that outdoors was not a thing. (17:18): I did not go hiking. I camped once on an air mattress in a tent for a weekend I think in fifth grade. And then I got a crash course hard into the outdoors when I went to college. So I had somehow inadvertently signed up for this outdoor orientation program at West Virginia University. That was where I did my undergraduate. And I was literally there for student check-in day. And there was this table in the student union building with this guy, his name's Greg Corrio, and he was this program called Adventure West Virginia. And I walked by the table and he basically said, you get three credits to come camp for a week in the summer in West Virginia before you become a freshman, you should do it. And I just thought, oh yeah, cool. This sounds fun. So I just signed up completely, just no idea what I was signing up for, wrote the check, walked on. (18:10): And then in August, so about three weeks before my freshman year started, I went on this trip and I vividly remember some of my guy friends making fun of me a week before the trip. I was like, do you think I can bring a hair dryer on this? And they were like, you are going to fail miserably at all of this. They knew what I was signing up for and I didn't. So we get there and literally spent a week around the wilderness of West Virginia. We did a whole road trip loop, we went rock climbing in Cooper's Rock.

I was just huffing and puffing along, almost crying thinking, what did you sign yourself up for? This is wild. But again, I didn't make it to the top of the rock wall. I was dead last an hour behind everybody probably they were radioing, where is she? (19:44): But I made it and it taught me so much and I just started to fall in love with the outdoors. Went on a spring break backpacking trip to Utah that same year, studied abroad New Zealand after that. And then I became a leader for that program three summers later. So I then got to be that leader and teacher for these incoming freshmen and the girls that were coming in specifically where they may have been so out of their element that I could relate to them and help let them know that it was okay and that everybody starts somewhere in the outdoors. But that was my crash course into outdoor rec. And I think once you fall in love with it, you start to get into gear culture and you see, I saw my leaders with Chacos and Nalgene bottles stickered up and I'm like, I want to be like them and look like them. (20:32): And that's how I discovered Keen and Keen. So Keen at the time, this is like 2007, they are doing this big sustainability campaign. show_notes_excerpt: Have you ever felt like you don't belong? As Carie says, the trees don't care what you look like or how fast you're moving. So why do we put so much pressure on ourselves? Why don't we feel like we belong in a sport or are qualified for a job? Have you ever considered what role marketing plays in making other people feel included? Carie Behe, the GTM Marketing Manager for Cotopaxi, shares her personal story and how after 12 years of working in the industry she still suffers from imposter syndro…

content:
Carie Behe (23:45): Got the internship and I moved to Portland and that was my first time really being on the West Coast and experiencing the northwest and got this three month internship with them to really see that whole campaign through, it was a big event at the end of the summer that culminated the whole campaign. It was called Stand. I got to recruit and have some grassroots marketing volunteers help me just promote the event. And then when I left, I had a semester left to finish at WVU, but when I left they had said, if there's a full-time position when you graduate, it's yours if you want. And thankfully, about nine months later they did. So 2009 I moved to Portland permanently and started working for Keen and was there for about seven years.

Cole Heilborn (24:30): Wow. And what was your role there?

Carie Behe (24:34): I was a marketing coordinator to start and just got to help support on a wide variety of marketing, different events, trade shows, was really helping with outdoor retailer and Keen's presence there and all the shoe sales that Keen would do. And then started to graduate more into public relations and having responsibility of managing the agency, developing PR strategy with 'em and then working with our product line managers to help bring all the product stories to life through PR and then some of the campaigns.

Cole Heilborn (25:06): Okay, gotcha. So that brought you up to year seven and then from seven to now can you fill where's, where's that time at?

Carie Behe (25:15): I spent time as a marketing manager at Danner Boots and got a taste of the hunt fish side of the outdoor industry. It was working.

Cole Heilborn (25:24): Bringing it back to your dad.

content: Carie Behe (25:25): Yeah, he was so excited. Oh my God. He was just so yeah, right up his alley. And then after that I went to Leatherman. So again, continuing with everybody was looking forward to getting Leatherman's and I got to learn a lot at Leatherman actually. I really got to take management and ownership of campaign development and really help building that from the ground up because Leatherman historically wasn't really building these big rich marketing campaigns. It was more like, here's a tool, it does X, Y, and Z for you. And then when I came on board it was really, we were working under a new VP of marketing, Bobby Parisi at the time, and she's been in the industry forever and is a wonderful person mentor of mine, learned so much from her and she really was trying to get leatherman to story tell and build that emotional connection to the consumer. (26:18): And I think today if a brand is not doing that, it's not going to be successful in resonating with the millennial generation and down. It's just like you have to tell these really rich stories to build that bridge between the consumer to relate to them because that's what they're seeking. And so we got to do that with leatherman and tell real life consumer stories of how a leatherman saved the day for somebody or even saved their life. And it was a very humbling experience to get to put those types of stories into marketing campaigns. And then I ultimately got to work on some international marketing before I left and really helped just building a consistent look and feel for the brand globally. And that was something that the brand didn't really have before that it's very widely distributed across the world, over 50 countries, but every country was sort of doing their own thing to a degree they were given assets, but there wasn't this global campaign and strategy that came from HQ and out to all the other countries. So I was really trying to spearhead that effort of getting everyone aligned on the same page, having a consistent look and feel and tone of brand voice across all different regions of the world.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:34): Gotcha. So I'm curious through all of that, through I guess your perspective of the outdoors and your relationship with the outdoors as it's evolved. How has that affected your perspective with the outdoor industry, with the marketing industry and the work that you do now?

Carie Behe (27:53): I would say it, it's greatly impacted how I look at I how approach my day to day, but just how the outdoor industry approaches building connections with consumers and the spectrum of the outdoor consumer is so vast. It's like you've got the very hardcore outdoor, the person that's going and doing laps up a mountain and then the person that has never even doesn't even know what a hike is or doesn't know what the word backpacking means. There's such a range there and each of those types of personas exist. So how does the outdoor industry, how does the epoxy a key and a leatherman, how do these brands really start identifying how they can talk to people that might not feel like they belong? And I think my personal experience, it resonates so much with that because I didn't feel like I belonged, especially on that trip. (28:46): And even sometimes to this day is like I'm not the fastest in what I do. I've experienced with, I think with the gear culture of the outdoor industry, you have to have the lightest, the fastest, the next greatest thing. Oftentimes a lot of garments haven't fit me. There's been jackets that it's like I can't fit into it. And then you start to doubt yourself of really, do I fit in? Is this, am I meant to be going and doing this? Do I have to have that jacket to then take me up to the mountain? What if it doesn't fit? There's this doubt that gets put in your head. I mean you put it in your head, but when you don't see yourself represented in marketing collateral, in messaging from outdoor brands, it might be a bit alienating. And I mean I think generally inclusivity is a topic the industry is talking about, but inclusivity across the board with your skin color, with how you identify with your body size and type of just, these are conversations I think that we need to have together and rally around. (29:50): It is a common thing that I think if all brands are rallying together, we're going to identify a solution to make everyone feel welcome. And I think I said this to you before, the trees don't care what you look like. They don't care how much you weigh or not what your skin color is. I mean the outdoors are for every single person. And I think at times where I felt like I don't belong, I mean for sure, am I in my head? Absolutely. But when I don't see myself represented at times it might help just subliminally amplify that. And how can we as brands make people feel comfortable in general of like, do you need that jacket to go out and hike a few miles away? Maybe not, but do you need the jacket to go scale Mount Hood or Mount Rainier maybe.

content:
Cole Heilborn (30:39): Interesting. I'm curious. I feel like kind of what you're describing is imposter syndrome, feeling like you don't belong

Carie Behe (30:45): A little bit,

Cole Heilborn (30:46): But I would assume anyone or myself looks at you and you're like, Carrie is doing an awesome job, she's in the industry, she's been doing it for a long time. But that still plagues you sometimes that doubt.

Carie Behe (31:01): I think so. I think especially when it comes to buying a garment and it might not fit. I have that moment of doubt. I mean that's for sure on me, but it's really cool to see brands starting to address their marketing collateral to make it more representative of anyone and everyone. That's the first very obvious and easy step. I think all brands should be getting behind at this point. And there's so many leaders in the industry that have been doing it for years already, but how do you keep, what's the next step in that? I mean it's inclusivity with sizes and building a more comprehensive range of sizes for people of all body sizes and shapes to fit into.

Cole Heilborn (31:45): I am curious, I think regardless of, I guess what people feel like feel an imposter about, I feel like imposter syndrome is a pretty common thing that a lot of people feel. Speaking personally, that's something that I experience more frequently than not. It seems like just around lots of different things, work related, not work related. I'm curious because I think a lot of people who are listening are probably going to resonate and connect with you on this level. What do you do in those moments of doubt? What truth do you recall? Do you anchor yourself in so that you can get through those hazy moments?

content: Carie Behe (32:27): I like this question. I'm glad that you're bringing this up. And I think the first step for me has just been a mental check with myself personally is just like, okay, why are you feeling this way? What's causing this? Is your work plate? Is there a lot on the work plate? Did you not hike that hike in a fast way? Were you super behind all your friends? I start to unpack why I'm feeling that way, but I think where it has been most beneficial, where I've started to feel less imposter syndrome is just talking to people about it and realizing that almost everyone I've ever talked to feels this way within their work and professional or even on personal things of just the doubting yourself. But if you talk through it and talk through it with a partner, a friend, a close coworker, just you'll find that they might be feeling similarly and that you can talk through it together. (33:24): And then I'd say on the professional side of things, just always having transparent conversations and wanting to learn where you stand in relation to your work plate and your responsibilities. If you're delivering on something and you're not getting clear feedback to help you progress and checking the box, then asking for it and being very blunt of just like, is this what you're looking for? And if not, can you help me understand why? I think a lot of the earlier years of my career feedback was given, I think from top down the executive level at companies, but there wasn't a lot of concrete explanation of I don't like this and here's why. It was just like, go fix this or go make it look different. And that wasn't, I think that helped continue to build this doubt of like, oh, I didn't do it right the first time, but I'm unclear of how to do it right the second time. And that really just comes from building the confidence to have those maybe difficult conversations with a manager or some other level. I always say powers that be is how I refer to executives is going to the powers that be. And just having that frank discussion of, you weren't looking for this, so just help me understand what you are looking for so I can come up with a solution

content:
Cole Heilborn (34:46): And feeling that way. I mean, it greatly affects how you're able to do your job. If we're just looking at it from the career perspective, then you start to second guess everything that you're doing and you're like, is this even a good idea because I'm maybe not the right person for this. Is this a good idea? And then it just spirals out of control.

Carie Behe (35:07): Yeah, I would agree with that. And I think there comes a point for me, I mean I'm speaking from my own perspective and experience in the industry is like my competence has been built over time. I mean, I feel like I was terrified my first five years on the job of just like, am I doing this right? Am I not doing this right? And if a mistake happened, oh, I remember this very vividly. This was the first photo shoot I'd ever had a bigger responsibility and was with Keen. And we were going to Smith Rock to do a photo shoot and VP of marketing was coming along at the time and she allowed me to come along on the shoot and that was my first work trip. And I, I was responsible for all the samples and making sure we had everything for the shoot. And there was one pair of winter boots where I should have brought both colors and there was only one color, and my head is melting on the inside. I'm like, I'm going to lose my job. This is awful. She hates me. I just spiraled in my head like, well, we can't get the boots. So the reality is what it is, and obviously you learn in those moments. So I think that's a great example of, okay, I failed to bring the second color of boots, but the next time I brought them,

Cole Heilborn (36:19): Yeah, that gut drop feeling, when you realize that you just messed something up, it's painful

content:
Carie Behe (36:26): And it doesn't go away. It's like even with all the years of experience I've had now, there's still been moments because as you progress, your project plate gets bigger and all the balls are up in the air and you have to figure out how to juggle them. But that comes with having very clear, honest, transparent discussions with your manager. And I think when I was younger, I was afraid to say that I was afraid to say no, because if I said no, this is me in my head thinking this. If I said no, does that show them that I'm unwilling to be a good team member? Does that show that I don't want the responsibility? What does that me saying? No. So I never said no. And then a consequence of not saying no at times was dropping the ball on things. Something as simple as should have grabbed the pair of the second color. (37:15): And I didn't turned out to be a relatively big problem at the time, but you learn. But it comes with having those discussions with people of like, okay, if you have all this on your plate, help me prioritize. And so that's, I've learned to say no, but I say it in a way of I can get to that, but something else might not get worked on at the time. So understanding project management and it goes with go to market too of how to prioritize because all these different campaigns are being worked on at the same

Cole Heilborn (37:46): Time. Sure. So yeah. With your role now, I guess, what is Cotopaxi doing to create more of an inclusive environment or what have they done? What are you hoping to do in the future?

content:
Carie Behe (38:00): I think that Cotopaxi is a brand has done so many awesome things right from the start. It is a brand that really is inclusive, I think across the board when it comes to messaging. I mean from a marketing perspective and building campaigns and showing representation of people of color, people of different body sizes. I think where I hope to see Cotopaxi go in the future, and I said this in my interviews and have talked with our product team about this, is the brand will have to at some point work on developing extended sizing. The size range that we offer in our products is the normal size range that you expect, but to offer additional sizes for different body types, that's my hope for it. And I know the product team feels that way. We've had many conversations about it and they're all really positive, great conversations. I think as the brand grows in terms and scales, we'll be able to do that.

Cole Heilborn (38:59): How do you consider inclusivity? What does that look like in the things that you're working on today? Has that influenced how you're working on this collaboration project?

content:
Carie Behe (39:10): Yeah, I would say it's influenced the collaboration project in terms of the way we're developing the messaging for it really of the message of the product itself can be used for a wide range of things. One of the things that I think obviously that comes to mind with Hoka is a brand is running. I personally not a runner myself, it's a brand I haven't identified with personally and have known of it. But I think where you get into the marketing messaging and storytelling is being able to explain, these shoes can take you on a run, on a trail hike, on a walk around your neighborhood. And the same on the Cotopaxi side with the pack. The pack could be a trail running pack. The pack could be for a day hike, it could be your commuter pack, but that these two brands are getting together and building a message of multiple different benefits that the product could serve the consumer. And then just making sure from the campaign, the look and the feel of it that people are represented in it, that people of color are represented. I would say from a lifestyle perspective with capturing imagery for the campaign and making sure that there is representation, that there's representation even in the activity itself of making sure that the images, that what you see being portrayed in the image makes sense across a wide variety of activities.

Cole Heilborn (40:37): You brought up something interesting that I'd be curious to hear your response to you as a marketer. You don't personally connect with the brands like Coca, but talking about imposter syndrome, does that bring about concerns about your qualifications to work on a project like this?

content: Carie Behe (40:57): God, I love that. That's such a great question. I guess maybe initially it brought up concerns. I think when I first started working with the Hoka team, I was nervous. I'm not a runner. I mean, I don't think I could even run half a mile right now, not my thing. There's other ways I get outside or other ways I'm active. Cycling or snowboarding is a thing. But even one of the first meetings, I pronounced the brand name wrong, how disconnected I think I am personally from the brand, I was so embarrassed I didn't say Hoka. And they were wonderful though. The team was like, it's not Hoka one, one, Carrie. So I think in the initial stages of it, I did feel like a huge imposter of like, oh my God, I have to represent my brand and beyond my game for my brand that I'm brand new to. (41:51): And then I have to help be a steward of another brand that's a really incredible, awesome brand. And when I can't even pronounce the name, what does that show? But I think we've grown a lot since then and it's been so wonderful. I've been working with Leah Lodge at Hoka. She has just been phenomenal, such a great partner to, we're just in such lockstep on this whole campaign and seeing it through from no ideas of how we're going to, what's the campaign messaging, how are we going to tell this story to then bringing our creative teams together to start making the building blocks of that, bringing in partners like Patty, bringing in other ambassadors and influencers, working with an REI and help tell that story through the REI lens as well. It's been really cool. So I would say the imposter syndrome is definitely gone. But yeah, I had some fun fail moments in the beginning, but like I said before, you learn, I now learn how to correctly pronounce their name.

content:
Cole Heilborn (42:55): But I am curious if you can dive a little deeper. I feel like that's, especially in the outdoor industry, I hear this everywhere. You get a job at a company that you personally are passionate about and that you practice outside of work hours because most people who are in the space live their passion and their passion is their work. But that's always, I mean obviously that's not practical for everyone and for every job in the industry. But I guess, do you feel like there's an edge or a value to either being outside of using this runner example, being outside of that industry looking in? Do you feel like there's added value being on the inside, looking out as you're in those positions? Is one better than the other? Is that a thing?

Carie Behe (43:51): I think they're both equally important. I think the fact that I'm this outside non runner looking into a brand like Hoka is hopefully offering that perspective from an inclusive message type of point of view of like, Hey, if this is so run focused, are we alienating somebody that might not be a runner? So I would say from the outside looking in, I think it offers huge opportunity to just, I mean, and this is true for any brand of internally, you are the experts of your brand, it best and the truth as you see it, but somebody on the outside might see it entirely differently. And so I think being willing to be open to hearing that perspective, it's so, so valuable because I think it helps shape and create something that resonates with somebody on the outside. So I would even say that might be the more important of the two, but I think being that expert on the inside of knowing it and you're eating, sleeping, breathing, if you are working for a running brand, a snowboarding brand, a climbing brand, that having that level of expert knowledge of the sport that your gear is going to support, I think is super critical as well. (45:03): So it's finding the right balance with it, of being the expert inside, but being willing to hear outside perspective too.

Cole Heilborn (45:09): Sure. Yeah, no, that's a really nice way of putting it. So we're almost out of time for today, but one of my last questions, I'm just curious, what's your hope as you look forward towards the future, both for you personally, for the industry as a whole? Any thoughts?

Carie Behe (45:28): Yeah. I would say hopes and dreams for, I think personally is I want to find a way I feel like I can be accomplished in my job and in my career. And if I've left a mark at all in the outdoor industry is I want someone who felt like they were excluded to feel included. I want the industry to just have this outdoors for all mentality. It doesn't matter the activity, it doesn't matter what you're wearing at the end of the day if you're getting outside. I learned so much during that adventure, West Virginia. I mean, that program truly changed the course of my life. I would not be in the outdoor industry. We're probably talking to you right now, but I learned so much about me and what the outdoors gave to me is so invaluable. And it's like that inspired me to want to continue on my journey and helping protect the places that we play, helping just get more people out to enjoy and learn as I have. (46:26): And so if I can inspire someone who may otherwise not have gotten outside to go take a hike for the first time in their local park or to go on a bike ride is I feel like I've done my job. And how as the industry, we can take that mentality of inspiring, especially the next generation of outdoor enthusiasts, like younger kids that are growing up today that maybe grew up like me that didn't have an outdoor experience. How can we find ways to expose them? Because the power of the outdoors is like, it's so magical. It's hard to put into words. I'm sure you know that too. And you've felt that. And so how can the industry really rally together to create this next generation of stewards and this next generation of people who are passionate about getting outside and exploring. So that's why, but I hope happens.

Cole Heilborn (47:20): I love that. If folks want to follow along with you or with the brand, where can people go to say hello?

Maddie Duffy (00:03): The biggest thing that I can say about any Ambassador program is just the relationship. Just really appreciate that relationship that you have with each of the ambassadors and nurture it. And I dunno, for me, I'm lucky because I can call all of our ambassadors, my friends. They're just such amazing people and it's always an honor to work with them and then an honor to see what they can produce for Mystery Ranch.

This podcast dives deep with leaders of the outdoor marketing industry as they discuss the gritty details of their work, personal challenges and latest adventures, whether you're standing in the lift line, shuttling to fresh loam, or cracking a local beer. It's interesting, I think in the outdoor space we see a lot of backpack companies, but there's not a lot of backpack companies that I'm aware of that go outside of the traditional hike and climb. How many other brands are in the spaces that you operate in forest firefighting, in military, in the hunting space,

Maddie Duffy (02:20): In the military, and in the fire, not as many. But in the hunting space, we've definitely seen an increase of different brands that also make hunting packs. But I think what makes us unique is that we're not only hunting packs, and I think that's kind of what you see throughout the different markets is each company only kind of their niche is hunting or fire or military, and it's not a combination of all of them.

Cole Heilborn (02:51): Sure. Yeah. So I guess kind of break that down. How did Mr. Man get started? How did you get into all of these different verticals?

Maddie Duffy (02:59): Yeah, so actually Dana Gleason, who owns Mystery Ranch, he started Dana Design and gosh, I think that was early nineties. And then he sold it to K two and just kind of realized that his backpacking days were not done. And with Dana Design, he really focused on the outdoor side of things, so whether that be climbing or skiing or hiking. And then when he started Mystery Ranch, the outdoor market wasn't doing all that great. We were kind of struggling to keep afloat, and then we were approached by the military to start making military packs. And so the military is kind of what saved Mystery Ranch and kept Mystery Ranch up and running. And then eventually we had a wild land firefighter approached Dana about making backpacks, and that's when we started doing the wildland fire side of things. And then we started to expand into the hunting side of things as well.

Cole Heilborn (04:02): I'm really curious to learn a little bit more about your job as a marketing manager. I know one of the things that you work on and oversee is the ambassador program, but kind of fill us in on the rest of your, I guess, job duties.

We have our hunting ambassadors, we have military ambassadors, we have brand ambassadors that kind of encompass more than just one market. We have ski ambassadors, climbing ambassadors, hunting everything. And just being able to have a relationship with each one of them has been probably the highlight of my job.

Cole Heilborn (05:50): Do you feel like you learn something unique from each of them? You wouldn't otherwise be able to learn if you didn't have the job?

So I don't really know a whole lot about hunting. My brothers hunted a lot growing up, but it wasn't until I moved to Montana that I just learned more about it. And I think the most incredible thing about our ambassadors is they get really excited to talk about their hobby and talk about the things that they're really good at. I think we all have those ambassadors or individuals that we look up to on social and we're like, man, I just want to be like that person because look at that epic trip they just went on. From the brand side though, I'm curious to hear your perspective. How do you manage an ambassador program? How do you decide to start one, how do you find people to be on your ambassador program? And especially with social media today, there's influencers that are popping up and they're kind of changing the way that maybe brands look at ambassadors or athletes. content:
Maddie Duffy (07:42): Yeah, so I inherited our ambassador program when I started, and a lot of the people that are in the ambassador program have had longstanding relationships with different employees at Mystery Ranch or within the Bozeman community because when we started, it was pretty small, and I think Mystery Ranch was one of the first brands to bring on an ambassador program. We just saw kind of a need for it. And to me, when I took that on, I'm like, well, what is an ambassador program? So I kind of just started from the very top of, let's break this down. And so I did my research of what I was seeing other brands doing and why they even had it. And for us, I'm like, okay, so what defines our ambassador program? And for me, I think it builds credibility to our brand and our products. When someone, especially in 2020, everyone wanted new hobbies, and so they were looking to social media to be like, okay, who's an expert in climbing or who's an expert in hunting? (08:50): And so I think by having an ambassador program of someone who represents brand and your products, it builds credibility. It also tells a story beyond what you are telling. So you're relying on these ambassadors to tell a story about your product. And for us, a backpack is much more than a backpack. We've had people write in and tell us that it's saved someone's life or when they were in the military, they used it as a pillow. And so you hear these stories of people who connect to their backpack. That's much more than just the product itself. And then it also just kind of expands your brand awareness. Maybe our followers aren't the same as one of our ambassador's followers, but in return it's just bringing their followers over to us, so it really expands your brand influence.

Cole Heilborn (09:43): Sure. You mentioned that at some point prior to you joining the team, Mr. Ranch saw a need for ambassador program. I guess what was that need and why did the company decide to go down this route?

Maddie Duffy (09:57): Yeah, so my boss actually is the one who started the ambassador program at Mystery Ranch, and I think from his standpoint, he was like, we need to expand our reach. Our company was growing really fast and we needed kind of help because it was only a three man marketing team. And so that's kind of where he saw the help, where it's like, okay, we actually get these extra hands to help push out our brand awareness and push out the reach. And then we also get these people who test our products because our designers, they're not the expert in the field. Some of them have never climbed before. So then that's when we rely on our ambassadors who are excellent climbers to be like, Hey, this actually would be really great in the field if you move to the strap over here or you added this buckle X, Y, and Z.

Cole Heilborn (10:47): I feel like there's kind of three phrases, the three words that pop up in the industry today, ambassador, athlete and influencer, what are the differences? Are they the same? How do they interconnect? I guess? Do you have a definition that you look at?

Maddie Duffy (11:04): So I don't know if I necessarily have a definition. I think it just depends. It goes from company to company on, you have to define what that means. For us. We didn't want to call them athletes, we wanted to call them ambassadors. And for us, I think that that's a big badge to wear. It's kind of the highest honor, and you just have to define what the expectations are and make sure that your ambassador, your influencer or your athlete, whatever you choose to call them, their goals, align with your goals.

Maddie Duffy (12:31): I think that's really cool. And it again goes back to each company has to define what that means. It's that extra element that you have other than your social media or other than your employees to tell the story of who your brand is,
