I am assuming you're looking at things like their social following, their social reach, but also things like their values and their level of expertise. Maybe for folks who don't have a program set up, what are things that they could consider as they're looking to build their team?

Maddie Duffy (13:25): So I actually sat down with a few other people in the outdoor industry and just asked them how they run their ambassador program and what works and what doesn't work. And one of them told me, you can't put all of your eggs in one basket. So just because they have a strong social following doesn't mean that they're automatically an ambassador. I think you have to look for other characteristics as well. What's their distribution? Maybe they're really good at trade shows and talking about product knowledge with your consumers. Maybe they do have a YouTube channel or maybe they have an Amazon channel, and then also do they give back to the community? I think that's a huge part, especially for us where we love giving back to the military. We love giving back to all the people who wear our backpacks because they're the ones that are keeping us in business. (14:18): I think the same kind of goes for our ambassadors too, just because you're good at your sport, what else do you do? Do you volunteer at different programs? Are you a part of RMEF? Are you a part of BHA? All of these different nonprofit organizations. The other thing that we look at is are they trustworthy? Do they have a strong reputation? Especially with all of our markets, we want to make sure that that person that we're bringing on as an ambassador can be a strong representation across all of the markets because we do have to be careful in that sense.

Cole Heilborn (14:57): Sure. Yeah. So maybe it was a few years ago or 10 years ago, but I feel like ambassadors or influencers were being chosen just because they had a massive following. Let's go find the people who have the million followers on Instagram and try to sign them on. As an influencer, that's starting to change though. The reach, as you said, is no longer the most important part. It's part of the equation, but it's not the most important part. Why is that? Why is changing?

Maddie Duffy (15:30): That is a good question. I think for us, one thing that we've always tried to do with our ambassador program is make sure it's authentic. And I think that's maybe why things are starting to shift is because if someone is just like nilly willy going on Instagram and they're just like, Hey, try these vitamins, but you can tell that it's not authentic. Maybe they don't even use those vitamins, and that was something that was really important for us. We wanted our ambassadors to have a nine to five job, and then their hunting or their skiing was an extra activity that they were doing that they're really good at because that makes it relatable. Not everybody has the luxury of being able to go hunting all day for their full-time job. So it's like the everyday folks want to look up to someone that they can relate to and it's authentic, and I think that's kind of where that shift is happening. I always use this analogy, but I watch a lot of the Bachelor and the Bachelorette and my friends and I, we always joke about afterwards, all of these people become Instagram influencers because they're like, look at all these followers that I now have and these vitamins that I've never used, but I'm going to say that they look good. And I think that's fine, but that doesn't work for our company, and I don't know if it necessarily works for the outdoor industry as well.

Cole Heilborn (16:57): You said something interesting. The people on your ambassador team are just regular people who have nine to five jobs. Where does that come from? You mentioned because you want it to be relatable and authentic. Is that your target audience for your marketing, or is that just a hope to kind of ground these people in the everyday average life so that all the rest of us average people can feel connected to them?

Maddie Duffy (17:21): I think it's honestly probably a combination of the two. Obviously, we want everyone to be able to use our backpacks, whether you're an expert or someone who's just beginning, that's kind of like our marketing tactic behind it. We want people to have always wanted to go climbing, to have the ability to go climbing and learn from someone who has started from the bottom and really worked their way up to where they're at. I think I've had a few conversations with people who are into backcountry hunting and they're like, sometimes it's hard to relate to the people who are kind of a celebrity in hunting because they have all the access to all of this gear and to all of this land or this camera crew. But I want someone who's just an everyday person that I can relate to and who can answer my questions and it not feel like they're elite. They can be at my level and be like, yeah, I've been there and I've struggled with that too, and this is what I've done. This is what I've learned.

Cole Heilborn (18:30): Yeah. How do you find those people? It sounds like you want people who are really qualified experts at their thing, but they're also relatable. You wouldn't mind getting a cup of coffee or a beer with them and you wouldn't feel pressure of like, oh, I don't know if I can talk to this person so cool, or whatever. How do you begin to find those folks?

Maddie Duffy (18:53): I think that they're all over, but I was saying a lot of the ambassadors that we have on our program right now, they've been there since the beginning. They've already had established relationships with a lot of the people at Mystery Ranch. And then I would say the ones that I have brought on since I started, again, they're known throughout the community. A lot of our sales managers will be like, you should talk to this person. And so what I do is I kind of interview them, and it's not a scary interview by all means because it's me. I don't think I'm a very scary person, but I have a conversation with them and I'm like, are these people easy to talk to? Just tell me about yourself. Tell me why you're in this market or you're in this industry. And I think when you can hear the passion and the excitement in their voice, that's where I'm like, okay, I want that person on my team.

Cole Heilborn (19:50): So then how do you get that person on your team? If you can share, is that compensated? Is that, what are expectations? Do you have a list of things that you require from them? Is it just like, Hey, we'll send you product and whatever you do with it is great. Where do you take it from there?

Maddie Duffy (20:07): Yeah, so I mean, it's kind of a mix of things. So when we have that conversation just to kind of get to know each other and see if it's a good fit, the next kind of conversation that I'll have with them is What are your goals? What are your goals for 2021? What are your goals for 2022? And then make sure that their goals align with our goals and vice versa, because it has to be a mutual relationship because that's where you get that authentic side of your ambassador where it's like, this isn't forced. We're not forcing you to post this. And then from there, I kind of meet with our sales managers and then the rest of the marketing team and see where we might have gaps of maybe content that we need. And then I go back with the ambassador and I kind of just say, Hey, this is what we're looking for. Does it fit with all the hunts that you're doing this year or the climbs that you're doing this year?

Cole Heilborn (21:02): So you've said that you'll make sure that your goals align. I guess, do you have specific goals for specific ambassadors that you're trying to match up with? And if so, could you share some of what that might look like?

Maddie Duffy (21:16): Every ambassador I think is different because we are in different markets and each ambassador has their own different characteristics. Some people love to be on camera and love to do photo shoots or any films, and then we have some ambassadors that that's not really their thing. So it's just finding out the goals that align there. And that also kind of goes with the different characteristics of your ambassadors. We know that this person loves to be on camera. We know that this person just loves to talk about product or write a blog post for us. So yeah, I definitely think also depending on the market, each person has a different deliverable or a different goal for the year.

Cole Heilborn (21:58): And how important is leaning into your ambassador's strengths and taking advantage of the things that they're passionate about?

Maddie Duffy (22:08): I think that's probably one of the most important things because like I was saying, we don't want a forced relationship. We want it to be very authentic, and if you're pushing something on someone that they don't want to do it or they don't feel comfortable, then it's not going to be a good outcome for either person. So just making sure that they're comfortable and asking realistic tasks of them, and I think, I don't know, that just helps build a better relationship with your ambassadors as well.

Cole Heilborn (22:37): Yeah. So I guess I'm curious then, so you've got your ambassadors, I imagine they're like you have 'em all on speed, Dolly, you guys hang out frequently, you go on adventures together, but then do you see, or do you work with I guess the influencer, maybe someone who isn't, I don't know. I guess we'll leave it there. Do you work outside of your ambassador program with other types of people?

Maddie Duffy (23:04): Yeah, we definitely do. It's something that I'm trying to establish a little bit more where we have an ambassador program and then an influencer program. And to me, the influencer program is someone who will write a blog for us in exchange for a backpack or write a review or help us with product feedback. That's always something that we look for. And I have people write in all the time, and we just kind of have a conversation about, okay, well, what would this look like if I did this huge epic hunt and I am normally a back skier, is that a story you would want to do? Can you provide us with backpacks? And so there is that different level of the influencer versus the ambassador. I think with the ambassador, I've just established a stronger relationship with them just because we do more consistent work with them. But that's not to say that we wouldn't work with any other influencer.

Cole Heilborn (24:08): Yeah. So I guess you've kind of described what the relationship with the ambassador looks like. What is the relationship and what are expectations that you guys consider when working with an influencer where maybe it's a one-time project or a much smaller ask? What does that look like?

Maddie Duffy (24:25): Yeah, so we took on a platform called Meltwater that kind of helps us track the engagement that our ambassadors are doing. And then it also kind of helps us look for different influencers. And I guess what that really looks like is, again, it'll be a conversation of what project are you working on and where do you see us fitting in? Why do you want to work with Mystery Ranch? Another thing I think that's really important is when you're working with an influencer, it's like, we don't want this to be a forced push of our product. We still want that authentic vibe to it, so tell us why you chose Mystery Ranch. What do you know about us? Do you know anything about us? And then if not, we're like, okay, this is still a good opportunity. Let's educate them a little bit more on our product and see if it's still a good fit.

content:
Cole Heilborn (25:18): And are those people that you are finding and reaching out to, or do the most influencers come to you and then you get to know them?

Maddie Duffy (25:27): It's a combination of both. Actually. Pre COVID, it was a little bit easier when we had trade shows and stuff, and you could actually have a face-to-face conversation with people. I definitely have had quite a few people come up to me at trade shows and we kind of have conversations and they tell me a little bit about the projects that they're working on. I've had people write into our Instagram, into our website, our different PR agencies, so they come from all over.

Cole Heilborn (25:58): Sure. Yeah. I guess for folks who are on Instagram and who are the type of people that reach out and want to share their adventures with brands from the brand side, is there anything that you would recommend an influencer or just someone mention or something that they could, if they're going to reach out to you, what should they say other than, Hey, can we have free product?

Maddie Duffy (26:24): Yeah, I think it's always important to reach out and just give us a little idea of who you are. That will help me quite a bit. Maybe just talk about, this is what I've done in the past for other brands, or this is what I've built X, Y, and Z. Just give me a little bit of who you are and then also tell me why you want Mystery Ranch. Why do you want our product? How will it help you in your adventure? Or maybe you've loved Mystery Ranch for 20 years, but tell me why. Because we get a lot of that of, I love Mystery Ranch. Our products are great, and it's like try and make it stand out a little bit, I guess.

Cole Heilborn (27:05): Sure. What is Meltwater?

Maddie Duffy (27:08): Meltwater is an influencer program, so for us, it measures all of our ambassadors, social channels. It just kind of helps me with the ROI to bring to my boss to help me set budgets for the year. And then it's also a tool where people can go and seek influencers at any different level. It gives them a rating based off of other companies that they've worked with before, their social reach, just kind of their reputation,

Maddie Duffy (28:12): For? One, just making sure that they're posting, so the actual content of it, and then just making sure that their posts, it is getting good engagement, it's reaching, it's resonating with their audience, and then that they're actually posting content too.

Cole Heilborn (28:31): Gotcha. And are there certain numbers that you're trying to hit when it comes to that information? Does that vary per person?

Maddie Duffy (28:39): It varies per person, and I think it varies per market as well.

Cole Heilborn (28:45): Oh, okay. So you would expect to see a difference in engagement between outdoors and forest firefighting?

Maddie Duffy (28:53): Oh, yeah. There's a huge difference for us. I mean, they both do equally well, but I think our fire community, because it's such a small niche of backpacks in the fire industry, that we do have a lot of wild land firefighters. We have a lot of military people, but what's cool is it all kind of overlaps because a wildland firefighter could be super into hunting or to backpacking all that, so all our consumers kind of dabble in each market.

Cole Heilborn (29:24): Gotcha. Yeah. Interesting. I never considered that, but I guess that makes total sense. What have you learned from being able to see those numbers? Have you guys observed anything that's kind of changed the way that you do things?

Maddie Duffy (29:43): We've only had Meltwater for a couple months, and so we haven't really done a deep dive into it. For me though, what I like is every month I kind of send a monthly update to our internal folks of this is what our ambassadors are up to, and I can kind of show them too through that platform, which has been huge for me because having Meltwater, I had to grab all of my analytics from Google Analytics and then actually going to our ambassador's page of taking screenshots and being like, this is what they're up to, but now it's all in one place, and so it's made my life so much easier.

Cole Heilborn (30:27): Yeah, I can only imagine. And I guess as you start to consider looking forwards, are you trying to continually to grow to your ambassador program? Do you try to keep it at a certain cap so it's manageable? Are you always trying to add people?

Maddie Duffy (30:43): I mean, yes and no. I think it's important to keep your ambassador program at a certain cap because it will lose its credibility and more people that you continue to add to it. It's like, oh, well, everyone can be an ambassador, and that's not necessarily the case. I definitely think our influencer program is going to start to build out probably in 2022, and with our influencer program, I'm always willing to have a conversation with somebody, but yeah, they have to meet all the qualifications that we set and all the characteristics that we're looking for to be an ambassador at ranch.

Cole Heilborn (31:26): Sure. What do you see as, I guess two questions. What do you see as the biggest opportunities around ambassador programs and also the challenges around them?

Maddie Duffy (31:37): I think one of the biggest challenges is just anything with social media or marketing in general. It's always expanding and it's always changing, and so it's keeping up with what's trending and what's not, what's resonating with your audience and what's not resonating with your audience? Is it bringing on more people? But if you bring on more people, it's like you need more management, you need, I don't know. And that's the other thing that's hard too, is all the content that you get from your ambassadors. Especially with us, we have 26 ambassadors right now, and so it's like managing 26 different content pieces that are coming in and making sure that it's getting distributed properly too, which that challenge is also a really good opportunity as well as we're running our social channels. I will never complain about getting too much content. It's hard to make sure that I'm putting it in the right spot and releasing it at the right time, but it's also a lot of fun and you learn a lot of things from it, and I think that's going to continue to be the biggest opportunity is you have these ambassadors that also have the time to learn different tools. (32:52): We have one ambassador who likes doing TikTok and reels, and that's not something that Mystery Ranch has dabbled in yet, but we have an ambassador to do that and help tell us a story on another social platform. I think that's the opportunity that Ambassador programs bring is just that broad reach of you might be reaching a new customer every day just because of your ambassadors.

Cole Heilborn (33:16): Yeah, that's an interesting point. How does, I feel like every year there's a new app or something that pops up, sometimes they stick around, sometimes they don't. How do you look at a new application and start to figure out, should we go down that? Should we not go down that? Do you kind of let your ambassadors test that out for you?

Maddie Duffy (33:39): Yeah, I mean, I guess it could be a little bit of both. I think for Mystery Ranch, you just have to make sure it aligns with your brand. For us, I think TikTok is great. I'm one of the millennials who actually watches quite a bit of TikTok embarrassingly, but I just don't think that right now, that's where Mystery Ranch is at, and we've had this conversation within the marketing team. That's not where our brand is at. I've also realized that Twitter isn't exactly where our brand is at either, but we still use it quite a bit. And I just use that platform differently than I use in Instagram or a Facebook with Instagram. I love having our ambassadors actually take over our Instagram for the day or two, and it just allows for our users to get to know them a little bit better and get to know this huge trip that they were on or their climbing expedition that they did, or skiing expedition that they did. But other than that, if our ambassadors want to start using TikTok, I think that's great. And again, it's just another avenue that kind of pushes people towards our product.

Cole Heilborn (34:54): How much do you look at your ambassador and see them as a way for the audience to get to know them and through them, mystery Ranch, how much of that is part of the equation?

Maddie Duffy (35:06): I think it's a huge part. I mean, it's a good balance because with getting to know the person, you can also relate it to that product. I think it's almost more important for the people to get to know that person so they can instill trust and understand why Mystery Ranch would want to call them an ambassador. And yeah, the trust component is a huge part of it because the more they get to know this person, they'll start to trust their recommendations.

Cole Heilborn (35:35): How do you measure that level of trust or how much trust you have with your community?

Maddie Duffy (35:41): For me, I think when we first start bringing on ambassadors, I hate saying it, but we kind of put 'em on a probation period, and part of that is are they meeting up to their deliverables? So I think that's kind of the way that you as a company can build trust within these ambassadors. And if they're living up to their deliverables and they're posting on social media or they're being to the place that they're supposed to be at, I mean that in itself instills that trust.

Cole Heilborn (36:12): Yeah, interesting. How does that trust connect to this rise in micro influencers or nano influencers, I think is a new one. I've heard also, I've heard brands are now starting to go after folks who have less than a thousand or less than 10,000 followers intentionally.

Maddie Duffy (36:29): I think that kind of goes back to what Mystery Ranch started their ambassador program with. It's like, maybe these companies are going after these people who have less than a hundred thousand followers because other people like you and me can look at them and be like, oh, they're just an everyday person and they're not just pushing a product to make money, they're pushing a product because they actually really like that product.

Cole Heilborn (37:00): Do you have a minimum follower count that you look for?

Maddie Duffy (37:02): No. Our follower count. It honestly is all over the board. And I think that's kind of what I love about our ambassador program. It's not like we're just targeting these well-known athletes. Not to say that we wouldn't ever do that, but I don't know. I like that some of our ambassadors don't have 10,000 followers. They have under that, and they're still absolutely amazing at what they do.

content: Cole Heilborn (37:30): So I feel like sometimes maybe the politics of it get a little tricky because historically, I feel like in the outdoor space, athletes athlete deals were like, those were the people that we all looked up to. And now with social media, like the influencer and the ambassadors become a part of the equation as well. I've heard in the mountain bike space that some athlete riders or phenomenal riders ride for big brands, and I'm sure this is all over, but I'm just thinking of mountain bike right now. There's been challenges on the brand side because athletes or brands are working with athletes, they're also working with influencers like YouTubers, and they might not be the fastest on the bike, but they have that connection with their audience. And so brands look at that and they say, well, we obviously want to work with them so we can connect with this audience from the brand side. How do you manage that? Because on one hand you have athletes and they feel maybe a little jaded or, oh, we've put in all the time, we've worked really hard to get to where we are. We're at the top of our game, but here's these YouTube influencers who are these new people who maybe aren't the fastest, who just make videos for a living and we're losing brand deals. Have you seen that? I guess I'm just curious your thoughts on that topic as a whole.

Maddie Duffy (38:57): I mean, I guess I haven't seen that on the Mystery Ranch side of things, but I could totally see that happening. But I also think that kind of goes back to setting up what you want your ambassador program to be and defining what makes an ambassador. Is it their social following? Is it that they're involved in their community? Is it their distribution? Figuring out why do you want that person to be an ambassador? Is it because they hit all the criteria that you're looking for? Or maybe they're really strong in three of 'em and not so much in the other. And I think I feel for those athletes that are getting frustrated, but at the same time it's kind of like, well, maybe this person is just a better fit for that brand. And it's not anything personal, it's just maybe the audience is resonating more with this person than it is with this person.

Cole Heilborn (39:53): Do you feel like we'll start to see more of that as more and more as the outdoor kind of become more accessible for everyone? And as we've seen through 2020, there's just been big push to get outside by the average person who maybe doesn't know who that athlete is, but they know who that person on YouTube is.

Maddie Duffy (40:12): I mean, I hope so. For me, I think, again, it all goes back to that authentic feel with that person where I'm like, okay, I feel like this person truly wants other people to know about what they're doing or what they're using because they care. I mean, for me, if I see something on Instagram of someone being like, I really like this product and here's why I'm probably going to resonate with that more rather than a celebrity being like, I love L'Oreal. And it's like, okay. You also got paid so much money to say that.

Cole Heilborn (40:54): It's kind of an interesting segue, something that I don't know when it came out, but Instagram recently, maybe not recently in the last couple of years, put out there, shoppable content through the app. Is that something that you consider with your ambassadors, or do you think about that at all?

Maddie Duffy (42:11): I don't know. I mean, have you watched the social dilemma on Netflix?

Cole Heilborn (42:16): Yeah. Oh

Maddie Duffy (42:17): Man, that gave me nightmares. I'm like, I'm part of the problem. I think that's, honestly, that's just the culture of the internet these days where it's like we just want that ease of use, and so wherever we can find an easier shortcut, I think that's just kind of how it's going to be from now on.

Cole Heilborn (42:40): I get that part of me wants to push back and say, no, let's not do it that way. But I mean, I guess I don't disagree with you morally. I feel conflicted about it all.

Maddie Duffy (42:50): Yeah. Oh, definitely. It's marketing.

Cole Heilborn (42:54): Yeah, that's a whole nother topic. Actually, that's a good plug for an episode we did a few months ago with the social media manager, Mary Kate over at Goal Zero. Andy Bethune (00:08:17): So the strategy role in an agency really revolves around being that person who can come into, into a client, listen to a client, explain some of the challenges that they're facing or the opportunities that they see, and really articulate those opportunities into a marketing opportunity. So a lot of times, one of the things we talk about in an agency is the difference between a client brief and a creative brief. A client will often come with something that they're trying to achieve or a problem that they see, but to get a creative team working on that problem, there's a whole step in the middle that involves uncovering insights and specific opportunities. So one of the things that we use as a strategy team is we write creative briefs where we take the input from the client, run it through a series of filters, do a bunch of background research, try and understand the target audience, really try and understand what it is about the brand and the strategy or positioning that that brand has, apply some cultural filters or filters about what's currently going on in society and look at competitors, bring that all together to create a strategic direction. (00:09:31): And that's sort of the role that myself and the other strategists on our team play is really being able to translate the client's ask into something that inspires a creative team to go away and come up with an interesting campaign idea or an interesting content idea or video series idea. It's interesting to look at it in the world of video because there are a number of production companies out there, and I know Cole, this is something that you are in the space and work a lot in, is trying to take things and understand, Hey, how does this video actually solve a business problem? And that's something that we do as strategists as well. It can be good to come up with an idea, this would be a cool video to go produce this and tell this story, but it's like, how do we actually connect that story or that piece of video content back to some kind of marketing objective? How do we understand how it's going to impact the customer's perception of us? How do we figure out how we're actually going to put that out into the market in a way that people are going to watch it or discover it? Yeah, I'm glad you asked that because as you were asking me that previous question, I realized something that's an interesting thing to speak about as it relates to why brand, why there's this intrinsic value in brands is that there's a lot of different types of brands and different reasons that people use brands, but one of the things that's common in the outdoor space is something we call an identity brand. And what that means is that I choose this brand because it helps me communicate something about myself and my identity. And there's a lot of value in that for people because a lot of people like to think that they don't, and there are people that don't make a ton of conscious decision about the brand of shirt that they wear or whatever, but most of us, whether it's conscious or subconscious, put a lot of time and energy into thinking about how we present ourselves to other people, what other people think about us, how the image that we portray to people, all those kinds of things and identity brands really leverage that to say a, to say, Hey, look, this is what our brand stands for. (01:04:14): This is what we represent. If you feel the same way or if you share these values and you want other people to know that these are your values, then we're the brand for you. And Carhartt's an interesting example of that. I think there's a lot of people that like that brand because they might not be doing a ton of welding or tree felling or something, but they like the idea of hard work and these classic All-American values, and that brand represents something to them. But if you go and look at that same opportunity and evaluate it against a really clean articulated brand platform and think about does it make sense with our values, does it make sense with our purpose? It might make you rethink that decision. And it might not always be a popular decision with stakeholders and with board of directors and things like that, but it's a long game. Branding is a long game, so sometimes you have to make sacrifices in the short term to achieve those long-term gains.

It was still really small. So our thought was, if we are going to really make a go of this, this is our golden opportunity. The company I was with was generous enough to give me a little bit of a stipend, a COVID stipend when I left. (09:04): So we had a little bit of money to live on and I had the time and opportunity to work on the business, but our thoughts went too, well, we have these other brands that we're carrying, but I didn't see a path forward and how to be competitive with all of the other stores out there. And our thought went to, let's develop our own brand further. Let's invest in ourselves and try and get the Alpen Field brand up and going. And so we sat down and developed a line of breakfast products. And so that was our summer. I guess this happened in July of 2020, and my last day was the day before Independence Day. And then we were full-time on ALP and Fuel after that.

content:
Cole Heilborn (09:48): So pre COVID, you were running Al and Fuel kind of this side hustle that you were distributing other products through your e-commerce store. Then COVID happens, you lose your job, and then within a couple of days you said, Hey, well, I might as well just try going full-time with Alpen Fuel. When you lost your job or when you were thinking about leaving your job, did you ever have the intention of turning Alpen fuel into your full-time job?

Shaun Durkee (10:18): Since the beginning? That's always been in the back of our minds, but we had never, I guess had what I thought was a great product idea or the timing was never quite right. We were trying to grow it steadily over time, and then all of a sudden it's like, okay, we're not ready to jump to this business, but we have to. So let's see how quickly we can scale this thing. And so in the months leading up to the layoff, I guess certainly I'd been thinking about other product ideas and whatnot, but we didn't really have a clear direction at that point. So that kind of crystallized, I guess with the layoff. And over the last, or the four months after that, when it took us four and a half months is all to get a product line off the ground, which I think was pretty quick compared to some of the other companies that are out there. (11:05): And they may spend one to two years. But we picked a simple product line that we could get off the ground fairly quickly and then just spent every waking minute trying to push that to completion. And so that process was fairly interesting. We had a lot to learn with it, but we picked, our products that we picked were just simple breakfast granolas, and so they're baked products and there's other products on the market that I liked, but I was trying to improve, I guess coming from an engineer mindset, I was trying to get my wishlist of everything that I wanted in the product and then trying and check all of the boxes. And so we have a product that contains powdered milk, so you can prepare it with hot or cold water. It's ready in five minutes. And then we combined a lot of fats with the carbs so we could get a really high calorie to weight ratio. (11:57): So the breakfast that we designed are 630 to 770 calories. They're the biggest, largest by calorie breakfast on the market out there. And they're really designed for endurance activities like through hiking or people who are putting on a lot of hard miles every day, back country hunters, that sort of thing. So we developed that product.

content: Shaun Durkee (10:18): We picked four recipes and then sent them out to our test group, and we had everybody from hunters to ultralight backpackers, and we had one endurance coach, a Montana endurance coach that coaches cyclists and ultra runners and that sort of thing. So we had a great group to give us feedback. We iterated quickly and then continued on with the process. And that process, there's nothing really written down that I could tell about how to develop a food product. We just got in it and started throwing punches I guess. (12:54): But we knew that we would need a label and nutrition facts and all of that. So we contacted a lot of design folks and got quotes between 10 and $40,000 to design four pouches, and that just wasn't in the cards for us to pay that much money. So we backtracked and actually I jumped in with a bunch of YouTube videos and bought Adobe Illustrator and with the help of some other marketing folks that I'd made connections with, just got in and started making the design for the pouches. So we got that ready and then we tried to submit it to the state, and in that application form, it outlines a bunch of other things that we needed. So they told us, well, you need to take food safety courses. We got that lined out. We had to send the food to a lab in Oregon to get tested for shelf stableness and a whole bunch of things like that. (13:50): We got set up through the city county and got a kitchen lined up that we could produce out of to rent by the hour. And so those four months were just filled with those type of tasks. But it's nothing obviously is as straightforward as it seemed. Every step of it was a little bit harder than I thought it'd be. Just if, for example, the nutrition facts on the back of every food product from the FDA, there's 132 page PDF that governs what can be in that nutrition facts and the food labeling in general, the label, the front and the back of the pouch. So we had to mine through that, figure out our tech sizes, fonts, what words we could and couldn't use all of that. So that was an interesting learning process there.

content:
Shaun Durkee (10:18): But eventually four months later, we were able to get off the ground and get our first sales and get product into the hands of consumers.

Cole Heilborn (14:46): That's incredible. When you look back, is it pretty mind blowing, seeing how much you were able to get done in that short amount of time? I mean, you're listing packaging, kitchens, all of the testing, all of the certifications that you need to go through. What was that like?

Shaun Durkee (15:04): It was fairly arduous, I guess. Just we didn't know what we didn't know. So we went through the food safety class and tried to submit our labels and they said, well, where's how many? I don't remember. It's parts per million or whatever. What's your water activity level on this food? It's got to be below a 0.8 or whatever the cutoff is. And I said, well, tell me more about that. I wasn't aware we needed that. So then we talked to the state labs and everything and got that approved. I think we had all of the motivation to do it in a short amount of time. I mean, this is everything financially for us was riding on this, getting this off the ground. And so we had every motivation in the world. I finally had carte blanche time-wise to just spend all the time that I had been working at my prior job. (15:56): Everything was freed up just to work on this one task of getting this thing off the ground. So we put everything we had towards it and it went fairly quickly. But yeah, lots more steps than I realized. We had to look at maybe almost 10 commercial kitchens before we landed on one that we liked that we could work under their management well and so on. So I think having all that time was a blessing, and I never could have done that if I was employed full-time somewhere else. It took, you hate to say it, but I don't think the part-time was ever going to become a full-time while I was working somewhere else. It took a big event like this to just get it jump started and allow me to put all my effort and time onto it. So it's been a blessing for sure from that regard. But now that we're trying to introduce a second product line and doing research towards that, we have some ideas about the products, but now that we're in full production mode with the granola, we don't necessarily have as much time to invest. So I'm seeing the difference now that I don't have as much time. It's certainly a clearer path to get to the end, but just finding all the time now is more difficult.

content:
Cole Heilborn (17:09): How does your connection, you alluded to it, how does your connection with your interest and your passion for engineering, which has been up until recently, your focus I guess, was that a natural transition for you? And if so, could you kind of break that down? How does engineering apply to food manufacturing?

Shaun Durkee (17:32): That's a great question. My background specifically, like I mentioned, was working in the aerospace with fifth Boeing and then more recently with flir. They're out of Portland where we built the laser optics. They're largely assembly operations, and those type of companies don't have to do a lot of marketing because they make something that just a handful of companies in the world make. So people come to you, they do a couple trade shows a year, but they're well known in the industry. And with food, it's more of a commodity. So I really had to wrap my head around that. I guess the manufacturing side, I'm well versed in how to make things more efficient there, at least how to think about it. I was able to cost the products out nicely. That might be a struggle for someone, but that's the world I lived in was how profitable are these things? (18:25): What are our margins? How can we tweak things to be more profitable? So that was a fit, but the marketing side, how to do a newsletter, thinking about social media, running online, giveaways, that part was foreign. I had a lot of learning there to do some of the design aspects, but the networking side, I wasn't completely foreign to. I know a lot of engineers tend to live in a bubble maybe, and they do design, but that was never, I picked industrial engineering because it's the most people oriented version of engineering. So I was schooled in business classes and things of that nature, but while I was working at FLIR Systems, I was in charge of interacting with all of the dealers isn't the right word, the suppliers that we had that put coatings on our optics or machined them in certain ways. So I was used to dealing with a lot of different things, a lot of different irons in the fire. And so right now I am dealing with dozens of companies throughout the weeks. And so that part I really enjoy and is more of a natural fit based on my background. But I'd say the type of engineering background that I have was well suited for where I'm at now.

Cole Heilborn (19:41): Yeah, that's interesting to see how those dots connect. So I'm curious, you mentioned a couple years ago you started the food box subscription

Shaun Durkee (19:53): Deal,

Cole Heilborn (19:54): And one of the reasons why that wasn't successful is because, as you said, no one really knew that you existed. How do you get the word out now about Alpen fuel if that's a challenge you faced with the previous business going into Alpen Fuel a year ago? content: Shaun Durkee (20:33): That's a great question. Just to give people a little bit of perspective or context on the subscription box. Like I said, we ran that for 10 months, and this is embarrassing to admit, but I haven't even really shared this with anybody. The best month that we ever had on that was selling nine boxes. It was pathetic. We lost money on it every single month. We gave more boxes away than we ever sold. There was other companies out there that maybe the person that ran them maybe had a podcast, so they had an audience to market to. We had a hundred newsletter subscribers when we started the business. And so our sales reflected that it was, we weren't prepared. I didn't fully understand the effect of our reach at that point. You just assume that you create a product that has value and people will flock to it. (21:30): And I was dead wrong on that. So I had a lot of growing up and learning to do there. So over the course that first year, we didn't really grow our newsletter subscribers that much. We just tried a few things and stuck with the business model of having the online store. And then it was in the second year, 2019, where we decided, okay, we really need to get more eyes on our brand. Nobody knows who we are. We're still completely unknown, we're still unknown at this point, but at least we have a little bit of a following. So that year, I decided after doing some research that online giveaways with social media would be a way that we could grow our following. And so we started doing those Instagram only type of giveaways in the beginning with two or three brands, and I just slowly leveraged my way. (22:22): I picked a brand that we had in our store and they said, sure, let's do one. And we got a couple hundred Instagram followers out of that one, and they'd be 30 to $40 worth of product, and we'd leverage that into more brands. And then I decided after more reading, if we are going to grow our newsletter following, which appears to be one of the best options for direct to consumer sales, far better click through rates and sale rates than just an Instagram post, for example, if we're going to do that, we need to get a much bigger newsletter following.

content:
Shaun Durkee (20:33): So we switched over to doing bigger giveaways with companies, and the first one we did, I think was in August of 2019, and my thought process there was, we're the smallest guy in the room. Why should anybody work with us? We're not going to get invited to any giveaways with other companies. (23:16): We've got to do this ourselves. And so I took it upon ourselves, my wife and I, just to kind of lead the charge there. And so we started doing not quite monthly giveaways, but several throughout a year where I went out and I took on, we went through gleam.com, I guess is our first one, but that's just, they help create the landing page and the code that you can embed in your website to collect email addresses for these giveaways. So instead of just getting Instagram likes, we just thought, well, let's do a much bigger prize and collect this data from people and get their email. So that's what we did, and it's worked really well. We've done that now, this'll be our second year in doing that, but it's been great. We're actually launching a giveaway next week, excuse me, two weeks out, and it's going to be 14 brands and about 3000 in prizes. So I was looking through folks that have been on your podcast and saw a lot of folks I've worked with from oru, kayak and Duckworth and Clean Canteen and others. So we just try to leverage our network, get these other brands online and give away much bigger prizes. And so that drives website traffic for us. We get recognized with our logo alongside all of these other big brands, and it adds legitimacy to who we are, but people still don't realize that I'm creating those campaigns in my guest room here at a fly tying bench.

Cole Heilborn (24:55): Oh my gosh, I love that. I love that idea of trying to ladder up and play a league up from yourself. Yeah, I think that's sometimes what it takes. That's pretty cool to hear that that's worked out for you, and that hasn't been something that you've looked at and said, ah, I don't want to try to go and ask that bigger brand if they want to partner with us. But just having the gumption to go out and reach out I think is pretty cool.

And now we've got folks that have been in three, four or five, six giveaways with us. So we're helping brands now that we're kind of a middle player as far as newsletter size goes, we can help brands that have zero following by getting them involved in the giveaways too. content: Shaun Durkee (26:40): We learned, I guess when we did our product launch for our granola last October, we did a presale for two weeks. And so now that we had a good track record with these people, we'd been emailing them a couple times a month. They knew who we were. When we decided to tell people that the best email response we've ever gotten was the one that I sent out that said, we're creating a food brand. And that was the one where it was just a lot of texts telling people, here's what's happened in our lives. We've got laid off, but we're going all in on this opportunity to create our own food products follow along with us. And so we kept people updated on that leading up to our launch, and we had a tremendous response launching a product in November in the dead season. We were just overjoyed with the response that we got, but at that point, we were marketing to thousands more people than we were when we launched our brand back in 2018. And these people had followed along with us, and really the story resonated with them. So it was night and day, I guess, from when we launched the company to our first product launch a couple years later. So that was tremendous. And then this year as we develop new products and bring on new brands into our store, we can communicate that immediately with people, and they're obviously people that have consented with us to a market to them. So it's a great audience and a low cost for us to do that.

content:
Shaun Durkee (29:20): That's a great question. I would say my mindset, my wife and I when we were in college or when we got married, rather, we totaled up how many jobs we'd done between us, and I think the total was between 30 and 40 at that point. It was crazy. I've always been interested in random things. In college, I worked at a feed store selling pig food, and I had never pig and cow food, grain bags, that sort of thing, bird food, dog food, and I'd never been exposed to any of that. So I tried to learn as much as I could so that I could sell people the right products. I worked as a bank teller. I worked for a log home company, just a crazy amount of things, putting in sprinkler systems, so I wasn't a stranger to learning new things. And I think I changed jobs a lot in college out of necessity, I guess seasonal jobs, that sort of thing. (30:19): But when I worked for Boeing for two years and then at the Optics company for nine, those were the longest jobs I'd had by a long shot. So I am used to bouncing around and learning new things. I don't consider myself really a stereotypical engineer. I have some of a mindset for design of buildings or something like that, but I'm more scatterbrained than that, I guess. I like to go in different directions and learn new things. So it was fine for me to, I knew the resources were there on YouTube or talking to other marketing folks. I'd say I've gained a lot of respect for other entrepreneurs and folks in the marketing community because now it was an unknown to me. Like I said, working for big companies, my whole job was to make production lines more efficient. I didn't get involved in the marketing side or the trade show side or social media or any of that. So it was just this complete unknown, I guess, for a lot of years. And I had some inklings about it, but jumping into it has been a lot of fun. I've learned a tremendous amount. And like you said, marketing's one of those bottomless topics that changes frequently, and it's tough to be on top of, but it's one of my favorite parts of working as an entrepreneur.

Cole Heilborn (31:42): Where do you want Alpen fuel to go? What's the goal? What's the vision?

content:
Shaun Durkee (31:47): The vision for our company in the near term would be just to be sustainable. We're still working towards being profitable, and we're still in that investment stage. So we invested all last summer in the business. We were building ahead on products for the winter and going into the trail season, and we're just looking to have the biggest or the best trail season that we can have this year and introduce other products so that we just have a more diverse array of things that we can sell folks and be valuable for them on their trips. So in the near term, I'd say this year that's the goal is just to get through our first trail season so that we have better forecasting going into next year. We know how to make our products and know what to expect really, and then just continue to add products and expand our dealer network. That's one part of the puzzle that I've worked on this winter with the help of some other folks, how to expand our dealer presence. And so that's been uppermost in my mind. We're in about eight different stores right now, so still just a lot of potential to grow what we have, and so we'll just look at different ways to capitalize on that.

Cole Heilborn (33:04): And just to be clear, remind me again, but it's just yourself and your wife that are every week, week in, week out, making the food, baking the food, packaging, and then distributing, right?

Shaun Durkee (33:17): Yes. We're doing everything from top to bottom, so we share half and half the load in the kitchen. We work mornings in the kitchen, and it's actually a restaurant that sells food to kind of a pay as you go operation for folks that are low income. And so they work afternoons creating meals for those folks for dinnertime. And then we just rent the kitchen in the mornings. So we're in there four days a week currently. And yeah, it's just my wife and I splitting the tasks, shipping everything and trying to hustle every day.

Cole Heilborn (33:53): Wow. A year ago, did you ever anticipate yourself being in the position you're in now?

Shaun Durkee (33:59): Absolutely not. No.

We want to make sure that this channel is just eyeballs impressions, and then demand capture would be basically more of the paid stuff or so really close to conversion, lower in the funnel and identifying, okay, if we know Facebook, we're never going to make a sale off of Facebook, but it's a pretty cheap way to get a million impressions. Okay, what's next? From there, then we can say, okay, I want to make sure I've got a million impressions on Facebook and on Instagram, and we're not worried about getting site traffic. So I think those are good goals that each one of your team members can come back with. Okay, do we think this channel will drive sales yes or no? If it's no, what can it do for us? If it's yes, how do we do that? And then so look at that in that way. You're not disappointed when you only get a hundred dollars of sales from Facebook, but in the whole click path, Facebook might've attributed to the awareness of that product and the whole what do you have to show somebody something seven times where they purchase or something like that, whatever changes every day, whoever you're reading. But it's like that reinforcing sort of thing. I think that's really important to look at. (00:46:00): And again, it doesn't have to be overly complicated or super granular. It can just be like, my goal here is to get video views and that will be awesome if we get video views and that could be a success because I don't think it needs to be all tied to revenue because once you tie everything back directly to revenue, you start to commoditize your brand and you lose some of the brand and the fun of it all and why people are really engaging with your content in the long term.

I guess depending on what that is, but it is a great place, and I think we were fortunate to move there just as the village was being built and to be in Whistler while all that development and transformation was happening. It was a super exciting place to be, and it is a special place just in terms of its access to the amazing skiing and now mountain biking and all kinds of other outdoor activities, and its proximity to everything else in the area. It's a special spot, for sure.

Cole Heilborn (02:19): Yeah. Well, I want to give a quick shout out to David Bergoff from RA for connecting us. If folks haven't listened to his episode, it came out a few months ago. I highly encourage it. We talked about leadership in the marketing department, how to be a leader, but David was kind enough to connect us, Rob, and we got to chatting, and I'm just super excited to dive into story. Our topic for today, we're going to talk in about an event, we're going to talk about Crankworx, which is a pretty phenomenal event that I think a lot of folks are familiar with on this show. Maybe they've been to it, they've probably watched it or at least heard of it. But I'd love to kind of dive into this event. We're going to talk about marketing, we're going to talk about experiential marketing and the intersection between all of these different pieces. But Rob, I'd love to hear a little bit more on your background and your relationship. I guess what was your involvement with Whistler? What was your relationship with Crank Works and how did all that get started?

Rob McSkimming (03:18): Yeah, because worked there for so long, it's a bit of a long story, but I'll try to get to the point as quickly as I can. So as I said, I moved there in 19 80, 81. I actually started as a ski instructor, so that was my background on the ski side of things. I claim I was the first ski instructor to actually be hired the year that glaucoma opened. So that's how far back that goes. And then at that time, glaucoma was new on the scene. The resort was just developing summer in the resort was, it was non-existent in terms of actual business and that sort of thing. And so over time, I worked in a variety of positions on the ski snow school side of things. Eventually kind of moved into the sales and marketing area for a while with Blackcomb. And then after the company's merged, it was from Black merged into one company. (04:20): I got involved in this position, which is kind of unique in, and I think kind of a good thing, but kind of unique in the ski industry, at least as their business development manager and eventually the VP of business development there. So that role, it was interesting in the sense that I had some pretty big operating responsibilities, but also it was a position that was designed to help develop the kind of experiential side of what the company was able to do and what the company was able to offer. So operating side was really, snow School was the biggest part of it. Got involved in all of our major events, which is the connect into Crank Works. And then as Summer was developing, I was really involved in that in developing the kind of experiences that we could diversify into and build into in terms of the things that we could actually do on the mountain. And so the mountain bike park was, mountain Bike Park was a big part of that. And yeah, that's kind of the short version.

Cole Heilborn (05:32): So when did the mountain bike park first open?

content:
Rob McSkimming (05:36): Yeah, the story there was as mountain biking was developing kind of in the early nineties, there was a little bit of, at the beginnings of, I call it 1.0 lift access, mountain biking 1.0. So there was a little bit of lift access, mountain biking actually on both mountains was and black home at that time. They were competitive. They hadn't merged at that point, but it was pretty limited. Largely ride your hard tail bike up and spandex and kind of ripped down some fire roads, was kind of how it was. Early on, Whistler began offering some guided tours, and that was actually a third party company called Back Roads. And the owner of that company, Eric White, was kind of responsible for the beginning of building some of the first kind of purpose built lift access actual mountain biking trails on Whistler Mountain. And so he was involved in that for a few years in the mid 1990s. And then in 1998, the Fitzsimons chair was built on Whistler Mountain and that basically that construction took place in the area where all the lift access mountain biking was taking place at the time. So essentially that put the park on hold for that year. And then in 1999, we took over the operation of the park sensing that there was a bigger opportunity for the company there. And so we began operating as a whistle mountain bike park as we know it today in 1999.

Cole Heilborn (07:18): Okay, gotcha. So tell me a little bit about the origins or the idea for the beginning of Crankworx, because it was born out of Whistler, correct?

Rob McSkimming (07:27): Yeah, yeah, absolutely. I mean, from when we opened it to when the first year of Crank Works, which was 2004, so in five years it turned into something completely different than where it started in 1999. We were just kind of in that nexus of the evolution of Free Ride mountain biking, the change in actual mountain bike construction and bigger bikes, heavier bikes, bikes that were more suited to the kind of rugged downhill mountain bike style or mountain bike terrain that we had in the park. And so we were involved with trying to figure out how to develop the right kind of experiences in this rapidly, rapidly changing world. And I think we were just lucky to be in the right place at the right time. You had this huge scene that was building, these bikes are getting bigger. The Lift access was a solution for getting those bikes up so people could do what they wanted to do. (08:43): And then a big part of that was we were ski people that needed to try and figure out the business of mountain biking or the recreation or the sport of mountain biking. And so we definitely, again, we're fortunate to be able to connect with a lot of people who were much more involved in it than what we were, whether it's athletes, media, different suppliers that helped us along the way. And so part of that was actually developing the writing experiences, but then the other part of that is to develop the events and programs and other activities and get people really engaged in the experiences that we're building. And so Crank Works kind of evolved out of, in 2004, evolved out of having a number of different mountain biking events over, geez, I don't know, probably 10 years in Whistler starting from Cactus Cup and up through a bunch of other events until we tried to pull them together or tried to pull a bunch of these things together into what was an event designed to bring together all the different riding styles and attributes that the park had at the time. So that was how it kicked off in 2004. Okay.

Cole Heilborn (10:04): So gotcha. So it was really just trying to organize everything that had been happening on its own.

content: Rob McSkimming (10:50): Right, yeah. Like I said, just a rapidly changing journey that if you look back on 2004 or 2003 when we were thinking about it and to see what it's become today, you never would've really been able to see exactly what it became. But I'll see if I can remember some of the key moments. It really probably predated a little bit Crank Works where we had the Joy Ride Biker Cross was probably the first sort of big free ride oriented event in Whistler. And then as part of that, we did this little dirt jump competition, which was really the thing that led to the development of slopestyle. And so it was pretty cash, but we just saw with this dirt jump thing, just the number of people that came and how excited they got, there's something there. And again, working with a variety of different athletes that happened to be in the area, again, people that are really on the cutting edge of what's going on. (12:06): We started to work on this slopestyle concept, so that's probably, you look at where that is today, you go, wow, that's really come a long way. And you look at the courses, you look at what the athletes are doing, and it blows me away to this day you think, okay, it can't get any more amazing than the last event, but then you see the next event and everything stepped up yet another level. So that was pretty amazing. Other things that we did, we aired downhill. So obviously ALINE was a big part of the Whistle Mountain bike park, and it's something that we wanted to be able to bring to life in an event. We came up with this concept of running a timed event on a jump course, which hadn't really been done at that time. And now you look, there's a tour, right? There's an air downhill tour. (13:09): So that's pretty cool. One that I think was pretty interesting development was we sort of brought back dual slum, I forget what year it was. So we brought back dual slo, but I think we probably took the course to a little different level building in little bigger features, things that were a little larger in terms of their size. And we had, it's one of these things where a mistake actually led to something really cool.

content: Rob McSkimming (10:50): So we had Major, when we started the event, it was on a small budget, so we were working on the timing of dual salon, which can get kind of complicated given bracket stuff. And so the timing totally messed up, completely blew up. And so you had all these, and by that time we had a lot of the top pros in the world. So you had Kyle Strait, Brian LOEs, and others there, not really happy with what was going on at the time. (14:22): And so we were scrambling. And so as we were trying to figure this out, who goes against who? And it took a while, like half an hour, an hour of the, so back up just a little bit. One of the really cool things about Crank Works is it brings together all these sort of gravity oriented disciplines. And so you would have, in the dual Islam as an example, you would have downhill racers, slalom specialists, and you'd have the free ride guys. So whether it's at the time Cal Strait or others. So then as they're waiting for this thing to go, the guys are practicing the next thing. They're starting to do tricks on the jumps within the course. And so that we went, wow, that's actually kind of cool. So from that, the concept of dual speed style grew out of that mistake. Yeah, that's another beauty. (15:25): I think again, yeah, again, so much of such a fine line there. You try to stay really connected to the audience, really connecting, especially with some of the core influencers and that sort of thing, and try as best you can to make things happen. Sometimes they can be okay, I mean, it's a really cool idea, but you know what? It's just too, what would you call 'em, wild and crazy for a responsible company to get involved in. So finding those balances has always been something that we worked pretty hard on. And so the whip off was basically, I mean, it was a total underground event. It wasn't not part of the schedule. It wasn't officially sanctioned, and basically it would kind of filter out through the grapevine and they say, okay, show up on crab. Apple hits between blah and blah. And they had this completely separate from the organization of the event or the mountain for that matter, their own kind of casual competition.

Rob McSkimming (17:47): Yeah, so the history there was in the earlier Crank Works Whistle Blackcomb was owned by a company called Intrawest who owned a variety of resorts in North America. And one of the resorts that they owned was Winter Park in Colorado, and Winter Park was a great mountain biking destiny or is a great mountain biking destination with the mountain bike park that they were working hard on growing and establishing. So we were part of the same company. We were involved in working with them, giving them some of our thoughts and ideas as far as that's concerned. And then it just made sense, okay, we're the same company. We're trying to do the same things with the interest in Crank Works, both from an audience standpoint, a sponsorship standpoint, there's definitely an opportunity to move into the US and certainly some of our sponsors like sram for example, with David, the opportunity to move into the US just would make some sense. So that was sort of the first second Crank works, I guess. (19:09): And that lasted for a little while, and then some things changed and they decided they wanted to kind of go in their own direction, which was great. It totally made sense. But in the meantime, so that sort of thought of having more than One Crank Works was born. And then I would say the other thing that was happening there, as Crank Works became a bigger and bigger player on the world stage, we had more and more people coming to Whistler and going, this is a cool thing, how can we learn from it? But then more than going, Hey, could we do one of these at our place? So I guess part of it was we thought it would be an interesting way to continue to promote Whistler and the Whistler Mountain Bike Park on the world stage. The other side of it was we had people coming to us and saying, Hey, what do you think about this? So we gathered our team and tried to figure out how we could do this, and that was the beginning of the World tour,

Cole Heilborn (20:10): And Crankworx is coming back in 2022. And where is it stopping?

Cole Heilborn (20:45): So what I've found really interesting, and I think one of the things we chatted a little bit about is, well, one, aside from the fact that the event just kind of happened kind of naturally, but as you said, it kind of happened by accident. It seems like sometimes these types of events, I don't know, are they taken fully advantage of? Are they sometimes not considered from a brand's perspective, I guess how do brands view these types of events and how do they take advantage of them or how have they used them in the past?

content: Rob McSkimming (21:48): I do think it is funny. As we were starting these things, part of our vision for Crankworx was actually modeled after the World Ski and Snowboard festival that happens in Whistler every April and had been pretty well established at that time. So as you said, it was kind of, this was rare at the time, this mixture of sport arts called and call it entertainment, blending all those together into this one big happening. And so that was definitely part of our vision at the time. And if you look at Crankworx over its evolution as an example, there used to be a lot more music involved in Crankworx at the beginning. So there's a big stage, and music performances were a big part of it. It's kind of evolved over time, but the bringing together of all those elements was definitely a key part of it. And then I do think having these events in this resort environment really helps to bring it all together, as you mentioned. (23:00): And so if you're a brand and you're involved in an event like this, I mean, it gives you, at least that was our design. It gives you a few opportunities. So one, it attracts a lot of people. And so you've got this on, whether it's Sea Otter or whether it's Crank Works, you have a lot of your target market in one place at one time that you can display, demo, engage with people that are there. And for us at the event organizers, it was great because it added to the entertainment, it added to the value that people coming were able to get from the event. So it was one of those kind of win-win situations. And then the other thing that we worked really hard on, I think we're pioneered in terms of the mountain biking event landscape at the time was we were really hard on being able to take the action and broadcast that, or webcast that (24:13): We were pretty pioneering a little bit on the webcast side of things because broadcast was just hard. It's hard to get into, it's expensive. Whereas as web-based media was starting to happen, it gave us this opportunity to do it, well do it super professionally, but do it in a budget that was affordable. So for brands, we felt we could provide that opportunity not only to have the in-person audience, but also to have the worldwide audience. And so, I mean, I forget the latest numbers, but it's millions, millions of people turn in now versus in a resort, if you get a couple hundred thousand people over the duration event, that's the best you can possibly do. So I think there's both aspects to it.

content:
Cole Heilborn (25:04): How important is an event like Crank Works for your average bike brand as part of their annual plan?

Rob McSkimming (25:17): I think it kind of depends a little bit on the brand, but when you look at RA, for example, and they would be one of the bigger investors in Crankworx, if you like, both from the standpoint of a sponsor, but also from the standpoint of their actual activation. And so for Aram, yeah, it's big. If you look at their overall marketing plan, their overall marketing budget, it's a pretty significant portion of that for sure. I think on the mountain bike side, it kind of like Road guys would look at Tour de France, right?

Cole Heilborn (25:58): I think is really interesting is you have all these people of the right demographic in a location all participating, but at some point it goes beyond the companies that are there tabling and have their booth set up. It's part of a much bigger, it's a culture thing. How important is it for brands to be involved in these types of culture defining events?

Rob McSkimming (26:27): Yeah, I mean I'm probably a little biased, but I'd say, yeah, I think it's really important. I think it's a really, really interesting question, really. And so it's like, okay, if you look at Pink Bike when Crankworx is on, it's a week, two weeks before, during week, two weeks after. I mean, it's dominating the news in the world of mountain biking at that time. And so I think for brands to be part of that culture being where it's happening, being associated with a place where it's evolving, the place where it's innovating, the place where the influencers are there. And so I think being associated with that, if you can catch that critical mass, if you're thinking about it from the event side, you can catch that critical Mass Boy, things really start to explode from there. But it's not easy to do because the calendar's so full. And so even as you expand Crank Works events and you have ECIF, sea Otter, you, there's a number of different places people can invest their time and money. So trying to figure that out is not super simple.

Rob McSkimming (27:53): Well, yeah, I do think there's a rub off effect to your brand. And so I think most brands, especially in mountain biking where innovation and being seen as being leaders if you like, in whatever particular segment that they're in is really important. And so I think how can you communicate that? Can you communicate that in a magazine ad? Not these days, but it is tough. You do your own videos and things like that. You can work with athletes, but the thing with Crank Works is you can bring Crank Something like Crank Works, you can bring all that together in one place. And I think Crank Works just, I think Crank Works just adds to the energy of all that. It gives you that sort of context, that sort of backdrop. And I think because people are paying attention, it increases the likelihood that they're going to tune into your message.

Cole Heilborn (29:10): So kind of coming back to that culture idea, you might have Aram tent right next to a Shimano tent and outside of that event, they're competitors. But what about, or is there anything special I guess, about the world of mountain biking that because when you get to the event, everyone's having fun, there is no sense of competition or, oh, we don't hang out with those guys trying to beat them this year. I guess what about the event or what about the culture feels that way? I guess why is that brought out?

And so I find with the event, it's not just you have the pros going out there and performing, and then you have other people watching and then you go and do whatever you're going to do. This is one where amateurs compete with pros on the competition level. This is one where if you're not watching an event, you're out riding your bike yourself. If you're not manning your booth, you're out riding the park or you're out riding the trails around. And so I just think because it's more than just the business of what you're doing, it's part of the overall, as you said, it's part of the overall culture of mountain biking. And I think that's whether you're competitors or whether you are not, I mean, I think that is a shared attitude. And so I think that's part of how people who would otherwise be pretty feisty towards one another actually can be, especially honestly, especially see it the later the evening goes and the more the party goes on. Yeah, it's a full congenial mix of people having a great time no matter who they work for.

Cole Heilborn (31:19): Well, probably because of the shared lifestyle, right?

Rob McSkimming (31:22): A hundred percent. Yeah. And again, I think that the thing with the event there is you're actually doing that lifestyle at the event as opposed to promoting that lifestyle or promoting your product, you're actually participating in the lifestyle.

Cole Heilborn (31:35): Oh, interesting. Yeah, I never considered it from that perspective.

Rob McSkimming (31:39): I think of all the people that are there, the supplier group, they're all riding, even have some people that are, maybe they're businesses in outside of a mountain bike area or an urban center or even Asia or whatever, and they may not be huge mountain bikers, but when they're there, they will definitely ride a bike. They'll definitely go try out the park. And so I think it does because of those options are all there, I think it helps to bring people together.

content:
Cole Heilborn (32:10): How important do you feel like experimental marketing is in today's world? And I know it's kind of limited for the obvious reasons, but will it become more important as more events start happening?

Rob McSkimming (32:24): Yeah, yeah, I think so. I mean, think you definitely hear a lot about how our global economy is evolving and moving more and more towards a sort of experienced economy or experiential economy. And so I think as more businesses become predominantly involved in the creation, development and promotion of experiences, you'll get more and more people figuring out how they package and promote those things from a marketing standpoint. So yeah, think it's really important. I would add to that, I think one thing that will grow or could grow in terms of the world of experienced providers is the actual, I would almost call it product development. So what are people doing on the experience side actually evolve, develop, and improve their experiences over time. And I think in the hard good side of things, there's a really clear path to that. On the experience side, I think it's still evolving and developing.

Cole Heilborn (33:35): Oh, interesting. I want to go down that path a little bit, but back up really quick. You mentioned that experiential events, that's the way that the economy is moving. How did you phrase that?

Rob McSkimming (33:49): Sorry, I just meant probably a little broader than events, but just that when you look at the percentage of, I can't remember the stats, but the percentage of the economy, call it GDP or whatever, that will be taken up by experience, call them products, is expanding. So your normal goods and services are becoming a smaller piece of that pie as the experience side continues to grow. So

Cole Heilborn (34:21): It kind of strikes me as being ironic because experiences are growing, but so is the digital world, which seamen odds at each other, but they also can compliment each other.

content:
Rob McSkimming (34:31): I do think that's an interesting point. And on the one hand, you're seeing an increase in the amount of screen time people have around the world and across every demographic you can imagine. But on the other hand, you're seeing it and you saw it pre pandemic, but you're seeing it huge during the pandemic. You're seeing this massive, massive, massive increase in people seeking outdoor home experiences, both from the recreational side and from the softer, just getting outdoors really. And so both things are happening, and I don't think they're mutually exclusive at all. I think that's a thing that we thought was the case. I think we thought that screen time would take away from outside time, but in fact, I think we're seeing people're taking their screens with them and they're going out and actually there's more, there's a greater number and a bigger diversity of people seeking those outdoor experiences. And so again, I think there's massive opportunity as a result of that.

Cole Heilborn (35:42): Okay. So take me back to your comment earlier about evolving events and comparing that to product design.
