content:
Rob McSkimming (35:50): Yeah, I think it is, whether it's events or it's the actual experiences. So I would say in the bike park, how do you, as time goes on, as rider preferences change, as bike technology changes, how do you adjust the experiences that people are having on the mountain? What's the process to get there? And then the same with events. I mean, those things absolutely connect. So as those things are changing, what's the process for you to evolve your events to meet those changing needs that are occurring as a result? And so one thing that I always found that worked well with us is making sure that you're engaging with the right people and again, just the way you would on the product side. So what kind of information are you getting? What kind of research are you doing? For us, I think a lot of it was, boy, it's changing so fast. We can't be on top of everything, but we can broaden our base, we can work with bigger teams, we can work with a more diverse group of people to try to get an understanding of where it's going and then figure it out from there and drive that process from there.

Cole Heilborn (37:15): So that sounds kind of like a bit of a chicken and egg scenario. Do we evolve the event before the sport is ready or do we let the sport evolve the event? Yeah. How do you do that? You guys think about that. Were there, I mean, I guess maybe some of those examples you gave earlier, the whip off was kind of an example of how do we manage the evolution of the sport?

Rob McSkimming (37:39): You know what, I am not entirely sure. I do know that when it comes to mountain biking, I think experiences need to play a greater role in actually driving things forward and not be the passenger. And when you do, so when you create an A line or when you create a crank works, are you creating where the culture's going or responding to it? And I always feel like it felt to me like it was a bit of a blend of everything. One thing wasn't necessarily ahead of the other, you were just all trying to keep up with one another.

Cole Heilborn (38:17): Sure.

Rob McSkimming (38:18): Curious to know how you think about it.

And I don't know if it can be so simple as I'll say it, but is it the trail that's defining the bike or is the bike change and the technology and the bike creating the momentum for the types of trails that are being built? And so that's something I've considered a lot is how does that relationship look like? What does that look like on a very granular level, on a very high level view? I don't have an answer, but it's something I've thought about for a while.

Rob McSkimming (39:08): Bringing it back to the event side of things. I mean, I do think there's something there. It becomes this incubator where all that stuff's in one place at one time. All those people are in one place at one time. And then what happens in the future that had an influence over it is hard to know. But you got to think that because that happened, things will evolve in a certain way just because everybody was in the same place at the same time doing similar stuff.

Cole Heilborn (39:38): So yeah, considering that, I guess from your role in the management and leadership perspective of the event at some point where you just like, you know what guys, we're, we're going to do the best job we can, but we're just going to be along for the ride and see what happens. It is about the people, it's about the culture, it's about the community, and ultimately they're going to help us create the best event if we structure it that way.

Rob McSkimming (40:01): Yeah, a hundred percent. Always our attitude and continues to be the attitude at the group is running it now is staying really close to that. And then as I said earlier, then the job is finding a way to make it work. I mean, there's tons and tons of ideas out there once you start coming your way through them. But the chore if you're the operator is okay, how do you make it work? I think that was always our attitude was, okay, okay, you guys think that's good? We like that. Let's try and figure it all out. We would have every year the crank works that happen, we bring together all of the main sponsors and that sort of thing and have, I would call it a bit of a presentation, but really a bit of a symposium to go, okay, here's going on here, here's what we're doing, here's what we're thinking about for the future. What are you guys seeing and how can we work together to make things happen?

Cole Heilborn (41:09): And those types of examples, how much of the success of an idea is based upon timing and the placement.

Rob McSkimming (41:16): Yeah. Yeah. I think as I say, timing's a lot, right? Timing's everything. Yeah, I think that's a huge part of it. And so you can be too soon or you can be too late. So I'll give you an example with Crank Works as it's a good way of bringing to life some of the things we were talking about earlier. So as you think of the bike technology, it goes from cross country to these bigger bikes, and then slowly those bigger bikes get lighter and smaller, and then now you get bikes that are capable of pedaling but also very capable downhill. So you get the introduction of Enduro style events that we got heavily involved in, but I would say our ability to make, we probably tried five different things before the right concept, bringing together the right bike technology and what riders really want to do from an event perspective actually jelled into place. So I think you've got to work with those groups and then try some stuff and then kind of iterate as you go through and go, okay, that didn't work. Now what do we do? Right.

Cole Heilborn (42:40): Interesting. What were some of those events? What didn't work about?

Rob McSkimming (42:44): Well, I think part of it was Enduro was happening huge in Europe, in North America. It just took a little while for people to get outside of their, I'm an XE guy or I'm a downhill guy, or I'm a free ride guy or girl. And so you remember you had Super D and Enduros could be different lengths of time and different trails and certain enduros might require a certain bike, others a different bike. And so I took a while before the concept that we now have these sort of multi-stage events with liaison stages in between that aren't timed that really kind of jelled that. So part of that was part of how we got involved with that is we became Partners, ownership partners in the endur World series when it first began. So again, working with other people to try to make this happen. So in this case, people in Europe were way ahead of us, so we ended up taking concepts that originated in Europe.

Cole Heilborn (43:56): I'm curious, so through all of this, and I know you were part of a team and it wasn't just you, but I guess how does it feel knowing that you played somewhat of a role in helping develop an event that those in the mountain bike industry look at and they're like, yeah, this is one of the events of the year that I'm going to.

Rob McSkimming (44:19): You know what, it was fun. I miss it. It was really fun. I'm still on their advisory board, but that means I get to talk to them once every few weeks kind of thing. So yeah, no, it was really fun to be a part of a thing. It was so dynamic and involve so many people. And yeah, there's just an energy to it when you're involved in it and you're working with a really dynamic group and you're able to accomplish some things and you're able to see. Yeah, I used to, on the slopestyle day, I used to just get out onto the event area and just walk the whole area and just really kind of soak in what was going on there. It pretty exciting to be kind part of that energy. Yeah,

Cole Heilborn (45:25): I can only imagine. But Barb, it's just making, wanting to go back as you're talking, I'm like, shoot, I can't wait until it opens up and we can go again.

Rob McSkimming (45:35): Yeah, I feel it's really too bad. And so if people are out there thinking about what to do in August of 2022, I start booking your trip pretty soon.

Cole Heilborn (46:19): What made Crank Works successful? We've talked about a few different things that were definitely important, but I guess why did it all work?

Rob McSkimming (46:27): Well? Yeah, I think there's a number of aspects. I think some, just as we've been talking, being in the right place at the right time, so a bit of good fortune I guess. And then, which I think was really important. I'm not sure if you try to start that event at the time that we did in Eastern Canada that would've caught fire just given what was going on in the areas. But then, yeah, I think again, I think the key to its success over and above that is being able to bring the right people together and then be really dedicated to working hard to be able to shape the experiences that are going to be interesting to the audiences that you're targeting. So whether that's the onsite audience, the athlete audience, it was really important to us that the industry felt really good about it. So that was another important segment. And then really on the media side also was really critical. So if you can get all of those things working well and being enthusiastic about what you're doing and providing you with good information and you're smart about how you take that information and figure out how to make it happen, it can be really big.

How many people decided, Hey, I'm going to start a mountain bike company. I'm going to start something related in that industry. I'm going to start a company because I went to this event, or how many people went to the event and were like, shoot, I'm going to start. I'm going to get on a mountain bike I've never ridden before, but this looks like really a ton of fun. I can only imagine what sort of impact that's had on people over the last, well, 15, 16 years.

Rob McSkimming (48:45): Yeah, that's interesting. Yeah. Mean how do you know? But I do think it has enough critical mass that it has had some influence, that's for sure. Whether it's on the more experienced riders or people that are kind of new to the sport. I mean on that end, I mean it's always been a goal and kind of a hard one really, is to be able to use the popularity of the event to broaden its appeal to make it more mainstream. At the same time, the things that people are doing at Crankworx are so crazy that it could actually take it in the other direction. You know what I mean? People could see it, watch slopestyle and go, man, I ain't riding a mountain bike. I'm not doing that. Yeah. And I think now with the pandemic and the number of people that are riding and getting outdoors, that group has now broadened. It's getting close to mainstream. And so now you've got this bigger audience and are the experience that you're providing, what's the messaging that you're providing and how do you adapt to that going forward?

Cole Heilborn (50:03): I guess what would you say if you were in a room full of marketers or you're just talking to our audience, which are predominantly folks in the marketing world, from the things that you've observed and helping develop Crank Works, I guess, what should folks be paying attention to? What do you think is really important for the future of the industry in relations to marketing looking forwards?

I just think it's been really amplified as a result of the pandemic. So I mean, you look at bike sales, you look at anything to do with biking sales just through the roof. And so you've definitely got this quantum uptick in the market. And so now what happens? Do those people that tried it because they had nothing because all the other recreational sports were kind of on hold, do they just park their bike in the garage and not go? So you have this opportunity to get out there and really engage with these people. And I think in some cases it might be kind of tricky because in some cases your business, it is firing. (51:32): I mean, it's through the roof. And so you could certainly make an argument that, well, we don't need to do more marketing selling everything out, but yet there is this industry opportunity there to be able to go, okay, now how do we really make this thing happen? So I think it's having a better understanding of those people that are being introduced into the sport. And then what kind of messaging should you establish for those people? How do you get them involved? And I think a really interesting way there is getting them involved on the programming side of things. So how can you get more people to participate in clinics and programs and eventually into events and things like that. And so again, all working together to do that I think will help to have those people that are trying it stay involved with it. And so I think that's a huge of each part of it.

Cole Heilborn (52:34): Interesting. So unfortunately we are coming close to the end of our time today, but so one of my last questions I guess is yeah, how is Crank Works looking at this new audience? How are you, or not you specifically, but how is Crankworx trying to include and welcome them? Is that something that's being considered?

So I mean, if you look at prize money, prize money is the same women and men, you look at podiums, men and women are on the podiums, so doing a lot to try to grow that female side of the market. Cole Heilborn (54:24): Interesting. Well, awesome, Rob. Yeah, again, I'm super excited to come up and visit the next event. I appreciate you taking the time to chat today. It's been great to learn more about how the event got started. I think I know when I showed up I was like, this is just cool. I have no idea how it began, but I appreciate you shed a little bit of light on that. Rob McSkimming (54:59): Yeah, thank you. It's been fun. It's great walking down memory lane again.

content: Jordan Todoroff (03:55): So IEX was an icon brand, really founded kind of the birth of the Merino movement. So synthetics were on the rise throughout the sixties, through the eighties primarily they became pretty affordable to produce and companies jumped on with that, right? Some real legendary outdoor brands took those and ran because they gave performance characteristics that people needed, right? The ability to wick moisture, dry quickly, stretch, and move with our bodies as we need to temperature regulate those kinds of things. So they became really cheap and they got the job done. But in the early nineties we started to realize that this sheep, the Marino, which is very likely the oldest breed of sheep on earth, naturally grew this fiber. That's an absolute miracle. So it wicks moisture, it dries quickly, it temperature regulates, stretches and moves through your body, all just designed by nature. So really phenomenal characteristics and obviously there's a great environmental story there to be told. (05:02): And the fact that you're not deriving it from petroleum and brands started to realize that this could be used to keep you cool in the heat and warm in the cold both. And as it dries and wicks that moisture weight, it actually prevents bacterial and microbial growth so it doesn't stink like other fabrics do. So you're able to use one piece for this huge variety of different applications. So in the early nineties we started to realize what a miracle fiber this was. And two gentlemen on the East coast based out of Vermont took this idea and really fell in love with the fact that this was when we consider the fact that polyester and nylon have been developed for 40 and 70 years, somewhere in that category. But renal fiber is the oldest breed of sheep likely on earth. You think about the amount of time that goes into that design and the consequences if the design is bad, if you're a bad scientist, you get fired. (06:04): If you're a bad sheep, you die. So nature is quite the teacher and yeah, two guys who love the outdoors and saw the potential in this ran and built this apparel brand that gained incredible traction throughout the us.

(07:11): And it went through several iterations as the company grew and changed and flexed over time, they made phenomenal, pretty legendary cycling gear and they made garments for backcountry skiing and mountaineering, but a lot of firsts. That's what I think when I think of IEX in the Marino sphere, I think of a lot of firsts. So really pioneering things like seamless construction, windproof, highly water resistant, a hundred percent merino textiles, a lot of real textile innovation. And the company grew and changed over time. And unfortunately in the end of 2017, early 2018, IE started to wind down and came to a close. And so that's where Bonnie came into things.

I loved the product and I remember receiving an email that said that IEX was going to be relaunched and I could be invited to this Facebook page, which has gotten 13,000 followers or something. It's a huge following of IEX Insiders. And then another secondary group founded itself called the IEX Junkies because people were obsessive. And so Bonnie really threw herself into those groups to get feedback and to stoke and ignite that excitement for the brand. If you go through, I mean if you type in ivex closed, you'll just see article after article that the comment sections are filled to the brand with people saying, I've got my pieces from 15 years ago and saying how sad they were. (18:04): That was their favorite brand going under. So we've tried to be really good about listening and making sure that feedback was heard by people. We're a brand of real human being people and we care about discussions and think collaboration is how we excel. Like we said, IEX is really founded on that idea of relationship and community and that was all the way from consumers, wholesale partners, international partners, the team itself. And some of that did get lost towards the end, especially with cutting off wholesale accounts. And we are still, I'd say the thing that we love most about Ibex 1.0 is relationships. We believe in working with people and being good teammates and good partners in this symbiotic relationship of making a brand and making a company. It's a huge team effort and there's no way we can do it on our own. So I mean, I respond personally to customer service tickets way too late at night, but we're entrenched. (19:09): Bonnie I know is responding to customer service tickets today and generally that's not something that falls within our types of scope for our roles, these job titles. It's very rare that you would have someone even acknowledge customer service tickets or even interact heavily with the customer service team. But I mean, Bonnie's gone out to coffee with people. I write to people on LinkedIn, I have phone calls with old customers and old partners and really just pouring into that to make this give and take a real open communication. And sometimes that communication is us saying, we're actually not going to bring that product back. We loved it too, but it wasn't functional. Bonie Shupe (20:18): I personally think that the community was born well, one, because the people who ran Ivex really cared so much that it was obvious to all customers and they were drawn to it, but also because the product was more elite. And that is something that I have continued to try to push. I really truly believe that Ives brings the Merino product to the market and I will continue to push for that every day.

Jordan Todoroff (20:54): And I think iex also, when I think about the brand, one of the most iconic stances I think is that IEX was one of the early companies to pull out of. And they had a strong belief in a variety of things, but they weren't scared to take stances where they felt was important for the outdoors. They were original founders of early partners with the renewal workshop and with Conservation Alliance really involved in passion projects about their environmental footprint was huge for iex. They took it very seriously and they took defending outdoor spaces very seriously. And I think when you see brands of real people, like Bonnie was saying, it was a passion project. This company, it was founded, it was somebody's baby. And when you have a team that's so deeply involved and so passionate about their own love of the outdoors plus products that they want to use, they're actually and consumers of, it's something special and it's something you don't see very often. They were the stakeholders, right? At the end of the day, it was the product they wanted to use. And so they weren't pitching for someone else. It was the company they wanted to run, wanted to be a part of, wanted to purchase from. And having that big holistic cycle mix, a very different type of company.

And we took that distilled information and we built it into what we internally we call our brand pillars, but we took those real core essential elements of what made the company work and what made it special and make sure that our decisions are interpreted through that lens. That's an important one for us, that there's a real timeless aspect, I think is a real defining characteristic of the first IEX iteration mindset over a skillset is also kind of developed from their original iteration, but it's the idea that we work with people who love the outdoors and who care about the things that we care about. So you make this, not only do we have a community who's already there, and I totally misspoke, it's 8,500 people in the insiders group, but not only do we continue those people, but when we make partners, we try to choose partners who share the same values that we have. And when you rely on that, those buys that you've made originally for your own company's finances, that's a huge slap in the face and especially if you've worked with someone for almost 20 years. So I feel excited to come in and I've had a lot of conversations with these shop owners and say, my first thing is just apologizing. And while it wasn't my mistake, right? Well, we didn't make those decisions for the first iteration of Ibex. I'm still sorry for what they did because I've experienced those kinds of things and it's pretty devastating and it's hurtful and it's pretty disrespectful. (31:43): And our goal is to be respectful, good partners who can under promise and overdeliver. So we are currently slugging through that. We talk about that made to last pillar. That's one of those things. And even if we love it, and even if it's a product that we as individuals really want, it has to meet that. (36:00): It has to pass that litmus test. And so on the one side, people want things and they don't understand why it hasn't come back yet. Bonie Shupe (38:30): I can tell you lie right now in the Marino space, for example, what we have currently is we have our top leading brands that have been around for a really long time, and then we have all of these new Merino brands that are coming into this space and they're rushing into the space. And those Merino brands that are rushing into the space right now aren't developing new textiles. The ones that are leading the space, they're at a point right now where they're trying to figure out how they can get to a bigger mass audience. You said the job is so much more than a job, but through the job, what lessons have you learned? I don't know about life, about yourself, about others. Is there anything that stands out?

Jordan Todoroff (44:30): Yeah, so I worked in retail for a long time, and like I said, it's a hard line of work. I've been clubbed with roofing hammers. I've had people chase me. I've had a lot of things stolen. I've worked a lot of long hours and showed up late in the night when my store was broken into or early in the morning. I've had people yell at me, but I've also had people hug me and I've learned how to respect people and understand that when they're upset, maybe it's not anything to do with you. All that to say, I'm in a very different role now than I was as a store manager and I've had to pivot a lot. But what I've realized is the core values that I learned of great customer service and building a business the right way, being willing to do the legwork, to not cut corners, to treat everyone you work with respect. (45:24): I just earnestly respect everybody that I work with at Ibex and retail workers are like, they're just kind of known those guys are running all day. And I did not expect to find people who outworked me. It's pretty rare. I tell that to my employees all the time. On day one, I'd tell my employees what I made in retail. I wasn't scared of that. And I said, because you're never going to outwork me. And I found a community iex of people who could just, I don't know how they do it. Bonnie runs an ultra marathon every day at work, and I'd say our whole team does. Our owners are absolutely slugging along just as much because we have so much passion. So I've learned that being able to mix that, just that core sense of respect for your partners and your customers and deeply caring about that and being willing to say, I'm wrong. (46:12): I messed up. I want to do better. And keeping open communication has been huge. We don't care about being right. We care about doing what's best. And I'd say a lot of that was like did come from my retail background, being able to say when I was wrong. And part of the reason I wanted to work for Bonnie is that she told me she took a fail first approach. I love that we are absolutely willing to embody that. And so personally, I've learned how important that is to be okay messing up and own it really quickly. And then as far as the sales perspective, it's just same kind of thing. It's relationships. All these guys who we care about. I've just reached out to old iex partner after old IEX partner, and for the most part, when I tell 'em my background in the industry and how I love the same things that IEX 1.0 was about, they're on board. They want those relationships. Human beings are, as much as we're changing and developing, technology is so crazy. Humans are the same as they've always been. We care about good relationships with people. We care about good communication. And fortunately for us at iex, we love the outdoors. And so such a great point that we can all get behind. So just meeting people on a human level. And I think being a company with a face means a lot to me, and I think it resonates with a lot of consumers.

content: Dave Taylor (03:39): Well, I guess we could start, we'll go chronologically in some way. Way back as Baby Dave, I landed a job as a junior production designer at an agency called Christopher Porter Guskey in Miami, which at the time was about 45 or so people. And we were working on things like Truth, which was the anti-tobacco campaign in just Florida at the time, as well as a number of bike brands. The ECD of the company is an avid mountain biker, and so got to work on Schwinn back in the day, Shimano gt, et cetera. And then that agency grew and I started becoming an art director. We launched the Mini Cooper in the United States when that got relaunched. And so it was really interesting experience watching this company go from 45 people in Miami to now it's about when I left there, there's a few hundred and now it's thousands of people around the planet, which is wild to be part of that in the very genesis of it. (04:39): From there, I bounced around just a little bit, landed at a great place in Madison, Wisconsin called Planet Propaganda, where I'd say I kind of grew up in the industry a bit. I led creative for Gary Fisher for about eight years doing catalogs and advertising videos, et cetera. And because of that, that really got me really deep into the mountain bike world and started traveling to all these amazing destinations with a level photographers. And then I'd go home and ride my home trails in Wisconsin, which while the access is great and they're fun, but when you're getting to ride on the north shore of Vancouver for a photo shoot, then you go back to Wisconsin, you're like, okay, I need a little bit more. Which then led me to moving to Seattle and bounced around to Seattle a little bit, did a stint at Amazon doing product launches globally. (05:38): So the scale of work that I was doing there was just massive, was a huge amount of education that happened during that time. Got recruited out of there to a small agency that was starting up and got to work on stuff for Frito-Lay and Mr. Coffee and a lot of more mass brand stuff. And that ran course. And I was just thinking about, well, what exactly do I want to do with my life now dad with two kids and a wife to support in a really cool city in a great place and wanted the most amount of flexibility to do the kind of work that I wanted to do, go get a powder day when I wanted it, and if the dirt's good, I could go bug out for a morning or an afternoon and go for a bike ride. And that's really the genesis of where I started. (06:26): Okay, bro, is it was really a lifestyle choice and the type of work and the type of life I think are kind of melded together quite a bit for me. And I think for a majority of creatives, they're almost one in the same in some way how they influence each other. And I wanted to see what I could do about taking the most amount of stress from the workday out of the equation. And now I'm what, almost five years? Well, a little more than five years deep as okay, bro. There's been some ups and downs and more people a part of the company than there are today, but the future's looking pretty good.

And very, or just very drunken frac guy is the bro these days. But back then it was like lowered Monte Carlos and tight Edwin jeans and lots of bass and I love that stuff, but bro is like the third word at everybody's out of all those guy's mouths. And so I just started ok bro. And that became our freelance moniker and somehow had the foresight to buy that URL on 98 or 99, and somehow that credit card never expired. Expired. And I still have it today. The cool thing about doing it right now is it turns every presentation into not a me versus you or a business type of thing. Everyone becomes human because you have a silly word up on a big screen in a fancy conference room. And so all of a sudden CEOs of companies are just like, the walls come down very simply, very simply than if I called it, I don't know, made it sound like a law firm.

Dave Taylor (08:44): Exactly. Or marketing services or something

But no, it was great to see that project come out and that's actually how we got connected and one conversation led to the next, and now here we are. So I guess we can thank Diamondback.

And as so much of the time because of bandwidth or just the willingness to roll their sleeves up, clients will let those things fall through the cracks. (11:34): But in this project, pretty much all of those ended up happening. We did this huge video. I'm really proud of the work that came out. One of my favorite things that we did was we sent pinatas to bike shops and that were filled with swag, and if they smashed the pinata and put it on their Instagram, they got entered to win a pizza party for that bike shop. That's one of those things where, yeah, there's a bunch of logistics that need to happen to make that go off, but it's one of those things where you could hit all the different touch points that they need to. It helps with the success of the campaign.

Cole Heilborn (12:10): Yeah. Oh man, that's cool to hear. So you alluded to it earlier, you said in your introduction that, okay, bro is a company of one. Let's dive into this. I think there's a lot of questions around freelancers turning their business into a business and making that transition between freelancer to agency owner, but I haven't seen a whole lot of resources out there about how do I structure my business? How do I want to think through what my business looks like? And so I'm curious to hear from you, how is your company set up and why have you chosen to set it up this way?

content: Dave Taylor (12:48): The key reason why I chose to set it up this way is keep the billings high and the overhead low, right? Because especially when you're starting out on your own, there's a lot of ups and downs that you need to be able to carry yourself through. There's going to be a month where you had four scopes go out and nothing come back or happen on time and things get pushed back. You need to be able to deal with that, especially when you're starting out. And then there's other months where, holy cow, everything happened. We're completely pinned and we're going to make a year's worth of money and six weeks. And you need to understand to be able, how you can weather those things. A big key to making sure that you're successful, I think as a solo entrepreneur is not to do everything yourself, but find great partners who are experts in what they do that you can trust and you've worked with before. (13:48): And I'm not just talking about producers and writers and other illustrators and other creatives. My favorite person on the planet is Vic at Ranta Accounting, who I pay a monthly retainer two to help me with my invoicing and taxes, bookkeeping and all those types of things. And it just keeps everything on track. And it's one of those giant monkeys that is always on your back as an independent company that you don't have to worry about every single day, right? We touch base every week, we see E, I get my p and ls from him at the end of every month, and we touch base and having an expert like that that has a network that I don't have, which then helps you find things like lawyers and mortgage brokers and insurance brokers, because out of the blue, one of your clients might say, in order for us to renew your MSA, now you need $2 million worth of business insurance. (14:50): Ask any solo designer starting out what that actually means and how much that costs or how you can even find a reputable person to do that for you. That's an entire day's worth of work. So you find those people that can help bolster your business that do what they do well so that you could do what you do well. And I think that's part of the key.

Dave Taylor (12:48): And what that starts to do is that brings a lot of value to your clients because it's totally fine for me to pick a small few thousand dollars project where we just need some lightweight creative strategy because the client's in a rut, they don't have time to come up with stuff. Let's just do three or four brainstorming sessions with an output of X, Y, or Z. If my company was 15 people, that's not a profitable way for me to spend my time. But with a small company, I have 25 years of experience working for large companies and small companies across a whole bunch of different industries. (15:52): I'd say that's valuable experience that normally a client's not going to get because when you go and hire a larger agency, that ECD, which would be my job at some agency that I worked at, you might see me, if you have 300 hours of scope, you might see me for five or six hours of that scope. And everyone else there might be super talented, but you're not going to get that same level of experience and guidance from someone that's in ECD because there's just that time to do it because they need to. Their billing is really high, but it's also spread out across five or six people.

Cole Heilborn (16:32): Sure. Gotcha. So what does your model look like now for an average project? How many are you working with contractors? You said you don't have any employees, correct?

But how projects work today, it really depends on the project and the depth breadth of it. For example, I restrict for one of the many sectors within the world of Amazon, and in that one I contracted out a writer as well as another designer. And so we tackled this together as a team. There was naming as well as visual design that's associated with it. And for a project with Amazon, they're really about option value and not deep thinking and ideas because they move so quickly, they don't have time to really dig into those things for a client like that kind of staff accordingly. Whereas the Diamondback project, which had a lot of different moving parts for that one, myself and my copywriting partner partner, we split this project up into two phases with Diamondback. So the first phase was conceptual development, and the second phase was production. (17:49): So what are we going to do? How are we going to go make it happen and then making it happen. So that first part was really just myself and my copywriter, concepting and ideating, and then myself doing a large part of the design work and collaborating with Evan and team to start to bring those things to life, and then helping them sell that whole thing internally. And so that was from the entire creative strategy. What are all the different launch tactics that we want to work through? Are we going to do teasers? Are we going to do swag? Does video make sense? How is this stuff going to land on their website? Coming with all of that type of thinking first, and then through that whole process, they're getting a good idea of what the budget is. And then once we got into the world of executing, then the team grew exponentially because we needed to produce this video. (18:46): So I have a dear friend who's a level executive producer who created that entire team. We brought in a director and a DP and an editor. We had a crew about 25 or 30 cruising around downtown Seattle. Overnight. We were shooting the video, and then we had a series of posters that we needed to create. And so hired a couple of really great illustrators to bring some of those ideas to life because as you're doing something that's across what three different categories, if everything looked like it was done with my hand, you're not going to have that extra bit of difference. So we hired a couple of different illustrators, and then we also hired a photographer, para scores, who's in Bellingham where you are, and he brought in on a producer and some talent. And we did that whole photo shoot over two days in Seattle as well. So it can expand really large very quickly, or there's other projects where it's just myself in my studio banging away on stuff.

Cole Heilborn (19:51): So essentially one of the benefits that you're describing is that you can scale regardless of the jobs need.

Dave Taylor (19:58): Yeah, definitely. And I think you're really similar to any other big air agency. When you hire a bigger agency, depending on the scale of the project, you're still really only getting a dedicated crew of three or four people. You're going to get an account manager, a project manager, but that project manager's job is really just to move it through the agency across all their other projects. And then you have a core team of creatives, usually a copywriter and an art director who are thinking about your business or the project every day. And then there's layers of approval. So then there's an A CD and a design director and a creative director who are just popping in and out for meetings, guiding the direction of stuff. So really when it comes down to it, you're still kind of getting with this tiny agency, the same people that you would get. They're the same number basically that you would get at a larger agency. Now where it gets a little bit different is let's say Nike called Nike has a basketball division, they have running division, skateboarding, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And each one of those things needs a dedicated team to work against those pieces of business. And if they don't have the layers of people above that, then there's no continuity across all of those different things people need to focus on.

Cole Heilborn (21:18): I see.

Dave Taylor (21:18): Whereas a lot of the scale of the work that I do within the outdoor industry, most outdoor brands are not even close to the scale. Even one of the sectors in business in Nike, it completely works because there just isn't the amount of marketing need and creative work for it to make sense to have that many layers and that many people working on it.

Cole Heilborn (21:40): Gotcha. So you're saying at a certain point your model doesn't work for businesses that are extraordinarily huge, but there's kind of a sweet spot for your model?

content: Dave Taylor (21:54): Yeah, there definitely is. And it's interesting because some of those larger companies like Amazon almost works as a whole bunch of tiny companies that ladder to the larger one. I mean mind, some of those little pieces of business are absolutely ginormous, but the scale and the way that that company works suits my company really well because quick, they need smart thinking really fast because everyone at the company that I've touched or worked with has a very high capacity and tend to be whip smart and have very high demands. Whereas working with the smaller brand, like say a Diamondback or even some of the sectors within Specialized, which I've worked with, it makes a lot of sense because it's just you have a partner that you could call. You have a one-to-one relationship with the person that's guiding the work. And so when my clients call, we could come up with a solution on the phone because you're dealing with the person making the work. (22:58): Whereas in some of those other places where you're dealing with a slightly larger agency, it's like, okay, you talk to the project manager, there's going to be a meeting. There might be two or three days until that meeting could get scheduled da. And so in today's world where things tend to move a lot quicker, we can move a lot quicker. And it's not because we're using buzzwords like nibble, it's because there's a phone that you can pick up and actually talk to the person doing the stuff, which also helps when you have a lot of companies, even smaller ones are bringing a lot of the day-to-day design work they can because 25 years ago, in order to bring, or 20 years ago in order to bring that work, a huge investment for graphic design costs five or $6,000. And now you could do that on a computer that costs 1500 bucks. (23:52): So just like the numbers alone makes it easier, let alone how easy it is for someone to get to that base level of competency of being able to do some work. And so there's a real, and that used to be how agencies and design companies used to make a lot of money, have this blocking and tackling type of work that was just ongoing billable retainer level work. And then you pop in every few months for a new campaign initiative where you need that strategic thinking. And so the strategic thinking is difficult for someone to do. You need that outside perspective, whereas the blocking tackling work, at some point, it's almost assembly line work. We have images that need to be set up and retouched to go onto our website. Do you need a great strategic creative director to manage that work? Probably not. You need someone with a great eye and attention to detail to do that work. And that's a little bit easier to find than a strategic creative director and less expensive too. So it makes sense to bring that work in house. And then you still need that creative thinking and that strategy to help move things where you want it to go.

Cole Heilborn (25:07): Sure. So you've described a lot of the pros. I'm curious, what are some the challenges lie underneath the surface of this model?

Dave Taylor (25:20): The downside of it is there are some days where you just don't want to do it, and there's no one to hand something off to you, and the pressure is real to ensure that your supported clients the way that you need to so that they call back for the next project, or when they leave that brand, they move on. The challenge is when you're going up against a larger agency, some people just don't trust that you're going to be able to pull that kind of work together, even with five plus years of quality work, that makes a difference in references from those clients. So that's definitely a challenge as well. But what really lies under the surface is sometimes it's Thursday and you've been grinding away and you've been really busy and you just want to talk to somebody at the water cooler. And over the last couple of years, that's been really difficult. And as things are opening up a little bit more, at least here in Seattle, and starting to feel a little bit more safe, kind of getting back to that rhythm of, oh, meeting people for coffee or having a beer at the end of the day. And that totally changes the outlook from being solo in the office.

Cole Heilborn (26:37): Sure. Yeah. Oh dude, that can be brutal. That mental health, when you're just isolated jamming away and video calls are great, and maybe you've got a Slack channel going on with your editor, but it doesn't replace the water cooler chat.

Dave Taylor (26:54): No, no. The 15 minutes of BSing in the morning while you're getting the coffee and fist bumping and making fun of each other. That happens in an agency in the morning. You do kind of miss that. And before I got my new studio space the last couple of years, I was working out of coworking space and there was a number of other small businesses working in there. So I had a little bit of that then, and I really enjoyed that. But having this kind of dedicated space is pretty sweet. That's also one of the reasons why I want to bring on some folks.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:31): How do you handle capacity? Because you're one person, and I realize a lot of the work that you guys do, you have other people helping out with it, but you're still kind of the final gatekeeper for a lot of stuff. And that comes at a cost when you only have so much time and time, sometimes not often equates to so much money. How do you manage that?

Dave Taylor (27:58): I think that goes back to having an overhead conversation because I have the power to be able to say no when it makes sense. And being smart about the work that you bring into the studio and the types of clients that you're working with. I purposely don't pursue clients or work with collaborators that I know whose hair is constantly on fire. The Diamondback Project, for example, that had a really wonderful long tail to it. And so being able to do things in the right way where your hair's not on fire on a consistent basis really allows you to work in a way where the work is better, your hair's not on fire, your capacity is manageable. There's ups and downs and things do come through, and we do help out clients when they need something in a pinch. But in general, you just have to be smart about what you say yes or no. (28:59): And knowing that you have a deep bench that you could work with. But sometimes one of my greatest joys sometimes in this business is saying no to something because I'm too busy and handing it off to a trusted collaborator or friend who then goes and crushes it and creates another great relationship because I feel like there's a lot of room at the table and everyone can eat. And I love sharing. My plate is full. There's no need to gorge. And when you're doing things the right way and you're managing your finances in a way that makes sense, and with my little office here, I totally could have dropped $6,000 on a sweet build out with bookcases and all the things, but I got my couches from an office that closed that I got for 70 bucks. It's super sweet. And then my desk is made out of a door and sawhorses. (29:55): And so it's like, but where I spend my money is on is I take vacations that have nice bikes and then my computer and everything else that I work with is completely dialed where it makes sense to spend money. And my accountant is a place that makes sense to spend money. And the amount of bandwidth that I get from having that part of my world handled for me opens up a ton of capacity where I could just earn more money. So it's having an understanding of where you spend your time that's going to be profitable, where you're going to spend your time that's going to be personally mentally profitable, and then where you're going to spend your money that's going to aid those two things to happen.

And they're like, why would we trust the small team or the solo person with a job that why trust someone who's doing it by themselves when you could have this full suite of people who are at your beck and call?

Dave Taylor (31:08): Well, I think one, there's a scale conversation there. And why didn't Kenny does hire, I mean, not wide. Nike for example, customer mentioned Wide does hire a lot of solo people to do projects, whether it's design or t-shirt designs, et cetera. But as far as a ginormous global brand campaign around the Olympics, sure, myself and my collaborators, maybe we could come up with this just as great of an idea, but then how are we going to execute $300 million worth of media spend? That doesn't make sense. But what it comes down to really is do I trust this person I'm talking to execute what my hopes and dreams for this campaign or this work is going to do? Because when that person calls White End Kennedy, they're still talking to one or two people, and are they going to be, is that client going to be able to trust that those two creative directors that they're talking to at the time? And that's really what it comes down to. (32:14): Is it a relationship that's going to work between the people that are on the phone making the decisions, is what it really comes down to. And just about anything that you do in business ideas or ideas. And they could come from anywhere. And a lot of my work comes from referrals. Oh, you should check out, ok bro, they did a great job on this project for us. And then Magic comes into the email machine. And then next thing you know, we're off on a new journey with a new brand and a new client executing work that we've never done before. And that gets really fun because for myself is if I get a referral, I want to do extra better for that person that referred me because your reputation is everything. And if you blow it and for whatever reason, you're not just losing that client that you're working on, you're also losing the client that referred you to them. They don't want to look bad either. And so it is this virtuous cycle of trying to be successful and building relationships how the network really grows and people give you phone calls.

They still need to roll up their sleeves and get their hands dirty and understand how to do something for 20,000 bucks because you never know that small activation might be the thing that triggers a big wellspring of goodwill to your brand. And so I think from that perspective, that helps big agencies. And then from the other perspective, understanding how big agencies do their strategy and their market research and things like that. That's good. And that's how you're finding yourself and your place in the world, and that can end up being detrimental, spending a lot of your time in this negative place where it's even looking at really good work. And I think consumers see that if they're really far away from that process, but they see it and they can feel it. Someone told me once that selling is really being a salesperson. A good salesperson is really just the transfer of enthusiasm from one person to the next. (39:27): And I kind of believe that. And when you're a fan of the work that you're doing and you're enjoying the process, that enthusiasm goes through. I've made a point for myself. I've just started looking at design annuals and add annuals and stuff like that.

And you try and bolster yourself up by putting people down and it doesn't feel good. But flipping that on its head and saying, you know what? That other agency might've won this pitch because their ideas were better. Awesome. And look, that work is actually fantastic. I wish I could have done it. I actually, I was chatting with Jill at Diamondback on Instagram sharing this great illustrator that I worked with a while ago, and I was like, just hire her and have her do a bike for you. It'd be amazing. And that both helps that relationship with Jill and I just as human beings sharing cool things. But it also turns me into a resource and a trusted collaborator, not just holding that to myself, but if you start to share and support other people. And I think the karmic energy of all that, not to sound too trippy on that, I think it comes back.

Cole Heilborn (43:01): No, well said. It is interesting why we often as creatives default to that cynic perspective when you're looking at someone else's work and some of those reasons that you just listed off, they're like, well, they only got the job because of X, or they really botched up this one element of whatever I'm looking at. We're super hypercritical of other people's work, and yeah, I wonder if that's, as you said, to make us feel better about our own work.

content: Ben O'Meara (04:52): Sure, yeah. Huckberry, as we briefly mentioned, was founded in San Francisco 10 years ago. Huckberry is, we're a retailer. We're online. We were started online, and I think going into where Huckberry started and where we are today still foundationally, the core of Huckberry is product curation and content and storytelling. And so how that comes to life from a product standpoint, really the inspiration behind Huckberry was Andy and Rich, the two original co-founders and still founders of the company today, saw this void in the market, if you will. You hear the term like scratch your own itch, and they're sort of the epitome of that in all the right ways. They were guys who lived in the city. They were both working nine to fives. They were both working in finance, but on the weekends craving adventure, whether that was skiing in Tahoe, going mountain biking in Marin, hiking, exploring the city, trying new restaurants, traveling, and they obviously loved the outdoors, but also appreciated everything that a city has to offer and the things that you do, whether it is in that nine to five window, but really that five to nine experiences after work. (06:10): So the original inspiration behind Huckberry from a sort of product curation standpoint, you have the outdoor traditional brands and then you've got the, let's say, more style forward everyday fashion brands, if you will. And those are two very sort of generic ends of the spectrum. Any and rich love to be outdoors, they love to travel again, they lived in the city, they cared about the things that they bought, what they're wearing to work, what they're wearing when they're going out with friends, but they also weren't necessarily interested in the most technical on the outdoor side and the most stylish, trendy fashion forward things on the other end. And from an actual experience standpoint, this was early on in sort of the rise of e-comm, if you will. Traditional retailers were still really dominated by big box department stores and physical retail stores, and then obviously Amazon on the other end of the e-comm spectrum.

Ben O'Meara (04:52): (07:10): So they saw this opportunity that kind of married their love for the outdoors and adventure, but then their love for the city and all the things that lifestyle implies and provides and wanted to create a place where you could find brands that lived in between those two sort of spectrums that were functional and high quality, but more versatile. And so the idea for Huckberry was born. And I think the other really important piece to that all was this. The stories behind a lot of the smaller brands. Again, back then, a lot of the cool smaller brands didn't have the ease in which the world of Shopify and e-commerce is now created to get their messages out and connect with customers. And they were really inspired by a lot of the smaller cooler regional brands in their travels to other cities they'd experienced and met and wanted to create a place where you could learn about them and find those products on a one sort of centralized platform, if you will. So taking that combination of smaller brands with story and brands that spoke to people that loved the outdoors, but also loved living in the city, that was where Huckberry began, and still very much is foundational to where we are today. We carry everything from traditional outdoor gear to incredible leather shoes made in Italy, and it can be a four letter word overused these days, but that sort of lifestyle, the nine to five during the week, and then the weekend adventurer.

So I feel incredibly lucky to sit in the position that I do.

Cole Heilborn (12:00): And how many brands do you sell? And to be clear, you guys aren't picking necessarily flagship products from these brands. You're picking some of the products that are maybe under the radar, correct?

You've never seen this product before because we're the only ones that's ever sold

But before we go deeper, I think something we should address is how you guys approach storytelling through all of this, because that's kind the bedrock I feel like to a lot of the piece you're describing. So how do you weave that into everything that's done at Huckberry? Maybe that's a really big question.

Ben O'Meara (14:15): It's a really big question, but it's also, I think it's a big one and that it touches everything and it is so core to our brand, but I think if you also simplify it and not in the sense that it's easy and simple to do, but it is, like I said earlier, it is so foundational to Huckberry. So it's really at our core, this idea of storytelling has been one of the number one product value promises that when Andy and Rich created this brand was going to be consistent from then until however long the brand was alive. And so when you think about how that then gets brought to life at the very beginning, how we talked about brands was different than you saw in other retailers. That was our promise to everyone from day one. We didn't have a big budget. Andy and Rich bootstrapped the business for the first six or seven years, but what we did bring to brands was this point of view in this editorial lens to their story and to their products that other retailers were not doing at the time. (15:24): And so that was quite literally how we built Huckberry, how built our newsletter was telling these stories of these brands. So that was just how we did things, and that becomes just a muscle that becomes so natural as you continue to build it and grow and add new people. That's just how the business operates. That's our business strategy. And so when you have that foundation, it makes things, I don't want to say easier, but it's just what we do. And that's when, I don't mean to oversimplify it, but that is what we do. And everything from a product page, we're really intentional with how we talk about products, making sure, of course we hit on the important features and materials, but how we describe that product has more of a voice, more of a point of view. We think about the customer and what they're going to be using it for, how Huckberry would recommend using it and what we're inspired by based on this product and this brand story. (16:17): So yeah, if you think about from a product level, our product pages, we consider a part of the storytelling pie.

Ben O'Meara (14:15): And of course we want to make sure that we are hitting on the important features and materials and how something's constructed, but our copywriters do such a great job of taking all of that information, all the ingredients, and contextualizing that in a way that is in a huckberry voice. It's relatable, it's approachable, but also putting the customer in the shoes of actually using this product. So I think from that sort of first touch point, if you land on a product, you feel that voice and then as we've continued to grow and scale and you find these incredibly inspiring stories and it's like, wow, there's a lot to unravel here. We can't describe all of this in one email or one product page. That's where our journal comes into play. (17:07): That's where our email comes into play. Again, going back to we want to be working with brands that are doing things a little bit different, that are focusing on quality, that are differentiating from all of the sort of mass that's out there. And when you have these amazing people and products, it makes our jobs, I don't want to say easy, but it's an incredible group of ingredients and amazing stories to start with. And then it's our job to figure out the best ways to unpackage those stories.

Cole Heilborn (17:45): You mentioned that part of the goal is to figure out how to differentiate. Is that why the founders have placed so much emphasis on storytelling or was storytelling just the natural way to talk about things as you entered the world?

Ben O'Meara (18:03): I think again, going back to that cliche, but scratching your own niche, that's how they wanted to be talked to. They didn't want a bunch of marketing jargon and cliche sort of copywritten taglines. They wanted someone. I think one way that we think about our voice and our content in a lot of ways is you're sitting down at a bar with a friend and they're telling you about a cool new bag that they bought, or you ask them, those are really cool boots, where are they from? And sort of keeping it real is one of our brand values and it's a tenant to our sort of voice. So it was something early on that Andy and Rich and all of us want to see and feel when someone's talking to us. And the more that we did it, the more we realized it also makes a stronger connection to our customer, our community. It creates trust when you do have that, making sure that you hit on all the important points and you give them the details. We've got a really smart customer base. They want to know how things are made and where they're made and what the materials are made of. But then making sure to contextualize that in a way that is also relatable and thoughtful to them, it creates that greater bond and that greater trust.

Cole Heilborn (19:21): Do you feel like people these days are tired of the marketing jargon and they're just looking for essentially a friend to be like, Hey, this is what I use, this is why I like it?

content:
Ben O'Meara (19:31): I think so. I mean, I'm obviously biased, but I do feel like that. And I think the combination of there's so much choice out there, and that was again one of the origins of Hucker at the time. There's a lot of choice, there's a lot of amazing brands, but there's also a lot of crap. Let's create a place where we can curate that. That's a really important part of our strategy is the curation of brands, but also the curation of products within those brands. So I think that combination of distilling down what we think is the most relevant and what we think is cool and what we think you should know about, and then combining that with actually explaining to you our point of view there. I do think that that is something that I don't know is needed more. I do think people are tired of getting hit up with the same ads that follow the same format, that say the same thing, and there's a reason for that. And we have an incredible team and strategy in our performance world, but we try to insert our brand voice into those and not just follow the formula, not just follow the algorithm if you will. Use the data, know what's working, obviously it's an important part of the pie, but making sure that the brand voice and the brand identity is consistent through every touchpoint.

Cole Heilborn (20:50): So there's other product curation retailers out there, but is story the thing, the perspective that I guess you guys take, do you think that's what set Huckberry apart from a lot of other similar models?

Ben O'Meara (21:04): Yeah, yeah, definitely. I think again, that was when Andy and Rich were first hitting the trade shows going to or and some of the New York trade shows back in the day, they didn't have a website. I remember some of the first trade shows that I went to and we were much, much smaller and no one knew who we were. What we sold them was our newsletter, was our content, and we're going to tell your story in a way that has not been told. Of course we're going to sell your product, but we're also going to work as that friend who is reaffirming your brand and telling your story in a way that lifts your brand up and is great marketing frankly for them. So that's always been the promise, and that has been, again, what has I think set us apart and you're now seeing content strategies and storytelling. (21:55): It is kind of required at this point in the game, but because we've been doing it for so long, I think it has become again, that muscle and that trust that people do continue to look to us for. And again, we've got such great data and insights and we've certainly tried a lot that hasn't worked. And all of that allows us to continue to, I think put out really interesting story and content and have a really strong perspective on the products and the brands that we're working with. And it is about trust. And when we do say, you should pay attention to this brand, this is a really cool brand, this is a great product, this is a great story. And then you decide to trust us with that, and you buy something, you read something and we come through with that promise and then you come back and that happens again. I think that is also one of the pillars to Huckberry in our success to this point. We've got an incredibly loyal community. Once we get a customer in, our retention with that customer is quite high.

Cole Heilborn (23:03): So that loyalty aspect is really interesting. Why do your customers become so loyal?

content:
Ben O'Meara (23:08): That's a good question. I think it's consistency first and foremost. Not to overgeneralize, but you can say that you're really good at something or this is the best x, y, Z product, and the next reaction is, okay, well either you read it or you got the product and was it true? If it is true, you're more likely to go back for a second time and then a third time and then a fourth time. And so I think because we are so focused on the quality of the brands and the quality of the story and the obsession of our customer, what they want to see, what they want to read, I think those interactions with our brand, whether it's your first one or your third one, it is consistent to what brought you in there and got you interested in the first place, if that makes sense. A lot of people that say, this is the best X, y, z, and you should read this, and then you get in there and you're like, this product is crap, or the information that's actually in this article is bullshit. You just got me with a catchy tagline. And I think again, at our core it's all about quality, quality, quality, quality, and that's the quality product. Quality brand and the quality story and content,

Cole Heilborn (24:32): But then showing up consistently for every,

Ben O'Meara (24:34): But you have to do that consistently. Exactly. Constantly tinkering and iterating. But I think the consistency is so, so important in creating that you can't just create trust in one interaction. You have to have multiple positive touch points with any person, with any brand, with any product before you really create that relationship. And then once you have the relationship, that's where the trust comes in, that's where the loyalty comes in. That's where you feel like you're part of the community.

Cole Heilborn (25:04): I think I read somewhere that in the restaurant industry, it takes three successful experiences at a new restaurant before a customer becomes a loyal customer of that restaurant, which when you consider what it would take to get three out of the park experiences at a restaurant, that could be tough to hit.

Ben O'Meara (25:27): And I think an important part of that too, and I don't want to sound like we do everything. Like I said, we make a lot of mistakes. We've made a lot of mistakes, we continue to make a lot of mistakes, we've gotten a lot better and we make a lot less of them. But going back to that point of having an approachable voice and a realness to your brand, it's much easier to rectify those mistakes. If you're real, you own it and you follow up with a great experience after the fact. Sometimes our best customers actually come in, they bought something for the first time, it didn't fit, but then they interact with our customer experience team and they're like, holy shit, this is a different experience. I talked to a real person and they got on the phone and they talked me through other options. And that experience is also a positive experience and a consistent experience. So I think it's also what you do with the negative interactions, and that's also a big focus of ours is making sure that when we mess up one, we own it. And two, we are incredibly proactive in finding the right way to fix it.

Cole Heilborn (26:22): Yeah. What other ways have you guys screwed up? Any big blenders that you can think of that you've learned from?

Ben O'Meara (26:31): There's so many. That's probably a whole podcast. We've actually joked about that we could create a podcast on the mistakes that we've made. There's a lot of success story podcasts, but

Cole Heilborn (26:40): I think people would love that.

Ben O'Meara (26:41): I agree. Here's an example from a product curation standpoint, I think one of the challenges and sort of the watch out if you will, as sort of a lifestyle brand that can play in a lot of different places, and again, as I said, we can have the really rugged traditional heritage outdoorsmen, but then we've got the more modern EDC minimalist traveler in our customer base and in our brand identity. And you can start to think, okay, what else can we do? We can be everything to everyone. And so there was a point where we went pretty hard at dress wear nine to five buttons up and suits, and we can own the entire closet from going into the office and wearing a suit. And obviously the world has changed in terms of what you wear to the office or will wear to the office again. (27:36): But we went pretty hard at a more nine to five element to Huckberry, and our customers came back to us and they're like, Uhuh, we of course appreciate a lot of the products that you do sell that I may take to work the Fils and Briefcase or the more versatile five pocket Chino, a great pair of boots, but the button up and the suit that's not Huckberry. Your brand is rooted in adventure and versatility and a number of those other things that we've talked about. And it was one of those, we spent a lot of resources, content strategy, we got our buyers bringing on a bunch of new brands and obviously investing in the product and it was just a good reminder that we can play in a number of different places and personas and styles, but don't lose your brand identity and what's core to, that's why people are coming to you if they want to suit, they can do that in another place that is that expert. So that's definitely one.

Cole Heilborn (28:40): Yeah. And was that feedback, how did that come across? Was that social? How'd you hear about that feedback

But then you get that anecdotal feedback, those different touch points, you start hearing people chiming in on social when you're posting a picture of a guy in a button down in a tie and they're like, that's not huckberry. You have longtime customers writing in and saying, Hey guys, not really what I'm interested in. I'd like to see more of X, Y, and Z. So it was a combination of things. I mean first and foremost it didn't sell, and then you start connecting the dots with some of the anecdotal comments here and there, customer experience writing in. So it was a variety of things. I was just say, and also it was one of those we got really excited about it, like opportunity, opportunity, but then once it went live and we're sitting back and looking at the brand and you have all these great images and great brands that we've spent years curating and telling stories around, and then it just didn't feel right. So it was an interesting one. Now we certainly not to keep going down this rabbit hole. We certainly sell an Oxford shirt and we sell really cool unstructured blazers and even fun linen suits from great brands, but even those are more connected to the Huckberry brand identity. It's a smaller brand, it's more versatile. They're typically things that maybe you're wearing to more of a destination wedding or a more casual office in a more creative space, but that nine to five buttoned up loafers did not work for our guy.

Cole Heilborn (30:30): What a great example of your consumers or your audience or really your fans, I guess in your case kind of checking you guys and saying, no, that's actually not who we think you are. I don't remember who said it, but a great brand is measured not by how the brand describes itself, but by how its people describe it.

Ben O'Meara (30:52): Yeah, was that Ogilvy said something similar and maybe it was him, but yeah, absolutely. Yeah, absolutely. And again, we have a lot, we were all more traditional nine to fivers and we have a lot of more traditional nine to five amazing customers, but just what they come to us for was not that.

content:
Cole Heilborn (31:13): Let's talk a little bit about your collaborations. So you mentioned there's kind of two camps where you collaborate with an existing product and maybe do a cross branding or something, or you guys create an exclusive product. A recent collaboration you guys have done is the Coors Banquet project Fill us in. How did that go?

Ben O'Meara (31:31): That was a fun one, and that was I think all of the different components that we've talked about, the storytelling, the content, the product, the exclusiveness. That was one of the best examples of wrapping all of that in one integrated campaign. So I think that different components of that. Of course Banquet has this incredible archives of old logos and amazing old branding and they've got a cool heritage in Golden Colorado and they let us have full access to the archives and designs. And so our product team was able to design a bunch of really cool exclusive and hats and we did a really cool custom boot. We did a cool cooler. And so from a product standpoint, there was an exclusivity angle. Obviously these were special. Once they were sold and gone, they were gone. They were also really interesting product. And so they checked all the important product qualities and pillars that we stand for. (32:34): And then from a content storytelling standpoint, we put together this really interesting video series where we profiled three different individuals who sort of in their own worlds in ways represent adventure and creating access to adventure in their communities. And so we had this incredible graphic artist and surfer in Santa Barbara and does a lot of really amazing, important work in his community and getting kids into the water that maybe have not had access or felt welcome there. We worked with a former hotshot firefighter and his efforts in conservation and documenting forest fires and sort of the challenges and devastations that obviously we're seeing across the west right now and really telling their stories as sort of individuals who again represented venture and what they do to make venture more accessible to their communities. We worked with this incredible fly fishermen and comedian in Denver, and so again, similar type approach working with his communities to get kids that don't have access to fly fishing and have felt included in fly fishing out onto the water. So it was a really cool cohesive campaign that tied together really interesting product with really thoughtful storytelling and involving the communities and the places that we profiled.

content:
Cole Heilborn (34:02): What are the intentions behind the collaborations?

Ben O'Meara (34:05): Just broadly?

Cole Heilborn (34:06): Yeah, why?

Ben O'Meara (34:07): I think there's a couple different reasons. I think from a product, maybe this isn't the sexiest answer, but collaborations are exclusive to your brand, and so they allow you to one, have that moat and it's a product that can't be sold in other places, and you need that when there's a lot of competition out there. It also allows you to insert the information and data that you have from your customer base. Again, serving the customer best. We know the colors and the styles and the vibe that our customer loves most. We're able to influence that product and create what we think is an even better product catered to our customer. So from a product standpoint, that's a really important piece to the collaboration strategy. And then broadly, I mean, collaborations are a really important marketing channel. You want to work with brands to elevate your brand. (34:59): You are who you hang with, and so that's exposure into their audiences. That is brand association. So I think from a marketing side is that important, top of the funnel, brand awareness side of things. And for a discovery brand that focuses on content, the best collaborations come with a story first, and that story influences the content and the product just like that cores example. And so it just makes for a really interesting campaign and brings delight and interest and sort of a moment to the Huckberry website, the huckberry email, the huckberry content, and that's all in service of our customer.

Cole Heilborn (35:39): Is the journal kind of what sums up all of the content behind Huckberry or how does that work? You have an extremely robust journal that I think also connects to your email campaigns. So how does that fit into this equation?
