content: Ben O'Meara (35:56): Yeah, I mean it fits in every single touch point possible. So we have product specific content on our journal, so that's a deeper dive into how something's made, where it's made the story behind the founder. And so it's a great opportunity to expand on the product or brand storytelling of the things that we're selling. On the other side of the equation, we've got what we call interest-based content, and that's with a more sort of editorial media lens, if you will, and understanding what our customer is interested in beyond just the products. Maybe it's the things that they're doing with the products, but things like whiskey and cabins and adventure itineraries and beer recommendations and stories of entrepreneurship and inspiring stories of epic travels and sort of adventure. So that part of the equation's incredibly important to continue to again, build the sort of brand and the lifestyle, but also from a customer standpoint, we don't always want to feel like we're selling to you. (37:02): We don't want you to come to Huckberry just because you have to buy something. We want you to come to Huckberry when you need something and when you want to discover something, if you want to browse or you're shopping for a trip or with intention. But on the flip side with our journal and how much content we do put out, that crosses so many different types of interests and categories. It gives our community and customer base a reason to continue to come back and read something and learn something. So the journal's always been part of Huckberry, but as with any company and you're scrappy and growing and having to reprioritize how much time and resources you're spending on things, it's gone through multiple sort of iterations where there was a point where we're doing one article a week, there was a point where we're doing one article a month, there was a point where we're doing three articles a week, but we just kept doing it. And now we're at a point where we've got the data and we've got the confidence frankly in what our customers want to see more from us of to be putting out. We put out a journal article once a day at a minimum, and at least 50% of that has nothing to do with a product that we're selling. It's more the lifestyle, the interest of our broader customer base,

Ben O'Meara (40:38): The email is the bread and butter of Huckberry, if you will. It is the channel that is built huckberry in many ways, and I think the email represents everything that we've talked about packaged in one newsletter that hits your inbox Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays. It's a combination of a curation of brands. You're never going to open an email and it's going to be one single brand or one single type of brand. You're always going to get an assortment of brands of what's new and what's interesting and what's relevant to the season or the moment. So there's always something that's new and interesting from a brand and product perspective. And we use that email as sort of that appetizer to introduce you to the story of that brand or of that product. So there is a decent amount of editorial in these emails more than you see in a lot of e-commerce, more transactional emails. (41:31): There's paragraphs that are featured throughout. And then we incorporated, you mentioned this content throughout that email, so there's always a journal article at the bottom of the email, and sometimes that journal article is tied to a product or a campaign above. More often than not, it's something completely separate. It's something, again, interesting and relevant that our editorial team thinks is worth reading, worth learning about. And then we also, I think breaking down the DNA, so we've got the product and the product curation. There's always newness, exclusives, there's consistency in every single email that there's going to be variety, there's always going be content. And then another really important piece to our email is sort of the bottom half of the email, which we call diversions. And then see you out there and diversions every single email we feature three articles or three pieces of content, video, podcast, a lot of written articles that link off to other people's websites, other people's contents, other people's stories.

I mean this was something that, again, they wanted to create a newsletter that they wanted to read, and I love sharing interesting articles that I find interesting with my friends. We share a lot of the same values and share the same interests, so how can we incorporate that into an email? And so that's what diversions represents. And we had a lot of people tell us, you should not be sending links off your own channel to someone. But what that does is we went back to the trust and consistency. There are people that open our emails just to see our diversions. They want a good read, and that's okay because they're opening every single email. And then eventually when you need something or you want something, you're probably going to give us a try and buy something. (43:25): So it creates that we're creating value whatever touchpoint you're coming in with. And so it also gives us a good data point on what our customers are interested in, who clicked most on which article. And it's like, huh, we didn't think that that necessarily was going to be an interest, but is that something that we need to provide more content and more context to? So it's a great data point for us as well, but first and foremost, it's just we love sharing interesting stories, whether it's product or content, and let's make sure that we're doing that, especially if it's other reputable content magazines, creators that we take inspiration from that we want to work with. We want to be that platform that shares good things. And then we've got our CU out there, which is the classic email sign off, which is that inspirational window into something epic and aspirational. (44:15): Everything can't be top of the mountain and amazing adventure mobiles, but we all need that once in a while. And so to see you out there is just a nice little sign off that if you're sitting at your desk at nine in the morning and you're about to jump into a spreadsheet and you look at some amazing photo, even for that moment, it kind of takes you to a different place. That's what it's there for. And it's also an opportunity for us to again, feature a lot of our friends, ambassadors, the work that they're doing. A lot of our own photographers. We've got such an incredible group of creatives in our sort of network. So it's also a nice sort of nod to people that we work with and people in our own sort of huckberry world here.

Cole Heilborn (44:53): A couple episodes, I had Lloyd Vogel from Garage Grown Gear on the show, and we were talking about email, and I think you mentioned this as well, but he said Email is one of the last channels that's intact. It doesn't have a filter. I mean other than a spam filter, but there's something so much to be said about having that direct communication with your audience.

Ben O'Meara (45:17): There's no algorithm that can change, and absolutely it is an owned channel. It you're seeing emails is kind of back in trend, if you will. I can't believe I'm even saying that, but you're seeing the rise of Substack and COVID brought back a whole new group of people that are writing and getting out their sort of content and their perspectives, and it's the equivalent of what Spotify did for brands. The idea of people putting out their newsletters to, whether it's a niche community or an expression of their interest or expertise, it's just such an important channel. And again, it is quite literally what is Bill. I mean, that is when we were talking about storytelling, it was storytelling in our email, and that continues to be that I guess gold standard for us. And so it is so important and to consistently do it well, not only the content within, but as I mentioned also there's intention behind, we send it Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays at the same time every week. (46:20): We don't want to spam you. You're not going to get five emails from us in a week. But it also creates hopefully a little bit of that anticipation. It becomes part of your morning routine. We hear a lot of customers like Can't wait to read my Huckberry email. And so we also send it at eight in the morning because previously that was a commute time, but it's also a time where we all spend warm. You're drinking your coffee, you're checking email, you're not quite ready to dive into anything. So I think there's a lot of different tactics and intentionality into what makes a really good email and why people open it. But yeah, it is kind of going back to that point that you made. It's an own channel. It cannot change. It means you have to invest in it if you want it to be good and you want people to continue to open it, that's the other edge of the sword. But if you invest and we invest a good amount into it, it's the most profitable from a financial standpoint, but also from a brand building standpoint.

Cole Heilborn (47:19): But email, I mean it seems old school.

Ben O'Meara (47:22): Yeah, totally. Yeah.

Cole Heilborn (47:24): But it works.

Ben O'Meara (47:24): It works. Yeah. Think about the change in our own, how we use social media. I don't go on Facebook anymore. I don't use Instagram nearly as much, but I'm always in my email because professionally I need to be there and it's still the best way to stay in touch and send pictures of my daughter to my mom. And you can do a lot through text, but email's the most consistent and the most sort of trustworthy, if you will. So it is old school, but it's also, it's as relevant as ever.

Cole Heilborn (48:03): And was email chosen back when the company was started because it was the most accessible, or did you guys see, oh, email is going to be a thing we should invest heavily into it or?

Ben O'Meara (48:15): Yeah, that's a good question. I don't want to speak for Annie, and I don't know if they necessarily saw the sort of roadmap as email is going to be the thing, but I do think one, it was free in a way. Again, it's your own channel. You have to invest time and resources and obviously pay for whatever platform you're using, but once you get it going, it's a very cost effective way to get your message out there. And again, it was one of those, there wasn't a lot in the toolbox yet in terms of negotiation offerings from Huckberry. It was like we're going to put together an email, and newsletters was still relatively new. Again, this was 10 years ago, and so this is going to be commerce, but in a newsletter format. And again, it's going to be consistent and there's going to be story, and we're going to invest a lot of our time in making sure that we get a lot of people to sign up for this email. And that then is used as sort of a negotiation, if you will, when a brand that's never heard of Huckberry is like, okay, yeah, you tell me that you can tell a good story, but and who's reading it. And email's a very easy place if you can get people to sign up for it that you can point to.

Cole Heilborn (49:28): How do you get people to sign up for it?

Ben O'Meara (49:31): Yeah, it's a combination. I mean, at this point there's obviously lots of different strategies and ads that we run and Hard gate, soft gate testing, all of those sort of technical things. But early on we relied a lot on our brand partners, like the early brand partners, you sort of trade. We will invest in this content and this storytelling if you tell your community that you're on Huckberry and send them over to Huckberry and sign up for the newsletter. We were also pretty early in affiliate marketing when we were really, really young. People like Art of Manliness and Outside Magazine took a chance on us and liked the vision and what we were doing and would shout us out and recommend the Huckberry newsletter. It really was a lot of word of mouth, organic recommendations to start, and then that slowly starts to snowball, and then you start building the strategy and you start building the affiliate team and you start building the email acquisition strategies, if you will. But it was a lot of, you scratch our back, we'll scratch yours and let's drive people to each other's sites. Let's tell each other's stories. And for us it was tell your brand story, tell your product story. And for our brand partners, we'd ask them, can you let people know that you like Huck Bearing to come check us out?

Cole Heilborn (50:48): I feel like everything we've been kind of talking about, and we talked about it in the beginning of the episode, is this just concept of loyalty and building audience loyalty, and all of these things we've discussed are kind of tactics and ways to do that. How do you measure that loyalty?

content: Ben O'Meara (51:04): It's a good question. I think we're getting a lot better at actually creating dashboards and tracking different KPIs around that. And I think the tip of the iceberg, not even the tip of the iceberg, but one is sales and repeat sales. What's the lifetime value of a customer? We are a retailer. That's how we pay our bills. Again, content and media is part of our DNA, but how often are you coming back to Huckberry and buying something? And that is loyalty. I think broadly the consistency of our open rights and click through on the Huckberry emails in our content, that's the very top of the funnel. You can't get as granular which customers necessarily did that, but you can look at those data points and understand if we consistently have the higher open rates and strong click-throughs and also time spent on page, whether it's a journal article or a video, I think that's a form of, or it's a touch point that gives you that data of is the customer gravitating to what you're putting out. (52:14): But absolutely, it does come back to the lifetime value of a customer, how many purchases they're making, how much time, how often they come back to Huckberry and interact with us. And then we track NPS scores. So you buy some what is an N-P-S-N-P-S, it's called Net Promoter, and it's sort of a directional survey that gets sent out. You've probably gotten them before with basically, how satisfied are you with this experience with this brand? And ours is consistently high. And so not only do we track the number, but it gives you a chance to write in what you liked, what you didn't like. And so we hear a lot of, Hey, I'm a long time customer. This is my third purchase, my fourth purchase. So we track that. We're constantly aggregating that information, our CX interactions, and we obviously know who the VIP customers are and know how many times you've bought from Huckberry and have those data points. So it's a combination of a lot of things. And then some of it is sort of the more anecdotal where it's people chiming in and sometimes it may be a single comment or a couple comments, but when you consistently see I love Huckberry on an Instagram post, or people resharing our content like Love Huckberry, this is awesome, another great article or love this collaboration. Those are all things that we track and pay attention to. So it's a variety of things that sort of give us that indication of customer loyalty and consistency to the brand.

It's one of our major strategic initiatives, if you will, for this year, is expanding our media and content and really rallying around video and bringing the brand to life in more 3D. (54:45): And then we're going to continue to invest in video externally, like going out on adventures and making sure that we're capturing inspiring people in places and again, bringing these stories that we've been telling for so long to life and new mediums. So I think it's just going to be a great way to better connect to product, brand story and people. So I'm very excited. We're particularly bullish around video and eventually podcasts. I'm going to be calling you up and picking your brain, but again, we're just, as I've said many times before, and I don't mean to sound like a broken record or cliche, but we're just so fortunate to be surrounded by such incredible stories. And again, that's everything from we nerd out on products. We are gearhead, and so the stories of a product, the story of a brand to the story of someone who is an entrepreneur or an adventurer, and how do we tell those stories in more interesting ways and get it in front of more people? And I ended up going to Outdoor Retailer with him, and we were sitting outside of a brewery somewhere in Denver, and we were like, you know what? It would be awesome if we could just start a podcast basically, almost selfishly, so we could ask the people that we want to talk to us and tell us about their journeys and their lives. (00:05:08): So we did that. I mean, we got excited about the idea and we were like, what form will it take? Who do we want to have on? Who is our hit list? And then we started it, and that was the Stoke cast. And so we split up pretty evenly responsibilities between hosting and producing and outsourced editing on that one. And we just did long form interviews with awesome people in the outdoor space. There could be entrepreneurs, there could be athletes, there could be activists, artists, all kinds of different folks. And it was one of still the privileges of my life to be able to speak to these people who I looked up to so much and learn so much from them. And also about, quite honestly, myself in the process, because interviewing people is a great way to learn about yourself as well. So that was my start in Stoke Cast, and then in February of 2020, I stopped drinking and I was looking for something that had concentrated stories about people in the outdoor space who were struggling with sobriety or recovery or addiction, and I didn't really find anything. (00:06:20): There's definitely episodes of certain podcasts out there that have those stories on there for sure, but there wasn't a place where those people were coming together on a consistent basis. And so I thought about it a lot and I sourced some ideas from other folks or really asked people, would this be valuable to you, which we can talk about, because I think that's a super important part of starting a podcast. And people said yes, and I started to think about what that would look like and what I would want to represent as far as the interviews go. And then the Nature Unfold podcast was started, pre-production was started in August of last year, and then January I actually released the first season of the Nature Unfold podcast, and now we're nearing the second season end.

I think the first memory I have though of listening to a podcast is listening to all Things Considered from NPR. And the reason I listened to that is because one of my sister's most intelligent friends was like, I was listening to this podcast called All Things Considered, this is like 2014, I want to say something along those lines. And I as well was very confused about what that purple app was on my phone that kept showing up that I was like, why can't I delete this? They also were realizing for the first time in a long time, for a lot of people, what they actually were interested in, they're like, I don't want to do this X job. And so there is an incredible amount of content out there. And like I said, not all of those will go on to become the Joe Rogans or the Dak Shepherds of the world, but that's the amount of creation that we're seeing right now, and it's incredible. I'm so happy that that's happening because there's so many people out there that should have a podcast and that are interesting and have great perspectives or have great journalistic backgrounds, and they should be storytelling. I get excited about the exponential growth of the podcast space,

I mean, I guess you could say the same thing for audiobooks too, right? The popularity of those as well. But for podcast itself, it feels like you're listening in or part of an intimate conversation and with interesting people who you would never be able to speak to in normal life for the big ones in the world, for our outdoor space, certainly if you went up to an Emily Harrington or someone who's an outdoor athlete who has a big name, she wouldn't be mad that you went up to her, not like a regular celebrity. But in general, we're listening to these intimate conversations that are so interesting, are so engaging, funny. Sometimes I cry listening to podcasts. So I mean, there's no other medium that you can go about your day and take in the same time and go away with a lot of value. (00:11:41): So that's part of it, I think. Yeah, and then the convenience factor, I mean, I have to sit down and watch YouTube. I have to watch Netflix, I have to watch all these streaming services. I can take a podcast with me anywhere, and now that we can also download them offline, we can literally take them into the back country with us as well. So that mobility of the audio format as well is so incredibly awesome for us. And I think even more for people who go into the outdoors, the folks in this outdoor industry is like, we spend hours and hours and hours doing hard things in the mountains, and I don't know a lot of people who don't listen to anything while they're out there for hours. I mean, that's pretty incredible if they are. So that I think is a unique part of the outdoor industry where quite honestly, outdoor brands I don't think have tapped into nearly enough of the podcast space to date, and it's a big opportunity, I think, for brands to do.

Emily Holland (00:13:07): Yeah, absolutely. I mean, I think last year showed us that connection is crucial to our wellbeing. I mean, I don't know about you, but last year was really hard mentally for me to be away from the people that I want to be around, or even the interactions of meeting someone new. We all had our little pods in which we were able to see all the people we already know and knew their backgrounds and knew who they are, but meeting someone new, interesting at a friend's party that you're going to, or a wedding that you happen to go to, those types of interactions, whether you're extroverted or introverted, they're really life-giving. And so to have those available to you in your pocket at all times, that was a godsend to me for the entire quarantine and now beyond of course, too.

Cole Heilborn (00:14:03): Yeah, well said. So transitioning gears a little bit, you've recently started your consulting business. As we were chatting earlier, you mentioned that a lot of people are interested in creating a podcast, but they have no idea where to start. Let's start at the very beginning. content: Emily Holland (00:14:24): Yeah. Well, it's interesting that you phrase it that way because that's the exact question that I would ask someone if they came and said, I want to start a podcast. Okay, why? And the reason being is because like you said, anyone can start a podcast, which is awesome. You really just need your phone. You need a computer, and you need a platform to be able to distribute it. Those three things, you can start a podcast, however, it's very time consuming and there's a lot of BS as you know that goes into it. If you're not excited about editing and you're choosing to edit your podcast, that's going to seem like a slog. And I'm speaking from experience on that. I absolutely hate editing. So those types of things, all that admin stuff, that's going to feel really hard if you don't have a solid reason why you started your podcast in the first place. (00:15:18): So you got to have that solid why. The other thing is how are you going to dictate your success of this podcast? Because there's huge podcast companies that have millions of dollars that they're putting behind huge podcasts with big names and celebrities and all this stuff. If your success is deemed on you being in the Top 10 podcast with, I hate to keep going back to Joe Rogan, but he's just the greatest example of podcast success. If that's your success metric, again, it's going to be really hard to get there when you're just an individual creator. So understanding what success looks like for you, and that might be more intangible, that might not mean that you're going to hit 5,000 listens per episode. It may mean that one person reaches out to you and says, this conversation made me feel like I was seen or heard today, and that's your success metric. Sure, you can have numbers and all this other stuff, but you need to bring it back to the reason you wanted to start it in the first place when you think about success metrics. So I think those two are really, really important to think about when you start your podcast.

I'm looking to talk to people about it, and kind of sourcing out the idea. And then I had 30 minute conversations with 20 different people to see what they would find helpful. Some of those people ended up being on the show themselves, and some of those people just ended up being great resources for me to ask questions to and to see what they thought about the concept. There's great Facebook groups out there specifically. There's a couple for Colorado that are sober Coloradans or Alcohol Free Outdoor Women is one, I think. So just reaching out to groups like that and posting in there and saying, Hey, I'm thinking about doing this. Will this be valuable to you? And then not only were people like yes, but then following up with those people and asking for their time and understanding what would be valuable to you, what stories do you want to hear? And I think that that is not only relevant for individuals who are thinking about starting podcasts, but brands too. When you're thinking about creating your own podcast, how can you make sure that you're serving the customers you already have and then potential customers as well? Because obviously starting a podcast is about brand recognition and brand resonance as well.

Cole Heilborn (00:20:53): And I want to jump back to that in a moment, but considering a format, there's tons of ways you could do it. You could have a host, you could have a host and a guest, you could have. What I've really started to enjoy and have been actually looking out is podcasts that have amazing production quality, and they're almost like they're giving you an audio experience, and it's so much deeper than just people talking. content: Emily Holland (00:21:27): Yeah, that's such a good question, and I think it really comes back down to how much time do you have to give to this and what are you outsourcing and what are you doing yourself? If you're a lay person that has no idea how to use editing software, and you're going to have to learn all of that in order to be able to produce your podcast, I don't know if a narrative, storytelling, audio experience would be the right fit for you to start off with. If you are really yourself, you know how to produce something. And so if you already have those skills or you were a radio journalist before or whatever, you know how to piece together a story, then great. And maybe that format is what feels comfortable to you right now, and you can do other formats in the future, but you start with what, for me, I didn't have any background in doing anything. (00:22:21): And so for the SoCast, we were like long form interviews, that's what we like to listen to, so let's do that. And I think also in a long form interview, there's sort of this unraveling of the guests, and you can start to really get to know them in this really deep way, especially when it's not cut throughout the entire process. And for the Nature Untold podcast, I was going out on my own doing this thing for the first time, handling everything. And so what I decided to do is I'm going to stick with what I know, which is long form interviews for the time being. That being said, in this season, the next episode that's coming out will be more of a cut narrative conversation, hopefully audio experience. So I think it really is like, okay, what's your skillset? What do you already know how to do and what are you willing to learn how to do? So think of that in time spent, money spent, and then also what do you like to listen to? And then finally, what's going to make you most comfortable upfront? You can always change it down the road. You can always have different formats if you want to and play with different things, but I think those are the three areas that you should focus on in thinking about what format you'd want for your podcast.

content: Emily Holland (00:25:08): Yeah, I think the things that get in the way is that there is not one platform that you're using for everything you need to do to be a podcast creator. And I'm hoping that something like this will come out soon, but if you're thinking about monetization, you'll probably want to have a Patreon. For folks who aren't familiar with that, it's basically, it's like a tip jar for creatives. You can give them a monthly subscription of $1 or $3, and usually you get stickers or exclusive stuff out of that. So then you have to manage a Patreon. Then if you're promoting your podcast yourself, meaning you're creating all the graphics and all the images for it, okay, you might have to have a Canva membership For those who don't know about Canva, Canva is an awesome format or platform rather that is pretty inexpensive, and you get to create beautiful graphics for anything that you're doing. (00:26:06): You can use that for proposals, you can use it for Facebook graphics, Instagram graphics, whatever. Okay. So then you have Patreon, Canva, then you'll have a distribution platform. So wherever you're either hosting your podcast itself or something like Anchor that's owned by Spotify where you upload your podcast to it and you distribute it through there, and then I'll have all your stats in it. Okay. That's just three things. And then not even to mention all the social media management of doing all that, and then also if you have a website. So I think that is a big part. It's like you're creating content, but then there's all these peripheral things that are around that content that need to be managed as well. It's not really enough to just produce a podcast. You have to promote the podcast, and how do you do that? You do it with great graphics and images and copy and that kind of stuff. (00:27:00): Then how do you make money off of it? Well, Patreon's a great access for that. I know we already talked about time spent, but it's also where you're spending your mental energy throughout the day too. It's like content creation and promoting is a different part of your brain than interviewing a guest and editing the show, all of this stuff. So all to say, there's a lot of different pieces that go into it. If you're not trying to monetize it, it's not as heavy of a lift. However, you still need to promote it if you want people to hear your podcast. So I think that's the biggest challenge is that individual creators and brands alike, I mean, there's just these huge studios that have so much money to manage all the stuff that you really can't compete on that realm. So just knowing that having a podcast means managing all these different parts of having a podcast,

content: Evan Poitras (08:04): So we kind of went through a big rebrand about a year and well, it started two and a half years ago, but it came out in March, which is super exciting. It wasn't necessarily changing our brand, but more I would say making it more coherent both internally and externally. And so what we landed on really first and foremost was our BC roots and our backyard, and the fact that Norco has been here since 64, and if you look at the evolution of what, I guess you could call it recreational cycling has been since 1964, has changed dramatically and is continuing to change with e-bikes, right? It's just constantly in flux. But Narco has kind of been there at every point, whether it was banana seed to the seventies or BMX racing in the eighties, or I think everyone thinks of the shore, the 45 pound bikes, all skinny is huck into flat there then. (09:05): So yeah, it's sort of the first one we always think of. Those scenes were always happening in this area as well, and it was such an influence to the brand. And so with Vancouver being probably the most cycling dominant city as well, it's just part of our nature and who we are. And so trying to sprinkle that in even when we're not doing stuff in DC to keep that front of mind as our birthplace. And then our second one we use is more of our design and product philosophy. We just use the word uncompromising to basically encapsulate that our design team, they're never happy, good or bad, they're constantly pushing the envelope. And that also reflects in the athletes that we choose. They're constantly pushing the envelope and just never being satisfied and trying to do better and better and do more things and change it up. And sometimes they're just throwing what's been, oh, this is great, but we're just going to throw it in the garbage to start a new plan. We think it can be better. So that's our third one or our second one, sorry. And our third one is freedom, and it's a generic word, but it's that sense of being out riding in the woods that we all love mountain biking for. So we'll unpack those differently, but those are kind of the three terms that we try to be latching onto with everything.

I'm always sort of thinking, is there something we can do that's not photo or video or can we turn it on its head? And I'm not going to tell you have any answers right now, but it's certainly a place where we're going to explore and test and try and see what we can do. It's hard to explain sometimes why we can't get so creative, but when we come back to where the audience is and what we know works, you have to balance that too of sticking with the audience and knowing the tried and true and pushing. (19:26): You can't always just do whatever you want and hope people see it. You got to go know what people will see. So if Toyota's going out, here's a mountain biker, and you're like, no, that is not an accurate representation of what I do or who I am or anything. I mean, we've all tried to describe mountain biking probably to our parents or uncles at Christmas and they don't understand it. You ride down the ski runs with your bike, it's a thing. And so we all take these sports and we identify to them, oh, you're a mountain biker and a skier. Okay, I get you that. It's so personal. It's not like you bought cotton socks and this is everybody who buys cotton socks. It doesn't matter if you're not associating that with a brand. I think people just take these activities and lifestyles so to heart and you can't kind of devalue them, make them feel devalued in your marketing material when you're trying to be like, we're with you on this. And whether that's just ego, fashion show of every consumer of, I don't look like that. I don't ride that bike. You still have to be aware that that's kind of part of the sport. content: Evan Poitras (32:43): Yeah, so I dunno if I want to call us a big team or a small team, maybe. We're a medium marketing team and we have a content team. We have a creative team. Our creative team has three designers including a creative director and a creative lead and a graphic designer and a copywriter. And so for us, the process really begins with, for most things, it becomes a layout. This is a brief, this is what we're trying to do, this is subject matter. Here's the idea. And then depending on how developed that idea is, me and the creative manager probably talk about it for a while, to be honest, who's going to work? Should we do it? Should we not? Do we kind of pro and con budget is always a reality, and then it becomes shooting it, and then I go away and work on the distribution plan and go back and then it filters through our creative team, whether it's already been written, if something had been shot and written, it will go through them and myself for feedback and go through our copywriter for the written part. And it kind of filters through that team and with outputs from both myself and our social media specialist to make sure we're hitting all our marks. So yeah, it kind of probably runs by, I would say at least five people before it gets out. If it's something bigger, maybe six if we turn it to email and seven if it's web. (34:21): But that's pretty much like our whole team. So everyone mostly for the most part, sees it at least on the content and creative side. Everyone will see it and have a chance to feedback. So yeah, sometimes if it's just, Hey, this photographer submitted these photos to us, fire 'em over. Usually I'll fire 'em over to our creative team, be like, are you billing any ads he worked for? We can hold them. We won't post 'em on Instagram if we're going to make an ad a month later with it, they're usually like, oh, can you hold this one? Boom. We mark it as hold and we run. So yeah, depending on the project, it always filters through myself and usually through either our social media specialist, if it's just strictly a social play or if it's anything more than that, our creative manager certainly dives into it and puts his eyes on everything and make sure we hit those details that he's looking for.

content:
Cole Heilborn (35:13): Is there ever a point where content becomes less important or we use less of it?

Evan Poitras (35:19): That's a really good question. I think, yeah, it's a tough one to answer because everything during COVID just ramped up to content only. I think we're going to appreciate in-person experiences a lot more shortly or whenever we get to do that again. And I do think nothing does be word of mouth, but I think where content plays is you're trying to subtly increase your equity with the people who are going to be talking. It's an analogy I always use because we have a range of bikes. I always say our top end model sell our mid end model because the person who's buying the, I have $2,000 and I want to get a new mountain bike and I'm getting back or I'm getting back into it, or whatever is going to ask about with the 8,000 bike. So that word of mouth to me is always going to be the most important thing. (36:21): But if you can subtly start to build up some equity, certainly if I wasn't working at Norco, I would have brands I would recommend to people to look at, but you've got to build equity with everybody. And so I don't think it's the most important thing even right now, but I think those human touches and when we get back to events and experiences, and certainly we have an athlete, Jill Kitner, who is just magic at making people's day out of nowhere and they send us comments and things about it, like she showed up and just had a coffee with us at Crank Works, Jill, they're mind blown. And those things will always be the most powerful, but what we're trying to do with content is try to bring those in the intermediary times. Here's something to watch. You like it, you connect with it, that's a great story. You like that character or that theme or whatever we're telling, try to get there. But I think the human side will always be more powerful, that personal connection or the person you trust answering your question or the person you look up to, you engaging with you or whatever. I think those are always going to be the biggest. You can't make those up either, right?

Evan Poitras (37:42): Man, that's an interesting one. I think it's currently quite unlimited. I think I'm going to plug one of your past episodes with my good friend Andy Bethune. He did take a, I don't want to say he took a shot at the mountain biking industry, but he called the spade of spade, and it's a very engineering driven industry. It's very geometry, spec, kinematics. And while all that stuff is important to some people, not a lot of people or maybe a large portion of mount markers aren't necessarily as obsessed with those things and the pure technical side of it. And so I think there is room for doing things differently. I think we've started to see it with brands, certainly, I think, I wouldn't say we're doing things too crazy differently, but for us, we're building up stories of a specific set so we can try and get these emotions of riding across the people and connect with them on that level. (38:47): But I think of a brand like yt. I mean, they did a 35 minute movie about this goat cult to launch a bike. I mean, that is the director directed Peaky Blinders on Netflix. I mean, when that came out, I was so excited because they just moved the bar so far in one move and some people hated it, but it's like, well, okay, now we're doing 35 minute episodes of fiction to launch a, where are we going next? And there's all kinds of different things that people have done and brands have done, and biking is behind in that aspect. I would agree with Andy. We are behind in that sort of level of branding and storytelling. It's such a young industry and it's an industry sort of created by engineer and product people, so you can't blame 'em. I mean, I certainly don't have the brain to design a bike, so I wouldn't expect them to be able to do it all either. But now that brands are really investing in marketing and storytelling, I think we've got a long ways to go before we're going to run out. (39:57): I think of all the things that are going on in other industries, just around the boom of streaming and different live sports things, red Bull TV being the obvious one, there's just so many different platforms out there. Every once in a while someone's going to make a crack in it and something new is going to flow out. So certainly in our industry, I think there's a long way to go both in terms of how, like we said, medium and what you're doing within that. So lots of room, lots of room. Hopefully I have some job security on that one. I think there's no end in sight.

content:
Cole Heilborn (40:35): Do you ever feel like the mountain bike shred, it will go away. I have mixed feelings about this type of content, but I'm curious to hear your thoughts here.

Evan Poitras (40:46): I don't think so, and I kind of hope not. And here's why. I'm going to use an example from our side just to plug Norco. We did a video, oh, just about two years ago now to launch our new optic with Burn Atkinson. It was shot by Scott Secco and the whole concept was brought forward by those two, I can't exactly remember which one specifically, but they worked in tandem on it and it's essentially, it's a shredded, but it was quite successful. And the reason it was successful is it was shot differently or the premise was different. The whole thing was just about routing your bike fast. But what Scott and Brian were able to do was take inspiration from actually Robert Downey Jr's, Sherlock Holmes, where he slows the boxing match down and they translated it to Bris slowing down the trail at a thousand frames per second and breaking down what he's doing in narration. (41:45): You're in his head hearing what he's thinking and to people who'd be like, how is he thinking in that much detail? Honestly, he is. It's true. The guy's, he on another level and they brought that forward. It's just riding a bike. But the way they shot it and framed it was so different that it was unbelievable that I hope there's more of that how we take riding a bike and just show it a little differently and frame it or whether it's how you shoot Slowmo, no slowmo. I mean, raw 100 is a great example. I remember reading All they Wanted was no sound and no slowmo, and that was the briefer raw 100 because everything at the time was heavy metal and all slowmo, and they were just like none of that. And that became Raw 100, which is one of the biggest mountain bike branded content series out there. (42:39): So I hope that people keep going in that direction because the of the day it motivates me to ride my bike and my friends to go ride. And when you're out riding, you want to try and ride that person or emulate that a little bit, but I hope the creativity and how they bring it forward continues to go. I think some brands or people are still really doing the generic, set it to a heavy tune and show some shredding. And if that works for some people, that's great, but I hope that evolution of how we show it continues because every mountain bike ride is so different, so there's so much to capture and ways to do it. So I hope it stays with that caveat that people get keep getting creative.

Roberto Gutierrez (01:45): Sure. So the short version, I guess, is I started in academics after PhD, got disenchanted with that for a bit, pursued a little bit of the startup world in the Bay Area. Then ultimately became co-founder at ORU Kayak and built that up over the course of six years, stepped away to do some other equity crowdfunding type things. Then got into the outdoor sports marketing specific realm in at United Sports Brands with a group of brands, and now I'm helping to lead the reintroduction or introduction of Jack Wilkin to North America here under the Callaway brand.

Cole Heilborn (02:26): And somewhere along the way there, you also started a van conversion build out company, is that right?

Roberto Gutierrez (02:32): Yeah, my cousin and I founded a little van conversion company based in Boulder, the Van Smith, and it's doing really well. It's pretty fun,

Roberto Gutierrez (02:52): I think it's a great question. I think it's a couple of things. There's the brutal honesty of some stability associated with larger corporations, and then there's also, the way I explain it best is I've helped build, I guess 20 million or 30 million brands, but when I one day run a hundred million dollars brand, I want to know how that works. And that's sort of the hope and aspirations of it, is to see the inner workings and learn and glean from that. I know it's a bit of a pipe dream, but hey, I got to put one foot in front of the other, and what better way to learn than under the hood and get paid to learn?

Cole Heilborn (03:27): Sure. For folks who are unfamiliar, could you give us a background on the company?

Roberto Gutierrez (03:34): Yeah, so Jack Wilkin is 40 years old, founded in Germany. The inspiration actually came during a camping trip in the Canadian Rockies. So the founder was camping with a group of friends, heard wolves crying in the background. He had a fondness for Jack London and the Call of the Wild sort of combined those two concepts and aspired to build a very sustainable, eco-friendly and high performance product line that was centered around hiking. Again, the Love for Wolves and Jack London. He combined the two and got Jack Wolfs skin, a very German name, if you will, the combination of the two in that nature. But the company grew for 40 years and is one of the largest brands. Well, it is the largest brand in central Europe. It's one of the largest outdoor brands in the world. Huge global distribution, 1500 doors globally. We have two in North America soon to be more, but not very many at the moment. (04:32): We actually are opening with public lands in two weeks, so we're pretty excited about that. The only final things is our brand is interesting in that when everyone was talking about sustainability, we just were doing it. We had the opportunity to work with Gore-Tex, but they said, well, we don't have the transparency we hold ourselves, hold ourselves to. So they developed their own membranes and rain protection and all of that named it tech support because they wanted to know each and every person along the way and have full transparency where sourcing it didn't allow for that. So it's an interesting thing where we've just been doing it, and so it's just core to what the company does. We actually came up with the world's first fully recycled membrane or waterproof and breathable membrane.

Cole Heilborn (05:18): Wow. And I think I read that, was it 2000 or early two thousands? All of the manufacturing facilities switched over to Green Energy In Germany?

Roberto Gutierrez (05:29): Yeah, in Germany, yes. And then one of the coolest parts, honestly, is the level of transparency. So inside of every piece of apparel, you can look and look for a little white tag, and there's two numbers. One is the source. So you can find out where the materials came from. You can see the full pipeline. You just enter that number into the search bar of our website, and then the second is the manufacturer, and it'll take you to the address and sometimes even a picture of the facility and people who built the product for everything we make, which is really amazing.

Cole Heilborn (05:59): Wow, why do that? That's a lot of work.

Roberto Gutierrez (06:04): Again, I think it was from the very beginning, Jack Wolf, the whole Wolf skin concept was they wanted something that was as somebody that had as little impact on the environment as possible, like a wolf skin, which is all natural and all that. That's kind of the core driving inspiration. Of course, you can't be perfect. No one's perfect in that regard. We try. We try and be good or better and even best. So it's just been something that they really hung their hats on. When I say they, I mean the design team and the developers and all that. And it was just something they decided they were going to be uncompromising about. And so we as a company get to represent that. And yeah, it's pretty subtle, but it's very cool.

Cole Heilborn (06:46): Yeah, no kidding. And what a cool opportunity. So you mentioned that the brand has been around for 40 years. It's been based in Germany, but the brand is recently entering the North American market, and that's kind of when you got involved, correct?

Roberto Gutierrez (07:01): Yeah, correct. So 2019, Jack Wilkin was acquired by Callaway Golf, and prior to that they had done some really, I would say, rudimentary efforts to bring Jack Wilkin to North America and blamed it on brand or blamed it on fit or color that it didn't succeed. But honestly, they didn't ever necessarily invest to the extent that we are now. So we have a team and a headquarters here in Park City. We've got global support, new CEO, and we're really aligning on a global level from product to messaging to ambassadors to all of it is becoming much more of a global brand rather than having the Poland market and the Chinese market and the Japanese market and then Dock or the German Central Europe market, and then North America, it's now all branches of the same tree. And you'll see that realize itself over the course of the next couple of years.

Cole Heilborn (07:57): Is that common, that unifying global unification?

Roberto Gutierrez (08:04): It's a great question. I would say yes. So I mean, we've seen f Raven Heli Hanson and then going overseas, the mountain hardwares and Patagonia, north Face is branching out, and you have to have localization. Our top seller here is not the top seller in Germany. The color stories that win here may not win there, so you have to have those components. And then in Europe, in Germany in particular, trekking poles have to go on everything, but here, nobody, it's like 14 trail runners who have carbon fiber trekking poles. It's not true, but it's just a little different. So we have to try and retell those stories. But globalization is, I mean, it's obviously relatively new as the internet is relatively new. I know for all of us, it's a commonplace thing today, but in the nineties it wasn't early nineties it was pretty relatively unique. And so as the years have passed, it becomes more and more fundamental, and it's only 30 years ago, but still,

Cole Heilborn (09:11): You mentioned that previous attempts to bring the brand to North America were unsuccessful. Can you elaborate on why that was?

So first, lemme caveat that, and I'm sure the folks who put the effort in did do some highly strategic and hard work to take those efforts. That said, I think that it was a little bit of a, they were on an island, and so when they came over here, it was like, okay, figure it out and just report back on what you need. Here's one of everything. Tell us what sales. Well, that's pretty hard right now. You sold one thing and you have a hundred of everything else, it doesn't sale, so it looks bad on the books, but really you just had the wrong stuff. And so it was a mix of inappropriate investments in locations and processes. (10:01): And now we've got Diana Song, who's our general manager here, has a background in merchandising. And so a number one, she's helping to select key items in strategic manners so that we don't sit here with 900 hot pink jackets that nobody's, or 9,000 that nobody's ever going to want. Instead, we have a bunch of the styles and colors that people do want, and then we dive deeper in that. So I think it was maybe done haphazardly without a, yeah, maybe they're pushed out of the nest a little early type thing. Like, Hey, in Germany, if everyone knows Jack Wilkin, it's like, oh my gosh, what a brand. So they just assumed that that same status would be carried over. But American, the North American market is very competitive.

Roberto Gutierrez (11:03): Yeah, I mean, I think that's what we are trying to do is how best to answer that rather than reacting to exactly where we could fit. We are choosing to try, we haven't done it yet, but we're choosing to try and carve out a space where we feel we belong. So we think that in our space and in this space in general, there is room for what we like to say the difference between an adrenaline brand and an endorphin brand. And so we're a brand that helps promote that moment of awe, but it doesn't necessarily have to mean that you're hucking off a hundred foot cliff in Jackson Hole, Wyoming doing a back flip or something. That's awesome, but that's not what we want to tell a story about. And so it's, ours is a little bit of a changing perspective where our pinnacle athlete or adventurer is a Nat Geo photographer who's holed up in a blind trying to take photos of a rare wolf in the Arctic. (12:06): That person still needs epic gear and has done something really amazing, but they don't, and they're at a pinnacle in one way or in a different way, but they're not a gravity sports expert. They're not going to slam a red ball, throw it off, and then go pro their day. That's not us. And so we're trying to carve out that space of and helping people change perspective and found everything in education and fact, or at least debate. And that's what we're trying to do. And so we believe there's space in that, not just in the outdoor world, but also in society for people to hopefully search fact or search for. It's hard to say that I'm biased, but hopefully at least do research and trust science again, because science has definitely fallen out of favor.

Cole Heilborn (12:59): When you say promote fact and truth, what does that mean? How are people finding those or discovering those with the brand?

So for example, we're doing a bunch of, we're doing an embedded mini documentary on Wolf trackers in Yellowstone National Park. They are based in Montana. It's a really fascinating story. These two, Nathan and Linda from Yellowstone Wolf Trackers have been there basically as long as the Wolves sensory introduction. And so we get to hear their perspective, their stories, and they're very objective of it. They understand both sides of the arguments. They certainly are passionate about wolves and have a very special relationship with them. And I won't deny that they are willing though, to sit down with anyone and discuss it. (14:03): They aren't, and I think when we talked about this program originally, people like, well, we need to talk about why we protect the wolves, why we carve out their space a keystone species. I was like, awesome. But let's also bring farmers, ranchers and those who don't believe that the wolf should be protected to the table. Because if you present one side of an argument that's just a bias or an opinion, if you bring both sides, then people can actually make a decision based on an argument and let people make that decision. So in that realm, what we're trying to do is bring things to the table that we believe are, and we're going to support the things that we believe once we've listened to the facts or the right action. I mean, that's all you can really do. But we'd like to bring, I guess, an open table, if you will, an open conversation.

content:
Roberto Gutierrez (15:01): Yeah, I mean it's everything. Like I mentioned, the sourcing is a great example of that, right? It's just something the brand does. They're transparent, they understand that not everything's perfect and easy, and it takes a lot of hard work to accomplish the things. So I think that it really resonates with the, I don't know if it's grassroots or I don't want to say blue collar, but there's that upstart mountaineer, if you will, who's going on their first hike and is like, man, I did 2000 feet of elevation today. Awesome, great. Congratulations. That's a huge accomplishment. And then a few years later, they do rim to rim to rim or something like that and throw down 12,000 feet of gain in a day and cover 22 or whatever, 44 miles I think that is. So yeah, I think that it's that gateway to the outdoors. There's the back country and the front country. We're kind of the middle country, if you will, and we'll build pinnacle product and we'll build entry level product, but most of your consumers will lie somewhere in the middle.

Cole Heilborn (16:09): So there's this concept, I believe, called confirmation is bias coming back to this concept of presenting all sides to an argument. And I'm curious from a philosophical perspective on storytelling, how you would approach something like this, because I think the concept basically says if you give equal weight to all sides, then the audience assumes that all arguments are weighted equally, even if there's more evidence for one argument versus the other. And the example of your film, how do you think through something like that?

content:
Roberto Gutierrez (16:47): Well, I have a bit of a background in science, right? I've got a PhD. So I look at numbers and try and look at the bigger picture and how it affects the whole story. So for example, there's an argument that the wolf needs to be protected, a number one, because it's a keystone species. Well, in talking with other researchers, so a keystone species, it could only possibly be a keystone species if left unadulterated by any outside forces, including man. So as a result, even in Yellowstone where it's very close to it, man's still feeding elk, and man is still hunting this, and there are still false perimeters and roads, and it is not untouched by man. It is as close as we get in North America right now. Well, as in United States right now, lower 48, but it's not untouched. And so taking that into account, the other side will argue, well, they're not necessarily an alpha, or sorry, a keystone species man is a keystone species. (17:50): Well, the good news, bad news there is that that means the responsibility is on us. So it then reflects on us to take that into consideration. That said, wolves in the greater ecosystem make a very positive impact pretty much every level. And so the research does indicate that it is statistically and ecologically more sound to have the wolf there and to protect it and restore it. That said, there's the caveat of it's not a blanket, just do it 100. No, no, no. You have to be considerate of the fact that there are people who also cohabitate in these regions. And so that's all it is, is it's not taking a blank, a one-sided blind approach, walking blazing a path through the woods. That's how we got here in the first place. But taking into consideration that this is complex, we have a goal, and to get that goal done, it's going to take some work.

Cole Heilborn (18:50): Yeah, no, well said. The art of telling a story in itself, the science behind it is it can be frustrating and very complicated.

content:
Roberto Gutierrez (19:03): And I think what's interesting, so I was doing research on, I should have done the numbers so I can bring it up, but the number of cattle killed each year by wolves is far lower than the number killed by domestic dogs and then killed by coyotes. Yet we don't have the same visceral reaction. And so the numbers indicate that if you're going to use that as an argument, you have bigger fish to fry, right? Vaccination, like sick cattle is one of your number one killers. So if I were to take all the money we're spending to fly helicopters in and hunt wolves, maybe that could be better spent vaccinating cattle. So there's just interesting conversations to be had all around. I think that the hard part is then, as we mentioned earlier, with all the fake news and people sort of finding their own sources or finding their own information without checking the sources is becoming a problem. And that's what we'd love to highlight. But it's tricky. It's very hard to do.

Cole Heilborn (20:09): Well, it sounds like an amazing project. When will it be out?

Roberto Gutierrez (20:13): So we're going to release a teaser in hopefully two weeks. So keep an eye on our social media, Jack Wilkin sub score Na for North America, and then the little mini doc will be released at public lands in, I believe Pittsburgh in December, and we'll be offering a chance to win a free trip to Jackson Hole and then go track wolves with the wolf trackers. So keep an eye on that. Yeah, it's a pretty cool giveaway or sweepstakes I guess.

Cole Heilborn (20:45): That's awesome. That's super cool. So kind of jumping back to the work that you're doing day-to-day, bringing the brand to North America, what differences have you had to embrace just between the German brand and the brand here in North America? Are there differences that you're having to account for and correct for?

content: Roberto Gutierrez (21:06): Yeah, I mean, honestly, there's a couple of things. So this year is our 40th year 40th anniversary of the brand in Germany. That means a lot, but for us here in North America is what we would call one of our first years in North America celebrating your 40th year is that's like a for year old showing up to a one year old's birthday party and be like, I'm 40, nobody cares. And so we just have to adjust some of that messaging so that it's more relevant to people being introduced to the brand rather than, Hey, it's our 40th birthday. It's like, Hey, we're 40 years going. And so it's little things of that nature. And then I think one of the things we honestly struggle with is as a company founded in hike and trekking in Europe, that is just a thing you do in North America. (21:56): We've got this kind of, I dunno if it's cavalier or cowboy mentality, where everything has to be done to its pinnacle and peak. And so as a result, your fastest hikers or your best hikers are either mountaineers, rock climbers or trail runners. And those are different sports. We don't make climbing gear specifically, we make stuff you could climb in. So one of the interesting things we're trying to do is, but on the flip side, most people are out hiking, more people are hiking than they are summiting, even Whitney or Baker or whatever. And so yeah, we make the product for the people. It's just that in the ecosystem here, people have an expectation. So we're trying to build awareness, and that's been a tricky one without having, that's been probably the biggest thing I've struggled with is trying to identify that pinnacle piece. And then of course, our sustainability. In today's day and age, you have to be cautious because people just read it as greenwashing. It's like, no, it's who we are. And it's not like we're hanging our hat on, it's just what we do. So we find some obstacles there, but at the end of the day, the product is premium and fantastic and well priced, and so it'll carry itself. And once we are able to tell more stories like the Wolf Tracker one and other stories like that, I think we'll be fine.

Cole Heilborn (23:30): So you're saying that you're having to, the challenge is trying to embrace the North American pinnacle perspective on sports, or sorry, maybe I'm not tracking with what that challenge is.

Roberto Gutierrez (23:43): The system is built a certain way. So the influencers, storytellers, marketeers, adventurers and so on are all shaped around a few core stories. And then you tell your big stories about something special in that realm. So North Face has a stable of rock climbers and mountain bikers and trail runners, and they have a couple in there who are your Alex Hos or your Stephanie Howes of the world who are going to be pinnacle trail runners, things of that nature. So the system is built that way. So if I'm going out to find our pinnacle hiker, our person, it's tricky. The Pinnacle hiker is it, like I mentioned, Stephanie Howe, right, who's a phenomenal trail runner, probably not, right? She's somebody who averages like 10 minute mile for a hundred miles. That's not even through hiking, that's another level. So I'm probably a nine minute mile for that long, honestly. But anyways, yeah, it's just a little different for us there. Right.

Cole Heilborn (24:55): Why is that difference? What does that difference say about the culture difference between North America and Germany? Could you speak to that?

content:
Roberto Gutierrez (25:04): I think if anything, the culture difference is the, so to give you an example, and I hope I don't get thrown on the bus for this one, but so Columbia, right? My first camp first all probably, sorry, yeah, it was maybe a Columbia tent and a Coleman stove. If you were to show up at the base of Whitney with a Coleman stove, you'd probably get laughed out, right? You'd be like, dude, you're doing what now? And so then Coleman, because there's this pinnacle perception gets this B grade backyard old person camping vibe, whereas if you showed up with that same heritage trusted piece in Germany, you would be seen as like, well, that's a wise decision. That thing works. And so some of our tents, we have some lightweight ones, but the majority of our tents are actually quite heavy, but they are phenomenal. Whereas in the US it's like grams, grams, grams, grams, grams. (26:08): And so you just get this like, oh my God, that thing just works. That's epic. Whereas in the us, we'll fight with a pole until our nose is bleeding because we want to save three grams. And so I think there's probably the difference where you can still stay. I don't think it's going to be very hard for Coleman to ever regain a prestige back when the canteen or whatever it was was probably their biggest thing early on, that it'd be hard for them to gain prestige where in Europe and in other places, being quality and sustainable and durable earns you that same prestige. Just culturally, it's appreciated differently, I think, if I had to say.

Cole Heilborn (26:51): Okay. Interesting. I feel like though there's a space opening up and welcoming brands who aren't the classic elite Summit Pinnacle brand. Would you agree? Do you see that as well?

But yeah, there's absolutely a space for those brands and it's being much more welcomed into this space. I think they also have a bespoke feel where you can have the founder of Cotopaxi Davis is going to stand up and he's going to say something and talk, and he's going to be on their ad and he is going to post on their LinkedIn where the founder of Jack Wilkin, I think retired 20 years ago from Jack. Roberto Gutierrez (28:07): I do love the what Jack Wolff skin bikes keeping everything proprietary has been able to do is bring high quality product at a better price point. And so I think being able to introduce people to performance like an 800 fill down at a price point that they could for 150 bucks instead of 350 bucks, that opens a lot of eyes. And to sort of be the gateway there, I think that that's our opportunity. And then also to celebrate, as I was talking about those endorphins over adrenaline. So I always like to give the example of you can look at a grass field, just stand there, and it's a big field of green, but if you lay down on your stomach like you used to do as a kid, you'll see dew drops and bugs and the blades of grass look like it's something from Honey I shrunk the kids. And that even just changing your perspective, that is it five, six feet laying down, it's a whole nother world. And I think that we can celebrate those moments without having to set up an illuminated tent over a boundary line so that you get a good Instagram picture. And so I think because the world sort of has been waking up to that just for Instagram and Red Bull type, Huck Go big mentality, that was not a slight on Red Bull. They're a fantastic brand. But

Cole Heilborn (29:30): You've talked about some of the challenges to bringing the brand in North America. Is there one looming threat that kind of keeps you up at night?

Roberto Gutierrez (29:39): It's probably self-imposed. If anything, the expectation. I love the saying it takes 10 years to make an overnight success, and I think that we have to keep realistic expectations for each day and everything we're doing. We're not going to be sponsoring the climbing wall at REI tomorrow. It's not going to have our logo all over it, but hey, one, that's not the goal at all. But two, we just have to be realistic in those. We will do amazing things. The stories are going to be incredible as we go. We're definitely going to invest in a global level. The impact we make continues to be great. So we're doing all these amazing things, but like I said, it could be a minute before we're a household name, so we have to keep that in mind.

Cole Heilborn (30:29): Is that conflict, is that friction for you personally, because you're all about getting out there, making stuff happen as quick as possible?

Roberto Gutierrez (30:37): Yeah. Yes and no. I think eight years ago it definitely would've been, but now I think that knowing where you are is really important to figure out where you're going. You look back twice as far as you look forward type thing, but it's tough without a huge history. So the hardest part is celebrating the wins. We did more revenue in two months or three months this year than we did the entire year prior. That's incredible. But that seemed like it was off the mark because our forecasts were supposed to be higher than that, and it's like, okay, well keep in mind and celebrate those little goals. So I think it's just a, and then we made it up in the next month and it's like, oh, wow, we didn't expect that win. So it's kind of back and forth on that, and it's just trying to keep perspective, what is it? Can't see the forest from the trees type thing. So yeah,

Cole Heilborn (31:38): This might be a really long answer, but how do you even begin to bring an established brand to a new continent and just say, oh, tomorrow we're going to give it a go. How do you even begin that?

Roberto Gutierrez (31:54): Yeah, I mean there are a bunch of answers to that. So you can check the y'all Raven model where they brought a couple items over and then their backpack just flew off shelves and they basically built a brand in North America on 25 different colors of the same product. That's really boiling it down. I know there's a lot more that went into it, but that's kind of what they've been come to be known for. And even their site North America is backpack heavy. So that was one way is to pick a couple winners and carve out your space there than introduce more and more of the brand. I think one of the realizations I had to quickly come to was that I'm not building a brand in North America. I'm just exposing North America to a brand. So you have to take all of the steps of a more established brand to exist here. You can't sidestep or skirt or shortcut the way a startup or a super, super scrappy 2-year-old brand can, so there's no pivoting there.

Cole Heilborn (33:00): Why is that? Why can't you take those shortcuts?

Roberto Gutierrez (33:03): Well, I mean, again, Jack Wilkin is a global brand whose product development line is being built out years in advance, any other global brand. And if all of a sudden we see North America is like, oh my gosh, our bike touring line is just blowing up. We should focus solely on bike touring. Well, the company may have only made a certain amount of bike touring or planned for a certain amount of bike touring. We can't just be like we're now a bike touring brand because that's not what we are. We're a whole outdoor brand offering sleeping pads and tents and shoes and socks and hats and beanies and jackets and layers. So because it's big ship, small rudder, we can yard on our rudder as much as we want, but it's still going to keep going straight. So we have to sort of address that, and then you just have to address, you either have to change the boat or change the destination. And so if we're not changing the boat, we just have to adjust our expectations.

Cole Heilborn (34:08): But I mean, that's not always a bad thing. Being able to show up with the strength and the resources that you do probably makes a lot of startups be like, well, shoot, we would trade some flexibility for 40 years of history.

Roberto Gutierrez (34:23): Yeah, no, I mean, yeah, no, coming from the world where crap, are we going to make payroll this week? Hey guys, how much money do you have in your bank account? Can we pay our team to, man, this healthcare program is really nice here. They're different, those types of things. I think it's just frustrating for people who you put a players in a position where they're not allowed to sort of, and this goes across our team. We have a really, really talented team and not allowed to blossom at times or to flex all the muscles they wish they could. That gets hard. So

Cole Heilborn (35:01): Yeah, that makes sense. I know we're kind of coming up on the end of our time for today, but a couple more questions. How have people received the brand? Do most people know that it exists here?

It's amazing to be part of a, it's not a rebrand, but a brand adjustment and the globalization of, like I said, I think it's the fifth largest outdoor brand in the world. We're based out of New Smyrna Beach, Florida, and we're an independent company. We make our own stuff here in our little, it used to be a race car garage and out in the country, and we moved in and sort of revamped it a little bit and are doing our operation out of here, but we have a lot of people who are from this area and had worked for another sunglass company that's no longer here. And so we've got a great team of friends and about 15 people here and probably another 45 out scattered about the country. And we make performance sunglasses primarily for the fishing market, but really for any type of water activity, everything we do is very sustainable, sustainably made, the materials, the processes, so we're real proud of that. And then we use what little cloud we have at this point, but is quickly growing to make a difference in the world in terms of ocean conservation primarily.

Cole Heilborn (02:45): That's awesome. And I'm assuming fly fishing and being on the water is a passion of yours?

Al Perkinson (02:52): It is. My wife, Marguerite and I, when we were starting this company, we knew that it was going to be 24 7 and we said, Hey, what direction do we want to go? And said, well, we got to do something that we love and it needs to all be about that, so we'll have for the energy and the passion to take to make it happen. And so we love salt water, fly fishing, that's our big thing, Marguerite's from out west, and so we love western fly fishing as well, but the top of the top is bonefish and tarpon and permit on a flat and some beautiful place in the Caribbean or wherever else. So that's what we love to do.

Cole Heilborn (03:37): And bajo is Spanish for shallows, is that right?

I started in New York at Ogilvy years ago and started working, was in the agency business and got a little sunglass company in Florida called Costa Sunglasses As a client when it was a $6 million company, they asked me to come over and head up marketing, which I did for about 16 or 17 years. And we grew that into a pretty sizable brand and really did it with a lot of cause-based type of marketing and with an emphasis on brand authenticity because it at the time was a cool little authentic brand. And so I think that's a little bit what we're going to talk about today is sort of what the formula is for that. We were successful, I guess it was back in maybe 14 or 15. We were named one of the top 10 cult brands in North America, and that was up there with Converse and Yeti and Patagonia and some of the big guys. So our little strategy worked pretty well and happy to share it with some others.

Cole Heilborn (06:40): Back in the day when we connected, we were talking a little bit about this topic, and you mentioned 20 years ago or so, you and your team were trying to break down what does it mean to be an authentic brand really before I think the authentic thing became a buzzword, right?

content:
Al Perkinson (07:00): Yeah, that's right. When I first met Costa and it was a little fishing brand out of South Florida, the thing that struck me about the brand was that it was authentic, that it was a brand that was used for a specific purpose by specific people, and there was just kind of this, for lack of a better word, authentic nature to the whole deal. And so we were charged with developing the brand strategy for them. We kind of got hung up on that idea of authenticity and started asking the questions, what does that mean? Actually, you hear people say it from time to time, but what does it actually mean And what other brands are like that we might want to look at? So I think we looked at probably 40 or 50 different brands that we just said, I think that's an authentic brand. And that was everything from Hershey Chocolate to Chick-fil-A, Patagonia. (08:09): The list was of types of companies and types of product was really broad. But I remember we got this big spreadsheet, like an Excel spreadsheet, and we started putting just different things about each brand and each of the little boxes. And then after a while we looked at it and things started lining up and we were like, oh my gosh, have these authentic brands all been playing from the same playbook, all doing these four or five things that are the same? And so we feel like we felt like we had discovered the holy grail. And so we took those five things and just kept working and thinking about 'em and refining 'em and then use those as sort of the basis for the brands we were working on. And it just worked. It resonated with consumers and resonated with importantly people within the company who just sort of intuitively related to those things.

Cole Heilborn (09:20): And you mentioned that you just made a list of 40 or 50 brands. I'm sure folks listening could probably do the same. They could look at a roster and just pick brands that they feel like are authentic. What about a brand makes it feel authentic? If you had to do a gut check on 10 different brands, you could pull out the ones that you feel are legitimate. What goes into that process as consumers are trying to identify authentic brands?
