content: Al Perkinson (09:50): Well, I think you start with just kind of a feeling maybe that this is a real company, it's a real, it really is about the company as much as it is about the product. And when you get into authenticity, I think you have to look at the whole thing. You can't just look at one piece like a product. And back in the day when packaged goods were king and there was Proctor and Gamble who's still around, but there was this whole sort of detached management of these brands, but the company behind the brand was never really brought into it. Nowadays, especially with the visibility into companies that the internet has provided, it's hard for companies to do that to create a product out here while the real company pulling the strings is behind it. And so they're held accountable and things kind of have to be in alignment all the way through. (10:56): But I think you start out feeling like this is real, and maybe it's a company with a really cool story. You look at so many brands now, and it wasn't like this. It wasn't as prevalent 20 years ago, but now every brand has figured out how to craft that story of two dudes who started out as kids love to do this. And then that interest grew into a passion, and that passion grew into a business. So you hear that creation story, and from the beginning we believed in this and we still believe in that today. So that creation story is something I always look for in terms of brand authenticity and then a higher calling or a purpose as well in the brand where you're about something more than just commerce, you're about something more than making a buck. Consumers really expect companies to be given back and not just taking resources or natural resources or people's money, but that there needs to be sort of a balance. (12:09): And so there needs to be what we call it, a higher calling as part of that authenticity story usually too. There's a different look and feel. I mean, design has evolved to be such an important part of brands. Brand design is a whole discipline, and there's some great new brand design companies out there who've perfected it, but that design, just like your higher calling, it says something about your values. And if you look at a brand that's really simple and it's design scheme might be kind of primitive, that probably says something to you about what kind of company that might be. If you see one that's super high tech looking, then that's probably, you're a high tech company, but it should get at some deeper values as well. And then once you get out and start operating in the world, you standing behind your product, just like the dairy farmer did with his cow and his milk, you standing behind your product is super important. And then really being committed to your customer and treating them a part of the family and not just as somebody you're trying to sell something to. So those were the kind of four or five things that popped out at us, and I'm sure they're recognizable to everybody.

content:
Cole Heilborn (13:39): So I want to jump back and let's talk about this idea of a creation story. I'm curious first, what is your guys' creation story? Because what I find interesting is you're brand new four months into this, and so I'm sure a lot of these points are things that you guys are asking yourselves as you're in this development process, but why is this creation story so important?

Al Perkinson (14:02): Well, I think it kind of seats the brand in a specific place, and it creates a set of, I think mostly a set of brand values that, and it gives those values legitimacy. You can say these were here from the very beginning, and these are part, not of a marketing strategy, but part of a passion strategy. It's something that we really, really do believe in. We're not faking you guys out. This is always what we believed in. It's always what we will believe in. So there's so much skepticism about value stories that planting them in the creation of the company and even beyond that and the creation of the founders of the company, I think it's super important. And it's kind of like with a person, I think marketing, branding, it's all about being human and a brand is a human. It's like a person, it's an entity and it goes to work every day. It does stuff outside of work. It has a belief system, it has friends, it has enemies. It's sort of an organic being. And so if you're asking a friend lots of times the first question you ask when you meet somebody is like, oh, where are you from? Why do you ask 'em that? Because where they're from probably gives you some clues about who they are. If they're like, Hey, I'm from Texas, man. You're like, okay, he is a Texas dude. Or Hey, I'm from California. Hey, he's a California dude. (15:55): And it's not just like geographic place, but you hear people all the time, whether they're a musician or an actor or politicians, especially football players. I was born in a log cabin and I didn't have anything growing up. So I learned how to be scrappy and I'm still scrappy to this day. So yeah, I think those creation stories just help inform people in a legitimate way about who you are and what you care about.

Cole Heilborn (16:27): Could we not look at creation stories though and be like, well, how true really is it, are those stories just being made up to further legitimize the brand and question?

Al Perkinson (16:40): It's that way kind of across the board because marketing people are really smart, and when they see something that works, they want to copy it. The good news is though that the internet has become kind of the great leveler and the great investigative tool. And so usually the truth, I think it comes out and it is hard to fool all the people as to what the real underlying truth is, but it is definitely attempted. I think there's all kinds of brands, and we were doing some work with some folks in Nashville, and I started reading the bios of all of these country stars and their publicists wrote, they wrote these stories and these stories are not true, but they help that they know that that particular singer, that their audience is looking for a certain type of person, maybe it's like a strong few words, man's man. And so they try to pattern their story to fit that narrative. And consumer brands do the same thing. So you question it, you research it, which a lot of people do these days, and you try to find out what's really real.

Cole Heilborn (18:12): What is your guys' creation story? How do you articulate that?

Al Perkinson (18:16): Well, other people kind of create it for you sometimes. And several of us worked at Costa Sunglasses for many years and built that brand. And then Costa was bought and we felt like we built Costa into a very likable, very friendly kind of brand a few years ago before all this happened, people would say, they wouldn't say, I like my sunglasses. They would say, I love my sunglasses. And when we would do loyalty scores, they would be astronomically high. So there was this cult following that was built around goodwill, around good customer service, around quality products and all of that. And so part of our creation story is coming from that. And what happened was a giant corporation from Italy and half of us from France, half from Italy, bought that brand and laid off 300 people in this county. And so we've come in to give those people their jobs back and more importantly to the industry needs a brand that has the values that we personally hold and that we've had before. And so we feel like it's important to have a brand like that in the industry. So that's the short version of that is, hey, the old Coasta guys got the band back together and started a new company, and it's kind of supposed to be like the old one was. So that's how that gets translated in retail among people, I think.

Cole Heilborn (20:09): Okay, very cool. And that leads us then to the second point that you mentioned, which is having a higher calling standing for something beyond just commerce, as you said. I know you guys are heavily involved with a lot of conservation, environmental programs. What else? I feel like that's a very common higher calling piece for brands in the outdoor industry. Are there other forms of a higher calling?

content: Al Perkinson (20:41): Yeah, there are. It's interesting that the role that brands are playing in our society these days, and not to overstate it, but brands are kind of taking the place of the creators of the mythology. And it used to be that religion was probably the biggest driver of mythology in society, and that's probably not as true anymore. And mythology is super important to a society because these are stories that we tell each other that tell us how we should live our lives. And so there's a moral to the story and you're supposed to learn from it. And that's the mythology when we're talking about higher calling. You ask yourself, what is the moral of our story and what is the message that we want to put out in the world that's going to make that world better? So there are acts that you can do, go roll rocks in a stream or go plant a tree or whatever, but there's also sort of philosophies and mythologies that you can put out there. (21:57): And there's so many, there's so much emphasis these days I think on the narrative of money and that if it creates jobs, it's good. If it makes money, it's good. And it's the excuse that so many people use to do bad things. And so you'll see a company, a corporation that'll come in and destroy the environment and be like, yeah, but look how many jobs we created. Well, how many future jobs did you threaten or eliminate by doing what you're doing? So anyway, I think that sort of the narrative that you put out there and the mythology that you put out there can certainly be a form of higher calling. And one of the messages that we want to put out there is to the millennials and the Gen Z folks to say that money is not the end all be all. It's important to make money and support your family, but don't sacrifice your life because your parents told you you got to be responsible and go make a bunch of money, live your life based on what you're passionate about, live your life based on something that aligns with what you love to do, and it's okay to do that. (23:27): And so it sounds like an odd message to be coming from a brand, but I think it's a totally a legitimate one. And one of the things that we try to emphasize is exploration. And you don't know who you are until you've gone out and explored and put yourself through the paces and put yourself in situations that are scary where you're uncomfortable and you're not safe. And our generation man with organized sports and play dates and all of that stuff, the baby boomer parents have just sheltered their kids like crazy to where true exploration is almost nonexistent. And so I think as a result, these kids, a lot of 'em are lost because they don't really know who they are. I've talked to so many of them who say, you know what passion, man, I saw that on Instagram the other day. Somebody talking about passion. I know I should have a passion. I just don't know what passion is. I don't feel it. I don't know what my passion is. So helping through fly fishing, through exploration, helping some of these young people really find themselves and find out who they are is a big part of what our higher calling is.

Cole Heilborn (24:48): I love that. How do you do that though?

Al Perkinson (24:52): Well, you can support other folks who are doing it and then you can do things that sort of enable exploration or inspire exploration. We all make a lot of content, but content, I don't really like the word content. I like the word stories. And we know that story is so incredibly important to move people. No one has ever waged a war without a great story behind it. The soldiers are following the story. Religion is all built on story. Every great film is built on story. So to telling great stories that where the moral of your story is what the message you're trying to get across is, I think that is one great way just to tell inspiring stories. But we also work with other groups. There's a little group called Fish for Change, and a friend of ours, Steve Brown started it. Heather Harkavy is running it, and they do these summer camps where they bring high schoolers to Guha in the Bay Allens of Honduras or Costa Rica or The Bahamas, even Mexico and the Keys. And they spend a week teaching 'em how to fly fish. They teach 'em about conservation. They do all kinds of exercises to sort of challenge each other, and they come back transformed and changed for the better. (26:35): And so we're doing some interesting projects. One we're you're familiar with youth hostels and people travel and stay in youth hostels because it's a really inexpensive way to travel. Well, we're creating fishing hostels. So these are hostels where people can go and stay and fly fish, and it doesn't cost three or $4,000 a week like lodges do. It's 14 or 15 bucks a night. You've got the exclusive on this. We're just now kicking it off in the first part of October, but just starting to build the first one. But we plan to have these all over the world and to create a community of people who are traveling to fish and to explore and to find themselves.

Cole Heilborn (27:30): That sounds incredible.

Al Perkinson (27:33): Well, good.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:34): Yeah. Oh, man. Well, I'm excited to see that continue to roll out. One of the other points that you mentioned was this idea of performance around the product. Does it work? Does it perform above and beyond the customer's expectations? I guess it probably goes without saying, obviously the product needs to be of quality in order for these other points to even be valid.

Al Perkinson (27:59): Yeah, absolutely. And over the years, as part of that contract with corporate America, and one of the ways that that contract has been broken over and over and over again, it used to be you go and buy a pound of coffee and I'm dating myself, and then all of a sudden they took a few ounces of it and it looked the same, but it wasn't a pound anymore. And they're like, gotcha. We saved some money. And you still think it's a pound of coffee, and it's a tiny example, but that happened over and over and over again. The whole discounting of America with the big, whether it's Sam's Club or Costco or Target or Kmart, what those consumers have said, look, man, getting back to the narrative of money and possessions or everything, they're like, I can't really have the good stuff. I at least want to look like I have the good stuff. And so they buy these lookalike products at discounts that are made all over the world through these crazy supply chains, a lot of it in Asia, but elsewhere too. (29:11): And so I think what's happening is that quality has been sucked out of so many of our products over time. And it's not just quality of the product, but it's quality of the service. I mean, customer service, I guarantee you, we all have 20 nightmare customer service stories that we could tell. And with all the merger and craze that has happened, lots of times the customer service department is the one that gets cut first, and it's kind of like, eh, consumers, if it breaks, they'll just have to buy another one. So I think there has been this decline in performance in the last, I don't know, 15 years maybe. There's been a whole nother class of products. It's made for professionals. Well, it used to be that all products were made for professionals, but now you have to spend a lot of money and quality is really the only people who can get it are the people who can afford a Viking stove or a Mercedes-Benz car or super high-end type of stuff. So anyway, I do believe that if you want to keep the faith with the consumer, if you want to keep that contract intact, if you really want to be authentic, then you have to be serious about performance quality. And there can't be an asterisk by it. (30:49): It's got to be performance and quality even when it hurts. So you screwed up and something went wrong, well step up, own up and fix it and pay for it. That's when if people are really committed to quality and really committed to performance, I think that's, you're right, it's central to everything else. Although if you have a strong brand, it can at least buy you some time and provide some equity that it takes to fix some of these other problems that you have.

content:
Cole Heilborn (31:30): And from your guys' perspective, having quality product, does that just mean having a really strong quality control program or process, or how do you make sure that everything is up to code?

Al Perkinson (31:43): Well, yeah, I mean, it starts in design and you design in quality in a lot of cases. So for example, if this is very specific to the sunglass world, but if your frame is made by one company in one country and your lens is made by another company in another country, then those two, when they get put together, they have to have the same curve. If they don't have the same curve, then one of them gets bent out of shape. If the lens is plastic, then it's probably going to be the one that gets bent out of shape. And what happens when it gets bent out of shape is that the view is distorted. If it's a glass lens, then the frame's probably going to get bent out of shape and it's not going to fit the way that it's supposed to fit. So coming up with design that sort of builds in and guarantees quality is the first step in the process. (32:51): Then there's manufacturing and all the things that you have to go through to create molds or to select materials that are high quality materials to find manufacturing partners. You're trying to hit price points. And so there are limitations. You can't just make the most expensive best of everything. There's a value equation that comes into play. And then once it all comes together and you put it in the market quality control, and we make the stuff here, cut the lenses, put 'em together. And so each piece has to be inspected by somebody who knows what they're doing. And even then they miss stuff. So once it gets out into the market, then you have to have a system that allows people to return things and you can service them really quickly. You don't charge them if it's your fault, you don't charge 'em anything. If it's their fault, you're reasonable on what those repair charges might be. So it really goes from design concept all the way through to customer service. And there's so many places where it can break down along the way that you really have to stay on top of it at all times.

Cole Heilborn (34:05): One of the points you mentioned, which ties into this is design and using design, I believe, as you said, as a weapon. Explain more. How do you use design as a weapon to creating an authentic brand?

Al Perkinson (34:18): Well, I think you tie it into what your values are, and design is a visual way of sending a signal to people. I think one of my favorite brands in terms of design, but there's a bunch of 'em, but Arc TerraX is an outdoor brand, and man, you can spot an Arc Alteryx product from a mile away. We moved to Bozeman for a while, and so we went to the skis store to get some skis. We were going to be skiing a lot, and I was looking up at the wall of boots, the wall of ski boots, and I said, what is that? And he said, oh, that's the Arc Taric ski boot. I'm like, of course it is. I should have known that thing is unbelievable. And so before me as a consumer, before I even tried on and it was way out of my price range so I couldn't buy it, but before I even tried on, before I even learned more about it, the design of that product is sending me a message that this thing is simple, it's clean, it's high performance. (35:26): So it kind of sets the tone for that interaction. I think the Volkswagen Beetle was another incredible example. It was like a bug. It was super simple meant for the common person. So it really embodies all the values of that brand. So anyway, I do think it sets the tone. I look at other brands like Target is a great example of that. Their shelves and their stores are shorter than Walmart. And so that allows you to see over the top and give you a feeling of space that you don't get in a stack 'em high, cheap type of situation. They also bring in well-known designers to design their stuff. And so their whole thing is, Hey man, it's cheap chic and design doesn't have to cost a lot of money, and everybody deserves good design. And so that's a part of their whole corporate message of everybody deserves good stuff no matter what the price point might be. (36:39): So these design decisions that people make really say a lot about their overall product and service philosophy and their brand philosophy, and I just think they're incredibly important. Patagonia was also one early on that said, in all of our advertising that we do, all of our catalogs, the human is always going to be little compared to the environment. And that's because we believe that the environment is that we're just here for a short amount of time and that we're in service of the environment. And as you know, their whole corporate philosophy is use business to solve the environmental crisis. So those are just a few examples of design being a weapon.

Cole Heilborn (37:26): How do you use that weapon and your guys' own design?

Al Perkinson (37:29): Well, I think we started with packaging and certainly everything that we do has an environmental or sustainability story to it. And we came out with a leather case and like a cow hide leather case, which most people would say is not sustainable. But then we looked at our head of product design is like a sustainability freak and knows he can get super deep, he could spend a whole hour with you just talking about our case. But when you break it all down in terms of, Hey, this is a food byproduct and it's tanned with water soluble tanning materials, so it's not harmful to the environment, hey, it never wears out. So instead of buying four cases in your life, you can buy one. So that cuts down on the material and the manufacturing that's made. And guess what? If you ever do throw it away, it's completely biodegradable. (38:33): So the only bad thing, the leather case was that one of the big things that's causing the rainforest to be destroyed in places like Brazil is they're creating new pasture land for cows. We love to eat meat so much from an environmental standpoint, meat is not good and we should all eat less of it and all eat more vegetables. So that was the one sticking point that we didn't like. So we kept looking and we found a vegan leather case that's made out of cactus, and we just introduced that probably a month ago. And cactus hardly uses any water to grow, as you might imagine. And then they tan it or dry it out in the sun, doesn't take any electricity, and then their manufacturing process is lead certified. So it hits all however many 750 different boxes that have to be checked, and it has a little bit of polyester in it, but that polyester is all made very sustainably. So it does leave a little residue when it biodegrades, but we compared the two and said, we're going to go switch over to cactus leather. And so again, it's designing into your product these attributes that say, this is something we care about and this is something that we believe in, and yes, it costs us more money, but it's worth it because it is good for the planet. So that's one of the things I think that we're doing.

content: Al Perkinson (41:01): Well, part of it gets back to taking more of a human approach to marketing and to business than more of I guess a business approach. You hear a lot of people say, oh, it's just business. There's a different set of standards for business than for human beings when all businesses are a bunch of people. So it's a dodge and people hide behind this corporate shield. It's the same with the relationship you have with consumers. And we are seeing this real time because we're a brand new company. And so four months ago we had zero customers, zero. And so we have seen who has held up their hand and has come on board and saying, I believe what you believe. I love what you're doing. And they're friends and they're lifelong friends of our brand. And so to in the future, turn your back on those people because you want to chase bigger markets or you want to cut corners and grow more, I guess less expensively then, or to break the contract with those people in any way, whether it's through your higher calling or through customer service or anything else. (42:37): If you look at it from more of a human standpoint, it's just really doing your friend wrong or doing a member of your family wrong. And so we believe that instead of that, you have to listen to the core that these people came on and joined your brand, joined your tribe for a reason, and listen to what they have to say about where you're going to take the brand, listen to what they have to say about the practices that you're putting in place, the things that you're doing. Lot of times they hold up their hand and they're like, I don't agree with this. Well, instead of treating 'em like, oh, you don't know what you're talking about, you're just a consumer, you have to listen to 'em. And I think it's just smart to listen to 'em and they can just be a powerful force for your company and for your brand. (43:35): I believe that it's our job as marketers to build a tribe of followers and a tribe of believers. And that when you're marketing what you're going out and looking for, like Simon Sne says, you're looking for other people who believe what you believe. And if you can build a company and build a brand around a value system around shared beliefs around emotion, then you always have to do everything else right as well. But man, you've got people by the heart, you got 'em by the soul and they will fight for you. I know they will fight for you. I've seen it happen personally, and it's humbling to see. So respect your core sort of worship, your core value, your core. They're extremely important and they're the secret to you pulling in other people just like them. Super, super important.

content:
Cole Heilborn (44:39): So there's only five points. This all seems pretty easy.

Al Perkinson (44:42): Yeah, well, I think it's easy to maybe understand when it's kind of difficult to execute, especially when some of these things don't sound very profitable. Truth be known, purpose-driven brands, authentic brands, tons of studies have been done are extremely more profitable than brands that are not. Consumers see it, they demand it, they understand it. But one of the biggest barriers to brand authenticity is ownership structure. It's funny because years ago, I think probably like 11 or 12 years ago, we started this little group called cem, SEAM, and was, I always forget what the acronym was, but it was basically for society, for the enhancement of authentic marketing. There you go. And so we invited heads of marketing for a lot of big brands to come together and go fly fishing out in Bozeman once a year for about a week and just talk about what problems each other was facing and building authentic brands. (45:59): And it was sort of like a self-help group. It was almost like Alcoholics Anonymous or something, and we all would tell our stories, and so many of them were the same. And one of the biggest ones was just around the barriers that ownership puts up. So if you're a publicly traded company, you have a fiduciary responsibility to return value to your shareholders each quarter, not over five years, but every quarter. And so a lot of shortcuts are taken that are really against product quality, against taking care of your core against a higher calling. And so I think that is just a huge barrier to being able to execute these things. (46:56): Private equity ownership is pretty much the same. They have a big fund. They've got to fiduciary responsibility to return a certain number to their shareholders. Really the only one that does not have those barriers is the independently held company. And so one reason I have an independently held company right now is that I have the freedom to execute these five things and to build an authentic brand. I just came to believe, and you could talk to Yvonne Ard about it at Patagonia, he owns that company and he can do what the hell he wants to do and he can take a longer view instead of a short-term view. And so again, I think that these things sound easy, but when you get into this, money means everything type of world that is out there and the focus on the short term, they become extremely difficult to actually execute.

content: Al Perkinson (48:44): Wow, that's a good question, man. I'm not sure. There's a whole nother one that we didn't get to, which is around community, and so it comes out of committed to the core, but it's a whole nother way that the brand is like who you are as a person. But then when that person gets up and walks out into the world, how does that person behave and what does it do and how does it do it? So that's a whole nother section we call community-based marketing, and it's taking these authentic brand strategies and putting 'em to practice out in the world. So I think that is definitely one that's not the whole thing is there. And so we created this other strategy. The other thing I would say is the one thing that's not here is storytelling. And if you're going to be a really good marketer, we talked a little about it earlier, you really have to understand story and story. I'm a huge fan of Robert McKee and Robert McKee wrote a book called Story and he is sort of the story doctor for Hollywood. (50:08): When directors like John Cleese and I mean you name it, when they're having a problem with their story working, lots of times they'll go to Bob McKee and say, Bob, man, I need your help. Story doctorate. How do we fix this? But Bob, he's not like a technician. Bob a soulful dude, and he has these philosophies and deep hell beliefs on why story is so important to the health of our society and the quality of our lives. And he understands the power of story, and he's a student of story and he's gone through and he's sort of laid out what makes a story, how story works, and he does these seminars that are four days long, eight to 10 hours a day where that man at 75 gets up on stage with no notes and walks you through, here's how you tell a story. (51:10): It's an amazing experience and probably overkill for a marketer to sit through that, but the book is certainly great to read. But there's, you see a lot of these films out there in the outdoor industry these days, very few with any of 'em are done by people who know how to tell a story. They may have learned how to use a camera, and they may have some cool ideas, but very few of them have you sitting on the edge of your seat wanting to know how this is going to turn out and leaving the theater crying or laughing or wanting to do something that's going to make you a better person or change the world. True story does that, and if you can tell a real story with everything you do with your brand, you'll have a competitive advantage over 95% of the other brands out there, and you'll be able to move people to passion, move people to cult status, move people to care about you, to care what you believe in and to care about your brand.

content:
Cole Heilborn (01:43): Fair enough. Well, I'm stoked to chat today. We're going to get down and gritty with the topic of licensing in the photography world. Could you provide a little bit of background on your career as a photographer? I know you've done a bunch of different work you've shot for brands like North Face, Brooks, Columbia, but kind of fill in some of the gaps.

Ian Coble (02:05): Yeah, I've been shooting professionally for 18 years. I went to Western Washington University up in Bellingham and got my undergrad degree in anthropology and finished that degree and then really had that, I think a lot of college educated can probably relate to it of like, well, what the hell am I going to do now? I've got this fancy piece of paper that I spent a lot of money on and I have no idea what I'm going to do. And I kicked around a couple of years and was working full time, just working in the restaurant industries and eventually kind of realized that all my free time was being spent outdoors, particularly skiing, and it was a thought of how can I make money at this? I'm already spending all my time here. This is where I want to be. If I can somehow create something where I can get paid to be here, then maybe that this is the best thing possible. (03:01): And this was before social media? This was before Instagram. This was back in analog days of film, not because film was hip, because film was the only option. And yeah, started the process of learning how to shoot photos and submit to magazines. And a lot of photographers, the editorial is the first place they kind of cut their teeth in the photography industry, and that's how I started. And then in time that led to advertising work for brands and the ski industry stuff like North Face or Heli Hansen or K two or Red Bull. And then I'd been doing nothing but ski work for probably I'd say eight to 10 years and just started segueing into more commercial jobs because the money was there. And B, it was a challenge. I felt like, not to say that shooting skiing isn't a challenge, it's an incredibly difficult thing. It's really tough to do, but I felt like I'd been doing it for 10 years and the challenge of shooting a power turn didn't feel hard anymore. And it was like, well, okay, how can I do something new where there's a challenge? And it was like, well, learning the world of advertising, photography and all the things that go into a large production shoot, that was something new to learn and that was really exciting. So I dunno, I'm probably rambling, but that's kind of a brief synopsis of where I came from.

Cole Heilborn (04:30): Okay, right on. So you were kind of right on the tail end of film world and then have been digital since, I'm assuming? Yeah.

Ian Coble (04:40): Yeah. I think about the first four years of my career were straight film. I still have binders in the closet behind me full of old slides that I can't make myself throw them away. I can't do it. It's going to break my heart if I have to do it. But yeah, I mean it was a great learning experience. At the same time you learn how light plays with film or how light interacts and it's something that you don't get quite as much until you really nerd out in digital, but to have to understand what exposure was in camera because if you didn't shoot it right, you didn't have anything that was usable because there was no Photoshop after the fact.

Cole Heilborn (05:26): Sure. Were you one of those photographers who used a light meter? Was that something that you practiced with?

Ian Coble (05:31): I did, yeah. I have some peers that still use light meters, and I actually really like that now to the point I've been doing this long enough, I can pretty much guesstimate with my eye and looking at the internal light meter in the camera. But I mean starting out, yeah, you almost had to have one or you had to really nerd out on what the light meter in your camera was possible. And I used to carry around a little notebook in my coat pocket, my breast pocket, and it would be like roll number three internal light meter said X shutter speed this, aperture that. And then I would compare it when I processed that role of film and it'd be like, oh wow, that was a stop and a half too dark. And it was like, okay, well here's how I have to adjust for the next one. There was a lot of this really weird nerding out, and it wasn't instant gratification. It was stuff where you had to really be fastidious and take good detailed notes because otherwise you get back a week, you get thrown back a week later from a trip or something, you'd be like, I have no idea what role was from, so I really have to start looking here.

Cole Heilborn (39:25): Where do you feel like things are going?

Ian Coble (39:32): In what sense? Give me a little bit more of a, that could go so many different directions.

Cole Heilborn (39:38): Fair enough. Where do you feel like licensing and this idea of work for hire is going in the future? Will it become more of a thing, less of a thing?

Ian Coble (39:50): I think the future is going to, the bigger a company is, the more that legal gets involved with contracts and it makes sense. That's the legal legal's department is to make sure the contracts or boilerplate, they're going to see a possibility of being liable in a non-work for hire contract. So the legal department is the more they're going to push for work for hire, the bigger the brand is, the bigger the legal department is. So the bigger brands get the more big companies that start buying up small companies and operating them under one umbrella, we're going to see a lot more work for higher in the future, but that doesn't mean that it has to be rammed down our throat because as I've said, I've only had a couple of times where in 18 years where I've had to either walk away or take it. (40:53): Just because someone wants you to do it doesn't mean you have to. So while I think that's going to be increasingly more common to see contracts that are worked for hire, it's up to my generation to try and push back on that. It's up for the newer generation to hopefully do some research, talk to the senior generation to ask for help to reach out. And I think that's a really incredible thing. I will always talk to aspiring artists and I'm not going to tell them how to do their job. I'm not going to tell them everything because at the end of the day, they are my competition, but still educating them is incredibly important because if I don't tell them and they're coming to me for help, then who is going to help them? And not helping them means they don't have the knowledge they need and they could be undercutting the industry, not just me, but the entire industry.

Ian Coble (42:13): I think it's a yes and no. If enough people do it, yeah, it's going to generate a critical mass where it becomes the norm, but there's also going to be the artists that have been around forever that are just so good at what they do that brands are still going to work with them on their terms, even though it goes against what all the new generation is doing or what has the critical mass. If there's still that group of people that are just really good at what they do and they're sticking to their guns, they're going to do it. I mean, if you go to a really amazing restaurant and they're like, it's $400 a plate, you're like, God, I'm not going to spend that. And they're like, okay, well then you're not going to get this plate. And you're like, I really want that plate though. That food's amazing. Then if you really want it, you're going to pay for it. (43:13): Excellence will always be able to demand a premium, but for mediocre isn't super unique. That fills a need, but it's not crazy different. It's not something that anyone else can't do. Yeah, I could see that possibly getting pushed into a royalty or a work for hire scenario where it's just like, okay, well you're not willing to do it. And that's it. And I think that's where you get into a bigger conversation of not just the importance of licensing, but as an artist, the importance of being unique, the importance of having a viewpoint that is very you that no one else can do. And when you have an artist that is just, you can see their work from across the room and you're like, I know exactly who did that. It screams of their style, then brands are going to be willing to, they're like, okay, you're not going to work for hire with us. We still want to work with you. Okay, but if your work, yeah, I could see you getting pushed into work for hire five, 10 years down the line. It could just be one of those things.

Cole Heilborn (44:44): You mentioned that you had some mentors that you learned some of this stuff from back in the day. For people who are trying to learn more about licensing, do you have any resources that you'd recommend?

Ian Coble (44:58): Gosh, off the top of my head, I don't know if the book still exists, so I wish I'd done my research and maybe I can possibly look at it, but there was a book by the A SMP, which is the American Society of Media Photographers called Basic Principles and Stock Photography, I believe. And it's a really boring read, but it cuts into everything from contracts to invoicing to licensing, why it's important, all of those things. If that book's still not in publication, if you went to the ASP's website, they would have resources there. There's other forms out there like editorial photographers. (45:41): There's groups out there. If you go to a camera shop or something and you're a new shooter and you're buying your first cameras and you're like, I'm trying to be a professional, are there any local groups or local chapters that I can meet with? They're going to have a resource list of people that you could talk to or going to the art school. I still get hit up by the professors of like, Hey, would you be willing to have an internship for this particular photographer or would you be willing to talk to 'em? And I always will. I don't do internships anymore. That just became too difficult to manage, but I'll still always make the time for it. (46:24): Don't sell yourself short just on the power of reaching out of who's your favorite photographer on Instagram, drop 'em a dm. If you've got questions and you just like how this person's doing it, ask 'em what's the worst thing that they're going to do? Not answer you, oh, well, but the best thing they could do, maybe they get back to you and they answer some of your questions and you're never going to know unless you try. And for me, the way that I did that, and you have to also, when you're doing this, think of what you're asking. If you're in those shoes, you're asking someone that you don't know to take time out of their day, away from their job, away from their family, away from whatever they were doing in order to help you, a stranger out. So if that's the case, what value can you bring to the table for them? (47:17): When I was doing this, basically I interned and I interned for free. I went to photographers that this was before social media, so I literally just opened up the phone book a photographer and would call their office and be like, do you have room for an intern? I'm like, well, no, we don't have an internship. I'm like, can I sweep the floors? I just want to learn. Can I carry your camera bag? You don't have to pay me. And eventually some of those turned into paid side jobs while I was getting started, but I knew that if I was going to need a professional's time, I also had to be giving something in return for that. You're not going to get an education from someone that's been doing it for two, three decades. If you're just like, Hey, can you show me the keys to the kingdom? But all of a sudden, if you're doing a lot of favors for them and you're helping them out and you're creating value, then all of a sudden there's a reason they want to help you out.

That's just a simple, you believe it or you don't. And I think, as I said, it's going to become more and more prevalent that we see work for higher contracts just because the way I see the world shifting is Amazon is sort of the way things are going. The contracts that creatives see are going to be more right, stripping more all inclusive work for hire contracts where we're forced to leave things on the table. And you can either choose to accept that and charge accordingly because they're now getting a significant value and not just leaving that money on the table or fighting for it and saying, no, I'm going to stick to what I know is right, that what I do has intrinsic value or you wouldn't be coming to me. (50:21): And as such, it deserves to be compensated for. So I just think it's really a matter of from whatever side, whoever's listening to this, whether it is someone in-house, understanding the value in it and why that is important and why it's important to respect the people who are artists and why they're going fight. It's not they're greedy. I mean, maybe some people are, that's not why I'm doing it. This is how I make my living and the only way I can make my living is by charging appropriately for the work that's being done. So hopefully someone that's in-house can understand that. And then if someone's listening to this, that's an artist themselves, they can understand that, yeah, actually I shouldn't be taking those jobs if I see them come across the desk. If I do see that verbiage written in the contract, I should push back and I should have confidence to say, no, I can't do this. Or if they're like, Hey, you have to do this, and like, okay, well it's going to cost you 500% more. It's going to be a five time markup from what it otherwise would've be. And a lot of times companies will pay that then if they can't do work that isn't going to work for hire case, they're willing to pay for it, but don't just sign it because you think you have to.

Tom Moreno (08:19): I would say let's just start with the today and juxtaposing it with Europe versus the us. There are some pretty stark differences there. So skiing as an example may be really what would be called on piece. So really resort focused skiing. It's a more rental oriented culture, whereas in North America, the brand is really known for its free rate products, the QST, the stance lines, those are really what people are using to ski all over the mountain. And the visuals that go along with that are different. So it may be a stance campaign as an example in the two regions, but the imagery that you're going to use to speak to those are going to be a little bit different. And maybe I'm skiing on a groomed run, maybe I'm skiing in chopped up crut, same thing goes for trail running. It's really about where are you running on huge aspiring peaks. (09:12): The Alps is an insanely beautiful place and there's great amazing places here, but the trail running is a little bit different here as far as where you're going to go and what is more approachable. It's really thinking through those types of things. And then your question about six months from now, it's really about seasonality. So making sure that you have imagery that matches the season with whatever you're using. So if I'm six months from now and it's the end of ski season, things are tailing down, maybe that's more spring skiing orientation, maybe it's touring, et cetera. And then on the trail run side, maybe it's a little bit warmer and it's not winter trail running.

Cole Heilborn (09:50): How customized can you get with that? If I'm up here in the northwest, if I go to the website today, can you show me only ski products? But if I was living in Arizona, maybe you would only be showing me trail running products today. Is that possible

content: Tom Moreno (11:27): Yeah, cool. That's a good question. I think when you look at what are consumers interested in, it's what do they use a website for? Maybe they're coming to your website because they saw something inspirational on social media or through a marketing campaign. Maybe they're already members of your mail list and they're coming via that way. How am I inspiring them through that first page? I was going to mention this a little bit later, but when you think about where you come on the website, it's never just to the homepage. If you think about the ways that people get there, so rough metrics, usually across most sites, and this varies, but about 30% come to the homepage, 30% come to a listing page, which would be a category page, like trail running shoes or something like that. A third come to a product detail page. So looking at a specific shoe, so let's say the Ultra Glide from Solomon as an example, and those can all have different touch points, whether it's CRM, email list, text message, maybe it's a social media post. (12:35): And then the last little remainder really comes through higher search intent content pages. So if you run a Google search for how to trail run shoes or how to trail run, sorry, or how to buy trail running shoes or what are the things that I need in trail running shoes, there's content out there that is optimized to meet those search terms and there's different search volumes for each of 'em. So those are really the ways, and it's really, again, understanding what are those consumer needs, what are your consumer personas for your website, and what are the things that I'm doing to meet those needs? Again, how am I providing inspiration? How am I providing the guidance? Once I have kind of set that hook and maybe that inspiration came offsite and now I'm fully into a guidance mode. So it's benefits, it's tech specs, it's features, really the key things and really creating that immersive experience that helps a consumer imagine themselves using that product. Maybe I'm going on a hike out in Colorado and it's using that imagery that helps them say, you know what? I could actually be that person on that mountain.

That's always going to be dynamic and fluctuate based on whatever the trends are, whatever the activations are within a given period, so, so we understand those consumer journeys where I'd say our biggest work over the next couple of years is how do we go through those journeys, those core journeys and make it a more optimized experience? How are we suggesting once they've committed to the right product, how are we suggesting the right products that are within our catalog that might improve their experience as well? How do we make sure that they know these are the things that you need to go do this? If you're say, a more recreational type persona to here are the things that our premier athletes, our Francoise Haynes, our Courtney to Walters, our Cody Townsend, here are the products that they use to do all the amazing things that they do, and really talking to those personas in a different way, but making sure that the journey is consistent, recognizable, and doesn't feel forced.

Cole Heilborn (15:15): Why is it important that the journey feels consistent and not forced?

content: Tom Moreno (15:19): Well, the not forced thing is an immediate turnoff. Let's say, let's use a retail store as an example. If I walk into a retail store and the first thing that they're doing is trying to sell me something, they don't necessarily know that I'm actually there to purchase something. Maybe I'm there to look around and get intelligence about maybe say a specific product or I want to educate myself about what are the things that I need, but I'm not really right ready to purchase today. So that's how a forced interaction can push you right out of that funnel. I saw a post recently about retail shops on LinkedIn and about how consumers are coming in and they want to get fit, and then they're on their phone shopping while they're doing it, and then they'll go purchase elsewhere. In e-commerce world, that same thing exists. It's called bounce rate, it's called exit rate, and it's basically they're coming to the website, they're doing some intelligence gathering, and they may buy from you if they may buy from somewhere else. (16:16): Solomon as a brand has so many points of distribution. There's retail stores, whether that's a independent retailer, it's a larger chain to obviously our website. And at the end of the day, the consumer is going to choose based on their needs and preferences. Maybe that's convenience, maybe that's education, maybe that's some sort of loyalty program. Maybe that's some sort of affinity for the education they've got. If you look at independent retailers, some of the things that they are best at is educating the consumer about a specific product or about a specific category. We'll use boot fitting as the example. The story that I mentioned earlier was about people coming in and charging them for that time. That's putting a friction point to just come in and actually get that education as opposed to leaning into your experience say, and building some sort of loyalty, some sort of trust and standing behind your experience and your education to use that as a benefit versus a friction point, if that makes sense.

Tom Moreno (17:27): Not my area, but it is my area, not my favorite thing if I'm being totally honest. It is absolutely an important way to acquire new users to your email list. It also means that people are going to sign up. I mean, I do this on other people's websites. I'm sure you do as well. Sign up with whatever made up email you have just to get that discount to make that first time purchase. So that's not really building true loyalty. It's basically just saying you can have a discount of always this when you come to shop at our store, that is going to happen at retail stores as well, right? You're going to walk into a shop and you're say, okay, I want this pair of chair running shoes and maybe I'm going to have a top and a bottom, and you can ask for say, 10% discount. (18:09): Or maybe even the sales says, ask for a 10% discount. It's kind of the same kind of concept. That being said, when you pop up an interstitial like that, it does break the consumer's mindset about what they are actually trying to do on your website. It's like, oh, here, look at me. Now I'm going into this funnel. What was I here for? And sometimes that can create problems as well. So they're a necessary evil, but there are other ways to work through that. So we actually just launched our loyalty program called s plus, and I imagine as we grow that program, we will see less and less of the popups on our website when we first land.

Cole Heilborn (18:44): I appreciate that. So when you think about, I'm really intrigued, but you keep using the word flow and keep talking about how consumers flow through the website. If you look at the way that the website is today, we are working through optimizing those pieces. So we have a cross-sell module on our product detail pages. (23:51): A really good example is we had two modules. One was a cross-sell, so we called it complete the look. This would be products you would buy with a similar thing. We first replatformed the website that was at the top of our PDP, probably the most common best practice. And what consumers are really looking for is a comparison because of this product that I'm looking at, what are other products that I might be interested in? So we AB tested that, which is called a multivariate test. We had, I think it was two different variants, basically flip-flopping those two pieces. And the one that had the better results at the cart rate, conversion rate, et cetera, was actually the similar products. So we've made that change based on the things that we saw across the regions, across volumes and the metrics that we were really looking for to try and increase that. So the next phase of that is what are the recommendations across those sports specialties that you're adding to again, make it less forced and really feel like you're a specialist.

Maybe that's your typeface that you're using across different points of the website. So different font types to different banner colors. So I'll use the dropdown menu as an example. And honestly, I don't know, in the future, I feel like that is honestly best served at retail by someone who is hands-on every single day. (29:09): You have to address those consumer needs in a similar way. You have to be able to recommend the right products. It's the same orientation, it's the same consumer journey, if you will. It's just done in a physical space versus a digital space.

content: Tom Moreno (29:40): So EVO obviously offers different things from past seasons that allowed people to get maybe a boot that fits the same as a current one, but at a discounted rate and different options there. So fit was we trained up the staff to make sure that we have that. The second component was a foot bed. We want to make sure your foot is in a consistent space each time. We want to make sure it's supported. And then the third is a sock. We want to make sure you're not putting on this huge thick wool sock. It completely changes the way that your booth fits. (32:04): So if you bought those three components, we would stand behind it with a fit guarantee, and there were different versions of it. And it's kind of been, I would say streamlined for Sonic because Evo sells a lot of boots in the winter. In the time that we were developing that program, I was looking at other options out there. How do we take that physical experience and merge it with the digital experience? There's a lot of different versions out there. There are companies that scan your feet, but none of 'em that usually use this, which pretty much everybody has in a way that makes it super obvious. So the blue sky vision was to take actual boot dimensions. Think of this, I was at a retailer. So trying to get those boot dimensions across all the different brands was very hard. But then what are your physical dimensions and then what are your consumer needs? (32:54): And you use those three kind of components to help provide them a recommendation, which is literally what you're doing in that retail space, but you're bringing it the technology at the time, specifically, the cameras for the mobile devices weren't there, but there are some companies out there that do some things like this. Nobody has quite found the right thing. I would not be surprised if there is something out there today where this is done at least at a vertical level, meaning it's a brand where they're giving you specific dimensions, you scan yourself, maybe it's apparel, maybe it's shoes, et cetera, and then they're giving you different recommendations.

content: Tom Moreno (40:27): Yeah, I would actually start at just the overall business model. So Solomon as a brand has been wholesale since its inception within North America. We've been doing D two CA little over 10 years now, but not all categories. Winter Sports Equipment is a more recent edition where we're selling, we've been selling snowboards for a while direct to consumer. But skis and Nordic, you can find there's big supply chain challenges within that. So what's available today is literally today is a bit of a challenge and hodgepodge in what's available. But because of that, it's not necessarily that the business was built with D two C in mind. So I would say that's overall the biggest challenge is you've essentially, this is a bad analogy, but bolted on a D two C business to a wholesale infrastructure. So there's a lot of what I would consider, Evo, I think probably spoiled me in a lot of ways where they had a lot of internally built purpose driven tools that really helped them shine as a retailer, whether that was the site merchandising that they had. (41:29): Even, I'll go to just the retail example, probably my introduction to product development was I was in the receiving role at EVO at the time in the retail store, and one of our developers at the time who was also from Idaho, which is where I grew up, so we kind of bonded on that. I was telling him the way I have to print stickers to put a barcode in a price on every individual thing is I have to hand key in every single line and hand key in the quantity. And because their interface was so bad, if I made a mistake in that process, I had to start all the way over, and that could be an 80 line thing. So it was actually super easy to make those mistakes. You get pulled away to do something, and I don't even know where I'm anymore. (42:11): So we had this conversation, I showed him five minutes of what my process was. He came back the next day and he's like, Hey, try this out. And I basically pressed the button, and from the receipt that I input into our receiving system, the stickers automatically printed the exact quantities that I needed, and it saved me.

If you look at the way our businesses, there are a bunch of different iterations and a bunch of different pieces with that. Probably the biggest juxtaposition that I would say for Evo versus a brand like Solomon is Evo is talking about a bunch of different brands and they're talking about products, they're talking about stories within said products across said brands. (43:05): Maybe that's their own story. Maybe it's a story that the brands are pushing. Sometimes those align, sometimes those don't. With Solomon, it's kind of the same thing, but through a more product oriented lens, there is storytelling that can happen. Maybe it's a tech story, maybe it's an initiative like WMN, maybe it's an initiative like sustainability, and those are things that you can weave through different stories. But a lot of times, and this has been really insightful for me to see, is within a brand, you have a very specific kind of set activation window, if you will, and really you're thinking about trying to maximize that demand within that window versus necessarily selling over a season. So it's much more like a spike that then tapers down, whereas a retailer may have a more kind of even keel across that specific product as an example. So because of that, on the marketing side, I think with e-commerce websites don't shut off and working with our brand team to educate them on how do we come back to that and tell that story again and again throughout the season? Because consumers don't come to the same website every single day. They may not even come the same week, they may not even come the same month. So how many times can I surface this without it feeling inauthentic or forced or repetitive?

Cole Heilborn (44:25): Yeah. How do you do that? How do you think through that?

Tom Moreno (44:27): Yeah, that's a good question. The first thing is we built standards, right? So when I started, I would say it was a really small team, and we've reshifted the global team plays a component with it specifically on kind of merchandising best practices. They help build campaign banners, et cetera, give us guidance on different various things. But we really put in place more site calendars and then processes for how do we bring a product online for say, a specific kind of high heat event? How do we do different pieces on the website? But really working with those brand managers on say, a seasonal calendar for their categories. What are the things that we should be talking about in any given month? Some categories may only have two to four months filled in with a specific product activation, but that doesn't mean we shouldn't be talking about their category in, especially from an investment standpoint. What are the things that we want to talk about that help show us as a sports specialist throughout an entire season, right? Skis, snowboards, Nordic, maybe a tighter actual and consumer usage window, but those categories live on the website at all times. So just as an example.

Is there anything that folks who might be listening to this episode, a lot of people are in your classic marketing positions, anything that they should be aware of that you come across frequently in the position that you sit in? content:
Tom Moreno (46:06): Yeah, I think consistent communication and alignment. I think honestly, this comes down to your site merchandising managers, your digital product managers, really understanding what their needs are as a stakeholder within the business is that's actually the first step. So it's actually on the site merchandising teams to ask about that because a brand manager, as an example, is thinking across all points of distribution within a given region, and the website is one component of it, maybe a priority, maybe not depending on the category, depending on the brand, et cetera. But really making sure that there's clear alignment on who are the consumers you're targeting for that category. What is the operating best practices that we have for managing our calendar that helps inform what's happening on the website. And where I see probably the most consistent friction, honestly, is really not enough emphasis being focused on the creative brief for say, a campaign. What are the visuals that I need? What are the aesthetics that we need? Because after those are produced, you're playing catch up to try and figure out, okay, I need to tweak this a little bit differently, or this doesn't quite meet my needs. So making sure that everybody's hyper aligned on that creative brief before it goes in across whatever those digital touch points are is super, super important.

Cole Heilborn (47:28): So in a perfect world, would you want to see a creative brief before a campaign is put together to weigh input?

Maybe it's just our visual specialist needs to do a checkoff to make sure we're shooting and we have a horizontal banner or a horizontal photo orientation if they were only thinking about social, which may be more vertical. So making sure that we have those little touch points and checkoffs are super important. So I would say it depends. It depends on the scale. I'll use seasonal gift guides as a very current example where again, going back to those alpine differences, it's on peace in Europe and it's free ride oriented in North America. Looking at making sure that creative brief has the ability for either two deliverables that has both those images or the ability to quickly change though, but it's understood upfront as opposed to maybe during the process of those banner generations.

Cole Heilborn (48:43): Interesting. So you're starting to get into my world a little bit, and now you're making me wonder, I wonder if we can encourage folks to, we get a creative brief and we assume that it's good to go and all stakeholders have signed off on it. Maybe we could suggest that folks maybe take a deeper dive into their organization if it seems like a project that is going to be touching multiple different components,

Tom Moreno (49:09): Understanding how a shoot's expensive, right? I'm sure the quotes are not cheap, and obviously that's going to vary by different production sizes, et cetera, but you're investing the time and effort. You better understand what are my endpoints of distribution where I want this content to be digested. If the website's not part of it, that's fine. That is a brand choice that they can make, but they should still understand is this social, is it, let's use this podcast as an example, right? It's long form, but what are the things that I can chop up within that to use as digital distribution at any given point? So those are key things for marketers to think about.

content: Tom Moreno (54:50): This is actually a really interesting one because in EMEA in Europe, the cookie acceptance rate much, much lower, right? So your ability to personalize and understand who they are is much, much lower. Apple as an example, releasing cookie blocking essentially within their iOS, massively changed the way that people are able to be able to serve targeted ads or targeted even experiences. So I don't have a number for you, but it definitely affects it. It's an interesting thing when you think about just how we have been trained as consumers to just kind of click that box. We can use the app store as the first kind of vector for that, right? Who is going to sit there and read a terms of service or terms agreement? I know you don't. I know I don't. Would be highly surprised if anyone outside of the law industry is actually sitting down and reading these things. (55:46): But they have these massive teams of lawyers that allow you to allow them to have all of the outs for all the different scenarios or the most probable scenarios. So we've been trained and we have kind of like Pavlov's dog. We've just been trained to hit that button to say accept, to move on and move forward because it is a friction point. It's that same popup as when you land on a website and you're given that welcome code for new users. So it absolutely affects your ability to do those things. But at the end of the day, it's your personal needs. If privacy is super important to you, you're probably not going to use Chrome. You're probably going to not accept cookies. Maybe you have a popup blocker. And then on the other side of that, there's people who really want that personalized experience. There's people who some package tracking applications out there that will have access to your email. So they can harvest the tracking number and service you all of the things. But they have access to your email. So if they want, and obviously I wouldn't read the terms of service, but they could read through everything and serve you more targeted ads based on whatever is being said in your email as an example. So there's pros and cons, and you as a person and consumer have to understand what's important to you.

I order something and then I order something again. I said, Hey, I made two orders. Are you able to wipe off the shipping costs and ship these two things together? They're like, no, I can't do that. But that happened in my iMessage. It didn't happen on a website. (58:03): So making sure that you have those placements within, say, an order confirmation page. Maybe I have a checkbox so I can have order updates or have communication through text message or in other countries, maybe that's WhatsApp, et cetera. So absolutely, but they need to be built to solve your consumer orders. If I can't figure out questions on my orders, you're probably not doing it right to start with, or you're probably not addressing what are your most common issues. And so you have to be able to think through that as far as product recommendations and pieces like that, for sure, that can happen. But at the end of the day, if you walk into a store, is it a robot giving you that recommendation or is it a human? People want that human connection and that ability to have a little bit of back and forth play.

content: Adam Cramer (03:39): Wow, so many different scales. I give you two at two ends of the spectrum. So one, we passed this massive piece of legislation or help pass this piece of legislation called the Greater America Outdoors Act back in 2020. And it all arises out of this idea of the Land and Water Conservation Fund and dc everybody reduces things to acronyms. So LWCF, so LWCF was started back in the sixties, and this premise on this idea that you've got all this extractive activity across the country, oil and gas minerals. And a lot of times these resources exist on public lands and waters. And the way that it works is that the government will give licenses to companies to extract these resources. And you pay royalties. So you pull out oil and gas, you pay royalty to the federal government because these resources belong to everybody. And back in the sixties, they had this idea that, you know what, some of these royalties we should reinvest in conservation, in recreation, in access for everybody. (04:48): And back then they said, alright, up to 900 million a year could be reinvested back into conservation. And remember, it's back in the sixties, 900 million a year is a lot, but the hitch is that it was up to 900 million a year wasn't a guarantee. Congress was allowed to do it. So every year it's like, alright, how much we going to send to Land and Water Conservation fund? How much good are we going to dispense? And over the existence of the fund, they hit 900 a million I think twice. And there's always this big effort to get as much as you can and where does it go? And so we had the idea along with many others, that it should be 900 million every year. Then we're arguing because the money's already there, let's just send it out and focus on delivering benefits to American people for conservation, make sure it's equitably distributed, and it's something that people were working on for a long time, but eventually political stars lined up in a way that we can make the case. (05:56): So we educated people throughout the community, identified all different opportunities for them to weigh in with their elected officials. Built a massive amount of momentum around this idea.

So we work really hard to say yes for the parks, how hallelujah. You can't cut out Forest Service, you can't cut out VLM. And we worked really hard to expand that investment to include all the federal land Medicaid agencies. So two huge things. A ton of money for land and water conservation, more equitable investment in all public lands and got signed into law, made it happen. So it's a big deal, talking billions of dollars and the ripple effects are going to be experienced and enjoyed for a really long time.

content: Adam Cramer (07:58): Yeah, so oil and gas again, right? Oil and gas leasing happens all over the place. What we do is we recognize that there may be some intersection between development and recreational resources or conservation values. So we monitor the intersection and it came to our attention. There was an oil and gas lease proposed for the area that includes Slick rock Trail in Utah. So one of the most iconic mountain bike resources ever. And BLM was like, huh, let's develop some oil and gas leasing behind Slick Rock. We thought that's not a good idea at all. So it was because we had that awareness that these two things coexist, development and conservation sometimes to conflict. (08:54): We knew about the process, realized it was not a good idea, educated the community, created opportunities for them to weigh in, figured out who the best audience for this was. Wasn't at Maine Interior, but we focused almost exclusively on the state directors in Utah. And people responded with figure and BLM was like, yeah, sorry about that. We're not going to do that. We please forgive us. We didn't realize that. And what's really exciting, Cole, is that based on that, in part BLM evolved thinking about oil and gas leasing and how they plan things out moving forward. And now what they've been experimenting with is a recreational alternative. So instead of doing oil and gas leasing, they're like, well, maybe the best use of land, best use of this parcel is not to develop it at all. Maybe the recreational resources are more important than the oil and gas resources and keep that stuff in the ground. So it's an example of working on something that's very particular and how that can have a ripple effect on national policy.

Cole Heilborn (10:17): So I know here locally in Washington State, our DNR has been having lots of discussions about their trust mandates around logging forests. And for the long time, at least I think in most states, but in our state, the DNR logs, that funding that money then goes towards the trust mandate, which helps fund public education and a variety of other public programs they're now reconsidering or people are suggesting they reconsider. Is it in the best interest for logging to take place or is it in the best interest to keep trees and use them for carbon sequestration instead of cutting them down and sending the money to schools. I'm curious, this conversation with the BLM that's happening about recreation versus extraction, it sounds like a similar conversation that the DNR here is having. Is that a conversation that's happening all across the country? Are these more common these days than maybe we'd think?

Adam Cramer (11:23): Yeah, taking a more nuanced approach to natural resources has been going on for a while and it's in outdoor alliance's interest to dial up that nuance even more. Back in the day, nobody really thought about it. Okay, we need trees, let's cut some down. We need some oil and gas put a well in. We really thought about, I don't know, climate, the disparate impact on communities that might live next to oil and gas well or a transmission line. And the trend towards being a little more sensitive to the nuance of these decisions and being more precise and being more inclusive with, I think other people that are impacted and have an interest, have their say will result eventually in more refined decisions, better decisions. And then you could weigh the relative value of carbon sequestration, which is huge. And ecosystem integrity, which is very, very important with like, yeah, you got to pay for schools too. And so it enables a more refined, more informed decision making, which is on balance of good thing.

Cole Heilborn (15:26): What's one of the proudest moments that you have felt or you've been a part of or your team has been a part of?

Adam Cramer (15:33): Oh wow. Restoring Bear's Ears. That helped set the curve. President Obama designated it in a super thoughtful way at the end of his term, it was put together in such a resilient, compassionate way to protect the landscape and to honor the value to indigenous people in the area. Indigenous governments who were also very gracious about how other people, people value the area. So getting that monument designated and the way it was designated was just this peak experience. And then having that ripped away during the Trump administration was devastating. We fought really hard and having it restored quickly was wonderful. And some of us were invited to the White House for the restoration ceremony, and I was honored to show up there with colleagues that had been thrown down for this designation or restoration for a really long time. So it's very personally gratifying. And I guess the other thing is getting the Inflation Reduction Act signed. Nobody thought that would ever happen, and then it did and put in a huge jet in climate and having in a hand in moving that along, tremendously validating personally for the team. And I'll tell you, Cole was a similar roller coaster. Things were looking pretty good, and then they looked really bad in the summer, and there's a lot of head and hands like, oh my God, but it worked out.

How do we incite protection of these natural places? And I got to imagine if that's your sole focus, that also there's also areas that you probably could grow at or if you're not focusing on them.
