content: Adam Cramer (18:23): It is been an evolution, and I don't think it's peculiar to us at Outdoor Alliance. We're an NGO, we're a mission driven organization. We exist to pursue some pretty lofty goals, pretty consequential goals, and it's heavy. It's a long time horizon. It's difficult work. And we've become, I think exquisite storytellers could spin a yarn. We know how to convert all this policy Golf league good into terms that are accessible for the community. We do a good job, but it takes a lot of time. And I think over the last couple of years realized we are implicitly part of the story, telling the story, but we're not intentionally the subject of the story. We're not the subject of what's going on. We're enabling it. Our fingerprints are all over the place, but we're not front and center. We're not talking about ourselves. And in a sense, you think, well, we're focused on the mission. (19:40): We shouldn't be talking about ourselves. There's so many other things going on. But the realization that we've gone to is that if we don't talk about ourselves at least a bit, there's less people are going to know about us and know about the opportunity for them to get involved. So in a strange way, for us to really most effectively pursue our mission, we have to talk about ourselves. We've got a responsibility to talk about who we are, how we do our work, how people could be involved, the way to scale impact. It's a distribution issue. We've got the goods, we've got the content, and we've been so singularly focused on that. It's time to think about how to get the word out, and if we do, we'll be able to more powerfully pursue our goals. So we've only been around since 2014. I think we're a little bit beyond a startup, but it's time to start thinking about those things. I think it focuses on that realization that actually you do need to talk about yourself and being at peace with that big giant step.

And the fact that that exists is a story unto itself that they're working things out and we're able to forge consensus. How does that even happen? That's kind of interesting and inspiring, and we've got a responsibility to explain who we are, how we work, how it all fits together, and also who we are, our team, what we're based, what rings our bell.

content: Adam Cramer (24:54): I guess in the very beginning of Outdoor Alliance, the relationship to the broader community was through the member organizations themselves, right? American Whitewater, most authentic spokesperson, representative for the whitewater community, ambo for mountain biking. And we thought of ourselves as a beltway entity. So our audience wasn't so much the user community, but policy makers. And there was by design a way to just separate the two. So we would come up with material, the member organizations, and we'd also channel the sensibilities and values of the member organizations and by extension their respective communities into dc. But it wasn't until a number of years ago that we decided that that was a bit myopic and that we could get a whole lot more done by speaking out to the community itself. So it was first recognizing that we had a responsibility to speak to everybody, the entire user community, about the things that we work on as outdoor alliance. (26:10): So that realization was a big deal. And based on that, we developed a whole strategy around email, social media, and all the conventions. But it took us a step to realize that actually that's something we needed to do, that our audience wasn't just people within the beltway people, the Forest Service people in the administration, and that if we could connect to the community at large, we can empower them to lean into policy makers because all these folks are accountable to the public, to constituents. And if we pursue our mission, we have to be able to mobilize people at scale because yeah, does a senator care about what your staff has to say? Yes, they're interested, they take the call, they'll read our letters, but if a bunch of constituents also weigh in and say the same thing or something similar saying It's important to us mountain bikers in New Mexico or Whitewater Boat in Oregon, more weight in the scale. So I guess it's an evolution based on our devotion to our mission and our goals and realizing that a more effective way to pursue those goals is to deal in more people. And the way you do that effectively is you got to explain a bit about yourself. So it's conceptually in the market

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:46): At first, did it feel like by focusing on bringing in community members or telling your story to the community, that you were taking away from your mission, that you were not focused on your mission because you are working on something else outside of your sole focus?

Adam Cramer (28:05): I guess given orientation and the type of people that end up on our board and the type of people that work at Outdoor Alliance, there's this orientation towards the mission, towards the mission work. And because the mission work is so complicated, anytime you're stepping away, you're like, oh, there's another thing I should read. There's another person I should talk to. And I guess you got to take a pause and realize, yes, but there's other things that are important. I guess it was a maturation, I guess for myself personally and for the organization to realize that we had a responsibility to do other things in long-term service. And I guess it's not taking a rest day. You can't pin it every day. (29:03): And if you do, you're going to get worn out and eventually you're going to get hurt, and then you're not going to be able to do the thing you like to do. So I'm not saying that marketing is rest, but it's doing something that's not your passion or your initial orientation that's actually in service of your passion. And it took us a little bit of time to come to that realization, and we're still figuring out what to do about it presently making some good strides. But it wasn't because of conscious avoidance, like, no, we don't want to do this.

Cole Heilborn (29:48): So what do you see in the future? What are the biggest opportunities for the Outdoor Alliance to continue to advocate your message?

content: Adam Cramer (29:59): I mean, I think we got an opportunity to rethink conservation at scale. In the beginning, going back to the early part of the conversation, there was almost singular focus on development and extraction everything off, going back to a manifest destiny, let's go out and get everything as much as we can, build as much wealth as we can. And then a reaction to that historically was like, let's make some national parks. Let's come up with the Wilderness Act. Maybe we should have clean water and clean air, like the environmental movement was in part and formed by it like this, I don't know, guilt is the right word or remorse. And there was this focus on restoration of the natural world, protection of the natural world, that there was this swing from development and it's too much, and now we've got to protect it, and there's passion there, but that's, it's not really the most balanced, sustainable way to pursue conservation because people have been here in North America for tens of thousands of years, if you really want to think about it. (31:21): The country's been around as a nation for 250 years and pulling out people and what these places matter doesn't help people and society have got to be incorporated into these protections. And I think that there's an opportunity to evolve how we think about conservation, why we do it, the social aspect of conservation, the value to society of conservative, protected places of intact ecosystems, and using that to inform how we could serve and protect places being afforded. And who has the benefit of those conservations, which is protecting places that are really, really far away. That's great, but how about protecting places where a bunch of people live? How about making sure that people have local parks? And the old style of conservation was singularly focused on the intrinsic value of place. Our vision in After Alliance is thinking about the intrinsic value and the social value of place. And the thinking is that if you articulate social value, you could build more political and social support for those initiatives. And at the end of the day, you protect more places because more people care about it.

Adam Cramer (32:54): Well, in the experiences and the stories that people have to a given place, why it matters. I care about All Rivers, but I really care about the Potomac, and I care even more about the Great Falls section of the Potomac because I got a connection to that place. And there's meaning infused in places all around, and there's a responsibility to inventory that, to ask to listen, what do places matter to a lot of different communities too. And kind of pulling all that together. And then you'll have a justification or a theory as to why this place matters, who's going to care.

Cole Heilborn (33:44): I think I read an article on one of your blog posts or one of the articles on the website, and it was talking about the stigma or the belief that most people feel that politics isn't something that we can affect or isn't something that we really have the ability to incite change. And I think the article went through a bunch of reasons and refuted that and talked about how important it really is that we as constituents reach out to our legislators and voice our opinions. Is there a number of if a senator or representative received a certain amount of correspondence about an issue that it would then be on their radar? Is that a thousand pieces of mail, 10,000 pieces of mail?

Adam Cramer (34:29): Yeah. No, it's a positive integer, right? But it's like the input, it all matters, all the input matters, but it's weighted differently based on who it's from. If it comes from a constituent, it matters a lot more than it's coming from somebody who's not a constituent, because these elected officials are accountable to people that put 'em in the office. So not that they don't care about what other people have to say they do, but there's extra witness scale for a constituent if it's an informed constituent, if it's somebody that's explaining from their own personal perspective why an issue is important to them more so, okay, if there's some modicum of understanding of the timing, the urgency, why they're talking about something at a particular time, dial it up even more. And if the lawmaker had not made up his or her or their mind, and they're hearing from the constituent, dial it up to 11, man, it's fluid, but it never doesn't matter. It never doesn't matter. And then there are other ways beyond email, social media, you could show up at a town hall. Now town halls are virtual. So I guess one way to think about it is that if the more time it takes you to show up, think about propose, weigh in, that will be recognized and incorporated into the decision making that whoever you're talking to, whether it's an elected official or it doesn't matter. So it's the number, but the depth.

Cole Heilborn (36:40): What are ways that the industry, I mean obviously the industry is full of advocacy support and funding being contributed, but what are some ways that the industry hasn't been thinking about how we can be contributing to conservation efforts? content: Adam Cramer (37:06): Well, I think it's a joyous question in that the industry, they've got a business interest and then a values interest in conservation. There's an authenticity that is present within the outdoor industry in terms of advocating for conservation. Enviable. A lot of people show up and ask for certain things for a lot of different reasons, but the authenticity that's imbued within the outdoor industry in terms of on these issues is a tremendous asset. So I think that they honoring that orientation is important, and most brands do that. Some of 'em do more and some of 'em do less, but they're all by virtue of what of the industry that they're in, they're all in the game. (38:10): So I think that in terms of supporting advocacy, do one of two basic ways. One is providing support to organizations like Outdoor Alliance and other NGOs and all the member organizations of Outdoor Alliance who are immersed in the game day in, day out, and know what's going on, know what the opportunities are. So providing support for them to just figure out what the opportunities are because brands, and not just to pick on the outdoor industry, who has time for that kind of preoccupied thinking about product and design and sourcing and is like, that's complicated work too. So providing support to NGOs would be great, but also there is a role for them to do advocacy themselves to get into the game themselves, whatever brand there is, they've got at least a Congress person and a couple senators. They've got a governor, they could make themselves heard and learning a bit more about what's important to them and taking a look at opportunities to engage, almost like a menu. You don't have to cook the meal, but take a look at the menu and see what's out there and pick something and show up in terms of direct advocacy, their social media channels, there's so much for them to do. And going back to your question of how many emails does it take? (39:44): An overture from an outdoor brand on a conservation issue is going to matter. And more so if it's to your own elected official. So support and then looking for ways to get in the game themselves. And because there's such a wealth of experience and knowledge within the NGO community, the upper alliance member organizations and us, we could be your guides. You're not going to be wandering around in the universe. We'll show you what the wine is, we'll let you know what you need to bring so you could do it. Have a good time, come home safely.

Does that create the impact that we would hope for?

Adam Cramer (41:02): Yes. Does create news does create an impact. Its value, I think, is that it reinforces the values of the brands. You care about conservation, you care about protection, and you care about the way the public process to enable those things. You got to, you're standing up for your value, you're standing up for what you believe in. And by not doing that, you're signaling that these things maybe not that important to us, which I think would be devastating to the outdoor brands because it'd be completely contrary to their identity. So I think does it matter? Is it effective? Yes. Is it like a cure all? Does it fix everything? No, it's a little more complicated than that, but at least we're all being honest with ourselves about what's important and we're being consistent with how we present ourselves and the story we tell about ourselves and our actions.

Cole Heilborn (42:20): What gives you, I mean obviously you're in this day in, day out, there's good days, there's bad days. What's your general attitude towards the work that we have to do? Adam Cramer (42:43): I'm hopeful and concurrently realistic and honest about the state of the world. There's so many aspects of the world. They're awful and unfair and unjust and embarrassing if you really think about it. And you got to couple that with the realization that there is an opportunity to make things a little better. And it's hard, but it can happen. And because it does happen, I feel a sense of responsibility to keep it a go. That's why it's interesting. If it was a foregone conclusion, everything's going to work out and everything's cool. It's like why bother? It's like the difference between, I don't know, getting on a roller coaster, getting strapped in and letting somebody, letting a Carney pull the lever and then you go on a ride and you're up and you're down. Now, that was a lot of fun. Or going through a really difficult fraught section of sail track where if you screw, you're going to crash. It's way more gratifying to do stuff when there are consequences and it doesn't have to work out. And you roll the dice, that's not the right word. You're not rolling the dice, you're making an informed decision. You're mindful of what the risks are, and it's worth it. You do. It feels good. And sometimes you crash. Yeah,

Cole Heilborn (44:28): Because what is the alternative? That's not a better,

Adam Cramer (44:32): I mean for me, but also just being the essential optimist. I don't think that's especially helpful in this line of work because stuff takes really long sometimes, and it's a circuitous path that we take to being realistic. But being hopeful, coupling those two things together is helps you make some incremental progress sometimes. And that progress is when it happens. It's especially sweet.

We need you.

I have producers on my team that have worked for Brooks for 13, 14 years and have evolved in their role over time. So I think the studio has grown. There was just recently actually someone shared a PowerPoint that was done I think maybe four or five years ago, maybe not even that long, that showed who was on the creative team and it was maybe 15 people, something like that. I mean small enough that everybody had their photo and a little blurb and then now our team is 50 or more. So I think in my time at Brooks, it's grown dramatically. (00:14:00): So there's more that we're doing with that. And so yeah, it's just constantly growing. It can sometimes take a bit for companies I think to really reach that tipping point where it goes over into sudden growth. And I think that's one of the challenges too, is how do you maintain the culture of what it was When I know when I was at an agency, we all went to lunch together and then it got to the point where we couldn't do that anymore because we would take up the whole restaurant. And so that was kind of sad. So I think there's a culture shift as you grow from being small to being big, but there's also the benefits that come along with that as well.

content: Liv Faris (00:15:23): Yeah, so when I started at Brooks, I mean definitely the way that the production team has functioned has been that our producers have been in more of a supervisory role where they're hiring vendors to implement, to line produce, to do all of that work. And I think part of it comes from my background as well of wanting to shift that and then also the needs of the business needing to be more efficient, more flexible. And so I think when I started, there was a lot of fundamental things with the team that we wanted to work on of just as the company was growing process and all of those things. And so to sort of shake up this, let's do it more as prevalent as maybe it is now or the opportunity wasn't as great as it is now. And so yeah, so I just think as more and more work is coming our way and more and more asks are being made of us, it's just making me think about it a little bit differently of, Hey, can we look at this a different way? (00:16:36): I've had producers that have been more in a line producing capacity. I think it's always a balance of when do we do it and when do we bring in a partner? But I just seeing more and more opportunities for us to do it a little bit differently and also have a couple people on my staff now that are more used to doing things that way too. And so I think that will help us shift it a little bit. I think our first real foray into this, I guess was we hired associate producer that also had some photography skills, and so we said, well, let's offer up those skills to the team and make that available. And we saw right away that that was valuable and helpful to our teams. So he splits his time between producing and photography. So for example, on this Portugal shoot that I was just on, he was helping me produce the project, but also had the added benefit of bringing his camera along and taking some photos while we were there versus having to hire another outside photographer to come and do that.

Cole Heilborn (00:18:03): So you said you started to notice something that maybe you could do something differently or approach things differently. What are some of the benefits that you have found by doing things differently? By bringing folks?

Liv Faris (00:18:16): Yeah, I think one of the big things that I see is that people just the ownership and the pride and the passion for the work, when you're doing it more yourself, you just have more ownership and more pride in what you've done. And I think that comes through in the work. So for example, how we got connected was through a video that I shared that we did with the Snoqualmie tribe around respect for the land that you're running on. And that was something that people invested their heart and soul into that this was an important point for us as a brand to support that we're running on this land and we want to respect that and it's not just about conquest. And that was something where our team really needed to understand that and communicate that and feel that. And so that was a really good example of I think, where being able to fully invest their time and thought and have that pride in what they're doing came through in the work.

Cole Heilborn (00:19:33): Yeah, that's a great point. Any work that has a strong emotional attachment, it seems that it's so important for the team that's working on it to be as emotionally invested in the project because the story is told through the lens of the people who are actually making it. And if they're not a hundred percent committed, the story probably isn't being communicated as well as it could be. So you've seen stronger ownership and that has led to stronger emotional responses or a stronger emotional project because of that.

content: Liv Faris (00:20:07): Yeah, I think it comes through in the photos, it comes through in the work and it comes through in the sharing of the work. It's not just about winning awards. Winning awards is great, we love that, but it's, Hey, look at what I worked on. Look at what I did. I'm really proud of this. I think that that's a big part of it. I think there's efficiencies that come with it. So I'll give an example of a recent thing that we did that has a little bit of both. So we were wanting to do some content for Halloween, and so there was some ideas being thrown around our shoe, which is the ghost, and we were launching the ghost, and this is a great opportunity to tie it to Halloween. And so there was a challenge put forward to, Hey, let's make some content and let's do this all in-house, right? (00:21:03): And so were able to, our goal is eventually to have more of a studio and kind of build out the capabilities, but right now we have a small photo room. And so we were able to have our in-house photographer, one of our producers, one of our designers work together and pulled off this, it was photography of a cauldron with a shoe levitating above it and the smoke and all of that Halloween vibes, and we shared that piece of content generated sales, some really good numbers. I mean, metrics is part of the work that we do. (00:21:54): Ultimately, we're a brand that's supporting runners and giving runners the gear that they need and letting them make purchasing decisions about what's going to be best for them. And so this was a chance for us to share our shoe and people saw this content and decided to buy it. And so that's great. And so I think there was a note that came from my producer on that project to me that she said, Hey, we just got these numbers. Take a look at how this did. And I love getting emails like that from my team. I got another one recently, Hey, I'm really proud of this. I wanted to share it with you. I don't always see it first. They sometimes see at first. So I just think that Halloween example was a good one of they spent a couple days, they made this cool thing, they shared it out, it had a impact on the business. They were proud of what they did. And so I just want us to do more things like that. Not to say we're not proud of work that we do with production companies too. Absolutely. I just think there's a little extra level of pride for the team when they're doing it themselves that way.

Cole Heilborn (00:23:12): Well, you're talking about efficiency, and I'm curious to hear your thoughts on the opportunity cost of a timely piece of content. If you go outside, maybe it takes longer. Well, chances are it's going to take longer than it would if you could just pull it off. So there's that gap between when we can get this asset live and there's sometimes a revenue number attached. If it's not known, there is some sort of revenue number attached to that gap in time. How do you see that play out through the efficiency side of it all?

Liv Faris (00:23:45): Yeah, I mean I think there's always going to be give and take. Pulling a photographer and producer for a day or two to go shoot a cauldron in our photo room is going to take away from other work, right? It's going to happen, but I think it's on our own schedule and our own time and we're able to really evaluate that easier, I think, than relying on a partner. So for example, yesterday I was working on the video we shot in Portugal. I was working on a schedule for post because of some of the things that happened on the shoot, we've had to shift a little bit in the content itself. And so we've had to adjust our post schedule. And so I was working on a schedule yesterday to send back to our production company, but I have to take into account what's happening on their end too. (00:24:41): I don't know what their other projects are. I don't know what else they have on their plate versus if it was an in-house editor for example, which we don't have right now, but did we have that? I would know everything that's on that person's plate. And I would say, okay, if she's going to work on this, then she's not going to be able to work on this. And so I think there's always that give and take. Sometimes we're resource, we don't have the resources, so the only way to get it done is, Hey, I need to bring in a freelancer to do that, or I need to hire a production company to do that. So I think it's a constant give and take in what's going to be the most efficient thing and what's going to be the best thing for that piece of content.

Cole Heilborn (00:25:28): Sure. I'm curious if we could dive into the cost perspective because cost is often another reason that people bring up actually pro and con of bringing things in house sometimes I've heard it's cheaper to outsource it sometimes I've heard it's cheaper to bring it in house. How do you think through the financial side of it all?

Liv Faris (00:25:46): Yeah, I feel like this is a constant battle because there's no A ICP, the producers organization has contracts and all of this. They have things that help guide us, but there's not a rate sheet that is used across, I mean, it's like any business, right? Supply and demand impacts, rates and so forth. So I think in production over my career, I've seen everything from the one man band that is willing to do it for a lower cost to the 50 people on set crew that costs way more. And so I think it's no standard to go off of. And so I think it's just a matter of taking it project by project and saying, okay, what the most sense for this? What does the cost look like? We try to do triple bids so that we are getting a good sense of what costs are. (00:26:53): Is that something that we can do that we'll have a time cost? Because like I said before, it's going to, doing one thing is going to take away from doing something else, so it's not necessarily free. I just actually had that happen. I got an email from a stakeholder that was asking about something that they needed shot, and I said, Hey, that's potentially something that we could do in house. And then they said, oh, does that mean it's going to be free? And so yes, it will reduce costs because I don't need to hire an outside photographer. I don't need to pay a licensing fee, that kind of thing. But we still potentially need props and we may still need talent and there's time for Gavin to shoot that. So it's not ever going to be free. It's just weighing the pros and cons or the costs of the things and what makes the most sense for that project.

So it's test and learn all the time. I feel like try it out, see what works, learn from it, move on. Not everything's going to work. content: Liv Faris (00:41:08): Yeah, so one of the things that I did earlier this year was as I'm thinking about what the team's going to look at it and how we build it out is I reached out to some of my peers at other companies to say, Hey, what are you doing? How are you building your team? How are you splitting the work? Who do you have on your staff? What's your org chart look like? Just questions, questions, questions. And so I think I did probably five or six of those conversations just to really get a sense of what other people were doing. And I think we're all seeing have the same questions, seeing the same challenges, everybody's doing it a little bit differently. I don't think there's any magic answer. And I'm part of a group of people in the industry in a conference every year, and that's a topic of discussion too that we've had there. I think it's a constant test and learn, like I said, and every company has different needs and different structures, but I really appreciate and appreciated being able to have those conversations with my peers and just kind of hear what they're doing and hearing that we're having the same question marks and challenges and wins and successes too. So that's pretty fun. And there's one in particular where I actually need to reach out to him. He had offered for us to come and take a look at their studio and I want to go do that. (00:43:00): So just learning. I think I told you when we talked leading up to this conversation about a friend of mine that works at buzzfeed, and we had gone down, we were in LA for vacation, and I was like, Hey, can I come check out your setup? And particularly what they're doing for Tasty. And so we went in, saw their setup for how they were shooting all of those tabletop videos and took that, this is when I was at the agency, but took it back to my team and took lots of pictures and showed them what they were doing, and we set up our own setup to be able to do that. And it was really great. So I think for those of you out there that are listening and doing this and thinking about how to do this, just talk to your colleagues, talk to your peers, learn from what others are doing, listen to podcasts like this. I mean, I'm not an expert. I am learning as I'm going, and all I can do is share my experience. And I think that's, for me, that's a huge thing that I try to do is just learn from others and try things out.

You have a similar mindset, so hey, let's work together to figure out how we can do that here at Brooks. But I think definitely starting with your internal team and figuring out what it is that they bring to the table and tapping into that talent and experience and skills that they have is huge. And then fill the gaps, like I said,

content: Liv Faris (00:46:33): Yeah, I mean, my big thing with being a manager and a leader is supporting your team, giving them the opportunities to try new things, but also building on their strengths. And so I think that's important, whether it's a studio or any other team, just to make sure that your people are doing well, that they have what they need, are feeling fulfilled and excited about their jobs. Because if you don't have that, you don't have anything, right? If you have a bunch of people coming to work every day that are like, oh, I got to go to my job and I'm not excited about this, that's not great. So that's my number one thing, is just making sure that my team feels fulfilled and that they're not overworked, which can be challenging and giving them what they need. And I think we were having a conversation as a studio leadership team the other day about talking about how some people on the team were working at midnight to get something done. (00:47:41): And one thing at Brooks is that we really value a culture of work-life balance. Get out there, get moving, take time out of your day to take care of your body, to take care of your mental health. And that's really important to us as a company, but there are going to be times when we're going to have to put in some extra hours and things like that. And so I think on this call the other day, it was like, Hey, I want to recognize and give kudos to these people that were doing this because without them it wouldn't have gotten done. And one of the things that brought up for me is coming from an agency is that is going to be, I think, and I can't speak for our whole team, but from my perspective is as we become more of an in-house agency, we're going to have to keep a really good eye on that because anybody that's worked in an agency or knows about agencies, it's like when I worked in an agency, my boss was like, this isn't a 40 hour a week job. (00:48:45): And I think that's why a lot of people get burnt out on agencies because it's just a constant, you're never off. And so I think as we do more work, as we bring more in-house, as we become an agency, we're just going to have to be really mindful of our culture and our people and having enough resources and all of that so that we don't burn people out, and we don't bring in those sort of negative sides of an agency knowing that there will always be times when we're going to have to maybe do a little extra. And then when we do that, how do we recognize that and make sure people are acknowledged for the extra hard work that they're doing? So that's one thing that I see and that became very clear on that call the other day of like, oh, okay, we got to keep an eye on this.

Because that can be a big decision because you're trusting someone, as you said, sometimes the outside partner doesn't get it, get it, they don't quite understand your brand. How do you ensure that the people you do bring in from the outside can actually kind of fall right in line with your internal team?

And what I've seen is that they bring those people in to work on the teams, and that's huge, just having that mindset. So I think that's one thing that as we sort of review bids and things like that, is just where do they have an understanding of our brand? Where have they done similar work in the past, but also where can their work elevate and maybe change what we've been doing so we're not doing the same thing all the time? (00:57:33): So it's a mix of things. It's definitely how do they approach it? What do they understand of our brand to start with? What does their work look like? What is their project management is a huge, huge thing. Do they get that this needs to stay on schedule and deliver on time and make it easy for us, so we're not struggling to get things. That's huge. So it's a variety of things to look at for sure. And then cost is always a factor too, but really it's most of those other things that are kind of the higher priority in the decision making, I think. Although sometimes it does come down to cost, unfortunately, but we always try to work it out wherever we can.

Cole Heilborn (00:58:32): Makes sense. We are coming up on the end of our time for today, but is there anything else that we didn't cover that you feel like is super important to talk about, to wrap us up with?

Ryan Coulter (00:00:00): A common leadership failure is in trying to over control your team, you're trying to enable those people and you're trying to let them figure out where their limits are so you're an advocate for them and you're going to push on them in a way like a coach of mine for them to figure out what they're really capable of.

Cole Heilborn (00:00:28): Welcome to the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. My name is Cole Hilborn. Today I'm sitting down with Ryan Coulter. He's the founder and chief creative officer of the James Brand. Ryan, how are you?

Ryan Coulter (00:00:38): I'm good, Cole. Hey, nice to talk to you.

Cole Heilborn (00:00:40): Yeah, good to have you on the show today. Looks like it's a busy day in your life, taking this from the car.

Ryan Coulter (00:00:47): Yeah, sometimes the car is actually the quietest, warmest, most secure place to get things done. Our office is busy and has a lot of concrete, and so sometimes these things are actually better done in here than up there.

Cole Heilborn (00:01:01): I like it. Yeah, it's a good sound studio you've got.

Ryan Coulter (00:01:04): Yeah, well, damped should manage our audio well.

Cole Heilborn (00:01:09): Awesome. Where are you calling in from?

Ryan Coulter (00:01:11): I'm in Portland, Oregon. I'm actually in the northeast corner. We were doing a photo shoot over here at to coffee shop this morning and we're in there getting caffeinated and getting some things set up and so yeah, I'm here in the beautiful Pacific Northwest.

Cole Heilborn (00:01:25): Awesome. Well, I would love if you could give us a quick introduction to the James brand. I've only discovered it since connecting with you and have been pretty blown away by I feel like what I was missing out on. And so I'd love if you could give our listeners a breakdown of the company and who you guys are.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:01:42): Yeah, so we are the James brand. We've been around, at least on paper since 2011. We didn't really get things into the market until halfway through 2014 and didn't really get more serious about the business till about 2017. So it's been kind of a long slow burn, but it started for me, I'm the founder, so this was kind of my doing initially, but it was a project that I was working on in that I was a person that had always carried a pocket knife and a few other things in my pockets. My general triad was a field notes notebook in my back pocket, a pen, usually a cheap disposable pen and a pocket knife. And I used those three things all the time, every day for lots of various tasks. Sometimes they were really mundane cleaning out my fingernail or slicing up an apple at lunch. (00:02:36): Sometimes they were more serious like cutting a rope when you needed to cut it or something that actually had higher demands. But I was just kind of blown away at how utilitarian those objects were and how important they were in my life. And the real asset test for anything like that is when you forget it or you lose it or you leave it and you start to reach for it and it's not there and you're like, oh man, I really wish I had that with me. And I thought that that as an idea was a really interesting idea and there really wasn't a brand that was focused on that and telling that story. And a lot, particularly in the pocketknife space, most of the incumbent brands were very focused kind of in the realm of tactical applications, a lot of military contracts, and there's a lot of blacked out stuff and more weapons point of view or fairly traditional hook and bullet outdoor hunting and fishing applications. (00:03:36): And I think there's some great companies and they do a great job with that. But no one was really telling a story of, Hey, here's some fairly minimal design language. This one is really just designed to live on top of your dresser. This is the one you should kind of grab every day when you roll out the door and just use it for no one particular purpose, but just for those 10 little things that are going to show up throughout the day.

Ryan Coulter (00:01:42): And I was like, wow, that's a kind of interesting opportunity. In reality, most people I think were using these products to do that, even if they were buying them for other emotional purposes. (00:04:12): So that was kind of the brand positioning thinking. But from the product standpoint, the things that I like, I'm an industrial designer by trade washed up industrial designer, and so a lot of what I like and a lot of what I tried to do in my design work and in my work as a creative director was really try to clean things up and make them very minimal and be very reductive and get rid of everything you didn't need and sort of see what kind of essence was left. And especially back in 2011, in that period of time, a lot of the design language in the pocket knife category was very overbuilt and lots of big camo handles and lots and lots of exposed fasteners, and there was just a lot of adding of things to the products and not taking things away. And I was always like Joni Ives fan, a Deida ROMs fan. (00:05:12): I really liked the minimalism in trying to reduce things, but no one had really done much of that in this category. So we set out to say, Hey, if the brand positioning is about daily care, can the product positioning be about minimizing these things and actually reducing them down to their bare essence and just seeing what's left. So that's kind of how we started. And in the spirit, if you can't find what you're looking for, you might have to go make it yourself. We started drawing things. We started working with some folks to try to get some things made. All of the early days stuff was terrible. It took a lot longer to figure it out, but it really was a nights and weekends project. And it was somewhat selfish initially because I was really trying to come up with this pocket knife that I wanted that was in my head that I wanted to carry with me every day.

Cole Heilborn (00:06:08): When did the everyday carry category become its own category? I feel like I've only been aware of it in the last 10 years.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:06:17): And I think that timeline is about right. I mean, I didn't really know much about the category until about that timeline either. And I don't know how I stumbled upon it, but there was, the website still is the site. We do some business with them every day. carry.com, that was really, it just featured laydowns, like these are the things that people are carrying with them every day. And it was generally a photo of a pocket dump or a lay down and then a list of what those products were and then a bit of an explanation about who the person was and a little bit, at least about why they were making those decisions. And I was just blown away that that was a thing too. I was like, wait, there's a category. This thing has a name, there's a website around it. I had no idea. (00:07:04): I never thought about that at all. And so it was the first time for me again about that same timeframe, about 2010 to really see the category with the name and start to see other people doing this and thinking about it and curating the stuff and actually taking photos. So I think it's been, I'm sure people that are more versed in it than you or I would say that it's been around longer, but I think that's when I first noticed it. I do know that a little bit of the history in that space was really sort of tactically focused a lot around police and sort of special operators and people really trying to say, Hey, here are the things, there are a lot more firearms in the space in those days. And people were saying like, Hey, here are the things that I bring into these really high risk situations to best manage my risk. (00:08:02): And it was really a lot of information exchange around the decisions people were making around the kind of sidearm they would carry into a special operations mission or that a particular police officer or military officer may choose and why they were choosing it. And there was a very functional, I mean these people were trying to stay alive and keep them other people alive and were spending time sort of exchanging the ideas around that. And so it evolved from that into something that was a very practical application into something that became a little bit more emotional. And I was really enamored and still am, I think with this idea that these decisions that you're making and what you're curating and bringing with you can be very much a reflection of who you are and what your values are and how you spend your time. And that ability to move through 30 different lay downs in everyday carry and say, that person's interesting. That person's interesting. Wait a minute, this person is just like me. I can make some guesses about this person. And they're probably involved in creative endeavors and they like to go outdoors on weekends. And I just thought it was amazing how much you could at least philosophically read into a person and their motivations by seeing the things that they actually brought with them day in and day out. And I still think it's just a really fun concept to explore.

Cole Heilborn (00:09:33): So let's rewind a little bit and I want to spend just a little bit of time in the past because I know you've got quite the history of different career stops along the way before you've ended up with the James brand or starting the James brand. Could you give us the quick highlight reel of where you've been?

Ryan Coulter (00:09:49): Yeah, the highest highlight reels, I've spent a lot of my career at Burton Snowboards and at Nike with a lot of other things along the way. My career has kind of triangulated between larger corporate work, some startup and entrepreneurial work, and then consulting, sort of design and innovation consulting. And I've kind of rotated through all of those things at various times and they all kind of feed each other and keep me from getting bored. But initially, I grew up in the Midwest. I was a skateboarder since early, since I was five. I'm still a skateboarder, and that was my first love. And that led to snowboarding in the Midwest because we were really just looking for a way to skateboard in the winter where it was cold. And back in those you really had to hang your skateboard up in about November in Indiana, and you may not get it back out until spring because it was just cold and snowy and icy and there were no such thing as indoor skate parks or skate parks of any kind. And so it was really hard to hang it up and stop. I mean, I think it's more a 365 activity now, but we really had to just stop. And so we were looking for ways to continue to do that. Snowboarding was kind of showing up and believe it or not, even in south central Indiana, there are still some tiny little ski resorts. Paoli Peaks is where I learned it, still operated there and actually just got bought by Veil, I think, which is amazing. (00:11:24): So I was really into snowboarding and really into skateboarding. I went to college at Purdue. I was a mechanical engineering student first. It's an Indiana school, and I grew up really wanting to make stuff. I always drew things and I'm not really an artist. I never was. I was more on the technical side and I used a lot of straight edges and circle templates, and I drew a trillion spaceships and airplanes and other things, but I was always very interested in the idea of just making these things. I was drawing a reality from a very early age. I was into that and tried to do that. And so I became a mechanical engineer engineering student because I thought that's how you made stuff.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:09:49): I was in my second year of that at Purdue, and I ran into an exhibition in the Union of Industrial Design, and I never even heard of Industrial Design, but here were all these really interesting scale models of cars and devices and all these beautiful renderings and technical drawings at this point, kind of pre-computer, but done by hand. And I was like, wait a minute. This is what I always thought I was going to do. I'm actually doing sewage calculations and hydrodynamics and what is this? Is this a thing? And so I totally fell in love with the concept of industrial design, switched my major to industrial design. And then some of my final college projects were actually snowboarding projects. (00:12:52): I got connected with Vans and did a really early sort of step in boot binding combination for Vans back in I think 1995 with a guy named Kim Boyle, who I always credit is kind of giving me a chance at a really early age. I can't even remember how we got connected, but he makes amazing custom motorcycles now. But I've always remembered Kim as a person that gave me sort of a shot. So I did that with Vans way back when I got my first job after college working for a small snowboard company in Colorado called Solid Up in the Hills up in Fairplay. And my nickname there was college. I had two nicknames. College, I was the guy around there who had been to college, which made everyone assume that I could fix everything and solve everything. And in reality, I was no more qualified to do that than any of the other people that were there. (00:13:49): Or they called me Steaks too. A lot of people still call me that because I was this sort of pale guy from the Midwest and moved to Colorado and I had the world's craziest goggle tan that made me looked like marbled meat because just white eyes and red face. And I was the color of steak the entire time I lived there, but working for solid for a bit. And then I ended up in California very shortly working for Joyride and doing some other stuff in kind of the southern California business.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:09:49): And then I got a call and got recruited by Burton, and that had always been the dream job, the dream company, and the job was to actually be the product manager for snowboard bids for Burton, which was very literally my dream job. I mean, that was the job that if I could have had any job in the world I would've had, and I got it, which was amazing. (00:14:49): And so in my early twenties, I moved to Vermont and started working for Burton and was there for about almost eight years working mostly on snowboard bindings and then on a few other things. And then as a part of my time at Burton, I spent a chunk of every summer out here in Oregon at Mount Hood testing next year's gear, and really fell in love with Oregon and your ability to do anything at any time. Those days when I would come out here with Burton, you would get picked up by a bunch of people that were already out here. You would go to Burnside to the skate park and skate immediately, and then you'd drive up to the mountain and you'd be snowboarding for days on end in a t-shirt or a sweatshirt, and then you'd get tired of doing that every day. So then you'd drive to the coast to go surfing, and then we'd drive into town and see the pixies and all these things that for me, I had always wanted to do in the Midwest. (00:15:51): And you couldn't do, we didn't have skate parks, we didn't have a beach, we didn't really have mountains, and we surely didn't have the pixies, but here they were all literally within an hour and a half of each other. And I was just smitten with the ability to do any of that stuff. So I left Burton, I came out to work for Nike for, I've worked for Nike for a total of 10 years, kind of in two different stints, left to do an earlier startup called Uncommon, which was some of the world's first fully customizable iPhone cases, and then did some design consulting, went back to Nike for a while to continue to work on customization and the Nike ID platform, and then was doing the James brand through kind of nights and weekends and then made the commitment to do this full time just a few years ago. And here we are.

Cole Heilborn (00:16:49): Here we are. So I'm really curious, the theme of our episode today is all about leadership and leading creatives and being a leader of a creative team. I'm curious, when did you first realize that you were a leader? Did it hit you one day when everything changed? You're like, oh, shoot, I have this responsibility, I have this role. Was there a moment that you remember?

Ryan Coulter (00:17:16): Yeah, it's a great question. There is no one moment that I remember, but I think part of it was the good news and bad news about working for some of these companies, Burton in particular, and Nike is I was absolutely working with and around some of the very best talent in the world, the very highest levels of talent in the world. And I was not that, I'm not that still, but there's a lot that I have to offer. But I was starting to see this sort of multiplying effect of my ability to find those people and organize them around an idea and sort of bring them together to make this symphony of really amazing work. And that to me was wildly rewarding because it was clearly both in quality and quantity, it was stuff that I couldn't do myself. But one of the things about a lot of top talent like that is that they couldn't do it by themselves either. (00:18:27): It required more breadth, they required lots of direction and shaping of the thing and making it into an idea that you could actually sell into corporate leadership and a story around it. In a lot of ways, my primary skillset was verbal was written. I was able to kind of pull together these story arcs and stitch together a lot of individual things into a bigger tale. And so I think I started to see that sort of really for the first time when I started working for Burton, and I'm responsible for this. I mean, the thing about Burton, and I'm sure it's still the case, and I credit Jake for this, it was sink or swim man, I'm 23 or something, and I'm responsible basically for the majority of the snowboard binding business, which was tens and tens of millions of dollars at that point. I've never worked for a company and I've got a design degree, but I'm fairly fresh out of college and they're like, figure it out or leave. (00:19:38): It's up to you. We believe in you, but you're going to have to do this. And so suddenly I was kind of, I think the first industrial designer that Burton had ever hired. But we started working, I think Burton was already doing this, but working with design consultants in Boston, a firm called 11 and a few other folks.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:21:17): Well, I mean I think as a leader you really have two jobs and it's motivated and trained, train, train and motivate. And so on one hand you have to kind of paint this north star of like, Hey, we're all pulling over here and we're going to do this and it's going to be epic, but it's going to be a long journey, but this is where we're going. Do you see that North star? Yeah, yeah, I see it. Okay, so you see it and you're clear on it and you get it. Okay, so your part of that looks like this. You need to do this part, and that's your part of getting us here, and then it will follow it up with this and this. And so keep going back and forth between those two different polls in terms of the timeline and the vision. (00:22:31): And then on the training side, you need to make sure that everyone understands that they have the skills that they need to do that and that they have the confidence that they need to do that and that they are technically able to do it. They don't have the confidence and they don't necessarily know what they really can or can't do all the time. So you want to train them about what they're actually capable of and what they're not capable of. They need to understand for themselves where those lines are. But I think a leader is a person that can manage both of those things.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:48:59): So a couple of interesting answers on that. Cole Heilborn (00:51:53): Beautiful. What is one of the biggest failures as a leader that you have experienced? Could be recent, could be earlier in your career?

Ryan Coulter (00:52:04): That's a great question. I think if you think about leadership as a two-way responsibility, there's only so much that you can do in this game of motivating and training. And then there's only so much that the other person can do too. And so I think sometimes, and this may not sound like a great failing of mine, but I can internalize failures as my own that really may have been failures within the other people and their ability to even know thyself to get down with what actually motivates them and put it on the table and I can beat myself up about it. I can't get this person. And we've had to let some people go fire some people. And you feel bad about that because you say, what did I do wrong? Why didn't we retain that person? And so anytime you lose an important person, you really start to internalize that and think, I did something wrong. Something is wrong here and something may well be wrong, but it may not be you. It may well be them. (00:53:14): And a lot of it may just honestly be not in their skills, but in their ability to know thyself and come to the table, what really motivates them, what they really want to be doing and sort how to get there. I'm trying to think of major failures and I can't think of some, but I'm sure if you ask my people I've worked with, they'll go through a laundry list. But I do think things that I did early on in my career that I speak out against now are micromanaging others. Just trying to forcing their hand to get to where you want them to be instead of letting them kind of go in the direction you want to go and having that be good enough. (00:53:55): I think that balancing between, and it's a really interesting line to try to tease out all the time in the world of making things. It's somewhere along the line between putting an idea on paper, doing a 3D model of it, building a prototype of it really, and then actually making a production thing happen. You lose the perfection in it. It's perfect. Only as an idea in your mind and every step towards reality, it actually gets a little less perfect, and it's probably in its least perfect form when it actually becomes a reality.

content: Ryan Coulter (00:52:04): But your job is to make actual things to put them in the market, to exchange them for money, for value with people. And so you have to balance your perfectionistic tendencies with reality. The difference between art and design is that design is there to make products that people actually buy. Where art can just be self-expression. (00:54:54): You can surely buy art, but art can be perfect because it really lives in the space of just that one object and not thousands of things that actually have to be injection molded or machined. So I think I'm saying that to say that there have been times in my career when I think I've probably held two tightly to an idea of something and driven it too hard maybe to the point of making it not even happen, where it's like where if I would've backed up, maybe that would've happened and people would've really found value in it. (00:55:33): So I think that's a thing that I've done and I've learned to back up and realize what is good enough and still maintain what I think everyone would say is a very high standard for myself and for the brand and for things that we do now. And I think everybody goes through this tendency, and I know that I've done it too, I'll just do it myself and you don't get it. Just step aside, let me do it. We're running out of time. And if there's almost one thing that I would tell and I do tell people not to do as they're learning to manage other folks, it's like, don't do that because two things happen. One, it's wildly demotivating, and again, your two jobs are to motivate and train. So you've just not done your job as you demotivate these people. Two, you didn't train them on how to do it or what they're supposed to do, so you also didn't do your job again. (00:56:29): And three, you're never going to get any value out of this investment that you've made in this person until you can get them there. And so understanding that hiring people and growing a team over the short term is wildly inefficient and expensive, and over the longer term, it's wildly valuable, but you have to understand the difference in the timeframe and the investment that it's going to take upfront.

And I think a lot of people who work in this industry can probably tell you frustrations of those teams not being aligned or coming up with a really great idea, not having the product to support that idea and really that communication and making sure that everyone is kind of working together is my main goal in sort of a day to day.

content: David Russo (00:08:07): Yeah, I think for me, really what it came down to was I've always had this kind of curiosity and willingness and want or internal drive to do more to learn new things. My background at Outdoor Gear Exchange, I really got to work in almost every department in the store, and that was like every time I got to be in a position where I was doing the same thing and it was becoming too repetitive, I was like, alright, what else can I do? What else can I learn? Where are the opportunities? And that's always been that kind of internal driver for me. So I mean, early on at Mamo there were opportunities where back in 2018 we purchased this app Mountain Hub, and it was this really cool mapping software that you could map out different adventures, and there was think kind of Strava fat map style application. (00:09:10): And at the time when we purchased it, there was no one to run the app. It was like we were onboarding that team, it came in and it was sit down in the circle with the CEO and a few others and everyone's kind staring at each other like, Hey, who has the time to do this? And I had never run an app before. I had no experience in that, but I knew that Google has the answers to everything and that if I was willing to put myself out there that I could give it a shot. And so I think for me that attitude is what kept leading to these opportunities when everyone else was hesitating, I was willing to take that step forward and put myself out there, and it's a vulnerable position to be in because of course you can make mistakes and you will make mistakes, and that's all a part of it. (00:10:11): But I think for me, willingness to make decisions and willingness to be wrong is actually a separation for people in moving into a positions of leadership. And so that was really, for me, it was those increased opportunities of when everyone else was like, Hey, we don't know what to do. Who has a solution to come to the table, not only with a solution, but be willing to be the person to carry that extra weight and invest that time.

content: David Russo (00:13:09): Yeah, I think for me a lot of that comes down to setting, I would say setting the tone. And I think when you hear people say that phrase, some traditional examples of that is the CEO or the leader who shows up first in the office and they're there before everyone else and they leave last. And I think that's that classical setting the tone, if you will, or sort of establishing a culture of what work looks like. But for me, where that comes down to being most important is setting the tone when it comes to attitude and when it comes to energy. And for me, optimism is one of the most important attributes I think for myself in order to be successful in doing my job. And I really think a lot about how do I make sure I'm using energy for good? Because again, I think one of those separators and what I experienced in terms of maybe even going from being considered a manager to being in a leadership position is when you're a manager, you can afford to be talking with your team. (00:14:33): And when people are frustrated or someone's upset, you're kind of all just piling on. And yeah, that meeting was terrible and I can't believe it went that way, and I can't believe this person said that, but that's using that energy in a negative way and it's feeding into that. I think your responsibility as a leader, it really comes into always making sure that you're taking that one step back and saying, okay, how can I make sure that we can set that aside and keep moving in a positive direction and keep that momentum moving and kind of, yeah, really be, I wouldn't say in control, but sort of dictating the energy of the room and the energy of the team. Because I think more than anything, that energy in that momentum, moving in the right direction is what leads to success versus not. And it's sort of having a fast forgetfulness or sort of a very short memory of that happened, acknowledge that it happened, and how do we move on and how do we talk about a solution and moving in the right direction? That's really, for me, underlying all things for how I see my job and my most important responsibility is setting that tone leading with positive energy and always be sort of creating that momentum in a forward direction.

David Russo (00:16:13): Yeah, and I think just another thing I would touch on there, Cole, is for me, there can be times where I think one of the best pieces of advice I ever got around energy, especially when you're in a room with people, whether that's giving a presentation, doing a training with staff in a meeting with a vendor or a client, et cetera, is acknowledge the distraction. And what I mean by that is if everyone's about to sit down and you, Cole are in the back of the room making a cup of coffee really quick and the spoon is clattering and there's this noise going on, instead of ignoring that and trying to start your conversation, acknowledge that distraction and maybe even make light of it and be like, oh, looks like Cole had a long night last night, needs some extra time to make a coffee. Let's give him a minute and then we'll get started. And that's another way that you're dictating that energy in the room and you're understanding that everyone's paying attention to that distraction. So instead of trying to hide from it, you acknowledge that distraction, you draw that energy, and then you kind of pull it back in and move it in the direction that you want it to go in.

Cole Heilborn (00:17:37): I can see that applying in other circumstances as well, not just in a very particular, in a meeting example, I could see that being applied on a much larger scale. Do you have any examples of acknowledging a distraction at a much higher level?

David Russo (00:17:54): Yeah, I think another example of that might be, let's say for a business product shipping late. I think that's something where we've all experienced that during the past two years, supply chains were a mess. And those excuses about why something can't happen or why the team is upset about something or why something isn't going according to plan, to me, that's another time where you can acknowledge the distraction first and be like, look, I understand we're all disappointed by the fact that this product is late and that we had these plans. And you do have to create that acknowledgement and create that space that people's feelings around that are totally valid. But then you have to quickly create that opportunity to say, we understand this product is late, but we have 200,000 other products in our warehouse today. How do we get creative and come up with an opportunity to continue to move other product, continue to change our plan and do something different? So yeah, I think at scale that really can represent any opportunity or any time where there's disappointment, something doesn't go according to plan, quickly acknowledging that, letting people know that that's a valid concern, but then creating that opportunity for let's talk about a solution, let's talk about moving forward, I think, yeah, you see that happen every day.

Cole Heilborn (00:19:36): I love that we're talking about this now because I want to get into some more specific later in the episode. I want to get into some more specific scenarios or examples. But it sounds like as a whole, when you approach leadership directing energy and dictating energy is one of your key principles, I'm curious if there are any others that are kind of guiding beacons that you follow before we get into some of the weeds?

content: David Russo (00:20:00): Yeah. For me, I would say in general, I think being empathetic is something you hear people talking a lot about. And to me that's really important as well. And I would say where empathy for me comes into play or how I would interpret empathy in a workplace environment is when something doesn't get done, your first reaction being, okay, why did that not happen? And understanding it from a personal level. So Cole, if you were on my team and we had talked about, I don't know, putting out a new social media campaign and the post never happened, and we talked about it being published on Tuesday and Tuesday comes and it didn't happen, instead of right away getting upset or coming to you and being like, Cole, what the hell? Why didn't this happen? It's Tuesday, this is the deadline. Why didn't you meet the deadline? (00:21:05): To me, leading with empathy comes into asking yourself, why might Cole not have been able to accomplish this understanding, Hey, maybe Cole has a lot going on at home right now, or, oh, his wife's traveling and he has to take care of the kids. Or Hey, when I look at the task list that I have for Cole, I asked him to do 10 other things that were due today, so maybe that's why it didn't happen. And then have that conversation and understand from your perspective why it didn't happen, and then how do you adjust, adapt to make sure that you can be successful in the future. But for me, that level of empathy I think is super important because I think you hear it all the time, it's like every leadership book right now is talking about empathy, but how do you apply that and what does that look like and what does that mean? (00:21:59): And so for me, that would be an example of applying that, but I think that is a super important piece. And then I would say other things like in general, accountability, transparency, kindness in a way, and ambition is a huge part of, I think being a leader and some of the leaders that I've worked with, oftentimes people struggle with the gap of where we are and where the ambition is and those kind of steps of how you get there sort of in a very classical business sense of current state versus target state, that path and creating a clear path and kind of guiding people along that path. That's the tactical day-to-day part of the job, but setting that target far enough and having that ambition. You hear people throw around the title of visionary oftentimes for people, and I think there's a clear reason why, but I think having that ambition to me is a really important aspect. (00:23:15): But the counterbalance to ambition is always patience. And I think you need that as well, and you need that long-term view. And you need, for me, the way I evaluate my career right now, for example, I'm thinking I have 30 years left minimum of working. So whenever I'm upset about a decision in a one month timeline or three month timeline or a six month timeline, I'm like, I've got 30 year runway, I've got a lot of time to grow, to make mistakes, to improve. So how do I set myself up for the best next 30 years and not just be hyperfocused on the now

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:23:58): I want to back up a little bit. So you were talking about empathy and approaching challenges or things that didn't happen or misunderstandings with the team. From a state of empathy, how do you balance that with accountability? And in the example that you gave where maybe I didn't do the thing I was supposed to do, how do those balance, because I could see them, I mean they're, I guess I see them as balancing acts.

David Russo (00:24:24): Yeah. Yeah. I would say for me, accountability is something that I always hold first for myself, then second for the team, and oftentimes I would even say maybe a critique or weakness of mine would be I like to take ultimate accountability or almost in some ways a radical approach to accountability for myself, where accountability in a lot of ways helps with being able to improve something. If I put all the accountability on you, Cole, for example, I only can improve so much your ability to do something, a lot of that is going to lie with you, but if I take accountability for you not getting something done, it puts the kind of control back in my place. So just to kind of put an example to it, something that I see happen a lot, especially with companies going remote, all of us working with these new tools, organizing your team, organizing information is super challenging. (00:25:36): When we sat down to play in this conversation, you're like, oh, pick a time through the Calendly link and there's now a tool and a digital tool and an online tool for literally everything. And with that, people frequently can't find stuff, they miss an invite, it goes to the wrong place, et cetera. And those are oftentimes the quick easy knee-jerk frustration reaction would be, Cole, why did you miss the meeting invite? Why did this happen? And for me, my approach to the accountability of that is, if you didn't get the invite, that's on me and I take accountability for that. How do I understand for the team the most successful way to communicate? And that could be different for different people. You might have someone who is digital native, they use a hundred different apps, they're super comfortable with it, you roll out a new tool, they get it within the first 10 minutes and they don't lose the invite. (00:26:43): But maybe you have someone on your team who's 50 and you just move them to being a remote workforce, they've never had a laptop before. And then sending that person an email or maybe even calling them before a meeting to remind them that the meeting is happening is the personalized approach that you need to take.

How can I adjust to make the team successful? I think to me, that's a much better approach. But going back to that balancing act with being empathetic towards the team, but also being able to hold them accountable, I think clear expectations around when something isn't going to get done, how do you communicate it? (00:27:41): If you're going to miss a deadline, how do you come back and communicate that and how do we have enough heads up where it's not 10 minutes before the post is supposed to go live and you say, Hey, I had a really busy day. I'm sorry I'm not going to be able to get to this, but if we have a couple check-ins during the week, if a day out before that post, you're sending me a message on Slack or you're giving me a quick phone call or you're sending me an email, Hey, I don't see this happening, I don't think I'm going to be able to meet this timeline, how do we adjust? That to me is that balance of accountability versus being empathetic and understanding the situation.

content: David Russo (00:29:01): Yeah, so I would say for me, one of the biggest learnings, and really that was at mah mood, and that wasn't something that I don't think a book can teach you or I don't think you're going to learn in a college class, or maybe not even a mentor can tell you, but what I saw play out for us, and maybe this is a very specific example to our organization, but when there's a change in leadership at the highest level, so let's say CEO level change for a company, what people don't realize is that the history and in the kind of hierarchy of who are the top performers at the company, who are the people with the most responsibility or even who are the favorites of the leadership team, when you bring in a new CEO, everyone goes back down to zero. Everyone is at an even playing field. (00:30:04): And what you see very quickly is that showing that you have a positive attitude in that environment, showing a willingness to take on responsibility, showing a willingness to provide value or make decisions or create calm and certainty for the organization. Those are the really valuable skills during a time of change. And anytime you have that really high level change, it's very hard for people to adapt because you can have, whether that's like a C-suite or a team of directors or a team of senior managers who are making the decisions for the company, a new leadership's going to have a completely new philosophy over how to make decisions and how to lead the organization. And so those people who are used to sitting in the closed boardroom environment and planning out a strategy overnight, they might not be invited to that table anymore. And so for everyone, it very quickly becomes this place where you have to forget the past and bring that really positive optimistic mindset. (00:31:23): And so one of the ways that you look at building a team coming out of that environment is who are those early adopters to that change or that change in strategy? Who's coming with that positive attitude, who can create a sense of security and kind of really in that classical sense of like, Hey, follow me, we're going in this direction.

content: David Russo (00:29:01): Who can be those kind of trendsetters within the organization? And I think identifying those people is a really great way to lay a foundation for a new strategy or for a new change or for a new organizational structure and then create teams behind those people. But what's really interesting to see is if you go through multiple of those changes within a three year or five year, et cetera timeframe, that reset backed to zero in my experience, happens every time. And so even if, I don't know, let's say you were in a management position and you had one direct report, two, and you got a full new leadership change, they're evaluating the entire organization and maybe they say, Hey, we really love Kohler. (00:32:45): We really love this other person and the attitude and what they're bringing, and we think they have a great vision, you could get put into a new position leading five people almost right away, because those are those times where you really have to understand that timing aspect of this is a time for change, and everyone here is looking for who is going to be reliable, who is coming with the right attitude. And so it's a very much a time for opportunity for people within the organization. And so I think that to me is something that I saw happen a few times that I realized or understood the scope of what was happening. And then when put in a position of leadership, looked to who are the other people within the organization who are also understanding this and who also want to come with a solution oriented mindset and who want to bring that positive energy. (00:33:50): And those are really the people that traditionally, it's not performance based, it's not like this person doing the best job, it's capable, but attitude is everything. And I think that that's such an understated thing in business where everyone wants to check a box, everyone wants to get a certain degree, everyone wants to have a certain amount of experience. We all approach jobs through a very traditional job description lens, but those kind of soft skill moments are what's missing for a lot of people, and that they don't realize that attitude trumps a lot of those other things.

content: David Russo (00:42:11): Yeah, I think certainly there's the traditional way of establishing KPIs, key performance indicators around we want to see growth of X percentage in revenue, or we want to see engagement on social media at this percentage, or we want to see an increase of followers or whatever metric you want to measure.
