Setting targets and setting clear goals I think is a really important aspect of creating success not only for you but for the team as a whole. Some of the analogies I use for my team around why setting goals are important is if you were to go to a firing range and there's no target at the end of where you're shooting, you'll still probably have fun and you can do that for a while, but at a certain point you're actually going to get bored because you don't know, am I getting better? Am I getting more accurate? Am I hitting the bullseye or not? And you're just eventually just going to stop shooting, you're going to stop doing what you're doing because you have no way of measuring that. (00:43:33): And I think that, I don't know, let's say another example of that would be you're, I don't know, you're heavyweight boxer and you're aiming for a certain weight to be able to get into that weight class without a scale, it becomes extremely difficult to know if you gained enough weight to be able to compete and fight in that heavyweight weight class. And so you do need some of those metrics or some of those goal measurements to know, okay, I feel like the team is working well, but also the team has that buy-in. The team has something that they're working towards and that they feel good about that. And I think those goals have to be beyond just revenue targets. content: David Russo (00:53:27): Yeah, I think for me, what I saw happen time and time again is, and I would hate to have people listen to this who I've worked with and be too, but I think it's really easy for people to get impatient. And that patient's piece is really hard to grasp in that big, big scale. And when someone starts to have success or when someone starts to gain free time in their job or they start to get comfortable with their workload, the ambitious people are always going to be like, I want more. I want more. How do I do more? How do I take on more? And for some people, it's very much like, I want to be a manager. I want to manage people. I want to have a team. How do I do this? (00:54:54): And I think what that accomplishes is it really create a sense of ownership for that person of if I can follow these steps, then I can achieve these goals, then I can get this increase in my salary, this increase in responsibilities, I can gain these things. And so in kind of building out that framework, that's where I kind of saw this pattern of really what it comes down to for those team members is it takes most people a full year of really learning something before you get a grasp of it. And the outdoor industry, we're very seasonal in our approach, and everyone knows that there's sell-in season for the sales team for spring summer and for fall winter. And there's go to market plan for spring, summer and for fall winter. But oftentimes those products are actually different in spring summer and in fall winter. (00:55:53): And maybe those retailers you work with are different in spring summer than they are in fall winter.

content: David Russo (01:02:23): I think for me, one of the things I would say or maybe to own up to a mistake I've made or a learning that I would pass on is understand the impact of making time for your team and know what happens when you aren't able to make that time. If her supervisor has to reschedule their one-on-one because she's too busy, and even just pushing it back a day, hearing that disappointment of like, oh, it feels like she doesn't have time for me, that is something that I've realized and been able to internalize and say, Ooh, yeah, I think I've probably done that to my team several times. And you don't understand the impact of those things until you get to be the one on the outside listening and kind of hearing from my wife and understanding like, oh, wow, yeah, I've been that person and I've kicked someone's two days down the road or canceled it for the week and said, Hey, we'll just catch up next week. And understanding that your time is probably the most valuable resource for your team and also the biggest way for you to communicate that you care about them. And so that's something that I would say I've caught myself doing and I'm looking for opportunities to improve on. And I think for all leaders, understanding that and creating that balance of you're going to have to manage your time and in a very financial, literal way. Your time might be more valuable than other people's time, but you have to understand the impact of giving time and taking time away. The way and this sort of leads into the conversation about how to build brands without feeding the ad machine. So we thought, what if we took that experience and put it on a trail? content: Amanda Lee Smith (13:00): So it started in the last year, I think, when brands were feeling the effects of the OS updates and all of a sudden their ads weren't performing the way they previously had been. And the frustration at the dependence that everyone has on Meta and Google that we, you know, we always have to put a dollar in to get two dollars out. It feels like this endless cycle. And Brands have seen it. The minute you turn off that ad machine, all of your traffic and your revenue dries up. Like we've become so dependent on it. And so I've started having conversations, and this isn't a fully formed idea, but this is actually something I want to dive deep into in the year ahead about like, you know, how did we do marketing before digital advertising? And is there a way that we can go back to that? And and I'm not naive, like I don't think we can totally get rid of our digital marketing. But there are brands that have done a really good job of growing through word of mouth or through maybe some more underground or IRL activations and activities. They're, you know, they're not without a cost, but they're they're more like big upfront investments instead of that continual, just like, you know, like I said, feeding the machine. And so exploring what it would look like to go back to things like. direct mail, you know, like it's so novel to get a really great piece of mail. And that's actually something that came out of Tailgate Talks. Some of our friends at the Essential Oil brand Vitruvi have seen a lot of success with direct mail recently. And they've got a a millennial audience. You know, it's not our parents' generation that are reacting to direct mail. It's actually people our age. so direct mail poster campaigns, you know, if you have a product that can be really localized, what would that look like? We have one client that is still doing some like local broadcast television ads that have worked really well for them. They have like a very specific product in a very specific area. But what would it look like to go back to using radio and to be creative about using radio? So just trying to think like what I mean, I mean technically that's still advertising and you're still feeding it, but not the same way. Yeah, what would it look like to have such a compelling story that it can live beyond just those, you know, clickable moments? What are your thoughts on that? So it seems like if you could if you could get around that and build something that's sustainable on its own without the need for a third party to be injecting money into a third party, it would help help the brand build building significantly. I think from like a from what I've noticed, I mean the type of work that we do when it's when it's a brand building project. I think that's where we get the most excited because there's there's so much more potential on an emotional level. And I mean that's not to say that like a a quick thirty second social media ad doesn't need to be emotional, but you know, the goals between a piece of brand building content and a social media ad are very different. And I think, you know, video like production and storytelling is i in my perspective is like best served. in the brand building format. And so when we get to come in and you know, our goal is to tell a story about something and the metrics and the success defined by that project are, you know, continuing to grow you know, owned platforms or owned media to build brand, like that's where we get really excited because you can dive deep into a narrative, you can dive deep into emotion, and you're not just trying to make someone click through, you know, to a landing page and purchase a thing.

content: Amanda Lee Smith (25:21): Well, I mean, important for me as someone that likes to be in nature and lives in a cold climate, you know, so many of the activities that I do, and I'm sure you can relate to this, they depend on gear that is, you know, waterproof or sweat wicking. And the foundation of that gear has historically been petroleum products. And those products are not designed to break down. So once we started partnering with brands that are investing in circularity, it you know, it gives us hope that these things that we love doing can be sustained over a long time. There's there's lots of elements to circularity and you know I'm not a product expert, but as we dive deeper into this, my interest in these areas has been growing so really interested in raw materials. How do you create something that's truly recyclable or biodegradable that also performs in the outdoors? There's so much fun innovation happening and I just came from ISPO in Munich and getting to see all of the different novel textiles that are coming out of different brands has been yeah really inspiring. It's also sometimes prob problematic. Like I think, you know, the big theme in outdoor apparel for the last few years has been brands talking about how many plastic bottles a certain garment kept out of a landfill. and that positioning kind of ignores the fact that often the best second life for a plastic bottle is actually to become another plastic bottle. like there's you you can recycle a plastic bottle numerous times, but once that plastic makes its way into a garment, that's kind of the end of its life. It rarely can become anything else. So right now the the big thing that we're starting to see, you know, like that plastic bottle narrative pretty much was at every single booth in ISPO. And then the more forward-looking brands were talking about removing petroleum from their supply chain altogether and using plant-based plastic. So like I think they're sometimes called bioplastics. That might come from sugar cane or cornstarch or castor seeds, which is really great for reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, but it doesn't actually solve our landfill problem because so many of those those quote unquote bioplastics aren't actually biodegradable. and I think in order to be considered a plant-based plastic, you might only need to have like 20 or 30 percent plant-derived materials. So, you know. That kind of brings us to the topic of greenwashing, which we won't dive into, but but but circularity is is more about how can you design products to eliminate waste so you don't have that waste at the end, but also designing for for end of life. So whether that is biodegradability or separability, so designing a product. or a garment so that you can deconstruct it so that you can reuse key elements or so that it's easier to repair one element without having to totally throw away the garment or a piece of of hard goods. And then and then the kind of easiest piece of circularity is resale or recommerce. And that's where we've really been involved in where we've been helping brands to find their strategies.

content:
Cole Heilborn (28:48): So when a brand comes to you and they want to hire you to h for for help with all of this, maybe they're starting a circularity program, where do you start? How do you begin to wrap your head around this?

Amanda Lee Smith (29:01): So in the past, like when we first started doing this, brands were coming to us once they kind of already had their resale tech stack, I call it. kind of already set up more and more. And I had three conversations about this last week. Folks are coming to us at the very beginning of their circularity journey, which is really exciting because it means we can actually help them do it strategically. And there's some decisions that you want to make early in the re-commerce journey that are actually really tied to brand. So the first thing you want to do is think about your strategy. So what's your goal? Are you stepping into re-commerce for purely environmental reasons, or is it because you want to try to find a new profit center or you're trying to reach a new customer? Those are three really different things. And so you kind of need to know your your core brand positioning in order to know what strategy is going to make the most sense and resonate with your customers. And you really need solid brand positioning to do that. So the first piece is Define your strategy. And then once you know what that strategy is, it helps you pick your partners and and build your kind of circularity tech stack. So there's a bunch of different resale platforms. We are pals with the folks at Recurate. They're doing some really interesting things. Trove, Archive, and the platform you choose depends on a few different things. Do you want to have a peer-to-peer option or do you want to have like a really curated branded experience? If you know you want to go super curated, you might go the direction that our clients ArcTerx went and work with Trove. And and I think Lululemon's working with Trove as well. If you want peer-to-peer, then you might go with Recurate or Archive. Do you want it to integrate into your existing PDPs, your product description pages? So like if I'm looking at an Arterix jacket, but I can't afford the $900 one, maybe you're gonna give me the option to buy it for 30% off as a used option. Not every brand wants to do that. You know, like if you want to buy from Lululemon's used platform, you're gonna have to look really hard.

content: Amanda Lee Smith (29:01): You're not gonna find it on their homepage, they're gonna make you work for it. Because for them, it's not part of their brand story that they're ready to tell, but they still want to have that experience for consumers. You need to think about how you're going to approach cleaning and repair. So, you know, partners like TERSIS, which cleans technical products, or reverse logistics partners like our clients D-brand that will handle all your returns and sort your goods and allocate them. find the highest value channel for them. You need to figure out who all those partners are. And so once you have that tech stack, and you know, there's obviously a lot of work to get the the gear in to be able to list it on the platform, but then you want to actually shape that brand experience. So figuring out how you're gonna tell that story. Are you gonna give it a name? Like is this platform gonna have a a unique name and a unique brand experience? Or are you gonna let your customers define that for you? Because they're gonna call it something. And it's it's better if you d tell them what to call it instead of them telling you what to call it. And I love what ArcTerx is doing. you know, all of their circularity initiatives are wrapped into the brand rebird. And I think it's really catchy and compelling. People that love the brand understand that like the the bird you know, skeleton on their logo. It's something that they can really attach themselves to. And I think creating that experience is really important. But yeah, what is the story that you're telling? Is it a story about affordability? Is it a story about sustainability? You want to be able to define that. And then there's two more steps. One is you actually have to kind of go big on the launch. You can't invest all this money in this tech stack in in all this repair and cleaning and then just let it kind of sit and hope that people find it. So you have to figure out what your launch strategy is gonna be and you know, obviously leave some time to work out the kinks, but I think it's it's worth actually going big.

Is it gonna be part of your core email list? Or are you gonna develop a completely different email list just for this particular customer base and different social channels? you have to kind of keep that drumbeat going and keep driving people to the platform. But depending on your strategy, it might look really different. Like it might just be a footer in your weekly emails or it might be that you have a dedicated email once a month or, you know, maybe you're really gonna shine a huge spotlight on it and really drive people there.

So they're keeping waste out of landfills from other brands, but also creating like a really good quality of life for their workers. So you look at the core brand and that's the story that you lean into. The other piece is voice and this is core to any brand and a lot of the work that we do when we're developing a brand is around Voice. How do you make it sound unique and specific to you? Just like every brand visual identity is different, every voice is different. And those two pieces come together to, you know, be the external facing version of your brand. And so leaning into it, is it playful? Is it a little more serious and technical? Is it really like bold and in your face adventure? So we would lean into those different brand attributes to make sure that it feels unique on top of the actual brand pillars that we're borrowing from.

And that's probably organic and leveraging what the platforms want. So anyways, high level impressions and then we go to website, then we go to followers. So we want to see if we're reaching a bunch of people when they come to the profile and it's clear what we are and who we are, do they actually want to follow? Are they actually the right people? And if they are, how many of those people actually want to go to the website? And now is our website traffic changing because of our effort? If there's no, then I'm starting to be concerned that maybe you're getting followers, but they're still not the right audience member or you're right customers. So it's like you got to make sure that there's not a hole in the funnel of we get a bunch of people to be here, we get a bunch of followers, but they're all actually, we set up the profile so wrong that they're just here for climbing clips or they're just here for, I don't know, satisfying videos or something weird. Sam Van Boxtel (16:52): Yep. I would say that there's two main factors that will drive this, potentially a third, but the first thing I would think about is having a clear CTA. So everyone on Instagram, you have one link in the TikTok, most platforms you have one link. Having the last line of your bio have a clear CTA towards that link letting people know what it is. So on the one link that you have, having a clear CTA on the last line of the bio, letting people know what the link is, I think is huge. I always tell people I as a user, I don't like to click links. I don't know what they are. I think this is the classic email spam culture of don't touch that sketchy link. So I always try to be very clear, is it a shop link? Is it a new product, is it a free course, is it a email? Whatever it is, you should have a very clear call to action one thing, and you should be clear on what that is. (17:49): So that's the first thing. People need to know what the link in the bio is. Typically, if you can, I would try to not have it be the homepage. Sometimes it makes sense for it to be the homepage. If you don't have anything you're any freebie or anything you're running at the moment. But otherwise, I'd try to have it be something specific. And then the story highlights is typically the second place that you'll drive your other website traffic, which is, this goes back to the analogy of the account being a website, having your story highlights then would be to your tabs of your website. So these might be things like the different services you provide, the different products you provide. So like Friction Labs has their four main styles of chalk clearly shown so that you can click in and maybe you see, I think ours is pretty simple, it just has the link, but you could also click in and then show maybe a benefit or two of that product or what makes it different. (18:46): And then you have a link there to go to that straight to that page and you're not wasting any links. So I'm always trying to send people where they want. Again, going back to the website analogy, you don't want to have 10 million clicks to get to the place they want. So I like showing them the options in those story highlights.

It's not as easy as some may want it to be But it takes a lot more strategic thought. And there's a ton of PL that comes with this, with the growth. And so I think people look at the Yetis of the world, these incredibly strong brands, the the North Face, and they say, gosh, like that's awesome. Let's go do that. But there's a lot of work that goes into that. And you can see that for instance, Yeti has an incredibly strong brand and it can really generate a ton of revenue and manage a ton of that PL growth. Because of that strong brand. And it's a great product, don't get me wrong, but it's it's really the brand that they that they push and sell. And you see that most personified in some of their video tours. So they have an entire video tour that they do. I'm gonna butcher the name, but essentially a a film festival, if you will, that Yeti puts on and it's all these short films. And the last one that I went to, I think I saw two coolers in the background, if that. And but yet this thing packs out and everyone goes there. And so that began the conversation of well, how do you do that? content: Jon Bausman (50:09): Yeah. Appreciate that question. I'm a big believer in managing expectations in general. Like I expect you to do this, you did that. because most of the time those conversations weren't had. And when I started at Airhead Sports Group, for example, that was a huge part of that conversation I had with the board where they were like, Great, now that you casted this vision and you walked us through, how long is that going to take? And so walked them through realistically, like, well, it's going to take some time for us. it took literally about two to three years to really start getting to that point that I was talking about because we wanted to do it the right way and we wanted to make sure that it was gonna be successful. Now, of course. Money can help expedite that, right? Because you can't outsource certain activities. If you had an unlimited budget, you could be like, man, I'm just gonna hire all these photographers and videographers or or do anything like that. But you're working in reality, which is working with constraints. So working within the budget that you have to say, okay, how how do I how do I do this in a way that achieves the goal, meets that expectation, but I can do it in a very I don't say like practical way within the means that I have. And so One, I think it's being realistic and setting expectations appropriately. I'd rather over deliver than under deliver. I'd rather deliver before time than deliver late. So first is I think just managing the expectation for how long it takes. Two, I think you have to make sure that you have the right people in the right seats on the bus. and I think that's incredibly important. And what I mean by that too is I had a team member who had been with a company for over a decade. He's an incredible creative designer. probably the fastest person Photoshop I've ever seen. he's absolutely incredible.

content: Jon Bausman (55:41): Great question. honestly, I'm gonna say pride is probably gonna be one of them. I think that there's a reality of people that are like, I can do this, I can do this by myself, or I got this. And and success can be a very dangerous thing too, because you may have success in the past, but that doesn't necessarily mean that you'll be successful in this in this role. And I've I've seen in my career, that element, whether you want to call it pride or any other vice that'd be similar, really get in the way. And whether that's pride of I put a ton of work into this and you didn't like it, or I can do this on my own without you, or I don't need your feedback or buy-in. those those can be very damaging vices in that process. Because when you say, man, I put in a whole bunch of work, right? And you don't see the work. Are you curious to understand why they don't see the work? Are you curious to understand maybe they just didn't get it? Maybe you didn't communicate it the way that resonated with them. but that's also, to be honest, why in my processes we have ground rules for feedback. All of our feedback has to be constructive and has to be specific. I I know someone used to walk into our office and they would grab something off the wall and be like, This sucks and throw it on the ground. I'm like, I have no idea what to do with that. I mean, I I that's not constructive, that's not specific. And now I have emotions hurt in the r this room. but the reality is is that again, if you have the process in place that says, Hey, all feedback has to be constructive and specific. It allows a better environment for humility to thrive. Because you're able to sit there and to share something that matters to you. And if someone doesn't see it that way, you can actually engage in meaningful conversation because, hey, you're being constructive and you're being like specific. And if we're a good team, then I'm assuming that your benefit, that your feedback is for the benefit of our greater good. So I think pride can be a huge downfall into that. and I think it's also pride to say that, gosh, like we can do this without help.

The people I worked with who have gone on to do incredible things in their careers, you know, we were all there together and there were just the the the culture of learning and experimentation, even for a big company and a big brand, you know, being being a number two in a in a category gives you a lot of permission. Right, you have everything to gain and nothing to lose. And so I loved always sort of having that underdog mentality. And you know, to use another sports analogy, it's like, you know, we it was like we were hitting the field every single day and going up against one of the best competitors in the world again, you know, at Coke and and you learn a lot from your peers and you learn a lot because you had a you know, ton of permission to try new things. and I've taken that lesson with me, you know, everywhere I've gone. I left Pepsi to join American Express, where I had, you know, a very different sort of professional experience, financial services, but, you know, an incredible brand where they you know, really believe in the power of marketing. And I got to work on our Core brand, the the blue box is is kind of the core brand, but then also worked with the business units and launched a bunch of different products, one with Walmart, and one which was a new type of rewards card. But again, I think being around a lot of very smart, very savvy marketers. And all the while that I was there, the landscape, especially the media landscape, was evolving very rapidly. Social was becoming much more. found like much more of a a marketing channel and then just you know kind of the advent of Facebook and Instagram and a lot of that was happening while I was there and just navigating all of those different platforms was you know an exciting thing to do as a way of you know how do I connect to my you know user in a profoundly different way than I've been able to in the past. And so that was that was great. And then from there I I got back into beverages and I I you know went to work for Heineken and I got to work on probably one of the most iconic campaigns in the beer category, the most interesting man in the world. but you know, I had the unenviable role of sending him off into sp outer space.

And then Havas, who was the agency who created the campaign, you know, just did an a remarkable job of of bringing that to life. And you know, I think as with almost any idea or advertising campaign, after a certain period of time, y you you know, your cohort of people who discover the brand and you know, love the brand because of that campaign, well they start to, you know, they start to get older and as much as they embrace the brand, you know, in any beverage, the way you scale is household penetration. So the more buyers that are buying you, the bigger the brand gets. And over time, that campaign just proved to be less and less and less effective, you know, against a younger generation where everything they did was interesting. And if you don't believe it, just look at their Twitter feed or their Instagram feed or their TikTok because you know, it wasn't you were needing to wait for an advertising campaign to see interesting things. The whole world became interesting because the whole world had a camera in their hand 247. And so it was difficult to then compete with reality. And so the decision was made that, you know, it was time to refresh the brand and as Challenging as that was going to be, and it was w probably one of the biggest marketing challenges I've ever had in my career, it was the right thing to do.

And so a man of very discerning taste who doesn't really drink much beer, this is his only thing that he drinks. content: Andrew Katz (15:00): So I I also have sort of this passion project, you know, that I I've been doing for the last six years, which is I teach indoor cycling at Equinox. So I I'm an indoor cycling instructor, I love fitness. And you know, as someone who is in that world also, you know, I I had this nagging problem of my own, which was, you know, the the time and energy and effort it takes to prepare For classes is is not insignificant. And for the most part, fitness instructors don't get paid for that time. Right? Prep time is your time. So the more time you put in, the better the experience is for, you know, your you know, your users, and and the less time you put in, it becomes obvious that you put no time in and people don't come back. So I I just thought that there was this huge opportunity to fill that gap of like. It's basically workflows and how do you create a tool for our fitness instructors to create and teach better classes? So I decided that I was going to go scratch this entrepreneurial itch. I left corporate America and I started my own fitness technology startup company called Instructor. It was really focused on the creative class of fitness and it's it's you know very big. And you know, the goal was to create an instructor app. on the App Store, which we did. So we launched a product. We had thousands of users and thousands more in our database. And then COVID happened and all the gyms shut down. And raising money was very challenging because this was ostensibly a tool for our instructors. So we pivoted and created an online two way interactive tool, kind of like Riverside the program we're on, but designed specifically for fitness instructors to schedule and monetize and recruit new users. We we, you know, struggled to raise money and so I, you know, got a call from Athletic in the meantime. We've got this opportunity, are you interested? Number two, the foundation of the company is, you know, very much mission led. And it's really about, yes, we have an incredible product, but at the end of the day, our our mission is much bigger to really encourage people to lead happier, healthier lives for themselves and their communities. And, you know, in addition to being a B Corp, and in addition to granting two million dollars worth of our own profits to trails across throughout the world, so more people have more access to the outdoors. You know, like those things were so important and so compelling w for me where I was on my own personal and professional journey that like that those two things were just profoundly different than anything I'd ever experienced in my professional life. And so the reason, you know, they were ready for chief marketing officer is because, you know, they were getting to the point operationally where, you know, we just completed a a state of the R brewery in Milford, Connecticut. So we have the capacity of four hundred and fifty thousand barrels of beer can get produced in that one facility. And then we still have another couple hundred thousand on the West Coast in our brewery in San Diego. So it was a combination of scale. We also brought in a chief sales officer Alex Berger, who I used to work with at Heineken, so he joined at soon after I did. So now we're available in all 50 states. We're sold at Walmart and Target and Buffalo Wild Wings. So we have a national footprint. And the goal really is how do we become a famous household brand? Really? I mean, that's as about as simple as it gets. How do we become the de facto choice if somebody's gonna have a non-alcoholic beer, it's like I'll have an athletic, you know? So Iron Man is a global partner of ours, so is Spartan and Ragnar. we've started to branch out into venues, but how do we start to kind of you know, from a grassroots foundation, how do we kind of like work both the top and the bottom at the same time? We've got this incredible network of fifteen hundred ambassadors across the country, you know, that really love the brand and are our brand evangelists. content: Andrew Katz (33:48): First and foremost, the the biggest barrier is taste. And the perception is how is something going to taste really good with the absence of something? Right? So it's not in our particular case, the reason why we taste so much better than everybody else and why we're so award winning is because we have a fully fermented brewing process that removes nothing. So we make tweaks to the process itself that enables us to have this b product. that has never had anything removed versus most macro beers that are zero zero or you know, they they burn off the ethanol. Right. So there's there's a totally different process that we employ in brewing our beer that's, you know, very difficult to replicate, which is why, you know, we we've won so many awards for our our our products. so taste is like the biggest barrier to overcome. And again, One of the things that I love so much is when you give somebody our product and you have them taste it and you don't even have to tell them there's no alcohol and they're like, wow, what is this? This is great. And you're like, it's not it's it's athletic brewing there but there's no alcohol. And they're like, What? Get out of here. That's not true. How could that be? so that's a really that's a fun experiment that you can do time and time again. And I go to the sampling, you know, sampling events all the time and I love that interaction with people who are ex you know, discovering us for the first time. It's very fun. the second thing to your point is like what is the occasion? Like when am I doing this? You know, versus regular beer. And and a lot of times it's it's you know the biggest occasions for NA beer watching sports on TV, right? Because I'm I'm at home, I want to have a beer, I don't necessarily need the alcohol to Tuesday night and watching a a a random game. Right. And then hanging out with friends. So like lower key, like we're at a backyard barbecue, we're hanging out on the roof deck of, you know. somebody's apartment building, but it's like a casual gathering where again, like, I gotta get up and go to work tomorrow, or I've got a training session I want to get to and be fresh for. I've got to drive carpool. You know, so it's like all these moments where beer is a perfectly acceptable choice. Alcohol is not.

content: Andrew Katz (43:10): Not necessarily. we we have a very flat organization. There is no upstairs. We all sit on the same floor. So, you know, I think there's a very open, honest culture, number one. and I think again, being a founder led company, you know, Bill and John have seen it for themselves. I think they understand the power of it. And again, if we could truly scale that, we would. But it's a very difficult thing to scale. But we do look, you know, we have tools we look at. There's a provider we use called Meltwater. So we're always looking at like our share of voice, you know, in the conversation, in the social conversation, and we can quantify that. We can say like, you know, we had you know 60% share of voice in the category when people were searching. You know, we can see search terms, we can see organic search, we can see, you know, paid search and what's working. So I mean there are definitely ways and as and as a you know, we're very much more of like a performance marketing organization. We're doing both, right? We need to build the brand at the same time. We need to actively recruit new users to buy us. So it's not either or, it's both. and we can see it show up in the numbers because we can see our sales left, you know, when we run media. we can see, you know, the difference of certain social campaigns and how successful they are in terms of recruiting. But again, we're still so young as a company and still like trying and learning a lot. And I think that's also for me a a very compelling thing about how we go to market is we're not afraid to try things and learn and and say that worked or that didn't work and and then Okay, then what's next? And being very agile and iterative. And again, having worked with lots of software developers for a long time, you know, those kind of like two week sprints and the agile development, you know, putting that into practice versus like we're buying our media plan, you know, for the year in November. We're not doing that because that's just not real world anymore. You know, we're much more opportunistic, agile. Let's see what's working, do more of that, and if it's not working, let's scale back and do something else.

Andrew Katz (47:57): you know, three, four years from now, I mean, it would be incredible growth to to be able to achieve that. But I do think as again the consumer is shifting, brands, companies are gonna respond, people are gonna invest more in the category. Corona's launching a zero product this spring. It's gonna bring a lot of new shoppers to this section of the bureau aisle, right? The more money that people pour into the category, the more interesting it becomes, right? The more legitimate it becomes. So I think we stand to benefit disproportionately because of how good our product is. But again, we love that Heineken's spending money in the Super Bowl. We love that Bud Zero invests. We love that, you know, this is just gonna become another part of people's drinking experience. The difference is, again, and this goes back to the company you keep, right? Beyond price, what does this company stand for? Beyond experience, do I believe in their mission or not? Because you know, Gen Z millennials care a lot about, you know, who they do business with and who they spend money with. And we just do it differently. You know, we do it differently than the competition, which is why we're trying to really create this notion of like a customer for life. Like how do we how do we onboard somebody to the brand and then they discover a lot of the things that we do that benefit their neighborhood, their community, themselves that are just fundamentally different than I go to the store and I buy the cheapest thing I can find. And then I go back the next time and I buy the other cheapest thing I can find. And there are plenty of shoppers that are are doing that. And I again, I don't, you know, take exception to it because that's just kind of like if this is how much money I have in my pocket, this is how much money I'm going to spend. Right. So it's a luxury to think that we can build this lifelong relationship with people. But I do believe because of the dimensions of our company, because we do only one thing. You know, we make the best non-alcoholic beer in the world. All of our competitors for the most part are making alcoholic products as well as non-alcoholic. So no one is maniacally focused on this the way w we are, and put everything that we can into this one thing and do it better than anybody else. And again, you know, a transactional company is one that really is not invested in anything beyond just, you know, just getting the transaction. I think we're much more interested in. building relationships, offering something beyond the beer and the you know, and giving something a value that transcends the price.

content: Andrew Katz (51:24): So it looks nothing like when I first joined, you know. I think, you know, kind of the beverage category again, like the kind of the big kind of all-encompassing beverage category is just a much more interesting place than it used to be. I think that there are so many different types of producers. I think there's so much, you know, more innovation. I think the the playing field has been leveled because You know, all I really need to kind of go to market these days is you know, I just need a really good product and the internet and I'm good. That was never the you know, when it was Coke and Pepsi and Dr. Pepper, like, okay, good luck getting out to a store shelf because you won't, because the problem was always distribution. That problem has been solved. So I think, you know, innovation is, you know, driving even the big guys to think differently and do differently. In the beer category, I still think it's much more slow to evolve. I think that there's just a lot of legacy there that the way that, you know, the laws, which are very antiquated, the route to market, you know, is very complex. And you know, getting to scale is really hard. There are 9,000 craft brewers in the world. In that sorry, not in the world, in in the US. alone right so so again there's lots and lots of small players right and and again you can open a brewery you can open a a a tap room kind of anywhere so the barriers are pretty low but getting to scale is really hard and so again then kind of taking that and then in in marketing you know how do you get how do you grow how do you scale And and it and it's like I was saying before, I mean, I think the thing that doesn't change is like the human story behind all of this is still really interesting and compelling and telling that well is easier to say and a much harder to do. But I think telling that human truth, like beer advertising traditionally is not very it's it's not really doesn't kind of deal in the truth. I think we have an opportunity to be very truthful. about the experience and like what the benefits are versus, you know, others.

Patrick Finnegan (10:27): Yeah, one of the the big challenges I see over and over again is that brands tend to be really focused around their products, the the specs, the features, the functions of the products that they're bringing to market, and not as focused on what those products and features and specs actually enable the the consumer to have as an experience doing the thing that they love doing. So I think that's probably the biggest challenge that Brands face is how do we take this product, this thing that we are manufacturing, and turn it into an experiential thing for a consumer that transcends the physical thing that they're holding? Patrick Finnegan (11:31): Yeah, so I think it starts really with the brand being very honest and somewhat brutal with themselves about who they really are, what they stand for, and how they define themselves and how they show up in in the world. the brands that have a really good understanding of that tend to be ahead of the the game there. brands that don't Have that figured out or at risk of having that definition created by someone else. The market will define you if you are not active in defining yourself and creating relevance for yourself. So that's always the first step is making sure that the brand has a really clear understanding of what they're about and giving the consumers a reason to believe in that.

content: Patrick Finnegan (16:43): Yeah, so Humminbird and Minkoda are both known as kind of innovation leaders in their categories. Minkoda in trolling motors, Humminbird in fish finders, and sonar technology. And we were really looking for unique ways to show how these brands were designed, engineered, and built to work together for a better experience for those consumers on the on the water. And so we looked at Just different ways we could do that. And we we ended up coming up with this idea that was half reality show, half fishing tournament, where we took some anglers from a wide variety of fisheries around the country. We had salmon and steelhead guides, we had striper guides, we had saltwater captains who were you know fishing for pelagic fish on a daily basis. We had all of these enthusiasts from around the country that we brought together. And we put them into the best bass fishery in the world, El Salto, down in Sinaloa, Mexico, and put them with the best technologies that fishing has to offer from Mincota and Humminbird, and saw what they could do in a fishery that wasn't their own. And it was a great way to get this hardcore enthusiast perspective on using the technologies. Some of them weren't super familiar with the technologies and so they were kind of learning it as they went. But that was part of our story, showing how how easy the products are to use, how well they work together, and how much they can improve that experience of targeting and finding and catching fish on the water. so we were able to get down there and take a bunch of content, you know, un unveil it to the world in kind of a unique way as a web series. And really it was a a different way than phishing had ever seen before, the fishing industry had ever seen before of showing brand and product content with actual consumers at the at the core of that. you know, it was a great case study and how branded entertainment can really have an impact on how the the consumers are seeing the products and seeing the brand and affiliating with that.

Patrick Finnegan (19:15): Yeah, I think one of the key takeaways that we had is that consumers are really willing to watch a lot of content if that content is compelling. So we had it was about an hour's worth of episodes, you know, broken up into several episodes that we that we launched. And I I'd have to look back at the number, but we had, you know, it was 60,000 hours or 80,000 hours of view time of that content. So there was no shortage of Anglers and people who who love that kind of thing watching long form content about people, you know, doing the thing that they wanted to do in aspirational places and using the gear that maybe they used or aspired to use at some point. So I think one of the other takeaways that we saw is that the community around fishing is phenomenal. So we saw all of these anglers that we brought in from different regions. Who are typically fishing in different fisheries, and we dropped them together and and what stood out to me was their commonalities more than their differences. So, you know, what a a steelhead guide from the Pacific Northwest has in common with a sword fisherman from Florida didn't seem like it was gonna be a lot, but when we put those people together and had them start going after fish, the the love for, you know, the the love for the resource and the love for the activity really rose to the surface there and it it really did highlight that community is important in these kind of passion activities.

content: Roo Smith (36:47): I think the elements are like I think the first and the the most enticing one is where it all starts, is like. creating that anticipation. And we talked about it as like making people care when they shouldn't. Like what are they anticipating to happen? And I think in the video format it's most easy to talk about this new tree climbing film that I'm editing right now, like it opens with him climbing this tree that's like sideways and jutting out from the side of this rock cliff over this river. And like eight seconds in he falls and the title opens and you're like What is gonna happen in this film? What just happened, you know? And so I think building anticipation, but then building that curiosity as well and keeping people hooked and wanting more, is like where it all starts. And I think from there, that's when like I really like to dive into the details. I I think for rock climbing, rock climbing films do this so well is like capturing the details of a story, everything from like the specific fingers on a crimp or like a foot, like, you know, on a tiny little pebble on the crag. Like I think all of those things, like those details are so cool from a visual standpoint, but I think movies like Free Solo, they were really interesting and successful because they capture the details in a really comprehensive way, where you see Alex Honnold like talking through the specific moves in the van, and then you see him doing it up on the wall and you know like those details matter. And when you have gr a great story and all of these elements, like you can create that anticipation, you can build that curiosity, but it's only when you go into the details of the actual event, the actual story of what's happening, the backstory, the specific challenge they're facing, when you really dive in, like that's where those emotions are really held. And I think we feel it when we watch movies, like the climax of the movie, like those aren't the moments where we're pulling out our phone.

content: Roo Smith (42:08): Yeah, I think for me the emotion comes in the process of making it. For me, like being a documentary person, I am telling real stories of real people and I am along for their real journey. And so for me, this is a great example. I'm making this film right now about this blind skier. And I went in, not being blind, I went in with this, this is gonna be a super cool film about Her overcoming her blindness and skiing and what it's like to ski while being blind. And that's just like not at all what her story is. Her story is so much more about like she's had to overcome a lot of like prejudice and kind of condescending conversations, being blind, people don't really understand how to interact with a blind per person, and like she had some trauma in her past and had never really felt free as a kid. And now she's chasing these experiences that allow her to like feel really free. And the back The outdoors, like I said, is a backdrop for that to take place where she's ice climbing and she's climbing and she's skiing and she's doing all that while blind, which is sure, super cool. But the actual story is is her kind of overcoming and finding that freedom. So when I started, I thought it was gonna be a little bit more of like, you know, the emotion is gonna be this inspirational, touching, overcoming blindness from a outdoors perspective. But really the emotion that is is hopefully going to be communicated as more of like one of empathy and one of more genuine human emotions and and authenticity of she's like, I'm a normal person. I want to be invited to go ice climbing just like the rest of you. And we went ice climbing the other day and she like was just totally there. Like she was teaching me how to do stuff on the ice. Like and I think when you look back and you take away the bias of what you're hoping to accomplish as a storyteller, like and see what the story actually is, I think that's when the the feelings and the emotions begin to land. So I would love to have an idea of what the f the emotion is when I go in. I think it would make the process way easier. But I think surrending surrendering to the process and allowing those actual emotions to transpire is like is important. I remember when I was first starting to make documentaries, my goal was I want to tell a to tell a story in which somebody cries in the interview because that would be so beautiful on film to be a part of that and capture that. And then I realized that's like not up to my control at all and like super selfish of me to want, you know? and then inevitably, like over time when you're when you're asking people about their deepest, deepest, darkest secrets on film and they open up, like sometimes tears will come, but it shouldn't be my intention as a filmmaker to make people cry.

content: Roo Smith (46:33): Dude, I love that. I love that question. And it actually brings me back to when I was in college, I was in the politics of Middle East and North Africa class. And our professor gave us this assignment. And he said, You have 24 hours to solve the Palestinian-Israeli conflict. Come back tomorrow with a solution. Just do it. And we're like, what? We're like a bunch of, you know, like white college kids. I went to like a liberal arts school in Colorado. And we're like, okay. And man, after like twenty-three and a half hours, we're all like pulling our hair out like there's no solution, you know? And you know, this was all of our like senior year. We'd all like written a thesis about something in the Middle East, we'd all like done a a lot of research into into this area. And we came back, we're like, there's I just we don't know, you know? And I think storytelling, like I think there's a lot of power in it, and I think there's ways to share information and share emotion and provide a lot of insight and and value to the world through storytelling. But I think the same way that I I tell some of my clients, like, you can't eat stories for breakfast, you know, like I kind of need money too to buy food and eat food. There's like I think there's a place for all of it. And I remember similar in college, I was taking a an art class where a a similar big lofty question was asked of is art useless? And that was just this whole, you know, the week-long discussion about is art useful or not. And somebody said the same thing. They're well you can't eat art for breakfast and you gotta have food, you know? And I think storytelling, like albeit really powerful and really transcendent and can have a lot of lasting impacts. I think there are there's space for for other conversations to be had. And I think ultimately, my hope is with storytelling. And like I mentioned with sharing my my film festival experience recently with Kevin Wilson, the Paralyzed Skier, like I think ultimately if stories can wrap up and they can end and more conversations can come from them, then I think they're s they're serving well. So I think maybe no storytelling won't solve the world's problems, but I think yes that storytelling hopefully can start a conversation that can solve those world problems.

Megan Prettyman (17:02): Typically I look for a mix of demographic and psychographic data. So I try to hit on, you know, percentage with the household income that they're looking for, percentage of the age, the male female split. I take all of that into account. But then I also try to tie in some of the psychographic elements as well. So If we're working for an outdoors company and they're looking for people that like to travel for adventure, we'll tie something about that in. I mean it's not with certainty like I said, but it can it can say we are like six times more likely that somebody that is interested in gear patrol is and visiting our site is also interested in, you know, mountain climbing or something like that. So so that's a lot of the way that I connect the dots there too.

content: Tony Sattler (08:03): So an insight to me is something that is an obvious truth that you arrive at that may be something that you didn't know previously or contradicts something that you currently know. So it's compelling, it's a wow type of statement. I think there's a lot of confusion, particularly in the marketing world around what actually is an insight or what constitutes an insight. And unfortunately, this has been exacerbated by the numerous amounts of marketing platforms that are out there today, different technologies. We see it even with a lot of the things that we work with. They talk about speed to insight, they talk about data points that they call insights. Those are not insights. Those are simply data points. And the unfortunate thing about that is because of the vernacular that's used, it's often confused in terms of conversation within our industry. And so the thing that I coach my team about, and honestly the rest of the agency, is that those data points are valuable, but you have to be able to connect the dots between all of 'em. (09:26): Those different inputs, and it might be a data point, can combine with a conversation combined with some listening that you've done on a forum or on social media combined with some behavioral data that you have from interactions on your website. What is that telling you collectively? What is the thing that it's proving or disproving that gets you up to say that's unbelievable? That's the insight. So it's an unfortunate thing that the jargon and vernacular within our industry has kind of devalued actually what an insight is and how it can drive a great story. It's less about the casual observations that you see through data points, and it's more about weaving this tapestry of information together and understanding the nuance behind it that gets you up to say, wow, okay, that's unbelievable. This is something that we can move forward with, or this is really compelling to wrap a story around. It's getting to the human side of things. You have to be able to almost tell that story with the data before you actually get into understanding how you're going to apply it. And ultimately, to me, that's what an insight is.

They can be in a meeting. It could be from reading a transcript of an interview, or it could be, like I said before, where you're combining all these different things together and you're saying like, oh, there's something in there, right? (11:59): That's ultimately the insight. It's got to challenge you to a degree. It's got to challenge you in a way that maybe you're not expecting. And that's where I think the magic comes with us and why I say it's a collaborative process. I think we as individuals, we're stimulated by different things, but when you can collectively come together and talk about your experiences and what you're seeing with those things, then you start finding threads to pull it. And then collectively, you can come and say, this is ultimately what's really interesting. And I think as an agency, we've gotten pretty good at that to say, okay, let's put aside all the different data points. Again, they're good relevant things, observations that we can maybe pull from, but when we work together to understand what's the through line, how does this apply also to our clients and the advantage that they can provide to their end users, that's where the insight comes from, and we want to make sure that it's as compelling as possible.

It's a device in my mind, and a lot of the folks on my team, it's like we're searching for those tensions. What are those things that are almost conflicting with the things that we already know that ultimately makes it more interesting right out of the gate? It can make it more compelling. So we're constantly looking for those tensions and how they align then with customer needs or the actual ask from the client or the challenge that we need to solve in terms of this advertising work that we're doing. (14:15): So it's important to have all of those inputs and all of that background, but you've got to find those things that challenge you and start digging into 'em again, like I said, kind of pulling at those threads. And hey, I saw this other thing about in this article, how does that apply to this? That gets the gears going. If it's just a flat sort of thing that's like, oh, yeah, it's kind of reaffirming things that we already know, it's just not as compelling. It doesn't start a conversation. And so that's ultimately what we're always looking for are those points where it really challenges our thinking and it spurs better ideas.

So it's usually somewhat cut and dry, and it's our challenge to really dig into that and say, but what is truly the human problem behind this? And so as we go into that, we start thinking about, okay, well, again, these data points, it might say that, okay, this is 80% better than the competition. Well, that's an observation. Again, the insight is how does that 80% apply to the challenge that I'm having as an angler or as a hunter, whatever it might be. So ultimately, that's always what we're after is just to say, okay, these observations are interesting, but again, how are we weaving this together? What's the through line? And the best way that we can do that as advertising is to what's the human story behind this? So again, that's why for my team, it's really important to not even just sift through the data to better understand the audience. It might be to have actual conversations with them and to listen intently. That's when those things start to surface. That's where you really start to understand the human problems, and that's where you can start getting to insight.

Tony Sattler (18:35): It does happen. And we've been in situations where they're like, Hey, we can't do that, and that's okay. But because I think us in our line of work, we have to challenge our clients as well. I mean, that's the value that we're bringing to the table. And if we've been caught in those situations before too, Cole, where we've had something that we really thought was great, but maybe they thought like, okay, we're not going to be able to take this far, or it's just so big and audacious that maybe we can't necessarily handle it with the budget that we have. (19:15): We find unique ways. That's the other thing about advertising is there's so many different ways to tell a story. So what are maybe key components of that that can still help us elaborate on the insight that we have that still fit within the brief that the client is bringing to us that fits the budget that they might have available? So sure, we've been caught in those situations where it's like, that's amazing, but probably not going to be able to do it. It happens and it's just not everything's going to fly and we have to be adaptable as well. But again, if we have that unique understanding of the audience and the user and a compelling insight that can still help drive other ideas. Because ultimately for us in the advertising, the insight and what we elaborate on that and goes into a brief, and it's supposed to be workshopped with the creative team so that it can accelerate their process. It has to be inspiring and compelling, and that's all it's trying to do is that insight is just supposed to be inspiration to help drive an idea or a creative product. So they may not disagree with us on what the insight is. We always come with the best rationale. It's how it gets executed that sometimes gets maybe a little might change throughout the process.

Tony Sattler (20:59): Yeah, again, I think it goes back to the human problem and the tension. So if the insight has those components and there's some nuance to it, it really helps us then elaborate on all of the different things that the story can tell in advertising, just like I guess in any storytelling device, you have to have a platform to work from. I think of the bigger movie franchises nowadays. I just went and saw the new Spider Verse movie, absolutely amazing in terms of the animation and everything else. But the thing that was so compelling to me is that this connected up so well with a storytelling that they're going to be telling across multiple movies, but it's all based off of, to me, I think an insight that they had about the characters themselves. And they made it so human, even though we're talking about extra dimensional beings across a multitude of different universes, crazy to think about. (22:08): But really ultimately it's focused on a few characters' ability to grow up and make their own decisions. And to me, what's so exciting about being able to tell a story when you can build a platform or a universe around it that's ultimately born from an insight, it has so much legs, it has so much opportunity. And I think every advertising professional would tell you the best campaigns have started that way. And it's all just been based off of just an understanding of a human element that resonates so much that it's just undeniable. And the best stories are born that way. And so for me and our team, it's like when you're able to arrive at that insight, even before the creative is there, it's so inspiring and you just feel so good about it. It's just the world has opened up to you and it's just a blank page that you can then go exploring with. So being inspirational is just a big part of where we go, and if we know that we have that insight, it's just the opportunities help us.

Because I think sometimes as humans, we can overcomplicate things and they were just the first in an industry to just figure this thing out and understand how an insight can drive a storyline and a brand for decades. So you're right, Cole, it is never, always some big complicated thing. Sometimes it's just uncovering the truth or an inconvenient truth that is just like, wow, I've known this all along, but we've never really recognized it. It can still be an insight. It doesn't need to be some ultra complex thing. And I may have mentioned it before, but when we go through our process, sometimes we're going through reams of data, we're doing user journeys and personas and going through all of that, but sometimes that insight is literally a line from a transcript, from an interview, so obvious, but it has all of the core components that say, this is right, this is so compelling. (28:05): This is an idea generator, something that can be inspirational that maybe is super obvious, but still has all those core components of fulfilling that human need, understanding that it's a truth at the core, it's believable, true, and relevant, and that ultimately there's some built in tension that we're solving for. If you have those core components, that's all that matters. And so like I said, it can really come from anywhere, and it happens sometimes in the simplest way, and sometimes it takes a lot of work. But like you said, Nike's a great example of just one of those things that just seems so glaringly obvious, but hey, sometimes you're the first to get it and you're able to build a multi-billion dollar brand of it.

Cole Heilborn (28:57): So I'm curious to learn more about your process as to how do you develop insights? And I know it probably varies significantly, but when you're first tasked with, okay, Tony and team, we need to develop an insight, where do you begin? How do you start?

content: Tony Sattler (29:13): Yeah, that's a great question. So the process that we go through is really not all that complex, but there's a lot of tools and technology and stuff that's built into it. So our process always starts with the ask. It always generally starts with getting a better understanding from the client on what we're trying to solve for. And once we have that in hand, we try, and I was mentioning before, we try and turn that business problem into a human-centric problem. So we'll say, okay, we've got to increase sales in our Turkey gear line this season. (30:01): What's the human-centric story that we're trying to tell there? So in this case, we might say, well, in order to increase sales, we're going to need to get more eyes on this. We're going to need more prospects in order to increase those sales. Well, what's a compelling human story to tell about Turkey hunting? Well, it's ultimately kind of like it's an easy entry point into hunting, and it's a lot big game hunting. So for those that aspire to get into big game hunting, well, Turkey is a great place to start. Well, there's an interesting through line there in terms of the human problem that we're trying to solve for. So we always start there generating the as trying to turn it into the human problem. And then what we want to do is then identify the audiences that we're talking to, and then we'll run that through different lenses. (30:48): We have a number of frameworks that we have internally at Swanson Russell, one of them that we've really tried to adopt in everything that we do, we call it the four Cs. It's a focus on the customer, the competition, the company, meaning the product and everything else that they sell. And last but not least, the culture. And what I mean by culture is not like the culture within the company is. It's the trends. What's the cultural landscape that we're playing within understanding of the vernacular and the ins and outs? And that's been something about Swanson Russell that we've understood for ages, particularly in the outdoor recreation environment, is we have a good understanding of the culture because a lot of us live it.

content: Tony Sattler (29:13): So we go through each one of those components and we use a variety of different research, whether that's quantitative or qualitative, direct user interviews, website feedback, quantitative surveys, whatever that might take to gather that data. (31:51): We also have a number of big data tools that we use to build out audiences and segments. We then also have the ability to do a lot of online listening, whether that's through social media forums, review sites, whatever that might be to get that true voice of the customer and what's happening within the cultural landscape. So we try and get all those inputs, and then we do as much kind of culling and ideation and hypothesizing that we can, we call it, trying to find the dig areas where we want to go. So taking all that data is like, this is interesting, this is interesting, this is interesting. Let's dig a little bit further. So then we dig down deeper to best understand truly what's happening here, keeping that human problem in mind that we're trying to solve for. So once we have all that information and we've gone through those dig areas and pulled at those threads as much as we possibly can, we then collaboratively get together and we decide, okay, what's the problem? (32:50): Okay, we've hopefully already defined that. What's the human truth and then what's that tension? What's the most compelling of what we've found so far in each of those categories? Those things combined can then drive us toward what we would consider in at site. So if we have those components after we go through our four C process and do all the research and this 360 degree understanding of the audience that we have from all of our data sources, we can then arrive at those core components that can drive an insight. But like I said, sometimes it's all this data is great, but then sometimes it's just lying there in one statement that you see on a social media comment in some random Facebook post. So it depends, but it's like, okay, is it fulfilling these needs? Is it addressing these core components?

Cole Heilborn (33:56): So you cast your net pretty wide. You scrape all of this data, and then you just start going through it. And what you're looking for is ultimately the problem, the human truth and the tension. And if you can find those things, then you're probably onto something good.

Tony Sattler (34:09): Exactly, yeah. Those are, to me, the core components of telling a great story. And if you have those, you can create that insight that can be that through line in helping create that campaign or the brand or whatever it might be, whatever you're trying to solve for.

Cole Heilborn (34:27): This is interesting. I've never thought about a movie plot in this sense, but I'm looking at problem, human truth, intention, and those three characteristics. I think you could probably look at every movie and find those three, but that's just interesting. I've never looked at it from this perspective before.

Tony Sattler (34:44): Yeah. Well, and the thing about that is you probably will find all three of those in a decent or a good movie. How compelling are they? Sure, you might have an insight or what you consider an insight, but of all those things, is it truly all that compelling? It's the intersection of a lot of these things too. Cole, you might have a really obvious human truth, but that tension is super taught, and because of that, it ultimately becomes stronger, or you might have, it's maybe a weaker tension, but it's something you're playing against. But that human truth is so strong, it's the intersection of all these things. And if you've got both where it's just this super obvious human truth that is just dead to rights, and then you've got this really hard tension, ultimately that creates the best story. So we have our own rubrics internally that we can't give too much of the farm away here, where we kind of go through and assess where we land on those things to ensure that it's a decent enough insider idea to move forward with.

Cole Heilborn (35:49): I see. So will you be identifying, let's say you have three insights and then you're evaluating those and making sure, okay, are these actually compelling insights?

Tony Sattler (35:57): Oh, yeah. Sometimes it's like, yeah, we all arrive at the same thing, and if that's it, then we're like, okay, this is really good. Oftentimes it's like I might come with something, one of my analysts might come with something else, the account director might come with something else. The creative director has maybe a different thing, and then we're like, okay, well these are all good, but is there something here combined? And that's where the collaborative process really comes in. It is like the insight development and turning that and generating that into ideas is one that takes a lot of back and forth and collaboration and working through and helping each other understand and pull at those threads as well too. Sometimes it's super obvious. Sometimes it just takes some work and some collaboration and some brainpower to really get to what we think is right. And the reason why we do that is because it reduces creative churn. If we land on something that is really good, incredibly insightful that we are all aligned on, then there's less back and forth through the creative process. It's like we feel really good about the story that we're trying to tell. We understand how much legs and opportunity there is there. Let's all go and attack it with as much gusto as possible. So when we do that kind of stuff, it just ultimately feels a lot better throughout the entire process.

Cole Heilborn (37:15): Yeah, you're not developing a brief and then pulling it out from underneath your creative team because you come up with a new idea,

Tony Sattler (37:22): Right? Or challenging it months down the road, just we don't want to do that reducing that. This is just operationally as an advertising agency, we don't have the time to do that. And so for us it's like how are we getting to something that's ultimately really exciting that we're all getting behind as early in the process as possible?

Tony Sattler (37:55): Yeah, we do to some degree. I mean, not everything is going to be super compelling all the time though too, Cole, right? We also work in a number of industries where it's very business to business focused and what might not seem as super compelling still might have enough legs to drive a good creative campaign, but I think for us, what we're trying to get to is just, again, something that we all feel really good about and we fight that a bit with our group is like that. Sometimes an insight just isn't there, and that's going to happen in the creative world from time to time. It might be based on the assignment, it might just be based on the nature of what's there, but you try and move forward with the best thing that you can get out of it that's at least compelling enough to spark some good creative ideas. (38:53): So we talk about just not trying to just invent something out of nothing. That happens a lot in our industry, and again, it's speed to insight and those vernacular in terms that I was talking about before can really just cloud things. So for us, it's like, let's work our process. Let's go through all of this. Let's still collectively come to something that we agree with. It might not be crazy compelling, but we at least all feel like it's a good starting point and something that we can run with. So hopefully that answered your question. It's one of those things where it's just like, sure, we'll work through this stuff and make it find the most compelling piece that we can, regardless of the assignment. Sometimes it's not all that exciting or contradictory or compelling, but it's still something that we can work with. Something is better than nothing. If you just have a brief that's just based off of features and product benefits and stuff, that's really not going to get you anywhere. If you still at least have a story or a through line to tell, that's better than nothing.

Cole Heilborn (40:02): What power does an insight provide? I mean, I think we've kind of discussed this, but I mean, what does it ultimately allow you to do?

Tony Sattler (40:10): I guess the best way that I could describe an insight is that it's excitement. It's a catalyst. It's that golden nugget that just when somebody touches it, they just feel like, I'm so excited to do this thing now. It is opportunity. It just feels fresh. And because of that, it's inspiring. And I think as an agency that is filled with just creative minds, that's what we yearn for. We want that level of inspiration that makes us feel so good about the work that we're doing and the results that we can drive for our clients. And so when we have that, ultimately an insight is just, it's the core of our work is the engine that makes things go. And we feel so strong about it that we can't put our brains to sleep. We can't put the pencils down, we can't get our fingers off the keyboard. It ultimately drives us and everything that we do.

Cole Heilborn (41:28): You'd mentioned that in our previous, our intro call that the outdoor industry has a tendency to kind of be the sea of sameness, and I wouldn't disagree. And I'm curious why you suspect that is. Is that because there's a lack of creativity? Is it because there's a lack of good insights that are being developed to differentiate? What's your take on that?
