content: Tony Sattler (41:53): My take, I guess the outdoor industry is just, there's a lot of competition, and it seems like there's always new brands or new technologies or anything that are entering the marketplace that are going to be the best. And so it's a lot of this feature benefit type of approach. Or the other side that I've seen of it in the outdoor recreation industry is that it's all about either machismo or putting you into the environment. So it's a lot of that sea of sameness, and I think most of that is just driven by the fact that there really isn't deep insight and that it's really product driven. It's not really human centric and that it's more like product driven. I would say that when you started baking in more of that, and we're guilty of this too, being in the outdoor rec industry for the last 60 years of that driving machismo sort of approach and broad vistas and all that. (42:56): Yes, we've been doing that for years, and that's table stakes. Now what we see is people who enter the outdoor recreation industry or getting into hunting or fishing, or they've been experts at it for years. They're all individuals, but they all have this nuance about how they go about it. They all feel like they've got their own handle on how they want to do things. Well, ultimately, we got to get to the human part of it. And that's what I think has been missing from the outdoor recreation industry is like, what does this mean to me? What's the emotional component that helps drive this story? Other than the product benefits or the product features? When everything's an arms race, you just lose that kind of emotional connection and component to the story. And we have to remind our clients that sometimes too is that, yep, these products are great and they could potentially revolutionize an industry, but what's it ultimately doing for the end user at the end of the day that makes their lives better? And you're just not really. Being clear with what your end goal is. So I think, I think that's like a really big thing is just trying to be way more simple with your message and just focus on one kind of value prop or message and do that really, really well. content:
Cole Heilborn (07:23): So tell me about the early days of 123 West. Allegedly, actually it's not allegedly, I think it's a fact. There's a photo. You guys started in a garage and that was kind of that was the initial the initial office for quite some time. tell us a little bit about the decision to jump out on your own. How old were you? At that point, how much experience did you have? And how did you end up with three other people in a garage?

Scot Keith (07:43): Yeah. Well even backed up right before one twenty three West is I I I was working in Toronto, ran a couple agencies, that was great. And my wife and I just missed, you know, living out west. We just kind of love the outdoor lifestyle and so on. And so I took a bunch of time off and and I read, I read, I read, and I kinda planned and where the business was going. So after two thousand eight when the world economy took a big hit, what happened in our industry is a whole bunch of very talented people got displaced. And they lost their job because the the brands that they were working on were stopped stopped spending. And then the big agencies got rid of the it's like they got rid of the really good people, making very experienced with a larger larger salary. So then when things started getting a little bit back together, they didn't want to go back to those agencies. And so so something kind of happened is that it created an opportunity. So my first company was called Community with a K, and it was all about a community of talent. And it was just like myself and this group of people that I worked with for twenty years or so, and we were doing special projects. Well, you know, I didn't know how it would go, and next thing you know, I've got an electronics arts project. So I was driving right across the country, me and my dog, my wife was still in Toronto. So we drove across the country and basically by Manitoba, which is halfway through pretty well, or or almost halfway through, electronic arts completely. Folks called someone I used to work with and worked on Need for Speed. So basically, I started my company and I started doing really, really well on my own with all these great, great people. I just missed though being part of a team. So what then happened is one day is Rob, Bryan, and Jeff, my partners, my original partners, we all went out for a beer. And I worked with Jeff before at DDB, Jeff Harrison, and is a fantastic person and just fantastic. talent had been nominated for Grammy Awards and done all this great work. And then I knew of Rob and Brian, but I had never met them before. And so we kind of got along but quite well.

content: Scot Keith (07:43): But I wanted to spend some real time with them and vice versa because having having been kind of the right hand person a couple of times at some agencies before, there was some things that I liked about it and things that actually I struggled with. And a lot of it's just personalities, including my own. And so So we spent a lot of time, the four of us. The first thing we did is we talked about what in what at work made us really, really happy in in the business. And then we spent time together of like, what did we not like about what we do and so on? And then we spent time of what in life do you like? Because our lives intertwine with work and so on, right? And then what do you don't like? So I just wanted to make sure that we all had similar values. I wanted to make sure that because I was a business person and there was three creative potenti potential partners at that point, that I wouldn't be like, Hey, we're a business. And they were like, No, we're creative. Like, you know, we're like together. And and then of course they probably wanted to know the same with me, right? And so we we spoke and we spoke, we spoke before we decided to even do this. And it got more and more excited. I think we got more excited because we're all like We're like a band that wants to play the same songs, right? And there was a really good energy. And then we were having some of the discussions in Jeff's garage. Yeah, he lived in East Van. And so we also then got to this point of like, well, you know, it's always funny how agencies, they basically work on companies, brands, and position them and do their ad campaign. But some of these agencies, like I'm saying, actually not some, most agencies, there's no positioning at all. I worked at a bunch of them. And so and so we thought like we need a position. The world does not need another company like us. So where's the space? You know, X, Y axis, where is the space that we could actually own and have an original story? Like we need to tell a story when people are trying to hire us. So we got into this whole bit is that our biggest problem at the start was basically you open up a company and you've got zero revenue.

content: Scot Keith (07:43): So if you do it the traditional old way, is you might be a half a million dollars plus in on lease costs, a whole bunch of things that agencies are famous for before you even make one dollar. And so we thought, let's just disrupt this. My other company was doing the same thing where it was like super low overhead. And so the guys kind of bought into that. So we came up with this positioning all about low overhead and high talent. And then even as we started to grow, the money that we we would make is we would put into hiring the very best talent. Most agencies are like a pyramid. How they make money, the traditional agencies. There's a handful of people at the top that really know what they're doing, experienced and so on, or at least they hope they know what they're doing, but they're experienced. And the vast majority of people at large agencies are at the bottom of the pyramid, like I was. And it's basically You don't get paid that much. And some companies they work you to the bone. and then they overcharge the clients. And people literally like I didn't even know what I was doing my first went three years. I just did whatever my boss told me. I was just tasked, task, task. And that's fine. But like I couldn't be running stuff, right? You know, and that was a different age back then too. You get nowadays, you get there's some agencies, they got people within like 18 months experience and are like running like, what? And so So for us is that we didn't want to go that model. Our model is upside down. Is so we wanted to be more of a Navy SEALs model. So so yeah, so we basically started off in this garage when we're looking for space and and it's just like, let's just work here. That's actually funny. You know, lots of great companies, you know, started off in the garage and they became, you know, mostly in the tech space, right? Billion dollar companies like HP and Apple and a whole bunch of brands like that. And then like and then because just into architecture and design, it was a kind of like a pimped out garage. So we started there and and it was ha awesome. It was absolutely awesome. It was hilarious.

Cole Heilborn (14:11): So that was that was what year?

Scot Keith (14:12): Two thousand thirteen is so we just we just basically are at our tenth year anniversary. In fact what happened is so we're about to start the company and I love getting PRs. So I email the Globe and Mail. So in Canada, that's like our New York Times or or Wol Wall Street Journal. So I email them and and especially the guys, like we'd all won if you care about awards, we'd all won, you know, thousands of them combined. so every one in the couple times over. And and so they're extremely talented. I'm okay. But so it was just like we're really excited, we're starting this company, we're doing it in the garage, totally different. Would you like to do a story on us? And then the writer, she got back to me in five minutes and she said no. And I s I can be fairly persuasive. So so come on, this is actually interesting story, right? And so next thing you know, They're sending over a photographer over. Next thing you know, she's interviewing me for the story. And she basically is like, When are you launching your agency? I'm like, Well, the day your damn article comes out and so we officially launched April tenth, twenty thirteen, when that article came out, and honestly, that we shut out of a can. Is that awareness piece on that was fantastic. We were on the cover of the business section in the national newspaper and It said four guys in a garage. It w had us just in front of the garage and we started winning seven eleven and and Mercedes Benz projects and a bunch of stuff locally in Canada. And so we started off real, real strong, which was great.

Cole Heilborn (15:56): And I think in that photo you had hair, is that correct?

Scot Keith (15:59): Yes, I had a little bit of hair. I was kinda you know, the worst part about being bald is that you're the left to know. Or balding, I should say. So I did eventually the shame because I was I spend too much time on the comb over every morning.

Cole Heilborn (16:14): And so that was that was ten years well, ten years in change ago and that model that you set out to create from the beginning has remained true ever since. you're no longer in a garage, but that that upside down pyramid is still how you guys continue to operate today, correct?

Scot Keith (16:32): Yes, yes. So basically from the garage we end up going later on to a factory. It was a linen factory in Vancouver. And it was like the you know, if you've s ever seen Breaking Bad, it was like going through the linen factory to get to the Meflab, and it was like even more of an insane space. But what that did is that really created a culture. So the people that came to work with us is they didn't give a crap about all the fancy stuff that often agencies had. You know, I've had corner offices before. Who cares? I would rather have way more talented people who are way more fun and awesome to work with and are gonna do great, great work for our clients. And so so it created this whole kind of like lunch pail, kind of like you know, factory of ideas, like just all about the work and enjoying the process, the process of making the work, right? And so So and to this day, you know, we like moved into another space and now we're that and we're in Toronto and partly virtual and partly in the office. But to this day, it's I think we got about 18 kind of working creative directors. And and so people come to us to actually get back and do the work. You know, like that's one of the crazy things about our business is that particularly on the creative side, is that all of a sudden you start getting really elite. Right? You start doing really good work, you figured it out, you've done your ten thousand hours, twenty thousand hours, like Malcolm Gladwell talks about, you're becoming an expert. And then what happens is someone taps you on the shoulder and makes you the boss. And essentially you're a manager. And some creative people are fantastic managers, but the vast majority, they're not a creative person to manage. They're a creative person because they love to write or art direct or design or film or whatever, right? And they're often miserable if they gotta sit in meetings and stuff all day long. I'm okay with that. That's what I actually like doing that, right? And so so they come to our place to actually go back to what they love and what they're good at. And that's the thing, right?

Scot Keith (16:32): Like the more you love what you do and the more you're good at it, the happier you are. And It's really that simple, right? So so getting involved doing the work. We still have some younger creatives up and comings because we all need that, but the vast majority of our team is still to this day. And and quite frankly, we could scale this and keep on scaling it as long as we're keeping that model. Keep your overhead low, put it into better talent. And the truth is the best people, the talented people with really good character, they just do the work more efficiently and so on. is I I I ran some agencies in the past where we had all these awesome up and comers. But the reality is like it just takes you so much longer when you're still figuring it out to then all of a sudden you start to actually really know what you're doing. Like when some when you really know what you're doing, you do it like maybe ten times faster. So and easier. Right. You don't take the hard road all the time and stuff like that. You kinda go, nope, this this didn't work when I tried that before. Let me try this. this is off strategy. Don't spend don't spend a week on off strategy work. Focus, right? And so so it just ends up being easier, right? Like, you know, like we I don't want us to be a sweatshop, none of us do a sweatshop at all. Is that like even on pitches, like we're done by like two PM. Like I'm not I'm not with the team rehearsing not twelve o'clock at night for a pitch the next morning. Never. But I definitely was before when I worked at other ACs and I hate I hated it.

Cole Heilborn (20:18): Hmm. So your positioning, your your perspective on how to build an agency, you know, keep your overhead low, keep your talent high. Like that doesn't seem like a a groundbreaking perspective. It's but but so what what's happened to the what had happened to the agency world? That seems like a very natural thing for an agency to focus on. Let's focus on the work, let's do good work, find the right people. What about the agency world is kind of skewed the other way, where agencies are investing in overhead and maybe not investing in in their people to some degree.

content: Scot Keith (20:51): Yeah, well, for example, you know, one of the challenges you have, like a lot of the agency world is owned by a handful of holding companies. You know, there's the WPPs and Omnicons and and you know the IPGs and a whole bunch of acronym type stuff, right? And so the reality is they're owned by shareholders. So and then they're really run by financial people. And so under those big holding companies, they might have a whole bunch of companies underneath that. So basically how it works really, how the real business works is that you do your job and you've gotta basically they've gotta make so much profit that they actually have shareholder return. And so even the CEO, when you're a CEO of a company, your number one priority by law as a CEO on a company like that is the shareholders. And number two, it's the entity itself and then you know later on it's the people, right? And so like it's a tough job having that thing, right? Because the shareholders, they they want them to have more profit. They especially the ones that have been for together for around for a long time. So so like a lot of that money, that overhead, like like that that money is going there. and then a lot of people just have different opinions on stuff, you know, the old big, big office downtown, people are starting to move away from that. You know, like I I s like I don't believe in stuff of like having foosball tables and pool tables at work because the reality is what they want you to do, they they buy you all these toys and then there's no way that they want you paying that playing that at two PM in the afternoon. They want you playing that at seven thirty PM at night. And so, you know, you go to some agencies, they got a hundred thousand dollar piece of art on the wall and you go, you know, and just Just all this stuff, right? It's just the the money just goes into other areas, right? A lot of agencies will have twenty to twenty five percent of their of of the money g goes into into that type of overhead, their lease, all these things, right? Whereas like you know, like our overhead is so so low that I'm already finding percentages of money that reinvest into better people. And so No, do we make less margin on stuff than a great big agency probably does? Yeah, probably. but do I sleep at night because we've got all these pros doing the work. am I proud? I'm not saying that they're not, but am I proud of what we're trying to do day in and day out? Like, you know, I just would rather be it's again, it's a positioning. I'd rather be Navy SEALs than a general army any day.

content: Scot Keith (25:36): Yeah, like well I'll come on on our specific role is that you know what's happening more and more, right? You know, is the the world's moving so so quick and especially with you know everything in the tech space, now AI, a whole bunch of stuff, is that brands that were very, very successful in the past are getting disrupted like crazy. Like just go through an industry. Look at some of the great big brands that were amazing, you know, 20 years ago that aren't even around. that were even around forever, the Kodaks, the Blockbusters, the you name it, and so on, right? So all of a sudden these brands can come out of nowhere and absolutely kill a big brand. So I think we add the most value when somebody is like they're running a company or have a company and like they were like, you know, they were a top one, two, three market leader. And then all of a sudden the world has changed. You know, consumer behaviors change. Maybe there's a competitor and so on. It's much more than making it an ad. It's basically we know you know clients will be like, We know we need to change our product or service and we're doing that right now. What we also need is we need a communications partner that basically can really help us redefine what our story is. So it's not even just an ad campaign, it's an internal campaign. It's about hiring talent, it's about re energizing their brand. And so everything starts at strategy, but then it's a combination of design. And then later on advertising said everything starts at strategy, right? And so, you know, what that positioning is, looking at the competitors, you know, I think it's Rick Rubin said, you know, just look what everyone else is doing, just don't do that. And so I would say some of the most successful things that we've done is exactly tight like that. It's just not analysis paralysis on the competitors, but just being clear on where they are, where the open spaces are, right? And then just using strategy to get to that kind of big creative idea that's ownable. It's ownable, has really strong brand linkage. You know, what are we asking people to do? Right. And so a lot of it's clarity.

So we're even starting to get a bit involved in that, which is great. So So, know, I love it where we add the most value on like, you know, what I call brand transformations is one. So we're helping transform a brand. and that could be anything again from re-energizing it and so on, complete transformation, or is it kind of an evolution? And then another one is I call it like it's almost like a brand acceleration. So the brand acceleration is like the company is doing well. The thing that's holding it back is the brand. content:
Cole Heilborn (35:08): Are there any brands, general outdoor brands, that you don't feel like a integration with a with a an appropriate channel is is helpful or or would be a good course of action? Or is this kind of could everyone take advantage of this?

Sam Van Boxtel (35:24): Yeah, I think anyone who if you do paid spend and if you work with athletes, you should be doing creators because it's kind of a hybrid in my opinion. Or if you work with media publications, which I think would be most brands in terms of if you work with one of those people, we're in that category. We're not all the way paid, we're not all the way athletes, we're in the middle. But if you do either one or both, especially, I think you should have some of the budget carved out to go into the middle. in my opinion, maybe more than both the sides, because like athletes just have one piece. Definitely still have value. I'm not saying write off athletes. and I'm not saying write off paid by any means. Retargeting all that stuff you can't do with YouTube. But there's this middle category that's really powerful, gets you return, gets you the lift.

short_description: Simply uploading a video to YouTube and expecting hundreds of thousands of people to watch are days of the past. I’ve always said that 50% of the work is making the film, and the other 50% is marketing it. Without a strategic distribution plan, your film is likely to flop. content:
Lindsey Hagen (01:48): You're starting with the real gut punch. well, you're asking the right person because I definitely think about this a lot, especially because I started off in the branded storytelling space and it's kind of the world that I've continued to exist in for the past six or seven years. Have we started to devalue? I think there's a threshold and definitely a gray area. And it's something. That when you bring brand partners onto documentary storytelling, I think we have to be very aware of this idea of guardrails. If as a storyteller, if you're working on a documentary film and you take that out to market, I think it's really important to identify those guardrails where you are and aren't willing to go, what the subject is comfortable with before you ever take anything out to market. you could take a documentary work and basically just sell out. And and at that point, we might as well be making a commercial. So I I hope that answers your question. But my answer is as documentary storytellers, as filmmakers, if you are going to be doing documentary work in the branded space, I do think you have to be very vigilant and do your due diligence to keep your story intact and unhindered. And that really comes down to just level setting with the client up front. knowing where you are and aren't willing to go before you get roped into something where then you end up having like product plastered all throughout your film or you end up in a situation where you know a client is asking you to ask the subject something that maybe isn't authentic or true to them. So you really have to do your due diligence and advocate for the subject matter up front.

I worked at a PR firm in Boston for some time. I worked at a ski and snowboard magazine. So that brings us to this podcast, backcountry. I learned how to do sales in the outdoor industry. Documentary was always something I really cared deeply about: human rights, social impact, environmental impact. I started at a company called Step Studios. I knew them from the ski industry actually. They started off making amazing ski films. I was like a total follower, loved their films. I used to go to all the screenings on campus at CU. They had moved on to Los Angeles and they were opening their first little office space. We were just getting started, and I jumped in headfirst. I knew how to do sales. I knew how to package projects and campaigns. I knew nothing about film. So they really taught me like everything, all the basics. And I just I hustled really, really hard. And when I was starting with them, I was living in Boulder, Colorado. The company was based in LA. I wasn't ready to leave the mountains. And I would fly out every two weeks and sleep under the Edit Bay on a little blow-up mattress. Eventually I got like a beater bike so I could at least bike around LA. content:
Lindsey Hagen (23:41): I mean, you see brands like REI and Patagonia constantly carrying the torch, you know, and and just making bold stands, especially within the outdoor industry. And I think that creates a ripple effect. We're we live in this consumer society, we capitalist society, and if brands can be the ones to help drive and spearhead change, I think it'll have a societal ripple effect. We've already seen it. There there's so much control. so many marketing budgets and and revenue streams, there is a there's a way to use all of that for good. And that is the the gap I'm constantly trying to bridge with branded storytelling is identifying what good these brands have the potential to bring to the world and let's use those marketing dollars to do so in a way that still can helps the the brand get paid, it helps them sell through their product, but Let's talk about the good work you're doing. Let's talk about the potential for good and keep moving things in a progressive direction through storytelling.

Cole Heilborn (24:48): I don't know if I agree with this, but do you feel like the industry is telling too many stories? Is the audience overwhelmed with the amount of stories that they can consume? And and I guess the reason I'm curious about to hear your answer is because like I hear oftentimes from brands and, you know, businesses all over, like they have an incredible story. They have an incredible why. They're doing amazing work. And then they tell their story whether it's through a video or a film or an a a a journal, an article, and it gets, you know, it's crickets. There's like there's zero response. And it could be the most groundbreaking story. story that that's ever been told, but no one pays attention, no one cares. I'm sure there's multiple factors at play there, but are we inundated with stories to the point where we're just at capacity, like we can't take on anymore?
episode_name: EP: 145 The Golden Age of Branded Films is Dead | Lindsey Hagen | gnarlybay
short_description: Simply uploading a video to YouTube and expecting hundreds of thousands of people to watch are days of the past. I’ve always said that 50% of the work is making the film, and the other 50% is marketing it. Without a strategic distribution plan, your film is likely to flop. As we look at the industry today, brands are cutting marketing budgets and these types of one-story-telling films are often the first to go. If there isn’t a direct result in sales it’s hard to quantify the impact these types of projects have.

content:
Lindsey Hagen (25:35): That's great question. Because it is such a competitive market and there are so many brands wanting to tell stories, I think we as filmmakers and on the brand side really have to ask ourselves, is there entertainment value to this story? If I were to send this out to organic media partners looking for organic media placement, can this story stand on its own as a story first? Or is this just a profile piece that aligns with so-and-so's values when it ties to sustainability? So I think brands need to look at the entertainment value. Can this pro that can this film or story stand on its own outside of their built-in audience? And if it can. then you have potential for a really compelling film that can break the mold, that can go on to have festival success, that can go on to have an educational distribution, potentially get organic media placement or acquisition with a streamer. I think constantly weighing like entertainment versus like just a direct branded film is really important.

Cole Heilborn (26:44): So feel like there's a the missing X factor in is this entertainment component. Not many pieces in your perspective have this entertainment piece. Is that is that what you're seeing?

Lindsey Hagen (26:54): I think if brands are only thinking about targeting their existing audience, that project can only go so far. For example, a brand like Nike. If you're going to be telling a football story, does that story have potential to resonate with an audience who maybe has never played football, has no interest in the sport of football? But maybe there's a compelling human narrative or a coming of age story, some sort of adversity. or hero's journey that they can relate to? Or is it timely? Is there a timely event that can help broaden the audience? If you have the ability to entertain and broaden your endemic audience, then that has the makings for a piece that can kind of break the mold. Otherwise just make a commercial or make your short doc, but then have all your auxiliary assets that are gonna, you know, best serve your ROI needs.

And I I think, I mean, coming from the outdoor filmmaking space, like there's so many projects that are objective based, you know, climbing that mountain, skiing that first ascent. but I'm really fascinated with the why, like the internal processes, the emotional why, the why it is that people are doing what they do, what circumstances brought them to this case, like what is the backstory? I'm always fascinated when I meet someone, like what is the backstory that made them so convicted in this aspect of their life? What happened to them, or what did they have to go through, or what did they learn along the way? I think backstories are absolutely fascinating in how it shapes all of us really in how we engage with the world. And then I love the in-between moments. so between that objective, what are the other things going on in your life? Who's the person you're you're sharing tea with at the tea house before you go up to your final, your final alpine ascent? or I I don't know, I just love the like when you go, you mentioned you just went for a a bike, a bike trip. Like when I go on a bike ride or a long trip, yes, the bike ride itself is wonderful, but I'm probably gonna be more interested in telling you about The really unique miner I met on the way who had this crazy story and he's lived up the mountains for the last 30 years, or like the amazing burger I got at the outside the gas station. So I think about storytelling in the same way that, you know, when I call my mom and I'm excited about something, it's not usually like the bolded objective, it's the little bits along the way.

Cole Heilborn (32:18): Do you think we forget about the little moment when it comes to telling stories? Like do we lose track of those?

Maybe they're nervous about something, maybe something happened earlier in the day. So I think if you can take that humanity and how we connect with people beyond your everyday life and apply it to your your filmmaking. that's where the viewer is smart. Like we are engineered. Lindsey Hagen (33:50): Mm-hmm. well, just like any relationship, you need to understand your client on a on a personal level. You need to understand their challenges, where they've come up short in the past, what what the hurdles are for them as a partner. and constantly as a as a creative outlet, a creative resource, a production partner, think how you can help problem solve. And whether they're paying you for that creative development up front or not, I think it's always going to be worth your time. you know, rather than just throwing things at the wall and hoping something sticks, it's really going to be helpful to have that insight, understand your brand partner's pain points, any upcoming launches or initiatives that they're working towards, and thinking of yourself as an extension of that brand in how you look at stories. So, for example, if I'm working with a brand. That has a new youth empowerment initiative and probably not going to bring them a cycling story around a nine-year-old woman who just cycled around the world. But perhaps there's a youth empowerment angle we can take. And do they have any nonprofits they work with? Is there the ability to grow their footprint in the the youth demographic? Can we play this in schools all over the country? Can we do an educational distribution run so that you know elementary schools can program this? So I'm really trying to understand their problems, practically come up with solutions through the lens of storytelling, always thinking about the emotional connection. But at the end of the day, I need to understand what they are deeming as a successful return on investment. So I'm building projects based upon their needs and how they're defining success.

content: Lindsey Hagen (35:49): I mean, sometimes it's as simple as brands just need to sell a product. or we're working with a a farming group right now and they they want more young farmers to get involved with farming and s and sign up for this like young farmer you know, training sessions. Or, you know, some of these other brands have affiliated nonprofit partners and they just want a call to action at the end of the film and they want folks to donate to the nonprofit. It really just depends. I'm of course we still have brands asking like, you know, we want to hit this many views and engagement, we want to see click-through. and that, you know, unless you're really doing like a targeted paid ad spend, I think it's hard to have those expectations with these brand storytelling pieces. So if you are going to create a short film, you know, let's say there's a new bike that's coming out and you have a short film that features the bike, but really the film is about a story. Maybe it features one of your athletes, you should you should have a commercial asset derived from that story. If you already have a film team out on the ground filming, why not just get yourself a 60 second commercial asset while you're at it? And then your social assets should have product integration. Maybe there's a bit of story in there and there's been paid ad spend behind it. And then you're clicking through to your landing page where your product launch lives, your film lives there as well. And so while your product is working. is working for you and people can click and watch the film if they want, they can fall in love with the subject matter. There's also the potential for that film to have a festival run and there's butts in seats waiting to engage with this more emotional, nuanced story. And then you have brand affiliation or potentially you grew your your your audience because maybe they wouldn't have come to your product launch otherwise, but they've been thinking about getting a bike and now they love you because you told a great story.

Lindsey Hagen (38:56): I mean, it honestly, it's pretty cheap to submit to film festivals. I think it's a great way to grow your audience. It's a great way to you can target various regions, you can target festivals that focus on different subject matter. since COVID, virtual film festivals have become way more of a thing. So you actually can hit a larger audience than you ever could have sitting in theater seats. And there is if you have A film that has emotional depth and it it exceeds three minutes, it's probably worth trying the festival route. because that is where your audience is ready to sink into those emotions or a captive audience. and it's potential for your marketing team to be out in the field meeting people firsthand who this story or subject matter is really resonating with. So again, it comes back to the human level. We did a film this past year. where Dickies came on as a partner and having the Dickies team at the festival with us, putting on this skate event for the youth in this local community and sharing, you know, sharing our film story with a community that is very different. Like we did a project that was filmed in Dallas, focusing on kind of like food access disparity in food deserts in in downtown Dallas. but it was through the lens of skateboarding and a skate park that provides access to fresh produce for the inner city. And we brought that story to Telluride. And those those two scenarios could not be more different. But what was so cool is that there is when you bring these films in person, these stories in person to a community and you almost spoon feed it to them, you'd be surprised the amount of connection and empathy. But it's really if you just put it out on Dickie's, you know, Instagram, Are you ever going to reach that audience? Probably not. So I think those are conversations that people bring back to their dinner table and can actually help change again how we see, how we engage with the world. So it makes it more human in my perspective.

So a map will tell you, Am I on land or am I on water? Am I on a flat area? Am I in a canyon? Am I am I going up a mountain? And that's the strategy, this the map is that's gonna tell you what is the right vehicle to use to achieve my goal, which is the destination. Right. So I want to climb a 14er in Colorado. Sharon Scott (34:42): Are two of my favorite tools to use at at this point are one is it's called the lean business canvas model. It's from a a tech guy named Ashmoria, and it's a really different way of looking at business a business model or or or even a product to sit there and say, Does this thing have legs? Does it work in the marketplace? You know what's where's the revenue gonna come from? And the first time you do one, it takes hours or days. And then after that, you can just spit through them in like fifteen or twenty minutes. And it's just a one sheet thing that because in my experience, so many people go not only from problem to solution, but a lot of brands and businesses say, here's the solution, go find me a problem. And and and instead it starts with who this one starts with who are my consumers? Who is gonna do this? Are they an early adopter? Are they a Johnny Come Lately? Are they are are they somebody whose core this is their core activity that they're committed to? Okay, how does that work? Then I go, what are the problems that no other product or brand solves for them? And we go from there. So okay, what's our solution? How do we solve for those kinds of issues and challenges? And then it takes you through all these different pieces and parts of of that that canvas. To say where's the revenue coming from? And the the crux of this one is the unique value proposition, or what some people in business will call the moat. What do you bring that nobody else can? And if you can't bring something to solve that issue for that consumer that nobody else can, then it's not the right strategy to pursue. So ideally it's a little hard in that day and a half, two days to really get to working through that canvas or there's another test criteria that that I'll recommend in a moment. So sometimes it takes, you know, a week later and then there's a follow-up. Okay, these are the things we thought about. Now I and the internal point of contact ran it through the lean canvas and these are the pieces that are missing. You still have to go somewhat granular and then it's a judgment call what's too much and what's not enough because you know otherwise you come up with we want to build pants for people with legs. Just because someone fits in the culture doesn't mean they can do the job. And so, you know, on a search for Highland Outdoor Group, you know, we're going to look for people that fit, you know, what we call a success profile. Here is the profile of what the person who can hit the ground running in the job. And then after we have We have the basics, right? Cole Heilborn (33:22): And if you had to define what the purpose of the interview process is for, how would you describe it?

Tony O'Neil (33:27): Well, the purpose of the interview process is to evaluate one individual against a pool of other individuals that are on your short list. You know, there's there's different components, right? There's, and I'll give you an example of how we do our interview processes. We call it the candidate scorecard. And the candidate scorecard for us is really three things. And you have motivations, and we're gonna call them motivations personal personal motivation, professional motivation, and financial motivation. And if you go deep into each one of those three motivations, then you truly know if you have a candidate or not.

Cole Heilborn (34:05): Hmm. Why is that?

Tony O'Neil (34:07): Well, you've got personal motivation. So you've got to figure out one, what drives this person as a human, right? Are they driven to to grow? Are they driven to learn more? Are they driven to lead a team? Are they trying to have progression in their career? Then you've got what we'll call it the professional the professional motivation. The personal motivation is, you know, do they do they is vacationing really important to this person? Is climbing all the fourteen fourteen foot peaks, is that a motivation? Do they, do they want to live in Asia for a month out of the year every year? What is that personal motivation? And then you had the financial motivations, right? Is this person going to fit within what compensation you have allocated for the role? Is it going to make them feel like they've had the progression? Does it make their living circumstances better than what they had before? And so those three motivations are absolutely critical. But when you know what motivates that individual from their personal their professional and their financial financial motivations, that's when you know you have a true viable candidate.

Okay, so now back to the person who is in the organization, who comes to the office, we'll say three days to five days a week. And what I think trumps everything is human connection. And that's whether you have a standing meeting for the first eight weeks with a department head or a team or a small team that you're going to interface with. Maybe it's not even your direct team. And then you have the leader of the organization, the CEO or the president or the general manager or the brand director. That person needs to stay very, very engaged with their new hire because that you know that ultimately is what's going to motivate them. They're going to build a stronger connection with them. And so how do you do that? It is an it's actually, you know, from that general manager or CEO perspective, it's asking questions beyond just the business, right? You know, what do you see the deficiency is here? Where can we improve on this? What do you think of what we've done with this department? How are you how are things going with the transition for you and your family now that you have relocated to this city. There are literally hundreds of questions you can ask, but it's a combination of the business focused, professional questions, but there's also personal questions, right? Changing jobs is a life-changing event. content: Tony O'Neil (51:43): Hiring is very difficult and it's extremely painful. It's painful financially, it's painful emotionally, it drains your time, your energy. You spend all this time trying to talk to these individuals, have them sell themselves. You sell the organization, you sell the vision, you sell the teams and the support that's already in place. And while you're doing that, really talented individuals. Are likely talking to other organizations or people like me, right? So they have more opportunities. And so when you think that you've got that right person, and if it doesn't work out, that is a very painful experience to go through. So part of minimizing the pain call is getting really super clear on two parts. One is structuring your process. Here is they're going to the interview process is gonna look like X, Y, Z. They're gonna talk to this person, that person, and this person. And not deviating from your plan. Set your plan and follow your plan unless you have to change it. But the second part of it is being extremely clear on the profile, the individual, what are the must-haves and what are the nice to haves. And put as much as you can in that nice to haves and be very finite in your in in your must-haves, and you can be more broad in your nice-to-haves. And the component that's most interesting that happens frequently on searches for us with our customers. is once we start the search and we're surfacing individuals and they start having conversations, that's when the position and the profile becomes more clear. They may actually realize after talking to a few different individuals that maybe something that they were really, really hyper focused on is a must-have isn't really a must-have, it's a nice to have. Or maybe it's the opposite. Maybe there was a nice to have that they've realized this person has to have that. And so be open to that and being able to shift and adjust as needed and that you're gonna meet some people that may not fit your mold perfectly, but that doesn't mean that you should always try to hire someone, the square person, the square hole. If you got a trapezoid and you're trying to hire for a triangle, you can take those corners and push them out just a little bit and you may have an even better person to help you drive a certain part of your business.

We got started in the hunting space and then moved into off-road, both snow and dirt, and then into the backcountry space. As you said earlier, I'm the the senior access and stewardship marketing manager at Onyx Maps and I work across all three of what we call our verticals, hunt, off-road, and backcountry. Access meaning how to protect and conserve the physical and legal access to the public lands we all love. And stewardship meaning the more of that human responsibility of using these lands. And it wasn't until I stopped and thought, is there a difference between these two words? And I Googled it and then found out, there is a difference, and there actually is quite a large difference, that I then realized something that I thought was very similar, which they are similar, but they have different different applications or they're they're used differently in the world. those two words are very different. And if you use those words in different user groups or with different people, they might respond differently based on what they associate the meaning of those words with. So one example that we think and and use a lot is the word stewardship. it's a great example. We can kind of kind of dive in there. But many human-powered recreationists have a fairly strong grasp of what the word stewardship means. They might know the Leave No Choice principles or at least understand that a steward is is one who respects the land. the word stewardship is also used in marketing campaigns and messaging. all over the place these days, thankfully, because the our world needs it. but chances are anyone who's who was tuning into marketing from from various outdoor brands has heard the prompts to be a responsible recreator out there. but because my work at Onex spans to off-roaders and hunters as well as as human-powered folks, we think about like the word stewardship in hunting, it's way less of a thing. And it's not that a hunter doesn't know what a steward is, although sometimes they might describe it differently. The the discrepancy here more so lies in the heritage of hunting and what they know to be good practices in their sport. The word conservation is the word that rings way more authentically with hunters. whether that's conservation of wildlife populations, conservation of the habitat in which those creatures live. and conservation of access to the lands where hunters can hunt. So is one word better than the other? Stewardship or conservation or environmentalism? I don't think one's better. They're just nuanced and they mean slightly different things to different people.

Becky Marcelliano (19:33): I don't know what if at Onyx we have any great example of where we've been completely disruptive with words, aside from trying to integrate a word like stewardship more into the hunting or off-roading community. But something that Onyx does take pride in in doing is trying to find commonalities between user groups and really celebrate where we're actually aligned or where we're actually more alike than we are different. we live in a very polarizing world today, as we all know. And that can be really challenging for brands like Onyx and and others in in a similar realm of serving such a wide breadth of of recreationists. but we really try to celebrate the good that e each user break each user group brings to the table and celebrate that we're perhaps in many cases more allied than we are just completely on opposite ends of the spectrum. We did a study last year and found that 96% of outdoor recreation participants feel it's important to preserve and maintain public lands, resources, and recreational access. And then we also pulled a more general American audience, including those that don't necessarily recreate outside. And 85% said that they also value these things. That is a staggering and extremely unifying American belief. So, really fun fact that like we all care about these places, and we're all just trying to get out there and go farther. But, you know, then you get into like access policy and things like that, where things get more polarizing. But if you take it right back to the beginning of we're all just looking for. these wide open spaces that we can go explore and unwind and immerse in the beauty of our landscapes, like that is a very unifying American dream.

That is going towards something that all user groups are are benefiting from and really care about. So that is something like huge kudos to the hunting industry for actually really dumping all of that money back into a good place. something that we're seeing from off-roaders that's really incredible today is they are there's very various groups around the country that are leading these large macro cleanups on our public lands. And unfortunately. content: Becky Marcelliano (25:42): So when you're talking about users of so many different recreation types, they all have different objectives. They call different cultures home, they vote differently, they need different gear, seek access differently, and ultimately stand up for different things. So of course they speak differently too in a lot of cases, and the junction really gets interesting when word choice becomes polarizing. between user groups in recreational access policy. For example, the word wilderness has different meanings. Wilderness often has a broad meaning of being in the wild or in the backcountry. And it represents these lovely places like we like to go to explore or immerse in our landscapes, and so on. And it's it's dreamy and it's all over branding today. We've all seen it, you know, like built for the wild Yeti claims or a Land Rover slogan, all the most dominant species start out in the wilderness, or Jackson Hole's very famous stay wild campaign to promote responsible tourism. so it seems that wilderness it's a it's a good thing and aspirational place, right? But there is also then Capital W Wilderness, the land designation, which is managed by the Forest Service. And there's 803 wilderness areas in America today. And whether this is a good thing depends on who you ask. And like this is the this is the junction or the crux. because the use of motorized or mechanized equipment is prohibited in wilderness areas. And this includes vehicles, OHVs, motorbike, motorboats, and even bicycles. So if I'm an off-roader or a mountain biker and I want to explore these lands, I can't. And that doesn't mean that those users don't don't appreciate or value preserved lands, but when it really comes down to policy and travel management plans that determine who can go there, it matters greatly. So that mountain biker might vote against land becoming a wilderness area so that they can maintain their access. and this is the delicate balance with land management and recreational access policy today. But thankfully, going back to that commonality between everyone, The things that unify us are we all care about lands in the first place and then wanting to protect protect them. Things just get really sticky when we talk about who the heck is allowed to go there and on what type of of method or vehicle.

content: Becky Marcelliano (32:24): Yeah, great question. That this is another doozy of a word or fascinatingly complex word. what the heck does access mean in the world of recreation? So there's the definition that states the legal and physical allowance to go to a place. And then there's the intersection of where access turns into accessibility. when you talk about barriers that are other other than physical or legal, such as like proximity to public land, monetary barriers, know-how, gear. and in those cases, access is more figurative, as in like a do I belong here? Can I go type type of messaging? At Onyx, the access work that we do primarily aligns with this physical and legal allowance to a place. that's what we That's what we really lean on within our access and stewardship program. But then things get complicated because of course at Onyx we care about and support access and accessibility topics beyond issues such as am I allowed to camp here? And when we tell those stories and work with our DEI committee to help fund and resource those types of organizations, We just have to use different language that speaks appropriately to those topics to to avoid confusion, just so that people people know when Onyx talks about access, it it means holistically this, but then we can actually care about other things beyond that and tell those more micro stories. But then you can see the importance of defining like key words used in your branding. At Onyx, we we have spent hours agonizing over what access and stewardship mean. to Onyx. Like those are two pillars of this of this purpose-driven program that we have built within our brand. But the definitions that we have written for access and stewardship are definitely not the same definitions that would show up in Merriam-Webster's, right? They're ours. Like what do those two words mean to us as Onyx, not to the entire world as a whole or how a dictionary might define them? and then these definitions that we have written, they anchor all of the work that we do within our access and stewardship program. And then because we have a lot of those sharp definitions, it alle it alleviates questions internally, it provides guardrails for us and provides us something to really rally around as an entire company that everyone can proudly buy into, support, share, and promote.

So that intersection, that delta of athletes having a primary focus on sport, not having a primary focus on finance and the other skills, and these brands also not having those internal resources to develop those skills, that that's where the problem lies. There's no one coming in and saying, Hey, we're going to develop these athletes in this way.

Lindsay Rogers (00:07:31): It's not the reality. I think there's so many assumptions with athletes. I mean, you had mentioned this, but I work with the United States Olympic and Paralympic committee, and those athletes are some of the poorest. They make hardly any money except for the top 2% of the athletes in that world. We're garnering a lot of attention. One is that, and I hear this from every single athlete I work with, they say, I don't want to be seen as just an athlete. I'm more than that. And I think I hit that too, where I had all these interests and other things that I wanted to do. I wanted to write, I wanted to be a freelancer, all these things. But you kind of get pigeonholed as you can't do both. You're supposed to be good at this one thing, stay in your lane. And so it's really hard for athletes to be sort of multidimensional and break outside of that stay in your lane box. And it is shifting. I feel like in the last year, this has changed pretty dramatically, and we can get into this, this is very representative of why athlete rosters are changing really dramatically. (00:09:47): But I do think for a long time you were supposed to just be an athlete, and there's people like Caroline Gly, she just announced that she is running for Senate. She's getting a lot of pushback. I am a huge supporter of her doing this and young people being multidimensional and doing other things besides just their sport, but she is getting a lot of flack. And so I think there's still this hangup of athletes, stay in your lane, do your thing, head down. Just do that. We only want you to inspire us with your physical ability. We don't want to see you as something else. So I think what happens is that singular identity can be the kind of mental death of athletes because they don't see themselves as anything else. If they do start to lean on other parts of themselves, it starts to become really chaotic. Who am they start to ask themselves, who am I? And so other people start not understanding who they are, what they represent. So there's a mental health component to that. Absolutely.

content: Lindsay Rogers (00:10:57): Yeah, so I started, grew up in Aspen, Colorado, and I grew up ski racing, so I ski raced through Noam and then a couple of Europa cups over in Europe. And so I was on, I think they organized the US ski team a little bit differently now, but they had this development team of the US ski team. So that's the point I got. And then I had a pretty huge injury that I, I'll spare you the details, but I was a pretty kind of career ending injury, had lots of fractures up and down both my legs, and so it was really hard to recover from. And I was just speed a speed skier, so mostly super G and downhill. And so when I went to college, they only focus on tech events, GS and sla. And so that's kind of when I started to hang 'em up. (00:11:43): And then after I left college, I opened the door again and started doing more big mountain skiing, did a few of the competitions, but then started doing more expedition skiing, so traveling over the world, try to climb and ski big peaks. And that's when I started working with several different brands. Again, growing up ski racing, I had the sponsors, but it was very, very siloed in ski racing. There was no personal brand back then. And so when I started doing more of that expedition style skiing, I started working with Mountain Hardware and all the ski companies and brands and K two, it was interesting, and it was also one of those experiences where it left me with a lot of questions. What do you want me to be doing? What am I supposed to be doing? Am I supposed to be talking about you out there? How do you want me to be talking about you out there? So I felt sort of this wash of confusion. I didn't really get any really clean answers from anyone or any directives. And I think that's the case with a lot of athletes. They sort of feel like, well, I know I'm waned by you, but what do you want out of me and how am I supposed to do that? You are expecting these things from me, but I don't really know how I'm supposed to do it. So that's what I experienced as well. (00:13:02): I started kind of pouring my athletic endeavors into writing as well. So I would pick expeditions where I could write feature articles for magazines. So I started working a lot with outside and National Geographic and all the other ones in between. And so that started taking a little bit more precedence for me is working in terms of what I could get a story out of versus what's the big thing I could go ski. So I started working heavily in that genre of writing more and more. And then I also went to what the industry calls the dark side and started working more with brands. Also, it was the time when that narrative side was starting to embed itself into the marketing mechanisms, and a lot of brands were iron writers. And so I started working a lot with brands on how do you integrate that narrative infrastructure into your marketing messages, and that's when things shifted pretty dramatically.

Cole Heilborn (00:14:01): If you had to describe a perfect relationship between a brand and an athlete, what does an ideal state look like?

Lindsay Rogers (00:14:09): Okay, I would say it's funny, there's a few different brands who are doing pieces of this really well, and I won't name them quite yet. But what I would say is a brand needs to look at an athlete as a holistic vehicle, so a holistic brand, not just their athletic endeavors, not just the things that they're interested outside of their athletics, but as a whole, the characteristics, the values, what they've been through, what they can talk about, and then also go in and say, Hey, these are our brand values and how do you connect with our brand values? And then really set the stage for we have all these different athletes as part of our roster, and you have this really solid message. Why don't you focus on that? This other person has this other solid focus for their messaging. You focus on that and also look at the intersections of those athletes. (00:15:06): How are those relationships being developed between athletes? Because people are very fascinated in that with how the athletes interact with each other and how they do the things that they do on their own. Because a lot of these athletes are very independent and training on their own. So for brands, I would say really look at a holistic person, not just their physical abilities, and then also look at how can that person connect with their core consumer or even beyond their core consumer. What are those things that are interesting as a human? Because ultimately there's a lot of studies being done on how people react to not just athletes, but how people react to messaging. There's two things that we as humans are really, really react well to. One is creativity and one is humanity. And I think in the past 15, 20 years, the humanity of the athletes has sort of been pulled out a little bit in lieu of focusing on their athletic achievements. (00:16:12): This is the Red Bull model of we're going to bring you in, we're going to wash you off, clean you up, and we're only going to put you on the roster if you are ping over and over again. As soon as you stop performing, you're out. So that I feel like that model is slowly being retired because it's really hard to connect to as a human. So I think brands really need to look at the humanity behind these athletes and what are they doing that's creative and interesting, and not just climbing Everest, not just doing that big peak.

But one is that we were looking at athletes are now really, really becoming the facet of those sports teams leagues, et cetera, more than they ever have been. Women, obviously, the women in sports became a huge trend last year, and brands are really starting to shift their focus into the holistic female athletes. Then we have obviously there's all these shows on streaming platforms. So there's this almost like a democratization of sports, and I think that's trickling down into the rosters where you're looking at how brands are really taking that, for lack of a better term, citizenry of the people who they want to connect with of their consumers and infiltrating it into their brand or their athlete rosters. (00:19:12): And so what that looks like is the North Face, for example, last year I've worked with them for a while with all of their different athletes and they had something called, I think it was called the Athlete Development Program, where they put out this kind of call for pitches and applications for everyday athletes out there in the world. And it was really I think a statement on, Hey, we're not just looking for the Everest climbers of a Jimmy Chen's of the world, and those are great, they kind have to have those as the top of the pyramid. But we're also looking at how are we bringing in this idea of different races, different cultural backgrounds? A lot of the DEI is kind of starting to come into this fold and this conversation around who are these people and how are people connecting to them? Because brands see that if they focus on one type of athlete, they're going to get one type of consumer because they are the face of the brand.

Lindsay Rogers (00:17:54): (00:20:11): So if you look at that spreading out or democratization of those athlete rosters, I think it allows people to connect more deeply emotionally with those athletes if they have these different tiers. And I know you and I talked about this really briefly, but last year Eddie Bauer kind of made this big splash. They literally overnight fired their entire athlete team, and I think some of them had a hint that it was coming, but they did it. They fired their high level athlete team, but then they rehired a bunch of people that were more like a highly varied group of photographers and fishermen and adventurers because they did want to spread that across a wider spectrum of people so people could connect more deeply with who they were and they could see themselves in those athletes because as you just said, sometimes it's really hard to connect with people who are climbing marrow or Everest. I am not going to do that. Most people are not going to do that, but I will connect with someone who's going on a five hour about bike ride or pushing themselves at a particular event. So really understanding what those human elements of those people are, those everyday people, and highlighting that humanity behind those people I think is really where it's going.

Cole Heilborn (00:21:30): It sounds like the industry is filling out the pyramid of athletes.

Lindsay Rogers (00:21:35): I think so, yeah. But I also think what's interesting too is I mean you can look at the outdoor industry, but if you look across just sports in general, more traditional sports, there's really interesting things happening as well where there's creative directors are being hired by teams. So never before has a hockey team had a creative director. So it's not the brand that's hiring a creative director, but it's actually like these teams because they are seeing that culturally people are really interested in athletes being these everyday people who are wearing clothes and going to the grocery store. They're like us. So yeah, I think there's that, that natural evolution towards back towards how do we connect as human beings now on a very basic level.

content: Lindsay Rogers (00:23:04): Yeah, I mean I think not to pick on companies like TGR, but sorry, TGR, I'm going to pick on you for a second. So when I go to those films and I grew up seeing Warren Miller, the Warren Miller films and you have all the bloopers and it's really funny. And what I think TGR has missed unfortunately, and I think there's the other companies like them have missed, is that people walk away, the kids walk away, the adults walk away wondering who are those people all is how big they win. You have no idea who these people are, you have no idea where they grew up, what their hardship was, what they went through, what they've learned, how they have become who they are. And ultimately that's what people care about because again, it's like a disconnect between what they're doing and what I'm going to be able to do. (00:23:52): But there's also this universality of the struggle, the hardship, the pain, all of those things that we all go through as human beings living in the world that I think companies like TGR brands can really leverage what these athletes have been through. Because one of the big things that we talk to athletes about is this, and leaders actually this is very, very important for them as well, is this idea of you want to connect on this shared identity, right? I am this, you are this. We are both this thing. So if you can say we are both this thing, it really builds this kind of intimacy and trust between you and them. So there's less of that tension between you and them and more of that connection. But then the other piece that I don't see very often, and this is where we really do a lot of our work, is really figuring out what have you been through? (00:24:50): What has it caused in you? What reaction has it caused in you? How have you righted the ship, changed your process? What have you done because of that hardship when your back was up against a wall, you had to make a decision. And then how has it changed what you do today? And then the key thing that I feel like we're really trying to hone in on is how does that impact other people? How does that impact other people? Because athletes are so focused on the lens being on them that as soon as they start to shift over to how what I've been through can impact other people, the brand wins, they connect way deeper with audiences, et cetera. So that piece is a really, really key piece of how we start to coach athletes is how do you shift your experience into something that other people can benefit from? And as soon as brands start thinking that way too, all of a sudden they have influencers that go far, far deeper than selling clothes, than selling gear. They have those people that are deeply connected to their audience. So that's my mission. I want people to share that stuff.

Cole Heilborn (00:26:00): Why do you feel like that is, why do you feel like those aren't things that are typically shared or are flushed out?

Lindsay Rogers (00:26:07): I think it's hard. I think it's harder. It's a lot harder than saying, I went to the grocery store. It's a lot harder than saying, I have this dog who cuddles up with me on the couch, or I trained 10 hours lapping the ice, fall in your ray. It is harder to figure out and you need someone sort of like an outside source helping you and asking you really hard questions and then saying, Hey, this is an opportunity. And really pointing out the patterns and connecting those dots with you is it's like I'm a big fan of therapy. I think everyone on the planet should go to a therapist because what they do is they can help connect the dots for you. Oftentimes we just need someone else to do it for us and help us. And so I think it's partly that it's just not a vernacular that these athletes or brands have really been taught, but I think to compete today in the world on that human level, you have to go there or else that kind of vulnerability and intimacy is just not going to come.

Cole Heilborn (00:27:09): So you mentioned that athletes historically are typically one dimensional. Do you feel like if athletes can start to answer this question or kind of round out this part of their life, it will make them multidimensional?

Cole Heilborn (00:29:40): Is that possible with the way that most brands work with athletes today? Are brands equipping athletes to encourage them to round themselves out and figure out who they are and who are they beyond just the podium? Is that doable in today's world?

Lindsay Rogers (00:29:59): Absolutely. I almost think it's a must do to be able to kind of compete at that level. And I think the beauty of all of this focus on mental health with athletes is that they are shining a light on, we do need to route out these athletes. We can't just put them in this pressure cooker and expect them to be everything we want them to be, but we need to kind of round them out. And so absolutely, I think it's a hundred percent possible. I think brands are more and more open to it, and I think they're seeing success of other athletes and other brands doing this very well. And I think there's people that I could point to. I mean one just because worked with her, Hillary Nelson, unfortunately, she passed. She was really starting to do this a lot and really starting to open up that vulnerability door and people were looking at her as kind of this person that's piercing this veil, finally, you're talking about these things that no one has elevated before, and now I get you more. (00:31:01): Now I can connect with you now I see why you do these things. Whereas before, she may have been judged for being a mom on an expedition, when she explained why and drove her, people started to get it and support her a lot more. So I think when brands see those success stories or brands kind of take a risk in elevating those elements of the athletes and they see how well it resonates, then they're more willing to do it over and over again. And so I think it's shifting from brands seeing it as a risk to brands seeing it as a must have, and they're figuring it out. I mean, hopefully they'll bring, whether it's me or someone else in to really help do this in a thoughtful way because you don't want to do this. I think you can do it very inauthentically and have the opposite effect. So I think you want to be thoughtful, slow smart, and really elevate the stories that enter deeply meaningful to the athletes, but then also deeply meaningful to the audience.

Cole Heilborn (00:32:00): Do you feel like audiences are inspired differently today than they were say 20 years ago?

Lindsay Rogers (00:32:08): Yes, but I also, it's interesting. I think they are inspired differently. Actually, I don't know if I would say inspired differently. I would say their expectations have shifted. I think if you look back across humanity in general, and there's all sorts of, again, not to point to studies, but there's all sorts of studies being done on this right now where from a psychological perspective, people really want a few different things. They want a sense of meaning in their life, they want sense of belonging. I belong to this type of group that I connect with or that I have similar functions in. And then there's this idea of psychological richness. And this is something that's kind of come up more and more recently where people want to experience something that makes them their life more rich, more interesting, more challenged. And I think that's a shift that may have happened from a brand and athlete perspective is that people are still inspired by those kind of deep human stories that Johnson and Johnson does at the Olympics, for example. But so I don't think what they're inspired by has changed, but I think their expectation around wanting to be enriched by these stories has shifted. They're not just looking to be in inspired. They also want to have that aspirational could, that could be me. I understand them, maybe I could do that. So that has shifted a little bit I think.

Cole Heilborn (00:33:40): Interesting. I've never considered the difference between inspired and enriched and where that line is. But it sounds like you're saying if you can enrich someone, maybe another word for that is empowered you them, you help them see a potential path they could take where I feel like inspired is just like you kind of walk away with your mind blown and you're like, oh my gosh, but there's no way for you, me as a viewer to feel like I could follow those same steps. Is that kind of what you're saying?

Lindsay Rogers (00:34:08): A little bit, yeah. And I think there's this other element when we talk about that enriched, it's also this idea of shifting perspective. So it's not just I get to see the potential of what I could be because you're showing me a way, but it's also this idea of, wow, I've never thought about it that way. That's so interesting. Now I have this different view of it and I'm going to come back to you for more because that was really cool. I've never heard someone say that before. So that type of enrichment where you're just literally giving people this slight shift in perception and perspective that they didn't have before. And that's a big one. What we coach athletes on and a lot with leaders is that how do you shift someone's perspective? Because ultimately if you do that, they start to pay attention because our brains say, oh, that's new. I got to come back. That's new. I learned something there. So I think it is more than, how can I also do that thing? It's about saying, wow, I learned something there that I never imagined to be true, and that's enriching.

Cole Heilborn (00:35:13): It's 2024 and we're in this crazy world of digital marketing and the attention span economy is, well, there's tons of studies out there, but it's short and it's only getting shorter. It feels like this need that humans have to feel enriched could be at odds with the way that we're consuming and engaging with media, but I almost feel like that creates more of a need for enrichment in our lives. But how do, as an athlete, how do you break through that if the way that you're interacting with people is changing? How do you see those two pieces playing and evolving?
