content: Moez Faruqi (01:48): Yeah, for sure. So I'm Moose. I'm calling in from Pakistan actually. So ever since all the Lockdowns and COVID and pandemic started, I've been spending a lot more time with family and now I've kind of created a situation where when I have some free time, I fly back over here, spend time with family, and then whenever I'm required to be stateside for trade shows or meetings and so on, that's when I'm in the States. So yeah, that's where I'm calling in from. I am the head of marketing at White Duck, which means I cover pretty much everything that has to do with marketing from the website, conversion rates to email marketing, to video content, to influencers and ambassadors and what have you. We are effectively a one and a half person marketing team. I say half because there's a contractor, Samantha, she's awesome that we work with for social media and community engagement. (02:34): But other than that, for the last couple of years it's been mostly myself and we have one person who helps out in marketing ops. White Duck is an outdoor lifestyle brand, which means we build mostly, we manufacture all of our own gear and we retail direct to consumer. And I say outdoor lifestyle because it's not the intense hardcore hiking or backpacking gear that you might find from say a North Face or someone like that. It is more about just getting outdoors and reconnecting, and that's kind of what leads to our hashtag Reconnect now as well, which is we just want to encourage people to get outside, relax and enjoy themselves and reconnect with themselves or friends or family or nature. And so our bread and butter right now is tense and we have a complete range of canvas density build, but we also have a complete range of gear, which includes bags, dog beds, lock carriers, tarps, and so on. (03:23): And we are slowly and steadily moving our way towards becoming a full one-stop shop for everything for the outdoors and down the road, hopefully we're looking at other outdoor products as well. And yeah, I'd say our main focuses for why we exist as a brand is we want to build products that are durable and built to last, and they don't let you down. So if you're out and it's raining hard and you're in your tent, it's never going to blow away or collapse on you. We have a major focus on sustainability. So for example, all of our tents are made from VCI cotton, we recycle any waste products, and we're also part of the Climate Action core, just trying to reduce our emissions and impact on the planet. And we have a big focus on product design just to make sure that everything that we build is easy to use and for one of any experience level. So that's who we are.

content: Moez Faruqi (06:19): Definitely. So I can start off with the history. So we've been around for, I want to say about five years now. I've been on the team for two years, and we started almost exclusively, as you mentioned, an online retailer, which means we had a website and we were selling on say, Amazon and eBay. So the goal of the business initially was just manufacturing product, listing it online and making money. And so our main marketing spend or marketing strategy was direct response marketing, which means for anyone who does know, it means spending on marketing that will essentially results in a direct response from consumers by way of a purchase. So that could be paid ads or it could be display ads on Google for example. I was brought onto the team specifically to focus more on the brand side of things. So how do we expand beyond just being someone who's present on online marketplaces to being a full fleshed out brand where we develop direct connections with our employees, with our partners, with consumers, with brands or other retailers that we work with. (07:24): And so that's what I've been working on recently. I think where the distinction might lie or where that inspiration might come from is what you're trying to achieve as a business when you're first starting out. If I'm someone who say has connections with a manufacturer and I'm just trying to make some money, I may go produce a product as the cheapest possible cost in wherever my manufacturer is located, get that exported to the us, list it online in some marketplaces like Amazon, eBay, and so on, and just try and turn a profit and make money as quickly as I can. Where the difference might lie with a team like ours is we were trying to look beyond that, and while we started out as an online retailer, you could say once we were able to invest more into the business, it becomes more about having a positive impact on the community, for example. So all of us as people who are passionate about the outdoors, just listing something online and making money off of that isn't enough. And we could do that through any other industry or any other kinds of products, but if we're specifically in the outdoor space, which all of us love and we love getting outdoors, how can we provide more to the people who work at the company or our customers or partners or retailers and so on with a better experience overall and a better connection with who we are as a brand.

content:
Moez Faruqi (09:20): Yeah, Amazon is important because it's just so convenient for consumers. So a lot of the times people won't even search Google for the brand's name. They will just go to Amazon and that will be their first try because almost everyone has a prime account. They want whatever they want to buy that same day. And so if someone's looking for say, gear or a tent, they might go to Amazon first and search canvas tents, or they might search duffel bags or tarps. So it is important to be present on those different platforms just to have that awareness and be in front of consumer's eyes. And so if someone's doing their research and they go to Amazon and search for White Duck and we have three star or two star tents or other gear, that doesn't reflect well on us as a brand. And so while I think most people know you don't make any money on Amazon, it's still important for us to have a great storefront, to have a great customer experience, to be rated extremely highly so that people know that what we make is something that they can rely on. (10:19): Then for us, it's a marketing challenge to get them to purchase directly from our website versus on Amazon, but it's still extremely important to be performing well on Amazon. So if we get a negative review or someone didn't have the best experience, we do everything we can to make that right, just because that in the end does reflect on who we are as a company. So we move a lot of gear on Amazon, tarps, bags, dog beds, all that kind of stuff. I think if you search for example, tarps as well, you'll see we have one of the highest rated tarps most reviewed, and again, that just helps get product out the door, helps move inventory and helps us fund all the marketing efforts that we're doing towards building a brand. But yeah, so if we're on it, we can't ignore it, but yeah, it doesn't make us money.

Cole Heilborn (11:09): You made the point to say that the goal is to use Amazon as kind of an awareness tool because most people go there to search for products or find new products, but then drive people to your website where they make the transaction. Why is that? Is that to circumnavigate the not making money part?

content: Moez Faruqi (12:34): I think it's going to be ever evolving. The challenge, you never really reach that final stage, and I think it's just because the outdoor market and the world of marketing is constantly changing. So I'd say we've come pretty far in the last couple of years from where we were. For example, we were just a brand that had a website and it was listed on some online platforms. Now, for example, we work with a PR agency. We have tons of video content that we put out. We produce vlogs on YouTube, we have a pretty great Instagram account and we have an ambassador program. We work with influencers. We have a full fledged email and SMS marketing strategy. So we have our hands in all the right buckets of ensuring that we're doing what we can to build this community out and build a brand. We're providing education to our consumers. (13:27): So for example, if someone buys a product, they will automatically receive a post-purchase email workflow with all the details about their product, set up videos, how to maintenance, all that kind of stuff. Then we also on our blog produce long form content around how to take care of your tent. It could be how to pack for a winter camping trip. It could be how do you start a glamping business? And so we're making sure that we are providing our customers with the education they need, not just about using our products, but how to make the most of their time outdoors. And then as someone who's active in the outdoor community, we also have responsibility say to make sure that whoever is getting out with white duck products isn't negatively impacting their campsite or the planet, for example. So then we also need to provide resources on leave no trace or leave nothing but footprints or how to make sure that we're reducing our impact as much as possible as someone who's active in the space. (14:20): So that's kind of where we are as a brand, I'd say. But again, as is a constant challenge with marketing that's always changing. So just recently for example, this year we had a conversation internally about how do we take our marketing to the next level where engagement on Instagram for example, is dying. I think most people are aware of that or organic follower growth for us is extremely slow. Let's just say if we're not running a giveaway, for example, and so then the question becomes, okay, we are all millennials, but none of us are particularly well-versed in TikTok, but we know that that platform is blowing up, so what do we need to do as a brand now? What steps can we take to make sure that we're on this trend before it becomes too late if we've already missed the Instagram one, for example? And so that's just a very basic example of why this pursuit is never going to end because there will always be the next Instagram or TikTok or new marketing channel or new kind of engagement with your community that pops up, and we're going to have to find a way to accommodate that into our marketing and brand strategy.

Cole Heilborn (15:29): Sure, yeah, that's a great example. How would you define the health of a brand? Just speaking about brands as a whole and what makes a brand strong or what makes one healthy? We've talked about the relationship with the consumer. Would you say that the health of a brand is equal to the relationship that a brand has with its consumer or the strength of the relationship with its consumer

Moez Faruqi (15:54): Health can probably be measured in two main ways. One is qualitative where you have the interactions you have with your consumer. So what are you hearing on a day-to-day basis from them? But then maybe that qualitative aspect of health of a brand goes beyond just the consumer and expands to the greater community. So when we have conversations, for example at PR or media shows with journalists and they come to our booth and see what products we have and the kind of feedback we get from them, if they hear about our sustainability initiatives or they hear about what our products are made from or they actually go inside the tents and experience them for themselves, what feedback are we getting from them? Are we going along the right lines or are we totally missing the mark? And I think it's also the kind of positive feedback that you get from everyone that you speak with. (16:37): So when we're first, for example, looking for a PR agency, do people sound excited to be starting to work with us when they hear about what we're trying to achieve? Or are people like, nah, I'm not so into White Duck. I'm not totally understanding the message, I'm not vibing with this brand. We don't want to bring these guys on as a client. So when it comes to say, retailers, if we're having conversations with wholesalers about Reselling White Duck, whether it's having conversations with journalists or the media, whether it's direct consumers, are we getting the right kind of positive feedback that makes us think we're moving in the right direction? And then again, if we aren't about certain products, so we launch a new camping chair and we don't get the right kind of feedback about that, are we nimble and agile enough to be able to change that and then respond to the feedback we're getting and increase our health if it was falling for any certain product in certain area? And then the quantitative aspect is of course in the numbers and the dollars. So are we healthy as a business? Are we not losing money? Are we spending in the right places? Are we seeing the right kinds of return on ad spend or is our average cost of say low enough to ensure that we're healthy and we're running and we're able to keep functioning as a brand and we're not syncing ourselves basically?

Moez Faruqi (17:56): I like to think we do a pretty good job, and that's not to toot my own horn, but I think like I mentioned before, we place a very strong emphasis on the customer experience. And so if we see that a certain product isn't performing the way we'd like or customers aren't getting their products fast enough, our shipping is broken or something else in the entire sales funnel isn't working the way we want, we do everything we can to fix that. And I'd say we're a pretty good team that operates that way, and I'm pretty proud about how far we've come in that sense. We're having meetings about how are we improving the customer experience, how are we responding to what any kind of negative reviews or feedback we're getting and staying on top of that. So I feel like we're doing a good job and I think we're moving in the right direction for sure.

Moez Faruqi (19:16): I'd say one of the main ones is bandwidth. As I mentioned at the start of the podcast, we are a one and a half person marketing team team. And so the biggest challenge for us is how do we get as much done in as little time as possible? So just the way we're structured at this time, we are a fairly lean team, so it just isn't inherently possible to be full throttle in every department that we want to be, which unfortunately means it isn't possible to be going a hundred percent on influencers and trade shows and PR and everything else that there is under the marketing umbrella. But that's just the reality we live in. And it isn't so much of a problem right now, but it may start to become one as we continue to scale. And I think it's also, that's kind of the internal one in terms of a SWOT analysis, what would we call that, the weakness at this time? And then if we talk about threats looking outwards, I think it's again, things we can't control but that keep popping up like new marketing platforms or a new competition or people who have more money to spend. And it's always about how are we doing everything we can in the context of the environments that we're working in to make sure that we're not falling behind. And I think, again, that TikTok example is a perfect example of that.

Cole Heilborn (20:33): Yeah, I mean it's easy to make a list of things and initiatives, projects that you want to start, but if you have no budget restrictions, you can do anything. But in a reality where everyone has to deal with a, how do you decide where to allocate that budget to try to move the needle as far as you can with any given dollar?

content: Moez Faruqi (20:55): Yeah, a lot of that is based on just straight testing on digital platforms. That's a lot easier because you have direct numbers to work with tools that Google Analytics give you that information at your fingertips. And so for example, if we're working on Facebook ads, we can test out different creatives, we can test out different copies, we can do photos versus videos versus collages versus discounts and no discounts. And within a matter of a few weeks, you'll have the data to tell you which way you should be going. And we have certain roas or return on ad spend targets that we aim for. We try to keep our average cost of sale below a certain percentage, and as long as what we're spending money on is falling within the KPIs that we've set, then we know that we want to keep pushing in that direction. (21:40): And that isn't to say we aren't willing to spend money in new areas of marketing, which I think you have to do. For example, I'd say we're still fairly young in the influencer marketing space. We're still figuring it out. It's a little difficult for us because our tents, for example, are of a higher value. The average value of our tents is like a thousand dollars. So it's not something like apparel that we can send out in hundreds or thousands to different influencers or creators that we want to work with. So we do have to be a bit more intentional about how we approach working with creators. And so that's just an example of a space where we haven't quite figured it out. We're spending money on say, Instagram versus YouTube versus TikTok and just trying to get a sense of where we are getting that return on investment. And it could be in the form of reach or impressions, it could be in the form of direct sales, it could be in the form of affiliate sales, and it's just a matter of what targets we set and how much money we spend and what kind of return we're seeing. So it is testing within platforms, but then also testing across platforms and then seeing where we're hitting our targets and just kind of going gung-ho in those areas.

content:
Cole Heilborn (22:52): Yeah. I'm curious if you could share specifics and give us two examples. One scenario where you've set the target, you set the KPI, and then the results have far exceeded that. And maybe one example where you've set the goal and then you've fallen short and you're trying to figure out what isn't working.

Moez Faruqi (23:08): Are we talking in any aspect of marketing,

Cole Heilborn (23:11): Any of the initiatives or programs that you're running?

Moez Faruqi (23:15): Yeah, for sure. So one area that we saw a ton of success or have seen historically even across a few different campaigns is working with creators on YouTube. I think especially the kind of space that we're in, because it is a fairly decent investment for people. It's a long-term buy something that people hope to hold onto for many years. There's a lot of research that goes into understanding who has the best canvas stand, what White Duck is all about. And so a lot of times people are searching YouTube for white duck and stent or the best belt tent and so on. And so we've done a couple of campaigns with YouTubers. There was one who had over a million subscribers. We sent out a Wal tent and just that day we saw five or six x extra return on that product that we sent out, which was insane. And then there was a different YouTuber that we worked with. We sent them a log carrier and they had a 32nd mention in the middle of their video and we had a 10 x return on that spend. And that is the exact kind of thing that starts to tell us, okay, maybe YouTube's the kind of place we want to be focusing on. (24:24): I'd say just kind of sticking in the same vein, Instagram is still something we're trying to figure out. It also is just a matter of the nature of the beast and how it's different from YouTube. I think YouTube directs a lot more relevant traffic directly to our website, which is why it often results in sales Instagram. From my experience, I like to think of it more as billboard advertising, where you put content out there, people see it enough over time, and eventually they will be convinced to make that purchase when the time is right. But people aren't always ready to convert at that point. And so we have spent money on Instagram, but we don't always see that return on investment directly. But again, it just might be because we have to kind of judge it differently from the way we do YouTube.

content:
Cole Heilborn (25:10): So all this seems like a lot of work, and you've kind of explained why you're on this journey. I'm curious though, who is this journey right for? Because I don't think not every online retailer needs to be a brand or even wants to be a brand. If someone is an online retailer, how should they decide? How should they weigh the pros and cons of doing what you're trying to do?

Moez Faruqi (25:37): I think not to get too philosophical, it comes down to why you got into the business in the first place. I think one of the things that excited me when I was joining White Duck was the vision and where they were trying to get to. If when I was first having a conversation with the founders, they told me that we are just trying to be an online retailer. We just want to be an Amazon and make money and spend money on ads. That wouldn't have been as exciting for me. But when I hear things like we want to build a brand, we want to invest in sustainability, we want to build in education for our consumers, we want to be present at trade shows, we want to build relationships with retailers and wholesalers and the Reis and Bash pros of the world, that starts to get a lot more exciting and get me interested. (26:19): So really I think that's the first aspect of it. And then obviously it requires investment. It's not something that you can just pick up, wake up and be like, okay, I want to invest in my brand but not have or not be willing to throw money behind it. And then also it is a waiting game. It does take time when you are, for example, working with a PR agency, when you're investing in influencers, when you're building out an ambassador program or throwing money at video content, it's not something you'll see the return on investment on the next day the way you might with paid ads. I can invest $5,000 in Facebook ads and I will start to see that return immediately when I am building out a YouTube channel. I may not see that return for a couple of years, but that's something you have to be okay with. So it depends on that situation and whether you're willing to endure that for a bit of time. And I think that's probably what it comes down to for me at least.

Cole Heilborn (27:11): How long, so you've been doing this for a couple of years. How long, I know there is no finish line, but if you had to set a finish line date to when you hope you will have kind of figured out some of these components, how much longer do you expect to have?

Moez Faruqi (27:29): Don't get me wrong. We've figured out some stuff. It's not like we're totally working in a haphazard way. We know how much we need to be spending and how much money we need to be making and in what areas we have a good sense of what works for us and what doesn't. And so I think we have figured out a lot of the parts, but aspects are still unknown to us and it's such a difficult question to answer. I think for me personally, as long as there are new avenues for marketing coming up, as long as there are new competitors, new products that we're building out, that challenge never stops. And so short answer is, unless we stagnate as a brand, unless we lose that passion for some reason, I don't think that's ever going to end. I apologize if that's a non-answer.

Cole Heilborn (28:19): No, but it's all out. I kind of gave you a loaded question.

Moez Faruqi (28:24): Yeah, fair enough.

Cole Heilborn (28:26): What are some of the aspects you mentioned there's a few other aspects you're trying to figure out, and we've kind of talked about Instagram as being one of those, or maybe TikTok. Are there things outside of social platforms or channels that you're still trying to sort out?

Moez Faruqi (28:43): Well, the PR world is one we've gotten into recently. We just started working with the PR agency in January, so that's extremely new to us. And when we were first signing on with them, one of directors of the agency mentioned that PR ages like a fine wine. And so we're probably not going to see the results of that for some time. We already have started seeing some results, but that's one of the aspects that we're working on newly. I'd say trade shows is something that we just started doing last year. We exhibited at one show and we're going to six this year and hopefully even more next year. But again, that's still new to us. This year was the first time we went to a hunting show, so that was totally new. It's the first time we're going to Overland Expo, first time we're going to be exhibiting at or, and then next year we'll be even more shows. (29:28): Website conversion rate optimization never ends. When I open up our website, it is a beautiful website and our devs and marketing team have done an awesome job, but there's always work to be done on the optimization side through AB testing and different tools, and that's something that never ends as well. And then I think just also just everything to do with product branding. So are we packaging our products the right way? Do we have the right catalogs and instruction manuals? Are we making the right kinds of video content for our consumers? Are we providing the perfect post-purchase experience? I think that's also an evolving thing. And just in that aspect, for example, we haven't revised our instruction manuals for our tents for maybe a couple of years now. So that's something that's an undertaking for us this year specifically. And that's a huge area of focus for us is the branding of our products, how they look and how we present them to a consumer. So those are just three examples of what a big focus is for us this year. And that might just change completely next year or it might just carry on into next year. It remains to be seen.

Cole Heilborn (30:31): Yeah. Awesome. What keeps you going

Moez Faruqi (30:36): At White Duck? Or

The day's always busy, there's always stuff to be done, and the outdoor community is just awesome. Everyone I've met so far, and whether it's customers or it's partners or it's people at trade shows and just everyone has been amazing to get to know, and it's such a welcoming community. I think we met on Basecamp, which is such a great resource on Facebook as well, for anyone who doesn't know, it's an awesome way to find talent. And we posted on there for our TikTok creators as well. Got an awesome response. And I think everything about working in the outdoor community is great. Being able to get outside camp with our products, do product testing, speak to people, go to trade shows, yeah, build this awesome brand that seems to be moving in the right direction thus far. It's awesome to be part of. And yeah, short answer is it's tons of fun.

Cole Heilborn (31:48): Awesome. Well that's good. I'm glad it's fun. It sounds like you've been on a pretty fun journey and there's more to go. Yeah. Is there anything else that we haven't talked about so far that you want to go over today?

Moez Faruqi (32:01): I think we've covered most of it. Yeah. I think in short, just when it comes to brand building, if I had to summarize what we've spoken about, the main thing for us is Insulin Conference in our community. So they know they're buying from a trusted brand and they can feel good about their purchase. And I think if any marketers are listening to this, the benefit of building a brand is that it's one of the best kinds of top of funnel marketing. So when you invest in video content, when you invest in your website, in sustainability, in building the right kinds of partnerships, that inevitably helps potential or prospective consumers find your brand online or YouTube or wherever else, and over time, it leads to a bigger community for your brand and in turn a better bottom line.

The landscape is constantly changing and evolving, takes really great smart people to run a successful brand, and that's what this podcast is all about. So if you're interested in learning more about what it takes to run a top brand, I hope you'll love this podcast and find something educational about it. Enjoy today's episode. Welcome to Brand Story. My name is Cole Holborn. I'll be your host today. Today I'm sitting down with John Drake, the Chief Strategy Officer at Drake Cooper. John, how are you doing?

Cole Heilborn (00:44): Doing? Great. Thank you for joining us. I got to say it is a special episode because this is episode number 10, which means we've broken into the double digits.

Small business typically isn't a client of ours, and you get over into large enterprise and we're not usually there except in certain circumstances. So we're in the mid-market for companies to help grow their brands. And our motto, if you will, is we build brands for the ambitious. And so we seek clients who really believe in the power of creativity, who really believe that good branding, good advertising, smart media, can really improve their organizations. And we have two offices. We're based in Boise, Idaho, and then I'm out of our Seattle office.

Cole Heilborn (01:58): So as the strategy officer, kind of paint us a picture of what your day looks like, what do you oversee, what do you get to work on?

John Drake (02:06): I've done this my whole career, Cole, and so I've been doing this 23 years. And so now as chief strategy officer, I sit in the middle between understanding our clients and what they need to achieve their business objectives and trying to take those things and help distill it down into ways that creative people can understand what needs to happen to the business and then apply really creative and innovative solutions to do, for lack of a better word, really cool things that help a business sell stuff or communicate something. And so I sit in the middle and it's a really cool, I love sitting there because on one side you've got commerce, and on another side you've got art. And it's about trying to get the best out of both and putting stuff out in the world that people actually like that they respond to and say, yeah, that's helpful to me, or that's interesting, or that was entertaining and I want to do something with that. So I sit there and I oversee, oversee is a weird word. I work directly with our account management team and our account planning team, which writes all the creative briefs and our media insights and analytics teams which evaluate if the work was effective or not and where we can be better.

Cole Heilborn (03:26): So that's interesting. You kind of got your foot in two different camps, the left side of the brain, I suppose, on the right side of the brain. How do you translate and help communicate between those two parties?

John Drake (03:38): It starts with finding the right people first. On the client side, you get clients who really believe in what you do. You don't have to sell them on doing good stuff. They want good stuff and they want to be shown ideas that make them think differently. So if you start with that people, that type of person on one side, and then you've got on the agency side, you've got people who really care about having an impact, they really want clients to succeed. And you take that initial mindset. And then my philosophy towards strategy, and by the way, it's strategy just with advertising, it's not strategy. Strategy goes a bunch of different ways, but in my line of strategy, always kind of think of things as a little bit. You have to be a one part focused where it's like, this is the thing, think about that. Try to get away all the other parts and say, okay, this is the area you really need to think of. But within that area it's a little bit, you want to have a little bit of a mentality that's like a garden that you're doing. It's like (04:51): This is the thing we're really focused on. We really need to move this metric. This is what we need to get people to do. But within that, there's several ways we can probably do that and think about these things. And it could be that this idea here if done really, really well will do the job, whereas this idea here, yeah, it's a little bit different of a shift, but if we do that really, really well, that can make a difference too. So it's really about what can the client team and what can the agency team execute on really, really well that hits that one key objective that we need, we need to move.

John Drake (07:03): Yeah, we worked with Visit Idaho for a long, long time. We learned from that we have to, we learned a few things. First of all, we have to define the problem really well. And the problem was visit Idaho is largely outspent. I mean, a lot of states and areas have a lot more revenue to put for tourism than Idaho does. And so it's like recognizing that from the outset that were significantly outspent. And then what we did is we really tried to hone it. We really honed the media target down. So we said, okay, who are we really trying to, we've got this little pool of money, so who do we focus it on? And so what we decided on, we coined this target, which has been really helpful, which was we wanted to spend, we wanted to mostly spend to get families with kids. Lemme see if I can do this family with kids under the age of 18 living at home who have an affinity for the outdoor adventure and live within an uncomplicated day's journey to Idaho.

Cole Heilborn (08:07): Wow,

John Drake (08:07): That's

Cole Heilborn (08:08): Specific.

And then once we know a little bit about you, you visited the site, you've done something, then we can say, oh, you're interested in this thing, so let's let you know what can happen there. So we learned to be really focused there and that was good. And you take learnings. That's one of the great things about this industry, I think, is you take learnings from one industry and you can see where that sort of learning can apply to others. And so it was good. And across the mid-market it's fun because you work on different things. So we have industries that we do a lot of and we like to think that we do an okay job there, but we also, I think what clients come to us for is we really try to understand their brand and do it well. And they like that we have a little bit of experience maybe in the category, but we're not a dedicated agency in one said category, and we find that our clients like that.

Home builder based out of Boise, (09:41): Idaho Central Credit Union, which is a great organization doing all the right things. We worked with 44 North Vodka for many, many years, many years. We work with Newland Communities, which is a master plant community, which is a great organization. And then we do a lot of work with Blue Diamond almonds. We work with Boeing a little bit. And then we have a lot of clients where we just won a best of show award for a company called Bornstein Seafood up by where you're based, which fantastic company. So we span across several areas and really just look for great clients to work with.

We find that clients who work there in the midmarket, they're really still a mid-market company, can still be a big company, but it's not a gargantuan company. And we find that that environment really creates, people who work there still have a connection to the CEO, they know that person often or they see that person walking around and that size of organization you get into. People really try to, they really understand what the company often, what the company's trying to do, what the brand is all about. They all treat the brand very seriously. They also really enjoy a personal relationship. They're very collaborative, we find and very pleasant to do business with. And it's just a great, if you can summarize an entire size of doing business, which is of course almost impossible to do, but to be very general overall, it's great because you get really good people and they've generated enough revenue to do some things with advertising and branding, which is interesting.

Cole Heilborn (12:10): And

John Drake (12:11): They appreciate the fact that we are a little bit more off the grid than a lot of agencies. I mean, we're not in New York or la and that is we find sometimes welcome to buy clients. They like that. A lot of good agencies obviously in those markets, but we're not, and we think that is an advantage for a way of doing business and a way of thinking.

Cole Heilborn (12:38): What can you do when your clients are maybe a little, are more okay with that creative freedom and passing it off to you guys? What does that allow you to do?

We don't have to say, can we talk to this team over here and bring them in and have a bunch of meetings about that? We just kind of do it. And that's really good for creativity. (14:18): Malcolm Gladwell, wasn't it, who said that? You got to know what you're solving. The puzzle or the riddle always kind of like that where it's like the puzzle is like you're missing a piece and we need to go find that piece and we do research or we do something to get it. Then there's the riddle, which is you've got all the pieces. For the most part, they're there. It's the vantage point of how you look at it. I think that there will always be a need for organizations to go out and realize they're solving a puzzle or they're solving a riddle and they need creative people to look at it and say, we've gotten it this far. We think it's about these things. What do you think? I just can't see that ever changing with the future. Is that all it takes or does it take more than that?

John Drake (15:29): It takes brilliant execution. If you're a company who can give people a good value, however you define value, and if you can execute it brilliantly so that they have a great experience, that's first and foremost what it takes. We think that we have this, we talk about consumers in three ways. We think that at Dre Cooper, what we say is that the consumer, however you define it, people really, they kind of want three things. They expect to easily find what they want and get what they need wherever they are. That should be, they want that. They dislike being bothered by things that don't help them, and they want to win. They want to win. And however you define winning, if that's, they want to save money or they want to be acknowledged for something, or they want to be delighted with something they want to win. And so they want those three things. And so if an organization can do that at its core, bring that out into the world, and then we can help them see that we can help articulate it or we can help get it noticed or be distinctive about it. (16:40): That's where we can be a helpful partner.

Cole Heilborn (16:43): And is that where you see differentiation coming into play between brands?

John Drake (16:49): I do. At least from our line of work. I think that it starts at the beginning. Can an organization be, can they do something that's valuable? And then are they saying it in a way that people understand it and believe it and get excited about it? And yeah, I think that's how a lot of companies can stand out and be different from each other.

Cole Heilborn (17:13): Yeah, yeah. So tell me a little bit, we're going to change gears a little bit. Tell me a little bit about your background. You've got a ton of experience in the ad world. Give us the highlights.

I was kind of an advertising nerdy kid, and I started reading advertising age when I was like 15 or 16 years old, and I for some reason really liked it. And I was one of those kids who put ads up. I would rip out ads out of magazines and tape them up my room, and I always liked that. And so I got my degree in advertising and I moved to LA after I graduated college and worked at Daily and Associates for a while, worked at Deutsche for many, many years and Wong Duty. And I've done account management, I've done strategy, and I've done business development all in advertising agencies. I've only worked in that agencies. (18:12): And I got really lucky because I worked at Deutsche LA at a time when I was the 19th employee there. While I was there, it grew to four or 500 people, and it was the first time that an agency based on the East coast had ever established a really successful office on the west coast to such a degree. And it was a time they won, and Deutsche won advertising agency the year, five years in a row from Adweek and Adage, and it was just this amazing run. And so I got to work with you. You take hundreds of people and you put them quickly into an organization, you're going to bump into amazing people. And I got really, really lucky because you meet and work with people in that environment, not just because it was big, but because of the nature of what was happening there. I just got lucky. It would've been like Kristen Porter in our industry a few years later, and those people went on and did really interesting things. And so I got lucky and that really helped me. And then from there, I joined Drake Cooper and had been with the agency since 2007.

Would you say for people who are fresh out of college or wanting to get into the ad world, it sounds like you're saying is it's really all about the people that you meet and the people that you know. It's really interesting work and you can do it from anywhere. That's what's really neat about it. I mean, almost anywhere. I mean, you have to go to a really small city, really small town to not have a need for some sort of advertising or branding or marketing. And it's really cool because you can live in the city that you want, the place that you want and do this. It's great. I encourage anybody who, and it picks up a lot of interesting people because it picks up the people who don't always know where they fit.

Cole Heilborn (20:23): They

John Drake (20:23): Like to be artistic, they like creativity, they like people often and they kind of like business, but they may not like myself. Business that doesn't come naturally. It's not like, but they like it. And so advertising exists to capture all these really interesting people where you can use your art or use your writing or use your strategy or use your people skills or use your affinity for the media or your ability to think about data and get insights. It captures all these really interesting people and puts them together. I think it's a really great thing to do.

Cole Heilborn (20:59): Yeah. Do you have any examples or, I don't know, memories of moments in the industry where you had, I don't know, you felt the most joy or you felt the most contentment with what you were doing?

John Drake (21:12): They all come back to when the team works really, really hard, you think of a really interesting idea. You think it's good you, and then you show it to a client and they say, that's good, let's do that. And that moment is so gratifying because you have a lot of people who work so hard and then somebody else looks at 'em and says, yeah, that's really great. We should do that. And just take that every time that happens on small things and big things, it feels great. And then when you see your workout in the world, that's kind of cool. That's neat.

And so he built it very quickly to be the largest agency in Idaho. Within I think five or six years it became that. (23:54): And it's been going ever since. And it's always this, it's always wanted to be, Cooper is a brand, it's always wanted to be a highly creative organization where the work is really, really important and we want to have clients for a long time. We think that we get the really good work. We get sometimes the best work when we know somebody for a really long time. So you want to have an environment where we really love our clients, we want them to be happy and successful. And so it's blending those two things together, which can happen. Sometimes you hear that can't happen, but it can. And we really tried to do that. And so I joined in 2007 after working elsewhere to work there. And Jamie Cooper's the CEO and president, and it's been fabulous working together with him.

But I never really knew what to call him in business. And so for years when he was still at the company, I would never call him by name because it just felt so strange in either scenario. And that's something I didn't really think about until it was occurring for the first time in that meeting in 2007.

Cole Heilborn (26:27): And you guys never talked about that out of work or after he retired?

Jay Matthews (01:31): Yeah, so Sitka is a technical, outdoor and hunting apparel brand here in Bozeman, Montana. Just give you a backstory on how we got to where we are. It really started, I think the story goes back to a mountain hillside in Nevada when our founder, Jonathan Hart was out hunting elk in Nevada and just started with a problem. He wondered why hunting apparel was so inadequate at the time for the experiences and the expeditions that he was out on at the time. You had to look to the mountain sports brands to really get the fabric and material solutions to solve the problems that you face hunting out in these super dynamic environments. So it kind of just said, Hey, we can do this better. The mountain sports brands make an incredible product, some of those leaders in that space, but there's parts to the equation for a hunter that aren't necessarily factored into the development of those products. And so that's really what the genesis of the brand was, and that's really who we are today, is to service that hunting and outdoor minded consumer with technical apparel and gear solutions that solve problems that they'll face in the field or in their everyday life.

Cole Heilborn (02:47): And I got to imagine as a hunter, you're wading through, whether it's muck and mud or through trees and sticker bushes and all of that stuff. I love my puffy coat from one of those giant outdoor retailers, but it doesn't hold up in a bush full of thorns. It gets tattered.

The other one, I think that's uniquely a hunting problem is just the idea of concealment. It's how do you stay visually and audibly and olfactory concealed, which is a unique problem when you're trying to solve for moisture management and thermal regulation and protection from the elements. But you have to wrap all that in a package that's quiet, that is optically concealed and can suppress cent as well. So it it's a Rubik's cube of problem solving that has to go to making the whole thing work together and function as a system.

Cole Heilborn (03:57): Yeah, no kidding. So it sounds like from day one when you guys opened the doors, you've been really focused on trying to solve the problem that the hunter faces. I know one of the things that makes up who you guys are is that you guys are really dedicated to solving the problem versus just churning out another product. So everything that you guys do is designed to solve whatever problem you're trying to solve. So what does that philosophy look like? How does that affect the day to day?

content:
Jay Matthews (04:25): Yeah, this may be a long answer. No, it's a really good question. Yeah. The idea of being committed to solving a problem is really core to our ethos as a company, and really what that stems from is this really intimate understanding of the types of experiences that we're seeking to enable. So we firsthand understand the types of places you're going to go and the things you're going to see and the experiences you're going to have, be it on a expedition style hunt somewhere, or be it sitting in a blind with your young son or daughter in the backyard. Those are all really intimate and connected and integrated experiences (05:09): And any problem you face, be it, I'm too cold, I'm wet, my gear failed, my jacket's too loud, all of those things can distract from that experience. And what we believe is we really want to enable people to go experience these things that we love so much as hunters without any distractions. And so that's really what leads us to the idea of solving problems. And the company started with that ethos in mind, and that's still what's kind of alive in us today and really drives all the decision making from product design to supply chain to material selection, to the stories we tell. It's all about enabling experiences.

Cole Heilborn (05:49): Yeah, that's cool. And I got to imagine it's easy to say that, but it's much harder in actuality to practice that when you're looking at a decision and looking how much, for example, if you're looking at a product and you ask yourself, is this solving a problem? And then on the other hand, maybe it doesn't solve the problem, but you're looking at how much that can make the company, how do you guys make sure that you stick to that core when you're facing a difficult decision like that?

Jay Matthews (06:14): Yeah, I think the most important thing in making those decisions is focus on who we are and an eye towards the long-term view of the brand. Me too, products are pretty easy and there's opportunity out there for that. But I think you have a really short amount of time to earn the loyalty and the trust of a consumer. And if it doesn't do what you say it's going to do, then the consumer will figure you out in a really short amount of time. And so that's a driver. And I think the other key call out here is just having a building that is really all grounded in the same belief system, and it's an incredibly principled group of people here. And standing on that ethos of what value does this add, what problem does it solve? Why does it exist? And if you don't have a good answer to that question, the conversation kind of stops there.

Cole Heilborn (07:16): Yeah, well said. And you actually kind of opened up the next question that I wanted to ask, and it is the idea about brand trust. And I feel like there's a few companies out there that most people could probably look at and say, they've got my trust, I support them. I think you guys in your industry are one of those brands. How do you go about creating that trust and what does that mean to you guys when you look at the trust that your customers place in you?

content: Jay Matthews (07:46): Yeah, the idea of being a trusted resource to our consumer is something that we take a lot of pride in. I think the commitment to earning that trust comes from standing on the principle of that we guarantee that our products will do what they say we will do, they will do. And that really kind of takes you back through the design process of how do we actually get there? Starting with the idea of solving a problem and letting that drive the discussion and the development all the way through the end of the life cycle of the product is how you earn that trust. So we start and we say, what do we need? What do we need this garment to do? And that drives material selection. So if we don't have the textile, we need to solve the problem, we will scour the globe for it or we'll go make one. (08:35): We have a great example of a product that we launched recently where there's a lot of great installation fills out there, but we didn't have the perfect tool for the job that we were trying, wanting that garment to do. So we went and developed our own. The other part of trust is testing. So we have some incredible resources, be it lab or field testing, and we'll put our products through the ringer. I mean, some of the guys that we use for testing, we'll get a product back from them after six or eight months in the field. And it looks like a standard consumer had used that for years and years because we really put it through the ringer in the testing process. We want to make sure when that garment arrives in the consumer's hands that it's, we know we're confident, we've put it through the lab test, we've put it through the field test and knowing that it's going to do what we say it's going to do. (09:23): And then the other part of trust is the idea that we're not designing products to end up in a landfill. I think that's another important aspect of earning trust, is we believe in these things so much and durability and repairability all factor into the equation to extend the lifecycle of that product. And that's kind of core to our belief system too, in terms of appreciating the landscape that we get to recreate on and building from that ethos from the guarantee that it's going to do what we say it's going to do all the way through the end lifecycle of that product. Knowing that we factored all that in is kind of core to driving what we believe, how you earn a consumer's trust.

Cole Heilborn (10:08): And I think for folks who are listening, if you want to get a good idea of, I guess, how far you guys take your product design, there's a great film that I was just watching last week or the, what was it called, the Science of Sound, I think that you guys put out. Yeah, it is super cool and you should go watch the film, but it's this mini film, five minutes or so about, I don't remember what product you guys were designing, or actually, why don't you fill us in? You were the one behind it.

Jay Matthews (10:36): Yeah, totally. So I actually wasn't here at the time, but intimately understand the concept and the product specifically. The team did a great job illustrating the ethos of the brand through that product. It's called the fanatic jacket and bib. It's specifically designed for bow hunting white tails in cold weather environments. And if you step out in the white tail woods, everything sounds like a freight train. And so the whole concept of fanatic was chasing this idea of quiet and how do you deliver comfort and performance and wrapping it all in a package of making it as quiet as possible because if you make a sound that's unintended, you're going to miss your opportunity. And so what the team did there is they actually went, we built a sound chamber and we recorded what's the difference in decibels of the sound of a hunter drawing as bow in this jacket versus previous prototypes versus competitive products versus all of this. And we said that's the scientific proof of concept was actually seeing a significant difference in the sound that was generated by different materials and selecting materials based off that, because the whole idea was around solving the problem of quiet, hence the name science of sound. (11:59): So yeah, it's a bit obsessive in nature, but ultimately that's kind of what makes us who we are, is that constant questioning of how do we make this better? And the fanatics a great example of that.

Cole Heilborn (12:11): Absolutely. So as your role as the director of marketing, tell us a little about your day to day. How do you take these core principles and apply them into the things you oversee?

Jay Matthews (12:21): We're a relatively small organization, so my role as the director of marketing can mean a lot of different things just on a different day. I guess to kind of start with the linear process. On some days I'll be building with our product teams three to five year category strategic plans that are ultimately going to help us achieve the goals of the business. And then it's my job to work with those guys to identify the problems that we want to go solve and what products are going to allow us to do that. And then the geniuses in the product department, which I'm not a part of, obviously go and build these things and they do an incredible job of it. And then it's really my responsibility to coordinate the business around bringing these to market. So I'll partner with our brand and creative team to build an editorial plan and strategy around key product moments, and then ultimately, how do we communicate this and how do we make sure that this product gets the attention that it deserves, and how do we unpack who we are as a company through the effort in design and perspective that went into the development of this process and this product. (13:28): So yeah, end to end, it's working three to five years out on what those category plans look like, and then ultimately executing and driving through a well coordinated launch when it's time for it to actually hit the market. And that can be a three to five year process.

Cole Heilborn (13:45): Sure. Yeah. I got to imagine when you're putting that much detail into designing each product, it takes quite a bit of dev time, and that just takes time, I suppose

Jay Matthews (13:57): At the very minimum, I'd say two and a half years would be fast, just given all the steps that we have to go through to make sure that we're standing by what we say this thing's going to do. There's products in our line that have been at least an ideation for five to seven years from the time it's an idea in somebody's head to an actual physical prototype to actually hitting the market. It can be a really long process when it's that involved for sure.

Cole Heilborn (14:27): How does storytelling fit into what you guys do, whether that's through films, through photos, through blogs, how does that manifest?

Jay Matthews (14:38): Yeah, I mean, I would say that just we are storytellers what as marketers we do. I think a product is a story. I think something that's the story of a hunt or a trip is a story as well. So I would say that storytelling is everything that we do. So I would say it's the most important thing that we do for sure, and really permeates everything. If you're just saying, Hey, we have a new product, that's a story. What value does that product add and what ethos did it come from? That's all a way to unpack the ethos and belief system of your brand.

Cole Heilborn (15:23): Yeah, yeah. Okay. So I know I just asked you what role does storytelling play, but let's maybe dive a little deeper into storytelling in itself, because a lot of marketers today talk about storytelling and how valuable that is, but oftentimes we see stuff that comes out from a company and they might call it a story, and we might say, eh, I don't know. That doesn't really resonate, or that doesn't seem like a solid story for you guys. What is real storytelling?

Jay Matthews (15:52): I think this is me speaking as an individual, not as a representative of the brand, but to me what makes a great story is one purpose. So that's what makes a powerful brand is something that stands on purpose and intent, and that can be manifested through a product launch or through something that's completely product agnostic, is illustrating what drives people at your company or your brand to do great work. And I think you see that reflected in the behavior of consumers anymore is they're looking for brands with purpose. And so you'll illustrate that purpose in a variety of ways, and ultimately that's what in my opinion makes a great story, is you have the storyline of said creative itself, but there's something underneath that that you're attempting to illustrate. And I think that's ultimately what makes a great story is what's the underlying purpose that you're trying to convey? And if you can touch on that and you can illustrate that through people or through products or through stories, I think that's when you're onto something.

Cole Heilborn (17:09): Why do you think we're seeing such a rise in storytelling and advertising and marketing as a whole these days? I

Jay Matthews (17:17): Mean, I think people are out for experiences, and I think we have very conscious and conscientious consumers. I think the idea of conscientious consumerism is on the rise, and people want to know that they're affiliated with a brand or a company that they see as a responsible organization or that identifies with some of the same values.

Jay Matthews (17:41): And

Jay Matthews (17:41): I think that probably drives a lot of it is just a deeper level of connection with consumers and storytelling and experiential storytelling is a big part of that.

Cole Heilborn (17:55): Yeah, yeah. I know well said. We're going to shift gears a little bit. Tell me a little bit about your background. Was marketing something you were always into or how'd you get into this?

content: Jay Matthews (18:04): It's funny if you had asked me, I don't know, call it seven or eight years ago if I was going to be in marketing, I'd have looked at you like you were crazy. (18:12): It wasn't something that I had ever really pictured myself professionally moving into. It just happened due to the circumstances in the journey that my career kind of became. Prior to Sitka, I was at Nike and ended my time there as a brand manager. I guess to back up a little bit further and kind of illustrate how I got into that role, I had spent the first call it 22 years of my life dedicated to being the best team sport athlete that I could be. Football was my focus, it was my passion was I thought what I was put here to do, and it kind of became the thing that drove the decisions I made as an individual. And I woke up every morning with how am I going to make myself better today from training to nutrition, to preparation, to study and tape all of those things. (19:08): Football was a lifestyle, and so I had a really great opportunity when my career ended to go to a brand that I had been a fan of for a long time in Nike. I had studied kinesiology actually at Washington State University while I was playing football there. And the door opened for me to go to Nike and be a part of an organization called Spark. And what Spark was was essentially it was a performance brain of the company and what we were intended to do there was to study some of the best athletes in the world and then distill that into information that enables our consumers to be better. It was how do we learn from the best and then educate the rest of the population to be better athletes? (19:54): That's where my career at Nike started and do just some natural progressions of the organization. I moved into a grassroots marketing role in Nike football, and then from there kind of progressed into my marketing role as a North America brand manager there towards the last year and a half, two years of my time at Nike. And then the step to Sitka to back up a little bit really came from my progression out of football was kind of happening simultaneously.

Jay Matthews (18:04): As I grew in my roles at Nike, there was this parallel path of my lifestyle shifting a little bit. I mentioned that football was kind of like, it was my thing for so long, and when my football career ended, I got sat down at a desk and I was like, all right, I know I can't just drive a desk for a living. I love my job, but I need a little bit more with this competitive energy that I have. (20:48): And hunting was really the thing that filled that void. And there was a friend of mine who was in a similar trajectory at the time just in terms of figuring out what we were going to do life after football. And I saw that. I saw what hunting could be in terms of a holistic 365 day lifestyle from practicing and mastering the art of archery or training your body to go to places that other people aren't willing to go or have these really intimate experiences on the mountains and be able to take this meat home and feed your family. So there was kind this two paths where I was moving myself into a role in marketing and really diving into this lifestyle that is hunting. (21:33): Then those two crossed when I started beating the doors down at Sika Gear because it was a brand that on one hand was a marketing powerhouse and a really powerful storyteller, and I thought did an incredible job of illustrating the lifestyle that I was living. And so that's when I just started knocking on the door and said, Hey, I want to be a part of this thing. And after a period of time, somebody decided to give me a shot. So made the switch not too long ago. It's been a little over a year and a half, but yeah, it's been a really exciting journey. That's probably a longer answer than you were looking for. No, how it unfolded.

Cole Heilborn (22:09): That's great. How was that transition between you wake up every day and you're focused on football to then having to realize that football isn't your future? What was that transition like for you personally going through realizing the thing that you thought was everything turned out to not be what you thought it was?

Jay Matthews (22:33): Man, that is a tough question to answer. I'll tell you, it was a really challenging transition for me, and I think there's a lot of people who go through a similar transition. Maybe it was a pipe dream to think that I could have played professionally. In retrospect, I just wasn't good enough. But yeah, you commit yourself wholeheartedly to the process and the people and the pursuit of that goal, and then one day just kind of at the snap of your fingers, it's over. It was a pretty challenging journey and I just wandered around for a while trying to figure out what was next. Yeah, so a tough transition for sure, to kind of be unsure of what's next for you, especially when you've committed so much of your being to being great and more importantly to the people that you get to pursue that goal with. My teammates were one of my biggest motivators for sure, and to not have that environment and that community anymore, it's kind of a shock to your system. It's a little bit of culture shock for sure, to go from a locker room where it's a pretty intense environment and everybody's working towards the same thing, and you're kind of in the grind together to be out in the corporate world where there's parts of that same culture, but it's definitely a little bit of a culture shock to make that transition. It certainly was for me.

Cole Heilborn (24:05): Yeah, I can only imagine. That's got to be intense, especially you go from the football field where you're surrounded by tons of other people to the hunting field where oftentimes you're just out in the field by yourself.

Jay Matthews (24:19): We have a pretty great little community here at SITA and Bozeman holistically who are all kind of on the same path, and fortunately there's some guys that are as involved in the process and the journey as I am, and so we get to do that together. And so yeah, hunting is, I think largely an individual journey, but there's still a lot of the same kind of teamwork elements to it in some pursuits more than others. But I've definitely appreciated having some guys that we will get up and go train and go shoot our bows together and we're kind of all on the same path. So it's been really fun.

Cole Heilborn (25:01): So I feel like your opportunity to work at Nike is something that I think any person in the marketing world would kill for. And you obviously earned your place there because you put in the work in your good. If you could share one thing that you picked up at your time there, what would you share?

Jay Matthews (25:22): Yeah, I definitely picked up a lot. I think a lot of the things that I picked up there were probably intangibles is working with large teams when there's a lot of points of view in trying to navigate just the environment that it takes to be successful at that scale. I think maybe a little bit less of an intangible is just the importance of a passion for the purpose behind the brand. One of the things that's really special about that place in my opinion is everybody there bleeds the brand, and that's what's really cool about, one of the things that I really appreciated and learned and definitely took with me was just a competitive nature and being on offense all the time and really believing in the purpose of why you're doing what you're doing. That's super key is if you don't yourself believe the story that you're telling consumers, they'll sniff that out in no time. And that's one of the things I think that brand specifically does really well is you've got a large group of people there. It's a big company and it seems like everybody there is marching to the same beat in that regard. So that was definitely something I picked up and took with me. It was just the competitive nature of being in these spaces.

Cole Heilborn (26:46): Yeah, that's super awesome and it brings up another question that I'm really curious to hear your response on. When you have an organization that size, how do you make sure everyone is aligned with the direction of the Y?

Jay Matthews (27:01): It's funny. I think it's always challenging for sure, but what they did a really good job of and I think is a learning for everybody, is having a really focused and sharp point of view on who you are and why you are that way. And I have an old document that I actually still keep today. It's called the original Nike principles, and I can't remember the exact year that it was circulated, (27:29): But that document still circulates the office of those building or the hallways of those offices. And it's really cool to see that culture that was built in the early years of the brand still be alive today. And it's pretty fascinating that the brand's been able to scale at the degree that it has, and they've been able to keep the same kind of tenants alive in terms of serving athletes and being competitive and all of those things that are core to that brand. And it's true here at Ska too, right? I mentioned earlier that the brand started with a problem, and that's really what drives us here today from an evolved perspective and point of view about why we're solving problems, but the idea of being committed to that idea of solving a problem is still alive very much today. It probably is more so than it ever has been, which is great.

Cole Heilborn (28:21): Yeah. What drives you to do great work?

Jay Matthews (28:27): Yeah, I think one of the biggest things, if I'm just being completely honest, is just a natural, intrinsic competitive spirit. Call it a desire to win or call it fear of failure. I don't really know if I could put my finger on it to be honest, but that's definitely one of my biggest motivators. And the other one I'd say is the people around me. I'm learning that more and more about myself as I just navigate my career is when you see the vehicle in motion, it's clear that it's like an assembly line and every specific piece has to be functioning at its optimal state for the whole ecosystem to work as it's designed to work. And those brands are Diamondback Bikes, Raleigh Bicycles, red Line Bikes, high Bike and isip. The latter two are our electric bike brands.

content:
Cole Heilborn (01:54): Wow, so many bikes. Do you own all of them?

Jill Nazeer (01:58): No, and if I did, I'm pretty sure that actually my husband would be thrilled, but our neighbors would probably not be happy if we'd have bikes spilling out into the sidewalks.

Cole Heilborn (02:07): Fair enough, fair enough. So tell me a little bit about your role. What do you get to do? What do you get to play with as the director of marketing?

Jill Nazeer (02:15): I get to play with everything. So my role at Alta is, so I'm the marketing director, so I manage the marketing team and I say that loosely because we are three people, which is surprising for a lot of people when you see that it's five brands. So I manage a marketing manager and she works specifically on high bike and Isep our e-bike brands as well as a field marketing person who actually lives up in Bellingham up near you. And so I personally also manage the other three brands. So I am the brand manager for Diamondback, Raleigh and Redline.

Cole Heilborn (02:55): Okay, gotcha. It's a small team, but you guys do a lot of great work. I think what's really cool too is the brands that you guys work with have been around for a really long time. How long has Raleigh been around?

Jill Nazeer (03:07): Raleigh's been around since 1887. So for those who don't know the very brief history, it originally started in the uk, but Raleigh USA has obviously been around for a very long time. So it's a lot of fun and very different from the electric bike brands. It's a perfect compromise to have this brand that has over 130 years of history and a history in the Tour de France. And so a lot of people know Raleigh from its heritage.

Cole Heilborn (03:34): One of the things that I find really fascinating about your job is just you're a small team, yet you manage five different and very distinct brands. I have a few questions about that idea, but I think the thing that I want to try to talk about is brand differentiation and how you manage all of those. What makes them different and how do you guys organize all of them? I guess let's start there.

content: Jill Nazeer (03:58): Yeah, that's a great question. So as far as what makes them different, these brands, again, some of them have had a very long history and they've been different. No brand I think has ever really stayed true to its one to one thing, especially with bikes which are constantly evolving and there's new technology, the brands have to evolve with that. So as far as separating out the brands, we have put a lot of work into making sure they are all different. I mean, in the end, we all sell bikes and although the bikes are different and the product is different and they have a different end use, it's still a bike. And so you have to think, okay, well how can you possibly make that look different five different ways? So especially when I started, which was just a couple of years ago, we really sat down and we put a lot of work into how are all of these brands different? For some it's completely based on product. For instance, high Bike is an electric mountain bike brand. That's what it is. I zip is kind of more of like a California Cruiser e-bike brand. Those brands are not going to be confused from a product standpoint. (05:13): So when my colleague Annie came on, she was tasked with making them look stylistically different and the marketing plans were different. And then for the non-electric bike brands, it's almost a little bit more challenging because these brands have had a lot of overlap. Raleigh has some mountain bikes and Diamondback is known as a mountain bike brand, but also had some road bikes and Diamondback was formally A BMX brand and Redline now has BMX. So you do can't ignore a brand's heritage, but you do want people to know that these are separate distinct brands. So we put a lot of work into it. And where we've shaken out is redline is BMX, people know the history, it's been around since the seventies, so a lot of people know the race history of Red Line. For Diamondback, it's been Road and Mountain bike and Gravel and we focus a lot on, we call it the dirt story, it's gravel and it's mountain, but we put a lot of work into Diamondback placing itself as it's kind of like your friend on the trail. (06:28): We're not the highest end mountain bike brand. We're also offering a variety of price points. We have low price point bikes and mid and high, so we try to make riding a lot more accessible. So we always say we're your buddy at the end of a trail that you high five and you have a go have a beer with. So that's where we've really positioned Diamondback. We want it to be a community feel. We don't just want to sell a bike and never see anybody ever again. And then for Raleigh it's a lot more diverse. We have tons of product in Raleigh and it's a lot more of that history and that heritage of the Raleigh fan. We have people that have been riding Raleigh their whole lives. It's definitely a family brand and stylistically it's fun and light and bright. And so we put a lot of work, both the marketing managers and the design team into how those brands are going to look and feel different when we talk to people.

content: Jill Nazeer (07:56): That's a fantastic question and it's an interesting one. And I will say it's interesting not just from the consumer standpoint and how you look externally, but it's an internal thing that we have to deal with first. Our company is very small. People would be shocked to know that there's only about 40 people that currently work at Alta Cycling and that's everything. So 40 people managing five brands. So first of all, think about it that way, that having 40 people that can think five different ways (08:34): Is a truly unique situation. I've worked at brands or at companies where every brand is siloed and every brand has its own team, and those teams do not overlap because they compete with each other. And that's not how it is at Ulta. We all work together. And so the first challenge is kind of what we were talking about earlier where you're selling a bike and how can you make it look five ways of different? So then you have the team of people that are all also trying to think five different ways that adds another level of complication to it. And then we look at the people that are all putting this all together. And someone like myself has been with the company for a couple of years, but my creative director for instance, has been with the company for 15 years. And it's fantastic to have that mix of someone who's a little bit more new and maybe has a fresh perspective and someone who's been with the company for a very long time and can speak to the history and the how's and the why's so we can learn from the successes and the mistakes. (09:44): And then even above and beyond that, we have people who have been in some ways involved with these brands for their entire lives. There were probably red line riders when they were kids or their first bike was a Diamondback or whatever. So you have everyone's personal passion that also adds in this level of complication. So I'll tell you that even internally, we all sit down and when we talk about what is the new product, we are a product driven company. And then we also talk about do we want to do some kind of heritage throwback bike?

Jill Nazeer (07:56): (10:18): Do we want to take a step back in history and intentionally to speak to those people who know our history? And then there's always an internal debate in that of like, is it right to take a step back in time? Do we only want to move forward? Are we moving forward so fast that maybe our consumer won't keep up with that speed? It's always these different answers. And so it's always a debate, and I honestly think that our product team along with us, they get feedback from everybody does a really great job at which brands can move forward faster. For instance, the Diamondback consumer, they're very knowledgeable about product. They know what the newest spec is, they know what they want. If we don't have a bike that they want, they have no problem telling us. And we listen. I really do tell the product team the feedback we get from the consumer and they're out there talking to people every day, listening to them. So for Diamondback, it makes a little more sense to push technology further and faster. For a brand like Redline, people really want their old school BMX race bike. So it's a great and really complicated question because you don't want to alienate the people that have loved you their whole lives, but you also do of course have to move forward. So a lot of it is based on making sure you're offering a little bit of something for everyone without making it look like you are just catering to them. You want to make it look intentional. (11:59): When Raleigh had a whole heritage line a few years ago, and that was a conscious decision to say, Raleigh, this year is going to make this product and we're going to speak to our heritage and celebrate it. And so I think that as long as you're putting that message out, people get excited about it and I think the consumer enjoys being along that ride with us.

Jill Nazeer (12:22): I got a lot of good bike puns. We'll see how long this keeps going for.
