content: Jill Nazeer (13:01): I'd say the business answer to it is there's definitely a fine line between a halo effect where one brand will help lend some light to the others and cannibalization of when one brand's sucking up the sales of another. And I think it's completely okay to walk that line, but I think that when you see that a brand is starting to cannibalize way too much, that's when you have to make some hard decisions. And certainly that's happened and that's why brands change and that's why some brands disappear. And that's why sometimes it's the product that changes. And from a business standpoint, sometimes companies make that decision in different ways. For us, right now, we make that decision based on product. We have different products for different brands and that's how we keep them separated. But in the past, there was a time when they alter their distribution based on the brand. So one brand might only be in a retail shop and one brand might only be sold online, and they thought that was the solution to too many brands. And I think that the retail landscape has changed so quickly in the last, even just the last five years, that it's difficult for companies to look at the different brands they offer and try to make a channel strategy based on it because frankly now everybody sells almost everywhere. So that's how we are. We consider ourselves an omnichannel company. So from the business side of things, we want to support the local retailers, we want to support online sellers, and we sell direct (14:49): And with all five brands. So then the next question is, well, the next question was how do you separate the brands and when is it too much? Well, that's why now we have differentiation in product. So (15:03): That's why for right now, Diamondback doesn't sell BMX redline does. I'm not going to say that there won't ever be overlap in product, but certainly sometimes you can separate it as much as you want. And then from the marketing standpoint, and this is just from my seat, is that sometimes I know it's a little too much. When you start to feel yourself falling down that hole of almost being robotic, we laugh about it a little bit. So I manage three different brands that have three very different voices, and I think a lot of people are surprised when they learn that it's me that's the one behind all of those voices. It makes me sound a little bit psychotic sometimes, but I find at times, for instance, right before a Black Friday sale, when I have 50 pieces of marketing copy that I have to write, and you start feeling this roboticness of sounding like a used car salesman, like sale or best sale ever, biggest sale of the year, come get your bike When you know that you yourself are starting to feel robotic and when it's not really you and how you would speak as that brand, that that's when it's a problem. (16:24): And so that is why it's so great sometimes to either take a step back and examine what you're really doing and what the goals of that brand are, or you look and you say, okay, maybe this is too much for this brand, and then you reevaluate what your plans are.

What would you say to someone who's trying to, they figured out the first part, now they're trying to figure out how does media fit into this?

Jill Nazeer (16:59): That's a really good question. So depends on if it's traditional media or paid media, which we do both. Traditional media is a little easier. There are electric bike specific publications that the e-bikes would be in or something like a bicycling magazine that does a really great job of covering every kind of bike. So that's something that Raleigh might be interested in or Isaac. Then for a brand like Diamondback, which is a little bit more tech and a little bit more dirt focused, that's when you go to the media that is also a little bit more tech and dirt focused things that help grow your community that are already there. And then from the digital media perspective, it is interesting. There's again been different iterations and different theories on should every brand get to be in digital media because then aren't we cannibalizing our own buy and aren't we competing with ourselves? And

Jill Nazeer (18:04): Is why some companies keep their different brands on separate teams so they don't risk cannibalization. It's almost like competition within your own company to see who can do better. For us. I'm kind of glad we don't do that. I would rather all of us work together so we all know what the other one is doing. So I'd rather just all play nice in the sandbox together. So we luckily have a really great buying team that helps us with this, but it is making sure that you're walking that delicate balance between addressing your existing community. Again, for Diamondback, it would be like somebody who might already be interested in mountain biking, but especially for bikes, you also have to grow the community. Buying a bike is something that most people would only do maybe a couple of times in their life, and it's an expensive purchase. It can be a very emotional purchase for people, and you kind of have to grow the consumer base, otherwise there's too many bike brands you would flat out just run out of people. So the media part of it is challenging because you don't want to ignore your existing community, but you absolutely have to grow the community as well.

Cole Heilborn (19:21): Yeah, interesting. Okay, cool. So let's change gears a little bit and let's talk more about your background. How did you end up here?

Jill Nazeer (19:30): So I've had kind of a roundabout way of getting here. So right after, so in college I was an art major and I was an absolutely terrible studio artist. It is frankly shocking that I graduated with a degree in art. Any designer that I've ever worked with or any creative I've ever worked with laughs when I tell them I was an art major. So it's an embarrassment to their profession. So I started out doing that and then I got a master's degree in humanities actually focusing in art history, which obviously my job has nothing to do with right now, but that's okay.

Cole Heilborn (20:11): I mean, you guys work with 120 year old brand that has history, right? That's true.

I laugh because my art program was a very conceptual art program, so I laugh that being a bad artist made me a better marketer because it made me think a little bit more creatively even though the art itself wasn't that great. So from there, I am from Chicago originally, and so if you're an art major and you live in Chicago, basically you work at an ad agency, that's what everyone thinks that you should do. This was the age when Mad Men was very big, so that was a natural next step. And I worked at a massive ad agency in Chicago on the MillerCoors account. And so that's my first step into managing a lot of brands at once. MillerCoors owns way more brands than people even realize, and so it takes a lot of multitasking to work on all of those. (21:13): And from working at this massive ad agency, I decided that I need a karmic balance in my life. And I totally switched gears and went to go work at a nonprofit and I worked at the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. They have a campaign, it's a revenue program for them called Team in Training. At the time, it was the world's largest endurance training fundraising program. So essentially we had coaches and training programs and we would train you for some massive endurance event like the Chicago Marathon or the Chicago Triathlon, and in exchange you would fundraise for the organization. (21:57): So although I was a fundraiser, it really was my experience with managing events and customer service because you're just managing a lot of people and grassroots marketing, because it's a nonprofit and every dollar you make needs to go to the mission. So you really have to get creative and make sure that you don't mind getting a little bit grassroots trying to get marketing done. So that was truly a lesson in how to do a lot with nothing. From there, I took a role as an account marketing rep for the North Face's Sales Agency. So at the time, the North Face didn't have any internal salespeople, it was all external agencies. So I supported them essentially as a field marketer. So any of the non-North Face stores, like small independent retailers and bigger stores like Dander Mountain and Shields and all those, I would work on the marketing for them. So I was employed by an agency, but worked a lot with the North Face's marketing team, and that was awesome. The North Face is just such a cool, fun brand, and they're so far ahead of technology and their teams are so creative. It was a lot of fun to get insight into a brand and how it works. (23:18): Even though I was in the field, the North Face makes you feel very a part of their entire family. And so that was my first foray into that. And then in 2016, we moved to Seattle. So from there I worked at K two Sports for a little bit, and I managed two of their Snowshoe brands, Atlas and Tubs, as well as their Nordic brand, which is Modus. So that was three brands all by myself. I was basically a one person marketing team. So that in itself was also a lesson. And then from there went to my role now, which originally was at a company called Excel North America, but now Ulta cycling.

Cole Heilborn (23:59): Gotcha. If there's one thing that you've picked up in your career career that you take with you or you apply to the next day, is there anything that comes to mind?

Jill Nazeer (24:11): Yeah, I mean, I would say this is if I was going to give my niece and nephew advice in life, it would be, and I say this jokingly, that it's totally okay and sometimes actually better to not have a clear path. Obviously, I've kind of done a little bit of everything that all led me to my role now, but I truly believe that not knowing exactly what I was going to do or what was going on has actually made me a better marketer. (24:43): I think that having the ability to have been in all these different roles in different kinds of companies and managing multiple brands simultaneously really teaches you how to take a step further back and see a bigger picture. I think that if I had only been a brand manager on a single brand my entire life, I would've only seen that. I would've only seen that little piece. And I think that it's actually a benefit to work in different places and do all these different things because it really teaches you how to use an outsider's perspective to solve problems. And my dad would probably laugh at that because our parents were all a generation where they stayed in a job for 45 years, and if you saw six jobs on someone's resume, you thought,

Cole Heilborn (25:32): What's wrong with them?

Jill Nazeer (25:33): Exactly. Like, oh my God, they can't make a commitment to save their life. So I'm so grateful that now that's no longer the mentality that now it's actually a benefit to have people that come from totally different backgrounds to solve these

(26:21): And from an industry standpoint, I think actually Casey might've mentioned this, and I totally agreed, and when you interviewed him on your podcast, that I do hope that the industry as a whole can kind of take a step back and look at what they've done in the past, and that's great, and use that as a reference, but to keep pushing forward into new things and not always rely on the old way of thinking. Just how do we make sure that this industry can continue to grow and support its future generations, and that might be a new and different solution that no one's ever thought of before.

Welcome to Brand Story. My name is Cole Holborn, and today I'm sitting down with Brenna Rosenthal, the owner of Great Escape Media. Brenda, how are you doing?

Brennah Rosenthal (00:39): Good, how are you?

Cole Heilborn (00:41): Fantastic. It's awesome to have you on the show.

Brennah Rosenthal (00:49): I am currently located in Denver, Colorado, in the guest bedroom of my house.

Cole Heilborn (00:56): Well, I have to give a quick shout out to Casey over at Raven for introducing us. He is a great guy, and it sounds like you guys have known each other for a long time. I've only just had the pleasure of getting to know him over the last month or so, but he's how we got connected, right?

Casey's a great guy with a lot of great personality and a great personal story, but anyways, Brenna, let's chat about who are you guys? What does Great Escape Media? What do you guys do?

show_notes_excerpt: Brennah lives in Denver, Colorado, and runs Great Escape Media. Focused on providing in-house quality production and strategy resources, she fills the need between large agencies and the smaller brands that don't need a giant working on their behalf. The video production world has gone through a tumultuous change over the last 10 years. Through advances in technology and low barriers to equipment, there has been a rise of one man, two-man shops that are producing amazing work. In this episode,…

content:
Brennah Rosenthal (01:49): Sure. So Great Escape Media is a company that I started about two and a half years ago that focuses on creative content, strategy and production, as well as merging the two of those together. So for the confusion that just caused for everyone, creative content strategy is basically taking a brand or company and looking at how they can present content to their audience through things like social media, YouTube, and their website and email campaigns in a creative way. So through imagery, video and creative storytelling. And then on the production side of things, we focus on basically taking that strategy and stuff and bringing it to life through both photo and video production.

Cole Heilborn (02:35): Yeah, absolutely. What was the biggest problem that you noticed and I guess that you're trying to solve by jumping out on your own and starting your own company?

Brennah Rosenthal (02:43): Yeah, I think one of the big things is that there's these huge agencies that exist and then these brands that have in-house marketing and content people that might not have the resources that some of these bigger brands have. So I think one of the problems I was trying to fix was kind of better helping these brands and companies tell their stories without the muddied Bs, I guess, of a huge agency where they're a million people in a room, a million a opinions, and then also added dollar amount that comes along with using an advertising agency. My whole, I guess, shtick with Great Escape Media is to act more of a friend and a connection versus this big scary agency that a lot of, they do really, really great work, but a lot of the brands today just don't need that robust of a system and are looking for someone they can feel a little bit more personally connected to work on these projects that they're going to get way better and more concentrated work out of versus working with a giant company. So

Cole Heilborn (03:53): For sure,

Brennah Rosenthal (03:54): I like to tell all my clients that they can pick up the phone and call me, whether it's having a bad day or they need help with a problem.

Brennah Rosenthal (04:12): Yeah, I mean I love working with smaller startup brands that are trying to get their company off the ground, whether that be with a photo or video shoot or with content strategy. But other times too, I love working with bigger brands on productions to make it feel like this production isn't this big corporate structure, that they have more of a personal connection with the producer that they're working with to have onset, that they can feel like they have someone to lean on.

Cole Heilborn (04:41): And how long have you been doing Great Escape Media?

Brennah Rosenthal (04:44): About two and a half years. So I've always freelanced in addition to the full-time jobs that I had before, but great escape's been a full-time thing for about two and a half years.

Cole Heilborn (04:52): Okay, gotcha. The advertising marketing world is definitely an interesting place, and I'm curious if you can kind of speak to just the things that you've observed over your time in the industry because there seems to be the rise of the small production shops or the small strategy shops. You're one of them, our company's one of them. Where and when did all of these small companies come forth and what's the opportunity?

Brennah Rosenthal (05:16): Yeah, I mean I think it's an interesting point and one of the main reasons I think is because of that giant dollar amount that comes along with some of these huge advertising agencies. It's like it's paying for a premium, which you do get premium services a lot of the time, but I think nowadays with the cost of entry for advertising itself with Facebook and social media is so much lower than it used to be where you had to pay hundreds of thousands if not millions of dollars to get a TV ad spot. Whereas now you can put a hundred dollars behind a social media ad with a video that was created through a smaller production company and get just as many eyes on it if not more, and get a way more targeted audience for it versus broadcasting a huge commercial to everyone that's watching the news that night and maybe that person's not into Nike and they don't do fitness and they sit on their couch and eat snacks all day. (06:13): So I think that there's been, because of that change with the way that advertising is running now, these companies I guess don't feel like they need to pay that giant premium with these agencies and they would rather work with someone that is going to give their company this full undivided attention for without that premium cost associated with it. It's the same thing that's happening with direct to consumer brands. I would say it's a very similar kind of crossover where you are seeing these brands that are launching in a direct to consumer way because of the fact that you don't need these bigger retail stores to showcase a product. It's very similar in the way that you don't need to pay this extra money for a really good product or service. Yeah,

Cole Heilborn (07:00): No, interesting. So with you, your tagline being, but you're not really in-house, the experience been for your clients. Do they like that setup? How does that provide value to them further than just being a contractor?

Cole Heilborn (08:02): I got to imagine for your clients there's a lot of value and knowing that they have someone they can trust who knows their brand, but also has that outside perspective that you can bring to the table if they're trying to solve something that they're not sure how to approach.

So having experience with one client will help then better even another one of my clients. So going through, for instance, running an ad that doesn't do as well for a certain brand, then I'll have that knowledge to bring to another one of my clients that says, Hey, one of my clients is struggling with this business and this, I think we should adjust this. Just having those experience that kind of cross over that I think are really beneficial to having multiple clients. But there is that, I'm like, yeah, it's hard to have this many different clients that I'm working on from different industries, but at the same time, it is beneficial to be able to have that crossover and learn from each different one to then better all of the clients as a whole.

Cole Heilborn (09:13): Yeah. Do you think that as you look forward, do you think we'll see more and more of the small shop style popping up? And if so, what does that do to the landscape for options or the ad agency or the ad industry? Excuse me.

I think I could find the resources to do it, but that'd be something where I would call someone that I know that works at a bigger agency that says, Hey, can we partner with so-and-so agency to bring this production to life? So I think it's almost the emerging, I don't know that there's day and night, they're just working completely separately, but the merging of these agencies with maybe smaller production shops. What's the journey been for you?

So if just them shearly having that thought in their head means that they have some sort of resilience or strength to do that kind of thing, versus just someone that's like, I'm comfortable in this corporate job, I would never suggest someone that has that thought process to start their own business. So I think basically what happened is I was in a job for three and a half years that I loved, but always felt the need to live out this dream that I had of starting my own business or being off on my own. So what I did from there is I talked to probably 10 to 15 different people that were freelancers or self-employed or had started their own companies to be like, what do you think I should do? (13:11): I needed to hear that from 10 to 15 people to be like, oh, you can do this. And that's something that I hope I provide to people that ask me the same question that the confidence instilled to say, Hey, you can do this, and if it doesn't work for some reason, you'll have fallback. You could always apply to another job. It might take a little bit to get, but you're not going to just be buried in the ground with no work. So that helped me a lot. Like the people that surrounded me that told me that I could do it, and then also shared their stories with me about how they quit their job, they filed their business name, started their own business. That gave me the confidence to say, Hey, I can do it myself too. I also had the support of my family as well. (13:55): My mom and dad are both business owners too, had the support of them to say, Hey, this is how you have to do these things. You don't know, they don't teach you that in school. They don't teach you how to start your own business in school when you have an advertising photography degree. So I think that the support system around me was huge in that. And then there was one instance at work that just clicked for me one day and I was like, I'm going to quit and do this. I registered a business name, got all my tax paperwork done and created a very mediocre logo, which is still in play, but I'm having it redone right now to get my business off the ground. And from there, what I did is I sent my entire network and email that said, Hey, I am doing this. This is what I'm focusing my time and energy on. I'm super passionate about it. These are the services I can offer. If you or anyone would be interested hit up. And since I sent that email about two and a half years ago, I haven't done a lick of marketing for great Escape media. All of my business has come to me through word of mouth or recommendation.

There's obviously platforms like LinkedIn that are actually super helpful if you're able to build that out and start adding people and are not afraid to connect and have conversations with people that are strangers. Instagram's another one of those too, that if you are projecting out that this is what you're doing, a lot of the people aren't afraid to get a direct message on Instagram as like a, Hey, can you get a cup of coffee with me? So I always tell people like that, if you look up to someone or want to connect with them, just ask to get a cup of coffee with them. A lot of people are going to say yes to that. And I make it a point to say yes to everyone who asks me to do that because I did it to so many people leading up to where I am today, that those conversations, even if sometimes they might feel like they take a chunk out of your day that's not worth it, they are always worth it for both parties. (16:25): So there's something to be learned from those people that want the advice of starting off on their own, and also for them to learn from the people that are off on their own. So I think those are two of the hugest things is just reaching out to people to connect. And then sometimes it's a means of taking jobs or projects that are a little bit smaller than you might want to start off with so that you can meet those people and create those network and show how hardworking you are. Networking events are always really awkward, but typically something will come out of it. I always tell people it's like, yeah, my strategy for those is I just post up at an empty table and wait for people to come to me, which might not be the best thing in the world, but it always works.

The other one is, are you going to meet someone there that is going to help with upgrading your network or future work and is it a good portfolio builder? So if it doesn't check two of the three of those boxes, probably say no to it. And that's kind of how we go through things in the office too. If we're getting proposals from clients that are like, oh, the money's really bad, but this is a super cool project, it'd be great for my portfolio, and this is something that could turn into a bigger project because of that, take it if it's maybe something that's not that exciting to work about, but that dollar sign's really good, take it. (11:29): And for me, I can relate that to snowmobiling. I bought a snowmobile many years ago. I still have my snowmobile, and I envisioned myself loving snowmobiling. If it's just you and you're the one guiding the conversations, you're the one guiding the work. It definitely, when you open up to collaboration, it's like, okay, do our core values as a company, are they inclusive enough for everyone at this company? Are they inclusive enough for everyone that we work with? And then it becomes so much more about me as an individual and more about wheelie as a brand. And so for me, sticking to my core values really has been interesting. And because I started the business when I was 22, a 22-year-old punk kid with a snowboard, and now I am a woman, I find more depth in certain things than I used to be honest, I'm not nearly as shallow and ridiculous as I was when I was 22. I've evolved a lot as a person, and so being able to not identify with, I have a pretty irreverent brand. Wheelie is kind of, we throw down, we charge hard, everybody's sending things. It's a pretty irreverent brand. I'm really proud of it. Also though, for me, there's this huge side of me as a woman, I'm soft and gentle and thoughtful and super, super introverted. This podcast dives deep with leaders of the outdoor marketing industry as they discuss the gritty details of their work, personal challenges, and latest adventures. Becky Marcelliano (00:57): You know, it is it is a beautiful place. I moved here to start working at Solomon and really wasn't sure quite what to expect, but it's right nestled in the mountains, just thirty miles or so north of Salt Lake City. We have, you know, a lot of a lot of podiums and Olympics in our in our historic timeline, like all of that stuff. But what that has done from a consumer level for a long time, we we were appealing to that that pinnacle athlete as well. And while that's a really an important consumer to to to bring into the brand and to to build loyalty with, at this point in our, in our evolution as a brand, we're really looking to, to branch out from that and also be a lot more inclusive and appealing to somebody that's maybe not at that pinnacle athletic level in their lives. so that's where core and more comes from. It's like I said, really just internal language that speaks to we have always been really core and like nailed that, but now we're going to continue that, but also branch out into, into, into more, right? And that might be the urbanite, that might be the newer to the outdoors person. that might be, that still might, you know, might be the the person that's bagging 14ers on the weekend and and everything in between. So that's really where the core and more concept is coming into play. One campaign that has really brought that concept to life is our women's campaign. We call it Solomon WMN. And that was launched in spring of 2019.

It was my first desk job ever in my life and You know, here I am entering the outdoor industry like at a desk. I was like, Am I doing it wrong? content: Becky Marcelliano (15:44): Yeah, so something that I have struggled with for the last twelve or so years of my life is chronic illness. And really it's been a journey of discovery and I'm still not sure I fully n have all the answers as to what's going on in my body. but I I have mold illness, which essentially means that my body doesn't know how to clear mold out of the system and so it can cause some chronic inflammation. And over time, when your body is is tripped up by a lot of information like that, it can it can be more likely to cause autoimmunity. So I also have Hashimoto's and Shogrin syndrome, which are two autoimmune diseases that all kind of spiral together. So it's it's really as as hard as it's been and as annoying as that's been over time to try to figure that out and deal with symptoms that have come in all sorts of strange ways, such as a lot of joint pain and fatigue and inability to to exercise just due to like a complete kind of system crashdown, rashes and just lots of strange things over the years, but it really has taught me so much about the long-term game of perseverance and patience. And I still necessarily wouldn't call myself a patient person because I'm pretty darn driven, but I do think it's really helped me understand just how to sit tight. And keep trucking and to to really see the benefit of the long haul. I think a lot of people sometimes give up somewhere in the middle of that and and therefore don't get to their long-term goals and achievements. But I think working with chronic illness, unfortunately, has really helped show me the value of that skill set. so it's something that I'm I'm thankful for. But Yeah, I mean, how it's integrated into my career. Thankfully, I've never been in such dire straits health wise that I have missed work or anything. It's it's more just chronic symptoms that are more in the annoying realm than the debilitating realm. So again, super grateful for that. But that's not to say that it hasn't been really emotionally and mentally exhausting as well. And yeah, it's definitely. Definitely impacted me in in a lot of ways. It also, interestingly, there's been a lot of year, there was a few years there where I really couldn't exercise much. I was just so tired. And like the one thing that I could do was sit at my desk. And so it it kind of caused this blessing and curse of working so much that I accomplished amazing things in my career during those years, I would say, but it also caused a a pretty unsustainable work-life balance. So you know, again, pros and cons. I think it's we have to work with what we what we have and try to keep keep all of the important things in life on a teeter. But anyway, my health journey has definitely caused some some things that I didn't expect in my in my career in strange ways. Yeah.

So I think the difference between a Me Too and a brand that really does have a story to tell is exactly that story piece. Clean Canteen for example, has the family owned side of things as well as all the third party certifications that we use to keep ourselves on track with our brand mission. (08:59): And then we're also a certified B Corp. So basically that means we meet high standards of social and environmental transparency and performance. So I think a story like that is sort of the root of authenticity, and I think without that piece, you can't create content as a brand that really truly is authentic. Then I think also there's the product side of things. So a lot of the brands that I've worked for have sort of existed in a very specialized niche. So I worked for a company called Mont Bell early on in my career, and they're a manufacturer in the ultralight backpacking space. So they create ultralight jackets, ultralight shelters, that kind of thing. So very specific products that are filling a specific use that are designed by people that have a very specialized knowledge in that world that's kind of driven by experience. So I think that kind of concept versus a brand that is just coming in and saying, Hey, here's another object that may look cool but doesn't really have this use knowledge behind it or this sort of business for good piece to it, I think that's where things become problematic.

We've already sort of seen that to a pretty large extent in the last few years. I think that's only going to amplify, and I think that's just going to increase the need for this authentic content, and I think the consumer is going to even demand that more so than they have in the past. I think it's on the technical side of things like content creation has become, I don't want to say easier than it ever has been because it's an incredible art and skill, but it's more accessible. I think equipment is cheaper. There's more people out there doing it. The whole back to the influencer piece, there's people who are legitimately making a living as sort of a brand ambassador or influencer. So I think that whole sector is going to ramp up and I see things only getting bigger in terms of demand for that type of content.

Ian McWilliams (17:14): So looking at that then, how do you guys react to that idea or that future?

So one of my first jobs in the industry was working for a small mom and pop gear shop in downtown San Francisco right on Market Street, no longer around unfortunately, but worked there for quite a few years and have some fond and not so fond memories of cleaning out rental tents and doing the grunt work and never really imagined that that would take me to the brand side of things and didn't really have that foresight that that was an option when I was doing that. And then my day would look like, oh, the phone would ring. I'd take that dealer workbook and reference it while I was selling the product to a dealer on the phone, and then go out to the warehouse and package that order and ship it off, and then a couple months down the road, go to a retailer and talk to that dealer in person.

Ian Mathias (00:02): Welcome to the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. My name is Cole Helebo and I'll be your host today. This podcast dives deep with leaders of the outdoor marketing industry as they discuss the gritty details of their work, personal challenges and latest adventures, whether you're standing in the lift line, shuttling the fresh loam, or cracking a local beer. I hope you enjoyed today's episode. This is the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. This episode is produced by Porch Line Productions, an outdoor, commercial and film production company based in the Pacific Northwest. Let's make waves. Welcome to the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Ian Mathias, the director of Marketing Creative over at Strava. Ian, how are you?

Cole Heilborn (00:46): I'm good. It's a pleasure to talk to you.

Ian Mathias (00:49): Yeah. Where are you joining us from today?

Cole Heilborn (00:51): My home office, like everyone else in San Francisco. In Richmond, San Francisco. Yeah, just chopping wood at home.

Ian Mathias (01:01): I like it. So tell us a little bit about Strava. What do you do?

Cole Heilborn (01:04): Strava is the number one app for runners and cyclists. We are a social network training log and a tracking app for people who love to run and ride. So basically you can record your run or your ride with Strava. Then afterward, kind of geek out on the details, analyze your ride, compete against your friends, and then also the way that we are, whereas social networks, so you can post into the feed with your activity and then check out your friends' rides, your friends' runs, and leave comments, stuff like that.

Ian Mathias (01:38): Make sure your friends aren't beating you in those segments or taking those kms. Right?

Cole Heilborn (01:43): Yeah. If that's how you want to use Java, that's great. It's different for everybody, but yeah, a lot of people do love to compete with each other on segments around town.

Ian Mathias (01:52): Yeah, no, it's great. The app is used worldwide, right? I mean, I think almost everyone I know who runs recycles has used it or does use it.

Cole Heilborn (02:00): I'm glad to hear that. Thank you. Yes, we've been very fortunate and grown a lot, especially in the last five years. We have about 60 million athletes all over the world. The US is our largest market, but actually about 80% of our athletes are outside of the us, particularly concentrated in Western Europe, especially the uk, and also a really, really big community down in Brazil. But yeah, we're everywhere. Very lucky to say, and it's just been such a pleasure and a privilege to get to work with athletes all over the world.

Ian Mathias (02:36): Yeah. How do you get to do that in your job? What do you get to work with?

Cole Heilborn (02:40): I'm responsible for the marketing team's creative output. I get to work with a bunch of amazing writers, designers, producers, marketers to basically make our marketing and help shape our brand. So as it pertains to getting to interface with our athletes, whenever we have videos to shoot, whenever we have campaigns to make, we really want to be representative not only of the athletes that are on the platform, but the athletes that we want to be on the platform the way we wish sport looks. So we're always looking to meet diverse, interesting, out there people, and that has taken me on shoots all over the world. And also just the beauty of the internet. You can talk to someone pretty much anywhere whenever you want. So yeah, that global nature has just made this a really particularly fun job and has really stretched my understanding of what it means to be a cyclist, what it means to be a runner or an athlete in general. It's different no matter where you are,

Ian Mathias (03:38): And I think that's cool too. You probably have a pretty unique perspective on athletes worldwide and through cultures and language, people everywhere run or if they have a bike cycle and they're kind of these cross culture methods of, I guess, experience that everyone gets to partake in. That's got to be really cool.

content: Cole Heilborn (05:33): Sure. Yeah, I'll do my best to speak for the entirety of social media. I'm not working at a social network myself, but there's certainly all different kinds, and I think it is fair to classify Strava as one if the very basic material parts of a social network are a feed where you can post comment, give, like stuff like that, and that's certainly a part of the Strava experience. I think what makes us different is two things. One, I think that Strava is a participant network. And what I mean by that is if you want to be active on Strava, you kind of have to post content. And that's meaningfully different from a lot of other social networks. Most networks actually have users that are far more interested in watching other or looking, consuming other content than making content themselves. It's kind of like a lurker or a voyeur network. (06:29): And the vast majority of situations like on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, all that, and I'm not here to say that's bad, but I have noticed an important difference with what happens on Strava is basically the way that you post on Strava is to upload a run ride. The activity is the central way to participate on our network. And in doing so, I really believe that it creates a sense of shared vulnerability that is missing in other networks. If you follow me on Strava, you are going to see more than just the destination of wherever I'm going. You're going to see the journey, you're going to see the ride I did the other day where I was kind of hungover and feeling like total crap and the run where actually I had to stop in the middle and find a bathroom or just those days that are just normal, just devastatingly normal. (07:27): And we all share that together. We all kind of upload these runs and rides together. And in doing so, I think it just chills everybody out that how can I have anything to say about your pace if the day before I posted a run that was even slower, and conversely, I can really share the excitement of seeing you finish your first marathon or seeing you win your first race on your bike or whatever experience that you get excited about.

content: Cole Heilborn (05:33): I can just so relate because I've posted that too and I know what it means, and I saw the eight weeks of suffering and work and grind that you put in place to get ready for that race or whatever. Whereas I think the same version of that experience on Instagram is just the picture with the metal around your neck at the end. So I think that's part of it is that when we have networks where people have to play, where you have to show up and you have to say, this is me and I'm trying my best and maybe I suck, but at least I'm brave enough to put it out there. (08:32): I think that really matters. And I think it affects the nature of the network and how people interact. And what we've noticed on Strava is a far more positive motivating kind of sense of belonging among the people in the community who use it and way less curation, hatred, trolling, and I think that's a big part of it. The other aspect I'd say that is really important to us being different and I think is very promising in this world of social media is Strava is a vertical social network. And what I mean by that is it's related to a niche interest. It's all about running and writing. And I've come to believe, and I don't think I'm alone in this belief, that one network might not be able to capture everything. Imagine being invited to a party. That's everyone you've ever met, and you can talk about anything you want. (09:36): It's just too much. It's too big of a container to fit in all these different things and ideas and kinds of people. And we're increasingly seeing people self-select into groups rooted in their interests around things that they want to talk about. And in doing so, it gives them permission to just nerd out and get really, really geeky about if I post a picture of my new bike on Instagram and a picture of my new bike on Strava, I expected people on Strava to be grilling me about my stem height and my gearing selection and what kind of bike is it? They're just going to give me questions and I can really go deep, and it's just a whole different environment. If I'm sharing that with everyone I've ever met on Facebook, I don't expect the same type of interaction.

content: Cole Heilborn (11:06): Yeah, it's hard for me to speak for everyone, but I can easily speak for myself, and I have a real hard time with the context switching of the mass social network where if your feed is anything like mine, it's very difficult, especially lately where the first thing I see in my feed, just as an example, it might be related to the COVID death count, and that's just incredibly hard to process. And I'm one swipe away from seeing a baby photo that from someone I haven't met or I haven't even seen in years, I might even know them, and the next photo or the next thing I see has something to do with the Black Lives Matter movement, which is just so heartbreaking and important, and the next thing I see is somebody's sourdough recipe. It's just too much. I think that the human brain might not be cut out for that type of really heavy context switching where it's just so hard to know what are we talking about and do I like it all the same? (12:06): Do I like that sourdough recipe or the picture of your big bubbly crumb? Do I like that the same way, I like the same tool that I like this Black Lives Matter protest? It is just too much. And I think you would never conduct a conversation that way. You and I would never talk to each other that way. We would stay focused on a subject and gently move from one to the other. And I think that that, at least for me, that context switching and that free for all, that feeling that anything could happen at any moment, we can talk about anything here is just too much. And instead, what I want to do is focus on one thing at a time and have the freedom to go deep to really get into it and talk about the minutiae and feel like it's a safe space where I'm only talking about that.

Ian Mathias (12:53): So back to your first point, is it the platform? Is it the people that use it that are, when you post a photo on Instagram, it has to be absolutely perfect, but when you post something on Strava, for example, you post that picture with a snot rocket coming down your nose across your cheek and you don't really care, I guess, what is different about those two platforms that has such a difference in the content that's published?

Cole Heilborn (13:20): Yeah, I think it gets back to that notion I mentioned minute ago about the journey and destination. And in a way I could see how this also explains the success of Instagram stories and that what we were noticing on social, which has inspired a lot of the branding work we've done at Strava, is that desire to curate this instinctive, it's very unspoken, but everyone feels it that they should be presenting their best selves. And this is about celebrating your accomplishments and in a way even projecting what you wish you were to your very, very, very best moments that are actually really fleeting and rare. Whereas on Strava, the way to use this platform is to post your activity good or bad, and acknowledge that it is building up to something greater, that if you want to run a marathon, you have to run a lot of really short runs. (14:11): You have to have a lot of training, and everyone who's been there gets it that you just can't show up and do the thing that you want to do. So I think that emphasis on the journey really matters. It really matters that everyone knows that this is a step along the way and I'm trying, I'm doing my best and maybe this wasn't my best run, but it'll help me get to a better one. And can you imagine Instagram and Instagram feed like that? It'd be so cool. These were the hundred awful photos I took to get this one photo that looks really great and maybe have to swipe through. I think that'd be a really killer post. I mean, it would clog up the feed to be a mess, but you know what I mean? It's just so cool to see the journey and see the effort and through that, the vulnerability and the acknowledgement that, look, I'm just trying. Yeah, I think that really matters.

And I think that's a lot of the problem that we have with social media is we see all of these summit moments and then you look at the amount that we have and we're like, well, shoot, I don't have nearly as many of those, but in reality, those are pretty far and few between for most people.

Cole Heilborn (15:19): Yeah, it's true. And I also think that a good network should have utility, and a big part of what Strava is up to and what we really hope to be for our athletes is just incredibly useful that it's not just about seeing the summit shot as it's a great example you just made, but also of like, Hey, this is the route to the summit and you can go do it too. Here's how I did it. Go try it yourself. And what we really want the feed to be for our athletes isn't this source of doom scrolling, just never ending, scrolling, scrolling, scrolling. What we want it to be is a source of motivation, a way to discover new places to play to see incredible achievements or really grindy workouts and get inspired by them and go do 'em yourself. So that's I think another aspect of these vertical networks. When you get really specific about a subject matter, you can then start to add utility and tools to make that subject matter come to life and just be more useful to your users as opposed to strictly about sharing content.

Ian Mathias (16:21): I

Cole Heilborn (16:21): Really hope that when people use Strava, they get a sense of motivation that they close their session ready for their next runner ride. That's like the dream. The last thing we want to do is have someone just feel like they wasted 30 minutes of their lives, they should be fired up and ready to go do an epic run or plan their next big ride, whatever. I think that's an important part too.

content: Cole Heilborn (17:22): Sure, yeah, I'm happy to talk about it. So as some background, we came to a crossroads as a business probably like many people and many businesses did in 2020 and really had to decide what we wanted to be. And our founders came back to lead the company and made it very clear that we are going to dedicate ourselves to our community, especially our subscribers. Strava is unique among networks that we have a paid offering, it is free to use, but you can pay to get our best features. And we felt that now is the time to invest in those who have invested in us and to build the best subscription service for athletes in the world. What that meant very practically is we added a bunch of free features that were outstanding requests. We really tried to get better and continue to try to be better at listening for what our athletes are asking for. (18:16): We also ripped out a lot of aspects of Strava that didn't feel like they were serving the athlete, that they were serving a different kind of customer. So for example, we had a algorithmic feed. So when you looked at Strava, the feed was sorted in a way that we thought you would've liked the most. A lot of our athletes did not like that, so we switched it back, even though they may or may not be able to find what they're looking for easier, just that logical ordering worked better, so we wanted to give them that. Another example is we took out sponsored integrations, which is a feature that is really the closest thing we've ever had to ads in the feed. We thought it just wasn't adding to the athlete experience, so we took it out. And then the last thing as part of this change was we added more value to our subscription. So we made some net new subscription features and we took a few free features that were really expensive to maintain and made them part of the subscription. (19:14): I can't get too much more into what it means for the business, but I can definitely talk about that, how it makes me very excited to be a marketer and build this kind of brand because this gives me such a more eye to eye relationship with our customer. It's simple and honest. Actually in a traditional way.

content: Cole Heilborn (17:22): I bet anyone listening who sells a normal product thinks this is sold fashioned and normal, but in software, it is not novel to make a product so good that people are happy to pay for it, and that's what we want. It's that simple, and that's a new model for networks. Many software companies put their focus on customers who are not their users. We don't want to turn people into a product to sell. We want to make an awesome product for awesome people to buy, and at the same time, we're going to keep making improvements to our free product for people who can't afford to subscribe or we just haven't convinced them yet that it's worth buying. (20:18): And that's such an exciting job as someone who's building a brand at a software business to just compete for that, to want to convince you of that as opposed to just finding a way to keep you using the platform. As I said a minute ago, we want nothing more than to be useful. If you subscribe to Strava and use it once a week and you're happy, I'm happy, but on many other networks that ain't, so once a week wouldn't be enough. We want to keep you back, keep you coming back, keep you using so that we can serve you more ads. And that is just so plainly not our business model now, and I think that creates a very exciting opportunity for us as a brand, but also as a business. And I hope that this is one of the revelations of a society that we have over the next five to 10 years. Our relationship with technology is changing. I think we're past that period of irrational exuberance where every app should be free and using free technology has no consequence. We saw that in media five, 10 years ago, and I bet it happens soon enough with technology too.

content:
Ian Mathias (21:43): Well, if an app is free, the company is making money and they're making money in other ways, and oftentimes that's ads. And I think now more than ever, people are dissatisfied with ads. They're obtrusive. And when you're spending time on your feed and you want to look at that photo of your new grandchild or your friend's baby, and then you see an ad for, I dunno, spark plugs, it takes away from that experience. And so dive a little further into why you guys decided to remove the sponsored element from Strava.

Cole Heilborn (22:18): Yeah, I think you just articulated it so well. It's about experience and we are not yet a profitable company, so we're in a great place where we're able to decide how do we want to profit, how do we want to become a company that is profitable? And it's so much more desirable for us and for our customer to invest in their experience and making an experience so good that they want to buy it. It's just such a natural relationship to have with the customer. And we are also not a huge company. We're very flattered by how people think. We're a big company and we're so lucky to have so many athletes on the platform all over the world, but we only have 180 employees and we can only have them do so much, and they're more motivated and our customers are more motivated by having them focus on making awesome experiences for athletes. And making an ads business is not just a switch you flick on. It's something that you spend a lot of time to do, and it's just so much more pure to go after making that experience. Great. And I think that's what we want to be.

Ian Mathias (23:35): Yeah. So from your perspective in the marketing department, you get to take all of this and figure out how to talk about it. What is that like, and what are some projects that you have worked on that you're really excited about, or what are some things that are coming up that you're working on if you can talk about 'em?

content: Cole Heilborn (23:52): Sure. Yeah. Well, I mean, we talked a lot about this change with our athletes and we knew it would be hard. It's always a challenge to take some free features and make them paid, but I found it pretty easy to do as a marketer in so far as that. One of my favorite quotes is a twain quote. I'll paraphrase it, and it's tell the truth and you don't have to remember anything. And that's really our approach to making this change is if we're honest about what we're doing as a company and what we think it could become and how we really genuinely believe we're acting in the best interest of athletes. You don't have to spin it. It's not a big flashy campaign. You just tell the truth and then just keep believing and keep investing and making that experience great. And what we've been doing all year long and we'll continue to do is focus our marketing on how we are improving the experience of Strava, acknowledging that some people love us already and some people don't love us enough. (24:49): You have to subscribe and we need to earn their trust in their business. And I'm happy to try just to continually showcase how our product engineering and design teams are making great new features and helping them bring those features to market. It's kind of old school marketing, but I really appreciate it as a low flash, honest way of just grinding out like, we're going to make this thing better and better and better until you subscribe. And even if you don't subscribe, you can still use it for free. That's not a bad deal. So that's been a lot of the work lately. We've also done some brand work that I've really loved that's related to a lot of the things we talked about earlier. We had a campaign a couple of years ago called Athletes Unfiltered. It happened not long after the 2016 election where the idea of social media was really taking a nose dive very quickly, went from a good thing to a bad thing in the eyes of the world, and we really took issue with that generalization and for everything we talked about earlier about Strava being positive, motivating people, feeling that they belong on Strava, they don't have to curate their posts. (26:02): We made the simplest campaign. It was actually so simple as we were making it. I was worried it was too simple, which is probably a great sign that you're doing something great. We just went out with a video crew and asked our athletes how they felt about their sport and about Strava and made a bunch of vignettes and a hero film that showcased the difference between the experience on Strava and that of other networks. And it was probably our most successful campaign ever, just because I really think we were able to isolate that tension happening in the world and that Hal Strava was an antidote to it, which I think is always the basis for a good campaign insight.

Yeah, the YouTube channel would be a great place to start, and definitely you can follow us on other social networks or on the Strava Club. Yeah, we've been doing a lot lately building this Strava Club up as a place to maintain that positivity, motivation, support inside our own wealth.

Ian Mathias (27:56): No, that's cool. So as you're looking forward into the future of Strava, what do you hope for? What do you hope the outcome of the app is for your athletes?

content:
Cole Heilborn (28:11): Well, a couple things. I hope that they find it incredibly useful and additive to their lives. The last thing that we want to make is technology that just keeps you occupied and that, like I said earlier, if you have a 10, 20, 30 minute session, you get to the end and wish you had that time back. That'd be such a shame. If nothing else, I hope our athletes use Strava and they put their app down and it just inspires 'em to go out. Actually, how fast can we get you off the platform and out there running and riding? That would be a great goal for us and something that I hope we just get better at, better at being useful. (28:51): The other, which is very related to the moment, is just increasingly diverse. Running and cycling are prevalent among mostly privileged white communities and affluent areas. Yet they are in many ways, very accessible sports that are experienced all around the world. And I'm really interested in building a world that we wish was how we understand sport versus one we have now and introducing all kinds of new people to the sport and bringing their cultures, their experiences into our sports in a way that makes the whole thing just even more fun and different. I think Strava is one of the few companies really positioned to do that because we have 60 million athletes already using it and from all over the world. I think it could be a really powerful force for unity in a time of division and diversity and inclusion in a time where that's really hard to come by too. So we've got our work cut out for us, but that's just so interesting too, and I think a place where we can make a difference.

Ian Mathias (29:57): Yeah. Well, that was beautiful. I think we're about out of time for today, but if people want to follow you, I mean, I know people can find Strava, but who want to find you, where can they follow your work

Patrick McCarthy (01:39): Yeah, I feel very fortunate. 6, 8, 6 brought me on to do the team management and work in marketing for them, and being able to work remotely is key. It's key for them too, because they need to bring authenticity to creating outerwear and snowboard and being in the mountains. So them being based in Los Angeles, it's important to have a voice here in the mountains. They're constantly sending prototype jackets and new concepts and ideas up to me, and I can go out and wear it up at Baker and pound on it in the rain and in the conditions and actually get them the proper feedback. And a lot of the riders want to come through the area, and it's a good hub for them. So it's really nice. It's nice to, I always enjoy my time going to Los Angeles and working there too, and the juxtaposition from Bellingham to LA and everywhere in between. So yeah, I love it up here. Don't really want to move too badly. It's a really fun place to live and lots of cool outdoor activities, which is what I'm really into it is getting out, being in the snow, being in the mountains in any way, shape or form. And I mean, we have the islands here too, but yeah, I feel very fortunate to get a chance to work out of here, and I think it's a very creative, good space.

Cole Heilborn (03:00): Yeah. Well, tell us a little bit about six eight.

And we have other products now with this multi collection that we created where we're making things that are really good for going out climbing, going out hiking, going out, mountain biking, a lot of new offerings from the brand to diversify and grab a larger amount of the population. content: Patrick McCarthy (05:19): Basically, I was like every other human being. I love to go to the mountain, love to snowboard and skateboard and do whatever those things, but I also, I was worried about my future. So after high school, I got into Western Washington University and started at the college, and then going into my third year, I was offered the opportunity to drop out of school and become a professional snowboarder. That lasted for the greater part of 10 years, maybe a little bit longer than that, 10 to 12 years. And then after traveling and filming for various movie projects and doing various photo shoots and traveling all over the world and enjoying that lifestyle for a super long time, 6, 8 6 approached me and they asked me if I would be interested in helping manage their team, managing some photo shoots in the beginning, kind of becoming a team manager slash rider, and it grew from there and they asked me to take on more marketing roles as time goes on and continue to run that side of it. (06:27): So I think I always have known that everything that I learned along the way of being a snowboarder and dealing with the various team managers that I dealt with and working with all the different sponsors that I had, I learned a little bit and took a little bit away from every single experience that I had. And now, luckily enough, I'm doing the team managing and I'm able to share all the insight that I gained from working with 20 different sponsors over my career and helping share a little bit of the insight that I have. And I'm already in tune with all the filmers. I'm already in tune with all the photographers. For me. I have a lot of interpersonal relationships that I can pull from, and I have that mental Rolodex that I can go into and all the riders and I can always see things from team rider's perspectives. (07:22): I went through everything. I know when you're out there and you're filming for crazy movie project and you're just trying to get those last shots and you're running out of travel budget and sleeping in your car to save money and doing what you need to do to make it work when you're on the road just trying to get that last double or 10 80 or 900 or seven 20 or whatever it is that you want to really make yourself proud of what you're working on. I know what those riders are going through. So I try to share the insight and kind of be a liaison from the company to the riders and underst it. Now I can totally understand it from both sides and understand both sides perspectives. The company wants to continue to sell gear and be progressive and give back and do rad things, and the riders want to follow their dreams and push themselves and represent the brand. So it's like helping that become one cohesive working unit. That's my specialty.

So from the brand side, because the world ambassadors have been around for a long time representing brands, and the word ambassador is almost kind of turned in, there's another form of it now, an influencer. It's a little bit different than an ambassador, certainly for 6 86. Why do you guys invest heavily into your ambassadors? What's the goal there?

Patrick McCarthy (08:47): I think the goal there is finding these unique people from the different regions all over the world that have made a huge impact in their region that have some of the best, I feel like 6 86 has some of the best professional snowboarders and skiers in the world on our team. And from Gigge rough over in Europe, who's been one of the biggest Austrian snowboarders, bavar area like snowboarders in the world to Forrest Bailey and now Hanna Beman on our female side and Parker White on the ski side. These guys all bring a really insane dynamic element to the sport and make it cool in their own way. And I think the kids look up to them. They have big social media following, so they post stuff about the gear, they post stuff that they're hyped on. The kids love it, and it creates a following. (09:46): And I think it's really important for brands. I'm really proud of the way 6, 8 6 does this, and it's like a way to give back to the sport to support these taste makers and to make their lifestyle and to bring that to fruition. And yeah, I think you bring up a really good point. There is a whole movement of influencers and people that just have these crazy social media fallings, and they might not even necessarily have all that much skill, but they know how to post about it. So I think there's a place for that here and there, but that's not really my wheelhouse. And it is something that's growing and something that we're aware of, and it is starting to be like, oh, you want to get a product out, you send it to this guy, and he puts it up on social, and there's part of that, but I think it's so important still to support the real core snowboarders that are out there going for it and pushing the sport and progressively. (10:44): But what you got to do is look at what kind of demographic you're trying to sell to.

Patrick McCarthy (08:47): 6, 8, 6 is not only selling to the top best kid at every resort they want to be for the beginner and for diversity, and for every element, we want to create something for everybody, whether you're going on a hike with your family or whether you're doing a front side 10 80 over the Mount Baker road gap, or whether you're competing in the Olympics doing 1440 bloody Dracula, or whether you're a rad chick from the Midwest that's having fun with our friends. We want to create something cool for everybody. So the influencers, there's a time and place for that. It's something that I have a hard time grappling with because just when people have a big following, I've been around a lot of these influencers and I'm just like, what do you do? (11:39): What do do with your time? Are you willing to sacrifice yourself for this? Because the snowboarders that I work with, they do stuff that's like do or die. If they don't make what they're trying to do, they could literally die and they're pushing themselves and they're just going off. And an influencer just is going on Instagram every two seconds. And a lot of the time when I've hung out with big influencers, they just sit there and post all day and they don't even live it. So that's what I feel. That's my own personal, that's not really necessarily maybe the brands we're all learning this new landscape, but that's just my own personal take on it.

Cole Heilborn (12:19): Yeah, no, that makes sense. I mean, you've been there, you've been in that world. So when you look at the ambassador program that you guys run, it's not something that it's not a small expense. There's a lot of time and a lot of resources that are put towards it. So when you guys look at quantifying, why should we keep investing in these riders, A lot of what you're saying it sounds like is you guys choose to do it because you want to invest in the sport, you want to invest in the people that are pushing it. So is that why you justify that expense, or do you also look at it and try to, I guess, what are the marketing tangibles that you try to extract from that as well?

content: Patrick McCarthy (12:56): The marketing tangibles that we're looking to extract out of having a team, and that is basically every season, we will create a line that will come out the next year. And so throughout the season, what I do is I'm traveling around with this rainbow set of the key items from our company that will come out the next year, and I'm putting those on the team riders and taking them out doing photo shoots. So we're shooting all this gear that comes out the next season in the current season. So when this next season starts right around those early preseason, beginning of December, we'll go out and we'll have all next year's gear and we'll start shooting the guys in it. They'll be hiking, they'll be hitting jumps, they'll be making turns, they'll be riding lines, they'll be ripping it. We'll be doing even just some lifestyle stuff. (13:53): But then they help us create the assets. And then also when they wear the gear, they say, oh, if this pocket was a little bit switched or a little tweak change, or maybe this pocket doesn't even need to exist, and this vent needs to come down a little bit more. And I don't understand with this hood, this hood needs more circumference. We need to have more room in there. So we get our feedback from them, we get our assets from them that we can utilize in the magazines that we market with or on our online social pushes. (14:32): And then not only do I have that Rambo set, but each one of them get certain key products that we want to focus on with each person, whether it's our street style riders that are hitting more urban stuff, or our big mountain skiers and our free ride tour riders will all be wearing the most bomber, Gore-Tex, our highest end pieces and out there in the field giving us feedback and representing the brand in those ways. So that's why it's so important to have those people because getting, bringing true authenticity to all the people that sell your product too. You're like, dude, look at this guy wears it and he swears by it, or this woman, she always wears this piece and this piece and this piece. And we try to hopefully tell that story down through our reps and so that they can pass that along to the retailers and we can tell the right stories and we can stand behind it and feel like we're proud of what we're doing.

content:
Cole Heilborn (15:39): So how has the ambassador programs changed since you were in it?

Patrick McCarthy (15:43): I think it's changed a little bit over time. I think that there's more people out there doing it. There's more riders. There's probably more talent out there than there was before, and I think a larger range, but I don't think there's been that much that's changed about it. Social media in general, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, all these new platforms that have come out have definitely made it different. When I was a pro snowboarder, you were going out with a photographer and he was shooting these photos on a slide, and the filmers were out there in the back country with 16 millimeter Bolex cameras and they're filming it on film. So you're out there and you're doing all these things. Then it's like, okay, you wait until September to fly to San Diego and they're going to do a huge movie premiere at the trade show, and you're going to be there for it, and then your photographers are going to submit their slides to transworld and to snowboarder into frequency, and you're going to wait and see if you got a few photos. (16:53): Well, dude, that has been the biggest shift in my opinion because it's like that's what it was like for me, and now it's today. It's like you go out, you get a few shots, maybe you're like, okay, that one's going up on Instagram. This one's going in my story. This one's going, I am going to use this one on this social media platform. I'm going to throw this. I'm going to save this for my little video project that I'm going to drop on Vimeo or whatever. And so there's just all these elements to it that have evolved so much and changed. So I think that that is just basically, that has made it quite a bit different.

Cole Heilborn (17:34): Does the social media element, does that change how your writers or you interact with the sport? Do you feel like that takes away from the sport at all?

content: Patrick McCarthy (17:42): I don't think it takes away from it. It makes it here now right in front of your face. It's like a lot of the times, one of the things that I find a little bit disheartening, but you can't get around it, is the whole concept of the viral video or whatever. Sometimes you can put up a stupid little thing from your phone that you didn't even think was that important, and it gets millions of views. And then you might make something in a really well-produced, amazing piece of digital cinematography and spend a ton of money, and that might get 3000 views because a kid won't sit for 12 minutes to actually watch something that's heavily produced like that, and maybe we can't market it to 'em properly. I have a really funny example. It's actually happened to me this last month. (18:38): I actually didn't even shoot it. So one of my team riders was following a group of us through this snake run, and it's like everyday thing and everyday thing. Anybody could go ride. It's on the normal run. You didn't put any extra effort in. It wasn't beautiful snow conditions. It was just five guys running through a little trail. And my buddy had filmed it and I saw it and I was like, I'm just going to post this. It's been the pandemic. Nothing, didn't think anything about it. So I posted it and people loved it. People were like, oh, I missed that. That's the element that I love. Well, then Snowboarder magazine DMed me and they're like, Hey, do you mind if we post this? And they posted it, and then when they posted it, they got 400,000 views on it, and then not only 400,000 views, but then it got 287 shares. (19:32): So what happens is there's all these, this is part of social media that drives me insane, but there's all these people that have board world and board great and board board all these different apps, and they just steal stuff from SNOWBOARDER Magazine and post it on there and they get like 20,000 followers, 30,000 followers. They don't do anything. They don't do any of the content generation. They aren't cool. They didn't go live it. They have no credibility, but they have groups of people that come in and follow them. They steal stuff from whatever they want.

Patrick McCarthy (17:42): So in the end, dude, I think that this little video that I actually didn't even film, I was the dude in the front, one of my team writers film. They thought it was me. It all went through, it got posted on all these things. It got probably two or 3 million views and it was a pointless little moment. (20:30): And that's where it's changed. And so then you think about I go out and I'm pushing myself and I get an amazing shot that I'm so proud of, and that'll go up and it won't have that sort of viral element to it. So it's something that we don't even really have the control over. You don't have any control over it. You don't know what's going to go viral. I mean, obviously if a dude has a ton of followers, he's going to get big views or whatever, but there's no rhyme or reason to how it's working right now, and it's evolving so fast. It's like I have tons of my younger riders on the team now are all like, oh, you still post on Instagram? We're all on TikTok now. And they're getting millions of views on that. And so I don't know, it's a quickly evolving game, try to stay up to speed with it all, but also try to bring as much authentic things to it as you can, I guess.

Cole Heilborn (21:37): So knowing that, that there's this huge appetite for just small, random stuff, how do you guys plan out your media if the big, huge films are successful, but also just the random cell phone shots are also extremely successful? How do you guys plan out what you post and what you need?

Patrick McCarthy (22:00): The way that we plan it out a lot of the times without giving too much away is we look at the line. What's important in our marketing is look, what do we do? We sell snowboard, ski and mountain culture outerwear. So we look at the line, we look at what pieces are important to us, what our key pieces are. We go out, we get the assets, and then we create a battle plan of how we want to drop the assets. The following year. We are like, let's focus this week on the smarty technology. Let's focus this week on the new Gore-Tex offerings. Let's focus this week on the women and what they're doing. Let's focus on this rider. Let's focus on this product. And we base it around the products. I think a lot more now. And then also, it's like another way you could look at it is like, let's say we come out with this thing and we're just really excited about it. (22:59): Well, what if everybody's really excited about it and then all of a sudden you realize the week before you're about to post about it, that you look at inventory and that entire collection is sold out? Well, you're not going to get another big shipment of this selection. That's it. So it's like if you come out with this year we did a CoLab with Seinfeld, we did Colabs with nasa. We have no idea. If the NASA CoLab collection is just fully sold out and there's nothing we can do about it, then we're not going to waste a bunch of time and energy on social media trying to push the NASA collection sold. So then you just move on to the next thing that you have big inventory in. So what you're selling and what you're that way can also dictate the way that the marketing goes.

Cole Heilborn (23:49): Sure, that makes a lot of sense.

Patrick McCarthy (23:50): Yeah, that's one of the behind the scenes thing that I think a lot of people wouldn't really notice.

Cole Heilborn (23:57): So for other brands that have ambassadors, any, I guess any advice or anything that you've learned along the way that works really well for managing or working with ambassadors? What would you, I don't know, say to these other companies that are trying to start an ambassador program or looking to refine what they have?
