content: Patrick McCarthy (24:14): The way I like to do it, and it's different for everybody, I like to look at it like a family and a team element to it, and it's like, dude, get out and live it. Do it real. Go and experience what you want to. Don't try to make it look authentic. Don't try to make it look cool. Don't try to pose the person doing something. If they're not doing it, go do it. Go snowboarding, go skiing. Go do the sports that you love, document it in a really organic way and have rad team dinners together and break bread and share your moments and talk about it and be authentic and enjoy it. Enjoy the process. Enjoy the fact that you're in snowboarding or you're in skiing or you're in the mountains or you're mountain biking or whatever you're doing. Go and enjoy it, push it, do rad shit and document it and share those experiences and create a really fun team identity. (25:20): Don't just grab a bunch of athletes and pay 'em top dollar if you don't think they all get along. It takes time and energy and effort to really build a really cohesive group of ambassadors and team riders and make sure that, yeah, when you guys go on trips, it's an awesome experience. And then document that and it'll show in what you're doing and it's better than just running out and paying the next Instagram model to post about your product. That just doesn't fly in my world, but there's a space for it for sure, and everyone else is dying. You want to know why everybody's gravitating toward that right now? Because it doesn't take any work. You just sit there, you send them the box, you didn't have to do anything. They went out, pretended they were doing something cool, took a photo of themselves, posted it on there. It didn't take you anything. You didn't have to earn anything. So go out and live it, earn it. Be proud of the work that you put in and create something with real identity and authenticity or just pay somebody to do it and sit there and try to make your sales and look at yourself. I guess in the end, you want to look at yourself in the mirror and be proud of what you're doing.

content: Patrick McCarthy (27:22): So if they're interested in parlaying it into the industry, I think the key, I mean, that's a really good question. I think that be true to yourself. Work hard when you're, work hard at it. And then, I mean, dude, for me, one of the biggest elements of it is networking. You've got to network. You've got to put yourself out there and put yourself in uncomfortable situations where you're around a bunch of people you don't know and thrive. Get to know these people get to know back in the day, for me, one of my biggest things, the reason why I am still relevant is go to trade shows, talk it up with people, meet people from different brands. Go out in the mountains, share your experiences. Don't let it all be dictated by thinking that there's some perfect algorithm to it, because there's not, the way I look at it is the more heart and soul that you pour into it, the more you're going to get out. (28:31): So I would say you're aspiring to work in the industry afterward. Then start learning about it, reading about it. Pick up some books. Think about all the different sides. What side of the industry do you want to work in? Do you want to work in marketing? Do you want to work in sales? Do you want to work in production? Do you want to work in shipping? Everybody's got a different dream. So it's like, go find what you want and learn about it, read about it, ask a lot of questions. Don't be afraid to ask questions. Don't be afraid to get uncomfortable and put yourself in weird situations that you're not normally. I always grew the most personally when I was taking myself out of my comfort zones and making myself do something that didn't always sound like exactly what I wanted to do, but what I felt like I needed to do to move on to the next stage. (29:28): So I think just networking, being true to yourself, being honest, being upfront, and ask a lot of questions, no one's going to be bummed to tell you the answers that you want to hear. And I don't think anybody ever got frustrated with somebody who asked questions. If that's what you want, put yourself in the position to go out there and get it. There's a lot of opportunities out there and everybody, there's something for everybody. So I mean, actually becoming a pro snowboarder, that takes a lot of energy and effort and guts and things. And also, you're your own brand, so you need to market yourself. You need to learn all those elements. It's insane what some kids are doing these days to grow these followings and to build themselves into a brand. They can do it a lot faster, just all sitting there, right on that little smartphone in their pocket. So yeah, I would say go out and network and put yourself in uncomfortable situations and be comfortable and be comfortable in your own skin, and believe in your own vision and the person that you are, and you follow your own heart and you'll get where you're going.

Cole Heilborn (07:43): Again, this was 10 years ago, and at the time I think that a lot of companies that were launching physical goods on Kickstarter were launching them in a much earlier stage. We came with a finished product. The first campaign we ran was 75 days long. And during the campaign we actually started fulfilling. We fulfilled a pre-production run of 200 units during that campaign. And I think part of the success of that campaign was that we were able to post updates of like, Hey, it's being made, check it out. We were able to give very tangible progress updates on the product, and it got people really stoked. And then once the campaign ended, it was only a matter of weeks before we started shipping these things out worldwide to 10,000 people. And so it built something that I think is kind of important on Kickstarter is especially when it's your first time launching a product to the world is establishing trust and goodwill that you, you're not just talking about this great idea, but you're also executing on it really well. And we were able to do that and show that to a bunch of people. And I think it helped us parlay a successful campaign into a business that was sort of immediately thriving, immediately profitable.

Adam Saraceno (09:32): Yeah. So how did you take that trust that you earned in that first campaign and roll that into the next project and subsequent projects?

And the next products we developed, which were the leash and cuff, they were essentially these kind of minimalist, versatile camera straps that you could use in conjunction with your camera clip. Were sort of based on customer feedback. And then, yeah, another part of it was when we launched that second campaign, there wasn't really any precedent for companies doing that. For companies starting on Kickstarter and then going back to Kickstarter to relaunch products. There wasn't a playbook for that. And we were really concerned actually that are people going to see this as us kind of going back to the honey hole.

Adam Saraceno (10:57): Oh, interesting.

And we were very upfront with why we were going back to Kickstarter. We were very transparent and it was just like, Hey, this worked really well for us when we launched our first product and we made all these fantastic customers through it, and we see no reason why we shouldn't do that again. And people were extremely and immediately very stoked to see us back there. We didn't hear a peep of, I don't know, resentment from Kickstarter or from any of our customers. And so we kind of at that point realized, Hey, maybe this is a sustainable way to keep growing our business.

Adam Saraceno (12:32): I guess beyond the immediate benefits of Kickstarter, why do you guys continue to go back?

Cole Heilborn (12:38): Well, I'd say it's equal parts, a financial tool for us, a cashflow management tool and a marketing tool. The cashflow part is, so peak design is we don't have any outside funding. We don't have any outside investors. We occasionally take on small loans here and there when need be, but we're essentially entirely funded by our own revenue. And Kickstarter gives us the ability when we are doing a big product launch and we need to make a huge product development investment and all the tooling expenses and all the manufacturing expenses for that first production run, (13:38): It essentially allows us to acquire that cash upfront via a presale so that we can, it just allows us to manage our money that way. And you can tell how much I actually know about financial management by the fact that I'm stumbling over the simplest of explanation of how businesses work. But yeah, become a very kind of important part of our month to month financial management. And a lot of our relationships with our suppliers now are sort of built on this trust of when we launch this product, we're going to have this huge injection of pre-order cash to kind of pay them with. So that's like the financial part. The marketing part is just, there is, I guess, bang for your buck. I can't think of a higher ROI more impactful way to build awareness and buzz around a new product. For us, at least for a company that makes consumer goods, especially in the space that we're in, we make kind of these high-end products that are photo video related, that are targeted towards higher end consumers of everyday carry gear and people that live in cities and just people that are concentrated in high numbers on the Kickstarter platform.

Adam Saraceno (15:26): So what's from your first campaign to your more recent campaigns, what's one thing that you've kept and repeated one principle, and what's one thing that you've changed from things you've learned?

Cole Heilborn (15:44): That's a good one. Captain repeated is definitely the transparency, and it's been something that has just, I think because of our Kickstarter roots, we learned very quickly just how much, being transparent sometimes too, a fault is beloved by your customers. And it's just like, seems like, I mean, it's kind of a no-brainer, but it's just a better, easier way to run a business when you're brutally honest about everything that you do. And so whether it's transparency about keeping a high degree of update about the status of development of a product and boots on the ground footage from our factories and that kind of stuff to transparency about when we fuck up. There's been a few occasions where we've launched a product and then later discovered some sort of manufacturing defect. And I think through Kickstarter, we've learned how important it is to just be very honest about it. And in terms of things that we've changed, that is a good one. We've certainly, over the years, I'd say developed and sharpened technically our video production capabilities and just our abilities to tell a really good compelling story. And that's kind of been a very natural, organic progression. And it's how all companies do it. And

Adam Saraceno (18:02): Yeah, I think when I go to Kickstarter and I'm looking at a new campaign, one of the first things I do is check out the video. How important is the video, I guess, what are the things that you're thinking through as you're creating it that are necessary for a successful project launch?

It is your opportunity to quickly and succinctly explain to somebody why they should buy your product or support your project. And ultimately, in my opinion, the thing that makes a Kickstarter successful is actually not the video. It's the thing that you're making or selling itself. You have to start with a good idea that has been executed on well and is just kind of business 1 0 1. It's a product that has to address a need that enough people have and are willing to pay for a solution for. And I do think that there are a lot of campaigns out there that end up being not that successful, even though they have a really good polished video, it's just kind of like, well, it's just not something that there's a huge appetite for. But when it comes to the video, it's just kind of like marketing 1 0 1. I wouldn't say there's a silver bullet. It's explaining to people what it is you're making and help 'em understand it and help 'em understand how it's going to make their life better. And then maybe share also the story about who you are and why you're making it. (20:07): And yeah, I think that the storytelling is always an important part, but not as important as the thing itself.

If you're making a travel bag to say travel, it is such a wonderful way to see wax eloquent on why travel is important and why we all care about it and all the great things it's brought to us. And then use that as sort of this lead in this grandiose lead in to be like, and that's why we developed the perfect tool, but at the end of the day, people back your campaign of the thing. And for us, for our type of customer who is a pretty tech savvy, gear minded person, people really like seeing the details. So we definitely try to spare no detail when we're talking about the products and the materials and when we're providing Kickstarter updates, like the thought behind why we use this type of aluminum versus another type of aluminum and the machining process that it takes to make this specific part and all that kind of stuff, that helps build the story as well.

Here's why all of these things are inadequate for these types of activities, and here's why this solution is actually a much better one. And so it's, I dunno, again, pretty classic marketing, just problem definition, and then explaining how your solution solves the problem in a better way, and what are the benefits that you can get from that.

content: Cole Heilborn (30:22): Yeah, that's a good point. I mean, I'm pretty sure that most Kickstarter projects are unsuccessful. If you look at just all the numbers, there've been more unsuccessful ones than successful ones, I think by a significant margin. The things that sort of the most high profile or common kind of mistakes that I see made a big one is around overpromising. And that can be caused by a few different sources. It can just be caused by maybe the idea, maybe the product that you have is just either not that great, or the execution on it has been not that great, the design, the construction or whatever, and you've hyped something up then, but the pictures and what you're actually showing is evidence of this thing aren't really supporting that hype. And I think people see through that pretty quickly. Another thing is, and this is something that is actually not necessarily keeps projects from initially succeeding, but keeps people with successful projects from growing that into a successful business, is basically not getting your ducks in a row from a product development and manufacturing standpoint (32:05): Early enough. Like I said, when we launched that first campaign, we were essentially already ready to press go on production. And it's not like that was a conscious strategy. It was more just out of this naivety of like, well, yeah, if we're going to sell a product, we better be ready to make it. And I think there's a lot of people that go to Kickstarter more so to validate an idea than to sell kind of a concrete thing that they're already ready to make. So a lot of campaigns, I mean, the coolest cooler, if you remember that it was, no, I don't. It was like Kickstarter's most funded project for a while, and it was a cooler with all these bells and whistles on it with a Bluetooth speaker and a built-in blender to make your pina coladas and stuff like that. And they had this huge campaign, and then it took them years, years to fulfill because they weren't ready for their success, and they did not kind of get their manufacturing together with enough time. They were also not great at communicating with their backers about it, and it just kind of turned into this angry mob with pitchforks in their comments section on their Kickstarter page. (33:47): So yeah, I think that that's a big area where I see, I would suggest folks that are, especially if you're bringing a thing, a consumer product to life, really try and get that stuff in order as early as you can.

content: Austin Whitman (02:16): Well, I launched climate neutral with with our two founding funders a year and a half ago. I had worked in carbon carbon offsetting, carbon markets, carbon finance about fifteen years ago and I spent really the better part of the last two decades thinking about carbon and energy and climate decarbonization and the environment and you know, I guess getting I'd gotten kind of increasingly frustrated by the slow pace of policy. when policy's the big thing that everybody seems to be looking for as a solution to climate change, but having worked on it for a long, long time. I guess I was feeling personally very frustrated by just how things are just not moving there. And so when I started talking to Peter and hearing his experience with his own company, kind of looking at their carbon impacts and trying to figure out what to do about them, it got me got me itching to leave my job, which was in clean tech at the time, and launch What We Are, which is a nonprofit that is doing A kind of that is working to get consumers engaged in the fight against climate change by giving them a label. And the label basically indicates that a brand has measured, offset, and reduced its carbon footprint from the prior year. And the brand has to certify with us every year to keep the label current. And we are running kind of a consumer awareness campaign. We've got the label and then we've also built a carbon footprinting software tool, which is really getting some pretty good feedback from the market. So it's a few different pieces to the to the organization, but fundamentally we're trying to get brands excited about becoming net zero with their carbon emissions and then consumers to get excited about brands that are becoming net zero.

Austin Whitman (06:25): It looks a little different depending on whether they're small, medium, or large. Small is less than five million dollars in annual revenues. Medium is between five and a hundred million, and large is over a hundred million in revenues. And I won't go into detail on each one of them, but but essentially what each what all companies have to do is first estimate their carbon emissions, which includes not just their direct operations, but emissions from their value chain, you know, the things that they buy, like raw materials to make their make their products or airline miles that they travel, that sort of stuff. And then they've got to purchase carbon offsets to offset the entirety of that footprint. Our our philosophy is those emissions already happened, their last year's emissions. It's too late to reduce them. So they have to be offset. And then the company's got to identify some things that they'll do in the next eighteen to twenty four months to reduce their footprint. So it's a fairly simple framework, measure, offset, reduce. And within the reduction step, we're enabling companies to start to think about where they might be able to lower the carbon intensity of their operations.

Cole Heilborn (07:37): I see. Okay. And so if you looked at carbon emissions as a whole, how much of it comes from manufacturing and consumption versus things like travel or, you know, other sectors?

Austin Whitman (07:50): Yeah, so there's this language of carbon footprinting, which is called the greenhouse gas protocol. It started about ten years ago, and it gives a common language across any type of company to talk about where your carbon emissions come from. And the greenhouse gas protocol is broken down into what they call scopes. Scope one, scope two, scope three. Scope one is basically the emissions that you could see if you walked around your company's physical. property. So you could see fumes coming out of a diesel generator, or you could see up the smokestack of your oil burner for heat. those are some simple examples. Scope two is mostly the line share of it is electricity use. So it's emissions that are happening from energy that you're using, but where that energy was produced somewhere off site. Scope one and two is what most people just think about when they think about their emissions. Scope three is everything else. Scope three is employee travel. Scope three is the impact of the things that you buy that are in your supply chain. Scope three is waste from your operations, scope three is shipping of products around the world, the emissions tied to you know trucks and planes, trains, and automobiles to move your stuff around, right? for a typical company that makes physical goods, it's pretty fair to say that ninety or more percent of their total carbon emissions will be from scope three. those things that are somewhere else and don't immediately appear to you that you're causing them. and so it's really the big one and it's something that we require companies to take a look at and be accountable for.

They are just they're worried. And they're not getting any of that worry addressed by positive messages out of Congress or the White House as to forward progress against climate change. Erica Rosen (15:41): What power does a brand have? Yeah, I mean, I would say that the simplest answer, which could then turn into an eight hour conversation is it's a way to build trust and measure permission. Interview over, no, I'm just kidding. Yeah, I would say that for brands, number one, really using your brand or not using, but just building your brand as a way to build trust among your customers helps create that affinity and helps create recall, and then more importantly, helps protect you against competition. And it really does mean that, listen, for BioLite for example, we're always going to want to be as affordable as possible, but we also know that our products, they cost money. And so we want you to feel like you're getting valued. We want you to feel like you're getting a great experience. And so I think that building trust and that kind of routinized and reliable association is really one way to really leverage and build your brand. And then in terms of permission, which is the kind of corollary of that is that if a brand wants to be around for a long time, we might want to expand into new categories or we might want to look at new offerings. And some of those offerings are going to be more competitive than others. And so what I would say is by building a strong brand, it's not even necessarily that you get more permission to do more things, but it's that you get really good feedback on where you have permission to go.

Adam Vicarel (02:05): Yeah, so my background is I have basically a degree in graphic design. Prior to getting that degree in college, I fell in love with painting. So I've always kind of grappled, at least early on in my career with am I an artist or am I a designer? The two starkly different things in the sense that design solves problems and art is intended to make people think, and or art is more of an interpretation of an artist's emotions or feelings or perceptions. And then design solves problems. That's maybe better said. And so I always kind of grappled with what am I? And over the years as a designer, I fell into hand lettering, which is literally just drawing words for lack of a better explanation. And as I started doing that more and more, I really fell in love with the artful nature of hand lettering, but how it's applied in a design sense. (02:58): So over the last couple of years, I've been working for myself about six years now, and just the beginning of this year, beginning of 2020, I rebranded my studio as a hybrid creative studio that specializes in the artful implementation of strategic design. So the idea is that I think and execute, or I think like a designer, but I execute a fine artist. And so what that enables me to do is bring a kind of unprecedented level of approachability or that cool factor to the work that I'm creating, but while still really being cognizant of the target demographic and who is the competition, what's the point of difference of this company? So it enables me to kind of tiptoe that line of, this is cool for cool's sake, or this is cool because it speaks to me because I am that target audience.

So they pursue that in college. So in the world of design, everything is created to solve a problem or to serve a purpose. So everything you make does something intentional. So as a graphic designer, everything I do, I'm considering why if I choose the Sam Serif versus a Crif, why did I do that? If I choose blue versus green, why did I do that? So I think they're starkly different in some ways, but at the same time, they do have a lot of overlap. So it's like a fun little thing I'm always playing with.

Gary Boulanger (00:04:20): On? My job is primarily to be the storyteller and the brand journalist, for lack of a better term, for Fox, because I come from a journalist and PR background. We realized up until a few years ago that so much of what we're doing was OE focused, where we would work closely with our OEM partners. They would design chassis vehicles and so forth. We'd come alongside at a certain point, we'd provide suspension with our name on it. Sometimes we'd share the space with our OE partner, and that would be it. We didn't have to do a whole lot of marketing. We would go racing, of course, and our athletes would be branded with Fox, so they would be our mouthpiece. It wasn't until our team was started, not quite two years ago, the power vehicle group marketing team, which we never had before. We always had a small corporate marketing team that would do the storytelling, but that was split amongst all our division, motorcycle, snow, A-T-V-U-T-V, truck off, offroad, mountain bike, you name it. So you can imagine that if a certain segment is grabbing more attention or more popular or more maybe identifiable with a larger segment like mountain biking can be worldwide, other categories are going to get neglected. A bit like case in point Motorcycle, I was senior editor at Cycle World Magazine, and I had no idea that Fox made shocks for Harley's (00:05:55): Because they didn't really put the time into it. They only had limited resources. So we realized that a big part of what we needed to do was tell our story. It's lovely when you have companies like ours that has four, almost five decades of heritage, history, victory, innovation, the fact that Bob is still with us and we're still located in the heart of where we started all those years ago, that meant that we needed to have a considered effort to tell and share the story. So with that back about a year ago, we realized that as the media is struggling to maintain its footing, tech editors, feature editors like I used to be printed publications, even online publications, there's a lot of branded content. And I think readers are feeling a little short shrifted in that they want information, they want tech.

What makes this athlete maybe a bit more special, not just because they're on the podium or winning, but what drives them. And conversely, what drives Fox? All of our engineers, when they go out playing, they're loading up the trailer with the side-by-side and they're towing it with their Ford or Chevy or Toyota truck, and there's usually mountain bikes in the back that are all specked out with Fox. So that's what we do. And even that story is one that I know we're going to be sharing at some point, so there's quite a bit going on. But with the storytelling, we also uncovered the fact a little over a year ago that education is something that needs to come first. Education and what is suspension all about? What makes a shock work? What other parts of a shock? (00:08:04): I buy a vehicle, I buy a very expensive vehicle to the tune of $65,000, either a Jeep Mojave or a Ford Raptor. I paid all this money. My suspension should work perfectly well. It's much like a guitar. You need to tune it, you need to lay hands on it. And we realized that known in the industry was really giving permission to the end user, the person who owns the vehicle to actually adjust, tune, set, sag, all those various things on their suspension based on the use case. What's this person going to do with this vehicle or bicycle? So we developed what we called Fox Academy, and it's a video series that goes along with telling the basics. We use our ambassadors and racers, and they give testimonials as to why certain upgrades matter versus stock or what we call standard. But the fact that we identify just all what the moving parts do and what they mean, and it's actually evolved into something that we use for onboarding new employees.

And for us to be able to share that story, then we've been able to cross pollinate with what we call Fox Stories, and that's our digital publication and Fox Academy. And we launched Fox Stories at King of the Hammers this past January 31st, right before the Super Bowl, and we had to do a virtual launch on June 9th of Fox Academy. And the reception that we've had from consumers, from the media, from the industry on Fox Academy specifically, has been very powerful. It could be playing on screens in store, and as customers are milling around looking at things, here's a chance for them to learn a little bit more. And we don't specifically break down suspension for just one category. Each episode we run the gamut on what it looks like for snow, what it looks like for (00:10:34): Jeeping, what it looks like for riding a side by side. And that's been, I think probably with the benefit of hindsight, one of our strongest initiatives that has caught the attention of leadership and has received their support leadership is now based in Brazelton, Georgia, near Road Atlanta, where we have a new tech center, an r and d facility, and there's so much going on in the power vehicle world that to be able to get on top of it and really message it clearly has been a huge challenge because Fox, previous to our coming on board, was also very heavy on events. Let's take our big rig out to Sturgis and do installs for 10 days. Let's take our big rig to King of the Hammers and do installs for 10 days. Let when Fox goes out traveling, Fox goes big. (00:11:31): We have tuners that lay hands on people's race vehicles, like I mentioned Daytona or Sturgis, in years past, we would lay hands on people's bikes and we'd upgrade their shocks and fork springs and so forth. But when you do that, it's important. And we've been as one of our marketing cohorts on the bicycle sites, so we've been spreading the magic ferry dust of racing for decades. But in this digital age, especially with shelter in place and the uncertainty of what's going on, how do you reach more people? We were hamstrung with literally not being able to go. I mean, Sturgis just ended this past weekend, and for the first time in a while, we weren't there to support either our friends at Indian, our super hooligan race team, things like that. So the timing, the benefit of hindsight on what we're doing with Fox Stories and Fox Academy has been spot on. The big key is making sure that now that we're focusing on aftermarket as well as oe, that our aftermarket partners have product that's any company's challenge, right? It's all about fulfillment and distribution. That's what makes Amazon so amazing. That's what makes Apple so amazing, right?

Gary Boulanger (00:12:57): The biggest one for us was the fact that we had the shelter in place. Both of our US factories, we have a rather large facility in Watsonville, California, and that's where our power sports stuff is made. Motorcycle, A-T-V-U-T-V and snow. And then in El Cajon, California, near San Diego is where our truck and off road suspension parts are made. And for a certain amount of time, not only were we told, sorry, can't have your people making stuff anymore for the time being, same thing happened with Polaris Ford, FCA, which is Fiat Chrysler. So everyone that we do business with here in the States, everyone was in limbo. Meanwhile, companies like Revzilla that sell motorcycle parts direct online that we deal with, they're having record days one after another. So we're trying really hard to keep up with that. (00:13:59): Thankfully, a lot of our distributors really do some strong forecasting, and we were able to fill those pipelines. But the biggest challenge is it's a real catch 22 now that we're getting a lot of very high profile OEM spec. All of a sudden now, all this marketing and all this word of mouth and all the good effort that we've been striving for means that we have this rather large demand. So when, case in point, Brian Fuller is a custom car truck and motorcycle fabricator near Atlanta, a really good partner of ours, really good friend of mine. He reached out recently. He has a TV series, and he needed some suspension for 1961, international Harvester, (00:14:48): Beautiful. Basically the predecessor to the Bronco and all the cool stuff that we're seeing. And I said, I could get you something Brian, like we always do, but I'd have to take it away from a customer, a four wheel parts somewhere in the country, which means I'd have to call that person, that customer and say, do you mind if Brian Fowler has take this away from you? I know you've been waiting a few months. So that's the catch 22 is we have this demand. Thankfully, I dunno how Brian did it. I recommended that he get ahold of some four wheel parts somewhere in the country that doesn't have dibs on that product. (00:15:23): And he did.

And a big part of what we're doing to offset that is we just finished a building, a 340,000 square foot factory near Brazelton, Georgia that is not fully up and running, but it's getting close because the off-road and truck segment of our business, there is such a large demand on production that we just cannot keep up blessing and a curse really. So a lot of that demand is from our OE partners, and they just want more. We just saw the forward Bronco was just introduced. Fox is not equipped on that vehicle, but the Bronco Raptor is going to be foxed out, and that's coming next year. We have a lot of things in the works with Polaris because Polaris does the snowmobiles, the side-by-sides, and they also own the Indian brand. So we're doing more on the OE side, which is wonderful. And we're also doing more on the aftermarket side. (00:16:51): Thankfully, Watsonville is so dialed that they're able to take the over spill production from El Cajon and help us keep up with the demand on the Jeep stuff. So it's been good, but it needs to be better. And that's where this rather large facility in Georgia, which is the same footprint of our two California facilities combined, is really going to help relieve that pressure and allow us to really position El Cajon to be ideally suited to do more r and d race development, tuning so close to the desert down there. And that's always been important for Fox as we go tuning every vehicle that we spec, whether it's OE or for aftermarket, there's a lot of miles that are put on those vehicles before things pass muster and make it to market.

Gary Boulanger (00:17:45): So

Gary Boulanger (00:17:45): That would explain why we've been so West Coast centric all these decades. So it's evolving. It's definitely evolving.

Gary Boulanger (00:18:01): Yeah. Yeah. And I guess for the first time, probably since I can remember, it was actually a detriment to be a US manufacturer, because on the bicycle side, we transitioned manufacturing to our Taiwan factory about eight, nine years ago. Because as bicycles have evolved, mountain bikes specifically, virtually everything on that bicycle is made in Taiwan. So up until nine years ago, all the fox forks and shocks from mountain bikes were made in Watsonville, (00:18:34): And we realized we were making all this great stuff here, shipping it over there, the bike in the box would been shipped back here because North America is the largest market, Germany's close second or maybe their neck and neck, but it was very cost prohibitive. The challenge with Taiwan is you really do need to own your manufacturing, have your people quality control, intellectual property and all that. So it took a while to do that, which also freed up a lot, quite a bit of manufacturing space in that Watsonville facility as our power sports segment grew. So you can see, so the point being is our bicycle business has just exploded something like 75% increase over the last few months with demand, because now we're getting a lot of specific orders from our partners, whether it's Pivot, whether it's giant, whether it's Trek, whether it's specialized, because as you've probably seen bicycle shops, I think it's been unprecedented since the oil embargo days or early seventies where people are just buying everything off the shelf and bike shops are doing everything they can to keep up with that demand. So that was the exception for Fox Factory, actually to have Taiwanese manufacturing, but our domestic manufacturing suffered because of the shelter in place and all the protocols.

Cole Heilborn (00:20:08): I see. Okay.

Gary Boulanger (00:20:09): Yeah, very ironic. Very ironic.

content: Gary Boulanger (00:21:21): Soccer in the early seventies too, in the United States was very rare. So that gave me my first taste of maybe the unconventional, the eclectic. I remember vividly freshman year in high school where our history teacher was also the freshman football coach, and he did not like soccer players. He didn't really think we were athletes. I remember there vividly, right? (00:21:48): Not realizing that I think between Moto GB Formula One and soccer, they're the most physically demanding sports on the planet, but I digress. So I had this mindset of going for the unconventional. And when you start playing different sports, soccer, bicycle racing, cyclocross, all those things, which now everyone's aware of, a lot of people partake, it's no longer unconventional. It introduced me to books, movies, people, places, things that kind of open up my eyes beyond my perch in Allway, Wisconsin, outside of Green Bay. And because of my love for soccer, that's what took me to a college in southeastern Wisconsin where I was able to play soccer. But I went to school for marketing, which back in the early eighties meant most likely it meant sales slash marketing, which meant if you were lucky, you might be a fax machine salesperson or you'd end up selling things door to door. It was very cloudy. And the only reason I went to school for marketing is because I wanted to be a cartoonist in grade school, and I was a very good artist, but I would seek the approval or maybe the advice of different adults, Hey, I'm thinking of going to this school, what do you think? And because it's so unconventional, I'd get the response, well, why would you do that? You can't make any money at that. (00:23:18): So I thought, all right, I'm in high school. And I realized, well, my art skills, my good friend Louis's dad's an architect. I want to be an architect. Not realizing at the time that you needed to be really good with maths and science, and I was not good in math and science, but I remember Louis's dad telling me, well, the computer age is coming. I don't know if architects will exist anymore. It's going to all be computer driven, (00:23:43): Right?

content: Gary Boulanger (00:21:21): This is early eighties before Macintosh came out, before really saw the personal computer segment grow. So once again, a well-intentioned, but Ill-advised adult telling me that you can't make money at that or something's going to change it. I ended up going to school for marketing, which is all well and good, but I floundered for a few years, first few years of college playing soccer. And I realized that part of what I enjoyed about art was that visual storytelling. And I would read comic books, just like most writers read a lot to sharpen their cognitive skills for wordplay and structure and so forth. I would always read, probably read more comic books and actually read textbooks. Maybe that's why I wasn't good at Math of Science. But what prompted me to switch to journalism halfway through college was I just wasn't into playing soccer anymore. I enjoyed it, but I would find myself asking. All my teammates always had questions, very inquisitive, and I decided, well, I'm going to switch to journalism. I'm going to give up playing soccer. I had a good couple solid years on the varsity team, but I became a sports reporter for the school newspaper (00:25:04): Because I also loved music. I was the music reporter. So I'd go to concerts and interview bands. I got a job, a part-time job, as well as a sports reporter for the local daily newspaper. So this is back in the late eighties where I'm taking my own pictures, interviewing people, I'm developing my own film. It was college and high school sports, and I was just gobbling up what journalism meant. And I also was fortunate to have a solid professor or two that really encouraged me. So finally, an adult beyond my parents. Of course, my parents always encouraged me, but an adult whom I respected that said, you've got something here. But I learned the mechanics, the fundamentals, and the foundation of storytelling through the hard news journalism, of course, it's very dry. Your sports reporting, court reporting, news reporting isn't as exciting. So I was able to segue into more long form Narrative magazine stuff.

You start asking other people their opinion or something, or you ask them to tell you their story. So in a sense, what I was doing for several years as a journalist is I was learning other people's trials, tribulations, highs, lows, successes, failures, and I've got this ability to soak it all up like a sponge. And as evolved, and I was wanting to be that full-time music journalist, I realized, well, I don't have the courage to move to New York to work for Rolling Stone. I really don't have the financial ability or courage to move to California where a lot of the other publications were. So I kept my nose down. (00:27:02): And when a big recession happened in the early nineties with the first Gulf War, I also found myself after leaving the advertising world kind of in a pickle. A lot of people are now, you're really overqualified. The jobs aren't there. There's a bit of, not a bit of, let's just call it, there's huge uncertainty. I also didn't have a master's degree, so I didn't quite have what it took to slot in where there might've been opportunity. So I kind of did a bit of a self audit. Let's call it an auto audit. What do I really enjoy? Well, I liked storytelling, but what do I really enjoy? Bicycling? And when I worked at my first magazine job when I was just finishing up college, before I got into advertising, the only other younger person, there was a guy named Steve Smith, and he was in the cycling. I walked into his office and he had jerseys hanging there. He had posters on the wall tour to France, stuff. I had no idea. It just wasn't in my thing. I was a hundred percent soccer and comic books, right? (00:28:05): So I said, hold my hand. Walk me into this world. What is bicycling all about? And this is 1988 following year, Greg Laman wins the second tour de France miraculously and the Champ final time trial. So late 1990, early 91. I'm like bicycling industry. That's for me.

I knew plenty from reading magazines, but I didn't really know the mechanics of the industry. So I took a job at a bike shop, and this is in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, when Schwinn was the brand, and it was Top Dog to everybody. And I was able to get a job managing a Schwinn shop. Well, that Schwinn shop had been around for close to 40 years by then. And we did good things because we were named the bicycle dealer Showcase Magazine, top 100 dealer in the country. (00:28:56): So we were part of 100 dealers out of that time, probably close to 7,000 dealers in the US or in the top 100. So I called up the editor and I said, Hey, man, this is really cool. Can you tell me more? I want to do a press release and let look a media know. And he said, well, this is unique. Usually bike shop managers don't respond. They just get the plaque in the mail and they hang it on the wall. But do you have some sort of business degree or journalism degree or PR degree? I said, yeah, journalism and pr. He goes, oh, and you're in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Yeah. Well, we we're here in southern California. I'd really like to, if you're interested, if you want to write a monthly column, that would be great. In fact, if you'd like to do more with maybe interviewing some people in the industry, because Trek is in your backyard, we had a lot of companies that were in our backyard, so to speak, between Wisconsin and Chicago and a little further northwest in Minneapolis. (00:29:54): If it could be our man in the ground in the Midwest, that'd be great. Like, oh. So that was a paying gig that I was doing while I was managing the shop. Well, as you can imagine, after a while, I thought, I want to get into that world. Retail's great for learning. But at age 25, newly married, I kind of wanted to expand a bit. So that led to doing more freelance stuff while I was doing a other things wasn't always easy because lost the bike shop job because we had two locations, and Schwinn went bankrupt, got new ownership in 1993. So all of a sudden, Schwinn wasn't top dog anymore.

So I was able to continue freelance riding, but because of the affiliation with bicycle dealer, showcase bike, Europe, velo news, bicycle retailer, industry news, that gave me entree into a lot of bike companies. (00:30:52): Trek, for instance, was about 60 miles away. So here I am interviewing the new CEO and owner of Trek learning his story. So I was able to do the same thing with as I did, interviewing all the soccer players to begin with, with all the musicians for a spell. And it really encouraged me to continue that. But I didn't land my first full-time bike journalist job until February of 2007, because it was interesting. It was real catch 22 because of what I was doing, interviewing different people. I caught the attention of a guy that started a company in Madison, Wisconsin called Airborne Bicycles, and he developed a brand that was just like Dell Computers used to be where you would go online, configure it, customize it, and within a week it would be shipped to your house direct. And we did that with bicycles back in 19 98, 99. (00:31:47): Well, huffy caught the, caught our attention, or we caught Huffys attention rather. And they bought us lock, stock and Barrel and moved us to Dayton, Ohio. And I didn't even know where Dayton was. I had to look it up on a map. I didn't head southeast a whole lot. Moved down there, and it was great for about a year. And then the internet bubble burst. So buying things direct wasn't great anymore. And so four years ago, we made the decision that was just too much and we decided to say, Hey, we're going to collapse all these brands into one. Sean Fields (04:25): We used to be called Mcne Corporation, and Dwayne and Nancy Mcne founded the company in 1981. So they were always interested in looking at new products. They kind of landed into care and repair back in the day with kind of outdoor rain suits, and they needed to develop products that would repair those. So that's where that kind of all started. Building the different brands, house of Brands was kind of the thing back then. And so Gear Aid was one of the brands and RevX, or not, sorry, not revive, X Gear Aid, M Essentials, which was a dive specific. There was Outgo, which was a brand specifically around towels. We had Mcna tactical. So all of those played together in different categories, but when we were purchased, that was something that was looking at the staff that we had and the resources we had to run all those brands, you need a lot of resources and a lot of money. (05:39): So that was something that was a recommendation that we did and we moved forward with. So that that's been a really rough transition to do that and to go from more of a B2B behind the scenes global brand into something that's very in your face. And we want to expand that. The name, the impression, what we do, because consumers demand it. It's becoming more and more important that consumers understand the companies that they're purchasing their goods from. Sean Fields (15:42): I think of it historically, you've had dirt bags that just go find stuff and use it until it literally disintegrates, right? They like to go climb and they don't have a lot of money because they like to climb. So just being conservative with their money and looking on ways that they can just do what they love to do. That's all they do is resell, use stuff. So there's a huge push for that. But specifically in the outdoor industry, there's an awareness of the damage that we can do with the things that we make. Yvonne Chouinard says, the only way to be sustainable is to not buy anything. (16:50): We know that that's not realistic, and Patagonia realizes that that's not realistic, but they put their funds and their efforts into mitigating that as much as possible. And that's where we come in with being able to educate people on how to take care of things that if you just buy it and then it doesn't work and they toss it, then all of a sudden that has an impact. So we internally have a program where we upcycle all the marketing materials that we use. Not all of 'em, but as much as we can into new things. So our fabric banners, we turn those into the little pouches and little satchels and things like that, creating old into New. So there's a big push for that, and there's a lot of people that are doing really, really great work in that realm. But I think also getting deeper into the product development, designing for repair, looking at materials, look at processes, supply chain's a big thing. All of that goes into it is really under the scrutiny. And big brands like REI, Patagonia, north Face are doing huge work in that as well. And we try to be involved as much as we can as well. And then that starts to open up the ability to start to be creative again and to solve problems through just relaxing and getting out there and doing something that's not work related or your traditional day to day.

Today I'm sitting down with Todd Bischoff, the global creative director at Gerber. Todd, how are you?

We've been around since 1939 and through all that, the company's definitely grown and evolved over the years, but ultimately, we're an outdoor brand. We're rooted in all things outdoor from camping, hiking, fishing, hunting, foraging, anything and everything that you like to do outdoors.

And so, yeah, there's definitely, when you think about all things outdoors, from survival to camping, to just going back to tools in general, a knife is definitely a tool that's needed and relevant in that space, whether it's hunting, fishing, camping, building, shelter, making fire.

And so with that, like we mentioned, we get so many consumers that are telling us about their first experience with Gerber and how long they've had their knife and how they got it. And those stories mean a lot to us. And over the years we haven't really truly presented those stories and told those stories. And so part of my role is to bring those stories to life through not only legacy products, but through a lot of our new products, new innovations that we have, as well as just all the activities that we're relevant in ambassadors and consumers that participate. So, so I oversee a team of creatives that include graphic designers, packaging designers, copywriters, oversee social media, pr, as well as our ambassador program. So everything from campaign development to packaging design to naming products, to coming up with crazy wild events. It's all part of the brand story and what we're after.

When we were chatting earlier, you were telling me a little bit about the history of Gerber, and I think it was surprising to me, I got to assume it would be surprising to other folks as well, because you guys weren't always a gear manufacturer. Knife manufacturer. Tell us a little bit about that story.

Todd Bischoff (05:17): Yeah, so again, it's one of those stories that wasn't really told. And it's interesting that Gerber actually back in, I believe it was around 1910 or so, but Joseph Gerber, Pete Gerber's father, those two started a advertising agency here in Portland, and they over the years developed this reputation for creating these handmade knife sets that they would gift to their clients in and partners during the holidays. And they became so well known for these handmade gift sets that Abercrombie and Fitch actually requested to bring these to life and more of a less gift giving and more of a product line into their catalogs. And so that really took off in about 1939 when Gerber Legendary Blades was born and it went from this holiday gift idea to knife brand.

Cole Heilborn (06:33): So was it just like one day when they said, we're going to close the agency and just start making knives?

Todd Bischoff (06:37): I mean, I don't think it was as simple as the flip of the switch, but I do feel like they were onto something and they realized that people enjoyed receiving this not only custom made gift, but high quality and premium. And it's super ironic because every year as a marketing department and team, it's like we always talk about what are we going to gift our partners? This year the bar was set pretty high with them. And so it's just kind of ironic and a cool story to tell that they started off as an app, especially me as a creative and being in marketing and advertising. This company started in those roots and has now evolved into this tool.

Cole Heilborn (07:33): Talk about a 180 and not being afraid to ditch what you were doing.

content: Todd Bischoff (11:35): No, no. And leading up to that point, the brand had evolved quite a bit. And over the years, the logo and the identity and the brand, obviously in that amount of time, things change and evolve, however, that story hadn't evolved and experience. So from that day on, we set ourselves this goal of we will never go back to that point. And we wanted to have this experience where engaging with consumers and not just being a brand that throws features and benefits and products over the wall and supports them with pricing. And we wanted to be more than that. We wanted to be truly that outdoor brand in that and that energy and that vibe. And so progressively got better and better. And the following year at Outdoor Retailer, we had a bald eagle in our booth, and that became known as the or Eagle. And it created such a buzz where people were just lined up and stacked in to get into our happy hour event. And we had at that point too, we started partnering up with a local brewery called Boneyard Beer, (12:58): And they started doing small batch of custom made brews for us. And so we wanted to break through, we called around the office, we like to positively disrupt, and so we wanted to break through all the other craft beers that everybody was serving and have this limited run special time. Only get it now in our booth and you'll never have it again. And so driving that excitement with having a bald eagle, having a beer that nobody else will probably ever have again, that drew a lot of crowd and a lot of buzzing. So we started thinking around, Hey, we're starting to connect with people. We're starting to engage with them and entertain them and bring them in and get them comfortable and start sharing our stories. And so year after year, it just started getting, it's like, okay, well, we had the Eagle and that set the bar, and so how are we going to go above that and how are we going to go above that? (13:52): And over the last five years, it's evolved from Eagles to tattoo parlors to, we almost had a 1200 pound Kodiak grizzly bear trucked into the booth to what I feel like is probably one of the most exciting events we've ever had.

But it was to the point of it was so executed from a team aspect as well, just logistically getting the Guinness Book of World Records adjudicator out having, we had to basically tear down half of our booth because the world record we were trying to attempt was the most beer can smashed and in a minute with an elbow. (15:02): And so everybody was like, how does that relate to Gerber and what's the point of this and why are we turning down half of our booth during prime selling time to put on this event? And it took a lot of planning and a lot of thought and a lot to go into it to get the confidence in the company to allow us to, for two hours basically tear down half the booth and prevent people from selling, showing products. And it was insane. We had people lined up for, I think six hours to get into the booth that day. And it seems to be a normal thing now where come 12 o'clock, one o'clock in the afternoon, people are starting to line up for our five o'clock happy hour event. But yeah, this world record, it was a highlight. We had media come in, we had special ponchos made, so everybody had these big ponchos standing in line

Cole Heilborn (16:01): Splash zone.

Todd Bischoff (16:02): Yeah, everybody boneyard flew out and they again made a special brew for us to support one of our US made autons that we were launching at that event. So it all came together. content: Todd Bischoff (18:29): Yeah, I think honestly it's getting to know who our consumers are and what their interests are and what they like to talk about and what they're passionate about. And you hear all these stories about somebody getting their first knife or their first tool, or for a while, Gerber was the number one supplier to the US military with Multitool. And so within the military and tactical space, Gerber's the Kleenex brand, and everybody says Hammy or Gerber, it could be six other brand of, but we're that brand. And so coming up with these events and stuff, again, it's not just about drinking beer and partying. It's more or less, I shouldn't say any, but it's like most consumers that we've talked with and we've interviewed is when they go out on a hunting trip, it's nine out of 10 times. It's a failure. But there's always a story that comes with that. And there's chances are that on the way home from that hunting trip, they're stopping at the local watering hole and they're going to share a pint with their buddy and talk about it. (19:42): Or when they're out fishing, there's so many fishing stories out there and the same thing on the way home. They're likely to share a beer with their buddy and talk about the one that got away, or just it's common things that people enjoy drinking a beer and hanging out. And so it's those simple things that come together. It's how we can connect more and engage more and sort of open the doors a little bit further. And with having a tattoo parlor in our booth, it's like what? That has no significance to knives and multi tools. But when you think about it, all these people that have served or people that have these moments in time that they want to remember, and a lot of times people, they'll get a tattoo to remember a moment in their life when something happened. And it's that sort of mentality of you see somebody that's got a tattoo and it's like, oh, man, I got a tattoo, or there's a story. (20:37): What's that tattoo mean then? So we were able to solely evolve this. I always rewarded our product managers for every US made product that they brought to market.

I mean, we had a contact sheet of 13 different designs that they could choose from one of those being the Gerber logo. And two people ended up getting that on. And that's two people out of hundreds of thousands of people attending that show. But those two people are going to have that logo on their body forever, ever probably. And they're going to remember, they're going to think back at that event that one day that they were in the Gerber booth and they got that done. And so it's not necessarily trying to appeal to everyone, but it's those moments that quality over quantity, those two people, that means something. And that's cool.

Cole Heilborn (23:32): Yeah. So you said the key to, I don't want to say unlocking, but building this brand loyalty and this brand enthusiasm has been through understanding who your customers are. What internal changes or mindset changes did you guys have to go through to start thinking about who your customer was?

content:
Todd Bischoff (23:53): Yeah, so that's a good question. It is tough because we say we have the burden abroad. We don't just make knives. We don't just make multi-tool. We have a whole spectrum of tools and gear that we make, and it covers across many different activities from hunting to fishing, to foraging to camping, backpacking, everyday carry to military, tactical. I mean, it's hard to just mean something to everyone. And so we really wanted to take a step back and just go back to our foundation and who we are and what we stand for, and truly the outdoor industry where our heart and soul is. And over the years, it's the military side of things and the contracts during times of war, that impacts our business because those products excel and those orders come in and those sales go up. And so there's always this shift in depending on what's happening in the world, and as we're in a pandemic right now, it's like people are buying tools and knives, and there's this fear out there that they need this stuff before it disappears. (25:16): And so we struggled or are we a military tactical brand or are we a camping and hiking brand? And so there was always this battle and it came down to just a lot of research and development. And just from a marketing side, it's easy to talk to yourself. We sit around in a room like all of us creatives and everything, and we toss out all these ideas, and at the end of the day, it's like, are we talking to ourselves or are we talking to the consumer? And to go a step deeper, it's like we shouldn't be talking at them. We should be talking with them. We should talk to them as if they're our buddies sitting in that bar stool next to us, sharing a pint, talking about the deer they missed or the fish that broke off the line. So we did a lot. We took our time and conducted a lot of consumer research studies and interviewed consumers and just collected a lot of data and a lot of facts and just to kind of support how we needed to go back to our foundation, our roots of where we came from.

Cole Heilborn (26:31): So now how do you describe yourself

content:
Todd Bischoff (26:35): Now? Honestly, our focus is again, coming from the outdoor aspect of it. And truly, we're a hunting brand. We're a fishing brand. We just launched this huge line of fishing products. When you think about people that there's a lot of conversations and opinions around hunters and anglers and is it catch and release or are you the ethics? Are you just out there to get something to mount on your wall? There's more to it that, yeah, we can't make everybody happy. We're not going to try and be everything. But what we truly believe in and what we want to support is that hunting's hard. Fishing's hard forging is hard, but what's meaningful is that you're outside. You're getting connected to nature. (27:34): You're out there providing for yourself and your friends and family, for somebody, especially coming out of a pandemic where you have to wait in line to get into the grocery store, and you get in there and the shelves are empty and you get back home and it's like you panic a little bit versus you look at the person that hunts every year and has that freezer stocked full of meat in their garage. I don't think they were panicking too much. There's a lot more meaning behind saying, Hey, I went out and I harvested that elk or that deer provided a freezer full of food for my family versus saying, I drove to the grocery store, purchased that meat, not sure where it came from, and came home and cooked it. And so again, it's that story. It's that adventure. It's that nine out of 10 times that hunt ends up in a failure, but they keep going back out there and there's this energy or this call to do that. And we want to be a part of that, and we want to support those people with the products they need to help them hopefully come home successful.

Cole Heilborn (28:52): Well, that's a whole nother podcast topic, like hunter ethics and all of that. But I mean, I think it seems more respectful to the animal to go out and harvest it yourself versus buying it from some supermarket where it wasn't free range or out in the woods,

content: Todd Bischoff (29:58): Yeah, I mean don't, there's not really an equation that we follow to disrupt something, but I think it just depends on what it is. I mean, for example, two years ago we launched our entire fishing line of products. And when you walk through any retailer, say Cabela's, whatever it may be, you walk through those aisles and all you see is Ziploc, baggies, clam shells, plastic, everything. And when we were bringing this product line to life, we knew we wanted to enter this space. We weren't the first people to enter this space. So you got to think about, okay, are we just showing up? Are we coming in just guns blazing and just out of control, or are we coming in with meaning and purpose and then doing so how can you sort of disrupt that space? How do you break through the threshold of the aisles and aisles of plastic and baggies and plastic in general is just a big topic, and especially from an environmental standpoint and what's happening and cleanup efforts in the oceans and waterways and stuff. And so one night I woke up just with this, I had this dream of out in the river fly fishing and a piece of our packaging floating past us, and I was like, okay, we got to eliminate plastic from our packaging. And from that moment on, that's how we were going to positively disrupt that space and introduce this product line. It's like we were going to, in what people are comfortable with and are used to seeing within the fishing category of all that plastic, we were going to come into that space with no plastic. (31:59): And for us having knives, that's a big deal. I mean, having a completely exposed knife blade at retail, nobody has done that. (32:11): And if you look at our fishing line of products that you go to any retailer and see that product on the shelves and pegged, it's everything from knives to pliers to whatever tool it is in the fishing category. There's no plastic. And so you can touch every aspect of that product and experience the grips, the textures, the cold hard steel, the filet knives. I mean, it was exciting. I mean, it sent ripples out there. Our legal team was definitely a little nervous.

content:
Todd Bischoff (29:58): Retailers were a little nervous, but at the end of the day, it's like what? I mean, we want to make sure that everything we're doing has meaning and purpose. And yes, it's the product. We're out there promoting new products, but it's also packaging is a big part of the product, and they're selling features and information on the packaging, but also it's the one thing that the consumer is going to just, they don't keep the packaging. (33:22): They're not buying an Apple computer and afraid to let go of that box. This is what people are used to seeing in a clamshell or a blister or a baggie. And it's like they're not going to keep that. And so we wanted to make sure that the packaging that supported this new innovative line of fishing products truly resonated with that consumer from an environmental standpoint as we want to make sure that we're helping to support those waterways and the environment just as much as we want to see you out there in that environment. So yeah, in a sense there, it's like we can positively disrupt a trade show by hosting against Booker World Records event, or we can come into a retail environment and disrupt a space by doing something that nobody else has done before.

Cole Heilborn (34:10): So you can do it on the large scale, you can do it on the small scale, you can do it in between. It doesn't have to be huge. It's just doing something different is what it sounds like.

Todd Bischoff (34:20): And a lot of times it can be overthought too. I think a lot of people come in and that's why we call it positively disrupt. A lot of people just come in and fucking disrupt the space, and it's bad. And you got to be careful with it. And I think that all comes down too, to just knowing and understanding the consumer or the audience that you're talking with.

Cole Heilborn (34:43): Yeah, no, well said. So what's the future of Gerber look like? Is there going to be another 180 switch in its future? Are you going to go back to advertising or, I don't know, jump into something else?

content: Todd Bischoff (34:54): I joke around with them because just my history of coming from the apparel industry, I joke around every day that I'm going to turn it into an apparel company. But no, we're always after maintaining that leadership position in the industry and making sure that we're staying ahead of trends and consumer insights. And so right now it's really just, it's not so much coming out with all this new stuff, but it's really going back to, again, Gerber became well-known for their custom quality gifted knife sets that people wanted and inspired to have. And so truly, the product lines that have been coming out over the last couple of years are just, I mean, the quality for the price is nothing that we've ever done before. And so we have all this momentum with the brand and building this culture and the abilities to engage at a deeper level with our consumers. (36:01): And now the product line is matching that too. We're not the most expensive product out there. We're not the least expensive. We're within reach. And so we get a lot of like, oh, that's cheap and made overseas, or Why can't you make more? If that was made in the US I would purchase that. And it's like we are always going to have those consumers that are either unhappy with the price or where it came from, but at the end of the day, it's we're trying to just make sure that we're producing, we're not fixing something that Snap broke. It's that quality over quantity. Making sure that within our price range that we're providing the best quality materials. And if that can be done in the us, awesome, we're going to do that. But if it can be done better and overseas, then we're going to do that because that's what's best for that product versus trying to let one or the other dictate what that needs to be. And so, yeah, I mean, super excited about the product line. We have a lot of, again, about half our products are us made, and so just trying to maintain that balance of supporting local industries as well as being able to, some things you just get better overseas than you can here. So yeah, so I think just from the next steps for us, it is really just connecting with those outside hunters, anglers, forgers, as well as just bringing to market the best quality products that we can for those activities.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:02): Welcome to the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. My name is Cole Helebo and I'll be your host today. This podcast dives deep with leaders of the outdoor marketing industry as they discuss the gritty details of their work, personal challenges and latest adventures, whether you're standing in the lift line, shuttling the fresh loam, or cracking a local beer. I hope you enjoyed today's episode. This is the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. This episode is produced by Porch Line Productions, an outdoor, commercial and film production company based in the Pacific Northwest. Let's make waves. Welcome to the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Eric Porter. He's a professional mountain biker. He rides for a number of different brands, I think most prominently, maybe not most prominently, but Diamondback is one of your big supporters. Eric, how are you?

Eric Porter (00:52): I'm doing awesome. Yeah, thanks for having me on.

Cole Heilborn (00:55): Thank you. Thanks for joining us. You're calling in from Utah today?

Eric Porter (00:59): Yep, I'm in the Park City area of Utah.

Cole Heilborn (01:01): Okay, right on. Quick shout out before we jump in. Jill over at Alta Cycling for connecting us. She was on episode 14 and she connected us and a couple months later we're finally sitting down and recording.

Eric Porter (01:15): Yeah, she's awesome. She's been great to work with.

Cole Heilborn (01:18): Yeah, she was a lot of fun to chat with and dive into branding and how to manage brands. For those of you that haven't listened to that episode, she works at Alta Cycling. They manage five different brands. Diamond Back is one of them, and she dove deep into how she is. A small team manages five different brands, so if you're interested, go check it out. But Eric, tell us a little bit about yourself. What's stay in the life of a professional mountain bike athlete look like?

short_description: "When you find a sport that you love and you're able to go do it and get out of the real world and go ride a bike. It's the best feeling ever."
show_notes_excerpt: Eric Porter has had quite a career as a mountain bike athlete. The highlights include being the first rider to grind handrails on a bike, competing in slopestyle for 8 years, then filming and traveling for multiple big free ride videos. A few years ago, however, he reached a point where he asked himself what do I want to do? His career as a competing athlete was slowing down but he still had a burning passion for bikes and adventures. In this episode, Eric shares how he re-branded himself, work…

content:
Eric Porter (01:46): It's all over the place. It's same as what it's always been, but different like everybody. So I have a lot of aspects to my job. The main one is being to be in magazines and videos and TV shows, all that sort of thing. So I'm getting exposure for the brands that sponsor me and that I work with. And it's typically more than just a sponsorship. I usually do a lot more with those brands as well, and that's something that I look at as a value add as an athlete. So I also help with product development. I also help with PR things and just really try to be able to do whatever the brands need me to do to better support the selling products. Basically, that's what makes this all happen. They're not just sponsoring me because I'm good at riding bikes, which is something that everybody thinks when you're getting into it. I want to be sponsored because I'm good and because I want free stuff. But the bottom line is that my job is to help them get their name out there and create a good image around their brand and in the end sell products because if bikes aren't selling, then I don't have a job.

Cole Heilborn (03:02): Right. Yeah. So tell us a little bit about your background as an athlete. What has that journey looked like?

Eric Porter (03:10): Yeah, it was kind of a interesting one. I grew up in Louisville, Kentucky, which is not known for producing professional mountain bikers.

Cole Heilborn (03:17): You guys make bats?

Eric Porter (03:19): Yeah, Louisville sluggers right there, and I was just lucky enough to have trails that I could ride from my house. So when I was 12 and it was time to get kind of a big kid bike or an adult bike or whatever, we went to Kmart and got what we could afford, which was probably a hundred dollars mountain bike. And I just started exploring the neighborhood and then beyond, which took me to Trails, and then I got a mountain bike magazine and found out that there's a whole sport about this. And then my first job was at a bike shop going into college. I was on the mountain bike team, which was, I was the only kid in high school that mountain biked or snowboarded.

Cole Heilborn (04:01): Oh, wow.

content:
Eric Porter (04:02): Yeah, so I was definitely not doing the cool thing, which awesome. It's awesome. That is now. So then going into college, there was a mountain bike team there at Western Kentucky University, and so I started racing Collegiate, did well with that, raced the Novas, and I was trying to make it as a downhill racer, but the whole time while I was trying to race downhill, I was dirt jumping and riding street and doing all kinds of fun stuff on the side when I probably should have been training, but I was having fun and doing what I wanted to do. And eventually that ended up being kind of a movement in mountain biking, which was street riding and dirt jumping, and I just happened to be in the right place at the right time (04:51): And surrounded myself with the right people through racing with Aaron Chase and Jeff Linsky and Kyle Abbott and those guys who were kind of pioneering that and fell into filming with them, which ended up leading to a magazine cover. It was, I mean, everything's connected. So the guy that shot my first cover for it was Flow Magazine was the best slalom racer in the Midwest, Scott Hart. So anyway, and at that time that was actually grinding a handrail on a mountain bike without pegs, which no one had done before. And it was just something that made sense to me and it worked out. So that got me my first Joel Smith, who's another industry legend and used to run a magazine and his dad's Malcolm Smith, legendary Moto guy that cover produced my first, he gave me just a cold call, Hey, I'm the Manitou guy, you have a fork sponsor. And of course I had nothing. So yeah, one thing led to another there, which slopestyle started at the same time. So the first crank works, I did really well on that and all of the dirt jumping slopestyle contests, and within a year I had a job riding my bike.

Cole Heilborn (06:08): Wow. So how did you go from dirt riding, dirt jumping wasn't really a thing to then competing in slopestyle and a year later having brand sponsorship. How did that happen so quickly?
