Eric Porter (06:24): I think it was just, I'm not really sure. I mean, it was something that was happening in mountain biking, so the media was looking to cover that, (06:36): What was going on, and I was one of the names that was doing things and I was pushing the boundaries there with what you could do on a bike. And we were kind of doing BMX tricks on a mountain bike and originally on streets, and then we started doing that in the mountains, building cool features on trees and dirt and everything as well. And then the industry really got behind it because they wanted to be a part of it. And so that's when slopestyle, they realized that that was such a great way to showcase what people could do on bikes and get a crowd. It's not always easy to get a large crowd for a race because you can only see 'em cross the finish line at the end, whereas this is a full on spectator sport, and Whistler has thousands and thousands of people crowded around the base area watching a slope style contest. So it's a really spectator friendly sport as well. Yeah. So that was from then for the next eight years, that was my primary job, was competing in slopestyle. So there ended up being kind of the world tour of stops all around in Europe and everywhere else, and then in between the contests we were filming video parts and yeah, it was really cool.

Cole Heilborn (07:53): What type of progression did you see in the writing and Slope style over those few years? I feel like you go to a Crank Works now and you watch the Joy Ride event and it's nothing like what it was. It's progressed so much, the rider have changed so much.

Eric Porter (08:08): Yeah, I would say it's kind of as crazy as it's ever been because every year there's new tricks that have never been done in a contest before, and that's the way that it was then too. So it was even the very first year back flipping a 30 foot jump was not a normal thing. (08:28): And that was my first crank works. I got second place, it was called Joy Ride that first year, and it was because I was, for whatever reason, it made sense to me that I could back flip this big jump. It was, and then it kind of went through this phase where they were trying to see how big they could make things go. So the features just got bigger and bigger, and then there's 20 something foot vertical drops and there's 60 foot gaps, and they wanted to see how big the sport could go. And then now they've kind of reeled it in and arguably made it quite a bit safer. I think there's less injuries and better success rate of runs and it's better than it's ever been, and it's still really big, but it's actually made safer and not trying to push the limits of what the riders can do as far as the biggest thing ever, but make it look good as well.

Cole Heilborn (09:28): Sure.

Eric Porter (09:30): Yeah. Same thing with Rampage where it's like, it's always been as crazy as it is. It just keeps getting crazier and the level keeps coming up as well.

Cole Heilborn (09:40): Right. Yeah, that makes sense. Okay, interesting. So you competed for a long time. Eric Porter (10:56): And so I wanted to pull that in because the more I thought about it as well, what you're doing in a contest setting is a spectator sport and it's really cool, but it's completely unattainable to anybody else. And second of all, I saw that I'm not a personal fan of vlogs and someone holding a camera and talking for 10, 20, 30, 40 minutes and saying everything they're doing. And I've hated that part of Twitter and Instagram and everything. I think it kind of ruins your heroes a little bit. I don't want to see Sean Palmer making coffee. I just want to see him winning. So then Bryce Winker, who was the marketing manager for Diamondback a few years ago, he was a fan of Seth from Seth's, spike Hacks, probably the biggest or second biggest personal YouTube channel in mountain biking. So I ended up getting to be really good friends with them through being teammates and doing stuff together and learning more about it. And the more I looked into it, this YouTube was where people were going to get their information and going to not only learn how to do something, which is if you need to do anything, you YouTube it now so you can watch a video of how to do that skill, whatever, but also for their entertainment. So they're going there instead of TV instead of any of these other places because they have it everywhere with them on their phone and it's free. And the other thing that I realized is it's the personal connection. So they're following people on YouTube because they want to feel like they're hanging out with them and going for a ride with them and that sort of thing. So it's really a different experience from watching an anthill video. That's the craziest cinematography and riding ever. (10:09): We went really deep with 'em. I think at first Haley was kind of like, wait, why are we thinking all this stuff? And we sat there and figured out what kind of car would this person drive? John Holdmeier (26:06): I would say the biggest challenge of this whole year in this whole brand refresh process has been the scale of everything. So we try to do a good job of stepping back and kind of keeping the big picture and the big goal in mind and just reminding ourselves of why we're doing what we're doing.

Cole Heilborn (27:39): Yeah. That's great. I'm curious, how did you keep, a year ago you were like, okay, we got to go down this path. We have all these things to do. And so it was really cool for us to be able to sit down upfront and kind of take the time to say, these are the things we know we don't want to be, and these are the things that we do want to try to be and plan it all out that way.

But really the brand was born out of a long-term effort that I had to simplify the things that I own, pair down the gear, pair down, especially the clothing that was in my closet and get to a few of my favorite things as opposed to just so many options, so many shirts, so many pants, all that kind of stuff. And so really what we're born out of is owning less stuff, but better stuff. (04:53): We're going to make a few things and we're going to make 'em as high quality as we possibly can and then iterate fast to make 'em even better as fast as we can as well. Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (05:51): We started officially in 2018 beginning, and then we launched our first Kickstarter campaign in September of that year. And then we've done another Kickstarter the next year, and then we've kind of gone on to direct sales, but pretty in the market for about two years.

Cole Heilborn (06:10): Okay. And how many products do you have? Do you offer?

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (06:15): Currently we have two available. We have the flex canvas pants and the high wool fleece, and the high Wolf fleece is great. It's a polar tech high LT body with a polar tech power wool panel. So in layman's terms, what that means is very breathable and if you put a shell over it, it's very warm. And the wool panels while being stretchy and warm are also anti odor. What's funny is though, and why we focus so much on pants now is that we've been outselling pants to fleeces three to one. Even when we were sold out of pants, people have been the world kind of said, Hey, I'm not sure we need another black fleece, but you're onto something with these pants. And so coming up, we're actually launching a new pair of pants called the Ecot Trail Pants, and they're built on what we've learned from the Flex canvas, but they have zero cotton content. (07:05): They're a nylon spandex blend, and the nylons actually source from recycled ocean buoys. So it's really cool, it's really sustainable. But they've also, from a performance standpoint, they're great. They've got a good drape, they've got a good feel, they wear well, but they also stretch, they wick sweat incredibly. They're DWR, they're coated with a water resistant treatment and like I said, building on the same fit and a lot of the same features as the flex canvas pants, but something without cotton. So a lot of our customers want to take one pair of pants, and if you're going to go out for many, many days and you don't know what the weather is, you prefer to have something that's a full synthetic. So (07:46): That's coming out in October. And then we're actually offering a women's version of the Flex Canvas pants, a fully featured women's version with deep pockets and everything that the men's version has, which is something that's been important to us, is not to just offer not as good product for the women's version. And then we're doing shorts to follow up with that next season. So really below the waist and building on what we know, which as a small brand is really all we can do, and we don't want to overextend and overpromise and we feel like we can really do well in this category.

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (08:50): Right. I mean, it's a big part of, like I said, there's a lot of philosophy that's gone into this brand from the start. Before I ever started designing products, I wrote down our company values and our production principles and how we design products and how we go about this process. And it's really a quality over quantity approach. And when we have a small product assortment of something that we've really designed, that we've really tested that we really feel confident in, then we can really market it. We can really talk about its benefits, pros and its cons. If someone wants to ask, Hey, is this the right pan for me? We really know how to answer that question. And from a QC design financing everything, it's just easier when you have lower product count. We can really control that process. We can fund it easier. We can take less inventory risk putting in all of our eggs in one basket. (09:44): And some people are listening saying, there's an obvious con to this. There's a lot of risks because if that doesn't work, which is true, but I think there's more risk in putting out 12 products for your first collection of 10, of which there's no way you can really guarantee that they were developed well, they were prototyped to the fullest extent and they were qcd as they came off the line. If you're a new company, I mean, hell even, it's hard enough if you're a big legacy company, some of these brands have thousands of SKUs in each collection and they cycle every season. You can't guarantee quality at that level, no matter how many employees you have on your team. So like I said, it goes back to the DNA of what we do and how we think about it. It goes beyond just the kind of marketing and it goes into how we actually operate, and that's part of it.

Cole Heilborn (10:29): Yeah, no, I love that. That goes down the whole topic of sustainability within the industry, which I know you're something you're really passionate about when it comes to marketing. How have you guys decided to position yourself, talk about what you do, what's your approach?

content: Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (10:49): Yeah, it's hard. So I'm a wordy person, especially when I write, and I want to get the value proposition for what we do outright. I want to tell the whole story. I want to start with the genesis and the thought behind it, then get to why we did it and then the product and then how it supports that. And most of our actual advertising happens on social media. So our actual paid advertisement is Facebook and Instagram ads for the most part. And you just don't have the time or you don't have people's attention to really tell that story. And so we've been going through a pretty big trial and error process to try to market, especially on social media without using cliches, without losing people along the way. And without what I say, it's losing our soul. So it's tricky and the way, I'm not saying we've found the secret sauce yet, but there's some things that we've figured out that at least I feel comfortable with because I work with external marketing firms and I work with people that typically, especially in the Kickstarter and crowdfunding, you see a lot of all caps and this is the best jacket that's ever been built and this, it's very subjective of hyperbole. (12:00): And so I work with them and say, Hey, we don't want to do that. And they look at me like, oh, well you just kind of cut off our left arm. But what we found is that we can find the true value propositions for what we do that aren't subjective. So you don't say best, but we say this is really good. You say high quality, which is somewhat subjective, but I think it's objective if you really kind of know the product, we talk about the features that people are going to get, why they're good. And importantly, like I said, you don't have a chance to put down all 15 features of a pair of pants on a social media ad, but we will make several different versions that key in on one feature with an image of that, (12:48): And we'll test those.

(13:46): And especially in social media advertising closeup shots has been extremely powerful and we've been baffled sometimes We've gone through several rounds of studio shots for our products, and the first round was not very good. Lighting was kind of blown out. It was a version one of the pant, and we'd even change it since then. Our hypothesis is that it showed the stitch work, it showed the detail, it showed the fabric texture, and those are all things that are really hard to see on online shopping. (14:23): How many times have you bought something, a jacket or a pair of pants or even a backpack or a piece of gear that looked great in the shot, but you can't zoom in, you can't look at it, and you get in and you're like, ah, it feels cheap. The stitch works bad, this seam is sloppy. And so I think what we keyed in on there is that showing that detail gives people a lot of confidence in the product, even though that ad didn't even show the pants as a whole back pocket and it's been the best we've had.

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (15:57): What works and doesn't work on social media? Marketing really sometimes just baffles me. But like I said before, I think it's mostly because people are getting a sense that maybe we are a high quality because we're confident in showing the details of what we build. And that's something, it goes back to having a low product count. And one thing we really do well is there's not a stitch or seam or detail on this pants that hasn't been analyzed and analyzed again and redone and kind of minutely tweaked, which by the way, factories are not huge fans of that, but they're willing to play ball, right? We've gone through, I don't know, at least 15 if not 20 iterations of these pants because I wear them every day. Most of my friends wear them every day now. And so I see them on myself, I see them on them, even if they're too kind to tell me. (16:48): I look at a pocket and I'm like, that's flaring a little too much. So the next time I'll say, Hey, let's take a half inch or a quarter inch of ease out of that pocket opening just to make sure that it doesn't flare when someone sits down. And what I think people are responding to with showing that detail is that attention to detail. They're getting some confidence that this isn't a drop shift item from China that 20 other vendors sell. This is something that was designed with intent and a company that cares about what they do. And so we try to sell that aspect too, which is we are really trying to make a quality product and we have a customer service team that's going to answer your call and we have this warranty that's going to stand behind it, kind of get over this. It's 2020. I don't trust anything barrier that a lot of people have towards new products, which I think is a healthy skepticism.

Cole Heilborn (17:41): I think it's warranted.

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (17:43): It is. And I'm not saying they shouldn't have it. We have to fight, especially if we're not going to play the game a lot of those companies would like with the all caps and with the ridiculous call to actions and everything like that, we get to really break through that in a way that feels okay to us.

content:
Cole Heilborn (18:02): Yeah, interesting. So when you were outlining your, I guess we'll call 'em Andrew's rules of marketing, you said you've outlined those because you don't want to lose your soul when it comes to the marketing work you guys do. Have you lost it before?

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (18:19): No, I don't really think so. It's just more I'm been an outdoor consumer. I've been a cut consumer period for my whole life. We all are, and I'm just not entirely happy with the way the whole, I'm not going to say industry products in general are progressing in the world. There's just so much stuff being built and every niche, even the niches within the niches are being filled. And a lot of the times it's not because it's a great product, it's just because it's an okay product and it was built specifically just to make money out of that hole in the market. And then it was marketed by a firm that's good at marketing. And so that kind of thing. And we want to make something new. We want to make something new that deserves to exist, and if it doesn't, we don't really want to do it. (19:08): And so like I said, I don't think I've lost it now or lost it in the past. The previous brand I worked for Fayette Hill, we tried our best to market responsibly there too. We mainly made a t-shirt, which most people don't need another T-shirt, but we tried to do everything that we could to make it as good as possible. So made in USA organic cotton, recycled polyester, we did community support, we did nonprofit support, we did events. That was kind of our way of saying, Hey, we're making something that people maybe don't need, but we're going to try to atone for that. (19:40): And going into this, I didn't even really feel like that was even the best way to do it. I really wanted to make a product that deserves to exist on its head that for the sake of it, if nothing else, no brand, no anything, no extra support for the community, no nonprofit or anything, which we're going to do and we do do, but I want that product to exist by nature of people see it's high quality and they end up using it and get back. You mentioned sustainability and I'm passionate about it and I skipped over that for marketing talk, but that's really my chief view and our chief view it lives in of sustainability is just build things that deserves to exist. Don't build things just because you think you kind of have a hole in your lineup and you need to fill it, right?

If you're just making a hat to make a hat, it's just, and I'm not going to paint myself into a corner and make a bunch of enemies. (20:46): There is value to creating income for yourself. There's value in creating a company and jobs, and that is inherently something that we need in this society. So I'm not demonizing people for just making your brand to make money, but what is it that makes what you're doing worth it? And especially environmentally. So our view, like I said, is the product needs to deserve to exist, have some sort of use, but then falling right on the heel that if you're going to make it start in the design process and make it durable, start in the design process and make it versatile and then follow that up with a real warranty and stand by your products and help that product stay in lifecycle longer. Because the most durable, the most sustainable product that exists is the one that already exists. (21:38): So durability is really the most sustainable thing aspect of any product. It comes before, whether it's made with hemp or organic cotton or recycled polyester, it doesn't really matter. Okay, I will say this, it matters a little bit, but more than what a material is made out of making it in the first place is going to use a ton of carbon. So if you're going to make a product, right, and you have to weigh something that's made from an eco-friendly material, it's going to last half as long for something that's made from a raw virgin material that's going to last twice as long, you're going to use a lot of carbon getting either one of those to market. You got to ship it, you got to make it, you got to do all the things to service it and get it to the end consumer. So personally, I think making the more durable product is better, and that's what we launched on, but with the intention of following that up with environmentally friendly materials. So we moved to organic cotton, recycled polyester. Like I said, everything, all those products are listed out earlier are either organic or recycled for the vast majority of their content.

So we got this paper twine and a recycled paper hang tag. Oh, cool. Wrapped up. We ditched everything, plastic and everything, single use out of that process. Everything's recycled and recyclable. But that's after we earn those things as a startup through getting out into the market. And that's all somewhat subordinate to me, to making a durable product and making something that's repairable and also helping people get that done. We have an infrastructure to do it right, they can send it back for repair, but it's also educating the consumer and reaching the consumer that's going to buy with the intention of keeping something for a long time, keeping it in surface, wearing that same pair of pants, and if they have a rip in it, repair it. That's something that I'm very passionate about from a sustainability point of view is just this idea of don't build so much stuff and what you do make it durable. And that's just not what's going on in the grand scheme of things with product development,

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (24:13): I mean, it's in our DNA, I think it's in a lot of the outdoor industry companies. DNA too is just the way in which you get your value proposition out. And if your value proposition is sustainability and durability, I don't think you're going to get that out correctly or authentically to use a buzzword in the industry or even convincingly if it just looks like every other piece of crap that you see on Instagram feed. From a messaging point of view, I think there's people out there that are into long form content. There's people out there that want to read and research the details. There's people out there that want to look behind the scenes of a company and figure out who it's and what they stand for. And I think that there's just a little bit of a difference in the way that you have to market to reach that person to break through that. (25:04): Like I said, that initial barrier of this is all bs, right? And so we're figuring it out. I'm working with firms that do crowdfunding marketing, and we're having to do a little bit of that stuff. They're like, there's some things we're going to do that you may not feel a hundred percent comfortable with, but we're keeping in mind everything you told us. I'm like, okay, we'll see if I see the ad and I like it, we'll have to talk. But so far it's working. And like I said, they do run parallel, but I think they're kind of one in the same. If you have an intention to do something a certain way and it's deep in the value of how you want the business to behave, and if it's part of the DNA, then it's going to flow through everything. It's going to flow through the product, it's going to flow through the marketing, it's going to flow through the messaging, it's going to flow through your operations.

Cole Heilborn (25:55): Yeah, well said. That makes a lot of sense. Where would you like to see, well, lemme back up. Lemme rephrase that. How would you like to see advertising and marketing change, not just in the outdoor space, but in the, I don't know, just the world and commerce?

content: Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (26:20): That's a good question. Hence the long pause. If I could wrinkle my nose and give my wish, there'd just be less of it, but that's not going to happen. So I'll just kind of put it back to sustainability. I would like to see more authentic values-based marketing from companies talking about what they're doing to actually address environmental issues and sustainability and clean up their act. And that's not just outdoor industry, that's all industries. So I'd like to see that not just from, like I said, value when people know your values are, but it gets it more to the mainstream. And I think what it will do and is happening is it's somewhat taking the onus of responsibility for environmental change off of the individual and onto the corporation and the company. And what I mean by that is everybody, I try to live a sustainable life individually, but individuals acting sustainably and using their single use straw versus a plastic one contributing the most to global climate change. It's actually companies and it's it's companies. And so that's not to say the individual consumer doesn't have a place in this. I think what the individual consumer does have the job to do is vote with their wallet. And if companies put out their views, what they're actually doing, not just greenwashing, but what they're actually doing to change their ways and act responsibly and environmentally and consumers then follow that up by voting with their wallet and buying their products, then we can actually affect change at the top. (28:05): So just to clarify, I don't think people should start using plastic bags and ditch their aluminum straw, but because that's also, like I said, kind of voting with your wallet, but I do think that the narrative and the responsibility needs to be shifted more to the top from the bottom because that's where the real change is going to happen. I think people can help make that happen.

And I feel like we've hit a point now where the only way you can compete is either have go really high quality or you have to go just constant messaging, low quality, high volume. What's your take on, I guess that concept?

content: Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (29:57): I mean, I think no matter what product you make, I think you have to market it. There's this kind of old stereotype of you're either a product guy or you're a marketing guy, or you're a product company or you're a marketing company. And there's this idea that if you're an artisan, if you're a craftsman, if you really love your product, that marketing is somehow unholy. It's dirty. And I don't think that they go hand in hand. And your marketing we've talked about before doesn't have to be dirty, doesn't have, you don't have to lose your soul to do it. And I think that now at least to start, unless you have just, I will qualify this, different levels of funding at the start can allow you to do different go-to-market strategies and launch a brand or a product. But social media marketing and kind of pay-per-click marketing and things like that have really lowered the bar to entry for a brand to get out into the market and compete directly head to head with the biggest players out there. (30:58): And I think that that is both a good and bad thing. It's led to this rise of a bunch of brands that probably shouldn't be around, but it also lets somebody that has a good product get in the market. And I think you have to play the game a little bit. You make a great product, how are you going to get it into people's hands the first few times? So you have this kind of easily accessible outlet to do that through social media and Facebook, and you can very cost effectively market. Now, you can also waste a lot of money. I'd recommend people hiring a professional if you're not very good at this, but you can get your part out there and then you can start to do the things that let you spread by word of mouth that is delivering a good product that delights people. (31:40): That's like number one, you get the sale, they get a product and it's better than they thought that it was. They're going to tell their friend about it. That's when you get into this, no one's going to grow. And if your business only relies on social media like return on ad spend, you're going to go broke. You're never going to grow organically.

content: Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (29:57): But if you have that and then you follow it up with a good product, and then the next step is you actually have the systems in place, so the people, or at least the intention to stand behind that product. So say you send the wrong size or does it fit or it happens, there's a production issue with the product and they contact you and they get a real response from a real person and you help 'em figure it out. That's how you kind of grow that, like you say, quality or mass marketing. (32:28): There's somewhere in between. You can use the marketing channels, but you actually follow it up with quality and you'll, people know that you are a real person and you're a real company and you have a good product. And it's funny, I used to do customer service at the last company I worked for. I started the whole process and everything. There's an inverse relationship between how mad someone is when they initially email you and how big of a supporter they'll be if you take care of them. The more expletives and curt sentences that were in the email and the length of it, if you take the time to actually kind of address those things and get that person taken care of, no matter what, it takes the bigger fan, they're going to be coming out the other end. Totally. And that's something that's like, I think in the outdoor industry, it's understood. (33:11): The outdoor industry cannot be faulted for customer service practices. Usually that's likes just the water we swim and you got to have great customer service, but across just general consumer goods, that is not the case. We get emails from people that are just so rude because, and it's not because the people are rude, it's because that's typically the hat they had to put on to get a response. The more angry you are, the better you get taken care of. It's like the cable company rule or something like that and one kind of courteous response, that whole demeanor goes away and it turns into a real person. So anyway, that was a long answer to your question, but I don't think it's as black and white as the initial proposition. I think that there's a way to play the game well.

Cole Heilborn (34:00): Yeah, fair enough. We're about out of time for today, but one of my last questions for you. What's your hope for the future of Lipson? Your two years in, what do you hope for two more years or the next 10 years?

Andrew Gibbs-Dabney (34:15): Yeah, we just launched wholesale side of the business and brought on some really great independent reps. So we're looking for really great retailers. So my hope as someone that's lived and breathed the outdoor industry for as a consumer and then someone on the other side. For most of my life, I want to see this in the best stores around the country, the ones, the independent shops, specialty shops that really have that great floor staff that knows they're talking about that live the lifestyle that help people buy the best products. That's where we want to be from a product standpoint. We're going to slowly expand what we do. We're not going to stay in pants forever, but we're going to do that until we feel like we need to move out of that space into the next thing that doesn't exist in the way in which that we'd like to see it exist. (35:01): And so my goal is to make the absolute best, and I'll use it now because subjective, and it's my subjection or my point of view, the best products in the industry. When I say that, like I said, it's subjective, what that means to me is that they're durable, they're extremely versatile, they're comfortable and they fit well, and you turn 'em inside out and you're not let down. So there's refinement, and these are the qualities that we look for when we design and as we go through the prototyping process. If they don't hit that, then we don't release it. So in two years and five years, we want to be a, if not the leading brand in those categories, right, in the outdoor industry. But if someone's looking through the lens of durability and versatility and refinement and fit, it lives in to be synonymous with those things. And that's where we're headed, I think.

Cole Heilborn (35:52): Yeah. Yeah. Well, I'm excited for you guys. If people want to follow along, if they want to find more, learn more about the products you have to offer, where can they go to check 'em out?

(13:14): And ultimately it came to a point where I was go, go, go, and it came the holiday time and I didn't know what to do. I had two weeks free at the end of the year. I was kind of just like I could do whatever I wanted. I could go up to Mount Hood and go skinning or just go for a long run, and I was paralyzed. I couldn't do anything. And I started to have these daily panic attacks that just completely paralyzed me. And it was such a weird journey for me because although I've always been an anxious person and I've always had anxiety, it wasn't to a point that it was affecting my daily life. And then when we came back on to normal schedule after the first of the year, I was supposed to go to Germany for some meetings and I had packed my bags, and I just remember sitting on the couch looking at my packed bag just thinking, you couldn't pay me a million dollars to get on this plane. (14:22): I was just terrified of nothing. And that ultimately kind of made me retake a look at my life and relook at how crazy is this that I'm feeling this way from being so burnt out, but also just neglecting my mental health in this world that should be the most fun. So ended up making a lot of lifestyle changes that I don't think if I would've made before or I know for sure if I didn't make those lifestyle changes before this last year and a half would not have been, it wouldn't have been possible for me to do and do in the average way that I've done it, I guess.

And I definitely believe that being under the sky up in the mountains on a trail, whatever it is, is amazing medicine. And I think getting kids outdoors too is going to be really important as the next generation grows, not only for the business to be able to continue to boom and get people into the sports and buying the stuff, but also just from a mental health aspect as well. And then the other side of that is that performance culture and the us, and I can't speak to England as much, but the US is obviously so rat race driven. (23:39): And I think there's some beauty in certain cultures like climbing for instance, this dirt bag mentality that it's more about your accomplishments than the materialist side of it. But even that, I think can have its downfalls where it's still performance driven and you're constantly seeking to be that the top. And I think we as a culture and we as an industry have to find a middle ground to say it's okay to people to get outdoors and enjoy it and still work hard, but you don't have to work so hard that you're not getting outdoors too. And (24:25): My European counterparts do it right, for sure. I mean with the amount of time that they take off and the bank holidays that they get and everything else. So I think it's just also just a cultural shift for the us and a lot of our industry too is freelance. So it's like you have the hustle and if you're making money, you got to be constantly having that brain switched on and thinking about things, whether you're a videographer or a designer or whatever. You're constantly out there and it's so hard to turn it off and just enjoy. Patrick Tullos (32:57): Yeah, probably the largest one is just doing this, what we're doing right now and just talking about it and normalizing it. Because I think when it comes to anxiety, at least part of the things as you close up and in order to let it out, that's how you release it. And it's so hard to let those things out if you don't have the ability or the opportunity to talk to someone. So for me, it was seeing a professional for sure, but it was also talking to friends and family and people I trust. And I had a couple of really solid mentors within the industry as well that really helped coach me through that time as well. (33:47): And then also medication, which is another huge, huge taboo topic to talk about. And I was deathly afraid to go on any sort of medication. Actually, the reason I kind of was okay with it was Conan O'Brien actually was talking about how he's on SSRIs, and I was like, wow, that is a trip that Conan O'Brien is. And it kind of made me feel like, okay, I'll try it. And honestly, it's changed my life. It just took a fog out that I didn't really know was there. And I don't know, I feel like there's a lot of people, and it's not the answer for everyone, but for me it definitely helped. And then all those other things I talked about too, obviously exercise is important, creating the time for yourself, meditation, healthy, eating, everything else, but those are probably the most important ones. The other ones don't. It's not like a magic pill or talking to someone will make you feel all better, but it's really a mix of all of that that just allows you to view things differently. And so part of being a brand that's going to move forward is saying, let's take a step back and set ourselves up for big growth opportunities and really start diving into what this community that has been huge brand evangelists for us want to see and what's important to them and what do they value while still tying back to who we are and what our mission is. And so we really reevaluated how we're coming to the market, and we decided that we were going to take a regionalized approach and really focus on the core of who we are, which is the safety messaging going back to the first glacier rope that actually held you on so you didn't die while you were not married. (13:36): And taking that message and saying, this is who we are. This is resonating with our consumers, and let's pull all the levers and turn this up in these areas. Maddie Petry (14:48): Yeah, I think a lot of go through this, we kind of get in a state of, Hey, we need to be everything to everyone. And that's an easy trap to fall into. And I think that comes with a lot of different directions. The market's changing consistently. There's a lot of unknowns. And we said, okay, we can't be everything to everyone. That's not who we are. That's not who our brand is. So let's take a step back and really evaluate what's important to us, what aligns with our mission, what aligns with our values as a company and the goals that we want to accomplish, and how are we going to do that? And so instead of trying to spread our message across a product skew, we have 4,000 products in our categories and trying to spread that across all of North America, we said, okay, what are the products that make the most sense for the consumers that again, are our most influential consumers, the people that are true brand evangelists that are helping us craft this message for us, (15:47): And where do they play in these places? How do they play and how do we start to reach them? So we really took our marketing a step back and we said, okay, we're going to focus on these two markets. So for mammo, it's Colorado and Western Canada, and we're going to really speak to these consumers in a way that's going to have continual touch points in their communities. So they understand who we are, they understand the products that we're making, we're going to consistently innovate upon so that they can achieve what they want to achieve in whatever outdoor activity they want to do. And then we're going to introduce new products that make sense for them to help them achieve those goals. And so yeah, taking it from a giant objective down to a more focused objective and saying, these are the people that move our brand and these are the people that we need to be speaking to in a consistent and I relevant way.

Maddie Petry (17:13): I think the challenge is really playing a long game. It's easy for brands to really think, I have to see quick results. This has to happen right away. But for us, it was a process of creating a space for our community to come to us and listening and learning as marketers instead of always saying, this is who we are, this is how we want to do it, this is how you need to play, this is how you need to wear our gear. Allowing for that space of learning about our consumers and what's important to them and what they value, and kind of marrying that process of learning while also marketing into a way that was going to create growth for Mout. And I think it's always scary to take a step back and say, Hey, we need to look at this from a smaller scale, a more impactful scale to set up for long-term growth in the future. And so it's something where we had to really say, okay, trust the process. Know that the efforts we put in now, the ROI might not come for another two years, another five years, but we're setting up that foundation so that we can be successful in these areas in the future.

Maddie Petry (19:41): So for us specifically in North America, we've done a really good job of speaking to the core group. The people that are at the top of the mountain, the people that are very experienced, they know the product, they've been on the product for years and years, they trust the product. I think where our challenge is is being at the top of the mountain and coming down the mountain to speak to those people who are just getting into these sports. A lot of times they use the bike analogy. If you're going out and doing an Ironman for the first time, you're not going to buy a $15,000 bike, you're going to buy a bike that you can test out, see if you like it, and then you move up your bike, whatever you want to call it, you move up in the tiers of getting a better bike, having the carbon wheels, whatever it looks like. (20:36): And so what we had to do was come off this expert level of the top of the mountain, come down the mountain a little and say, Hey, the education that we do with these experts, the focus that we put in allowing them to be part of our brand, the conversations we have, we have to also have it with these people who are just starting to get into the sports and then funnel them up through those tiers. And so it's been kind of a balancing act of what are the campaigns, the initiatives, and how are we speaking to these consumers that's going to hit both those newcomers and those natives and be meaningful to them? And a lot of that is the education part of it. How do we educate these new consumers on products that's going to really help them achieve their goals? And how are we going to educate these experts on product that's going to help them achieve their goals and marrying the two together?

Cole Heilborn (21:36): Yeah. You're speaking to two very different camps there. You're speaking to Camp five and base camp. How do you craft the messaging, or how do you engage both of those groups in equal ways or maybe not equal, but in the ways that they need to be spoken to?

This is a place where people want to teach you. They want to make sure that you're comfortable in the outdoors. And especially from a brand side, we want to make sure that everything we're doing on our end makes you confident going into that space. And so that's one area where we touched on, whereas we work with the professional groups on safety and we have an avalanche program manager who's going deep into multi burials and what that looks like and how our equipment is really designed to make sure that you're doing your job the best you can as fast as you can. content: Maddie Petry (27:24): It comes from experience, and generally people who are in the outdoor space do it because they're passionate about it and they experience the outdoors both from a newcomer level to an experience level. So for me in particular, I was very comfortable in the ski space. It's the space I know very well. My whole family's done it. I'm ingrained in it. I've done it since I was two. I competed in it and felt very confident in how I shopped as a consumer, how I experienced the outdoors as a consumer in that space. But when it came time to, I don't know why I chose to do this, but I signed up for an Ironman one year, and I had zero bike experience. I had zero swim experience. I was a very novice runner and decided to do this crazy thing. And I was at a very beginner level and I was seeking out any information and any education I could find on people who had been in my position and how brands helped bridge the gap of, this is the equipment you need, here's how we're going to reach you, here's what this looks like, here's some training options. (28:39): And I found for me in particular that there was just a lack of that, and it was really frustrating to me. I wanted to see more. I wanted to understand how people, even from the basics where they put their bottle cages on their bikes and what swimsuit they had to do laps in the pool, and it just coming from this very expert level to this very humbling, beginner level kind of touched, I guess it struck a chord with me, (29:08): And I felt like I could really relate to the people that were coming to the outdoors for the first time and weren't getting that information they needed, but also on the ski side was like, Hey, I'm an expert in this space and I need you to really step up what you're talking about so that it makes sense for me as I try to accomplish some of these bigger objectives. And so having that experience really allows you to go into these marketing situations and say, okay, I understand this sector and I understand this sector and I understand how I need to a bridge the gap, but also how to speak to both of these sectors in meaningful ways. And I think so many people experience that in the outdoors where you kind of silo in into one sector and say, yeah, I'm getting expert level here, but when you try something new, you're not sure what that's going to look like for you as a consumer or as a participant.

We make what you would probably recognize as the green insole or the blue insole, but we also have a lot of new technology that's out there that has 3D foot scanning and gate analysis. We have 3D printed personalized insoles, and all of it really is designed with the idea of giving people an affordable, easy option to be as comfortable as possible. So we had a lot of doctor referrals, people that have major foot pain, plantar fasciitis, tendonitis, stuff like that. But then we also make products for professional skiers and runners and people that just really want performance and great comfort out of their footwear.

Cole Heilborn (04:00): I think every person who is ran at least half a mile is probably familiar with your insoles because they make such a difference. It's pretty incredible.

So yeah, all of those sports that really require you to be on your feet and give your feet take a beating Superfeet is there for you, and it makes a huge difference.

I had been a user of Super Feet, but actually met the CMO of Superfeet through the Conservation Alliance, and we started talking about what an amazing brand Super Feet is and how they're a hundred percent employee owned and what they had been doing for the past 39 years at the time for the community and what they wanted to do in the future. And it just sounded like this perfect mix for me, this trifecta of amazing well loved product, really great innovation and a vision for what we could be, and then just a strong ethic and great community, a great community builder, which I think is really important to me. So those three things put together, plus when I came up here and met the team, just such a strong group of individuals and really fun people, it was hard to say no to.

Linda Balfour (05:59): Yeah, so super feet's a member of the Conservation Alliance, and we have been for, since probably the year before I started, so five or six years now, I've been really fortunate to be on the board of the Conservation Alliance for four of the years that I was at Super Feet and four years prior to that. So with that, we get to go out to Washington, DC and lobby on behalf of public lands. We do a lot in the community as far as getting employees outside and volunteering and doing trail work or helping with cleanup with the Whatcom Land Trust. So it is funding great work, but then also putting the manpower and the sweat equity behind building the community that we want both here and wherever we sell our products.

Cole Heilborn (06:43): Yeah, that's well said. So as the VP of marketing, what do you get to do?

So when COVID hit, we looked to our brand truths, and one of 'em is people first and our leadership team and our executive team really did everything that we could to put some measures in place really quickly to make sure that our employee owners were well cared for, that everybody was going to have a job at the end of the pandemic, and that we were really making some smart moves. And so some of that stuff was really difficult. It looked like short work weeks for some people and reduced budgets, and of course, you always get a reduced marketing budget when you get reduced budgets. So we really had to think about what it was that we were doing and how we were serving our customers and our consumers the best, and then also just making sure that we were taking care of each other. (09:51): So I think COVID on a personal level was amazing for Superfeet because it really brought us closer together and as we're, I wouldn't say coming out of it, but as we're looking forward, it also really did make us look hard and long at what it was that we were doing and what we wanted to do, and then how we could do some of it faster. So like I said, we were founded in 1977, and one of the things that drew me to the brand was that we really are, while we are this really trusted brand by people in the industry and well loved by our retailers, we're also a really innovative brand. And in some ways we operate a startup. And I think that was really, it started, that mindset started from our founders and has just stayed with the company all of these years. And so back at the very beginning, one of the reasons that Superfeet was founded was that our two founders had looked at the market and realized that 80% of people who needed orthotics had a similar kind of foot problem that could be solved by a similar shaped insole. (11:04): So they introduced the first orthotic grade over the counter insoles. Dr.

And when you look at all of the studies that are happening right now, or if you just follow intuitively what you know, that change is not going backwards, right? Retail will always hold a place in people's hearts, and it will always be important brick and mortar retail, but online is going to become more and more essential for brands and for retailers as we move into the next phase of consumerism and shopping. So I'm now just talking, I don't even know where I started. (13:11): And it's a fun challenge, right? Because going to a running store website for a different reason potentially than you'd go to super feed.com and you're shopping differently on Amazon than you would at their running store website. So really understanding how shoppers are using each of those sites and how to best serve them on those sites is really important to us. But then also, I mean holistically, honestly, I probably shouldn't say this, but I don't really care if people shop on superfeet.com or if they shop on your specialty outdoor store.com, right? In fact, I would probably prefer 'em to shop on specialty outdoor.com because we need those retailers to really help curate and build this outdoor experience for us. (22:57): So I think we're looking at this world of how can we be the next generation of retail? How can we act like a digitally native brand even though we're 40 plus years old and bring everyone along with us, or at least support 'em in their quest to do the same thing? Because outdoor is changing, outdoor participants are changing, the way that people shop for outdoor is changing. And so how do we be as innovative as we were when we launched insoles? Now, how do we relaunch insoles online? Do we make buying them easy no matter where you are? How do we make it real easy to find no matter where you're shopping?

How do those two pieces work together? So I think while being a well orchestrated, really solid marketing team has always included being a good storyteller and working well as a team, we've just had to make kind of subtle shifts in the way that we're doing that in order to really do that well in an online environment. And so I think it's a skill. It's just strengthening your skills. It's kind of cross training a little bit, I guess. (26:10): So that's one thing. I think the other thing that has been, I don't know that it's a skill, but I mentioned our retailers a couple of times, and retail has always been really, really important to us, and relationships are really, really important to us. And so I think we've had to be better at working with our retailers, not only in that online environment, and how do we give them the tools that they need to be to be this destination really interesting, rich shopping experience when somebody is in, but then how do we get people also to embrace this idea that we are after that the world is after, which is that we also need to be equally strong online. And I think COVID definitely sped that up because retailers who never needed a website before all have 'em now. And so they're there and we're there for them. But that was definitely a skill or something, I would just say maybe an area that there was a little bit of a gap that we needed to fill.

And while we do a lot of things, including both of those, we started off seven years ago deciding that we didn't want to ski and ride on skis that were kind of the whole shrinking and pink it thing. We weren't really satisfied with what was available to us. We just kind of waited around to see if anything better would come out on the market, and it kind of never did. I think we got to a point where we realized that we were sort of transitioning from to a platform, so people were showing up and wanting to be a part of what we were building regardless of whether or not they were skiers or snowboarders, regardless of whether or not they skied or rode on our product. So we recognized that and we also began to recognize the responsibility that we have as essentially privileged white women in a privileged sport that we created this platform, and if we started our company based on a mission of inclusivity and diversity in snow sports, we really needed to walk that talk. And so looking at all the different platforms that, all the opportunities that were there for us to essentially open up this platform to other people and to stories that sort of challenged a dominant narrative in snow sports became really critical in terms of us upholding our values and also being responsive to our community as well.

content: Jen Gurecki (08:41): I would say at the beginning, it felt like a fight. It felt like we really had to push in a big way for any recognition people. I mean, snow sports with a lot of outdoors, it's just like, are you a cool kid or not? Do you know the right people? Do you have who holds the keys? Do you know that person who holds the keys? Do you? And we didn't come from the industry. We are just women who like to ski and ride, and we've been doing it for decades. And so we weren't industry insiders. Nobody knew who we were. And so when we launched, there was certainly disbelief, I would say. People were like, who cares? Who are they? Also, it's just a lot of not believing that we were capable of designing skis and snowboards and creating a product that was performance driven and outstanding. (09:46): We don't look like your typical ski bum. We don't look like your typical ski manufacturer or brand, and we never have. So I think at the beginning, it really felt like we had to pull out all the gorilla marketing tactics that we could. We had no budget, we had no connections, and we just had to really think about what was our competitive market advantage. And for us, it essentially was and still is, we're the only feminist ski company. We are owned by women. We're run by a hundred percent of what we do is women focused, women driven. And so we just really, that's what we know. So we went with it. And there's never been, I think what we've seen over the years is another thing that makes us different is that there's not a team of marketing professionals sitting around a table trying to come up with a campaign or what should we say? (10:42): Everything you see and read and hear is just a hundred percent real, real talk from us. It's how we feel. It's how we perceive the world. And I think that that's what really resonates with people is that authenticity over the years, because we have remained consistent in the way in which we show up in this industry and the world, and because we can continue to be responsive to our community, I would say that now in year seven, it feels more like a celebration than a fight, and it's still certainly difficult. I mean, I'm the dumbest, smartest person you've ever met to start a hard goods business in a seasonal industry that's male dominated. I mean, I don't know what I was thinking, but it does, I think that we've earned the respect and the recognition that does come with so many years of hard work and failing and succeeding and just picking ourselves up and just deciding to do this every day and really working hard to show up for people. So yeah.

In this episode, the CEO of Coalition Snow, Jen Gurecki shares her perspective on starting the company, becoming a thought leader, and giving a voice to underserved individuals in the snow sports world.…

content:
Cole Heilborn (11:56): What type of response have you gotten from your audience? How did they feel when you guys entered the space and gave themselves a voice where they could connect and just have conversations? What was that like?

Jen Gurecki (12:11): I think that it's important to acknowledge that not all women are the same, and not all women appreciate us. And we can see that right now happening politically where not all women represent all women. You can't put us in a box. So I would say that when we first started, there were heaps of women who were like, wow, this is amazing. Finally, somebody's here for us and we're being listened to and we're understood. And then there were other women who were like, just shut it up. Just shut it. Get out of here. There's not a problem. Everything's fine. Why are you so loud? Forget about it. Right. And that continues to be the case. We are not for everyone. We talk about things that some people do not like and they don't like the way that we talk about it. And that's okay For us, we have decided as a company that as long as we're being honest and true to ourselves and staying in line with our values, then we're not here to make everyone happy. We're not here to serve all women, but we certainly know what it is that we stand for and where we're willing to toe the line on that.

Cole Heilborn (13:23): What type of backlash have you received? Did that get in the way or did that deter you as you guys were first starting out?

Jen Gurecki (13:30): No, I mean, I just would say it's like your typical backlash that any strong, outspoken women get. It's not unique to snow sports. This is just life. And I think that that's probably why it didn't deter us as I was like, oh, just another day. Showing up in this world as a woman, where I decided to use my voice and stand up for myself, and that makes other people not feel good about themselves. I can't be responsible for people's fragility, their insecurity, their unwillingness to accept change. There's a lot of different reasons why, or just they just don't like us. I mean, there's a million reasons why, but it wasn't new. It's not like I've lived a life of everyone giving me a pat on the back and telling me that everything I do is fantastic. You deal with things as a woman, and I'm a white woman, so even what I deal with is far less than what women of color have to manage. But so no, it did not deter me, I would say, actually, I was just like, oh yeah, watch this. Here we go.

Cole Heilborn (14:34): And seven years later.

Jen Gurecki (14:35): Yeah, exactly.

Cole Heilborn (14:38): So describe your own journey becoming a thought leader. What has that been like for you and what have you learned and what's the responsibility that's come with that position?

content:
Jen Gurecki (14:46): Well, I think that one thing that's important to acknowledge here is that I had a long career and academic experience prior to starting coalition snow. So I have a master's degree in non-formal education and community development. I dropped out of a PhD right before I was getting ready to write my dissertation, and I spent years studying feminist theory, critical race theory, economics, sustainability. So there's a lot of theory bound in what we put out as a company, and I think that that theory combined with experiences is what has allowed for the thought leadership to naturally occur. I think also prior to coalition, I ran wilderness programming at the University of California. I owned a whitewater rafting company. I've started a social enterprise in East Africa. I've done a lot of things. And so I don't know if I would be as prepared to speak to the things that I speak to now if it wasn't for those years and years of research in years of experience. And that just kind of goes back to what I said earlier, that this isn't a group of people sitting around a table trying to figure out what to

Cole Heilborn (16:15): Say.

Jen Gurecki (16:17): It just comes out of my head and either out of my mouth or onto a piece of paper and it gets put out there. I feel really fortunate that that is a skill that I have and that I've cultivated for two decades now.

Cole Heilborn (16:32): With that though, why do you think we're seeing such a, I dunno, we're seeing such a push for thought leadership in marketing across all industries. I feel like specifically a lot in the outdoors with that though, there's a lot of companies or individuals I think, who are real, who are authentic, and then there's those who maybe are just out there not backing up what they're saying and are just trying to reach that level of credibility without the credibility. I guess. What's your take on what we're seeing today in the marketing world when it comes to thought leadership?

content: Jen Gurecki (17:09): Well, we have changing demographics of consumers, and consumers want. They actually want to see a brand take on the persona of human beings, and they actually want to know who those human beings are, and they want to know what they believe in and what they do. And so this is fundamentally different. If you look at generations, older generations don't necessarily have affinity for brands. Younger generations do, and younger generations also, I think just based on what they've dealt with in the few years they've spent on this planet is that they really look toward a lot of different avenues for change to occur. And they want to see change, whether it's about healthcare or universal or education, the economy, they weren't born in a good time in this country. And so they really want to see that companies are doing something to make the world a better place. (18:20): So what we're seeing in marketing is being driven by the consumer, and so you have to be responsive. With that said, what I'll say is that what marketers or anybody in business should take away from this is that this isn't something that you can just Google one day and write about, or this is lifelong work. Understanding what these issues are and making change is a daily commitment. It's not something that you just roll out in a campaign and then you walk away from it. And consumers are going to be savvy to that, and they will do their homework to see who is what behind the messages. So this is where hiring the right people who have the experiences, the education, the training to be able to tell real stories is really important. And what's beautiful about it is that in and of itself could diversify the workforce in the outdoor industry because you cannot have a 40-year-old, cisgendered, straight white man tell the story of a 25-year-old black queer woman. It is impossible. So rather than try to tell it, get out of the way and let those people come in and tell their own stories and and help you do your job better. And I think that that's what consumers are going to respond to.

content: Jen Gurecki (20:33): Yeah, I think one obvious one would be Patagonia, the work that they've done around the environment, around voting. Just recently it was disclosed that they put a little secret hidden message on some of their tags. They have some secret code on their website. When Rose decided to donate her entire 10 million tax refund she got from Trump, that's big. So Patagonia as a privately held company has been able to do some, I think, pretty spectacular work. Obviously they have things to work on, and I think they're aware of it and they're speaking to that, but they haven't really been afraid to talk about the environment and to talk about voting. And that message does resonate to some extent pretty well with their target demographic. I think a lot of brands will be challenged the more that they talk about race and they talk about gender, because at the end of the day, a lot of people who are consuming these messages from the outdoor industry are cisgendered straight white men. (21:45): So I think there's some challenges there, but I think Patagonia does a really good job. There's a number of brands outside of the outdoor industry that I look toward because I actually don't see, I don't see the level, I don't necessarily see what I want to see in the industry. I do think that the outdoor industry is very conservative. I think that some people recognize that and other people also don't because they don't realize how their message is really catered to white men still. So I tend to look like Wild Fang would be a brand that I look at. So they're women owned out of Portland apparel and accessories, but have always been very outspoken. I'm very supportive of the L-G-B-T-Q-I-A community. One of their founders identifies in that community, so they've always sent it pretty hard. So I follow them. And then there's just a lot of, I'd say smaller indie brands popping up in the sort of lifestyle, health and wellness space that I spend more time looking at because they are talking about the things and saying things in the way that resonates with me. And I think that that's indicative of the spectrum of interests of women in the outdoors.

Cole Heilborn (23:19): Yeah. Okay. Very cool. Yeah, it's always interesting to hear what are some other brands out there that are doing really good work? And there's so many that I feel like we haven't heard of who are just plugging away doing their thing. For you, as you look forward for the future of Coalition Snow, what do you hope for the future of the company? And what are some things that you guys look at and you think, oh, we could do a better job at X?

Jen Gurecki (23:48): Yeah. Well, I would hope that I can be replaced soon. I would love nothing then to be able to pass the torch on to somebody who can do a better job than me. So the future of coalition is number one, sticking around still being here, which let's be honest, year to year, when you're a small brand in snow sports, you kind of really, you're like, oh, hope we make it to next year. So I would like for us to stick around, and I would like to be able to step aside and let someone else come in and take the company to the next place where it needs to go. And I also think that what we have been attempting to do over the last few years, and I hope that we can continue to do it better, is just really demonstrate that when we talk about being here for women, that we mean all women, that we mean trans women, we mean black women, we mean queer women, even to be quite honest, we could do a better job of acknowledging that they're non-binary individuals who our values resonate, but we are not necessarily showing up in the way that we could. (25:12): And I think that's where having other people step into leadership positions in the company would be a really good thing. But I'd like us to be able to do that. And part of sticking around part of a transition in leadership and part of really ensuring that we're staying true to our values is all of that leads to substantial change in the snow sports industry because the industry is privileged. It can be very toxic. And at the end of the day, the outdoors are for everyone, and skiing and snowboarding is super fun, and everyone deserves to be out there and doing it and enjoy it. And that can look different for anyone or for everyone. So I would just like to see that happen.

content:
Jen Gurecki (27:21): I would say that we don't live in a time where you can be agnostic to the massive social, environmental, and economic problems that we face. Your consumers demand more of you. The world needs you, and stop being afraid and get over yourselves. You will make mistakes. You will say things that will make people angry. You will likely have to make public apologies. I have done many. They are embarrassing. And then you get over it and it makes you better because you learn from it and really stop focusing a hundred percent on the bottom line. If you cannot make that change. Now, the people who you're trying to appease now who don't want to hear these things, they're not going to be your customers in the next 10 years. We know by 2042, the majority of people in the United States will not identify as white. Start looking ahead if you're struggling, because you could make this as a values-based decision of there is an urgency around these issues and we want to contribute to positive change. Or you could just make a good business decision because you pay attention to the future and any way you slice it, you have to acknowledge that there's more than cisgendered straight white men participating in these activities. So you better figure out how to get all the other humans to enjoy your brand, and you likely will alienate people and okay, because at this stage of the game, you're going to alienate someone. So what side do you want to be on?

Cole Heilborn (29:06): I love it. If we're about out of time, we're reaching that 30 minute mark, are there any, I don't know, resources or leaders? You mentioned a few brands, but who are some people that you look up to that if people just kind of want to get exposed to more of this type of marketing, this type of philosophy and business, where could people go to learn more or just get a taste of it all?

Cole Heilborn (31:44): Alright, well have a good rest of your day and enjoy the snow this season.

content:
Rick Wittenbraker (01:48): No, I've actually been coming back since maybe late July, early August. Not everyone is just sort of a select few. And during quarantine, we primarily left our office to the design team just because they have so many physical samples and swatches and fabrics and stuff that they had all this need for the physical stuff, and so we sort of left it to them, but we have enough space and we're kind of spread out enough that I can be in and out and not interfere with them or in any sort of risk there. So I've been coming back. I'm grateful for resemblance of normalcy in a daily routine, and it's been good to, at least across the room, have some interactions with folks. That's been good and helpful.

Cole Heilborn (02:49): Yeah, that's got to lift a lot of morale too.

Rick Wittenbraker (02:53): Yeah, it's good. And I think everybody's probably having these same challenges. You can certainly do a ton via Zoom and calls and texts and Skype and email, but I think what you miss are the interactions, and what we've found is that we're able to do everything, but it's kind of twice the squeeze for the same amount of juice. And when we're all together, it's like we maybe we got a question about how we want to do this or what's our approach on X, and if we're all together, we can knock it out 15 minutes. If it's all over Slack, well then that's like, oh my gosh, like a day and a half to get everything finalized. So for the interactions we have been having, I'm very grateful for it. It makes me feel like we're getting more done each day and it's less just the tedium of always being on Slack.

So I'm really curious to learn a little bit more about the brand and who you are, who the team is, doing a quick search and going to your website and looking at the Howler Bros crew. You guys, I love your direction, your vibe. You've got a very serious but fun tone. So I'd love to kind of dive into a little bit of who the brand is.

content: Rick Wittenbraker (04:34): Yeah, well, Haller Brothers was started by Chase Herd and Andy Stepanian, two of my partners and really good friends and probably two of the most creatively talented people I've ever met. And so they went to UVA together, they are still in a band together and being in the band and having the creative collaboration of music and then the work of making the band successful and touring and all this interaction together and stuff. So they have the sort of creative collaboration together. And then they had the sort of effort work side of that together. And it was, without going into the full encyclopedic history, there was an opportunity. Chase is one of the most talented people in the world and he was a fine art painter. He then decided he wanted to go an architect, so he went and got his master's in architecture and was a practicing architect. (06:01): And this is all simultaneous to the band, but so Chase and through his painting and his drawings and stuff had been asked by another apparel brand a long, long time ago to come up with some designs and he did. And then they kind of went off into the sunset and never ended up making his designs. And he was really bummed because he really was fired up to have these things come to life and to wear these shirts and things. And so he just never got the chance. And so that sort of sparked this idea of, well, what if we went and made those? Well, if we're going to make those, maybe we should, this certainly the band project, this is a separate initiative, and if we're going to do that, then maybe we should start our little company. Well, if we're going to do that, then we should really put some thought and effort behind what is this brand and what does it stand for and what do we want it to be? (07:11): And so he and Andy, I give them all the credit in the world. They really spent a lot of time fine tuning and crafting that even way before they were launched publicly. And so there was a lot of back and forth and a lot of collaboration there and a lot of hemming and hawing on what it is and what it's not.

(08:25): And so that you, in the essence was that you could go do any of these activities you wanted to do. In this instance, a lot of it was around surfing, saltwater fly fishing, being active up in the mountains on a given day might involve five activities and doing all those things but still wearing stuff that you felt was cool and look good. And now we sort of jokingly say has to work just as well in the bar as it does on the water. But I think especially back then it was, I don't want to say, oh, I'm going to do this activity, which means all this specialized clothing that I then as soon as I'm done doing that, I feel like a total dork in and I want to go change, and then we go do something else, I got to change again. And so it was really like, Hey, what can I wear all day? (09:20): It looks great, it's comfortable, is very designed forward, but in a laid back way, a lot of attention to detail, a lot of bringing design and creativity forward instead of pushing it to the back. And so that's kind of where they landed. And then the other thing really, you had asked about the brand and the brand part of it was they wanted to do something that wasn't about, it wasn't ego driven, it wasn't about me. Look what I accomplished, look what I did. It wasn't man versus nature at all. In fact, it was sort of the opposite, like, hey, if we go to this place, we can take this trip to go surfing and it's flat. We're still going to have an awesome trip even though the waves were flat or fishing, we're going to go take this trip with our buddies, but even if we don't catch a damn thing, it's still going to be an awesome trip because we're on this adventure with our buddies and it's really about the shared experience.

Rick Wittenbraker (04:34): (10:39): That's why it's brothers plural and not singular or not like me or a single noun there. And really about just these, because the moments in between tend to be a lot of the memories that you make and the best times and the stuff you laugh about. And when you think back on a trip from 5, 8, 10 years ago, it's less about a single instance and more about the sort of collection, this sort of photo album, if you will, of all these memories. And the stuff that probably stands out the most is either the funny stuff or the inside jokes that came out of that trip or the flat tire in the middle of nowhere or whatever. And so those things, and really not only appreciating those things, but almost like doubling down on those things is sort of the ethos that came out of a lot of this and that it's shared. It's about the adventure along the way and the journey and the moments in between is really where all that came from.

Cole Heilborn (11:57): Yeah, interesting. How does that mentality, the idea that it's about the experiences, about the memories, how does that affect, I dunno, the brand's decisions or how does that affect the decisions you make in the day-to-day today?

Rick Wittenbraker (12:13): Well, and since the launching and we've gone on to further refine and define this, and I think what's equally important is to define what it's not and what we, what do not do. And I think that really matters as far as putting clarity around it, especially for the team. We don't necessarily broadcast all the things that we're on the not list, but we do that from a practice standpoint and it gives you a good sort of check to say, Hey, okay, this image or this design or this post or whatever in the world it's going to be, is this checking all the yes list and then does this have any infraction on the no list? Because that's a good check. It's also a great way to help. Our brand is very nuanced and a lot of people can get 80 or 90% of the way there, but that last 10% is the real detail. We put a lot of effort into this so that when we bring new people onto the team or we're working with a third party, it really helps to articulate that better and we can get them up to speed faster.

Cole Heilborn (13:45): Yeah. Okay. So what would you say the average person can get 80% there? What's that 20 or 10% that they miss? And then how do you guide them with your knots and the yeses and the nos?
