content: Rick Wittenbraker (14:02): Yeah, well, I mean I think that there's kind of two sides to that coin. One is what are they interpreting about us if they were to go try and type it up? And with regard to that, I think one of the best things we can do is in fact be anything we're putting out into the world, whether that's a product or a message or an ad or whatever it is that all fits within our framework. And so if you really went to study all this stuff, you would start to see these commonalities or these things and you would say, oh yeah, that feels very howery. And then simultaneously this thing over here, or it's close, but it doesn't, just as a simple example, we a long time ago made the decision that we weren't going to post, we're not about grip and grins, and it's not that we don't like to see somebody holding up this fish. It really was just about, it's not about me, which at the end of the day, the grip and grin is kind of about me. (15:28): So it's not about me and it's about this shared experience rather. I think we would probably rather post something that was, I don't know, the moment before that or the moment after that or it got away or we broke the rod or whatever it is, the high five afterwards or something like that. Having a beer after you let the fish go, I mean something like that is probably more in our sweet spot. But the other side of that is just that almost every other brand that interacts with phishing posts or utilizes the grip and grid, it doesn't just have to be a social post. And so we wanted it to always be like, man, that's a, if you covered up the logo on the ad or you didn't know who shared that or whatever, that you still should be about 95% positive that that's us and not someone else. (16:43): So a part of this is the perception, and so where we try to control or manage that is through what we're putting out. And again, that's why we wanted to define all this stuff. The other side of that coin though is I do believe that there is, and that's sort of people looking at us was the first side and the second side is people acting on their own. And the fact that someone who likes Hower Brothers wants to incorporate us into their world, they might do stuff that we're ambivalent about or I don't know, well, we don't really do some activity that they love to do, but but they want to incorporate us in that. That's awesome. We love that. And to that regard, if they want to get real fired up about wearing their howlers gear in their grip and grin photo, hell yes, that's awesome. That's them. And so we fully embrace that and it's not a we're against this type of thing, it's more just like, Hey, we made a creative decision. We didn't want to do this. The fact that our audience wants to do that, like hell yeah. That's awesome. And that's them being usually is pretty happy and we're a part of that happy moment then hell yes. That's great.

content:
Cole Heilborn (18:20): Yeah. So when you're having these conversations with the internal team, I want to lay some groundwork or some framework as we move forwards in this episode. As you're having these conversations with the team and you're talking about what the brand is, what the brand isn't, how do you first define not necessarily your brand, but a brand as you're having these conversations?

Rick Wittenbraker (18:43): Oh man. I think first off I'll say I think the word brand is totally over and misused this day and age. And I think it's people misuse it to mean the company. People misuse it to mean logo. I think there's a lot of ways that it's sort of misused. I like to think of the brand as at a very high level as sort of the personality. And if you think about it like a character in a movie or a book or a story that it is a character and that character has attributes and does things a certain way, and you have a really good actor that can really get into a character. And it's not them, it's the character. And I think that is really what this is. And so we can go right or define a character and it has a way they talk, it has a way they act, it has a way they move, it has emotions, it has all these things, and that makes up this character. (20:15): It's not just it one of those, it's not just the way it looks. It's not just the way it talks. It's not just a logo or colors, it's not logo usage guidelines. And I think where it gets hard is you have, there's something like a consumer facing business like ours and something that makes a tactile physical good like ours, you have way more interaction with a person or your audience than say a software Dropbox, for example, which is software that I like. But other than that little blue box logo, there's not a whole lot that is from the brand, you know what I mean? And so it's pretty sterile and it's about trying to be easy to use and functional and all that, but just picking colors and using a logo isn't really cutting the mustard, at least in our world. And so we think the better, the more thought out we can make that and the more deeper and richer, and it doesn't even have to be articulated from a definition standpoint, it just has to be, I think really again, back to that character example, it has to be really well-written, so to speak. (21:59): And look, we always want to make it better than what we're doing and we're always striving for more, but hopefully there's a tone that comes out in our copy and in the products we make and in the videos we do and in everything that we put out and the products, and that's different than the next brand.

And the things that they might enjoy, and you might not be able to articulate why or how it fits them, but you can say, yes, this works, or no, this doesn't.

Rick Wittenbraker (23:03): Yeah. I think again, it goes to that interpretation from audience and team is a part of that audience. They're just more intimately involved and sometimes on the inner circle inside of that character. But it's just like to use this sort of nerdy example, it's not Harrison forward, we're talking about Han Solo. And so every time that you see Han Solo, it needs to be with that smart ass sort of commentary with it's a little cavalier, it's a little this he operates, we know he is a little bit of a troublemaker, but he's got a good heart. (24:23): So we really try to impart that on the team and we have to, if you really think that through it is in the products, it is in all the content and things we're putting out, it comes to the way we handle customer service and interact with people. And there's just like any person they have the way they act, the way they speak, the way they dress, the music, they listen to the stuff they like. Cole Heilborn (25:11): We've kind of laid the groundwork I think for how you would describe a brand, what it is, what it isn't, maybe ways to think about it back in March when the world rapidly evolving around everyone, you guys, everyone in the outdoor industry. How did brand, did you guys think about what was happening and what you should do or how you should act through the lens of the brand?

Rick Wittenbraker (25:33): Yeah. Well, that's a really great question and I think there's kind of two parts to that. One is what do we do as a company? And we as a company did certain things and maybe added things or changed things or we had to revisit just our financial situation and how are we going to operate and what are we going to do? What changes need to be made? We had to do that just like anybody else. It doesn't matter what your company is or what your business is. And so we did a lot of that. We were very, I think very fortunate that we're in a good position and didn't have to make any sort of drastic cuts and didn't have to do anything that had a long-term detriment to the business. So we're very glad about that. We did also from a brand perspective though, and from the Voice, we did decide that we wanted to come out and message everybody. And now that seems like 10 years ago that all that happened. But looking back on it, we really just wanted to tell everybody, Hey, we're all in this together. We're with you. We're still going to be out there. We're not going to all of a sudden turn into something else, but we hear you and I don't know necessarily what we can do, but we're here to help. (27:25): And so I think it was sort of a welcome when we sent that first email out and we weren't trying to sell anything and we weren't trying to get you to come watch some new video, we were just saying, Hey, we know you're going through this. We're all going through this, we're all in this together. We got a lot of feedback that it was a very welcome and appreciated message, even though we weren't really trying to accomplish anything. I think what it maybe reaffirmed in people's heads is like, yeah, these are good folks and they're not just in it to try and shove me to the cash register and they're not going to change who they are just because they're under duress and that we're going to march on. And so we did end up after that. We ended up doing a couple different efforts that helped some groups in need, especially around here in Texas. (28:36): And that was great, and it was a real easy decision.

We had all the product ready, we had all the assets ready, and we were ready to push go on this thing. And it's usually one of those things that sells out in no time. And we said, Hey, we don't feel right and it doesn't feel authentic for us to just act like all this stuff isn't happening and we're just going to kick this launch out the door and say, yeah, yeah, now we're back to normal. Give us your money. And so we said, look, I think this is a no brainer. This needs to benefit some groups in need. And that was still so early on in the whole Corona scenario that we didn't have yet a full understanding of the scope and the breadth, but we made it around these two Texas groups that were organized and help. (29:44): And so it was great, and it felt right, it felt good. And then from there we proceeded to get involved in a lot of other fundraising efforts and contributed to a lot of other campaigns and then even sent a bunch of old inventory to be turned into masks. We didn't make masks from scratch, but we said, Hey, we have these friends that this is what they do. They cut and sew stuff and then they're sort of converting their efforts into making masks, so why don't we just give you all this material? And so we were able to work with, actually there's three that we did that with our friends, Fort Lonesome here in Austin. They're sort of our longtime friends and collaborators, a really awesome lady named Anna Ergot out of California who makes surfboard bags and she's used to making 'em out of other fabric and those awesome coffee bean bags, those jute bags, so it's called Sagebrush board bags. (31:11): And so she makes those and used to repurposing materials. So I reached out, we had sort of connected in the past and I reached out to her and said, here's what we'd like to do. And so she made these incredible masks and it was really neat and we didn't ask, we don't want them, we want you to sell 'em as a individual maker. You can sell 'em Fort Lonesome, same thing. Some of theirs.

So for us it was like, Hey, here's a cool way to get involved. It's not about us. I mean, we were sharing their efforts, but we weren't making any money from it. But we made some business decisions around it and it changed maybe what we would have done during this time and maybe how much or what we made back then, which is now affecting us here and six eight months later. But all those things we made after we had sort of calmed down and everyone sort of caught their breath and normalized a little bit. And then we said, I think that despite all this, us hiding in a cave is not going to help us or them, anybody else. And so I think we need to get out there, but we need to be very mindful of the scenario and situation people are going through. (35:39): And so we also don't just want to go guns ablazing and act like nothing has happened. And so I think being mindful sometimes that's how you communicate what you communicate and then what we did. And so I think once we started putting stuff out there and we got back to our regular routine, there was an incredible reception. I think one of those things was that people were, I'm trying to think of a great way to frame this, but I think people were stuck at home and maybe a little stressed and maybe a little working from home and figuring out all this stuff and it's strain and stress and there was a little bit of escape. Oh man, I threw that funky shirt from Hower and I think I'm just going to order that or whatever. And I think there was also a bit of optimism that man, when this storm passes, I am going to go take that trip or I'm going to go do some adventure. And so there was this man, I want to get this because I want to be geared up. And even if it's not something you don't buy anything new, maybe it just said, you know what, man, I am going to go do that cross country trip or whatever it is. It doesn't matter. And so I think we got a very welcome response and reception once we did get back out there.

Cole Heilborn (37:17): What have you seen now that we're in October and we're what, eight months into this, obviously the industry, a lot of the industry seem to have gotten really busy really fast and now there's manufacturing issues. What have you observed?

Rick Wittenbraker (37:41): I think we've seen a whole host of different things, and a lot of that has been, there's slowed load, there's been a lot of, from manufacturing and logistics standpoints, there's been a lot of challenges and a lot of delays and things that you used to take 10 days now take 15 days or whatever it is. And so that's had to account for a lot of that. And it means that we've had to be nimble and flexible on a lot of different fronts, not just our back of house, but also the front of house and say, okay, well man, just because we had originally planned to launch this new stuff on the first, we might have to shuffle some things around and now push that to the 20th and do something else today. So I think it's just being able to adapt and adjust and not being so rigid because everything has changed. I mean the good news is that everybody's in the same boat, so everyone has an understanding of why things are maybe a little different than they normally were or than what they had expected. But I think that you can also use that to your benefit in a very sort of open and healthy way and say, okay, well hey man, it's all different now. They may have been headed towards closing shop or headed towards some point where they were going to need to sell the business or do something else. content: Nikolai (12:12): That's a fantastic question. Great question. And it's funny you mentioned Yvan because I don't know for your listeners that don't know, that's the founder of Patagonia, and everyone probably knows that, but let my people go surfing. His book on founding Patagonia and kind of their business unusual approach has been kind of our almost like company bible in North Star. And we have all of our employees, all of our contractors, we have read that book, and we've kind of held true to their mantra and Patagonia's way of thinking, which is kind of we're not trying to pump a bunch of cash into this business and blow it up to a bunch of VC money. We're trying to grow slow, innovate smart, grow intelligently and organically and just listen to our customers and provide incredible customer service for our customers, take care of our customers, make sure that they are satisfied through every step of the process. And if they're not, go above and beyond to make sure that they are. And that's our mantra is just what can we do to make our customers happy? And just focusing on that slow growth mentality that creates kind of that foundation for a very solid brand.

Jensen (13:46): In terms of how we focus on steering the brand, we rely on a number of things. So we have a lot of great mentors that we talk to just about. Anytime we're presented with a difficult decision, we first acknowledge that this is a very difficult decision, and there's other people out there who have been confronted with these kinds of decisions. So we just reach out to the smartest people we know, pick their brains, get a collective opinion on something, and then kind of follow our instincts and are kind of own mantras on executing and making that decision. With Obras. We also just, Jensen and I both, we really value quality. There's a lot of crap out there, and we try to just put our best foot forward in everything we do, whether it's content, whether it's product, whether it's customer service, customer experience. We try to make things easy for the customer. At the end of the day, we treat ourselves like our biggest customer in a lot of different ways when we're rolling something out and we're testing it out at first, if there's any kind of discomfort, if there's any kind of anything that makes it more difficult or any frustrating in any way, we try to be as hypercritical on that as possible and try to solve that before we roll it out to the rest of our customers.

Cole Heilborn (15:19): So it sounds like you're not so focused on the future, but you're really just focused on making the best decisions that you can that are in front of you.

Nikolai (15:29): I think by making those good decisions and really being hypercritical of the entire every step of the process, you're almost paving the way for a sustainable, potentially high reward future. And there's so much crap out there nowadays. There's so many brands and there's so much junk. And that's the last thing we want to do is create a product that is mostly petrol based and just have it break and get thrown away. That's not what we're about. We're about creating a product that has longevity. It doesn't have a planned obsolescence. We want this to be the last price sunglasses you ever buy, and if something fails on it, we're going to fix it rather than throw it out.

How do you think about it? How do you put language behind it? You mentioned that you have every person that you work with reads, let my people go surfing. What are some other ways that you, either between yourselves as co-founders or with the rest of your team, help everyone get on the same page and essentially get on board with where the direction's going so that everyone understands where it's going and your guys's philosophy behind the business?

Jensen (17:03): Well, I think first of all, we try to be very genuine and honest with everyone we work with, including ourselves, whether that's our customers, employees, contractors, each other. That's really the first step is being critical and honest and creating a good feedback loop from everything we do. We try to be, I don't know, Jensen, what do you think?

Nikolai (17:35): Yeah, I think that genuine, just being genuine is so important and authentic. It goes back to just the same goes for creating a brand as it goes to the way you interact with your factories or your manufacturers or your employees or your customers. As long as you're a genuine person, you have good intentions, good things will come of it, and you're growing and building the right way.

Jensen (18:06): And that's, at the end of the day, we know that we have a superior product. Ultimately, we're building something that is more comfortable, more durable, better in so many ways than the traditional sense, and it's reducing waste and it's offsetting more carbon than it emits. And we just try to do the right thing when it comes to all aspects of our business just about. And that naturally attracts the right types of people. And when we're interacting with our customers, we're trying to add value, not sell them. We'd rather have a good friendly conversation with someone than have a sales pitch, a successful sales pitch that results in them buying a few pairs of sunglasses. That's just more interesting to us. That's the way we like to live our lives is it's more of just creating those good relationships. And success comes from that very naturally and organically

Nikolai (19:06): That goes with the way we kind market owners as well online in our ads. We're not trying to just shove product down your throat and our videos and our imagery. It's more about harnessing the emotional tie and the feelings around what home Brew entails and who we are as a brand and as co-founders, well as just people. We are a customer. We talk to our customers and we train our customer service teams to talk to our customers the way that we would want to be talked to and the way that we kind of talk to a friend, because once someone invests in a pair of ERs, it's almost like they're part of this armless, sunglass family where they get it. You run into someone on the street wearing a pair of obras, and we've heard these stories countless times where people are like, oh, yes, you get it. Our customers will find each other wearing them. And they're like, you get it. These are freaking awesome. And so that's kind of like what we're trying to just encompass and have permeate down from top to bottom through our company, that genuine, authentic feel.

I ran into a few people in the mountains, these backpacking this past summer, and one of them was wearing a pair of obra, and I came up to him and I was like, Hey, is that a pair of obra? Yeah,

content: Jensen (23:59): There are definitely challenges with thinking about the future. Right now we're a two to four person company, so Jensen and I are pretty much the only ones full-time, still in the weeds a lot, and we are handling 35 different things every day. So it's really easy to get down in the weeds and work on that kind of stuff, that kind daily operational stuff a lot. But we've been taking more time recently to take a step back and really try to plan out our future and challenge and think about the direction we want to take as we're kind of peeling back the layers of the optical market. We're seeing so much potential here. We started out really focused on backpackers and the outdoor community, and now we're seeing a market opportunity everywhere from aviation to equestrians to construction workers and ballistic side of the fence with military and stuff like that. And it's really a lot of those things they still have, everything still has to vibe with the brand that we're building and with the base and foundation that we've already laid. So it definitely does take an intentional approach in figuring out what's next, and that's from a branding perspective and from a marketing perspective, but then also from a product perspective, we are always just in touch with our customers asking for feedback and trying to think about the next generation of Obras, how

Nikolai (25:50): Can we create that better product? Our first version was a hand stitched pair that we made 5,000 units in our barn office that Nikolai is in, and every adjustable system was hand tied by us, and it took us almost three months to make our first 5,000 pairs working 12 to 14 hours a day, seven days a week. And that was just like, it made us so intimately familiar with the process, but it also gave us a good understanding of how we need to innovate and what we need to do to create a scalable product that can potentially someday reach the masses. And I think what Nicola touched on has been one of the most difficult parts of exploring growth and tapping into the new markets because like you said, we were focusing on that backpacking, outdoor hiking community, and we're still very focused on it. (26:54): And it's tricky because we're so small and we have really not even tapped into a fraction of that community, specifically the backpacking hiking community that where we're avid backpackers and hikers and still the most at home on the trail because they have all their aforementioned benefits. And it's been tricky because we want to, oh, what's the next market we can go after? Wow, these are so good for golfing, they're so great for pilots, yada, yada yada. But just staying focused and being like, no, this is where we need to be. Once you cast that net too wide, your message gets diluted, and I like to assimilate it to fishing. When you go fishing, you don't have a ton of lures on one line trying to catch whatever you can. You're going for one specific fish with one specific lure. And when you've been fishing with one lure for so long, you get a little bit, I don't want to say bored, but you just feel like you need to be moving on, but maybe you just need to move to a different location and fish for that fish and somewhere else. So for us, it's been tricky just being, staying focused and being like, we need to dial in and permeate this market and drive home into this market before we reach out and try and tap into it.

Cole Heilborn (28:23): Yeah. Well said. That analogy is really helpful. So then for you guys, when do you add more lures to the line?

When you think back on that, let my people go surfing model and how Patagonia started out as a climbing hardware brand, and then they started making some clothes and they noticed that people, the climbers were also skiers and snowboarders in the winter, and they were bikers and they were surfers. And that kind of naturally just progressed their brand, and naturally their brand just evolved along with their customers. And as their customers kept using their products for more and more things and letting them know how awesome their products were for all these different things that kind of propelled the brand to naturally go and explore those other avenues and niches and paths with their customers. (30:38): So I think that's kind of the approach that we're taking is just keeping our ears open and our eyes open, seeing what people are buying these for. And right now it's for the most part, it's to enjoy the outdoors. It's to in the outdoors. And we're seeing people reach out to us all the time with new stuff that they're trying these out for, and we're definitely listening to that stuff and we're kind of incorporating bits and elements of that into our marketing and into our brand and into our ethos. But it's really just like, yeah, we're letting our customers take the lead with, we have our North Star, we have our foundation. And now it's like the word is starting to spread and it's kind of starting to froth out a little bit.

Cole Heilborn (31:27): Yeah, no, that's so cool. So it's more about for you guys as you're trying to get a lay of the land, like letting the customer drive where you go, and then as they start to populate into these other industries, then you guys start to follow. Is that what you're saying?

And that kind of brought in a whole nother cycling aspect to and mountain biking and graveling and bike packing aspect to the brand. And we've integrated that a lot. If you go to our homepage right now on obergs.com, you'll see a really fantastic shot of a guy named Ultra Romance is this is Instagram handle. He is a legend in the bike packing industry, and we've definitely incorporated that into our brand. A lot of our customers also happen to be climbers, rock climbers, and so they started loved our sunglasses in the way that they worked with a helmet. They wouldn't interfere. But as we've grown, we've kind of started to outgrow some of our factories and just managing that relationship because ultimately when you talk about supply chain and inventory constraints, it all really comes back down to the factory and the relationship you build with them and how much the trust that you build with them, because at some point you're going to need them to kind of bend over backwards for you. Cole Heilborn (00:03): Welcome to Brand Story, the podcast where we interview individuals who are creating and designing the brands we interact with every day. My name is Cole Hoborne. Today I'm here with Michael Goldstein, the director at Goldstein Productions. How are you doing?

Mike Goldstein (00:14): Doing excellent.

Cole Heilborn (00:15): Thank you for having me today. We're here in beautiful Vancouver, bc.

Mike Goldstein (00:20): Yes. Yes. It's still beautiful for another day before it starts pouring rain.

Cole Heilborn (00:24): Right. So tell me a little about you guys. What do you guys do for those of people in the world who don't know?

Mike Goldstein (00:30): So we do commercial film production. A lot of our stuff is digital content, but we also do some broadcast work, and we work probably 50% with agencies, 50% directly with brands, and we're pretty heavily based in automotive lifestyle, active living, and the weld industry.

Cole Heilborn (00:50): Okay. Okay. And how long have you been doing it?

Mike Goldstein (00:54): So I've been doing it as a freelance gig starting in 2010, and then incorporated in 2013. Hired the first person in 2015, and now we're a team of four on the core team on the west coast. And then we have a Montreal partner as well.

Cole Heilborn (01:13): Awesome. And so your role as a director, I mean, I know you guys probably all wear a lot of hats, but if you're looking at the director role, what does that mean to you and what do you do?

Mike Goldstein (01:26): That's a good question. Yeah, so we definitely all do wear many hats, but if we're talking director specifically, I think it's the ability to have a vision in your head before you get into production and be able to communicate that before anything's shot to your client and then fulfill that throughout production and post.

Cole Heilborn (01:49): So you got started how doing mountain bike videos, tell me a little bit about that you get started.

Mike Goldstein (01:56): Yeah, so I was working up in Whistler at a bike shop, loved riding, raced mountain bikes and also just loved making images, whether it be photo or video. So had started just filming all my buddies up there and made some mountain bike movies. We did a full length mountain bike movie at one point that we premiered at the local bar up there on opening weekend in Whistler. And really just through that whole community of mountain biking, got to know people at Whistler, and it was in 2010 that I was chatting to them. And this was back when online content was still pretty up and coming, I guess you could say. So they were like, yeah, we want to make some video stuff. We don't know what, we don't know what it's going to be. And we ended up doing the first ever online video campaign back in 2011, and that was kind of the start to it all.

Cole Heilborn (02:54): Okay. Okay. So you were describing to me earlier, taking a DV camera, wrapping it in bubble wrap to protect it.

Mike Goldstein (03:02): Yes. My cocaine brick, my camera.

Mike Goldstein (03:07): That's a good question. Yeah, I think I remember when the GoPro three came out, there was like 2.7 K in 2009 I think it was. So this was, yeah, definitely before GoPro. And I think I remember too one, I think it was one time back ski racing where a buddy of mine got a GoPro. I remember he was like, yeah, you can stick it on your ski pole. And I was like, that's just a piece of shit. But they're really good now.

Cole Heilborn (03:33): They've changed a little bit since then.

Mike Goldstein (03:35): Totally.

Cole Heilborn (03:35): So one thing that I find really interesting, and I'm hoping we can kind of dissect in a brief manner, but you graduated from school and then you just kind of jumped into the commercial stuff or a progression down that path for people that are trying to figure out how to get into the commercial world, what would you say to them? What would be some of the things you've learned along the way?

Mike Goldstein (04:01): The biggest thing I think is networking. And I think it's one of the things in school that I laughed at a lot in our first producing class that we took. They were like, yeah, networking is super important. There's this thing called LinkedIn, you got to go and meet people. And I was like, fuck that. I don't like talking to people and whatever. Many years down the road now it's like it's the most important thing. It's what we spend probably most of our time doing is meeting people, building relationships. You got to build those relationships and people need to trust you and you need to be able to communicate the work that you can do. And it takes that, I think, to get in the door with anyone.

Cole Heilborn (04:42): Do you feel like there's the filmmaker, photographer world, people are hesitant to go try to build those relationships and network? Is that a personality trait of a lot of creative people that they want to be focusing on their work and not out in the spotlight, so to speak?

Mike Goldstein (05:03): Yes and no. I don't know, maybe it's just the people that have been around. I feel like there's a fair few people that I know who are not opposed to that at all. They're pretty out there building those relationships. But I definitely do think that, I kind of see we're getting at with that. There's definitely a bit of a divide, I think, between your super creative people and people with the business minds mines. It can be really tough, I guess, as a freelancer, but that's also not necessarily the only way to get into the industry either. There's a million different ways that you can enter in. But yeah,

Cole Heilborn (05:47): So maybe elaborate. What's number two and three on that list?

content:
Amanda Goad (08:27): Several. Oh, okay. So we went to Alaska in a 2011 FJ cruiser. That was Adrian, my husband's car at the time that he had recently invested in. And so it was fairly new, only a year or two old at the time. Since moving to Durango, we have also gotten a 73 FJ 40 and an 87 FJ 62. So those are our over landing rigs. I feel nervous to say we also have a Jeep that we take over landing, but I'm on the Toyota side of things. We just happen to, that's more of our commuter car with kids and we take it on easier trails too. So yes, we have a lot of cars, but we don't drive them all that much. So we try to stay economically and environmentally sustainable in that way.

Cole Heilborn (09:35): That's awesome. Do you guys run rooftop tents? Do you throw tents on the ground?

Amanda Goad (09:41): We actually don't do rooftop tents because they have a tendency to have your car tip a little bit or so on harder trails. They make your car a little top heavy. I used to want one so badly and recently the harder and harder trails we go on, the more I realized maybe it's not the best idea. And also with a toddler and another one on the way, being up in rooftop is probably not the best arena. So regular tens and sometimes we sleep in the back of the FJ 62, which I love. It's nice and cozy.

Cole Heilborn (10:19): Okay. Alright, well completely off topic, but I was super curious. So tell us a little bit more about some of the clients that you work with. Are there any recent projects that you can kind of talk about that give us a good idea of how you approach a project or work with a client?

Amanda Goad (10:35): Yeah, so one client that we've been really excited to work with recently that we've had a relationship for a long time through various networks is Coalition Snow. And we just did a rebranding on a visual level for them. So telling their story on a visual level, not necessarily on a verbal or copy language level. And that included visual assets for their fall campaigns, redoing their website, how they talk about their ambassadors and their programs, and then bringing that into all of their promotions and doing PR for it this fall. So I was really excited to work with Jen Gki, the CEO at Coalition Snow because she and I have mean anyone that knows us in the outdoor industry know that we've been friends and we've spoken on panels at Outdoor Retailer together for quite a while and we've worked together on and off in the past. But really being able to dig into an amazing women focused brand like Coalition Snow and seeing Coalition snow evolve over the last four or five of knowing Jen and then being able to take that gradual evolution of seeing their story evolve and seeing Jen grow, seeing Jen be really big part of the Bipoc community and the Jedi community and a strong voice and leader in those communities and being able to kind of bring that out in a visual level on their website was really exciting this summer.

Cole Heilborn (12:16): That's a perfect plug and I'm glad you did it so I didn't have to, but if you're curious, Jen has an episode that's come out before your episode, so folks are interested to learn more about Jen and Coalition Snow and all of the rad stuff that they're up to. You could go listen to that one. You mentioned that Bold Brew focuses on building brand voice and helping with visibility. I think actually I stole that from your website. In your mind, what is brand voice? I'm curious talk about brand storytelling, brand voice, but maybe let's define some common language around what a brand voice is in your opinion before we keep moving.

Amanda Goad (12:58): Definitely. When we are approached by potential clients or brands, we're often approached at a level of, I need PR or I need this social media campaign, or I need to push more people to my website. And that's all that the brand knows. And we work with clients from all sizes, from small, new emerging startups in the outdoor industry and lifestyle industry to larger established brands like Sherpa Adventure Gear in the outdoor industry. And when we talk to these brands, they just, sometimes there's just this goal of the end game, but they haven't really established who they are

Amanda Goad (13:51): And

Amanda Goad (13:52): What their voice is to the world and establishing that voice and that story really differentiates you from everyone else that you potentially competing with in your immediate arena and then other potential markets as well. So my favorite part of marketing and strategy is really digging into the gaps with clients and potential clients of you have this amazing, incredible product. You are doing this awesome new thing that is helping sustainability in the world, and I never even knew I needed your product until I started using it or things like that, even on our Alaska trip. But then being able to share that product with so many other people requires you to talk about it and to talk. You need to have a voice. We all have voices when we speak. And so I think building a voice really builds community and connection in order have longevity to your brand in the world that you're trying to build for your brand.

Cole Heilborn (15:11): Gotcha. Yeah, well said. Do you have an example of a client that you've helped unpack what their brand voice is? Just to give an example of maybe something tangible we can work with?

Amanda Goad (15:25): So when we first started started Gold Brew, we worked with another startup that was emerging that's much better known in the outdoor industry now called Western Rise. And we had a really strong relationship with Western Rise helping them evolve their voice from where it was in the beginning to where it is now. And so that took them from, they started Western Rise because they wanted to have a product that they wanted to use out on the river when they were fishing. And the founders of Western Rise are really big anglers, and you'll still find them out on the river all the time. They're based in Telluride here in the San Juan now. And they were originally in Georgia when we started working with 'em. And so we started working them from the ground up of what their voice was at the time and why they established their product and their business. (16:29): And we were with them for two and a half years along the entire process of what their voice evolved into as their business evolved. So they started looking at new audiences and realizing that the product that they were actually creating was much more versatile than just for fly fishing and that you could use it out on the trail or traveling or heading onto an airplane or anything of that nature. And so they wanted to appeal to a larger arena and they continued to evolve their voice from there. And they've definitely done a really big pivot from what they originally launched at to who they are now, but they've taken time and been thoughtful about it throughout the entire process in establishing this pivotal voice of who they are for the long run. And so I think that's a really good example of loving the product and loving what you're creating and why you're creating it for the world, and then building that into who needs your product and why, and then how to speak to them on their level as well.

Cole Heilborn (17:47): Yeah. So you're talking about helping them craft their brand voice. If you can give us a brief look into your process, how do you figure that out and how do you know when you've identified the voice, what does that look like?

content:
Amanda Goad (18:05): Yeah, lots of meetings with a client, lots of conversations. I mean, I think in any type of storytelling, whether it is establishing a brand from the beginning or doing public relations or sharing a marketing campaign, you have to really dig into and get to know the brand and the client. So it's not easy to just say, hi, nice to meet you. I'm Amanda from Bold Brew and now I'm going to help you build your brand voice and I don't know anything about you. So I think that establishing a really strong relationship with your clients and getting to know them and feeling like you are a part of their brand and not an agency, working for them is crucial. And then digging into who their audience is and who their audience could be. And then that from a tangible tactical standpoint, that can evolve into anything from consumer surveys, market research, digging into competitor audits, diving into mood boards and potential colorways. And so there's a lot of more qualitative tactical things and then quantitative tactical things behind it. And I really love how it all works together in collaboration. And our team is skilled and good at different variations of it from the much more creative side of things on our team to much more tactical, quantitative, let's look at the numbers and how we grow this business and where my role comes in a bold brew is how that all works together.

Cole Heilborn (19:59): So you kind of pull all the strings, bring it all into one cohesive PDF, for lack of a better word.

Amanda Goad (20:04): Yep. Yeah.

Cole Heilborn (20:05): Okay, interesting. So you help them find their brand voice that's kind of like the foundation maybe? Yes. Am I on track? Yeah, definitely. Then where can they go from there?

Amanda Goad (21:46): Yes, cohesiveness and consistency is key. Definitely. We always tell our clients, don't just put a social media post out there or don't just jump on a bandwagon. You see something happening in the news. Be thoughtful about how you're reacting to the world in situations and definitely make reactions when they need to on a timely level, but also make sure that everything you're doing is consistent with the brand that you've shown and shown up for. And then you are continuing to do that moving forward, past whatever reaction or promotion you have just in that time. So I think a really great and timely example of that these days is with the Black Lives Matters campaigns and everything going on in that world, a lot of brands want to show support for that. But if you haven't authentically been showing people of color in your imagery in the past saying that you want to photo shoot with black models or native models and not really bringing them into the culture and community of your company for the long-term and making sure that they feel included and that your company has an exclusive inclusive values and inclusive voice is not being authentic to that voice you've created and established. (23:23): So that's just one example of making sure the voice that you create is always evolving, but making sure that it is clear to who you are trying to talk to moving forward. So if you are just making sure that you aren't jumping into something without your voice sharing, that you actually do have that authenticity and that value.

Cole Heilborn (24:01): Yeah. Yeah. So I feel like brand storytelling is kind of like that next step you have to have in order to tell stories through your brand. You have to know who your brand is and have a brand voice brand storytelling seems to be kind of this next cool thing to do for marketing, but does it have to be such a big undertaking? Can it be small and done on the small scale or does it have to be these large initiatives? I guess what's your take on that?

content:
Amanda Goad (24:36): Yeah, I think that historically in marketing, storytelling has always been a part of a brand and I think that it's this sexy keyword that people are using now to sell their business or sell their services or anything they're doing. But overall, for centuries and centuries, we as humans gravitate towards stories that are engaging and tell us about a community or a place and give us an affinity and shared values to something that we want to also connect with (25:23): And have those same values for. So I think that you can tell your brand story and the story of others that represent your brand in so many different mediums in ways, and that can be anything from a gorgeous, beautiful, lengthy YouTube video that Yeti creates and those are fantastic, and they're really engaging to a post sharing your influencers and your new ambassadors on your social media pages, or maybe it is utilizing Instagram TV once a month to authentically interview your ambassadors or have them do takeovers. Maybe it's utilizing traditional PR methods to have a publication interview one of your ambassadors or athletes and tell their story, and in turn, they're telling your brand story. So those are all different forms of mediums that you can get your story out and this values behind your story and voice out, but I think the key is making sure you're sticking to that storyline and that value system in anything you do.

Cole Heilborn (26:42): Gotcha. So yeah, I guess I'm trying to clarify. Obviously stories have been a huge part of human civilization since forever, but you'd said that brand storytelling has been around for a long time. Has it though? I feel like brands, companies historically have just been focused on products and features and not so interested in the story. I don't know.

Amanda Goad (27:11): I think maybe from a consumer level it looks that way, and maybe I've dug deeper and kind of seen that the consumer is wanting stories more than looking at features. I think historically, if you look at the way a product has been promoted, for instance, the first thing that comes to mind is women in the fifties in their very traditional domestic lifestyles and being promoted through black and white television the way a new product is going to make their house make their life easier by helping them clean their house or get dinner on the table. Those are all specs and things that can happen through that new product, but the story that those brands are telling is you want to be this strong capable wife that does everything for her family and they're sharing a value system for that time (28:27): Of the value. And I think within that, and I'm not super familiar with lots of different promotions that have been on during that time, but within that they've even used things like celebrities, which at the time could have been considered influencers for these types of things. Maybe in a sense of utilizing the word storytelling these days we're, the direction we're talking about is really diving into influencers and not always focusing on a traditional athlete or celebrity and digging into the everyday person and hearing their story and a general consumer gravitating towards that person that they can really relate to, and the fact that brands these days will tell a story about an influencer and not even mention their brand the entire time and at the end through their logo up, that's definitely new and different and I think that it's super impactful these days to dig into featuring people of the same value systems of yours in order to build that connection and community.

Cole Heilborn (29:43): Gotcha. Okay. So brands and companies have been telling stories, it's just stories have evolved and how they're telling them, is that kind of what I'm hearing?

Amanda Goad (29:53): Definitely, yeah.

And so I think that when it comes to any brand telling their story, making sure that strategic thought and creativity and planning is still very strong, and that's high value in whatever content you're creating versus quick one-off content. And then along with that, your traditional high video production will be a part of campaigns when they make sense. So I'm taking a stab and a guess here based on some insider knowledge, but for Jimmy's video that he had about voting, he had some content that he had probably filmed throughout things. And so I just think that there are lots of different ways to create those videos. That story was still being told very highly impacted and really strong, but it was a montage of Jimmy's content and other things that they grabbed throughout the outdoor industry or I'm sure you're familiar with a lot of the social content that's happened recently where people are asking people of influence or anyone in general to video them talking about a specific topic or answering a question. And then there's been lots of montages created from that, and that is a lower production value content, but there's still a lot of thought put into the questions and the creativity behind things. And then I think pairing those types of content with these larger production campaigns is what grabs people's attention in the long run.

content: Amanda Goad (40:48): It's about that community and connection. In the last couple of years, Adrian and I have watched the YouTube show Lifestyle Overland, and they're growing YouTube show about overlanding. And the reason we first got invested in them was because they were going on a trip to Alaska with their daughter. And at the time I think we had a newborn. So we were at home bored watching the show a lot, reminiscing about our trip to Alaska, and then also thinking about the future of going over landing with our young daughter. And so that's a story that we immediately gravitated towards, and the production of that story didn't really matter to an extent it does matter because they have an intro. I've actually seen them evolve their production over the last couple of years to be higher production so that production does matter and it also builds your voice. (42:08): So one of the things behind their production that I find interesting is they do tons of technical content of rock crawling and finding campsites and stuff, but then it's also got an emotional element to it. So they will do a lot of B roll of the sunset or cooking at camp and put really emotional connecting music to it. And so that brings a different audience into what they're creating and the story that they're trying to tell so that different types of people will gravitate towards their voice. So I would say their brand voice is like this adventurous couple family that is really into the technical elements behind their two Toyota cars that they take around now. And even the mom has her own Toyota and gets really into the technical elements of rigging out her car, but then they have this emotional building memories as a family and connecting with the land and stewardship to the land type of element. And so those types of things right there would be building that voice and them sticking to it with whatever stories or mediums they use moving forward.

content: Jo Salamon (03:04): So Mustang Survival is a 50-year-old company, kind of started back in, I think, 1967, I'm going to say originally in Gastown, which is, if you know Vancouver, it's right down on the docks, it's right on the water. So they started with IRV down there making floater coats. So Irv started, he wanted to make an insulated jacket, and he was introduced to FOAM as an installation property. And then somebody was like, oh, and it floats. And he's like, it what? It floats. And it sort of opened up a whole new area for him that he hadn't initially considered when he was looking into insulation, but he decided to sort of move in that direction. So the Mustang Survival floater coat or the classic flotation coat that you'll see, it's iconic here on the Pacific Northwest. It's probably iconic across Canada for anybody who works on the water, in the water, over the water, commercial fishing, commercial water, anything. The float coat is a synonymous iconic orange jacket that keeps you warm, that you can work in and obviously has flotation properties. So keeps you safe on the water as well. The long-term goal being for any company that is involved in lifesaving products like PFDs, not just Mustang Survival, but we wanted a PFD to be seen a bit like helmets are now in the ski industry. You see somebody on the ski hill with a helmet on, you don't think twice about it anymore. (04:46): In fact, you look at the people who don't wear helmets and think they're crazy. And the same with PFDs. There's a lot of regulations around them, but a lot of people have them on their boat or on their paddleboard, but they don't actually wear them. And really at the end of the day, they don't save your life if you're not wearing them. So for us, and for all brands and all companies who make PFDs, our goal is that people wear the PFD at the end, you wear it. And so we try to work to make them light, to make them comfortable, to make you almost, to make them invisible so that you can just do your stuff, go fishing, go boating, go paddling, not even think that you've got it on, and just know and trust that if the worst case happens, it's there and it's going to do the job for you and safe when you need it most. That's kind of the plan.

Cole Heilborn (05:40): So yeah, tell us a little bit about your role currently. What do you do? What do you oversee? What are you working on?

Jo Salamon (05:45): So it's one of the fun things about going back to working for a smaller company again, is that you become the jack of all trades again. But I quite like that. It's fun. So my role is PR and communications. The PR side of it obviously is helping promote the brand and the product into the rec industry, the outdoor rec industry. And then the communication side evolves from everything from blog content management, working with the digital marketing team on emails, working with internal communications and brand communications and business communications as well. So it's a bit of everything. We are a 50-year-old company, but the marketing side of it is very young in the company, I'd say like four years old because the company has only just started to move into the outdoor rec side. So previously, most people know us and understand us from a commercial and professional products. (06:44): Mustang survivor has a long history of working with commercial fishermen, professionals who work in on or over the water, be that military to Air Force. We've worked with nasa, it's a big long history, and the last four years, they wanted to take all that knowledge and know-how that we were putting into a lot of these very, very specialized products. And we're like, how can we make paddling better? How can we make sailing better for people? How can we make other water sports on a more recreational level, more comfortable, safer, easy to wear products, keep you dry and allow you to really have a great time outside, playing outside. And so the brand is sort of, I wouldn't say split, but it's definitely sort of increased its design and its engineering and its marketing to focus on the outdoor recreation industry at the moment. And that's kind of partly where I came in the last year and a half to help them promote those products that we were making into the outdoor recreation industry so that people would see Mustang survival from a different angle. A lot see us like you do. They remember their orange PFD at the lake, at the cabin with the canoe, the seahorse on the logo, or if they've known anybody who works in commercial fishing, they know the floater coat, they know the gear, they know the salad pets, and they would probably try and wear them. But now we're like, okay, now we're making them with a recreation activity intended use as well. So we're making it a little bit more specific for an end user in the recreation

content: Jo Salamon (11:51): There's a huge amount of responsibility. Obviously anything that is a lifesaving product has regulations and certification. It has to go through and pass without a doubt. So we work very closely on all the UL certifications on anything. We're making sure all our PFDs, their Coast Guard or Canada Transport approved. Currently we only sell within Canada and the us, so we don't need to have European standards just yet. As we move eventually grow and move into Europe, obviously we'll need to work on CE certifications and stuff like that as well. And everybody's slightly different Coast Guard to transport Canada. The nice thing is Transport Canada Guard are now working on a lot of what's called harmonization of PFDs, allowing you to move between borders wearing the PFD, so that you know, especially where we are in Vancouver, Seattle, the ocean, the border is pretty close to move through, but you have to make sure that the PFD you're wearing is certified in both areas and things like that. (13:00): So there's a lot of testing that goes into it. A lot of protocols we have at the office, we call it the Water Life Studio. We have a full on lab for testing everything from fabrics, bladder strength, durability. We have a washing machine that's constantly going. We have put things into stuff with rocks for durability. They're testing so many things all the time to see how they stand up to abrasion, wear and tear. We have a pool at the office too, and so we can do a lot of buoyancy testing ourselves to make sure things are writing you in the right way. So with a lot of PFDs, everything's about bringing you back up. So your head is above water, and so you're always trying to make sure there's lots of very specific engineering and mathematical calculations that have to go into how it works and how it works for body types and trying to get things to work on as many body types as possible to create the right scenario. So yeah, there's a lot of work and a lot of attention to the very tiniest details that go into PFDs. So we take those things incredibly seriously. We have a very passionate team of people incredibly dedicated, who work really hard to make sure all those standards are met.

And that's where Mustang survival started flow to coats, PFDs, their lifesaving products. That's what we do. We're now moving more into sort of a recreational apparel line. (15:49): I'm not a sailor. I like paddling. I like being on the water. I have always worn A PFD, my comfort level on the water. I need to have A PFD. I know that about myself. So I have no qualms about putting a PFD on whenever I'm on the water. Other people feel super confident on the water. They've grown up sailing, they've grown up paddling, and they maybe feel a little more complacent about wearing A PFD. I think one of the things that the whole company has that I felt is that we all promote wear it. It doesn't save your life if you don't wear it. That's at the end of the day, it cannot save your life if you don't have it on and if you don't have it on correctly. So we all promote that amongst, I think our friends, our colleague, I know my friends who paddle with me now all wear their PFD, so I've at least managed to influence that many people. (16:48): And that's what the company does. That's what our marketing does. We try to always promote safe water use, safe water experience. We're very conscious of that. So even you'll see it even in our photos, we want to make sure that people are wearing PFDs. If we are using marketing photos of somebody on the water or in the water or near the water, that's sort of a policy we have. It's a policy that a lot of brands who work in the industry that in the PFD industry have too, that if their marketing doesn't support it, why would somebody, they're following you, they're following you for a reason, they're seeing your images, they need to see that you are promoting, wear it. You're promoting this safe space on the water. So we do that a lot. Obviously that's a key focus for us.

They already know about that. They already understand that and they see how well it's been trusted and used by commercial professionals, whether those professionals are Alaska crab fishermen, whether they're people who are working on oil rigs, whether they are people who have to fly over water for their profession. We do a lot of work with the Air Force, whether they're search and rescue teams, swift water rescue teams. You'll see a lot of swift water rescue whenever there's an area where there's hurricanes and floods. You'll have swift water rescue teams in there who are helping search and rescue with police. We talk about some of the other uses of our products or where they've come from. We have a story going out next year, which is all about the history of the inflatable PFD belt, the one that all the paddle boarders are using. Well that comes from the Navy Seals and it comes from the Navy and the Navy use. And we have this sort of history of how we've worked with the Navy on creating an inflatable belt vest for them that we took into paddling and into the paddle sports industry. (23:45): And so we have those kind of stories, history and heritage stories. Next year there's a story that we're going to try and talk about the innovation of PFDs in general and highlighting one that we make actually for the military and for law enforcement, which is amazing. It's so tiny, it's like less than a pound in weight, but it inflate and bring somebody up to the surface with all their gear on. It took a lot of engineering, it took a lot of problem solving to create this piece, but it allows them to have one less piece of equipment that's as heavy or as bulky and it can keep it out of the way. And that innovation moves into what we wear. So you'll see in the M mi T 70 that came out sort of this year, we were able to make a much slimmer, thinner, lighter weight PFD that you can wear all day and not notice you're wearing it anymore. And you can have an automatic or manual version. And we're able to do that because of the work we do with governments, with the commercial side that we work on. Innovation can trickle down into everyday recreational use, which is great.

Actually, the guy who created the company went there on a trip and saw that there were people there without power, without lights, anything. So it was kind of started as a philanthropic endeavor. And then word got out about our products in the US and people were like, well, I want that for whatever I'm doing, and I could use that camping and whatnot. So it kind of evolved into this company that it is today where you have all of the power products and light products and solar panels to enable people and empower people to really get out further, stay out longer, and do the things that they love doing off grid or on grid during emergencies, during work, whatever they need our products for. (02:33): And so that's kind of where we are today. And now we've kind of grown a lot in the past year alone because of all of the wildfires in California and all of the natural disasters happening around the world. People are seeking our company out more and more, and we've evolved past kind of the outdoor persona that we've had in the past, and now we're more of an emergency preparedness. In addition to the outdoors, we produce power packs, so they're kind of like large battery inverters. We make small ones from a hundred watt hour ones all the way up to 6,000 watt hour products. So the 6,000 watt hour ones can power an entire home for a couple of days. And our a hundred watt hour ones can charge your laptop, charge your phone for a couple of recharges at a time. So we offer a really wide array of products to help people charge and stay powered for whatever they want to be doing.

show_notes_excerpt: In this episode, Eli Kerr the CEO of Gnarly Nutrition joins me to discuss why embracing the holistic wellness of a person is crucial to building a strong company, a strong internal culture, and how that permeates into marketing and branding. Gnarly is on a mission to help athletes be their best selves. To do so, they first have to take care of their internal team. content: Eli Kerr (02:26): Yeah, so sometimes I can go off, so if you ever need to throw the lasso and bring me in, please, I'll lasso it. It's funny, actually, I consider myself a relatively quiet guy, but then when I start talking about gnarly and stuff like that, it seems like I just start rattling and going off. And anyways, so the lasso comes or the sheep hook comes in hand here. So we started about eight years ago really focused on, and the idea behind gnarly was to create quality natural sports nutrition products that tasted delicious. So we felt like there was this place in this very saturated market where there was actually a hole where natural products didn't taste very good. The other products that weren't natural did taste really good, but nobody was putting the two together and really making good quality products that were delicious that people could look forward to using. (03:34): And that's really where Gnarly was born. And then we saw this other hole in the outdoor industry where we felt like we could also feel we had a background in the outdoor industry and knew it and felt like we could bring products that were traditionally known in more of the fitness industry and less known in the outdoor industry, and bring them over and educate outdoor athletes on how to use products like these and thus fill this hole around performance and recovery for outdoor athletes. And so that's kind of the journey that we started on is really bringing performance sports, nutrition products to outdoor athletes. And it's been a hell of a ride. It's been really interesting. There's been a lot of barriers that we haven't or didn't see initially, but we've also been really welcomed. And I think that's partly because we've taken a pretty authentic approach. We've also been really focused on the science of products like ours and less just on straight marketing and sales of products like this. And then also we've had the opportunity and been, I guess blessed with a lot of phenomenal relationships with athletes that are outstanding in the mountain culture that have come to love our products and fully adopt them. So that's been super rad and a really fulfilling part of what we do. (05:21): Ultimately, we have wanted to create a lifestyle brand that supports outdoor athletes and helps them become better and do more of what they love. So our slogan is want more, do more, be more. It's this idea of a process that we all go through to become something greater than what we might be today or were yesterday and our products help a little bit with that process is what we believe we're here to support. We also want to ultimately support the athlete through more holistic approaches as well, and not just products. And I think that that's really where we are trying to go as a brand. And that's what I mean by a lifestyle brand is people who use our products and people who are associated with us see us much more than just a product-based company.

We don't do any food-based products right now, meaning like bars or anything like that, but everything traditionally we would put in the category of training products. So these are products such as everything from a pre-workout that you would take to help your performance during an event or during a training session. And then branch chain amino acids that help with recovery all the way to proteins, which have kind of been our traditional flagship product, both a grassed, whe, and a vegan product that you use for both help with macros of protein, but also post-workout or event to help with recovery. We also have a hydration mix. We also have a creatine product. All of our products are really focused on helping you with performance during training and ultimately prepare for an event, a game day, and then with recovery.

content: Eli Kerr (08:27): Well, so the two events happened simultaneously for, (08:32): It wasn't necessarily like an order of operations. It really happened simultaneously. And what we also saw during that same time is that functional fitness was growing substantially and functional fitness was also really colliding with the outdoor industry. And so for the, I would say not necessarily for the first time, but it became more generally accepted and or part of the outdoor industry for outdoor athletes to start moving more towards the gym, meaning training specifically for their sports. When I grew up, we just did more of our sport to get us better and stronger at our sport. Now the environment for an outdoor athlete has really changed, and a lot of outdoor athletes are using training programs, training at a traditional gym setting using trainers. (09:36): It's totally different. And that created a really, really cool space where we could come in with sports nutrition products, which there was a gap, and provide sports nutrition products specifically around training. And so what we've been working on is helping people understand the science of products like these, because traditionally they see products like these and they look at 'em and they're like, oh, that's for the gym rat, that's for the muscle builders, that's for the dude or gal that's getting super yoked. And that's just not true. That's not the reality of it. The truth is that these products actually help with your performance and help with recovery so that you can continue to progress and do more of the sport you like. They don't just necessarily make you pack on muscle. So there was definitely a gap in the outdoor industry around the knowledge of products like ours, and there still is and an acceptance of these kinds of products for the outdoor athlete. There are outdoor athletes who have been doing more traditional training forever, but there were few, and now it's become more accepted. Same thing with products like ours. There have been outdoor athletes that have been using products like ours forever, but now it's becoming more accepted and we've definitely been pushing and creating that desire or that acceptance of products like ours. So there's been traditionally products that are more carbohydrate based that outdoor athletes have been using, and these are more fuel based products that you would recognize whether there were bars or chews or a gel (11:32): That you use as a fuel substance. And we don't currently provide products like that. And that space is also very saturated in the outdoor industry. So everybody from Cliff to bar to go, those are the brands that we as being involved in the outdoor space and have been for quite some time.

content: Eli Kerr (14:44): It feels like a lifetime ago that I was doing something other than gnarly. Yeah. My background originally was in a field called recreation therapy, so it's really mental health. I went to college and got a recreation therapy degree here. I'm based in Utah and Salt Lake City in Utah, it's a certified position. And so basically recreation therapy, you use recreation as a modality to help people and it serves a lot of different kinds of people, like large demographics as far as it can be community-based programs or it can be more mental health. I specifically focused on more mental health and even more specifically focused a lot with adolescents. So working with kids typically from 12 up to 18 years old started out in what most people are probably familiar or have heard of wilderness type programs. So started there and moved through that into more residential programs and then also really focused on more adventure based programs, so using not only recreation but specifically adventure type recreation. (16:14): So the stuff that we love in the outdoors, so whether it was skiing programs, climbing programs, I mean backpacking, canyoneering, we used all these different modalities to help and build these adolescents up and used it as a form of therapy. And so I spent a lot of years doing that. I did a business minor in college as well, so I always had this inkling and desire to be more involved in business, and it was always very exciting for me to want to try to do something and then towards, as I was, I guess now I can say wrapping up my career in recreation therapy, I had a desire to actually go practice medicine in some way. So I went back to school and did a bunch of prerequisites so that I could actually go to PA school, and I had just completed all those and was applying to PA schools when the opportunity for gnarly came about and got whisked away. And I can't say that I've never looked back. So I've definitely looked back, especially during some of the hard times of trying to grow and build gnarly, there's these times it's like, oh, I would love to just have this consistent job where as a pa I can live wherever I want. I get paid well, I practice doing really rad stuff with humans, but I didn't go in that route. And so (18:16): That's kind of the background.

Cole Heilborn (18:18): Nice. So I'm curious because a lot of people, it seems like a quick antidote to a lot of people is like, oh, just get outside, go to a park, go on a run, you will feel better. I'm curious from your perspective as someone who's done this professionally, are there any success stories or any examples that you can talk about for things that you saw how people improved as they spent more time outside or gained confidence and skills outside?

Eli Kerr (18:53): Good question. So one thing I guess I could say is I would talk about this subject from more of a general sense, (19:05): And I do believe it's true everything that you just mentioned, I think it's totally true, and I think that we have a really, really good case study of that in the year 2020 where shit has hit the fan and has completely and totally disrupted our lives and what we expected our year to be like. And what's really been powerful to see, and for some people who love the outdoors and who were already in there, I think are frustrated or maybe even bothered or upset because there has been this calling of people just crowds heading outside because for a lot of reasons are normal forms of entertainment have been removed. And so people looking for things to do and they've headed outdoors. It's been a beautiful thing. I think that why I say it's a case study is that we have seen how people have found solace there. (20:16): We have seen how people have found some form of stability and connection back to our earth through that and connection back to humans, which is so wild that during all this COVID in 2020 that we're trying to create some social distancing and so forth. But I really believe that our participation in the outdoor actually creates more connection to each other as humans. And I think that we're seeing and experiencing that. I think that that's a very general broad case study, but I would tell you that I saw numerous times with the people that I worked with as a recreation therapist, them experiencing a couple of specific outcomes, and that's partly because we were focused on some specific outcomes and some of those outcomes were really helping them build what could easily be talked or mentioned as kind of self-confidence. But really the focus is what we call self-efficacy, building their self-efficacy, which is ultimately their belief in their ability to accomplish something or a specific task. (21:48): And we would do specific outings that challenged these kids coping mechanisms and what they believed they could or couldn't do and help them have a successful experience. And by having that successful experience, it showed them that they could overcome these specific challenges and by helping them recognize that they had what it took to overcome these challenges, we could help them take that belief in their ability to overcome that challenge and apply it to the challenges that they were working with. For example, in their therapy, their therapy with a therapist, that they were working through these other challenges, whatever they might be, and helping them direct that belief in their ability to overcome a challenge and relate it to the more personal intimate challenges that they were experiencing, whether it was in a family situation, whether it was about themselves and that we saw happen time and time again and it was like it's a beautiful, beautiful, cool process.

Cole Heilborn (23:08): Is that something you feel like a lot of people recognize? I mean, I'm sure we've all experienced it, right? You go out, you've never run a 5K before you go out and run the 5K and then maybe you're like, oh, I'm going to do a 10 K. Or maybe you then look at a situation at home and you're like, oh, this doesn't seem like that big of a challenge. We can work this out, we can tackle it. Do you think a lot of people, I'm sure we have all experienced that, but do you think a lot of people have been able to name that and help understand what that process is, what self-efficacy is?

Eli Kerr (23:42): So I don't think that majority of people, even maybe there's probably a very small amount of people that would actually label it and call it self-efficacy and that are familiar with that term. I think it's become more familiar or more popular, but I don't know about the general populace really understanding that, oh, I'm having a self-efficacy experience. Oh, my self-efficacy has increased. And really knowing and understand that it's actually a psychological theory where there's a substantial amount of research that shows that you can have and go through these experiences and that your self-efficacy in a specific area can be increased through a couple of different ways, and then that can be generalized to other areas of our life. I think some people can make that generalization on their own, but I also think that we as humans help each other sometimes make those generalizations and specifically therapists who focus on this theory really help their clients make that generalization into other areas of their life. But I don't know that we cognitively or deliberately do that. I think that there's some that it kind naturally happens, but it definitely helps to have somebody help you point it out and recognize it.

Cole Heilborn (25:28): Yeah. What does that do for you or an individual once you can identify that?
