Eli Kerr (25:33): Well, I think that there's a little bit of self actualization there where you start to learn that by building your self-efficacy in a specific area, that you gain more confidence slash really a belief in your ability to be able to be successful in other areas of your life too, which allows you to go after things to do things maybe that you normally wouldn't do to. I mean, I think a great example of this might be something is what we may think is as simple as applying to a job that you don't think that you have the ability or skillset to do, and so you just don't apply where because your self-efficacy increases, you would actually go apply to a job that maybe seems like it might be out of your realm, but you're still willing to try. So really trying things that you normally wouldn't try, if that makes sense.

Cole Heilborn (26:49): Yeah, it does. You said something there that was interesting when looking at self-efficacy, is there a difference between confidence and belief and what is that?

Eli Kerr (27:00): Yeah, so a couple of things. One is confidence is really associated with what you think the outcome could be, meaning it could be positive or negative. You can be very confident that you're going to fail at something. So self-efficacy is very associated with a positive outcome. So that's one specific difference. It is the belief that you will have a positive outcome in a situation. Self-efficacy also is typically is more specific in a specific task or area where confidence is more generalized.

Cole Heilborn (27:50): Gotcha. What got you interested in understanding, trying to understand how humans work, how humans process, where did that passion come from?

content: Eli Kerr (28:02): I don't know. It's interesting. I think back to when I first learned about this field of recreation therapy, I remember I was on a ski lift and I ran into a buddy that I played soccer with through college, and I hadn't seen him for years. And he's like, oh, yeah, I started this program. It's called recreation Therapy. And he's explaining, learning the recreation side and really focused in psychology. And ultimately the two things I put together, I was like, oh my God, you can do recreation and use the power of recreation and you get to help people. You get these two things and you get to marry them. It sounds perfect. I had no idea what kind of jobs were out there at that point. I had no idea what it paid. I didn't know really anything except that you got to do recreation and you got to help people. And it's like (29:02): Two things. I'm sold off things I love, so I pursued it and I got to learn a lot more about psychology and learn more about human growth. And I've always been interested with human growth and development. It's a topic that's so interesting to me. I mean, I guess there's this other component too that I'm from Utah, grew up in Utah, I grew up as a Mormon, no practicing or involved with their religion at all, but there is an aspect and principle with Mormonism that's very focused growth and very focused on development and becoming something greater. And I think that that's been really ingrained in me. And while now I'm at this point where I don't know that I fully understand or know what's going to happen to us in our lives and post life and all of that, but one thing that I still really believe and hold onto is the idea of developing as a human and becoming better and going through a process of learning, getting rid of old habits that don't serve us and taking on new ones that do. (30:44): I've always really loved that idea of the idea of progression. And I think that while I think that's interesting about what we do now at Gnarly Nutrition and my background, while my background really isn't like a typical background of say, a CEO or someone who runs a business, I think that that's kind of the beautiful part. And one of the differentiators for us at Gnarly is that because I have this pretty unique background that all of that stuff has come with me and it's become part of what we are about at Gnarly, and it's part of our brand, this idea of progression and helping people become better. And it's not about being the best, it's about being your best. It's about being better than you were yesterday. That's a component and a core belief of gnarly that we are trying to figure out how do we make this exude from the brand and so that people really feel it and are inspired by that. And that's a challenge for us because ultimately that's what we want people to see and feel from our brand.

We're all dealing with a lot of chaoticness a disruption. We're managing things that we never had to manage before, and it takes a toll on our personal lives. It takes a toll on our work lives. content: Eli Kerr (45:36): Yeah, I mean, to bring this more full circle and talk a little bit about marketing, talked about some kind of very theoretical stuff and our internal culture and my beliefs as a leader and as a person and how it's impacted gnarly. But ultimately what's interesting about all of that from the marketing sense is it does influence and impact our marketing. So traditionally the fitness industry or the sports nutrition companies really focus on marketing products like ours, for example, on the aesthetics of the body and really kind of focus marketing them is almost like a magic pill. Take this (46:25): And you'll look like this. And they use sex appeal to drive a purchase of a product. We market very, very, very differently with gnarly, like I mentioned in the beginning, we are focused more on the science, on the education of what products like this do for a person, and we're more focused on teaching the athlete how to fish rather than just give them a fish. We don't believe in a magic pill. You only get progression through work, and our products don't do the work for you, but they will support the work. And so putting products like ours in the correct context is what we ultimately do for our marketing. So we're focused on the education, we're focused bringing out the science or the research around how products like ours actually help, and we want to give that information to the consumer and empower them and ultimately allow them to choose what products they need to accomplish their goals, and in giving them that empowerment, hope that they look and see us or recognize us as a brand that they can trust, that they know creates a quality product when they are ready to turn to use a product like ours. (47:57): So rather than just selling more and more and more, we ultimately market to consumers to help them be successful. We're interested in their success. Obviously we have to and need to sell product because it's what keeps us alive as a company. So we have to make those cells, we need to make those cells, and as we continue to make those cells, it generates the revenue that allows us to continue to educate, to continue to support athletes and build or communicate ways to be successful as an athlete. And that process some people really don't love or just see us as a brand or see brands as machines that are just selling stuff and there's some truth to that, but also give us a little bit more benefit of the doubt that we're selling stuff so that we can do more cool shit so that we can support people more also so that we can create a livelihood for us and our families so that we can continue to produce phenomenal products and phenomenal education, and that's what we do. And so I would say the culture and the things that we've talked about so far in our conversation really has changed the way that we market, (49:37): And it's because ultimately what are our intentions and our intentions, I really believe are in the right place. We're trying to do the right thing and that you see that in our marketing.

Cole Heilborn (49:58): Beautiful. You summed that up wonderfully better than I could have ever had. So one of my last questions, we're running out of time. You look towards, let's say another eight years into the future. What are you excited for? What do you hope for the future of Gnarly and what are you excited for and hope for just in terms of your progression as a leader in the things that you want to learn and work through?

Eli Kerr (50:25): Yeah, we really want to continue making a huge influence on the outdoor industry. We really want to continue to build education that's focused on the outdoor athlete, so meaning make nutrition a larger part and a greater emphasis of on performance, how important it is on performance. And we want to continue to create a line of products that are really high quality, natural and delicious, that support the athlete in all their endeavors. So we're excited. We've got some really rad products that are coming out that continue to support the athlete from a nutrition standpoint, but we're also, we're going to be moving into other categories around nutrition, and one of the things I'm really, really excited about in the next six months is being able to provide a more fuel-based product for our outdoor athletes. And this will be a big game changer for us, and this is in line with our desire to ultimately support the athlete and providing a greater range of products. (51:46): So I mentioned that we've traditionally been kind of focused on training products, and we want to continue to build out that range of products so that we can support the athlete in whatever they're doing from a nutrition standpoint, and that's the direction that we will continue to head in the next eight years and ultimately become a greater household name for the mountain community. I think that we've done a great job with how small we've been and carving out this niche and helping to build a greater desire for outdoor athletes to be conscious of what they're putting in their bodies and how it affects their performance. And we will going to continue to do that and hopefully make a greater and greater influence on the outdoor community and ultimately be, I mean, I want us to be the sports nutrition company that outdoor athletes look to help fuel their adventures, help them be successful in whatever it is that they're wanting to accomplish, whether it's racing to individual goals, athletic goals, and that's fun. It's super fun and super rewarding.

short_description: An awakening that has lead to company-wide transformation
show_notes_excerpt: In this episode, Christian Lepley the VP of Marketing at GU Energy Labs shares how GU is adapting and embracing newly emerging markets. Historically GU has been a brand focused on the podium. But when podiums were shuttered in 2020, the GU team realized they needed to be more welcoming of everyone. As Christian says, "it was an awakening." This awakening has been fueled by the everyday athlete where 5ks are just as important as ultra marathons. Follow Christian and GU: @christianlepley @guenerg…

content:
Christian Lepley (01:46): Sure, yeah. Goo Energy Labs. Yeah. It started back in 1993 in Berkeley, California. Basically orbited around this idea where it was just a father trying to help a daughter run ultra marathons and not have problems with her nutrition. So being a good dad, he was into what his daughter was up to, and also being a scientist. He got back to his kitchen at home and started concocting these little experiments in nutrition for his daughter to achieve a hundred mile races in great time and with great nutrition and great performances. And so what ended up happening is he played around with different formulas. He ended up with this kind of gel-like formula that he shared with his daughter, and she shared it with her friends. And months and years later, a category was invented and a brand was born. So this happened back in 1993. Yeah, it was basically all around this idea that it was just a dad helping a daughter do something that she loved, and he didn't have the intention of creating category or a company. It was just, that's just what happened. As she started to share it around, it became a thing.

Cole Heilborn (02:49): And is that the first kind of goo energy substance that was on the market then? Was that the beginning of that category?

Christian Lepley (02:57): Yeah, that was the beginning was a goo like substance that also obviously inspired the name goo. It just became goo because that's what it was, gooey, (03:04): And so they just kind of stuck with it and played around with how to phrase it and spell it, and just ended up with GU, meaning exactly what it was. And then from there, over the years, expand into other form factors, chew drinks, recovery and capsules and a bunch of other things. But essentially it was all around the gel and also the packaging of that gel both very important, what's inside the packet, and also how the packet operates and works was also very important, and it was a huge innovation as well because Goo and Dr. Bill Vaughn are the ones who invented the packet design and the functionality of the packaging as well as the ingredients on the inside.

content:
Cole Heilborn (03:41): Okay, right. You got to have the easy terror access to the goo whenever you're doing whatever activity you're doing, and if you've got to fumble with it, like you do a prescription bottle, you're not actually going to be able to get the nutrients you need.

Christian Lepley (03:55): Yeah, exactly. I mean, the packaging and what's inside the packaging is a piece of gear. It's how we see it. So it has to operate efficiently, it has to have durability, it has to be waterproof, it has to travel well, and all these things just like a piece of gear, a jacket or a pair of skis, it has to have the same sort of, has to be used as a tool, just like any other piece of gear in the outdoors. So that's how it was looked upon. So a lot of thought and innovation went into the packaging as well as what's on the inside of the packaging. And so we try to do that with all the new form factors that we have developed over the years. It's all about the ingredients, but also about how you use those ingredients and the portability of the packaging and the convenience of the packaging and all those things. Because just like a Gore-Tex jacket, it can save your life out there if it's operating properly. So it's a piece of gear in our minds.

Cole Heilborn (04:44): Sure. So as the VP of marketing, I guess, how long have you been with the company and what does your role entail?

Christian Lepley (04:51): Yeah, it's coming on four years in April. Next year it'll be four years at Goo. And as the head of marketing, I basically have two pillars to my job. The first one is I have the opportunity to manage a crazy band of super innovative and talented marketing people where we cover off social media, web content, public relations, packaging design, event activations, anything that has anything to do with communicating with our community internally and externally. My team does, and I have the privilege of managing them. So that's the one pillar and the second pillar as being on the executive team, I also help drive corporate strategy for the future of GOO and all our sub-brands. So I have those two basic, basic pillars, manage marketing, and then be on the leadership team.

Did that for about a decade, just bouncing around, working with brands like the North Face and Levi's and a few other fashion brands, and also in the healthcare industry. I did some things for them, just kind on ad hoc basis, kept myself busy, just bouncing around from place to place. But before that, I was full-time staffer, ad ad agencies, car accounts, fashion accounts, all kinds of things, and then just branched out on my own so I could climb and travel and run and do all my things while also working. So that worked for about a decade, and then when this opportunity to go came up, I just could not pass up the chance to spend all my time with my people doing one thing, focusing on one brand and doing what I love. So it was a great opportunity. It's been great every single day for four years now.

Christian Lepley (06:48): Yeah. One of the great features and benefits of working at Goo is it has an incredible work-life balance. This comes down from the top, our owner, Brian Vaughn, he the CEO who runs the company, he believes in a work-life balance. He does it himself, and he allows all of us, all of the employees to do the same. So I didn't slow down a bit. I became more structured for sure, because I couldn't take phone calls from a beach in Croatia on the way to a climbing spot or something like that, and I couldn't have meetings up on Mount Tam on a Wednesday afternoon. But because of the balance, I'm able to kind of do all those things just in a different time slot. So actually I think I was kind of ready to have a little more structure in my life, so I appreciated the fact that I was able to do both, but just a little bit more on a schedule. And so it's fine. Most of our meetings, half the crew is in a bike kit or running shorts or something, so everybody's kind of on their way in or on their way out (07:43): As we're doing our work. So for me, it wasn't much of a change. I just had to keep track of my time a little bit differently than I had in the past.

Cole Heilborn (07:49): Sure. Sure. I feel like it's a good time for us to connect and chat on the podcast today, because it's currently beginning of December. This episode's going to come out later in 2021, but I've been doing a few of these podcast interviews. It seems like we've been doing a lot the last couple weeks, and it's been fun to connect and chat with brands as they're wrapping up this year. So I'm excited to chat today and learn a little bit more about what you guys have gone through in the last year, the opportunities that have come out of it, maybe some of the initiatives or things that you're looking for for 2021. Can you just kind of paint us a picture of this year and what next year is forecasting to look like?

content: Christian Lepley (08:29): Sure. Yeah. I mean, like everybody on the planet, the most unique year we probably all of us have ever experienced in Q1 of 2020. Things were sailing along great. We were having a great beginning of the year, had no idea what was about to happen, but we were feeling super optimistic. We had a bunch of new products in the pipeline. We had our marketing programs all set ready to roll, and everybody was super excited, super optimistic, but then all of a sudden things just changed. We're out of the office, we're working from home, everything's shut down. All of our channels for selling. Our products basically shut down. The events went away, our athletes got confused, our community was confused, what do we do now? And so we had to really make some very quick decisions about what to do about our operation and our company. (09:11): We immediately put everybody remote, made some adjustments, reduced our spending, because immediately our sales were impacted in many of our channels. And so we just spent the first few months just kind of refocusing and re-engineering how we're going to operate, knowing that we wanted to keep going and keep supporting our communities, but it took us maybe 30, 30 to 60 days to kind of figure that, figure all that out, thanks to technology. It was super simple and a lot of us travel a lot, so we were kind of used to doing things on the road anyhow. So for the marketing and sales teams and a few other teams, it wasn't a big change as it was for maybe somebody in r and d or in accounting or other really important departments. They just weren't used to being at home all the time. So it was a different experience for all the different team members at goo. (09:54): But for us in sales and marketing, it was pretty easy, but it was also kind of shocking that all of a sudden everything had changed. So we made that pivot and that was great. And then we started to see the smoke started to settle a little bit in terms of, okay, what are we looking at on the horizon? And so at that moment, we had to figure out how do we support our community?

content: Christian Lepley (08:29): And our community is not only, it's people that work at Goo, it's our retailers, it's the race directors that we're partners with, and it's of course our athletes and our consumers. How do we work with them to help them? We understood that maybe sports nutrition isn't the number one thing on their minds right now, especially if their training for races has stopped. Retailers were shut down or only delivering shoes out on the curb, all these kinds of things. (10:38): So we spent a lot of time focusing on the community because really GOO was born basically to support a community. It wasn't, like I mentioned before, it wasn't intended to be a company. It was intended to support people. And so everything we do is for the community. We orbit it around our communities. So we really pointed our lens on, okay, what can we do to help all the various communities that we're involved in, and especially race directors, where their races suddenly went away, and then they tried to flip to virtual races. And so one of the initial instincts was maybe, well, races are over, races are canceled. No, they're not canceled. They're just virtual. So it doesn't have to be a live event. You don't have to be together to have it be a live event. So we had to shift our focus and our thinking about how we get products to people, how we sample products, how much sports nutrition do you need If you're just doing a virtual on your own own timeframe, maybe not as much, but still, it'd be better if you're out there with some nutrition that's going to keep you rolling along in a good way. (11:32): So we just shifted everything as how we saw the world. We just said the communities are the same, the world is different. So that was actually a relatively easy shift for us, but we had to kind of go down the line for every discipline and make sure our communities are the same, but the world is different. So how do we support those communities in this changed world and know that it might be permanent, it might be semi-permanent, or it might go away in three weeks. We didn't really know. So we've just been rolling with it ever since.

We've learned different ways of sampling products. We've learned how to support people when we know they don't need as much nutrition as they may have needed before when they were in a serious training block. So we learned how to be more empathetic. So that was an opportunity that I can get to in a bit is like we learned a lot and we've also see opportunity, even though business has changed and the size of the category has changed and things are uncertain for next year, but we see a lot of opportunity in the future, especially in 21, where things are going to be a mixed bag, but we know what it is this time where it's like in 20, we didn't know it was even coming. (13:05): It just happened. And so now we know what it is and like, okay, we can do this. And so our team is very unique in a sense. The optimism and the marketing team is incredible, and they always look for opportunities. They disregard the problems and just look for the opportunities, which I think is a unique character trait. I think it's nurtured at goo as a culture. I'm sure they come to it with that ethos born into them, but it's nurtured at goo, and I try to keep that going, that things are not a problem. They're opportunities, and if there is a real, real problem, we deal with it and then we move on. So it's been a great opportunity for a lot of folks. It's been hard. We've lost some teammates. We've had to shrink the size of the company and do things like that, but also it's been an amazing growth opportunity for those of us that are at goo.

content: Christian Lepley (14:20): Yeah, yeah. I mean, one of the big revelations was for us, I don't know, for folks who know goo pretty well, they know that we have a high standard of performance. We like to be on podiums and we like to finish strong, and we like to win races, but we also mostly like to have fun doing it, but there's no joke. We might be smiling, but we do want to win. And so with that comes a certain, I don't know, a high standard elitism or something where like, oh, it is only for the super committed athlete and those kinds of products. They're not for me and maybe don't really need, if I'm running a 10 K or my first half marathon or I'm riding my bike for the first time over 20 miles or swimming across a channel or something, you don't really need that. (15:00): It's overthinking it. I'm sure there was. I know that a certain segment of the athletic population didn't really connect with the brand because that's what they thought of the brand of like, well, it seems cool, but I don't really need it. And we didn't necessarily not think that either because we were like, well, really, we focus on run bike and try and we try to do the best we can and enhance performances, great training, great performances, have a good time, achieve personal best, f kts, whatever it is. But it was always about have a good time, but do your best. It wasn't as casual, not as casual as it maybe it could have or should have been, but the pandemic slowed everything down. It slowed down our elites, it slowed down our committed athletes, our big broad consumer base, but then it also introduced us to a whole segment of the population that was either getting back into athleticism or exercise food for the first time or for the first time in a long time. (15:53): And so I had the opportunity to sit down really quietly with our team to say, and our owners, how do we talk to these folks? They are now part of our community. I would go out my door, my house where I live in San Francisco, and I saw more people out on the roads than I've ever seen in the years I've lived here. And I thought, wow, this is interesting.

They're creating new habits here. So how do we support that? Not in a way that we want to force products on them that they don't necessarily need, but how do we re-engineer our messaging and our communications around, Hey, if you're running a 5K in the morning or an actual 5K virtual race or a race, no, you don't need to carry a bunch of nutrition products with you, but you probably want to gel on your way out the door. (16:42): It's going to be better for you than a banana and a glass of water that you might have eaten before. And that certainly is fine, a banana and a glass of water, but actually an energy gel will do a lot better for you. You'll process it better. You'll have a better performance, you'll feel good, you'll recover better. All these things, you actually could benefit from that, but it's really only one gel. You don't need to buy all of the products and the whole lineup. It's just really about that. So we had to learn how to gently bring people into this notion that nutrition is important for everyday movement because ultimately goo as a company, we orbit around our community, but what we want our community to do is move. So we're all about supporting and feeding people's need to move every day. So if that is our brand mission, then of course we care about athletes of all levels and of all experiences in any activity, whether it's soccer on weekends or if it's training for an ultra marathon or for your first century or for swimming to Alcatraz or whatever it is, we care about all those people. (17:48): So it really opened up our eyes and opened up our opportunity as a brand to communicate to anybody who wants to move. That I think is an opportunity that in 21, we're really going to lean into that.

Christian Lepley (14:20): We're going to obviously stay committed to our core and a lot of brands, as you've, I'm sure heard in all the different conversations you've had with the core and more challenge, certainly we have it as well, and I don't think that we necessarily knew that we had it before the pandemic, but now that we've had a chance to really communicate and bond with more athletes, we realize, yeah, we definitely support our elite athletes and are really committed athletes that want to want to achieve personal best every time they go out. But we also really care deeply about folks who just want to move through their neighborhood, through their local park along the beach when they're on vacation, they want to run and go from here to there or ride from here to there. We care about those folks. So again, I think the opportunities that opened our eyes to that, and then also we had to learn how to communicate with them in a way that was not intimidating, but was empathetic to where they're at and what their goals are. If you've kind of built the brand and the company has been built on this, as you said, kind of this elite athlete mentality, I got to imagine for a consumer who's just getting out for an evening jog, it could be pretty intimidating to have a brand that they're not really familiar with, or a brand that is promoting Olympians and triathletes to then show up on their doorstep and be like, Hey, have you ever considered having a goo? content: Christian Lepley (19:39): Yeah, that's a good question. I think because part of our communication style, when we talk to committed elite athletes, it's a science-based science-backed product and also philosophy. (19:50): So there's a lot of science and a lot of technology that goes into how we formulate our products and including the packaging. So that stuff is important and that's why it works and that's why it's popping. That's why it's been around for 27 years. So that's important. However, I don't think it resonates with these other athletes. It's not going to be as important to somebody who's just really wanting to do really well running three or four miles in the mornings or actually running a 5K that's been organized. So what I have worked with the team on is just okay know that we have that science DNA, but that's not how we can speak to these folks. We have to have empathy. So for example, an energy gel, rather than giving somebody a nutrition plan for an entire four hours out on course or in the water or wherever it is, it can be as simply as we make 31 flavors of these energy gels. (20:45): There's got to be one in there that you love, from birthday to salted watermelon to whatever it may be, tastefully nude, which has basically no flavor. All of these, there's 31 of them, and they're made for fun and they're made. So you mix up your flavor profile as you're out every day or for long days. It gives you variety. Well pick a great flavor that if you like chocolate cake, then put a chocolate energy gel on your shoes in the morning, just one gel on your shoes. So when you go out the door, eat the gel, go out and have a great time. You don't have to do anything else, gel glass of water, and then you're done. So it's just that simple. Instead of having a bagel or a banana or a bowl of cereal, that is fine. It's calories, it's great, except it's not the right kind of calories in the right formulation. So the gels are crafted for that. And so if you eat one of these, it tastes great and then you're done. It's the simplicity of it, (21:38): It's the ease of it, and it's the taste of it. So I might want to, as a marketing person, lean more into the convenience and taste of it rather than the science of it, because our elite athletes care about the science and the taste. They love to eat well, but really it's about that science first. It's not science first. With these other athletes, it's really convenience and that it works and then it tastes good. So it's the tone by which you speak to them. So that's what we had to kind of teach ourselves that. It's not always about the nerdy science. It's really about does this stuff just work? Because I think people's eyes will gloss over if you start to get too involved in the science and the technology that's gone into it, especially when you're talking about amino acids and things like that. I just know that they're good for you and they'll help you recover, and you'll have more fun out

Historically GU has been a brand focused on the podium. But when podiums were shuttered in 2020, the GU team realized they needed to be more welcoming of everyone. As Christian says, "it was an awakening." This awakening has been fueled by the everyday athlete where 5ks are just as important as ultra marathons. Follow Christian and GU: @christianlepley @guenerg…

content: Christian Lepley (46:54): Well, we certainly, when everything shut down, our sales did change. They did reduce and everything shrunk. Everything just contracted. So that happened for sure. All of a sudden, especially when you lose expo sales and there's no longer events where we've actually sold product and then our retailers literally closed down. Of course then, like everybody, we all know this story. E-commerce shot through the roof. That was fine, but it did not make up for the sports specialty channel, the brick and mortar channel. It did not make up for that. It did not make up for all the fun we have at the New York City Marathon, selling thousands of gels to people. So all those sales just went away. So our sales did shrink. But then what we're seeing now based upon this is a leveling off, and it's solidifying and then kind of building back. So that's why I have a lot of optimism for Goo in the future because of the brand loyalty and the brand awareness with just even on just our core, that in all this pent up demand and the fact that one of our goals during the pandemic is to just remain, if nothing else, remain relevant. (47:58): Talk to race directors, talk to consumers. Let's do offers. Let's just be empathetic, but just stay in front, get, keep the brand in front of people. They don't have to necessarily buy right now or do what they're, but just keep it in front of people, entertain people, offer up help. Just be communicative with our community. And then when the time comes, it will grow back. Because one thing you might find in other categories where sales have just gone crazy, if it's bikes or helmets or shoes or whatever, I dunno if that's going to be sustainable sales once the pandemic is over, that might be a risk for some brands in some categories. Whereas we have the opposite. We actually have all upside from where we are (48:37): Versus potential. There's nothing in my mind that says we're going to, gore going to slide down. We're only going up from this point. We started down, now we're just on the way up.

So because there's the brand side and there's the product side and there's the business side of things. And so those brands have complex work. And so the more we can mimic and mirror that on our side, the better the relationship will be. Because a lot of it's about relationships and being good people that are carrying the torch of these brands and doing it with integrity is pretty key.

And the idea morphed quickly, I think for us in our minds is this is so much more than just living in the visitor center. This message is relevant right now in this moment in time, especially what's been going on with public lands and their popularity. content:
Sean Slobodan (00:10:21): I don't know if it was hometown treatment there, but I mean obviously it was pretty great to be able to have it premier at a festival so close to my home. And Shandy obviously from Alberta as well. So a lot of Canadian influence on this one, and it was cool to have it play there for sure.

Cole Heilborn (00:10:41): So a lot of things we talk about on this podcast are in the client side of things. We interview a lot of folks who are on the brand side, who are the people that are coming up with the goals of, oh, we need to be able to inspire people to appreciate our national parks and respect them. We haven't had a lot of voices on the other side of that, the people who then those people go to and figure out actually, how do we do that? And obviously film is such an amazing tool to be able to communicate a message like that or many others. That's why we love it, that's why we do it. But I'm really curious to dive into how you guys went through taking this goal and actually turning it into something that is effective and communicates that story and that emotion and inspires your audience. I guess from a big picture level, how did you initially approach this idea and what ideas did you try? What things did you avoid?

content: Sean Slobodan (00:11:41): Yeah, I mean it was interesting because they actually had a couple of ideas, even a script for the project. So the amazing part about it's, they'd always kind of put out an idea and go like, but hey, this is just us and we're just paying for everything, but I take it or leave it. This is just an idea. If you think it'd work, if you don't think it would work, let us know. And it was just they were always so like, Hey, this is something, here's something we could do, or here's an idea, but let us know what you think. And I think throughout my career as a filmmaker, every project you work on, you learn more about your own voice and your own style and your own approach. I think we all packed probably 10 years of experience into this one year because of this project, but you just have your past experiences to pull on and go, okay, well here's something that, an approach that I know works for me that I feels true to me. (00:12:55): And so we just use that as a bit of a blueprint to say, Hey, we've told a lot of short docus style stories in the past and that's where a lot of my experience comes from web content or commercials or things that you're dealing with real people and you're trying to tell an authentic story often in a five to eight minute window. And we felt like, okay, well they have all this information. They talk about wanting to educate on the geological aspect and the flora and the fauna and the water in the park and the colors of the rocks and the Colorado plateau and all of these things that are often a part of films like this where it's just very educationally focused. And so that was where a lot of the ideas were coming from and they felt like it's still important to have this in there. (00:13:53): And so we kind of took that and went, in our experience, what audiences have most connected with. If you're wanting to have somebody walk away from a film or a piece of content changed or with a different idea or with a different perspective, you have to obviously connect with them on a personal level. And I don't know of a better way of doing that than telling authentic stories of us of other people. And I think that's why we get inspired to do the things that we set goals to do or want to do or be like is we see other people doing it and we go, I want to be like that, or I want to try to do something like that. And so I think we took that and just try to apply it into, well, how do we take some real stories and work in some of these aspects that they're interested in still kind of being a part of this project that are important? And we found that you can do that through people that are personally connected through the park and just, we basically just said, okay, well how many people stories can we fit into a 25 minute piece or a 45 minute piece? And that's where we started. We went, okay, we can probably fit, I don't know, somewhere between two and 10. So then we just kind of started whittling down from there and trying to identify characters to fit in,

Cole Heilborn (00:15:27): But at the same time, you got to find those individual stories, but then those stories all have to converge and connect in some way, otherwise they just feel very scattered and they're not working towards something bigger than each of their individual stories. So yeah, this kind of gets into the grittiness of the characters and how you choose characters. How many did you end up with and what were, for folks that haven't seen the film, one, you should watch it when you can, but who were those characters for you guys? Who did you discover and why?

Shandi Kano (00:16:04): Well, so we had a little bit of a blueprint when we talked about they wanted to talk about the elements of water and sandstone and wildlife and safety, plants, safety, all these sorts of things. So since we are outdoorsy people and we had interests in these things via activities, we kind of linked certain characters or hopeful characters to different elements they wanted to talk about. So with geology, we thought, well, what is cooler than canyoneering and what is cooler than understanding the land and its use? Then hearing it from a native Paiute person, we had to link the characters to these elements of nature. I think that helped tie it together because all those elements were essentially what we're working to preserve. (00:17:04): We whiteboarded a lot and we set ourselves a blueprint of here's all the different elements and here's all the different things you can do, and here's all the different kinds of people. Because one of the goals too is this isn't supposed to speak to one kind of person or one kind of activity or one group. This is for everybody, people who come to the park twice a month, people who come to the park once in their lives, people who've never been. And so we had to make sure that we would cover bases with characters that would speak to all sorts of people. So between that, between the elements, between the activities, I think we started to line up on characters. And so the characters ended up being a couple of park rangers, a guy who's lived there for a very long time, a farmer, a local rancher

Shandi Kano (00:18:01): Yes, so Leon, a Paiute family, a foreign tourist who came to from Japan to Zion for the first time, a couple of rock climbers, a couple of canyon years school kids. Water was a character that we made intentional, like water was a character. It's not a person, but it was a character. That's only seven. Who are you missing? James. James

Sean Slobodan (00:18:26): And a planar artist,

Shandi Kano (00:18:28): A plain air artist.

Sean Slobodan (00:18:30): Yeah, I think we just kind started with what we had. The park had identified certain things they wanted to include history of the park, kind of how the park was formed. They wanted to talk about the geology and just the uniqueness of the rock formations there in the park, just the craziness of those cliffs and those walls and the beauty of that, the role of water in the park. They wanted to talk about safety, they wanted to address wildlife, wildlife, flora, fauna. So we had all of those things and it's just kind of going, okay, well here's a subject or an item. What kind of person would be able to connect in a personal way with this thing? And the focus? I think a big part of the discussion at first was moving away from just over flooding with information rather than and more focused on telling this person's story and it being connected to that aspect of the park. (00:19:52): So we often talked about less is more. I think oftentimes there's just so much information and so many things you want a viewer to understand, but when you give too much, you actually get less out of that. Whereas if you can inspire and introduce them to a certain thing, we can leave a space or leave a film and then on our own go and search and learn more about it. And I think that was the goal with a lot of this was to inspire people to learn more on their own, to start connecting their own dots, but to give them a starting place to do that.

Cole Heilborn (00:20:27): Yeah. So it sounds like you had your objectives from the client and from your just personal goals for the project, and then you started to map out who you ideal character would be to reflect those objectives. Is that what you're saying?

Sean Slobodan (00:20:40): Absolutely.

Cole Heilborn (00:20:41): Gotcha.

Sean Slobodan (00:20:43): If you talk about geology, first thing that came to mind for us, Zion is an iconic place for climbers, and climbers have played an important role in our national parks in the United States and really all over the world. And so we felt like that would be a great fit. We could find somebody with a personal story, a personal connection to Zion. It would also obviously visually give us an opportunity to really show off the beauty of that red rock in the park, but show a person who respects the place. And still climbing is an interesting part of the story because climbers have, and maybe we don't need to get into this, but climbers have a tremendous impact in national parks, some for good and some for not so good. And so it was definitely, yeah, I mean it was tough. I mean, just climbing in general, such a polarizing can we found out, I mean, firsthand experience can create such a polarizing effect on people. (00:22:05): If climbers are so passionate about these places, often climbing and activism kind of go hand in hand and they're viewed as going hand in hand. And yet you find out that there's the opposite side of that. People are very against those types of activities in the park, and do they create more harm than good? And so there was a whole kind of different discussion that came from that aspect, but you just kind of go, okay, well, who would be a good character to talk about history? Well, who's been around the park for 350 years, probably a local farmer. And so these are just ideas we're throwing up on the board, and a lot of 'em ended up turning into real people that we were able to connect with.

Cole Heilborn (00:22:56): So you come up with this dream character, a farmer or a native individual, and then you have to go find them and make sure that they're actually willing to be on camera and can speak to what you want and can actually articulate thoughts on camera. How do you do that from a logistical and from a creative perspectives?

Sean Slobodan (00:23:17): Well, it's funny because we hadn't actually won the project yet, but we were, as often happens, you put together ideas, a big pitch deck, and you go in and you try to go, Hey, here's our vision. Here's what we think would work, and here's why. So we had at that point, this is end of 2018, we said, okay, here's all of the kind of areas that we want to touch on in the film that we've discussed together. Here are the characters that we think would work best to get into those topics or get into those areas of discussion. And so we had these kind of make-believe characters climber that has a goal to climber here, old timer here, ranger in the park. And so we had all these kind of theoretical people, and then they go, this sounds amazing, let's do it. And then our team afterwards, we kind of look at each other and we're like, well,

Shandi Kano (00:24:21): It's go time

Sean Slobodan (00:24:21): Crap. Now we actually have to find people that fit into these. They've approved it, signed on the dotted line, and now we actually have to deliver these people that we don't even know if they exist. So luckily it worked out, but it was an interesting moment for sure. We were super pumped to be able to move forward, but it was definitely learning as we went. We'd made people up, and now we had to actually find the real versions.

Shandi Kano (00:24:51): But I think it wasn't like they were made up in a way where it was farfetched. They'd exist.

Sean Slobodan (00:24:54): I mean, I've been around humans before, so I knew people like that existed somewhere. I just didn't know them specifically.

Shandi Kano (00:25:01): I didn't know that was a moment where you went, oh crap.

Sean Slobodan (00:25:03): Oh yeah.

Shandi Kano (00:25:04): I went, oh yeah, I'm so excited.

Sean Slobodan (00:25:07): Well, we're walking out of the meeting and we're like, oh, this is stoked. We got the project. And then it's like, I don't know any of these people. The work was cut out.

Cole Heilborn (00:25:18): Well, that's where the producer really kicks in and starts to make things happen.

Shandi Kano (00:25:23): So okay, I think as you're speaking about this and the question comes up, I start to go, oh yeah, here's my answer. And then I'm like, oh, yeah, oh yeah. And I remember what a mountain this was to climb, and it was very exciting for me. I was very excited to, I'm not saying I was bummed out. I know you're not, but I was like, yes, uncharted territory. Here we go. I'm going to go find all these people. We had roles to fill, we had a brief to fulfill. We had a film to make with goals and sight. And so really it just comes down to hardcore networking and staying at it and really getting your elevator pitch down, understanding exactly what you're looking for and understanding how to use your network and how to connect with people to find and start to begin exploratory interviews with all of them, which is always a little bit of, well, what are you doing and why? And here's kind of what we're looking for, but it can't be so much like, are you this person that X, Y, Z? You really have to connect with them, understand what they're about, because those human elements start to come out and you start to see, well, this is how it fits in. And so I mean, at one point we said, are you just everything against the wall and seeing what sticks? And it's like, well, but it's not without direction. You know what I mean?

content:
Sean Slobodan (00:26:52): Yeah. I mean the main goal for the whole thing was the approach was, and it always I think will be for us, this is just how we have gone about our filmmaking, is telling real human being stories. And I think that's always going to be the most effective way to connect with audiences is if they sense they're experiencing something that's real and not fabricated. I mean, you're always going to have an agenda. I think even the most objective oriented person is still going to end up with an agenda. We definitely had an agenda with this. We want people to be better stewards in our national parks and to treat these places with way more respect than we currently do. And to understand our impact in those places, that's our objective. But I think telling real human stories is always going to be the best way to go about it. And whether you're selling a product or whether you are just sharing your life, I don't think it matters. I think the whole goal with content is to connect with people and telling each other's stories in an inspiring way is going to be the best way to do it.

Cole Heilborn (00:28:24): So you're sitting there listening to a hundred people tell their story. What are you looking for? What makes a good story from an individual? What stands out to you guys as you're listening to these people talk?

Sean Slobodan (00:28:39): Do you want to tell him about Hitomi?

content: Shandi Kano (00:28:40): I will, but I will say this too. That process is like I'm taking direction from Sean and Travis who's the co-director on the film. They're the ultimate, the last say in the creative decision. And they've got these ideas and we've all kind of mapped out the kind of people we want. And so as I'm going through doing exploratory calls and trying to decide ultimately who I can bring back to Sean and Travis for them to say, yes, we're headed in the right direction. So it's very much synergistic and how we're working together. And I'm constantly, okay, interviewed this person today. I don't think they're the right fit, but I would generally gather a few options per character, bring them back to Sean and Travis and kind of say, here's why I think these people can work. And I'd kind of go through things and it ultimately comes down to them being like, okay, let's talk more to this person, or I want to talk to this person. Initially, it's just me kind of sourcing and feeling things out. And if I feel like it's a good fit, bring it back to them, then we'll get on a larger group call. They'll do a deep dive with this person, but ultimately they have the last say in that call, it's a creative decision and I'm working to fulfill that order or that vision. (00:29:55): So that's the process, and it just kind of keeps whittling itself down until we get to a point where we are kind of dialing in their story that's going to be portrayed in the film, and we're going through that with them and pulling out the pieces we want to focus on. And anyway, that takes us in a different direction. But the question was how, and for me, the answer really comes down to it's made easy when you have talented directors who know what they're looking for and understand how to understand people, how to connect with people, how this person's story is going to play out on camera, and ultimately how the world is going to be able to see them. (00:30:38): And so I think this example that I was sharing with Sean earlier, I spent from, gosh, January until July trying to find a person overseas to come.

Shandi Kano (00:28:40): And honestly, probably before January too, the park had ideas on people who were overseas who could be visitors in this role. And we spoke to people in China and India and Japan, and it was like June, I think it was after or when we got linked up with one of our partners, they had a distributor in Japan who ran a women's outdoor company for retreats and things. And they said, why don't we link you with her? And this is after months. And we had a couple people and it just didn't feel right. And so I interviewed five or six other women from this group in Japan, and I felt like there were three good candidates and nothing was really sparking that was like, this is a home run. But I brought these three to Sean and Travis, we all interviewed them, and there was kind of this thing where it was like, well, who do you really want? Who do you really want? I was just like, I think they'll all be fine. But ultimately it came down to Sean and Travis feeling like this one person would be more able and more willing to be emotionally open and vulnerable, which was something we had to pay attention to. Because Japanese culture is so different from ours,

Sean Slobodan (00:32:20): My sarcasm does not transfer over very well, and pretty much I rely a lot on that aspect of my personality. So I needed somebody who was going to at least get that, you know what I mean? Or appreciate it.

Shandi Kano (00:32:36): But I think that decision was made because they could see something that I couldn't, quite frankly, which was that this person who we ended up choosing Hitomi, would be more willing, capable to open herself up and to share her feelings and emotions with us. And I cannot tell you how amazing it was to watch that idea that they had come true. She was incredible. And one of my favorite characters of the film, it's very hard to pick favorite, but I don't know what you want to call that was spot on. And her story just became such a beautiful moment for all of us. And I dunno that it would've happened. I mean,

Sean Slobodan (00:33:29): I remember when we were speaking with Hitomi and we were also speaking with a couple of the other women that we were interviewing over in Japan. I was on the road with my family, we were driving to, I think we were driving to Canada and we stopped at a hotel and I was trying to get all the kids, my wife and I have three kids, we're trying to get everyone in the hotel. I'm on my headphones, I'm trying to hold my phone like this. And I remember I just had to get kids in the hotel room. I gave my wife the sign off and the good luck. And then I closed the door and had to go out in the hall and then try to focus on me, okay, are you going to be emotionally available to me? And it was an interesting time, but that was just kind of how it worked through that process was it was all the time, and that's a whole different aspect of it, but it was all day every day for a good year. We were finding characters filming in the park already working on the edit. It was all aspects of the production were happening at the same time and at all times of the day.

Cole Heilborn (00:34:56): So yeah, that's a really good example. You're chatting with a few different folks, three of them stand out, but one of those three, you just kind of have a hunch about what is it about that person that makes you think they're going to open up and fill that role and surprise you with more than you could want when they're on camera, essentially you're taking a big risk, inviting someone into a film, inviting them not only from the financial aspect, but also from the story because you're inviting them into this story and they have to fit and they have to kind of meet this expectation, but you don't really know if they will prior because people change when they're on set and they're in front of the camera and they can clam up or they can open up. But what is it about those initial conversations? What are you noticing? What are those nonverbal things that you're picking up on that help you trust that hunch?

Sean Slobodan (00:35:58): I don't know. I mean, I think that's a good question, but I don't know that I really know the answer to that. It is just time and experience. I think just sharing time with lots of different people. I think for the most part it's just learning how to trust yourself. And I've made plenty of wrong calls with people and had plenty of horrible interviews and just trying to pull from that in moments like this, just to try to do the best you can and you just kind of have to live with the outcome. And sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't. But I think luckily over time you just get better at it. I mean, I love talking with people and getting to know them. And so I think an important aspect in thinking about it now is if you are real and open and emotionally available to someone that you're getting to know, they're more likely to reciprocate that and be open and available to you. And that's not going to happen with everyone. But I think everyone that ended up in the film, it happened with to a certain degree, and I think we were able to kind of trust that with the Tommy. I mean, we flew out to Japan before we'd ever met her. We didn't know what her apartment looked like. I had ideas of shots that I wanted to get, but I had no idea how we were going to get them. (00:37:41): Yeah, I mean it was an incredible leap of faith on both parts. She didn't know us, she didn't know what our process looked like. She didn't know what she was inviting into her apartment and her work and her kind of just circles of family and friends, her

Speaker 4 (00:37:59): Family.

If you're going to hire somebody to tell a story for your brand, you have to have complete trust in that person because I mean, that's why you hire people to do certain things, right? (00:53:50): Because you hope that they're better at that thing than you are, or that they can see it in a way that's going to connect with people better than what you can envision. content:
Doug Thielen (01:16): Yeah, that's a good question. I mean, I think Seattle and where Seattle has been and the Northwest in general, and the type of people that came here back in 1897, and you could argue that probably even in today's world of tech and pioneers that's drawn, folks who've had this adventurous spirit, be it in literally getting outdoors and going to the Klondike or making their claim in the timber industry or in the mining industry or in the tech industry. I think Seattle and kind of the attitude of what it builds and the people who come here who live here is woven into the people who work at Filson, who worked at Filson, who started Filson and came all the way through. Even today, looking at the folks who are on my team and I get to work with, they're outdoor at the core. There are people, it's one of those where you sit around on a Monday and it's fun to hear about the diverse experiences from people who are duck hunting to our mountain biking to skiing. It's fun to have folks who really enjoy being out in the outdoors and the northwest and what it provides. And I think you see that in the brand and in the products that Fen puts out there.

Cole Heilborn (02:25): So you walk into a store where we're looking down on your guys' flagship store right now, and you walk in and you feel like you're kind of walking back in time in a way as the marketing guy or as part of the team of the marketing. Tell me a little bit about the Filson brand and what that feels like and what that is.

Doug Thielen (02:45): Yeah, and it's one of those things where I think when I came on board, a lot of folks could see it and knew it, and they knew it was the brand, but they had a hard time talking about what it was. (02:55): A lot of you could see something and go, yeah, that's Filson, that feels right. But describing it was often difficult. We set out in that, in this growth size side of our business to build a brand guide. I think that's one of the things we were talking about earlier is we call it the Fills and Operation Manual, and unlike a lot of brand guides that would just talk straight about where you are today as a brand, your vision, your values, your purpose, your mission. We knew we had a big task where we're 120 year old company. We wanted to find a way to talk to people about the brand, but you couldn't do that without talking about the history. And I think that's something we talk and feel a lot where Filson has once foot in the past, but by no means do we feel that we are beholden to it, are tied to it.

Doug Thielen (03:36): We

Doug Thielen (03:36): Can absolutely have your other foot and our head focused on the future. We are an outfitter and we think through that a lot. What would an outfitter do? What we provide, what can we bring to the table? I often talk a lot about having a connection to the wild and then the wild and the unknown, and I think the wild can be a lot of different things for a lot of different people. What's wild to you? And I maybe vastly different than what's wild to someone sitting somewhere else in a different office doing a different thing. I think that's what starts to set Filson a little bit apart, is showing real people doing real things through our marketing, through our advertising, through our events that people may look at and go, I didn't know that still existed. I didn't know people still did those things. That's crazy. And it's a little bit of that wild and unknown, and that's one thing that's kind of fun too for me is those folks we see in features in our social, in our campaigns, in our creative, they're not models.

Doug Thielen (04:32): I

Doug Thielen (04:32): Mean, I guess they're technically a model because wearing a product and they're an ad, but those are real humans doing real things that we've got to know through our producers, through our content contributors that we're featuring, that we're finding. And I love it more than anything when someone's like, oh, look at that guy. He's never clearly wheeled an ax before. And it's like, well, actually, he's been logging for 37 years, so here, talk to Nick.

Doug Thielen (04:53): Do

Doug Thielen (04:53): You want to tell him why you hold the ax that way? So it is fun to find ways to feature people that may not be at the forefront of what people think about from a fishing industry or logging industry or any of those sort pieces.

Cole Heilborn (05:08): Yeah. What is the value of a brand? Why spend all the energy and why do you even have a job creating a brand?

Doug Thielen (05:15): Yeah, that's a good question, and I don't know if I have the right answer or the perfect answer. I think the value of the brand is all the things that you don't see. It's the intangibles, it's the places that fill in the cracks. There's the product, and a lot of places have the same product or similar product, and you can use the best fibers, and yes, you can use the best materials that are available and stitch it in a way that no one else has. But I think the brand and what it stands for, the things you surround it with and where it comes from, the providence of that thing is what really pulls on people from an emotional perspective. It allows them to engage and interact with it.

Doug Thielen (05:50): It's

Doug Thielen (05:50): One of the reasons you'll see at Filson. We have a ton of different events and experiences as a way to let people engage and interact with the brand to learn to experience, to dive deeper into be it an educational component or just a cool component, or to feel that they had a chance to be a part of something from conservation to education. And so for us, it's building all those different on-ramps to the brand

Cole Heilborn (06:15): And

Cole Heilborn (06:25): Okay, interesting. So you mentioned an aspect of the brand. You mentioned the emotional part. Can you dive a little bit deeper into that? Why deal with emotion? What does that do?

Doug Thielen (06:38): Yeah, I mean, I think we don't necessarily set out to say, let's touch on this emotion or let's find this thing and really bring it to the forefront as much as it is trying to show and highlight things we may not see up everywhere else. You mentioned wanting to talk about the Will to Live film that we recently did. (06:59): That's a piece that was a passion project that I got to work on with some really incredible people at FOS Media. Frankie and Adam over there were incredible. They were able to find a story and bring a story forward that I would say most brands wouldn't tell because it is a story for those who aren't familiar about a guy named Gary Edinger. He's written a book, which is phenomenal. So if you don't watch the film, read the book, either one or both, or both do both. And he's this incredible human who lived this life that read it was out of a fairytale champion dog sled racer, worked on fishing boats and was a trapper in Alaska. Comes back to Wisconsin where he's from, to be a logger, has a tragic accident where he loses his leg and he has to make a decision to pull himself back to the skidder from the skidder to his truck. (07:51): And then he drove himself out of the woods while on the phone with nine one one and made the decision to kind of fight to save his life and everything that happened out of that. That's a story that doesn't necessarily fit nicely into a box is an outdoor story. Is that an adventure story? Trust? It was like a human story. And so we look for those things. We look for those things that may not get always told or shown or featured or highlighted. We talk about harder or faster, tougher, meaner sometimes not as a joke, but a little bit of where is that going? Where are other brands necessarily not going to play, and how does that continue to evolve the story of Filsen?

Cole Heilborn (08:27): Yeah, interesting. Okay. So there's a lot of things you just mentioned there that I feel like we could unpack for a long time. But diving a little bit further into the film, I know you guys have done a lot of other films in the past. What about film is something that you guys choose to invest in and to create?

Doug Thielen (08:47): Yeah, that's a great question. I think we're still trying to figure it out. I mean, there's a lot of brands out there who've done phenomenal work in film for REIA place where I used to work does content. That's fantastic. Yeti obviously has done fantastic content, Patagonia as well. So I mean, I think we've got a ways to go before we're on the scale of what they're doing. That said, I think we've taken a chance on a few different things and have worked with a few different partners, and we've had to get creative with small budgets being a brand that isn't that size of those other ones I just mentioned.

Cole Heilborn (09:18): Sure.

Doug Thielen (09:18): So for us, one of the things we're able to do is partner with different brands like Danner Footwear to go out to find a story to come together, and for us, finding a partner that makes sense so that the consumer, when they see that film and they see those two brands together, they don't kind of squint and wonder like

Cole Heilborn (09:34): What? Yeah, it makes

Doug Thielen (09:35): Sense. Yeah. They go, well, of course Danner would work with Filson. That makes sense.

Cole Heilborn (09:39): Sure.

And then it was working with great storytellers and Adam and Frankie and that team over at FO to build something that we felt was going to be right for the story, right, for the brand. And then for us, it's taking a look at, and we do this with pretty much everything. We take a look at anything we invest in. It could be an event, it could be a product, it could be a partnership, a film, and squeezing every ounce of opportunity out of it. And so it's not just a film that we run online, it's a chance for our, put our brand in front of new people. So what's our distribution strategy and putting that film in front of the right audience? What's the event? What's the experience? Is it in store? Is it out of store? Are we partnering with a brewery to screen the film?

Doug Thielen (10:26): How

Doug Thielen (10:26): Are we leveraging all those different pieces? How are we submitting it to film festivals once it gets accepted? How are we showing up and activating where I think sometimes it's easy to say, this thing is this thing. We made a film, we put it on YouTube,

Cole Heilborn (10:40): Leave it on the shelf

Doug Thielen (10:41): Onto the next thing. I think one of the fun parts of being 120 year old startup being scrappy is you don't have that luxury where all of a sudden it's like, if we are going to spend this chunk of our budget making this thing or on this partnership, we've got to find every way to maximize that. What's the piece of content? What's the story? What's the social post? As a way to leverage all of that. I think a cool outcome of that is from a customer perspective, you're giving 'em a ton of on-ramps to discover it, to find it. It feels integrated. You're going a chance to go deeper If you want to go deeper, read a longer story, watch a bigger thing. And so those are reasons we look for films.

Cole Heilborn (11:20): So unfortunately, budgets are a very real thing. And so I know that you probably have to take, you look at an event or you look at a film and there's a budget associated with it. You have to take that to someone and I'm assuming get that signed off or it's part of your budget. How do you decide this film or this event or whatever you're trying to put on is worth the money?

Doug Thielen (11:43): Yeah, that's a great question. I mean, to me, everything comes back to what's the objective? What's the objective for the company for the year, what's the objective for the department for the year? What's the objective for the channel for the year? And to me, it becomes very simple to say yes or no to or in terms of what's the priority. So if our objective is to put new eyeballs on Filson as a way to drive customer acquisition and an opportunity presents itself that doesn't help with that, it's quickly gets filtered out.

Cole Heilborn (12:13): Sure.

Doug Thielen (12:14): It's also something where we take a look and say, okay, we have this much spend for the year and we're going to wait that opportunity, be it a film or an event, and look and say, okay, well this is what it costs. This is what it means by doing this. We no longer can do these other four things. Is everybody on board with that? Does everyone understand what that means by going through that? So it becomes relatively easy when it's all objective based and saying, okay, these were our goals. Does this help us get closer to it?

Cole Heilborn (12:42): I see.

Doug Thielen (12:43): Or does this detract from it?

Cole Heilborn (12:45): Yeah. So what did you find from doing that film? It's been out for a while. I think you guys are up to how many views on Facebook or in YouTube now?

I know back in November when you looked at Danner's, Facebook and YouTube and our Facebook and YouTube, we were well over a million views. We ran a targeted campaign too from a distribution perspective targeted towards new audiences. So we're using that as a way to bring people into the fills and

Doug Thielen (13:18): We also ran multiple screenings. So we did a screening here in Seattle screen in event Oregon screen in Portland, Oregon as a way to have an event and bring people together. We had Gary and the FOSS team out here in Seattle. We had Gary and the FOSS team at Ben. One of the more interesting events is we ran one in Portland at a brewery, straight screening. People could watch the exact same film on YouTube or they could come out to Rogue Brewing and have an evening with us and Danner. But we brought in a nonprofit back country, hunters and Anglers, a group that we work with quite a bit from a public land and access perspective, and we used it as a fundraising event. So Danner put in a great giveaway. We had a great giveaway. Rogue, I think it was a percent of sales that night, all went back to BHA standing room. Only packed house had to turn people away, which I love. That's people who want to engage with the community, meet other people, get outside of their home and watch a film again, they could watch online. To me, that's telling that there's a hunger within that community to get together. So we're continuing to do screens in the east coast. We've done 'em in Detroit and New York. I think we have one in Boston coming up, (14:30): Some in store as a way to drive store traffic, others at breweries and other locations as a way to, you want to have the man of the woman sitting there drinking a beer. They look over and say, well, what is that thing that's playing? So it's an easy kind of low key way to introduce the brand and film new folks.

Cole Heilborn (14:49): Sure, sure. Have you guys a chance to kind of come full circle, circle the wagons and analyze any metrics from the film? Have you collected those or is that still, I mean, the film is still kind running.

Doug Thielen (15:01): Yeah, the film's still running. So the wonderful part, I guess, of running the distribution campaign through Google is all the analytics and metrics is able to get you, so you're able to see, while we were optimizing that campaign for views, we were able to see click through rates as well as return on ad spend from that. So it's positive to be able to see and go, yes, not only did we make a film that yes can attract new customers, yes, people are watching 80, 90, a hundred percent of the way through, but it's also driving clicks to the website and it's also driving sales. So from a metrics perspective, that's a great story to package and tell leadership and say, yeah, this thing, yes, it cost us money, but it also made us money definitively through this channel. And so those are things that help get more films, more projects funded.

Cole Heilborn (15:48): Yeah, makes sense.

Doug Thielen (15:50): Yeah.

Cole Heilborn (15:50): So transitioning a little bit, what is Filson's biggest challenge? What are you guys working on? That's,

Doug Thielen (15:59): That's a great question. I mean, I think we face the same challenge that a lot of brands and businesses face that have retail locations is how do you grow retail while at the same time facing the ever present wave of online and online retailers direct to consumers who don't have retail at all or don't have

Doug Thielen (16:18): Wholesale.

Doug Thielen (16:19): How do we continue to develop product in a way that's innovative and true to the brand? How do you do those pieces while at the same time growing and hitting the growth rates that people want us to hit? (16:34): I think it's a good challenge. We definitely have, I mentioned that the mentality of being 120 year old startup, and it really feels that way. It feels everyone who is here has come in and has invested in the company. They really want to see this thing work. It's all hustle. It's pretty fun. I think it either attracts, I've used the analogy before when talking to new hires, potential hires that here it filson. If you see a leak in the roof, be careful to point it out because someone will hand you a hammer and a shingle and say, fix it. Go. I tell that to people and that either attracts them and gets them really excited about the opportunity that lies ahead, or it scares the shit out of 'em, and they're like, yeah, not for me. That's fine. That's not a bad thing. But I think the brand and the life cycle and growth cycle of where we are today, it's interesting to see us push on the elasticity of the brand and what we can do and where it can go. And good ideas have come from anywhere, and you have a chance to work on a lot of different things here.

Cole Heilborn (17:33): So I guess in the outdoor retail space, there's a lot of manufacturers making a lot of different types of products, some of 'em not so different. Where do you guys see yourself fitting into that market? Because in today's age of Gore-Tex and whatever the next fabric is, you have a much different approach to your manufacturing methods and the materials you use. Where do you fit into that?

Doug Thielen (17:59): That's a good question. It's probably better answered by our product development team who spends their nights, days, weekends, every week, hour, thinking about how to do that. I think from a marketing perspective, what's really fun is the dynamism of the brand. We've got our Mackinac wool cruiser, which is made the same way with the same material as it was when it was patented in 1914, hanging next to a technical rainwear product that is using some of the best fabric and best products and materials that you can get, and what other brands really going to be able to play in that zone. There are by no means, I think we're the only one, but that's a pretty unique thing to be able to pull on something that has history, that has providence, that's been around a long time, that's still warrants itself and is useful in the outdoor industry. But then we have things that are technical that are solving problems for our customers that we're able to create, develop, and give them so that they have that need met.

Cole Heilborn (18:59): Yeah, interesting. What do you enjoy doing in the outdoors? What's your go-to?

Doug Thielen (19:04): Oh, man. If it's wintertime, you find me skiing. That's literally where I spend every time that I can. I've got two kiddos, which makes it a little more challenging now, but now we just got them on skis. The youngest turned two early December, and she was on skis the first time on her birthday.

Cole Heilborn (19:20): Oh man.

Doug Thielen (19:20): And then the 5-year-old, she is a ski machine. She goes everywhere with me, we're Whistler. She's skiing at all. And if I would let her, she'd go even further and harder. So that's fun. And then the summertime mountain biking, which was a sport that I did for a while, kind of stepped away from, did road biking and triathlon for a long time. And then when I moved back to the northwest in 2014, just rediscovered mountain biking and the muddy messiness. That's super fun. And I really haven't, I think I've touched my road bike two times in the last five years. I always just spend all that time on the mountain bike.
