Doug Thielen (19:57): No, absolutely not.

Cole Heilborn (19:59): As you look forward towards marketing in the future, there's obviously a whole new wave of people that are moving in and taking marketing positions. What do you see, if you could say anything to the people that are stepping into it that are learning it, what do you think is, what's the takeaway? What should they consider as they're trying to figure out how to do this themselves?

Doug Thielen (20:20): Yeah, that's a great question. I think people and brands that have the ability to blend content and commerce and see them not as separate things, but see them as one, see them through the customer's eyes are going to win, be their brand or a person. I think the days of seeing things so separate, oh, I do. Oh, I do creative. I tell stories. I sell things. It's not how the customers look at

Doug Thielen (20:44): It.

Doug Thielen (20:44): And the more brands and people do to marry those two things, and I'm referred to it as story selling instead of storytelling, there's a piece to it at all points of that funnel where you're meeting that customer. But by no means are we doing it perfect. We have a long way to go to get to where I want to see SB. But when you have that ability to provide value to the customer, so if you come in and buy a fishing jacket and you get an email saying, Hey, here's your order. It's confirmed. It's on its way. I don't want to send you an email that has another buy now piece into it. I want to send you an email that has a story about fishing. Come watch the film (21:22): On the life of a guide. Come read a story on how to take care of your jacket, come read or view this trip, this photo tour this guy took down in Texas. That was crazy. I want to provide content that adds value to your experience. On the other side of that one, someone's engaging with a film or a story on the fill some journal. I want to be able to drive them to product that's relevant to the story that they're reading in a way that adds value. They read a great fishing story, they read a great hunting story. Now let's take them to product and information that allows them to dive a little deeper. If they see an image on the story, they're like, ah, that's a great jacket she wearing. Well, we should make it easy for them to find it.

Doug Thielen (22:03): Right?

Doug Thielen (22:04): So that blend of content and commerce, I think is something that people can bring to the table. Adding a layer of creativity to the numbers and adding numbers to creativity and not being scared to do so, knowing from a numbers side, not everything is black and white. There is some gray. Sometimes. We have to make that gray decision and knowing it's that not being held to the numbers on creative side, but being aware of the metrics, being aware of what's going on, letting that make you a better creative.

content:
Cole Heilborn (01:40): Okay. I'm super excited to chat with you guys today. I'm stoked to kind of hear a little bit about what you guys are up to. I've been seeing your name popping up over the interweb the last couple months. I'm assuming that's because you guys are doing something pretty cool and pretty rad, but fill us in what is super Pacific. What's this project you guys have undertaken and is now consuming most of your lives?

Peter Williams (02:05): So I can give you the quick and dirty history to date if you want. And Spencer and I worked together at a design consultancy in past lives, and when we left that job, we stayed in touch and maintained a friendship. And I have a five-year-old son, and as my life's transitioned from not being a parent to being a parent, I realized it became a lot more complex to get outdoors and started looking at how to make that easier. So I started looking at, do we want to do a conversion van? Do we want to get a slide in camper? What's our best adventure vehicle? And my life had some constraints. There's not great off street parking at my house, and we're kind of thinking about it with an eye on the budget and all those kind of real world constraints. So I started the pop-up camper market and got really interested in it and was just over at Spencer's one afternoon, two summers ago now having a beer and looking at 'em and was like, these are cool. These are looking sweet. There's a couple things I would do different about this one. I'd do that one a little bit different. And we were just over a beer. We're like, well, let's just make, you've got the metal skills, I've got the fabric skills. Let's make one just like we want it. These are sweet. We'll make one for your truck, one for mine, and that'll be fun. What a cool thing to do. (03:30): And that led into really digging into the design, looking at the designs real closely and really studying the decisions that everyone had made and looking at some feedback and reviews, just trying to educate our point of view on what we wanted to do, which in the process of that we started seeing a lot of back orders and it felt like there was an undersupply for a pretty big demand. And we then started doing some market research and sort of realized we were looking at what might be a business opportunity. And at that point we had breaks on our fund side project and started thinking about is this something we could build a business around? And now whatever it is, a year and a half later, here we are up and running and trying to keep up.

content: Peter Williams (06:01): Yeah, essentially we have the broadstrokes of our design intent was that we both own pickup trucks and use them daily, use them as pickup trucks regularly in our normal life. And we both really put a premium on spending time outdoors, especially getting our kids out and our families out. So we wanted something that would facilitate that kind of outdoor lifestyle without compromising the utility of our pickups. So we wanted something basically that was going to be a camper shell, just a canopy over the truck bed that weekdays you've got an empty truck bed, a dry empty truck bed, and then on Friday you can just throw a cooler in your kitchen in there and you're set. So really trying to streamline the whole transition from work truck to adventure truck. (06:50): So that's the broad stroke stroke sort of functionally of what we did. Then from there, we just looked at, we have a pretty good sense of what we want to do with them, but they're really useful for anyone that wants to go outside, regardless of what they do. If they're driving to the place outdoors that they want to go do that thing and they plan on spending the night, then this is a super useful piece of equipment. So towards that end, we figured we would try to do a really good job on about 90% of the build and then just set the people up, set everyone up to really finish the build easily and get it tuned into exactly what they want it to be. So even we've designed it with an eye for customization and trying to facilitate people's process of tuning it in, if they want to build out a kitchen and have it all dedicated to camping full time that we've got wire chases and threaded bosses and lash points all throughout it, and if they have a different intent, then it should be easy to bolt stuff to it and strap stuff onto it. (07:51): And I really get it dialed.

The wed shaped tent can also be used as kind of a standalone unit. So you can take that wedge-shaped tent without the canopy and put it on your Toyota for runner or your kind of SUV off-road, SUV, and still be able to just use it as a standalone tent, very low profile. One of the features of this is trying to have as little impact on your vehicle as possible. So making it lightweight, making it super low profile, making it so it's not like the standard kind of tent that you see on a Subaru or something, which is a box that has a lot of straps and a cloth cover and that kind of thing. We try to make it all hard. Shell very robust, the kind of thing that when you're not camping, you can throw sheets of plywood on it or two by fours or surfboards or mountain bikes or whatever it is, and drive down the road with very little impact to your daily driver kind of thing. So

That's the reason why you get a truck is because you want to be able to do a dump run and you want to be able to camp out of it. But if you have to go through this lengthy process of converting it between usage, it just makes it tougher to use.

Peter Williams (09:34): Yeah, that's exactly right. Yep.

And that niche I think is a tough one for those bigger brands to fill. But the rooftop space, I agree with you, is very competitive. There are a lot of people competing in it, and we have seen, we've sold a lot of our integrated truck shell camper and a few are rooftop tents, standalone rooftop tents. So we're kind of on feel that out, and if it makes sense for us to continue doing the rooftop tint, then we will. Yeah, I think we're, we're going to run that down and see what we can do with it.

Peter Williams (14:23): Yeah, I mean, the truth is we saw that opportunity because that was the reality that was solving a problem that existed in our personal realities. And like I said, we both have pickups, we both use them as pickups more often than we use them as campers, and we really value the outdoor recreation as part of the lifestyle and part of raising our families. So as we looked into it, it just kept looking like the market research we were doing, we kind of looked into how people were reporting that they used the products that they did buy, and it looked like there were a lot of people who were in a similar situation to us where their aspirations are certainly to spend as much time outside as they can, but the problem they're trying to solve is not necessarily to live out of the truck or to go drive across the continent, although if you chose to outfit this thing to do that, it would certainly support that we're building a product that can support that kind of objective, but that's not necessarily the use case that we designed it for.

Cole Heilborn (15:30): Tell me a little bit more about that market research. How did you conduct that? Did you have any expectations or ideas going into it? And what did you find?

Peter Williams (15:41): We looked through, there's a big trade show called the, what is it? The Overland Expo?

Spencer Houser (15:49): Yeah, Overland Expo.

Peter Williams (15:50): And they do quite a bit of research and they make it public. So we looked through that and there are a lot of public market research that's been done by, Coleman had a big report on camping, and we looked into those different publications, I guess you'd call 'em, or the data that we could find out there. And then we also did a bit of just looking, just observing the market and talking to people that we ran into that had products that we were interested in and that we felt like were in the right niche, getting a sense of what they liked about 'em, what they used them for. And yeah, there was quite a bit of information out there once we started looking for it, but I would say it was 90% desk work, 10% seeking people out and talking to 'em.

content: Spencer Houser (16:38): Yeah. Yeah. I think we started with the Overland Journal, Overland Expo people. They've got some really good stats, but that led us into, like Pete said, the Coleman big Coleman report. I think we started in the kind of the overland world, but it led us into the bigger outdoor recreation world. And outdoor recreation is a massive, massive market as a percent of GDP. It's actually bigger than energy (17:17): In the United States, and on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars a year. And as we did our research, we realized that a lot of maybe our competitors are looking at very specifically the marketplace, but as we looked at it, we thought that maybe there's a lot more opportunity as an outdoor company. We are definitely entering here in this kind of overlanding world. But what we're trying to approach it as is more of an outdoor point of view. Everybody aspires to have the gear and the lifestyle that you drive across Siberia and then you climb a huge mountain and every day is the best Instagram day you've ever had. The reality is is that most families, I think, are lucky to get out six or eight times a summer and you're using your pickup for a variety of things. And we wanted to build a product that met the reality of what families do, yet was robust enough and the serious, hardcore outdoor or overlanding enthusiast could look at our product and go, oh, yeah, I could live out of this for the guys that can't 120 days a year and build their stuff out. (19:06): They could look at our stuff and go, yep, this is going to hold up great. But for the suburban mom and dad and Pete with a five-year-old could look at it and go, oh, well that's really approachable. This will support what we want to do, and I'm still going to be able to go to Home Depot and haul yard debris. (19:30): People like to customize things, whether it's your mountain bike, whether it's your fishing pole, your camping gear, your kayaking stuff. People like to customize their stuff. And as we looked at what was out there, it kind of felt like it was an opportunity that the other companies were missing is that if we built something like Pete was saying with wire chases, with threaded bosses, with hook points, with T slots, that gave people the opportunity to build and to customize and to add things, we'd be setting ourselves apart and offering something that everybody else kind of was overlooking. And so we integrated that into our design from the get go, and it's proving to be pretty popular.

Cole Heilborn (20:28): So where are you guys? You're about a year old, you said it's been the last few months now you've been producing product and working through the production challenges. Where are you in your product line in terms of distribution? What are things looking like for this last year and looking for this next year?

Peter Williams (20:50): So basically we sort of built our business model and growth model based on what we felt were somewhat optimistic projections and had a plan of scaling up slowly over the course of several months. But as it's materialized, we have sold way faster than we expected. So we've been having to build up our throughput and our systems a lot sooner than we thought. And we've also had to do it a lot earlier in the life of the business than we expected. So it is definitely been full on. We have now got five employees, not including Josh Spencer and myself, who are all now. And yeah, we're ramping up. Every build cycle goes smoother and we're able to work more efficiently.

content: Spencer Houser (21:47): I've got quite a bit of background in manufacturing. I owned a machine shop for 15 years. Like I said before, I was an operations manager for an aerospace manufacturer for about three and a half years. I helped that company basically ramp itself up pretty significantly. I've helped build out factories and have a background in lean manufacturing and things like that. So as we looked at this company and our products, we designed it around the idea that we could scale this thing up from a manufacturing standpoint, made sure that the products were unique, the individual components were unique, but it was stuff that you could manufacture. We weren't going to have to invent an anti-gravity machine in order for our product to work. So we had this great game plan, and like Pete said, we had this nice little ramp up. We were going to sell four a month the first month and six the second month, and it was going to be great. We could build the shop out nights and slowly hire one or two employees, get everybody trained, and we completely underestimated the demand. And I think COVID has a lot to do with that. I think if we'd just gone our original, if there was no COVID, it would've run closer though, probably more than what we had originally anticipated. (23:18): So we've had to scramble because I figured that I would be the guy building things full time for the first month, and after three months we'd hire an employee. And within that first three weeks, it was like, holy crap, we got to hire our first employee tomorrow. And I think the game plan too, Pete had a full-time job originally, and we thought maybe after six months or so we could start talking about Pete coming on full time. And within two months I was coming to him and saying, dude, I think you need to quit your job and you need to come do this full time, which it is a big deal to ask somebody to do that, especially when they have a very good comfortable job. (24:09): So our challenges these days have just been, everything's going faster than we anticipated. The upside is that I think we all very much understand what we're doing. And our first hire was a guy who had worked for me before who was like an ACE assembly guy.

So I would say to start answering that question and break it down a bit, historically, PR and communications and marketing have been siloed and we had just talked about how we now, most cases the silos are kind of broken and working together, but historically they've been siloed and PR was used to gain awareness for products, services, or personalities of a company via trusted third party validation and gain that third party validation. (15:01): And so it often has borrowed measurement techniques from paid media sources like at equivalency value or readership or impression numbers. And that's okay, but it doesn't give you really a full picture of the impact. And this has slowly started to evolve into reach for unique visitors per month on the digital side, but there's so much more that we do. And so I think now is a really exciting time in the earned media and the PR world because there's less barriers to connect earned media with the impact that it's producing for brands, whether it be a brand awareness impact or a digital impact or a bottom line pact.

content: Cory Van Auken (19:43): Yeah, that's a great question. And I think it depends on the type of coverage that you get. So let's go with the holiday gift guide example, and we'll go with the holiday gift guide example where you have a specific product from a brand that we're working with and the piece of coverage links directly to their website. So we're able to link that piece of PR to behavior. And what I mean by that is we can connect earned media consumption to web traffic and then track those people's journeys. So someone, let's say I read that holiday gift guide. I see this product that I'm really interested in, I click from, let's say it was on Gear Junkie for example. They do a great job with their holiday gift guides and they have some awesome gear. So I click from Gear Junkie onto the brand's website. As a PR practitioner, I can measure the journey of that person. (20:38): And so we gather acquisition metrics, so user sessions, those kinds of things. We gather behavior metrics, what are they doing once they get to the site? Are they bouncing immediately? How many pages are they viewing per session? What's the session duration? Things like that. And then we can also measure conversion metrics depending on how people have their Google Analytics set up. But is this leading to e-commerce and last click conversions that's really easy to show ROI there, or is this leading to some goal completion? So if it's a larger product, let's say like a kayak and some kayaks can be a pretty hefty investment, sometimes it takes a lot of touch points and maybe I'm not ready to purchase just from reading that holiday gift guide, but I did go to a product view page and I scrolled down and watched the video and maybe I achieved a few goals. (21:34): There's certain value in that as well. So that's what we start to measure now. Totally. That's one example of a digital piece of coverage that directly links. And I think your question, and where PR continues to figure this out is in pieces of coverage that you can't automatically measure the direct impact. What do you use to get a good idea? And I think that's a question that PR as a whole in communications is continuing to grapple with. So a piece of print coverage, there's tons of value in that, but how do you express that value truthfully, and how do you express it without over-inflating its value or underinflating it? And so something that we look at is if we were just looking at what we can measure directly, brands would, you would think naturally it would eventually lead to brands just wanting digital pieces of coverage that link directly. But we can cover everything. But there is a lot of value in appearing on a podcast. There's a lot of value on a great piece of print coverage. And so what we've worked really hard at is trying to disseminate that value and analyze it and then present it in a way that's truthful. And so we've done a bunch of work on that in the last three or four years do that. And so our reporting system's pretty robust. And yeah, we're pretty proud of it. We work pretty hard on it.

(29:00): All of these things we look at. And the purpose of this then is each piece of coverage spits out two numbers and they're coordinates. content: Kansas Sartin (05:37): Yeah. We make aluminum hitch-mounted cargo carriers. The hitch mounted cargo racks. Cargo carriers have been around for 40 years and you can find 60 different units on the market by a dozen different manufacturers, maybe more than a dozen at this point, but they're all kind of the same. And honestly, there's a handful of ones that folks are familiar with. They're all manufactured by the same person. They're just sort of white labeled for these different box stores and none of 'em are real exciting. They don't do anything real well. And what I mean is that you're adding a cargo carrier because you need space, but a lot of them are pretty small and even the larger ones aren't all that big. And so you put one cooler and that's about all that it'll hold, which isn't necessarily a lot of space. And then the secondary sort of negative is that when you put that cooler on, you now can't drop your tailgate or raise a lift gate to your SUV. (06:37): And so what I was finding is that I had lift gates on my SUVs and I'm constantly carrying a dog with me, whether it's for retrieving or just for having my dog. He is a part of the family at this point. And you'd end up somewhere and you'd have to take the stuff off the cargo carrier so you could raise the lift gate so you could get your dog in and out. And I have very little patience for stuff that doesn't make a lot of sense. And so I'll spend a ridiculous amount of time and money trying to make something work really great, probably more time than it would ever take me to take that cooler off. And so through that pain point, I'd been thinking about how does this change and how does this become better? And there's some other storyline there about sort of that one moment of the steel one that my daughter cut her forehead on it, and then I tried to take it off and I dropped it on my foot and it was that like, oh my God, there has got to be a better way. (07:41): This is so ridiculous. And the steel ones are resting and there's no way to store them, and they're leaning up against your fence.

And I thought, well, that's it. And I'm kind of looking around the boat and all these boats on the Texas coast and in Florida of course as well. And on the East coast, well, any coastline really, but thinking more in the shallow water back bay boats, you've got these T tops and polling platforms and casting decks, and they're all made out of a bright aluminum. They're TIG welded, they look great, they don't rust, and they're strong enough where people can stand on 'em and cast from 'em and all that. And I started thinking, well, that's it. (08:30): And nobody was doing anything with it. And so I just laid it out. Honestly, the first pack mule wasn't a pack mule, it was just Kansas needs a better way to haul gear. And so I just made one straight up. I wanted to hold, this is still in the early days when Yetis were just starting to become, I mean people were aware of them, but it was still like, really? Do you spend three 50 on a cooler? And I had put a couple on my boat, which was kind of the inception for those coolers, and I realized, man, these things are great. They could be a tabletop on the back, you can cut on 'em, it's a bar. They're super useful to having a hitch carrier on the back. And so I wanted to hold 2 65 side by side and still be able to raise my lift gate so I could get my dog in and out of the back. (09:18): And everything's piped. So you can use our cambuckle mule straps, which allows you to secure the Rotomolded coolers underneath the lid. So you walk back there, you just open the lid, you don't have to unstrap anything. So again, it's about I don't have patience for things that don't work. When I get to my destination point, I want to open a cooler and grab a beer right away. I don't want to have to undo a ratchet strap or something. I better have easy access to that stuff.

It's an off-brand, it's maybe made in China or whatever, just another stamped out piece of equipment. (10:09): And you're miserable because either your feet hurt or you've got blisters or you're wet or you're cold or it's not doing what you really wish that it was doing or maybe what you thought it was going to do. And so that time that you've taken away from friends, family, the money you've spent on the travel, vacation time from work, and then you're kind of wishing that either you were already done with your height because your feet hurt so much, or you were in a hot shower drinking some warm coffee, so cold, or you wish you were back getting dried off. And so you don't get to engage in that experience. And so really the purpose of Pac Mule is to support people, make it easy to encourage them to load up, go see America, the wild spaces that exist. Go learn something, try something new, don't be intimidated by it. And then when you're there, we don't want you to even think about Pac Mule or how your gear is. All your gear goes in its place. It's easy. You can find it so that all your time and efforts focus on that place and the people you're with.

Cole Heilborn (11:16): Yeah, man. Well, no, I think we've all been in those environments where we're going out on some adventure or whatever, and we packed that piece of gear. That's not ideal, but it was maybe half off or it was a little cheaper than the other options. And then you get out in the field and you're going out there, you're like, oh, it can't be that bad. Think about how much money I just saved. And then you get out there and you're like, oh man, I realized why this thing was half as much as the alternative option. And you quickly regret your choice, and then you end up going back and spending spending money on the full price item, and now you've just spent one and a half times as

Kansas Sartin (12:08): Yeah, my wife is really the one that drew that to my attention. She said, golly, you keep buying this crappy stuff. And when you're young and you first get married and you're first working and stuff, you get into something, you don't have a lot of money to spend on things. But she saw that I was, I'd go out and buy a pair of snake boots and then they were miserable and my feet hurt and I was getting blisters. And she's like, do you even know if that'll protect you from a rattlesnake if one hits? And you're like, I don't really know. That's not a good sign. And so she said exactly what you did. Just wait. Just wait a little bit longer. Use what you've got and save up and get the right thing. Because spending more money, you eventually buy the high quality piece and then you love it and you have it forever and you use it, and then you have memories. And now you put on a pair of sims waiters that you've been fishing or duck hunting out of for six, seven years, and they're still perfect, and you have all the memories of 'em. Or you put on those old pair of snake boots and it's like, man, how many miles have I walked in these boots? And they're still working good, looking good, and you feel safe and confident, and there's a lot. And so her coin term that I've heard some other folks say too is just buy once.

Cole Heilborn (13:28): I like that. I've never heard that before. Maybe that hasn't made its way up to Washington yet. Maybe that's just a Texas thing maybe. So how long ago did you have that realization to start Pac Meal? What's been the journey? What has been the journey with starting the company and where are you guys at today?

content: Kansas Sartin (13:47): Yeah, it's been wild and crazy unlike anything I probably would've thought it would be. It's easy to have an idea and either A, be completely overwhelmed with all the steps that it takes to get there, or B, think, well, it's going to be pretty easy. And then as it is, in my case, four years later, you're like, whoa, we've really learned a lot here. And so the first pack mule, the one that wasn't a pack mule, it was just my own product. That was probably eight or so years ago that I built that and people were stopping me on the road all the time, where'd you get that? I got to have it. I'd be at a gas station, raise the lift gate to take the dog out to go, let 'em use the bathroom and the grass, and I'd have all this stuff on the back. (14:38): And they're like, wait, how'd you do that? You didn't have to pull a pen or move anything or use a swing arm or whatever. It's like, no, you pack it right? And it's designed this way. And so my wife and I talked about it and I said, golly, I'm not going to quit my job and just go do this thing. I'm going to keep, we have kids and mortgage and all the other things, but I'll double down on this. And I've got a pretty big tinkering intuition. I was always doing something outside of nine to five anyways. And so the idea was, look, if we can do this responsibly, if it can not just be something else that people feel like they have to buy, but if we're really making an impact on people, if we can encourage people to go outside where they can find that place to exhale, and then in turn they appreciate it, so they want to help conserve it, then I feel like we're doing something right. (15:36): And so February will be four years that we've had product available to sell. And the first three years of that, I was running a construction business for some other people and moonlighting working until one or two o'clock in the morning each night doing stuff. And then on Fridays I'd fly or drive somewhere for a trade show and then be home at one or two in the morning and then back in the office the next day and just doing whatever you could to try to grow it, but also keep paying the bills.

And that atmosphere is constantly changing. (16:53): Used to be print ad and billboards and mailers. And now of course, digital ads are more the driver. And so you're constantly trying to figure out how to make people aware. And so year one was really kind of a, let's make these available. Let's make a few hundred of 'em and see if people will buy 'em and what they think about it. And towards the end of year one, we made the sway back model, which is the lower rail for Jeeps, like the newer model Jeeps with the spare tire on the back. So it would slide underneath the spare tire, and you still have access and no extensions or anything. And that's been a great market for us because Jeeps have no cargo space inherently. And so you can enjoy the Jeep top down doors off wherever you want to go and whatever you want to do, it's easy to park. (17:42): And then when you need to go to the hardware store or you need extra space for a road trip when you're going somewhere, you've got that cargo space. And some people bring up ground clearance and some of those things. And we do have a ridge line model that has extra departure angle vis-a-vis an eight inch riser. But really the design isn't you're going to go climb Moab in this thing. The design is really, it helps you get to your destination. You can take it off at that place. It only takes a minute and then go do your trail riding and stuff, leave it at your campsite if you want to.

Cole Heilborn (18:34): Think. Yeah. Yeah. So that's awesome. Four years in, and as the company has grown, has the team grown, is it still just you moonlighting or?

Kansas Sartin (18:46): No, I quit my job September of 2019 and have just been fully focused on Pac Mule, which of course that's a scary thing too. You know that it's growing, but you really have to be a hundred percent focused on it and give the 80 hours just to this instead of doing 40 at night. And so it's great and it's exciting. And then COVID hits and nobody can travel anywhere. Nobody is spending money, we're not sure about jobs. And then you start second guessing a little bit like, whoa, is this the right thing to do? And I say, second guessing, you always second guess everything that you do to some degree, but still very confident in the business and what we're doing and the products we're making and what we're all about. And so this has been a tremendous year, and sales have been great and just we're working on a lot of new products, accessories that'll mount onto the Pac Mule and how you haul other things on it and make that more viable. (19:52): And then what other things fit within the portfolio of Pac Mule? And so of course we have a laundry list of things we'd love to do that's a mile long, and just trying to figure out which ones really make sense in a broader market. And then which ones first is the other piece of it, it's me and my wife. I have contracted most of our other labor. And so being in Houston in an oil and gas market, I've been through the 2008 recession where oil tanked and all the jobs shut down and people were getting laid off and it was crazy. And then managed the recent construction business through the 2016 downturn in Houston and going through layoffs and closing business units and all that stuff. And what I learned through all that is you have to be as light, nimble, lean, and variable as possible. (20:49): So if something happens, you can turn off some light switches real fast and it's not a major impact to you or your business or whatever else. And so we just try to keep it lean and people are always surprised by how lean we are. And even my accountant's like, Hey, listen, there's nothing else you can do to get leaner. I mean, how do you even eat?

It's a bright aluminum, like the same series, 6,000 series aluminum that they make horse trailers out of. So it's already naturally bright without having to anodize. They all seem to become more complicated with the variety of things that are out there, and I really try hard with the products that we develop to make them as universal as possible. I hate to have to have 10 skews for something depending on what you've got. And then you change whatever you've got and now you got to go buy a different one. I want it to be as universal as possible. And that's the way that the Pack Mule is. (27:15): The original one fits 95% of vehicles. The only thing it doesn't really work on is a Jeep with a spare tire on the back. If you've got barn doors like on a Sprinter van, you need the Swayback model with the lower rail. And then if you've got a 200 series lane cruiser with the tailgate that drops, the Swayback model works better. And then the Swayback works on a hundred percent of vehicles. So it's good to have units that are back to my OCD, I want them to work on all the vehicles. I want people to not have to make a bunch of modifications and cut stuff. And you can see all sorts of YouTube videos for the other hitch carriers out there that people are like, Hey, so I've made it work and all I had to do was cut this off and bend this and move it out of the way. And man, that's not right. That means that somebody didn't do the design work correctly.

And so we have a two and a half X safety factor built into the pack meal to account for the dynamic load. (32:58): And we have so many customers that come to us and say, Hey, we had a hitch carrier. It said it had a 500 pound capacity, we had two or 300 pounds on the back, and it's all bent already. And it's so many of those, and I don't know how they do this or why they even get away with it, but they have a static load rating on a hitch carrier that's meant to be on a vehicle that's got a dynamic load going down the highway or a trail or something. Kansas Sartin (28:52): And fact Neal's not for everybody for sure, but it definitely fits a need for a lot of people that are looking for an easier place to load their gear, an easier way to access it all and demand more out of the products that they use. And so we're proud of what we're doing and just the sustainability piece of it too, we're 70% or more recycled content in our products. So we have huge scraps of metal. We melt 'em down, we pour it into billet, we extrude all the aluminum shapes, bend them, cut it, and then weld it, and then we temper it for eight hours at 350 degrees. And so it's a serious process to build it, but every time you weld aluminum, you actually weaken it a little bit. And so we're the only cargo carrier on the market that is actually welding and then tempering afterwards. And that's very unique to us, and it's part of the reason that we're so substantially strong in our design and in our fatigue stresses and all those things.

Cole Heilborn (34:41): Yeah. Well, I think as you said, one, I don't think it matters how well your marketing is. If obviously if your product isn't good, then no one's going to buy your stuff. And I think it's cool that you guys have put so much effort into making sure the product is as good as it can be, but while still trying to improve on it with each iteration. I'm curious though, back up a little bit. You've mentioned, obviously your product is for a very niche audience. Not everyone needs a super robust cargo carrier like you guys make. And you mentioned you've worked with some groups, some agencies, some businesses in the past to try to do some digital advertising, but they weren't able to find your audience what wasn't working there. I'm just curious how you guys have now found the right people who Pac Newell is for and if there's anything that our audience can learn from trying to find where your demographic and where your audience is located and how to talk to them.

content: Kansas Sartin (35:44): I can't claim to be an expert in digital marketing, and it's still a little bit of a magic potion as far as I'm concerned. And so I think it's really about people paying attention to the data, the customer stream, the touch points, the interactions where you're showing up for them, all of those things that allow it to be successful. I really think you just have to be in it all the time just obsessed about it. The way that I'm obsessed about the welds that are on our pack meal is the way that the right digital marketer has to be obsessed. You can't just plug in some ads and let 'em run for a week and then let 'em fizz out. If they're not doing good, you need to call 'em. And if they're doing really good, you need to start bumping 'em and you need to learn from what went well there and modify it. (36:40): You got to change constantly. And so I'm excited about the ad set that we're just turned on today. We've got great imagery. Some of it's customer provided imagery. We got customer quotes from reviews that have been sent in. So we're just trying to, not from us, but look at what other people are doing and look at what they're saying about it. And then some of it's runtime and some of it's spend. And so the more folks that you can hit and the more that you can learn from those folks, the better the algorithm gets in trying to find those people. And then it's interesting too, I look at regional information a couple of times a week just looking at where pack meals are going. And it's interesting, we might send something to Massachusetts, a town of Massachusetts, and then I'll notice that after that one, maybe a week or so after it was ordered, and so now it's delivered that we'll start seeing another couple that get ordered in that area. (37:54): And I have to suspect that it's that person saying, oh my gosh, this thing is awesome. It's more than what I thought it was going to be just by the images and stuff. And then they're telling their friends and they tell their neighbors and they find somebody there that says, oh, I really need one of those. So then they buy one. And I love to see that. And I think it tells a story in of itself just in the quality of the product and its usefulness and it's lightweight, so it's something that's easy to put on and off. And with the hitching post, you're just hanging on the wall when you're not using it, and it's out of the way. And so just where does it live? Where does it go? How does it go on all those things. If they make sense and it's easy, then people will keep using it. But any other product, if it's too complicated, people won't use it because talk themselves out of it. I don't want to mess with that. I'm just going to cram my stuff in the back and deal with it.

Let's check and see what Pac Mill's got that can take care of that. I want to be a problem solver in the market. I want continual to be an innovation leader. But then doing it all responsibly where the majority of the products are built overseas, we're making stuff here in the US and so no greenhouse gases. We're using recycled content. When you open one of our boxes, it's recycled box or content recycled and there's no plastic on the inside. And all of that was predated the plastic movement and metal straws and all that stuff. It was just because I don't want to wrap this huge thing in a bag, and if it's got a little dust on it, it's an outdoor product, just hose it off when you get it, but you now don't have 24 square feet of plastic that you're just going to throw away. (41:42): It was one use. And so just being conscious of what we do and being a company that when I look at leaders in that regard, Patagonia does such a great job in the way that they look at business as a thought leader in environment and sustainability and all those things. And so it's interesting because you get emails from outdoor retailer, it's a trade show for dealers, and it's like how to become more sustainable and how to reduce your impact and all this stuff. And I'm like, man, I'm already in the green and I haven't been to one of these classes. I'm looking good. But I love that and I hope that I to see more manufacturing come back to America and improve jobs. And a lot of that's about safety too. What's the impact on the people that built your product? Are they in a safe work environment? (42:40): Are they able to hug their kids when they come home? At the end of the day, are they able to make a good living and in an environment where they're emotionally taken care of? And there's a lot of stories overseas about all sorts of crazy labor stuff, and I would hate to be a contributor to that by the things that I purchased. short_description: Pedal Damn It!
show_notes_excerpt: In this episode, Zach Vestal, the marketing manager from Niner Bikes and BATCH Bikes hops on the mic to give us a little insight into his changing world as he manages two very different bike brands. Niner has been around a while, having built their reputation on the idea that riding bikes on a 29" wheel is the best. Whereas, BATCH Bikes is geared for an audience who are re-discovering their love for biking and aren't likely concerned with their wheel size. This puts Zach in an interesting posit…

content:
Zach Vestal (02:16): Yeah, yeah, definitely. I'm glad you picked up on that. So, little bit about Niner, little bit about Batch Niner was started in 2005 based in Southern California, and it was based on the premise that 29 inch wheels for mountain bikes are better period across the board, every bike, every situation. And the entire brand was built around this love of 29 er mountain bikes, and we've since expanded to gravel bikes and e-bikes and everything, bikes for dirt, and they've all got the big wheels. The company moved from Southern California to Fort Collins five or 10 years ago, and like I said, I joined the company about two and a half years ago and moved to Fort Collins a year and a half ago. So that's kind of been my ride with Niner Bikes. About three years ago, Niner was acquired by a larger organization based in Ohio, and we were meant to be kind of the tip of the spear for an entire group of brands that's meant to be sold through independent specialty retail bicycle dealers. And that specialty retail group, Niners at the top of it with premium boutiques, high-end bikes for people who really know what they want, and they're probably experienced riders. Our prices range from 3000 to $9,000. (03:49): The company wanted to have a broader offering for bike dealers at every price point, and therefore the batch brand was started. So Batch Bicycles was started about two years ago, and it's really bikes in the $500 range. There's a mountain bike, there's a fitness bike, there's a comfort bike, there's kids bikes, and as with Niner, it's meant to be sold through specialty retailers. In this group, we have an affinity for local retail. We want to support independent dealers, but we also feel they need to have a broad spectrum of bikes to offer their customers. So that's how the batch brand was started. And as you commented earlier, it's been quite a year for that brand.

Cole Heilborn (04:43): Oh, I'm sure. Yeah. Does Niners still only run 29 inch wheels?

Cole Heilborn (05:07): Gotcha, gotcha, man. So yeah, I'm sure Niner Bikes has been super busy this last year. I'm sure batch bikes has been incredibly busy this last year as so many people as we know have just been getting into cycling and breaking into entry level sports kind of everywhere. What's that been like?

Zach Vestal (05:30): It's been a wild ride. I mean, it's almost impossible to describe the 12 months that we've kind of been through. I mean, obviously the world has been through just insane disruption and uncertainty and everything else. And that all kind of hit us around this time. Last year is when we started getting news of factory shutdowns and disruptions to the supply chain and everything because it's starting in Southeast Asia where an overwhelming majority of bicycles and bike parts are produced. So that started, we got, I'd say relatively early word about that in part thanks to the batch brand because their manufacturing is in China. (06:21): And then so as the shutdowns hit in March, our business dropped in half because bike shops were closed along with restaurants and businesses, everything. Well, not long after that bike shops were declared essential retail and because soccer and swimming and football, baseball, basketball, bowling lanes, you name it, it was all closed. But the outdoors was still open, right outdoors. So people are running, riding, biking, walking, hiking, and doing all that. And the run the demand on bicycles is like nothing we've ever seen. I mean, absolutely unprecedented. And the batch brand, for example, offering affordable bikes to new cyclists or people that haven't had a bike for a number of years, the company did twice its projection and just insane amount of business.

The company was located next to a bunch of aviation companies, and Eline became aware of some new technology that was being used in aircraft manufacturing around thermoplastics. So thermoformed plastics have a lot of advantages over composites, but also a lot of similarities. So it brings a lot of the same high gloss finish that you can get with composites, great strength to weight ratio, but it's a much cleaner and it's a much more, frankly, environmentally friendly process because the byproduct, the scrap plastic, you're able to recycle a lot easier than you are with composites, and you're working a lot fewer noxious chemicals than you are with some of the more composite fiberglass heavy production styles. So any line became aware of what was on in the aviation industry and started tooling around with it first with seats and combinings and bullheads, small parts switching that from fiberglass over to thermoplastics. The big goal on the horizon was obviously the deck and the hole, the main components of the craft, and eventually Edline was able to nail that. And so we became the first to thermoform a boat in the mid nineties, and over the course of the next decade, we switched all of our manufacturing from composite boats over to Thermoform.

So we recognized when we were going through the process of buying the company that we're really in a pretty awesome position. If I were to break out the paddle sport marketplace, specifically within Stillwater Kayaks, you still have the premium high-end composite boats that absolutely have a place, and there's some amazing designs, amazing crafts out there at higher price points as they should be. But the volumes there are quite a bit lower than what they were in the eighties or nineties, for instance. And then you've got a lot of price point boats, a lot of rotomolded, polyethylene boats that are principally sold through big box stores, and those volumes have exploded over the last few years and the prices on those, it's really been a bit of a race to the bottom on the pricing side, but that has the advantage of getting a lot of people into the sports. So we recognize the advantage that that has, and we're right there in the middle where we're able, again, with our manufacturing process and our designs to replicate a lot of the form function benefits that you get with the top end boats at a fraction of the price. (17:56): And we have, for the people who have entered the industry with a price point boat, maybe they bought it at one of the big box stores that have gotten into the sport, they love it and they're looking to upgrade to a sleeker, more efficient, lighter craft. We're a natural step in that progression for them. So it's a really cool place to be in the industry as participation rates have increased and people have gotten their feet wet to torture, pun there, we're able to give them a really great paddling experience for their next boat. And at the time we had built up quite a bit of inventory for spring shipments to our dealers that had bought on preseason, and at that point, no one knew what was going to happen. So we sent our crew home, turn off the lights in the facility. We did do a few things around bringing the crew back to help create personal protective equipment, which something we're super proud of that we were able to be one of many, many manufacturers who were able to step up in that way. (30:47): But otherwise we weren't producing boats, and we frankly had no idea if the demand was going to come back or not. Fast forward just a few weeks to Memorial Day, and it instantly became aware that people who had been cooped up inside who weren't able to get on a plane and go to Disneyland, were looking for ways to recreate in their backyard while maintaining six feet of social distance. And at our boat is 12 feet long and a paddle is about six feet long. We're sitting on the sport that was designed for the social distance era because we're such a relatively small industry compared to some of the service industries like tourism. Just that little bit of spend shift going from the plane trip to Disneyland into hard goods has created massive supply chain issues across the board. Again, one of the advantages of being a privately held company was we actually had made the decision in January to increase our inventory levels in anticipation of supply shortages. So we were able to get back in and really not miss a beat and get up to speed to meet the demand as best we could. (32:09): That said, we did sell out pretty quickly and we remain sold out. Our production is spoken for through the rest of the summer. Wow. At the moment, we're continuing to accelerate the growth of our production, I should say. We took occupancy of the new building a year ago, just a handful of weeks before we got shut down. That was the building call that you were able to take a walk through. And because that's where they chose to invest, we inherited a company that for 45 years had invested in product design, product quality that hadn't invested in as much in marketing and advertising as was the story told itself in the product. And we had them build us a website, which was we went from WordPress to a Shopify site. We wanted to have a clean experience across phone, tablet, browser, and really make sure that the quality of the imagery that we were presenting in the digital world was matching the quality of experience that people were getting when they walked into a showroom. So we had that new website go live in December of this year. (41:39): For the last few months, we've also been working with this agency on the social side and really focused on user generated content. We like most brands will go out and we'll do professional shoots, video stills, we will do on products, hang tags, et cetera, and we really want to make sure that we have those professional images. But in terms of helping people imagine themselves in a boat, there's nothing quite like the user content out there where authentic smiles, different water types, different paddler types, different boats, and the stories that accompany it. I know a lot of your guests have talked about the importance of storytelling. Every paddler has a story. Every paddler is a story. The story of that particular outing, the story of how they got into the sport, the story of what that sport means to them, and there really is no shortcut to telling stories when you're talking about your paddling community other than investing time and effort into listening, understanding, curating, and then from a very consent driven perspective, telling those stories to the general public. Stephen Matthews (09:43): Yeah. Well, for me, I got involved with mountain biking purely for the passion of it. I loved it as a kid. I was a mountain biker and super motivated to just have fun more than anything. And I'm really happy to say that it segued into a job, eventually took a while, but it did. You

Cole Heilborn (10:05): Made it.

Stephen Matthews (10:05): I made it, yeah. And so I think it's about maintaining that excitement and the passion for mountain biking and ideas will come. And so how do I take what I love about mountain biking and what Rocky Mountain stands for and bring it to a broader audience through that avenue? It's about seeing what it is, seeing what you love about mountain biking in our brand.

Cole Heilborn (10:50): Yeah. What challenges are you guys currently working through in the marketing department, in the bike industry right now?

We've introduced a lineup and it's been incredibly successful for us on a global scale, but it's really touch and go depending on where you are in the world. The US for instance, seems to have spots opening that are open to riding e-bikes and other trail networks that are closed, and it just feels really touch and go right now. So it is a new product and it's a really great product for introducing new riders to the sport. But there's definitely a bit of red tape when it comes to trail usage that just makes it, I think, difficult for a consumer to buy with confidence. And that's just not just our brand, but any brand people looking at at a point right now where there are networks that are just not to be ridden.

Cole Heilborn (11:54): So

Stephen Matthews (11:55): I think it's a challenge. Yeah, it's a challenge to market that globally when globally they're not accepted everywhere.

Some of the big brands have started to release them, and now locally, a bunch of people are asking their local trail groups, can we ride these here? And sometimes they're not even sure.

Stephen Matthews (12:20): Yeah, I think that's exactly it is. There's a lot of unsure, unsure ideas in the legislation and landowners and land managers because they are a relatively new thing. And as we know, bureaucratic process for getting new activities approved in certain land areas is slow. And so it's a bit of a cart before the horse scenario perhaps.

Cole Heilborn (12:48): How did you get to here? You got kind of an interesting story. Can you walk us through that?

Stephen Matthews (12:52): Yeah. I grew up in Calgary, Alberta, and I have an older brother who's super involved with mountain biking, and we both kind of got into it in our early teens, like I mentioned earlier, just for fun. We loved hitting jumps and riding all over the place, and it was really well timed with the free ride movement that Rocky Mountain latched onto. So when I was a kid, I wasn't interested in racing. I was super interested in riding off jumps and cliffs and log rides, and the creativity that was essentially formed in North Vancouver here was what was inspiring me back in Calgary. And so yeah, I wrote a ton throughout my teens and I got involved with sponsorships and a couple brands that helped get me going. And then from there, I just made a whole bunch of decisions that mountain biking was going to be a part of my life. So I moved to Whistler. I became a guide in Europe for a while, always just taking opportunities. If there was a chance to do a photo shoot or a video shoot being a part of it. They definitely didn't all work out financially for the most part, but it was a lot of fun. And I think for me, looking back, it was just like I took opportunities that there made the best of 'em, and I met some great people and eventually those people helped me get a job and that's where I'm today.

Cole Heilborn (14:14): One of the things I noticed and you've said is that you're really passionate about the bike industry. Is there ever a point though, in your job where the passion, it doesn't run out, but that fire kind of slows down for you? Is that a thing?

Even during the workday, we're really lucky being close to our trails, and if I have an opportunity to go for a lunch ride, I'll take it. And if I don't and I have to work through the day, that's fine, I'll go after work. But I think for me, I ride most days because I really enjoy it, and it helps remind me when I'm at work of why I work here. So it hasn't happened yet, but I definitely put a huge concerted effort into make sure that I'm on the bike a lot. Yeah.

Cole Heilborn (15:12): What's your hope for the bike industry in the future?

Stephen Matthews (15:17): I think it's an interesting time. Mountain biking that I fell in love with back when I was 12, 13 years old. It's changed a lot. The sports blown up like crazy. More people than ever are getting involved with it, and I'd like to just see that continue. Really. When I started mountain biking almost, it wasn't underground, but it definitely wasn't mainstream. I've also moved from the prairies of Alberta to the epicenter of mountain biking. So everywhere I go, it is not uncommon to see people on super high-end carbon bikes. But that was definitely not the case when I was growing up. So my hope for the mountain bike industry is just that more people get involved with it, that more people get involved with trail work and help build up those community sides of things. I think we're still in the grand scheme of things, if you compare it to an industry like skiing, we're really young. We're super young, and so we've had a boom, I think we're having another one here with e mountain bike. And in general, I think I'd like to see more people involved with the community side of it and then see where it goes from there. Because reality is, the more people involved with it, the more it's going to move it forward as a

Cole Heilborn (16:28): Whole. So if you couldn't have the job that you have now, what would be a dream job?

I mean, it's phenomenal, but they can't always see that. So if you add a podcast and sometimes repurposing a YouTube channel could be your podcast because a lot of that has audio to it. So it's really simple. I think as you've discovered, and I've discovered when we got into this, if we can do it, anybody can do it. And the equipment is, I have an a TR 2100 mic that costs me under a hundred bucks. So you get a mic in Zoom and headsets and away you go. So pretty simple to get started.

Cole Heilborn (10:17): Yeah, that's a great point. So if it is so simple though, why are there only a handful of brands that are actually out there creating podcasts?

Rick Saez (10:24): Well, I think it's another thing to add to the to-do list, right? I mean, I think it's a combination of, I'm worried that it's going to take up a bunch of time, which it's another thing to do, but as a brand or a retailer, you can hand that off to an employee or an associate and let them run with it, and then maybe it could be a different person every week or a different person every month. And if you're a brand, you get a product manager or someone. This week we're talking about packs, and this week we're talking about footwear and so forth. So there's just a lot of ways to cut that up so that it's not as daunting a secondary task to add your to-do list.

Rick Saez (12:13): It opens up ways that they connect. And again, it's back to that human voice thing. I mean, I think there's nothing, it's one thing to read a book, to read a blog post, but you don't really get the passion and the excitement or the trepidation that comes with the audio, the audio pieces. Man, you really know that that guy's having fun or you really can tell that, ah, he's a little sketched out here going over that jump or whatever he's doing. And I think that's one piece, because people, we all react to that even as we're sitting in a line talking to one another, you really responding to the voice, not necessarily the eye movement or some of those other things. So the voice is so powerful. It's the first thing a child hears too. The first thing they hear is the mother's voice in their womb. So it's just right out of the gate, we're looking for it and listening for it.

Cole Heilborn (13:00): It's interesting that the podcast format works so well because I think about for the most point, it's only audio, right? There's no video, and we're such visual people. I mean, humans are visual learners. That's how we interact with the world. But the podcast works so well. I'm curious why, I think you mentioned something interesting there, this idea that from the beginning of life, all we hear is audio, and then we learn to use vision along the way. Why are podcasts so successful now? Does it have something to do with that? Why has it only just become a thing recently that we're starting to see pop up?

Rick Saez (13:39): Well, I think it's a combination of they're new. They're still relatively new, even though there's millions of 'em out there. But it's also society has become so busy. We're on the go all the time. And again, that's more important I think, with the outdoor space because not only are we busy on the go with work life and just life, but then the recreational activities we choose take us outside away from the screen. And more and more of us are looking for ways to get away from that screen because screen time has been going up like crazy. And so the podcast is a way to do that. It gets you away from the screen. It allows you to do a couple things at once. And the other thing about a podcast is it's very portable. You can put it on your phone, and we all have our phone in our pocket almost twenty four seven. So as long as you take the time to download or set it up to automatically download, your episodes are right there in your pocket. It's like Steve Jobs said when he introduced the iPod, there's a million songs in your pocket. Well, now there's a million stories in your pocket. So I think that's one of the ways that it's impacting people.

Cole Heilborn (14:47): What are some of the less obvious opportunities that you see brands could be pursuing in the podcast space?

Rick Saez (14:54): What do you mean by less obvious?

Cole Heilborn (14:56): Well, I think, so we talked,

Cole Heilborn (14:58): Maybe? Yeah, we talked about storytelling. That seems like a really obvious option, but what are some things that maybe aren't as common that we could start to see?

content: Rick Saez (15:08): Well, it's storytelling. It's talking about new products that you've got in the shop or you're going to launch. It's education. A lot of podcasts are educational, so you can learn how to set up your tent, even though it's not visual. You can walk somebody through how to set up their tent or how to pack their backpack or how to, you could guide 'em down a trail. They could be walking down a trail and think, if you're a retailer here in the Eastern, Sierra and Bishop, and there's all this public lands around us with all these trails, and those of us that have been here for a while have been on some of these trails. What we could do in our sleep, blindfold me, spin me around, and I can probably find my way up to Southlake or to Northlake or to one of the back Country Lakes, Humphreys Lakes basin. (15:50): I could probably do that blindfolded, and you could do a podcast about that trail, hiking up that trail. I could start at the trail head, here's where you are. Here's what you need to plan for. Don't go hard right out of the gate because it's a little swampy, whatever it might be. And they could have that in their ear, and then you could be talking about features and things they're seeing as they're walking along the way. So I think it's, again, that story, that voice and that audio piece of it just makes it unlimited. Same with photography. You could go through photography and some guy's going to go up and shoot the beautiful fall color at North Lake, and you could guide him up the road. Here's where you drive, here's where you park. There's three options to go, or there's unlimited options to go take the photo. But if you want to get this, look, you can go down there at this time of day with this light. Here's your F-stop and here's your shutter speed. Just point and shoot. It could be that simple or it could get more complex.

One I've been toying around with this called the 3 95 Chronicles, and I've got a graphic and I've got, I think one episode in the Can already, but over here in Bishop Highway 3 95 runs up and down the Owens Valley and comes from way South, runs up and down California, really. But the outdoor piece of it starts in the southern end of this valley and goes all the way up through Reno. And as you drive that road, there's not only beautiful scenery, but there's all kinds of cool little towns that you drive through. And my thought is to just go into all these little towns and interview the outdoor shop owner, the fly fishing shop owner, the guy who's got the best burritos in town. (20:47): You want to stop at this coffee shop because blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. And a lot of them have been there for a while. Some of 'em are very, very old since this road was paved maybe. And so there's some history there that can go along with that. And I think that would be just a fun, not only for someone coming up here to do an outdoor thing, but if you're just traveling along the highway, because I remember as a kid, there used to be this booklet that you could get, and as you're driving north, you looked on the left hand side of the pages and it had all the outlines of the skyline and what peaks you were seeing and whatnot. And then as you're driving south, you looked on the other side and it showed you all that. So that's where the idea came from. But again, the audio piece to share all these guys' stories, I think it'd be fun.

content:
Rick Saez (22:36): Well, and that kind of goes back to one of the things that I teach in my course is you've really got to hone in on your ideal listener, because I dunno if a lot of people can look up a thousand True Fans by Kevin Kelly. I dunno if you've read that, but he wrote this piece. Kevin Kelly is one of the founders of Wired Magazine, and he wrote this piece on a thousand True Fans. And how he says that if you have a thousand people that consume everything you make, you can make a pretty damn good living. Because if you sell something or advertise something and those thousand people spend 50 bucks with you a month or whatever, there's some pretty good money. And so if you really hone in on that ideal listener, A, it helps you figure out and focus on the content. And B, it guarantees that you're going to have a good qualified audience to follow. And an audience is different than a follower. A follower will follow you and maybe not always tap in, but an audience will come back for more. They know what you're offering, they know what you're delivering. My audience comes back every Tuesday because they've heard 300 episodes and they know it's going to be another one with some outdoor person. They like to hear that. So audience is, I think, more valuable than followers.

Cole Heilborn (23:46): I guess there is an important distinction between those two.

Rick Saez (23:50): You want the guys that are going to pay for the ticket to come in the concert, not the groupie that's going to show up and buy the t-shirt and not come in, wait for the CD to come out.

Cole Heilborn (23:57): Sure. And honestly, I think that's some encouragement for people who have started podcasts and they're trying to figure out, how am I doing download wise? You look at your downloads and you're like, oh man, I feel like I should be doing way better. But how many of those people are the right audience, are the right people you want to be talking to? And it sounds like that's something you practice or you preach in your COING programs.

content: Rick Saez (24:22): Yeah, I preach that in my educational stuff and I practice it too. I can't tell you the times that I've been talking to somebody like we're talking today and that we'll be wandering off topic a little bit and I want to get back on track. And for whatever reason, my ideal listener pops into my head. And I mean, when you create your ideal listener, you want to know what color shoes he wears, I mean, right down to really get into the details. And it helps a lot. And I think the other thing about audiences, I think sponsors will find an audience more valuable than downloads if you're only talking to 500 people a month. I think that's the magic number. They want 500 downloads a month, and that's a good number. But some people don't always get that. And I think that's within the first, these metrics have changed a bit, but I think it's 500 downloads in the first 30 days is kind of the magic number. (25:15): I'll have to look that up and get back to you to confirm that. But as a sponsor, that could be 500 people, but maybe only a hundred people are going to be interested in my product. Whereas if you have a hundred people that are all interested in my product, that's more valuable to me as a sponsor than 500 people that might not be. And so that's one of the things that I'm trying to confirm with everybody too, is look, my audience is X, Y, z. I did a survey a few months ago on just trying to find out who it was. It just verified that it is the outdoor industry. It's all the folks that we see at the Outdoor Retailer Show. But now I can go to people like some of these tourism folks around the tourism boards. They're interested in talking to me because the one guy I was talking to in New Mexico, he wants to get some of these outdoor brands to go down there and do some of their photo shoots. They got beautiful country, beautiful outdoor activities, come down here and do a photo shoot. So there's a lot of different ways to cut that. But yeah,

content:
Rick Saez (27:21): That's a tricky one. I think for me, a lot of the success is based on, I mean, I would probably do it for free. I didn't anticipate having so much fun doing it. And it just, because I get to talk to all these great people, I'm like, Charles Caral or something. I mean, it's so much fun to talk to these people and hear the stories that I didn't know about. So I'd probably do it for free. I'd like to monetize it, but I'd probably do it for free. But I think success, it depends on what you're doing it for. I'm doing it to share all these stories. So that's the success piece for me. If it does turn into a monetization opportunity and I can quit a day job and just do this all the better. But I think I would still share these stories because there's so many great stories of, and I think you learn from those that came before you, whatever it is you're doing. (28:09): So I think it's that valuable. But everybody's got their own thing. So I would ask them first, you got to do something that you're going to like and enjoy, so you stick with it. So whether it's hobby based or something you're having expertise at, and as long as you're still liking it and enjoying it, keep doing it. It takes a while. You can't just throw it up there and start talking about it and five episodes in, okay, I want that. Where's that money? That's not how it works. People have to get you, find you and you have to market it and get it out to all the places where your people are. So that's the advice I give people.

Cole Heilborn (28:40): YouTube in the last 10 years has become a really popular and some might say necessary channel to be on. Do you feel like the podcast format, apple Podcast, Spotify, will eventually reach YouTube status as it is today?

content:
Rick Saez (28:54): Oh, yeah. Yep. I think so. I think it's already happened. I mean, I think it's not as big as YouTube yet, but I think it's getting there because you look at all the new apps. I mean, when I started this, there weren't half the apps or half the destinations to push the show out to. I host on Lipson, and Lipson just had a new destination called Ghana, which is in India. So you can push your show to India, and I get a handful of downloads every week from India, which is like, that's very cool. So I think it's becoming pretty global. I think it is global, international. It'll get there. And my show goes to YouTube. I don't do the video piece of it, but there's just a graphic up there. And for those of you that get all your content on YouTube, a lot of people do these days. You can go listen to podcasts on YouTube. A lot of 'em are there.

Cole Heilborn (29:42): Yeah. How important is that when considering your content ecosystem strategy?

Rick Saez (29:49): Well, yeah, the YouTube component itself is not that important. But the importance is, I tell everybody you want to and need to be everywhere. Because the thing about podcasts is it's not like YouTube. There are multiple destinations. The reason Apple's so big is because the Apple Podcast app is native on the iPhone. That's why Apple's and Mac have kind of dominated podcasts, the Android phones and all that stuff. You have to go download Spotify or Stitcher or Pandora or wherever it is you want to listen. Apple had a built in and they created podcasts way back in the day. So that helps. But I think you just have to be everywhere because of that. You never know what people are going to be listening to, how they're going to be listening. So you want to be everywhere, and Lipson makes that easy.

Cole Heilborn (30:34): And Lipson is just, I mean, that's the podcast hosting site that we use. There's a few others out there I can think of. Anchor is Sprout Bean, is that one

Rick Saez (32:11): Yeah, they're taking some of the work off of me to get the production side of it done, which that's not why I hired them because the production, I have my workflow pretty tight. But what they also do is they turn the show notes and they create a blog post out of the show notes, and they optimize it for SEO purposes, so it's more likely to get found by Google and all that stuff. So it's a pretty detailed show notes page with all kinds of links, and they research the terminology. I might say, Hey, we're talking to Cole about podcasting today, and that'll be the title. And they'll go, no, no, no, that's not a good title. They'll tweak the title and make it all SEO appropriate. So they do all that stuff. Yeah, that's what's really been valuable to me.

Rick Saez (33:03): I dunno how they do it like a blog post. It's like a true article well written. It's well optimized. There's links to everything. Yeah, I'm assuming they transcribe it and then they rewrite it, and I'm sure it's all done in Asia. I don't know. But yeah, just stumbled on 'em. I signed on initially with 'em to go back and republish, I think it's 15 episodes, show notes. So they created blog posts at all that, and then I just produced five episodes with them, or I think it was five episodes. I'm going to produce five more with them just to have them do all the audio and all that stuff. It does take a lot of work, and it frees me up to do other things like workshops and that kind of stuff.

content:
Cole Heilborn (34:12): Well, that's a good point. If you're going to start a podcast, you can do it by yourself, but you don't have to. There's plenty of resources out there. And maybe if you don't have in-house production capabilities, there's some places out there that you can find resources. What's the place you work with and are there some others out there that you'd recommend?

Rick Saez (34:31): Yeah, the one I'm working with now is called Po Ize, P-O-D-E-T-I-Z-E. I was using Resonate for a while, resonate just for producing episodes when I kind of got in a jam, but there's a million of 'em Resonate PO ize. I mean, just look up podcast production and you'll find all kinds of places. But I also strongly recommend everybody to do your first 10 episodes yourself, because you have to know it's better if you know how the soup is cooked so that when something goes wrong, you can fix it because something does go wrong. It's just the nature of the beast. Somebody either their side crashed or the guy was sick that day, or they flubbed, they missed this. I got to go in and edit this out because they missed it. Whatever it is, you got to know how to go in there and do that. So I always tell people, you should produce your first 10, five to 10 that way. What's going on?

Cole Heilborn (35:23): That's a great idea. As a host, do you listen to your episodes after they're recorded to see if you can improve?

Rick Saez (35:31): Not always. I try to. I use Script and I read them a lot to you. Descrip is a transcription. It transcribes the audio, and I just read, I can find faster, and I take pretty detailed notes as I'm interviewing. So I write down the timestamp. Oh, I just flubbed that up here so I can go back and look at, I don't have to listen to the whole thing. I know we screwed up at 1922 and 42, 48. I can go back and clean that up.

Cole Heilborn (35:58): If you had to make a prediction about how the podcast world is going to change or what sort of opportunities it's going to open up that people might not be expecting or even aware of. Do you have any predictions? They could be wild predictions. It doesn't have to be factual.
