Rick Saez (36:17): Wild predictions. Wow, that's a good one. I think it's really not a prediction. It's more of a, it opens opportunities that none of us see coming, whether it's an opportunity to work with another company on some other project that they're doing, whether somebody wants you to write a book, somebody like what you said about this, they want to dig into your thoughts about that more deeply. I mean, I just think it opens up so many doors that I think that's going to continue, and I think it's just going to continue to grow. I think it's going to be, I mean, it might be replace radio is what I'm thinking. Radio, I don't even listen to radio anymore. I have XM radio, so I just listen to music. So I think this could be podcasts, could be a channel on XM radio, for example, you could go to XM channel 1 97, and it's the outdoor podcast channel, and it's the tennis podcast channel, whatever it might be. That'd be kind of cool, actually.

Cole Heilborn (37:11): That would be,

Rick Saez (37:12): You hear that XM give me a call.

Cole Heilborn (37:16): Yeah, you could have a whole bunch of scheduled episodes just playing throughout the day, and you just tune into the channel and away you go.

Rick Saez (37:25): Yeah, and I think that's sort of already exists. I think that's a lot of the way people find shows when you go into my show on Apple. You can just scroll through and listen to what you want to listen to or put it on play 'em all.

Cole Heilborn (37:36): You mentioned that there's a lot of hook and bullet podcasts out there, and of the a hundred some that you found in the outdoors, a lot of 'em were that nature. Why is that? Any ideas?

Rick Saez (37:48): I don't know. That's a good question. You'd think that there would be as many other mountain biking or backpacking. I don't know. That's a good question.

Cole Heilborn (37:59): I wonder if it's because that demographic really embraces the storytelling. The fish was this big, and then the next day it was a little bigger type of story. So maybe

Rick Saez (38:13): It could be that, and it could be too. I think fishermen and hunters, they always like to know where to go. So I want to go, we're the big fish. So they talk about, I think, I haven't listened to very many of these, but they do describe the hunt or the fish. And we got on this boat down in Baja at Loretto, and we went to, here's the settings on our compass, and we fished and caught a ton of Dorado, or I was hiking in the Wind River ranges chasing a moose, and we found them at this spot, and this is how we snuck up. All that kind of things. There's a lot of more how to, I think. But the same could be said for hikers and skiers and mountain bikers and all that. The PCT could be, imagine the whole PCT. Oh man, that'd be a great podcast actually.

Cole Heilborn (38:58): I mean, if there's anyone doing the PCT right now, maybe you just grab a mic and start interviewing people you pass along the way.

Rick Saez (39:05): Wouldn't that be fun?

Cole Heilborn (39:05): That would be incredible

Rick Saez (39:07): Stories of the PCT. I know a guy that wrote a book. He was on my show recently too. But yeah, that'd be a cool podcast.

Cole Heilborn (39:13): My wife is going to be really frustrated with me. She did the Washington section of the PCT and Are they Trail Angels? Is that what they're called? Sounds like. I don't know a whole lot about that culture, but it sounds like that's a really, that could be a really interesting series. Like doing episodes on these kind of renowned trail angels.

Rick Saez (39:37): Yep. Or the Trail Angel could do episodes on the through hikers that come through. Right. Both of those would be good shows. Yeah, and the PCT association could be the sponsor. There you go.

Cole Heilborn (39:50): And I think when you consider the amount of production that goes into a podcast, comparing this to a film or a video series, that's what we do. We create videos and it's so much less work, and you still achieve incredible quality. So as you're considering, as we're talking about this, I'm like, huh, what would it take to create a Trail Angel video series versus a Trail Angel podcast series? And the lift is so much smaller.

I mean, when Apple had that big update recently and kind of crashed a bunch of shows and muck things up for a few weeks there, Lipson was all over it. They were on it. content:
Cole Heilborn (42:18): The host, the person, the voice, who's kind of guiding the show? How important is that component?

Rick Saez (42:25): Well, I think it depends on what kind of thing you want to do. So if I was a retailer, for example, I would start a podcast and I, I might have the store owner as the host, but only once in a while. So that all that pressure's not on that person to host every episode because you can have, in your store, you have the guy who's the stove expert, so you're going to have him do a month long series once a week on backpacking stoves, and the host, the owner can tap in every once in a while and make some comments. But then Jim or Bill, or whoever it is, the stove expert, can be the guy who's doing every episode about the stoves. He knows all the intricate how to fix 'em, how to do all these things. So I think it's important, but it's not as important as people think. People might think that, yeah, I got to have a good voice and blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. And I don't know. We all have our voice. That's the beauty of podcasting too. It's so available to everybody. It really doesn't matter. I have a face for radio anyway.

Cole Heilborn (43:28): That's the beauty right now. No one can see our faces. That's right. When you were getting started, how did you practice? How did you get warmed up to host a podcast? Did you do any training? Did you watch YouTube videos? Did you just trial and error it?

Like one of the guys climbs, he's been a climber for a long time, and he traveled around in his Subaru and he says, I just got tired of living outside. I try to do four episode minimum. You get the whole month and we talk about your, say it's a multi-product category brand, and you have different product categories. So we get your apparel designer on one episode, we get your PAC designer on another episode, we get your footwear designer on another episode, and you really can dive in to the details of how the ethos of your design and your products and why you do what you do. It's a transition from talking to the guest to a read about, he was talking about his four wheel camper. Well, four wheel campers are made by blah, whatever it is, and it's a different one in each four episodes. So I think it's a way to continue that. But add value, you always want to add value, in my opinion, on whatever you're doing on your podcast. And so if you do it right and you do the ad read write, you don't make it too long. (55:47): You can't make it another two minutes. It's got to be maybe 30 seconds to a minute and a half max. They want to get back to the story, but it adds value to them so that as they're listening to me talk with Jonathan Seagrass about his four wheel camper, then you hear the guy from Four Wheel Camper or me or Jonathan, come on and talk about some more specifics about his four wheel camper, you're probably pretty well guaranteed. They're going to go home and look up four wheel campers and check it out. And that's ideally what you want to do. And that's I think the beauty of a podcast is you can go the route of radio and just slap some ads in there, but I think people will blow right through it. But if you have something where you're, again, continuing to provide value in education, they'll listen.

So if you're interested in learning more about what it takes to run a top brand, I hope you'll love this podcast and find something educational about it. Enjoy today's episode. Welcome to Brand Story. My name is Cole Hoborne, and today I'm sitting down with Casey Lorenzen, the content manager from Fial, Raven Casey, how are you doing?

content:
Cole Heilborn (02:09): Okay, nice. So you guys are opening up a new store, you were saying that's going to be in Denver?

Casey Lorenzen (02:17): Yeah, so we're opening our Denver flagship this summer. Obviously with the COVID situation, it's kind of touch and go with a lot of those sort of operations. But yeah, everything's on track right now and it's going to be kind of our biggest and baddest store so far. So we're excited about it.

Cole Heilborn (02:34): Yeah, that's awesome. When will it be open?

Casey Lorenzen (02:37): We're shooting for mid-June, so yeah, right in our backyard. Our North American headquarters is based in Lewisville, Colorado, so just outside of Boulder. So yeah, we're excited to have that just down the street.

Cole Heilborn (02:49): Sweet. Tell me a little bit about the brand. What is the brand? Who is the brand? How do you guys describe yourself?

Casey Lorenzen (02:59): That's an interesting question. Yeah, I mean, like I said, it's a Swedish heritage brand, so there's kind of two sides to that. I think when you talk about the brand in Europe, it's a little bit different than how we talk about it here in North America, just because the brand, it is still kind of in its infancy here year, needless to say, the market is growing rapidly for us here, so business is doing really well. So yeah, I mean, when you talk to any suite, it seems like they've grown up with the brand, they know exactly what it is, what it stands for. When you talk to the typical American, I think the first question is how do you pronounce the name? So yeah, once you get past that, there's I guess this allure or intrigue associated with it because it is a foreign brand. But yeah, we focus and pride ourselves on durability, sustainability, and quality and longevity of our goods. So it's one of those things that when you purchase, you're going to have it for a long time. So that heritage backing is super important for us as we tell that story here in North America. So

Cole Heilborn (04:18): Yeah. So how do you do that? How do you tell that story here where there's a cultural difference and even as something as simple as just the name and how you pronounce it?

So it is nice because like I said before I started working for the brand, I always held it in high regard because I had owned the products personally and I knew that the quality was there and I really enjoyed using their product. And so when you speak to the brand to somebody that doesn't understand or know it, when you then say that it's been around since 1960 in Sweden, you have that kind of heritage backing and okay, this is a brand built for longevity and has been around for a while and kind of know what we're doing. So

Cole Heilborn (05:23): Yeah,

Casey Lorenzen (05:25): It's easier to tell that story because of that.

Cole Heilborn (05:27): Sure. I guess in your experience do Americans have, when they think of a Swedish brand, what do they think of? Do they think of that legacy heritage or I guess, what's the most common kind of thoughts about what a Swedish brand is or should be?

Casey Lorenzen (05:48): Yeah, I can just speak for myself and what my perceptions would be, which I think anything Scandinavian I think you immediately go to, you have to be built for it. I mean, it's a hardy people, they endure harsh winters, and so when it comes to outdoor equipment and outdoor gear, I think they have that to fall back on and put their stamp on. But not only that, but as a Swedish brand, I think Swedish design is such a huge thing just across the board. And I think that's just a result of the riding opportunities in the sea of sky. (13:38): And we had this idea of, okay, well what if we took Crankworx on a road trip and we showcased and highlighted other destinations around the province gave these BC opportunity or BC athletes an opportunity to shine most of whom are from BC or have moved to BC because of the opportunities. And they just thought that was an amazing idea. And from there we hit the ground running, we went to our partners of Crank horse, Whistler explained what it was we were trying to do, how it was going to be made for tv, digital first broadcast first, no one on site. And I think at the time a lot of people were, they weren't sure what they were going to do from a marketing perspective. And so we were sort of one of the first to come to a lot of them with this concept and this idea and the feedback was generally really good. (14:39): They were like, okay, we think this is a great idea. We want to support you guys because we want you to be around in the long term. And so they got on board in a big way. And so it allowed us to, I mean for us it was the ultimate pivot. It kept our whole team working. We had about 70, including the athletes, I think last year we had around 65, 70 people on the tour plus the people that were in the resorts. And it kept people doing stuff and it kept us top of mind. And I mean every year in Whistler we have to rebuild the slopestyle course, which is a great advantage. We get a new course every year, but it's also you have to rebuild it every year. And in May of 2020, there was no sign of any certainty whatsoever. And so the decision was to cancel Crank Corps Whistler in Innsbruck. They were able to identify alternate dates in early October. And so we were able to postpone sbr. And I mean it was a challenge because a lot of, I mean at the time the US wasn't allowed to travel anywhere, so none of the American athletes could really get to Europe. It was primarily European based athletes. I mean a lot of the North American athletes were just hunkered down, weren't really sure about traveling internationally. Cole Heilborn (18:17): So when you had to cancel Whistler, I mean I'm sure that was a giant decision that weighed on everyone's shoulders as you were making it. How did you think through that and how were you thinking about the future repercussions of potentially canceling it?

Darren Kinnaird (18:34): Well, it is funny because the way my brain works and it never stops is I had already gone in the direction of the Cliff Crankworx summer series as this pivot that only we could pull off. And so by the time it actually came time to announce Crankworx Whistler, it was almost more of a formality. I was just excited about this crazy pivot that we had come up with and was excited to show that to the world that it was something unique that we could pull off. Of course, we were the sadness and disappointment of not being able to do Whistler was we dealt with that really quickly, moved on, the whole team got excited about, here we're going, we're going to do something else. No one else in the world can do this. We're going to pull this off. And so I think the whole team bought into we're going to go in a different direction. (19:40): I mean, it was sad and tough to make that call on Whistler. It was probably tougher this year because so many people had thought this won't be a thing for more than 6, 8, 12 months, whatever the heck it is. And so when we were faced with the reality of a second year of not being able to do this, that was probably tough. Year one was like, okay, cool, we're going to do something fun and new and it'll be different. And then I think to answer the other part of this, what were the long-term or what is our view of the long-term ramifications of that? (20:27): From my perspective, it was super, super important to keep Crank works, going, doing something and continuing to be able to tell our key sports stories and to keep, for lack of a better word, the narrative going. And that's what we've been able to do by working really hard to come up with ways to deliver Crank Steinburg this June with we had 500 spectators on site Crank Works BC where it was all made for tv. And then of course now here we think we're going to have spectators on site, but we're not a hundred percent certain with that. But it was just really important for the long-term of Crank Works that we continue the stories, we continue to provide opportunities for the athletes, we continue to provide opportunities for our partners. They're different opportunities, but it is really important to just keep working with all of these stakeholders to keep things going.

There were some surfing events where they were just bringing people together that were already in destinations, and that was effectively what summer series was. And like I said, excuse me, like I said earlier, we have some of the best World Cup downhill racers. We have some of the best EWS Enduro racers, and we have some of the best crankworx focused athletes that live in bc. And we started out really early on by getting all of these athletes on a phone call and saying, Hey guys, none of us are probably traveling this summer. We got an idea. What do you think? And the athletes, they were the ones that first said, and I was really hoping this was going to happen. (23:02): They said, everybody has to race everything and it's a winner, takes all points for everything. And so we set it up over three weeks in July and August of 2020, we traveled and we had a bus pick people up from the ferry and in Pemberton and brought everyone to Silver Star. One of the athletes had built a really great slalom track there. We had the athletes race, Enduro Air downhill, downhill and slalom at every stop, with the exception of when we went to Golden Kicking Horse, we reintroduced psychosis to the world, which is this infamous race that hadn't taken place in 12 or 13 years since 2008. But it was really this, we would go a week, one week in Silver Star, one week in kicking Horse Golden, and then a week in Sun Peaks Resort. And I mean, these are three of BC's best bike park slash mountain biking destinations. And so it was neat to be able to share those locations with the rest of the world, but we had 24 athletes compete over three weeks. And I mean, the feedback was, it was a unique once in a lifetime experience. It was a lot of fun, heck of a lot of work, but was well worth it,

Cole Heilborn (24:35): Man. I'm impressed with how quick you guys came up with something else.

So typically Crank Works has a bunch of partners and sponsors that help put on the event. How do you work with them now and how are you trying to serve them and still provide value even though the thing that they usually sign up for is totally different?

content: Darren Kinnaird (25:39): Yeah, I think there was a couple of key things that I learned early on, and I'll give a shout out to Mark Harrison who owns an agency in Toronto called T one, and they also put on a sponsorship X or sponsorship forum called Sponsorship X. And I've known Mark for a number of years and he is also a member of our advisory board now, and I would almost say a mentor, but had been listening to some of the things he had been saying. And I think one of the most important things that I picked up from him was make sure you are telling your stakeholders, your sponsors, all the scenarios and work them through and have them involved in all of the scenarios that you're planning. And so that was one of the most critical things that I think we're able to do is have weekly or biweekly calls with all of our partners, all of our stakeholders, just to keep them up to date on what we were doing, what we were thinking. (26:52): So that was probably the critical thing, number one. Number two, we experimented a lot with different ideas. We said to our partners in particular with summer series that this is an opportunity to experiment with all sorts of new things. We created a, one example is we created a pre-show for our broadcast called Crankworx Connect where we would have athletes and ambassadors and brand people on to interview them, talk to them. And it was sort of like a 30 minute lead into our main broadcasts. We did all sorts of different things within the broadcasts. I mean, that was the other sort of crazy thing about the broadcast is everything was done remote. So we had our announcers like Camal and Elliot Jackson, I think Elliot was in his living room and Cam was in his garage in Oregon and California. We had our production team producing remotely in Quebec and our timing and data graphics team producing remotely in Germany. (28:07): And so we were trying all sorts of stuff to make this work. And I think we took some of that. It gave us an opportunity to experiment, but it gave our partners an opportunity to experiment as well. We took some of those learnings to Innsbrook. I mean we had to do that remotely as well.

content: Darren Kinnaird (25:39): We did have a few more people on site because there was a lot of people based in Europe, so that made it slightly easier. But I think post that, the other thing that we did was we spent a lot of time doing what I've sort of coined a benefits audit or a deliverables audit. We went through the typical list of things that we provide for our partners at the varying levels of investment that they're involved with Crank Works and sort of thought, okay, which ones can we still do? (29:07): Which ones can we not do? And is there alternatives for the things that we can't do or is there new things we could do? And so when we had done that and sort of looked at, okay, here's the things we can offer, we started to have conversations with our partners about these things and made them aware and truly listened to what were the challenges and issues and problems that they were trying to solve, what keeps them up at night with work and tried to come up with new, whether it was broadcast or new digital solutions for those problems homes. And this has taken a truly whole of team approach to do that. And our team has adapted better than I think I've ever seen them adapt. I mean for a number of years have tried to get the, I mean every year we have a retreat and we sit down and we've developed our stakeholder wheel and trying to get the whole team to understand that yes, you might manage the athletes, but you also have an influence on sponsorship. (30:34): You also have an influence on the media or you also have an influence on the destinations that we go to. And so as we try to develop this whole of team approach, I kind of felt like we were maybe halfway there, but this forced us to get a hundred percent of the way there was for it forced people to get uncomfortable honestly, but to reexamine how they could support other things.

content:
Darren Kinnaird (25:39): And now we're in a much better position where we work hand in hand with our marketing and our digital social team, and they're so involved in our broadcast team, they're so involved now in all the, not directly in the conversations we have with partners, but we are bringing all this feedback from our partners to these teams and going, Hey everyone, we need to solve this stuff or deliver on these things as a very holistic approach. (31:38): And I think that was what we learned last summer. And from inberg last fall, we really spent a lot of time over this past winter developing that and spent a ton of time planning and preparing. And it's gotten to the point now where our social media schedule is, every single thing is planned to the minute and it's all color coded. Is this a sport delivery? Is this a destination delivery? Is it a sponsored delivery? What channels is it going in? Who at which brand or who are we sharing this with on the other end? Is it an athlete? Is it someone responsible for digital or marketing in a destination or ATRA or specialized or whoever? And so that's been critical to how we've been able to successfully deliver for partners in this new world.

Cole Heilborn (32:44): Wow. So what are some of the deliverables that you had to take off the table and what were some that you were able to adapt or add to the list for each of your partners?

content: Darren Kinnaird (32:54): Yeah, I mean I think we've had to take away expo booths for obvious reasons, demo booths, sampling opportunities. I mean all the things that you would traditionally provide for partners at a festival we've lost for the most part, not fully, because I think in Innsbruck, they've actually come up with a really creative way of doing it, and I'll come back to it in a second, but a lot of those human to human connection, physical connection. But we think we've been able to come up with new ways to integrate branded content or brand messaging into our broadcasts or into our social really having, I mean, we've always tried to have this focus on everything we do delivers for all stakeholders as much as we possibly can, but we've kind of taken it to a whole other level in Innsbrook. They actually last fall and this spring they found a bit of a loophole. (34:06): So the event takes place up at this resort called Mutters, which is about a 20 minute drive out of downtown Innsbrook in Innsbruck. Farmer's markets were still allowed last fall and this spring. And so we held a farmer's market of bike expo in the city, and so it just needed to be fenced in, you needed to check in. There was a number of people that were allowed in and that was very successful, maybe more successful than the expo had ever been at the venue. And there's one thing that coming out of this, we will probably keep, I mean we went down a couple times into the city and the lineup to demo one of the new specialized e-bikes was 20 people deep all day long and just take a bike for an hour. And you're right in the city, but the mountains are two minutes away and you can be on the trails in a couple of minutes. So there's definitely been some great key learnings out of this.

I guess, and I guess I don't want to speak for other events, but what it sounds like you guys have really been able to do, and maybe this has been your mindset before the pandemic, but Crank Works is an event business. You are an event, but you're way more than just an event. And so that perspective shift maybe has allowed you guys to continue to operate and find new paths and avenues. The event isn't what makes Crank works well, it is and it isn't, but you see what I'm saying. Maybe?

content: Darren Kinnaird (36:04): Yeah, I mean, I think one of the things that struck me prior to the pandemic is, and I mean I sometimes live within the bubble of crank work, so I don't quite have always the perspective that someone on the outside would have. But internally, what has started to happen over the last few years leading into 2019 was this concept of the Crankworx family and that involved the different destinations we went to and the people that we worked with there, but also the athletes. I mean, I can remember in 2018 we did the first ever Crank Horse World Tour awards and we had a new award, the Crankworx Spirit Award, and Martin Soderstrom won the first year and the guy was almost in tears on the stage when he won the award because for him, it showed that he was embodying and living this spirit of what it meant to be part of the Crank Works family. (37:25): Anna Cab Beton won it the next year and she still talks about it as one of the most important awards she's ever won. And so I think this Crankworx family idea goes beyond just the athletes and the partners and the destinations and so many people just they identify with the concept of I love mountain biking, I love celebrating mountain biking, and that's what Crankworx does. And so even though they can't attend, they can still be a part of the action, whether it's social, whether it's through our watching or broadcast. And that actually just sparks a thought here. I remember something, one of the things we did realize in Innsbruck this spring was that people wanted to see these behind the scenes moments. There was a way for us to share these sort of non-broadcast non-sport moments to a wider audience. And so it was little things like the Scrub Off, which was an event that we literally made up the morning of Slopestyle as a alternative. (38:48): If the weather came in and we needed to kill some time, well we'll do a scrub off. And that was one of the best events of Crank sbr and all these photos and images. And we were able to share that even though people couldn't be there and tens of thousands of people watched this content of this scrub off about something that was just made up that morning. We've taken that into Crank Works BC to have a videographer just running around behind the scenes, capturing goofy moments that the athletes are having and that desire to be a part of this cultural movement that is crankworx that I think is carrying or helping carry us right now. I mean, if you go back to the roots of what Crankworx was about, and I think Rob talked about this when he was on nowhere in the world could you be rubbing shoulders in the lift thigh with the biggest mountain bike superstars in the world or riding in the same race as them. I mean, that was something we started way back in 2004 and say we, but Crankworx started back in 2004 as a goal is to bring all these people together to celebrate mountain biking. And that is still such an important part of what we do today and will be a massive part of what we do in the future.

content: Darren Kinnaird (40:54): Yeah, I mean I think, again, I'll go back to this. I think I sent you a note before the show of everything has changed and nothing's changed. Of course everything's changed. We can't travel as easily as we could, gatherings tougher, all these sorts of things. But what hasn't changed is a brand's desire to be affiliated with a certain property or a brand's desire to connect with a property's audience. So those things haven't changed how we as an event property can provide those opportunities. That's changed. So that, and so that's on us to figure out, and I think now it takes more communication, more openness, less cookie cutter type partnership proposals and the ultimate flexibility to be able to deliver for partners. And it takes truly, truly listening to what is a brand's goal? What are they trying to achieve? Like I said, what keeps them up at night? (42:13): Mark Harrison always jokes that your job as a property is to get the person on the other side of the table promoted. So how are you going to get Joe Smith at X brand promoted up the food chain or to his next job? And if you can do those things, you are solving their problems. And I think we're living this right now. It's uncertain here in New Zealand. I mean, they had their first COVID case in whatever it was like 12 months back in August. And that toothpaste isn't going back in the tube here in New Zealand. They're trying to vaccinate as quickly as they possibly can to get to a place a lot of other places in the world are. But we're two weeks out and we're uncertain as to how many people will be on site. A lot of brands are actually based in Auckland and they're not on to leave because there's a border around Auckland because they've been able to, knock on wood, contain COVID within Auckland. (43:22): So the rest of the country's under level two warnings, but things are relatively normal. And so we've had to work with brands that are based here in Auckland that are sponsors of Crank Horse rota and try and create, we're working with one just this week about how can we create money, can't buy experiences for them, but they're in digital. And so we truly listened to what it was they were looking for, and we're in the process of creating and developing digital experiences for them that will allow them to continue to achieve their goals and what they were hoping to out of Kraner rot wheel, but in a completely different way.

content:
Cole Heilborn (44:10): So when big groups can gather again, how will the things that you guys are learning now translate to the conventional format?

Darren Kinnaird (44:21): I think we will just have a whole bunch of new arrows in our quiver. I think mean, again, I cannot express how fortunate and lucky our whole team feels to have been able to push through the last 19 or whatever months it is now. But it has truly taught us a lot. We've got all sorts of new benefits and opportunities and things that we can provide for partners, and it's actually brought our team closer together, more cohesive. We, there's so much more emphasis on planning and planning to execute has been the focus. And so I think a lot of that will carry forward into the future, no question. We'll be able to, things are looking really positive in, I have my finger on the pulse mostly obviously in bc, but they just announced yesterday, October 20th as we're recording this, that as of October 26th capacities at indoor venues, there's going to a hundred percent for, they have a vaccine passport in bc. (45:58): And so if you're fully vaccinated, you're going to be able to go to the Connects game a hundred percent, which is really exciting. And so for us looking to next summer, knowing that our event is outdoors and there's so much of a lesser risk of transmission and who knows where we'll be anyways next summer, but we're really looking forward to being able to deliver Crankworx Whistler 2022, the full gamut. There might be a little few the things that are different, but we'll see. But we're really excited about the prospect of bringing everyone back to the mecca, as they say, of mountain biking. And so when we do, we're going to be able to bring back all of the old opportunities we had for partners, but have a whole new quiver of new opportunities as well.

Cole Heilborn (46:57): Great. If you had to, I don't know, give any message to fellow events directors or organizers out there who are still trying to figure out how to weather the storm, any thoughts, any advice?

content: Darren Kinnaird (47:11): Yeah, it's never too late to reach out to your community and you never know where those conversations are going to lead. When things did hit the fan last spring, that was one of the things that we started to do was just reach out to all sorts of people. What are you seeing? What are you learning? What are you doing? And I think that helped inspire us to come up with the ideas that we did. And I, I spoke to, I mean, spent weeks just on the phone talking to people, what are you thinking? What are you doing? How are you guys going to react to this? And that has led to some amazing new relationships, rekindling of relationships that people that we used to work with and all sorts of new opportunities for not just Crank works, but for us as a business. And so we're talking to people in France, people in the us, people in Quebec, people in Calgary, people in Australia about what are the future opportunities for Crankworx? And so for us, not only did it help us work with other entities to find common ground to keep things going, but also now it's led to all sorts of new conversations and new opportunities. (48:50): This whole idea of summer series, when we came up with it here in New Zealand, they're like, that looks amazing. Can we do one too? And so they pitched it to basically the south island, and we'll be doing the first ever Crankworx summer series New Zealand at the end of November for three weeks, end of the early December, and we're going to go to Alexandra in Otago, Queenstown, aka, and what's the place? I forget. But we're going to be going in and around Queenstown to share the stoke of Crank Works. All the athletes that have traveled here to be a part of Crank Works rota, a lot of them are going to stick around and race and be a part of this summer series. And so that's just one neat example of the things that have come out of this idea of reach out to your community, build connections, what are other people doing? And those that reaching out to the community did lead government entities to help provide direction and where are the opportunities for government funding to help get through all of this? And so we now have a direct pipeline to our NP in Cedar of Scott, and turns out he's a huge Crank Works fan, had been to the last 10, so you never know.

content:
Cole Heilborn (50:24): Wow, man. Well, anything, I think this conversation is one educational, it's a little inspiring just to hear that you guys are still kicking, still connecting the dots and providing opportunities for fans and for your team and for sponsors and athletes. We're kind of reaching the end of our time for today, but do you have any other thoughts, anything that we didn't cover that you feel like we should get out there?

Darren Kinnaird (50:49): No. I mean, I think if I can lead people with things, it's reach out to that community, talk to your partners, constant communication and keeping them apprised as to all the scenarios and the challenges challenging you are facing as a property, because sometimes they want to help you solve them too. And because people are investing in what you're doing because they want to be a part of what you're doing, and that also means they want to help you continue doing what you're doing. And so those conversations have been invaluable. But yeah, I mean, I think, like I said, nothing's changed and everything's changed, and it's important to remember that that's just how we do things is what's changed, but what matters and what matters to everyone that hasn't changed.

Cole Heilborn (51:48): Well said. Darren, if folks want to follow along with you personally on the socials or with Crank Works, where can people go to connect?

Darren Kinnaird (51:56): Yeah, so most of my handles are DW Cannard on Instagram and Twitter, and then at Crankworx on Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, all that, TikTok, all the things. Yeah.

Cole Heilborn (52:13): Awesome. Sounds good. Well, I'll let you get back to your exciting day of quarantine, and hopefully you can get out on more than one walk.

Darren Kinnaird (52:20): I got another one planned for this evening, so I'm looking forward to it.

Cole Heilborn (52:23): Beautiful. Well thank you and looking forward to rot.

Darren Kinnaird (52:26): Thanks, Cole. Thanks for having me on the show.

Cole Heilborn (52:27): Take care.

Darren Kinnaird (52:28): Cheers. Bye-bye.

Cole Heilborn (52:31): Thank you for listening to this episode of the Backcountry Marketing Podcast. If you enjoyed today's episode or learn something new, please consider leaving us a review on Apple or sharing this with a friend.

content: Jonathan Ronzio (00:22:25): So I have never intuitively been the process person, the organized operational person, the business playbook, which you just held up. My brother wrote that book, and that always was natural for him. And so me on the other side, I complimented him with my just impulsive wild kind of creativity. And so along the way, he, as the older one, got to be an expert at delegating to me and I had nobody to delegate to. I became an expert at priding myself at taking everything on and being able to get efficient and learn real quick and figure out how do I do it all. But that is not a sustainable way to really scale anything. And that's probably where I did hit a wall with Explore Inspired was I wasn't thinking about how to do anything beyond me until even though Emily came on board, that was more or less the first time, I had to start thinking like, alright, well how do I teach her how to publish blogs and WordPress? (00:23:30): Lemme document that process. And so from a creativity to process index, I guess what I had to learn is you can't operationalize the creative spark, the creative engine, the ideas, the intuition. That's not something that you can document, but you can document the systems that enable that spark to fly to have more freedom. And so that's what I learned a little bit along the way. Train was just a beta kind of prototype. When I went to Denali and I had to, for the first time document, I'm like, all right, I'm going to be totally off the grid for the next month. I'm going to be living on a glacier. I'm not going to be able to produce this client content. I'm not going to be able to keep this newsletter going or publish this and that. And I had to document those things in this early version of TRA and assign them to my wife and to some freelancers. (00:24:28): And that was my first aha to wow. It's not about replicating the creativity, it's about replicating the guardrails that enable the creativity. And so let's say in video production, it's like you hire somebody to come and produce videos for you, and do they know right away if they should be exporting in 16 by nine or two by one, where are these videos going to live? What frame rate should they be shooting in? What frame rate should they be editing in? There's just so much of the minutiae of actually the creative output that can be process driven and can be documented and can make things more efficient and give you less headaches when somebody does something wrong, is really what you have to figure out. That's why often process documentation is such a reactive thing because you don't even think about it until something goes wrong, until you hit a wall. And then you have to think, well, how could we have avoided that? Okay, I could have told you this and this and this and this and this. Alright, so that's where I had to start learning what needs to be documented around the things that I do so that I can delegate to others and how do I build the systems and processes around my creative output to help others do the same, but you can't replicate the experiences of your life that inform your ideas.

content: Al Perkinson (05:54): I used to work for another fishing brand and we were engaged with all types of fishing. So we were engaged with bass fishing, offshore salt, inshore, saw fly fishing, I mean muskie, stripers, all these different types of fishing. And it was funny because when I would go to an event for one of those types of fishing, I found myself having to dress differently. So am I going to wear my bass fishing outfit to the bass fishing event and to the saltwater, to the offshore saw or fly fishing? And then I really started noticing that each of these communities kind of had different personalities and different values and they each did things differently. And so it occurred to me that these individual parts of fishing were sort of little subcultures within the fishing community. And that fishing as a whole was a bit of a subculture, but really for fishing there were sub subcultures. (07:06): And so I kind of got to the point where, look man, I'm sort of feeling schizophrenic here and I have multiple personalities and not only do I have to know how to do all these types of phishing, but I have to have a separate wardrobe for each one and not totally adopt a new set of values, but there's some red state and there's some blue state types of angling communities. And so from that experience, I sort of developed this, just sort of thought it through and wrote it down and started playing around with it and came up with this community-based marketing type of approach. But it started with just an understanding of looking at things like a cultural anthropologist might look at it and saying, Hey, this is a group of people that hang together and exhibit similar types of behaviors to each other and have different characteristics. (08:17): And so if you go in and you understand that hey, okay, this is a community and this community behaves this way, then you can develop a strategy for targeting that community. But it's really more about becoming a member of that community and joining that community, being a part of that community as a brand. So that's sort of how it evolved.

content: Al Perkinson (12:06): I think this is one of the main reasons that I like to share sort of the secret of community-based marketing because I believe it's good for business and it's good for people. And so the more people that do this, I think the better off we are. And a lot of it is, I don't know if you look at AB boomers type of marketing marketing for the last 20 or 30 or 40 years, it's been almost militaristic and you're a company and you don't really respect the people you're marketing to. They are there to buy your product and for you to make money off of them. And so the consumer has kind of considered this almost anonymous type of entity or thing. And so lot of companies looked at the consumer as something to conquer. And so they developed these strategies and they developed target markets. (13:16): And so they would pummel communities with marketing messages until they couldn't take it anymore. And like, okay, I'll buy the freaking ring around the collar. I've heard it a million times, I will buy your product. It was almost an adversarial relationship. And with community marketing, I think it's not an adversarial, but it's more of a respectful type of relationship and it's one in which you want to become a part of this community. And one of the ways that you do it is by giving to that community. So you're not just taking targeting and trying to extract dollars, but you're actually trying to help build that community. And those communities are really important to people. If you're a cyclist or a mountain climber or a fly fisherman, your community is where you probably get the most joy out of your life is the time you spend in that community. (14:26): And so these communities, it's important that they stay healthy and it's no guarantee that they are going to stay healthy. And so the people participating in it, they want to come together and hold hands and say, how can we make this community better? And then the brands, if they take that attitude as well, which is more of a giving building type of attitude, then they're contributing to make that community better so they're contributing to people's happiness. And so I think having an attitude of you're not trying to take and target, but you're trying to join and build that everybody wins and that type of scenario.

Cole Heilborn (15:09): And when community-based marketing is being used effectively, I mean, what does it look like? What are some of the foundational elements that make a marketing initiative community-based marketing? How does that get played out?

Al Perkinson (15:25): Well, I think it does start with that attitude of how you're approaching it. And so you're joining and you're giving before you even ask for a sale. And so it is kind of organic and it takes a little bit longer and it's not as easy to justify sometimes internally in a company because it does take a little bit longer and what you're building, you're building relationships and those relationships are hard to quantify. And it's not necessarily a media-based where I'm going to spend this much and I'm going to get this many impressions. It's much more of a relationship based, so I'm going to spend this much time and I'm going to win over this many hearts and minds. So that's something that if you're trying to justify what you're doing up the ladder, it's a little bit more esoteric and a little bit more difficult to do. (16:30): But what happens when you're successful is that the community rallies around you. And so having lived through the great recession like 2007 and eight, what we found was all the other brands, let's say you're talking to a retailer and at that time they're open to buy dollars shrunk because people weren't buying as much. Well, instead of taking that smaller pot and dividing it between three or four brands, they gave all that money to us because we were part of the community. We also found when we would sponsor a conservation group and for example, and other brands would say they were successful at sponsoring that group, well, our sponsorship wasn't based on just giving them money, but it was based on us locking arms and working on problems together. So they would actually turn down other brands who wanted to come in and become a sponsor of a conservation of their conservation group and they'd say, no, we've got our partner and that's good. So you see a lot more loyalty between all the members of the community and you see 'em actually trying to help each other out. So that's pretty unique in business to have that type of environment.

And we call those events and a lot of brands will look at an event as a place to sell their product, and so they calculate what's our return on investment? We spent a hundred thousand dollars to sponsor this event that we sell a hundred thousand dollars worth of product, and that is completely the wrong way to do it. And so your attitude in that event should be, I would say bring the beer and pay the band because you want to make that a kick ass party. You want to make that event, you want to be part of that celebration and make it something special. (19:23): So people who go to that event and other people who hear about the event, they're going to know who bought the beer and paid the band, and they're going to know who's just trying to be there to sell 'em some stuff. You can see the people who work in the booth of that company that's just trying to sell stuff and they know they're going to get their ass beat when they get back to the office if they didn't get a good return on investment. And then you can see the people in the booth who are there to have a good time and to celebrate, and they'll probably sell more product than the other guys do, but the community's going to know what that brand did and that engenders them to that community and builds that brand loyalty and makes those deposits in that equity banks.

Cole Heilborn (20:13): Yeah, interesting. So let's dive into your five points. Can you summarize them for us and then we'll start back up with number one and dive deeper into what each of these points mean?

content:
Al Perkinson (20:25): Yeah, so all communities have leaders, and so one of the tenets is, and these aren't really steps necessarily, they're just sort of components, but so all communities have leaders, people they look up to. So our mantra there is win over the leaders, not with your pocketbook, but with your heart and your soul. We want them to believe in what we believe in. Then number two would be adopt the cause. So communities have sort of a set of beliefs and values, sort of a religion. So you want to embrace that cause and further that cause for them. Then the gatherings we just talked about, goose, the gatherings, play the band, bring the beer, super important, join the conversation is we call that chatter. So communities connect themselves by talking to each other and communicating and there's a conversation going on. Join a conversation, don't interrupt it. (21:29): There's a whole school of thought on interruptive marketing. I kind of think that's bullshit. Nobody likes to be interrupted, it's rude. So join the conversation and be a part of it, make it more interesting. And then the last one sounds superficial, but it's looked the part. And that's why we hire community leaders because they come from the community. They're authentically a member of that community, and so they look and they feel, and they are part of that community. And so you're faced to that community needs to feel like that you're a member of that community. So the five things, leaders, causes, gatherings, conversation and look the part.

Cole Heilborn (22:16): Gotcha. So jumping back to point number one, this idea of winning the leaders. How are you guys at Behe winning the leaders? What does that look like?

content: Al Perkinson (22:28): Well, I have my community leaders who've actually been with me for a very long time and have luckily followed me over to Behe. They have relationships and they know that there's certain people that fit our brand and there's certain people that it doesn't mean they're a bad person or a good person, it's just are they a good fit? And so that's kind of the first question that we ask is who is likely to believe what we believe and to care about what we care about and sort of have the vibe that we have our bros, our team. And so then they identify those individuals, and some of them they might not know yet. They don't know everybody, so they'll do some networking, they'll talk to other people and certainly share what we're all about. And people are like, yeah, I know exactly where you're coming from. (23:29): You ought to meet this dude. And so it becomes this just networking and talking and conversation with these folks. And then when we do have the conversations, I mean literally it seems like it would just take forever and you're never going to be able to talk to enough people personally to make a difference. But there have been a lot of studies done that says a very small number of people can affect a very large number of people. And I think some brands have gotten it down to a hundred people can influence the entire community. Others have been nuts, like 10 people. And so just that network of influence. So finding who those influencers are, but also who are the ones that actually fit your brand. And then sitting down and having the conversations and trying to win them over just one person at a time before you even talk money and contracts and all this kind of stuff. It's like, Hey, would you be happy here? Would it be a good fit for you? Are you believing what we're believing kind of thing. And then when it comes to actually doing a formal agreement, it's super easy. You've already know that it's a great fit and it's not about money, it's just about a belief system. So that's kind of how we approach it.

content:
Cole Heilborn (24:56): When you say the leaders for you guys, are those your athletes, are those your ambassadors or is that how you're working with these community leaders?

Al Perkinson (25:06): Yeah, leader to me is just, you could call 'em an influencer. It is just somebody that other people in the community look up to. And it could be, it doesn't even have to be the top dog. I mean it could be the president of another company in the community or it could be like some dude or gal who's in the marketing department or in the sales department, but for some reason everybody looks up to that person. It could be somebody in a conservation group, it could be a well-known scientist, it could be a writer, it could be an artist, it could be a professional athlete, but it's just people who influence other people and that others look up to.

Cole Heilborn (25:55): How do you work with these community leaders? You're talking about contracts. Are these employees, do they have their own lists of duties and responsibilities or are they just more of friends connections of people in the industry?

Al Perkinson (26:09): Yeah, our community leader would be an employee of ours. They're the ones who coordinate all of the activities within that community, the leaders of the community, the influencers, those folks, there's a range. Some of 'em will want to do a formal contract and get paid money or get paid free product, be obligated to do appearances or to do social posts or stuff like that. Mean you can look at Michael Jordan was an influencer for Nike. He also had his own line of shoes and did all kinds of other things. So that's way up here. So it can be a whole range of agreements. Sometimes it's, there's no formal agreement at all. You flip 'em a pair of shades and they're like, yeah, man, I'm in and lemme know what I can do to help. So content is really big these days, and so being involved with content creation or just being part of your content is something that's pretty popular as a way to get involved.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:29): Gotcha. So your second point adopting the cause or the belief system in the outdoor industry, is that, I mean, I think a common example of that is give back programs, conservation partnerships. What other ways or how does it go beyond something just like the 1% give back type deal?

Al Perkinson (27:51): Yeah, it's really interesting. I guess there's two parts, a couple of parts to it. Maybe the conservation could be a value because if you're using this resource to really do the thing that you're passionate about, then you care about protecting that resource. And so one of the values of that community is protect the resource. If there's no fish, then we don't really have a sport anymore, so let's make sure the fish aren't going to die and let's make sure they're taken care of the same for mountain biking or any other type of activity. So that's definitely a core part, but there can be other things that are important to the survival of the community. Are we bringing new people in? Are we bringing young people in? Are we bringing women? Are we bringing various ethnic groups into the conversation and into the community? Because if the community is not growing, then it's dying, right? (28:56): You're either growing or you're dying. And so helping a shared value could be about winning over new people and within that being more inclusive, more open, less sort of cliquey or whatever. And so that can be part of a cause that you adopt within that community. There can also be stuff that's a little more, maybe less tangible and it could be an attitude, and so it could be about independence or freedom or self-sufficiency, those types of, if you look at Harley Davidson, what is that community built around? It's built around sticking it to the man. It's built around expressing yourself and being free and not being smothered by the constraints of society so that you can actually go out and explore and be free. And if you create films for example, talk about that, that celebrate that, then I would say that that's part of furthering the cause of that community as well.

content:
Cole Heilborn (30:18): Gotcha. So it doesn't just have to be a monetary or financial component. There's a lot of other parallels or things to consider as well when you join the belief system. So joining the belief system kind of sounds like you're signing up for a religion. Do you have to wholeheartedly believe with all of the commonly accepted beliefs within a community in order to fully join it?

Al Perkinson (30:46): Yeah, it's a great question because it is sort of where religion meets commerce and you have to serve both masters in a way. So I don't know if it's necessary. I don't think it's necessary to hook, line and sinker adopt all aspects, but there needs to be something that you can embrace and that you can hold onto and that you can believe in. I mean, it just does because that's like the emotional tie that you have. And so many of these communities and so many of the things that hold us together as human beings are emotional, they're not rational, and the rational stuff's easy for everybody to do the emotional stuff super hard. I would say on some level, yes, it's important that you are part of that if you want this to be an authentic endeavor.

Cole Heilborn (31:57): Okay, yeah. Interesting. The third point, showing up at gatherings, being present, contributing. What does that look like?

content:
Al Perkinson (32:04): Well, sometimes it is literally bringing the beer and paying the band. Yeah, we did a college tour years ago and what we learned, and we just toured the country in an Airstream and threw parties for frat boys, and eventually there was a disconnect in the value system there. So we exited that eventually. But yeah, I mean the mantra there was cheap beer didn't have to be free, but it had to be cheap, great music and free shit is how, and if you had those three things, you would have a successful event and that's what the college guys were looking for. So you get the vibe of what makes this event cool and why do people come to it, and then you just try to pour gas on that fire, and that's what it's all about at the time was called the Teva Mountain Games. I think it's now called the GoPro Mountain Games out in Vail. (33:28): And for all the sponsors did a little summit and the guys who ran it, Joel Heath and some other guys, really smart guys brought in a guest speaker for all of us. And that was kind of the topic of his conversation that every one of you sponsors. If you're here to take something from this event, if you're here to argue about where your booth space is going to be and how big it is and just asking the people putting on the event to just give you more and more, then you're not going to be happy here and the event's not going to be successful. But think about what if everybody in this room said, how can I make this event better? Then we all benefit from that. And I just thought that was an incredible little speech that guy gave and it's very much in line with this whole community-based marketing approach. And so we've adopted that and I think it's a lot more fun to go about it that way and it is a win for everybody.

Cole Heilborn (34:42): It sounds like points three and four kind of blend together. You're showing up at the gatherings and then you're joining the conversation, but those are distinct points for a reason. Why is that?

content: Al Perkinson (34:55): Well, that would tend to be more around marketing communications in terms of joining the conversation, and certainly one type of communication is at an event where you're talking to people directly. But from a more theoretical standpoint, if you think about, let's say you're at a cocktail party and you walk up and there's a group of three or four people and they're talking about a, let's say they all love fishing, and so they're talking about fishing and they're talking about some trip that they've taken to South America or to wherever, and you walk up and you interrupt that conversation that they're having and you're like, sorry, I know y'all are talking about fishing, but let me tell you about myself. Here's where I went to school and here's where I work and here's my strengths and maybe I have a weakness, I haven't found it yet. (35:52): And then you say, what's going to happen? They're going to turn to you and be like, who is this jerk? And so they're not really going to want you to be part of their group. On the other hand, if you walk up and you kind of listen for a while and you understand, Hey, what are they talking about? What's the conversation about? And you're like, oh, well, I like to fish too, and I've been to that place that they're talking about. And then you say, with a little humility, I went there a couple years ago, I know what you're talking about. That was really cool. And then they're like, oh, really? Yeah, okay. Did you catch anything? Yeah, caught this fish. And then all of a sudden you're part of that little crew, you're joining a conversation instead of interrupting the conversation. And so it's just kind of an analogy for marketing communications. It's all about storytelling, and it's about telling stories that are of interest to the community and being part of that conversation

content:
Cole Heilborn (36:58): In that story, it makes perfect sense. No one in that social setting would want to go grab a drink with the guy who just interrupted them. But why is it that interrupting interruption? Marketing tactics are a thing and tons of people use them, but socially that's a very odd practice. But when it comes to marketing, that's the thing that people use all the time. Why is that? That seems really obvious.

Al Perkinson (37:27): Well, I think of brands as people, and it's really a company and a company is made up of people. And so marketing is really just you having a conversation with other people. So everything is very much to me in human terms. And you've had this expertise within business and marketing built up over the years to where it makes it not human, but it makes it, I don't know. I don't know what people think companies are, but it's almost like they're not made up of people and of humans, but they're this other thing. And people will say stuff like, oh, it's just business. Well, what do you mean? It's just business? Is me as a person having an exchange with you, a person, how is that any different than a social conversation? So I think they're one and the same. It's more of a humanistic, human-based type of approach to business and to communication. (38:42): And people are going to either be on receive or they're going to be on send or they're going to be on block. And so if you're trying to tell them about your product, what's the easiest way to get them to open up and be receptive to that conversation? I think it's in the way that we talked about as opposed to just, and the thing is, people, we used to not have control of the commercial messages that we were fed. There used to be three networks and you sat down and there were 32nd commercials and 62nd commercials, and you had to sit there and watch those commercials. You didn't have a choice. And so it was very much sort of a force feeding type of arrangement. Now the consumer has finally pretty much gotten control over what messages come to them and they can pick. And so it better be a message that they're receptive to or they're not going to let you in.

content:
Cole Heilborn (39:50): So in your guys' marketing today, what's your messaging? How do you speak about your product? Are there certain tactics that you just won't touch or even recognize because of this pillar of joining the conversation rather than interrupting the conversation?

Al Perkinson (40:12): I have to be pulled, kicking and screaming by my people, my staff, to talk more about our product. But I think if you talk about the product, you talk about it in terms of the benefit, and if we have a lens that blocks significantly more blue light, which reduces haze, makes everything clear, and it has a rose base so that it has high contrast. So the benefit of that is you can see more fish and you can catch more fish, and so you're going to have a great time on your trip, then that's a message that folks might be a little bit more receptive to than just talking about the features, talk more about the benefits. But then there's a heavy dose. We have a series now called Fishing with Jay, with Jay Johnson and Jay is in the old Bojo school bus traveling around the country talking to fishermen and fishing with fishermen and just having a great time. And that's something that we don't talk about the product at all. It's obvious because Bahi was written by a tattoo artist tattooed on the side of the bus, but it's not in your face. And really the star is J and the star is the story.

Cole Heilborn (41:39): But it sounds like you make a cognitive decision to talk personally to talk less about the product. Is that correct?

content:
Al Perkinson (41:48): Yeah, if you make a product, I had a PR person one time and I said, I want to get some feature stories and some magazines, something that's like a real meaty kind of story. And she goes, okay, well what are you doing that's worth writing an article about? I said, well, how about our product? And she goes, no, man, everybody wants to talk about the product. They think their product's the best everybody does, so give me something interesting. Give me something that's real, that's something that's not product. So that kind of forced me to think about that. I'm like, wow, what are we doing as a company? What are we doing as a brand? What are we doing to improve the world? Help the world? What are we doing that's funny, that's crazy. I better go do some of that stuff. And so I think that's just kind of human nature, not to just listen to people talk about themselves and talk about their product, but to want to hear something that's cooler than that.

Cole Heilborn (42:55): When is it appropriate then to talk about the product or the service?

Al Perkinson (42:59): Well, if you're into online marketing and you got the funnel, then top of the funnel is the really fun, interesting stuff that's going to get people to say, oh, I'd like to check that out. And then as you move down the funnel and you're like, okay, I'm considering buying this product and so I'm going to want to know certain things. I'm going to want to know about what is the base lens color, what is the light transmission? What are those specific things? Because that is going to impact my decision to buy it. It's going to impact how it performs doing the thing that I want it to do. So when you get sort of bottom of the funnel and get close to that purchase decision, people are going to demand that you give them that information.

Cole Heilborn (43:44): So your fifth point, look, the part you mentioned earlier that when you'd show up at different gatherings with different, you'd have to put down different types of clothes for the different events. Is that what you mean? Putting on the right wardrobe to fit into the right crowd?

And so I think looking the part on the outside and the inside, on the outside though, it becomes a, for that community that helps you identify yourself and others identify you as a member of that community. And people are proud about that. You want somebody to stop you in the airport because wearing a certain type of shirt or wear of glasses or a hat like, oh, you like to trout fish? Yeah, I do too. Man, I can't tell you how many conversations like that I've had in airports and just out in public where you instantly make a friend because they see that you love the same thing that they love and they identified you by how you looked and whatnot. So I mean, I remember being out west and we got our Southern Prep boys who were out there working in a fly shop for the summer, and they're driving a certain type of vehicle, probably an old beat up four runner. They got the baseball cap on, they got their Patagonia shorts, and they've got their guy Harvey and their sunglasses hopefully. But at this point, but you're like, that's our guy right there, man. I can tell he looks the part.

Cole Heilborn (45:43): So how does a brand look the part, I mean obviously the employees could wear the right clothing, but the outside the image of the brand, how do you guys look the part?

Nicole Handel (00:03:58): Yeah, so marketing, I mean I think it's kind of funny, especially after the TV show Mad Men was released, marketing really has this reputation for being this kind of thing that anybody can do as long as you're a little bit creative or charismatic or something like that. So I think truly I feel like most people are interested in marketing and I was one of them. I studied psychology simply because I wanted to study all of these different things like anthropology, sociology, poetry, philosophy, and in my head at the time as a 17-year-old when you're deciding what to study, psychology seemed like the thing that was most likely to sound good on paper and get me a job. The irony of course, is that I actually don't work in the field of psychology, but I'm pretty convinced that having a degree in psychology is really beneficial to marketing. (00:04:55): So I was always interested in marketing and after I graduated college I really wanted to go on to study consumer anthropology or corporate anthropology, which is essentially why are consumers doing what they're doing, what is motivating them, how are they using products, how do they associate with a brand? And that kind of aspect of anthropology or any kind of study of people was really interesting to me. I ended up not going to grad school. I kind of inherited bear and my life changed a little bit and I bartended for a while. I taught spin classes and Pilates, and then I eventually ended up in a sales position working for the company that owns Jameson Irish whiskey, and there was a lot of marketing components to that role, and that's when I kind of started to develop some marketing specific skillset. And Instagram certainly I think has helped shape lot of people who have no formal background in marketing to be marketing savvy individuals. So I think that played a role as well.

content: Nicole Handel (00:06:19): Oh, interesting. Well, my favorite learning that has stuck with me over the years as somebody who has a lot of opinions and is a fairly loud person, I find myself in conversations pretty often where people are sharing feelings and so it can be emotional. And one thing I learned actually in a mediation class was about position versus interest. So in any conversation, and this is relevant in how we speak to others when we consider things like sustainability and DEI, when we think about the political climate that we've been in this country for a while now, and to anybody who's currently studying psychology and who's fresher on this than me, I apologize in advance if I'm doing this concept of disservice. But position and interest is about what people are saying in a conversation or an argument or a debate, and then interest is what they mean. (00:07:21): What's at the root of that. So an example is, I don't know if we're talking about the environment and you say climate change isn't real, that's your position, but maybe your interest is you are saying that you don't want to believe that we've done this much damage to the earth because that doesn't serve you or your lifestyle or whatever the case is. That's really at the core of what you're saying. Or if somebody says, I don't like that you did this thing, what they mean is that hurt my feelings and it didn't feel good. So considering position versus interest comes up for me all the time in my personal and professional life because what people say isn't always what they mean. And anytime anybody says anything, there's a feeling behind that they mean something. And so finding what's meant over what's said is I think really powerful. And I know that wasn't so specific to marketing, but that's the thing. I mean, it's specific to just existence as a human who communicates. It's like the primary thing that has stuck with me. It's less sciencey and flashy, but it is interpersonal and I think that's important.

Cole Heilborn (00:08:39): Yeah, so I mean personally that, well, personally and professionally, I suppose you could see that playing out frequently. Is that something you're cognizant about while you're doing your job, while you're making decisions, while you're putting together messaging?

Nicole Handel (00:08:54): Yeah, totally. I mentioned earlier, I don't know if somebody doesn't agree with something we've said or done on social media, it's easy to say why do they have to be confrontational when we are trying to do a good thing that's a human feeling or emotion that's easy to feel in a case like that. But then you consider what's the interest there? They're concerned about safety, they want the best for others. They want to make sure that information being shared is accurate. That comes up. That certainly comes up. And anybody who works with people has to keep that in mind. It's super relevant for I think just anybody who has to function in a group.

Cole Heilborn (00:09:39): So it sounds like the position statement is where people can disagree, but the interest perspective is maybe the common ground that a lot of people find themselves feeling the same way,

Nicole Handel (00:09:51): Same way? Well, it's irrefutable. You can disagree with a position you can't disagree with, I feel X, I experienced X that can't be argued with, which is really why that's a much stronger way to communicate in the first place if you can manage. But yeah, you're totally right. Interest is the common ground and interest is the thing that anybody can understand. Maybe I can't understand why you voted for a certain candidate, but I can understand that you had feelings about something that that candidate was referring to. I can understand that you have a vested interest in your loved ones and maybe that can, that's the thing that we can all relate to.

content: Nicole Handel (00:16:07): Yeah. Well, I think we already touched on the primary big picture one, which is emotion. I think that everything we do is informed by some emotion, even charitable act when we do something good for the environment or for someone else. I think, and this is not to be pessimistic, but just to be kind of scientific or realistic about it, are we doing that because we really care in a very selfless way about that thing? Or are we doing that because we want to believe that we are the type of person who would do something good? And really the conclusion I've come to is the answer doesn't matter if we're doing good, let it be doing good is still doing good. And I think we don't have to look at decision-making in that way apart from just having an interest in it. But I think back, kind of one step is emotion is the number one thing that I think all brands capitalize on or should or could capitalize on, and that's really big picture. (00:17:13): So we talked about dogs, people have a strong emotional affiliation to dogs campaigns that tap into negative emotions, for example, like diet culture, you don't want to be X or you don't want to feel X, or if you want to be better or whatever, or do this, buy this. And that's certainly emotional if anybody has any level of insecurity or self-loathing, which I think most of us have, some of that's an attractive campaign emotionally speaking. So I think mean without sounding like I'm simplifying, I think behind you were asking what are some kind of behind the scenes things and tactics? Emotion is probably everything. I mean, certainly there are other tactics like save money do this. But isn't that sort of an emotion too? You want to feel in control or you want to feel responsible financially. Of course, technically saving money is not emotional. That's the survival mechanism. But I think emotion is really at the root and at the core of all of the kind of tactics as you put it.

Nicole Handel (00:19:04): Yeah. Well, one thing I think that is important to mention is I think when we talk about psychology in marketing, the first thing people think is psychology as a dirty word. Like, oh, they're trying to scheme us or they're trying to pull one over on us. But really psychology and marketing, at least for us, because psychology isn't just how do I get somebody to do what I want them to do? That's certainly one factor in psychology, but psychology is also what does somebody want? What do they need? What will make them feel safe? What will let them know that they're welcome or what will help inform safe decisions for that? Those things are all psychology. So we certainly aren't huddling around in our marketing team meetings, like going through psychological research studies, but I would say it's more the latter, which is it just is in everything we do. I don't think you can work in marketing without tapping into psychology a little bit. And again, not necessarily in any kind of manipulative way, but more so figuring out if our goal is to help our consumers to bring more consumers in to create this community around the outdoors, then psychology has to be involved because we have to know how can we get people in and what can we do to be a leader in safety education in DEI and sustainability. So I think it's just sort of in the corner of everyone's minds.

And that's fine, there's nothing wrong with that. But if we're talking about brand and consumer being about human services, nobody really needs to see that. That doesn't really serve anybody. I'm guilty of doing that on my own social media, and we certainly still do that on that mood, social media, if we have a really beautiful photo that we want to share.
