Nicole Handel (00:28:05): Yeah, so it's interesting because everybody, your point about not everybody being consciously aware of needing safety unless they're in these high risk situations, in Maslow's hierarchy of needs, safety refers to obviously so much more than that. We all need to feel safe, whatever that means. And to your point, I think totally it's ironic that on the hierarchy of needs safety is orange. Well, it's not ironic, it's intentional. In our industry and in other industries, safety is the color of orange, and we have a color safety orange that denotes your avalanche safety tool pocket in our packs, et cetera. But I think you're right. Safety is something that everybody wants to feel and needs to feel because safety at the end of the day means survival. Safety is life. And being a brand that makes lifesaving products specifically airbag, beacon, shovel, probe type products, safety, it's no coincidence that safety is one of our three pillars because it is so core to human survival and belonging and fulfillment. So yeah, that's a good call out.

Cole Heilborn (00:29:23): So when we first connected, you mentioned that you guys don't call your marketing department a marketing department. You mentioned that I believe you call it a brand and consumer department. What's the reason behind that and how does that connect to this conversation?

Nicole Handel (00:29:38): Yeah, so I think marketing takes into account ad campaigns, assets, content, copy. Those things are important, but for us, when we think about what we want our marketing department to do and how we can serve the brand, the consumer is really at the core of all of that. Everything we do, our three pillars are safety, sustainability, and DEI, the consumer's at the core of all of that, safety is to keep the consumer safe. DEI is to bring every consumer in and make everyone feel welcome. And sustainability is to make sure that there is a world left for all of us, the consumer to be a part of and to enjoy over time. So when we think about what brand and consumer means, brand is kind of like all of those aspects of a traditional marketing department, and consumer is the consumer. So our department, I think our department probably has our hands in more areas than a standard marketing department. Meaning the marketing department consists of avalanche safety, education, trainings, clinics, et cetera, consumer service, lots of different elements that really relate directly back to the consumer, not just to marketing with a capital M necessarily.

Cole Heilborn (00:31:01): Gotcha. So you see it going beyond the kind of conventional boundaries?

Nicole Handel (00:31:07): Yeah, absolutely. It's not just a flashy title meant to confuse people. We literally do a lot of work that directly relates to the consumer.

Cole Heilborn (00:31:17): What are some examples of how you guys might go beyond, above and beyond in that instance?

So both gym to Craig for climbing, and then a skiing mentorship program as well. And that's through the brand and consumer department. We've also had a bunch of different projects that I'll share about when they're further along, but basically one of our biggest goals in the brand and consumer department is finding ways to offer resources to the consumer. So we are really passionate about not just being a brand or a company or a business who creates products and sells them, but how can we do more and how can we be more? And the root of that, especially as a safety brand who specializes in technical outdoor apparel and gear, is safety. So we're working on a lot of resources right now that specifically speak to safety and education in the outdoors and bringing that to the consumer, which is not just a safety story, but also a DEI story because we know that so many people feel excluded and that there are barriers to entry. And if we can play our part in minimizing those barriers, we plan to,

Nicole Handel (00:33:08): Yeah, it's this kind of, I think, well, there are a few technical answers and then there are some more interesting psychological ones. The technical answer is Instagram has made everybody feel like they need to do everything and be everything. And when I say be everything, I mean it's not enough to just be, for example, I dunno, a small business owner, you have to be a photographer, a videographer, you have to follow trends, you have to be an algorithm expert. And so I think people share that kind of thing because there's this pressure to always be on and to always be engaging. And if you don't have anything particularly engaging to say or to show, you just show something or anything because there's this desperation to keep up. And then there's also the wow factor, big beautiful mountain shots. People love that we all double tap for that kind of thing. So I think that's an easy showstopper for people.

content: Nicole Handel (00:34:23): Yeah, so I mean the most basic way that we're trying to change that is just not feeding into that kind of empty content void. Nora who's on my brand and consumer team, runs our social media. And the conversations we have pretty often about social media are related to, like I said before, what can we share that's meaningful? So we share a lot of our partners content, like we work with the American Mountain Guide Association, we work with Airy, we work with pow. They often have important things to say, and we feel like if we don't have anything more important to say than them, we should be sharing what they're saying. We also feature our athletes and ambassadors and their insights. They all have such a diverse range of experiences and knowledge to share. So amplifying that is another way that we kind of get past the posts that are kind lacking in depth. (00:35:28): And of course, we share when we have a promotion on our website or we share when we have something going on as more of a notification. But we have really tried to shift to mostly offering resources on our social media and also sharing a more diverse set of faces. We are really, really proud of. Recently we've received some dms and some comments from people saying, Hey, I wasn't familiar with your brand. I found it through whatever X, Y, or Z, and I'm so happy to see so many women or so many whatever. Our feed is definitely coming further along in being a place of diversity and we're working on it. We are not experts, but we're consulting with experts and we're doing what we feel is our job to do in the industry, which is to not just show the same things that everyone is showing over and over and create this echo chamber, but to offer something more.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:36:30): I got to imagine one of the reasons why the Epic Mountain photo gets shared so many times is because I got to imagine at some point you just run out of things to say, and so because you feel like you need to say something just to stay top of mind or feeding the algorithm or whatever, you throw something out there. Are you trying to only say things when you need to say them? Or I guess, what's your thoughts on the algorithm portion of it all?

Nicole Handel (00:36:59): Yeah, we had a really, I think it was a two hour meeting several months back about social media. And we first were looking at it from this stereotypical approach that I think most brands look at their social media strategy through where we were like, what are we going to post on Monday? What are we going to post on Tuesday? What are we going to post on Wednesday? Because everybody who uses social media at any professional level knows that you do have to feed the algorithm. But like I said, when we took a step back and started asking ourselves, why are we sharing this mountain photo? We started to develop a strategy that was focused more around making sure that everything we shared offered some value and things slip through the cracks. Especially like I said earlier, if there's a photo from one of our athletes or if even a social media user, like a mam, consumer shares a photo with us and it's just super epic and we really want to share it. (00:38:02): We still do that from time to time. But I would say what has shifted is our mindset and our approach to social media and feeling less like we need to share at any cost and feeling more like we have all of these great things to share. How does that fit in? When will we share it, et cetera. Because really, I mean, we're a pretty talkative crew and we have a lot of opinions and thoughts, and we have tons of athletes on our team and we work with so many incredible partners. So really I think there's always something to share, and it doesn't have to be from us. It can be sharing something that a partner has shared that we think is important. So like I said, we're really moving away from the approach of feeling like we need to share just to share, and we're finding better ways to share.

It's guesswork and because the algorithm is scientific, but human behavior, there's more gray area. So my best guess at why we are seeing more engagement is because what we are sharing is more engaging. So the mountain shot does get a lot of likes, but the not tutorials or the right now today is giving Tuesday, and we're sharing a Giving Tuesday promotion where 15% of our e-comm sales support the AGA's Bipoc scholarship fund, that kind of thing. That's real. That's a real thing, and that is naturally more engaging. So our numbers have not suffered from this new approach probably because what we're doing is all more relatable to humanity than this sort of shallow pretty object.

Cole Heilborn (00:40:01): Sure. Yeah, no, well said. Continuing with this idea of human behavior and needs, what are some other applications beyond social media that you guys are reexamining or reinventing the ways that you have done things?

content:
Nicole Handel (00:40:18): Yeah, I mean, we talk about sustainability and I would say here we have a ton of really, really strong initiatives that we're working on currently, and human behavior is a part of sustainability because the conversation that I think a lot of brands who feel like they have a responsibility to the outdoors are having is like, how do we get people to care and what can we do as a brand and what is our responsibility as a brand? We can adjust our practices, we can donate to organizations who are doing good for the environment. For example, we're partnered with POW at the global level. That's one small thing that we can do, but when we think about the big picture, which as I said is how do we get the consumer, how do we get humans to care about sustainability? That's a more challenging conversation because motivation is nuanced. So those are conversations we're having, but I don't think there are any clear answers, just some hypotheses.

Cole Heilborn (00:41:27): What do you mean motivation is nuanced? What does that mean?

Nicole Handel (00:41:31): I think I touched on this earlier. If we're motivated to do something, understanding why isn't always clear. A thought that I've had for years is I'm motivated to wake up early and run. Is that because it makes me feel good? Yes. Is that because I like identifying as somebody who is motivated to wake up early and run? Yes. Is it because I have dogs who need exercise? Yes. Those things are all my motivation. Those are my motives for doing that. But I think when we try to find a singular motivation, like a true core motivation, I think that's more challenging. There's a lot of gray area there.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:42:20): So you did mention this earlier, but I want to come back to it. This idea that maybe one of the reasons why you run is because you like the idea of being someone who gets up early and runs. I've always heard that the why is the most important piece of how you do something or why you do something, but if the why is inauthentic, it seems kind of shallow, is that not, I don't know if problem is the right word, but that just doesn't seem as legit as I just like to get up and run because it feels good.

Nicole Handel (00:42:56): I think about this a lot, and I'm not shy about being very honest about the thoughts that come to mind. I think if we're all honest with ourselves, there's plenty of things that it would be easy for me to say I exclusively run because it makes me feel good. And frankly, that would be a lie. And I think anybody who runs skis, bikes, who does anything, I think anybody would be lying if they said that they could pinpoint this one clear singular motive. And I don't think that it's problematic because what's wrong with that is that hurting anybody. And like I said, motivation is nuanced. It does make me feel good. It is good for my dogs. It is a way for me to bond with others and form deep human relationships because usually you run with someone and that's one-on-one time that you get to spend with another human. It's pretty rare nowadays to have that concentrated alone time with someone. So there's lots of reasons, but I don't think it's harmful. I think it's just realistic to identify that among the reasons why we do something. Some of them are maybe selfish, some of them are maybe performative, but if we're doing something good in this example running, it's good for my body, it's good for my mental health, then the motivations can be nuanced and across the board of in quality.

Cole Heilborn (00:44:31): Because the outcome is ultimately a positive thing for you or whomever you're with, is that right?

Nicole Handel (00:44:38): Right. Yeah. And I'm not saying that outcome is the only thing that matters in any situation ever. Motivation is important in a lot of conversations, but this one feels pretty harmless. Same thing like I mentioned earlier, with donating to a charitable cause. Whether or not we do that because we genuinely care about others or if, because us caring about others is just an expression of ego. Does it matter if we're doing good? Does it matter? Some people would say yes, and in some contexts I would agree yes, but I think this is really more subconscious. I don't know that most people would identify one way or the other. If they're doing something good, they are a good person, and it doesn't matter if super subconsciously, that's an ego thing. Ego is a part of good acts and good things, and so I don't think that that's necessarily harmful.

Cole Heilborn (00:45:40): Sure. Yeah. Well, to expand on, I think what you just mentioned, this idea of if you're donating to a nonprofit and if you're doing it because you like to have, for instance, the 1% for the planet logo on your website, are you doing it because you really like the logo or are you doing it because you genuinely believe in the act of giving and supporting? Maybe it isn't one or the other. It's probably

Nicole Handel (00:46:04): Right. It's usually both. To be clear, this is not me calling out people who do things like that and saying they're doing it for selfish reasons. My point is more that human behavior is complex and so many people do good things and also have other subconscious motivations, and that's okay. And I think that's just a reality that we could all recognize.

Cole Heilborn (00:46:30): Is that why you enjoy it? Or what about it? You could just spin circles around yourself.

Nicole Handel (00:46:36): And I do. I certainly do. I have on this call in our conversation. No, that is why I love it. I don't think you can escape human behavior or the concepts of motivation and wants and needs. None of us can escape that, and that's daunting for some people, or it's exciting and encouraging for some, and I get really excited by that. I think that's kind of what keeps me really interested in marketing, because systems and processes and technology, those things all change and specific motivations change, but the concept of human behavior, that's always there. That's always going to be there until we're replaced by robots who are incapable of human emotion, which probably will never happen because if humans are creating robots, they'll have to have some human-like aspects, but it's always going to be there. So that's what I love about it.

Nicole Handel (00:47:47): Oh, interesting question. I mean, I think I stand by the fact that psychology is in everything. I was going to say maybe in one of those stereotypical flashy email subject lines like attention open this, but that's psychology. We're appealing to a human's sense of urgency, or I think a lot of times it's not intentionally ingrained. I don't think psychology is always intentional in marketing, but I do think it's always there.

Cole Heilborn (00:48:27): Could we use the psychology? I feel like what this conversation is helping me realize is knowing these tools, they're really tools. You can encourage someone to do something by speaking a language that they understand or speaks to 'em. I feel like we could all come up with examples where we feel like we've been prodded in the wrong direction. And that kind of gets back to your early comment about this feels kind of slimy and gross, but there's also ways to use these tools in a positive way. Nicole Handel (00:49:13): Yeah. Well, again, not to oversimplify, but not even a tactic, but a framework or a perspective would be what do people want to see? And in a non slimy way, I don't mean what do people want to see? Diet culture mean? What do people want? Do people want to feel knowledgeable? Do people want to feel safe? Do people want a cause to support? And we can help direct that. What is it that people are looking for? And that's the most basic question in marketing, is what do consumers want? But if you can shape that in a way that's beneficial mutually to the brand and the consumer, sure, we want consumers to love our brand and our products, but we also want consumers to love what we do and how we treat them and what we stand for. So I think I don't have a big flashy secret to what you're asking, but the very simple answer is just asking yourself what consumers want. That's the tactic, that's the tip or trick. And it's really quite simple in theory. It's of course more complex when you get down to it because you can identify what consumers want and not know how to provide it or not know how to give it or be it or do it, but it's not too hard to figure out what people want.

content: Nicole Handel (00:59:20): Yeah, so my favorite example when I talk about this because it comes up frequently, is that my partner is a fly fishing guide. And I grew up hunting, but for food, very, very utilitarian, upstate New York, like family tradition kind of thing. It was not, nothing about, it was for sport, and we never looked at it as a sport. My partner is a catch and release fly fishing guide. And when we met, the concept frankly felt gross to me because I kept thinking about why are we doing this? Why does a human have the right to put a fish through stress for our own enjoyment and our own sport? And my partner, Dominic, isn't like that kind of person. We stereotype what sport fishing or sport hunting people are like, but I learned that not everybody has the same motivations and there's actually a lot of good that can be done. (01:00:17): So in the conversations we've had about why catch and release fishing is or could be ethical, taking into account using ethical practices like how to handle the fish safely, et cetera. His position was that he is a conservationist. He volunteers for some organizations that put a lot of work into river conservation. And he grew up fly fishing. I didn't grow up fly fishing. I had no connection to rivers or bodies of water, really. I hadn't spent much time on them. So I didn't know anything about river conservation or the species that exist in those environments. I didn't know a single thing. And if you ask me, do you care about water conservation? Yes, but have I ever done anything for water conservation? Did I know a single thing about it? No. So what he explained to me was you, in order to get somebody to care about something, they have to have an emotional attachment, a specific experience. (01:01:16): So the reason why he cares about river conservation is because he grew up on a river. He grew up figuring out which species of fish are eating, which species of bugs, and at what time of year and at what time of day, and what is the water temperature, where they're most comfortable and can thrive. All of these factors that people don't realize go into fly fishing.

(01:05:32): We can get someone outside, but how do we make sure that they continue to pursue an interest or how do we support them continuing to pursue that interest to create that emotional attachment? And it's, again, it's not a scheme like, oh, how can we manipulate people into caring about the environment? But it's more like we know what we feel on our brand and consumer team. You can think of scamming people or just being really pushy and disingenuine. I think we're really moving away from that in the outdoor industry as well as In marketing as a whole. That kind of icky marketing and copy and advertising, it really turns people away. our consumers are too smart these days to fall for it. And they want to feel like your company aligns with them. People are really values-based in these days, in this day. So they want to align with companies and purchase products and work with service providers who also have values that align with their own. And so values-based marketing really gives companies a position to build something that truly aligns with their customer base so that their marketing doesn't have to be icky or trick people into buying. People want to buy from them because they resonate with these companies on a deeper level.

I found myself entering copywriting and marketing, saying my my core value is freedom. I want to give my clients more freedom in their lives by freeing up their time through the services I can offer and helping them. And I want to give myself more freedom. one, the freedom to work remotely from wherever I might find myself, the freedom, my the freedom of freeing up my own time because I do have so many hobbies and things that I love. Chloe-Ann Swink (13:38): Yeah, absolutely. So as a copywriter, I do come from this at this from kind of the standpoint of messaging and tone. And a company's values are super important in developing your brand messaging, your tone, your entire brand positioning, really, what is what's the hill you're gonna stand on here? And if you don't know what that is, you can come off as very scattered. And one thing that Consumers want is they want consistency. They don't want to be surprised by something, thrown off by something. they're gonna connect with you because they connect with your messaging and they connect with your values. They like the way you're marketing yourself. And if that way that you're marketing yourself is way out of left field one day and in a completely different spot another day, you're gonna lose the interest of your consumers because. It's hard for them to build trust in you when they really can't identify who you are or what you stand for.

Cole Heilborn (14:43): Hm. Is there a way to quantify that cost? Is that a thing?

You can put your your foundational values into place for free, essentially. You don't have to make a monetary investment in that, but it is gonna take time and consideration. Because we're gonna get into how to actually build this foundation, but paint us a picture of what we're working towards here. Like why are we doing this?

Chloe-Ann Swink (17:14): Yeah, so I've actually worked pretty closely with a company called Wild Cabin Studio. They are also kind of a branding studio. And the owner of this company, when I first spoke with her, was very clear on kind of what she valued and how she wanted to come across. She wanted education was a huge value to her. So she didn't want to have her clients walk away from her and not understand why she did what she did and how they can recreate it. Basically, if she were to create a website for a company, she doesn't want them to walk away and have no idea how to update their website a month later. so education was really important. Nurturing her client base was very important, and she is very empathetic and understanding of her clients and the issues they're facing. And the space as a whole. So we kind of, I worked with her to create first off a brand voice and messaging guide where we dove into these values that she cared so deeply about and wrote basically an outline of how Wild Cabin Studio acts on these values, how they convey these values through their messaging on different platforms, and how they share these values with their consumers. So What was really great is over the next six months or so to see her values start to come across in her social media. And her actual client base seemed to be growing just because, for one, her marketing and content ideation and creation process ended up going so much more smoothly. She could pull. phrases and snippets of copy directly from this brand messaging guide that we had created based on her values and basically copy paste them directly into her marketing materials. So that saved her a ton of time. It saved her money on continuing to have to hire me or someone else as a copywriter or a marketer because she had this whole foundational document that she could basically just branch off and create social media posts from. create web copy and content from and emails from and even use little bits and pieces of it when speaking with her customers and clients.

Cole Heilborn (19:46): Wow. So so establishing your values is kind of the first step. And then there's more value than just establishing your values that comes from this process because everything ideally emanates from from these these this foundation, right?

Chloe-Ann Swink (20:00): Absolutely. The idea of values-based marketing is kind of that your values are what is driving the actions of your brand. So once you have your values kind of set in stone, you can refer back to them and say, okay, so I mean, if profitabil if profitability is a value of yours, you can look back at that and say, how do we act on profitability? If Philanthropy is a value of yours and you don't really know what direction to go in. Say Black Friday is coming up, or like we just passed Black Friday, but think of a big moment like that where you have, say, a new product or maybe a product that didn't perform very well, and you wanna amplify this product and create a campaign around it. It's kind of watered down to just say, okay, it's Black Friday. I'm going to create a Black Friday campaign around this product. It's 60% off. What if philanthropy, like I said, is your value and you can find an organization that aligns with you and your customers, and then you can say, this product is 10% off, but for every purchase of this product, we're giving 5% back to this foundation. It just kind of gives a really clear guideline of the next steps you're gonna take. You're always guided by those values.

Cole Heilborn (21:25): Sure. How do you how do you go about doing this when a client comes to you and they're passionate, they have values, but they're not necessarily sure what those values are for their business, they're not identified on paper. How do you walk people through this? How can people develop this for themselves?

Chloe-Ann Swink (21:41): Yeah, so I generally will work on strategy sessions with clients when we're doing something like this. They'll last about an hour to maybe a few hours long throughout a few sessions. And we really just distill down the core of for an owner operate a business, often who that person is and what they value. Because when you're an owner operator, you have to resonate with the values that your business is. Founded on, or else you're never gonna be able to have the passion and the drive to continue pursuing these values. So I kind of like to get to know the person, what matters to them, what causes have they contributed to in their life? I like to look at what companies inspire them and what values are those companies based on. Do they align with that? and we'll kind of do an executive session where we just write all of this down, whether it be on paper or in a Google document. And then we kind of connect the common threads. We'll even go as far as to say, what companies in your industry really kind of turn you off? Like, so is it their marketing? Is it what is it about them that you do not want to emulate in your business? And then we distill that down. Okay. These are the values we definitely want to stray away from. And then these are the common factors that we're seeing come up that affect the person's personal life and also that the potential customers of this person might align with. Because if your values align with you in your business, but do not relate or convey at all to your ideal client base. they're probably not going to serve you very well. So it is really important to make sure we can find personal values to implement into somebody's business that also align with their customer base.

Cole Heilborn (23:47): Yeah, that's an interesting point. For owner operators, oftentimes there is no distinction between the values of the business and the values of the individual. How do you guide people when they're trying to decide? Should there be a separation between my values and the business's values? How do you navigate that?

I'll I'll delve in and I will personally reach out to people who would be their ideal customers and I'll do little mini interviews with them. that way I can come back to my clients and let them know, okay, so you value this thing. but I don't see that as a common thread in the market research I'm doing. So, where can we kind of look to make these things align a little bit more? So that market research, it can be a lot of things, but I've even gone as far as to join Facebook groups that my clients, ideal customers, are in and kind of dig around there, do a little bit of sleuthing and then reach out to people directly who seem like good candidates. and ask if I can just send them a quick questionnaire via email or hop on a call with them. So this really comes down to knowing your audience. And knowing your audience is sometimes just digging in and doing the dirty work of finding your audience and getting to personally know them.

Cole Heilborn (25:17): If you only had three questions that you could ask an owner operator to identify their value set, what three questions would you use?

Chloe-Ann Swink (25:26): I would probably say, what is the ideal dream goal for your business? what would look like absolute success to you in this business? And then I would ask, what personally would you say are your three core values that you hold in the highest regard in your personal life? And what do you want this business to make people feel? when they see your marketing or when they click to your website, what kind of feeling do you want to invoke with your potential customers?

Cole Heilborn (26:04): Yeah, interesting. And I mean that sounds really simple. Like if you can just answer those three questions then you've already identified your values. But I'm assuming it's a lot more challenging than that.

Chloe-Ann Swink (27:24): Yeah, I think this is the part where it does get a little bit more difficult. there is more strategy involved, and this is where you're really delving into your brand positioning. for an owner operator who doesn't have a ton of hands on deck, my first recommendation would probably be to start with your major sources of traffic. So start with your website or your social media presence, if that's where. A lot of your potential customers are hanging out and begin redefining your brand there. So if you're starting on your website, I would say find a way to tell your story and connect those values with your audience, whether it be a brand story page on your website or an about me page if you're a service provider. This is where you're going to really position yourself to stand behind those values. So a really simple first step would Be go rebrand your website, rewrite the copy so that it's based on your values and speaking to your ideal client who aligns with those values. Redo your brand photography if you need to, if it's totally off-brand, you can fully refresh everything. You can redo your design if you feel the need to do that. But basically, I would say start where you're getting the most traffic and just Refresh that space. Even if it's social media, I would say maybe come up with 30 posts for the next month or month and a half and make sure all those posts align with your values, speak to your values, speak to how you're acting on those values, and really start to connect your new brand identity with your audience.

Cole Heilborn (29:14): Yeah, interesting. What's the difference this exercise? What is the difference between this exercise for a big brand or a small business?

Just give yourself a week to go through everything and just pick out, pick away at it with a fine-tooth comb. What are you proud of? what kind of style or tone of communication did you take that you really like and would like to keep around and make maybe a part of your business moving forward? And what maybe did you not handle so well, or what content did you put out that you look back and you're like, that's not how I want to portray my business? So just run a really in-depth audit of everything from the past year and then set to one side what you love. Set to one side what is absolutely not coming into 2022 with you. And then maybe if you have a gray space in the middle, you can that can also help you define kind of, okay, so maybe that gray space is where you were putting too much of yourself into your business and your customers weren't relating with that. Or just see what you can identify based on each of those categories and then go from there and identifying how you want to move on in 2022.

(04:19): We had to just evolve and add services. So now we're a fully certified Google partner, we're a fully certified Facebook partner.

So it was a two part campaign where first we were getting a broad message about how important recycling is and creating a full supply chain, not just putting your plastic and cans out at the curb, but there has to be demand at the other side of that chain. And that's something that Patagonia has done really well is more and more of their fleece, their face fabrics, their nylons, their polyesters is coming from recycled base material. (11:20): So we teed up the message, and I think it was about a 14 or 15 minute long film, which is hard to capture people's attention online. They want to watch something that's 15 seconds long. And then I think our execution on driving traffic to it was also well done. content: Liz Esche (06:40): Why? That is a great question and I actually gave a presentation earlier this year with some other folks in the outdoor industry about when is the right time to rebrand? And it all comes back to the why are you doing this for the right reasons? And we had really strong reasons, which was we felt like our branding wasn't communicating to our key audience. So we cater to the outdoor industry, we work with outdoor athletes, with climbers, with runners, with bikers, and our branding was a little bit more reminiscent of a just in the gym kind of nutrition brand. So we were talking to a different people than our branding seemed to be talking to, which was a bit confusing. We also wanted to be more playful and we evaluated our values and realized that a lot of nutrition companies seem to be talking about being the biggest in the Buffett or being the best person at X, Y, and Z. (07:46): And that's not the conversation we wanted to have. We want to talk about individual efforts, we want to talk about what we changed our motto to was push your possible, really those individual goals versus just being the most extreme and the absolute best. Everyone has a journey that they can go through and that was key as well. And then the final reason was we were going through a period of really evaluating our sustainability. It's always been important to us. We've always tried to source really well and have the most recyclable versions and we just could not get past these plastic tubs, which are a staple in the supplement industry. And then Eli and our CPO, Shannon O'Grady, she's brilliant, found this amazing solution and figured out a plan on how we were going to switch to steel tins. So there was also this opportunity, if we're totally switching to these steel tins, we're going to rebrand, we're going to come out with a new look, and on the other side it's going to feel like exactly who we are and who we have been and just be a better visual presentation of that and in a much more recyclable, better for the planet package. (09:08): So that was what I walked into day one.

Ideally you get it done with and then you're good for however many years, but when it's happening you find yourself in this really unique position where there's all these new things being developed, new looks, new deliverables, new assets, but you still have to keep the day-to-day running. You still have to keep the current operations running. So we're going to get a little bit into some of the weeds of how Liz, you kind of kept everything going while developing this entirely new brand. Could you kind of set the stage for us though, and describe though what were some of the deliverables that you guys were looking to refresh with this rebrand so folks have an idea?

Liz Esche (10:48): Yeah, so everything changed, logo changed was updated, colors changed, motto changed. We reevaluated our values. Our website is completely migrating to a new platform because why not do that at the same time? We had to definitely look at all of our assets, all of our content and start building again from scratch. That doesn't mean you throw out all of our great content from the past. It just means that, alright, we're going to need these new assets, new labels on everything. It seems never ending, but it was a full restart.

content:
Cole Heilborn (11:31): Gotcha. So how'd you begin to approach this because you can't just shut things off and say, I'm only going to focus on the rebrand. You have to keep things moving forwards while simultaneously developing everything new. So what was your mentality going into it?

Liz Esche (11:46): Well, it started with a deep breath. So I walked in Gnarly's out of Salt Lake City. So I flew in to meet the team and we kind of sat down and looked at everything that needed to change and it became apparent very quickly that this was not, we're not going to wake up one morning and have it all be new and fresh. That's just not, maybe you can do that as a larger company. Maybe you can do that as a smaller company. And it's just the mid-size companies that really struggle. I'm not sure, but we could not align our inventory with that process. We could not align the creation of our creative assets with that process and we definitely couldn't align our web migration. So then it became a phased approach and we looked at, okay, well what can we do right now and how do we make this clear for our customers and explain what we're doing and why? (12:44): And that was really important to us. We didn't want to try and hide what we were doing and keep it under the radar because at some point you're going to have different logos on different product and you're going to have a freshened up website with old labeled product being displayed and we couldn't get around that. So it really began with what's the timing and how do we release information to our customers? So we started very basic. We started with the logo and the colors. We had the rest of the branding figured out, but that's what we started with. And we sent out communications to our athletes who actually helped us spread the message and to our customers saying, this is step one of many and here's why we're doing it. We're doing it because we found better packaging because we want to connect better with you and this is truly embodying our spirit, this gnarly spirit. So being really transparent I think helped and just sending that constant communication, not an overwhelming amount, but acknowledging that things are happening was really key.

content:
Cole Heilborn (13:57): Gotcha. You mentioned something interesting. So you guys rolled everything out in different phases because you couldn't do it all in one go. Would you have preferred to have done it in one swoop one day someone wakes up and everything is new or was this trickle approach, how did that work out? I

Liz Esche (14:17): Don't know. I think that's the dream, isn't it? To wake up one day and have everything be new. And in previous companies that I've worked for that are really dependent on seasonality, you can almost do that because you can set it for your spring launch and you can do that, but we don't work that way. We're not that big. We order inventory X amount of months out and we are keeping up with a kind of constant schedule. We have some high, but it's really pretty constant. So there was no clear stopping point based on our inventory where we were like, you know what? We're fine if we just throw out that amount of inventory that was never going to be okay with us or our values. So maybe it's the dream to launch all at once, but it's also opened the door to have this continued conversation with our customers and our long-term customers. I mean, we have people that have been using our product for six, eight years to explain why we're doing this and to keep them in the loop and give them previews and little tidbits of what's coming next. So overall, I'm really happy that we did it this way because it allowed us to have a longer, more in depth conversation with our audience and gave us a lot of little moments to highlight along the way. Whereas if we had done it in one fell swoop, how long can you really keep that exciting?

Cole Heilborn (15:52): How did you communicate with your customers through all of this? That sounds like an interesting component and maybe people don't think about when they think about a rebrand is like how do you communicate with your audience through all of it?

Liz Esche (16:04): So a lot of emails, I mean emails going to be the go-to. We definitely post it on our social channels and we asked very routinely for feedback and we're continuing to ask for feedback. We want our customers to be engaged, especially with our far more recyclable tin cans, we want our customers to give that feedback and show their excitement. So we've actually had a really high number of reviews coming in asking, can we put all of our product in these cans and you still have some stuff in bags, why don't we just move it all over? And they, they're really excited. And so it is just generally been emails and asking for that feedback and checking in. We definitely updated a lot of our flows at the post-purchase level to remind people, especially when we had, there were points where we had double products. So you might order a vegan protein and you may get it in the old label or you may get it in the new steel can. So a lot of post-purchase flows saying, Hey, this might be happening and here's why, and we're really excited about this and it's a bit awkward. We know it, but we're happy that you're here with us on this journey to something better. And everyone was on board. I wish I could say you just got to push through the detractors, but we didn't really have to detractors everyone, and that's kind of our target audience. So it made sense. Our audience are outdoors folks, so they're going to care about reducing the amount of plastic out there.

Cole Heilborn (17:48): Yeah, yeah, that's great to hear that it went fairly smoothly from that perspective. I just had an idea how you look back at some of the legacy outdoor brands now and you look at some of their old products with the old logo on it and they've become collectors items and you can spend way too much money on these old things if, because now I'm like, well, every rebrand that a company does in 50 years, that old product could be some heritage item. I wonder if there's a way to still create that collectible, instigate that collectible spirit with where you guys are at right now.

Liz Esche (18:25): Oh yeah. There's some products we will never give up. We had a very popular slogan, gnarly till death was one of our popular swag items. We have it on some hats and some t-shirts and I don't think those are going to be phased out. They're just way too popular. But maybe we will face them out and bring them back for special occasions. That's not a bad idea.

Cole Heilborn (18:51): Yeah. Well, any royalties you collect, you can send them my way. So tell me a little bit more about the switch from plastic to tin. That sounds like a really, sounds like an easy thing. Sounds like though it was not an easy thing. What was that process like?

Liz Esche (19:09): I have to give credit to our CPO Shannon because every week she'd give us updates and just kind of push through the haze. It was a really difficult time to switch all of our packaging when supply chains were in chaos and still are in chaos. I think they're estimating chaos until 2023, who knows? So we knew it was going to be a process, but it had been a really long time coming. We wanted to switch to the steel cans and we knew we were almost going to have to do it product by product. We bought as much as we possibly could and then waited for current inventory to run out. And sometimes that timed well, we just got the new product in other times product ran out and we had a gap of three weeks and we had to go to our customers and say, I'm really sorry we were out. (20:13): That took a lot of foresight on Shannon's end and on our team's end to say, well, okay, we need to set aside X amount of product for our subscribers and for our current customers who we know are going to want this, and it's just going to be those new customers that have to wait, but it'll be worth it. So that was quite the process. We are down to our last, we're waiting on one more flavor in BCAAs to switch over, and then we are completely over to the new steel tins in all of our Tubbed products. So it's been a long journey. It started six months ago and it started seeing those changes and we're finally here.

Cole Heilborn (20:59): Wow, that's awesome. Well, congratulations. That's got to feel really good.

Cole Heilborn (21:23): Well, and yeah, and it sounds like even though some parts were messy, people were on board with the reason why, and that committee comes back to why knowing the why is so important because it gives you your audience reasons to stick along through some of the bumps in the road as the company goes through the transition, right?

Liz Esche (21:43): Yeah, exactly. I mean, we had to raise our prices to one to $2 across the line per product in order to support this new packaging. And sometimes as a marketer you have to be the bearer of bad news when things aren't going great, but they're going great, but raising prices is never a fun conversation. And we addressed that head on and just sent out a bunch of notifications that this was happening and really no one said they either didn't say anything or they said, don't care. It's one to $2 to get plastic out. So that was nice.

Cole Heilborn (22:27): Yeah, interesting. What was the moment, was there a moment, like a crux moment in the last year or so that was the hardest piece for you guys to overcome? What was that?

content:
Liz Esche (22:39): The crux moment? We had some moments of really low inventory just waiting on new cans, and I guess that's kind of a scary prospect for a marketer is how do I continue marketing when I running out of product when we're still waiting because of everything that's going on? Because steel is suddenly three times more expensive and people are snapping it up as quickly as they can. How do I market when we're out of our top sellers? So that was something we leaned on consistently through all of this change is, well, what are we good at as a brand? And that's our education. So we just leaned more deeply into our education, into our clinics, into our content. I have an incredible content manager on my team, Tim biac, who's just done some absolutely stellar work for us. And we leaned in and we continued to provide what we think is almost our primary goal as a brand before a product, which is nutritional education and knowledge from the experts that work for us as athletes or on the team itself.

Cole Heilborn (23:59): Interesting. You focus more on the content marketing side of things because you didn't have product to sell. Is that what you guys did?

Liz Esche (24:08): Yeah, I would say we leaned into, I mean, we got to sell product at the end of the day, but in order to keep that top of funnel really flush, we want to keep bringing people in. We don't want to stop everything just because we're going through some painful moments. We definitely leaned into the content. We have some really incredible partners in the industry. We're a sponsor of USA climbing. We work with vacation races, we work with Circ Series A vipa, so we continue to support those partners, those efforts, develop those relationships. We leaned heavily on our athlete team. We have an athlete team of over a hundred athletes, and they're just great people and they are the best when talking about our product because they're the ones using it every single day to go out and do incredible things.

Cole Heilborn (25:00): Okay. You mentioned that because product was limited, it sounds like you pivoted a little bit more towards the educational style of content. Was that to lessen sales but still keep cycle the funnel churning? Or what was the motivation behind that?

Liz Esche (25:18): Yeah, so when you have minimal product to sell, you lean on people like your content manager, Tim Baac, great guy, very skilled. In order to keep that top of funnel just flush, we wanted to keep providing value. Even if we weren't able to give them our top selling product at that exact moment, we still wanted to communicate with them. And we've always believed ourselves to be an education first company. It's in the nutritional arena. A lot of folks just don't even know what they're supposed to be using or how they're supposed to be using it. So those are conversations that we're very used to having and we continued to create those conversations and we did that on our social accounts. We had webinars, we host clinics, we support our partners very in depth. We're a sponsor of USA climbing, we work with vacation races and we make sure that all of the people they're touching have access to our information and our knowledge. (26:24): And we also leaned on our athlete team. We have about a hundred athletes who are just filled with their own additional knowledge and their own expertise using our product daily because they use it pretty much every day to do incredible things. So we reached out to them, we got their buy-in, they were creating more content for us. We really used that time to keep our, we already had a great content machine going, but to make it even better to what can we do even more than we are right now? How can we make this better? How can we make this more accessible? A lot of times we were creating content and we felt like it was getting to our core audience, the people who already know to come to us with their questions. And so we were really focused on pushing that out, putting advertising money behind, pushing that content out versus as much focus just on quick product sales.

Cole Heilborn (27:24): Did you learn anything about the brand through the rebrand process that you didn't anticipate learning or discovering?

Liz Esche (27:33): I would say I really learned how much people appreciate companies doing the right thing. We expected. I was mentally prepared for so much backlash with all the change and just leaving people a little bit stranded and not having the exact flavor that they wanted and raising prices and we didn't have that experience. They were willing, and I think that shows kind of the outdoor industry, but also consumers today, they want to work with companies that are doing the right thing. They want to support smaller companies that are taking big leaps in making the effort. And that also came through in our athlete team. We asked them to support us when times were a little bit rough and chaotic, and they were 100% behind us spreading the message of the sustainability and backing us up and saying, this is worth it, this is worth it. And we'd get emails from them that were like, you know what? It's okay. Don't send me product this month, give it to your customer, but we're totally behind what we're doing and we want to support you in whatever way we can. So that I think really surprised me and that lends credit to, I think the early founders of gnarly taking those values seriously and building great relationships with our athletes and our partners.

Cole Heilborn (29:08): Right on what, in what way did you grow the most?

Liz Esche (29:12): Oh, so many ways. This has really been the best experience in understanding more way beyond the marketing aspect because it's not just about marketing, it's about the company as a whole and seeing how marketing fits into that process and how we can do more than just focus on conversion rates and cost of acquisition. How can we focus on the bigger picture, who we are as a company? That has been a huge growth phase for me. It is also taught me how to deal with change and how to respond quickly and stay nimble if we need to. In the beginning, I think I kind of had this idea that I was going to kick all of our marketing spend or a lot of it and save all the money for when all of our ducks were in a row and we could just really come out with a bang and be like, this is gnarly. And that did not happen. And I realized you have to create stepping stones and be able to continue to push your brand and continue to create that story and talk to your customers even when it feels like everything's on fire.

Cole Heilborn (30:30): Yeah, no, well said. For someone else or a team, anyone who's trying to do a rebrand or is thinking about doing a rebrand, what would you impart on them? As someone who just went through this?

Liz Esche (30:44): Be extra realistic about your timelines. I think everything takes longer than you think it will, even if you're a smaller company. And I would expect delays and have contingency plans for those delays, and just be transparent with your customers about what's happening and embrace the awkwardness if you have some weird mixed branding. Okay, tell your customers why, show it off. Be like, Hey, this is the last 10 of this product with this label. Kind of like what you said, it's an exclusive item. Now stay lighthearted and keep your head up. It's going to be a little bit goofy and it will be a little bit painful, but you'll get through it.

Cole Heilborn (31:38): What do you hope the new brand will communicate to the world?

Liz Esche (33:01): Let me see. Anything we didn't cover? I think I'd just go back to what the thing I would say, this is something we maybe didn't touch on is, and I've kind of spent the last, I don't know how much time talking about pain points and getting through and over these hurdles. And it may sound scary and it may sound like it's not worth it, but it absolutely is. If your reasons are correct, and I've been a part of many teams over the years that have been afraid to make big changes because of the challenges that it would incur. And the longer you wait, the harder it's going to be. I mean, I can't imagine doing this twice the size or doing this when all the current subscribers we have doubled and tripled, and now the earlier you do it is probably better if your reasons are really good and kicking it down the line and just saying like, oh yeah, we'll do that when we get to this point or when we get here, it may not be the right plan because you're just going to incur more of everything, more customer data, more things that need to be changed over. (34:24): So just take a deep breath, make a plan, cross your fingers and get through it.

Cole Heilborn (34:31): Well, no, that's really well said. Good things don't come easily. Sometimes you just got to buckle down and jump in feet first.

Liz Esche (34:39): That's absolutely true.

Cole Heilborn (34:40): So I know as we're recording this episode, pieces of the brand have been released. When can we expect everything to be updated? When should we all go and stock gnarly's presence on the web?

Liz Esche (36:16): I think it's even easier for outdoor industry brands because lean on your athletes, lean on your community, show their awesome adventures, show them. We have a slew of nutritionists that do a lot of work for us and help our customers, and we've got tiktoks of them with their favorite recipes with gnarly products. We've got tiktoks of them talking about why they use certain products when you use certain products. If people are interested, then they'll watch it. I mean, they got to kind of test your own brand. I don't know if I can give all encompassing advice, but I mean, if Book Nerds can get on TikTok and have a whole book talk, then the outdoor industry can get involved.

Cole Heilborn (37:03): Okay. Well, I know what I'm doing. As soon as we wrap up recording today, I'm going to go check out your guys' TikTok because I don't know, maybe I'm just old. I just don't understand it.

Liz Esche (37:14): We are old and it's okay. We're not that old though. Mike Artz (03:52): Okay. I tried to get better with my quick breakdown because I'm usually a rambler, but my business partner and I, Frank Phillips, we met working at Burton Snowboards over 20 years ago. Frank was the head of engineering and overseeing the prototype shop. I was more on the marketing kind of team side of things. Frank and I became great friends. I moved into his house. He had just bought, we had a big shop there. We were always building stuff, tinkering. I'd be out in the field with the team. I would take that feedback back to him and the development crew. So I don't know. The way I summed it up now is you take the two of us, we've had 20 years of just getting to sit on chairlifts and dream and hike and dream and snowboard and you take the mind of me being a bit more on brand and content and Frank more on design, fabrication, custom build and 20 years go by, start a couple businesses and that's where we are now. (04:52): That's my quickest way of trying to explain how what we do actually makes sense because the Public works is a pretty unique agency. I like to say. I think what sets us apart is we do a lot of the creative work that creative brand agencies would do, but we also do a lot of execution. We have our own fabrication shop, we have photo video team editors, our own studio. So we're a very executional bunch of creatives. I think that sums up the public works heavy outdoor industry, but working with a bunch of different kinds of companies we just love, it's more about the spirit of the company than what they put out the door or whatever. So quite a range of types of clients. Battery 6 21 is a creative workspace. We don't say cowork. We bought this building in Denver about 12 years ago and it was 30,000 square foot empty building. (05:50): It was super intimidating. I mean Frank and I were still working out of our houses, so it was a big kind of step, but our was to find a cool space that we could actually have our workshop and photo crew and studio and have all of that under one roof, but we wanted to be surrounded by other awesome people and companies. We didn't want to just be sitting in a building by ourself. So that's kind of how Battery started. The whole co-work kind of. We were a bit on the, I'd like to think on the front edge. We by no means invented it, but I will say we launched Battery at the same time WeWork launch. So we were at the front edge of the whole thing, battery. We have about 20 tenants now. We're in the busiest intersection in Denver. Stop in anytime and everyone's around, come by and grab a coffee or whatever. But battery, I felt like we dreamed huge and then it exceeded so much of what we ever hoped for with just the events we've been able to host nonprofits, just the random collision of, I mean Denver is such, Denver and Colorado are such great places to begin with and I think what we've got is just one little 30,000 square foot spot that captures a little bit of that and then just good things happen.

Mike Artz (07:15): Well, let's see, I think we're 16 maybe we're 17 years in now with Public Works. So at the beginning it looked like me and Frank just saying yes to everything. You need some photos? All right. Red Bull was one of our first clients, so we did a bunch of really cool custom infrastructure type stuff, like the kind of things you see for Red Bull on Hill branding at one of their ski events or DJ booth that would go to a club that they work with or custom bars, trophies. We did so much different stuff. I think we lucked out. Red Bull hit us up before we'd even launched public works. The first things we did, it was just me and Frank and the shop he built at his house, and I think what Red Bull saw in us was that we could be creative. We really listened to what they had to say about their brand and when they shared the look of the brand, red Bull is probably one of the best companies at controlling the look and feel and execution of their brand. (08:21): So to get to work with them early on, it challenged us, but it also gave us opportunity to make these beautiful pieces. And like I said, we hadn't even launched a company yet, so all of a sudden we just became, these guys call them, they'll build it. I mean we built an arch over a racetrack, you name it, and that was just me and Frank we're like, we got to go weld this. So we'd weld it, we'd build it. I mean that arch we built over the racetrack. Frank and I worked seven days straight and built this 60 foot steel arch powder, coated it, delivered it, installed it and shot photos of it and the race started two hours later and that was the beginning of the public works is it's just sort of that entrepreneurial spirit where even if you're smart enough to say no, you don't, it's all in. So that's kind of how it started. We just got to be known as if you have this sort of crazy idea, then call Mike and Frank. And so that was then. Now we have people that are so much better at almost every aspect of the business than we are. Frank has an amazing design build crew. I've got a media team that I don't even know how to use some of the cameras we have now, which is funny. We're pretty hands on.

We all go into work on a Monday and they were just like, yeah, it's over. You all need to pack your stuff and get, oh man, that's how fast it imploded there. I'm a bit shocked that somehow it all came together, but they really support each other. I've worked with some amazing photographers that are just not easy to work with. You want to be someone that your clients want to call back and that can't be just a good photo or a good video clip. It's got to be that you made their life easier. You actually got them what they asked for on budget, on time. It's cool that you're in the same industry because you get it. My creative would execute so much stronger than whatever these people did. And then it took me a while to get to the point where I was like, you know what? There's actually a reason that this client worked with this company. And sure, the creative is really important, but they probably care less about the, I might bite myself if I say this, but the client might care less about the creative and they care more about the relationship and the ability to work with said creative. And so what you don't see on the portfolio is the relationship that that company or that individual has with the client

content:
Cole Heilborn (19:40): For you. It sounds like the creative and the business have been balanced pretty naturally throughout your career. I don't know that that's true for everyone though. It feels like one or the other Jekyll Hyde situation. Why is that?

Mike Artz (19:54): I think there's something to be said for kind of right brain, left brain of sometimes the best artists. Sometimes you see amazing photographers, but if they have to shoot to a brief or to a brand, look, they might not always be the best person. I think that's a little bit of it. I think sometimes it's just listening in this world, and I'll fault myself for this too. People aren't always good at listening. You often want to go do what you want to do, but when you're in the commercial world, we are. Someone's paying you to do something that's different than me saying, I just want to go out and just shoot the most beautiful photos I can and try to hang 'em in a coffee shop and sell 'em. Right? So I don't know. I think it's interesting dynamic and for Frank and I, Ian was the third member of the team. (20:54): He pretty much hopped on when we launched public works, so he's been with us a long time too. All three of us are definitely creatives. We use a business operating model that it generally breaks people between visionaries and integrators, right? I'm going to get this right. But more or less, Frank, Ian and I all knew that we were kind of more worked on a visionary kind of mindset, but if you don't have the balance of that in the crew of people who actually can execute and stay organized and make sure that little pieces don't fall off, it's real tough. And we struggled with that for a while trying to find those right people really in our world, they tend to be the producers or the chief operating officer or whatever, but that's harder to find than visionary. It's easy to find the dreamers. I think it's a little harder to find the people who actually see it through and execute. I think that's part of that balance. Having an amazing CO slash producer right now, the amount of freedom that gives me to be able go chase a new client or go be on a shoot and execute. It's a total feeling of freedom.

content:
Cole Heilborn (22:12): So you guys have an operating officer or an executive producer who's managing that stuff for you?

Mike Artz (22:19): Yeah, a couple. And we also have the building management, so there's a lot going on, but we have some great people now that help execute and aren't afraid to tell us where we're not holding up to our side of things.

Cole Heilborn (22:36): Sure. Yeah, I mean that's a really interesting subject in itself. So I guess I have two questions here. My first question is, so for folks who aren't in a position to go out and hire someone or who don't want to hire someone, how can they personally try to do a better job of staying organized? Was there a point in your guys' career where you couldn't afford to bring someone on so you had to figure out how to get organized yourself?

content: Mike Artz (23:01): For sure. I think getting really good systems in place from early on matters so much, and if that's an area that means spending a little bit of money. We did all our own QuickBooks, like all our own accounting for a long time, and then we'd hand the books off to a fractional CFO to tune them in, do the filings, that kind of thing. But we waited way too long to hire a fractional bookkeeping, kind of fractional CFO kind of role. We waited too long on that and not only was it time that Frank and I were spending working in QuickBooks that we probably should have been doing other stuff, but we also weren't building systems as well as we should have and getting advice, having another set of eyes that's more financially driven, that kind of thing. When we finally hired that team, there was quite a bit of process to just clean up the way we had been doing things. (23:59): That was one area where, and I still look at how much we spend each month on those services and it's like a standout item, but I also think about how much they're doing for us and how else would we do it. So that's the biggest example that comes to mind for me. I think I can remember being that sole entrepreneur and just trying to land the next shoe and all you're thinking about is shooting the best photos and when you send an invoice and a check comes in, it's the most rewarding feeling in the world that someone paid you for your work. So it's hard to spend when you're at that point, but the certain areas like finance and if you're going to be a professional photographer, videographer or whatever, you've got to have your asset digital asset management super dial too. So whether that's asking around and finding a mentor or actually paying someone for some help, getting that kind of stuff like the foundation of what you do proper from the beginning I think is hard to see when you're at those early days of looking at every dollar. (25:01): But here we are 16 years down the road or something and could really feel the change. When we got more dialed in with those kind of systems, we got multiple photographers shooting, putting all our photos into one Lightroom database and now we can look through a million photos or something pretty quickly and drill in, find them, share 'em, use 'em and know that we're triple backed up and that kind of stuff that I think was at least hard for me to see far enough out at the beginning and probably not invest in help. And now we're in this awesome world where whatever service you need, whether you need an hour of help or a week or someone on retainer who lives in Bangladesh and feels like they're sitting next to you, everything's available now. Right. There's almost no excuse anymore to just finding some good help, man. I got to start trying to give you some shorter answers, but

content:
Cole Heilborn (26:05): No, this is great. So you mentioned that you felt like you guys waited too long before you started hiring help. When is the right time? When did you realize it was too late or not too late but that you should have done it earlier?

Mike Artz (26:18): I'm sure. I can't imagine there's any perfect answer. I would look at it as saying what's the value of your own time and what can it be best used for? We still do a lot of our own QuickBooks entry and stuff ourselves where we could just push it off because on a lot of those expenses and stuff that are shoot driven or we want to put the time into making sure that the accuracy is there, that clients get billed back, that we know where we spent that we're tracking it in QuickBooks, that the way it's going to report for us. So I mean that right there is an ongoing debate we always have of how much time is our team putting into it versus farming it out, trying to value your own time. I think one of the most helpful things for me is we've started talking a lot more about what we do is we have a certain amount of capacity as a company with our core team, we have a sense of how busy can we be, how much can we do? (27:19): For me, I have to look at it the same way. How much am I willing to work? How many hours do I have? So with that capacity of time that I have, what is my best use of time? And if I'm going to drop a FedEx off or I don't want to belittle anything, but if I'm doing that instead of calling a potential client lead, it shouldn't be a hard decision. There's always going to be gray area. I mean, I'll probably leave this Airstream and end up cleaning up a pile of dog poop behind the building or something. But you also, you care about where you are and you also don't want to walk by something like that. But while I'm cleaning it up, I'll be like, is this really what I should be doing with my time? (28:04): I think that's the way I keep trying to think about it. And then to finish that thought, someone, another good friend of mine, we've talked about this capacity thing a lot, but it also gives you a sense if we're going to do a retainer with a client, then we look at, okay, how much time is that going to take up of our crew for the year and then we can budget a bit better, whatever. If our goal for the whole year is X and this is going to take up 20% of our working time, then that better be one fifth of X.

content: Mike Artz (29:17): Once again, I don't think there's any easy answer and there's probably no perfect answer. Currently what seems to be working for us is we use Wrike as a project management software only with our team. That's been pretty good. So every project gets tracked, make sure we do things like invoice and get paid, which is always nice at the end, but it just works well too. We can put reminders in of when that project's going to go live with the client, so we remember to push it through our social and support them, whatever. So Wrike has been a really good project management software for a bunch of different people from our crew to all be working on. We just went through our Monday meeting and we go through Wrike and that's our update for Monday. How's each project tracking who needs to follow up, who's getting assigned to do what? It works great for that. We're using Slack as more of our at once communication within our team, but we also have a couple of our biggest clients also in Slack now, which has been really, really good. (30:28): It's just, I think everyone sees Slack and if we see something pop up from our team or from one of those clients and we just know that it's got to be taken care of, it's easy to organize, set reminders, whatever. So Slack's become a bit more of our communication tool when we can. And then, like I said, QuickBooks is our financial, the hard part is trying to set our systems between all of those, right? A project will kick off in Slack, then we have to be like, alright, who's setting it up in Wrike? Did you make sure to assign to me that I'm going to invoice at the end? Then it moves into QuickBooks and at some point if it's not paid, then we see the AR report and QuickBooks, right? It's not perfect. We still screw up. I can be honest on here. I mean there is one client we miss sending an invoice to, and by the time we figured that out, that agency that we had done the job for, it pretty much imploded. (31:25): And let's just say you don't want to make that mistake where you do the work and you don't get paid and it's your own fault. You learn from that and we'll probably do it again at some point.

content: Mike Artz (29:17): But I mean it's all of that which is how do we make sure we're communicating timely and accurately to clients and that we're tracking the project through. We have some other great tools too. Our head of post-production has made some amazing shared document spreadsheets that for those clients, it's kind of one-stop shopping. They click, they can see every project in process. The ones that have already finished are all, it's all indexed by date, everything. They have links to those projects so they can go and download again. We'll have one tab for video, another tab for the stills so they can look and find any folder of shots. (32:23): Yeah. But to me that's still kind of messed up that we have to, if you count email, text, phone, that's still probably eight different communication channels. The occasional person wanting to use WhatsApp and whatever else, Facebook Messenger and you're like, can we please stop? But there's that many different channels and when we switched to Wrike, we had been in Basecamp before that. We spent a bunch of time with our crew. We really wanted everyone to look at all the different options that were out there, Asana, wrike, Basecamp. We tried to have it be a team decision, but we also said when we decide it's all in, you don't get to question this anymore and if you come on as a sub or whatever, we explain to people early on, this is how we're working and we need you to work in here. And sometimes we'll get some resistance and you'll have the occasional person that's still texting and we're like, please move this conversation with the client into Slack or whatever because it's how things are going to get messed up if we're kind of all over the place. Long answer again, but it's a painful one and it keeps me up at night thinking about, I go into the Monday meeting today and I'm like, man, I haven't heard about this project in a little while or this project. And then the team today everyone's just firing and just giving updates and I was like, okay, everything is on point. So the better the software, the more I sleep the (33:53): And the team using it. Right? You have to embrace it. Yeah.

content: Mike Artz (34:21): I think the better the systems and the crew, the more we get to be creative. That stuff gets a little bit out of your way. It varies so much too. If we're going on a shoot and there's only two of us on the crew and it's photo and video, I mean we're doing everything right. We've got to get lunch, we got to do everything. Part of what we try to explain to clients is with, if you're willing, invest a little bit more in the shoot and our team can get a little bit broader. It does change a lot when Ian gets to be just director, then he gets to just think through a creative mindset and just focus on what is the best deliverable we can get out of this shoot if he's got to be there just because it's smaller job or the nature of the beast or whatever. (35:10): But if he's got to be there and be director and kind of producer and still guy, your mental focus keeps getting pulled in different directions and it's been a place I've had to really listen to the team because I lean more towards come from the snowboard background. We're going to go out into the backcountry or whatever you want the leanest, tightest crew, no one's doing craft services on a freaking backcountry snowboard shoe. You just hope everyone brought a cliff bar and you get through the day. But when shoots get a little bit bigger and budgets get a bit bigger, that is the beauty of getting to specialize, getting to focus, and it goes right to post of if you're going to invest a bit more, we can put more time into color, more into sound sweetening. It's all the little steps. And if your budget's 10 grand, that's fine. (36:06): We'll figure it out. You just can't get all of that. If the budget's 200 grand, then we can really think about where it gets spent, how it gets spent, and you get some advantages out of that. So I do think it's an interesting place, and I'm sure you've felt that where you're in the middle of a shoot and you're in this creative focus and the light's good and everything's coming together, and so you get a phone call or something else, and I know there's some theory about when you get distracted while you're in a task, how long it takes you to get back into it. I think I forget what the smart people say, like 12 or 15 minutes or something, but that's real when it's happening over and over
