Cole Heilborn (36:51): And by that time, golden hour is gone and you've missed your moment

Mike Artz (36:55): And no one has dinner.

Cole Heilborn (36:57): Right? It's interesting, those types of tasks. We were on a shoot a couple of months ago and we had, fortunately we had someone, an amazing line producer who helped manage all the talent for the day, helped manage craft our schedules, all of that stuff. And I wish it happened more because it was so amazing to be able to have someone who could just focus on those types of details. And it sounds like, oh, figuring out what to do for dinner. That sounds like a really relatively simple thing, but for whatever reason, when you're in production mode, you're making so many decisions all the time that coming up with something like that in a timely manner and scheduling it for 15 people at a local restaurant, that takes time and it takes effort and it takes planning. And sometimes those details do get missed if you are doing everything.

Mike Artz (37:58): The difference of having budget and time to do an on location scout at the right times a day before you just show up to shoot what you get out of it is an amazing difference. When you go in with you've already seen, you know what you're going in to do. That's an area I feel like we're constantly trying to push. And also talent. It's like, I get it, you have friends that can stand in, but there's a difference between a professional model or actor, actress, whatever, and someone's friend. And we will say to clients, okay, this is a $40,000 shoot. Do you really want to save a thousand bucks on talent? And then you have the friend who all of a sudden can't get the day off from work or shows up late or there's a lot. It's easy to watch Zoolander and just laugh and modeling can be funny, but when you work with people who are the master of their craft and they see what you're doing as the photographer, they're reacting to it, they're moving, they're doing different things. When you get to work with professionals, you get professional results.

content: Mike Artz (39:52): I should have started with a disclaimer thing. Just because I'm on this podcast does not mean that I am an expert in any of these things we talked about. We're all constantly learning, and I mean just getting to know you and for us to share time, we learn from each other. That's never ending. So I don't want anyone to listen to this and think I'm sitting here trying to speak some professor of pulling this off every day that we get to do what we do and someone pays us. I'm super thankful, but I also know we have a long ways to go and learning. So I mean, that's some of my advice is just surrounding yourself with the best possible people resources. I joined a global entrepreneurial organization that there's about 13,000 business owners in the world that are part of this group called eo, and that has been a game changer for me. I've been in about eight years, but the people I've met, what I've learned, it kind of feels like just one more step in the education process. (40:51): A lot of those people have helped me get through some really tough days where you just feel as an entrepreneur, you feel like the world is caving in on you and you need resources. I think everyone needs those kind of resources. So I think that's one thing is just finding those amazing people. They're everywhere and people want to help each other. You just need to lean into it and look for it. That's one. I feel anytime that we've been able to give back or put our skills towards helping other people. Once again, we have a long ways to go with this, but we work with a couple organizations that we've been able to use some of our media skills or whatever to help support them. Anything we've been to do where we're trying to help other people, I feel it has always come back tenfold in morale for the crew or new business leads or people out there in need that just see that we're a group of caring people and we're trying to help. (41:49): So the give back part I think is huge. I want to do so much more of that.

Mike Artz (39:52): I think it's a unique place that it's one thing to give 1% of revenue or whatever, but when you look at what you can actually do as a skill and how we can help, it's often, I think we've been able do a lot more by putting ourselves towards these tasks. I think those are two of my favorite things. The family personal work balance is this never ending? I'm trying to think. I believe my kids, I think my daughter, yeah, my daughter was born right around the time we launched public works. So you're going through this entrepreneurial journey at the same time, you're trying to be a parent at the same time. You're trying to maintain some sanity and do your own thing. And I don't think there is any answer to the balance between work, family, and personal. (42:43): That's a place that the entrepreneurial group has really been helpful for me, but I feel anytime you're winning on one side of that triangle, the other two sides are suffering. But anytime all three parts get to come together, if I can take my kids on a shoot or to me that's the best day ever. If it feels good for me and it kind of connects to my family and work, that's the ultimate. So the reason I say that is because back when I was starting this thing, I wasn't thinking that way. Now I'm sitting here and my daughter's going to be out of high school in a year. Have I embraced every moment I could have, but I wasn't thinking that way 16 years ago as I was trying to define the life I wanted to lead. And so, I don't know, maybe that's three areas.

Cole Heilborn (43:31): Yeah, no, that's great, man. Yeah, I mean it's never ending. It just keeps going. You keep learning, you keep trying new things, and I appreciate you sharing some of that stuff.

Mike Artz (43:39): Yeah, it's been really fun. Always open to talk more with folks too. And

Cole Heilborn (43:44): Yeah, Mike, so if folks have, I dunno, you mentioned a couple resources so far in the show today. Any other resources that you'd recommend people look into if they're trying to navigate some of these conversations?

content: Mike Artz (43:59): A SMP has been okay for me, the American Society of Media photographers. I think I could have gotten even more out of it if I was just more active with it. But if you're a photographer or a filmer or an assistant, being an assistant is a great way to get out and learn from other people. A SMP has some good resources. They also have a lot of documents. When you become a member, it's not that expensive, maybe 400 bucks a year or something. They have a lot of documents that help you with your talent releases and they have people in Washington lobbying to protect our rights, copyright, that kind of thing. So A SMP has been pretty good. When I was first freelancing, I became a member of my local Chamber of Commerce and it was cool. Once again, it was a couple hundred bucks a year. (44:47): I met a lot of people in my community of Evergreen, Colorado that it grounded me a bit. And when you join some of those groups that people really start looking out for each other. You want to support the people that you met there and stuff. So me and a couple buddies started talking about Join the Elks Lodge. Now I feel like that's such a, I dunno, I dunno if we have to wear crazy hats or what, I don't even know what they do, but we're like, it seems like a cool thing. We should probably join it. (45:15): I think any of those organizations that help to curate random collision of other people that are thinking somewhat like you are worth their weight in gold because anyone who's joined already joined for a reason, you kind of already passed that part in eo. I can bump into any one of those other 13,000 members around the world and we instantly can get into a conversation deeper than most other people I know because you just already know. This organization is about deep sharing and confidentiality and all that already puts aside, it's an entrepreneur and immediately I can be talking to a guy who owns a business in Catman de and it's on immediately. So I think just looking and looking and finding those other people in your community who you aspire to be or you like what they're doing and yeah, see what they're connected to. And it could be like a Wednesday meetup and go snowboarding group. Everything gets solved and planned and figured out on a chairlift.

content: Jonathan Wegner (03:07): So part of why I was actually brought on to SOG was that I my experience in the last couple of companies I've worked with has been for you know helping early mid-stage or even late stage companies pivot and work out where they want to go next, be it either go public or sell or enter new markets or you know. change their public perception. So SOG was kind of a lot of those things. And so you know early on I came in to be the the marketing guy because the board said, hey, we've got a marketing problem. And I came in and said, no, you have a much bigger problem. I'm sorry to say it. So unfortunately for all my sins, I was then gifted e-commerce, even though that was really spearheaded by a really excellent guy that that Steve. So he's you know brilliant at what he does. He works with Eddie Bauer and other places and you know they had a product strategy problem and Chris Cashbur, whom you had on the show previously, he he speedheaded that and you know, and there was a you know product design problem and so Josh Mizilleron, who's guy that I work with here, is another Seattle guy who works for a couple of different brands. And so, you know, I think. All in all, what ended up happening was I, you know, we built this team up of subject matter experts that just look really passionate, really driven. and I was really just the catalyst to to get things moving in the right direction. So that was kind of the first piece of the puzzle. But then when we came to selling, it's something I've been working with the the board for the last shoot, eight months now, I think. It's been some time. So it was, you know, working with the CEO and the CFO and others to craft what the message is, the positioning statement. you know all of the the proposition it's basically like selling a product like you would in a store but you're doing it at much bigger level and you're talking about things like EBITDA and margins and you know volumes and all that fun stuff. So just marketing through a different name.

content: Jonathan Wegner (10:46): So the the brand is 35 years old this or sorry just last year really I think the year anniversary and there's kind of what I'd call three stages of the brand. It was the very first stage where Spencer Fraser, our founder, came across a Bowie knife that had no markings on it, had no branding, no country of origin, nothing like that. And was fascinated by it, found it like at a yard sale or one of those, you know, one of those things. And he Started researching and found out that it was an original McAvee Sog Bowie knife. McAfee Sog is a special forces unit in Vietnam that did all of these, you know, incredibly risk, risky missions. and they needed tools that were specially designed for what they needed to do, a lot of close in combat and hand-to-hand combat, and you know, in the jungle and lots of problems to solve with this knife. And so There was a guy that designed it for them and worked with them and then got made in Japan. And so Spencer fan out this entire history by talking to veterans and reading, you know, Soldier of Fortune and all those sorts of things and wanted to make it for others to be able to celebrate the history of Maccabees Sog. And so that's what he kicked off with. He sold out within a week. He put an ad in Soldier of Fortune. I actually came across that ad with the very original logo. the very first one. And yeah, he sold out within a week and then thought, okay, I'm I'll make some other things associated with this and made a folding version of it. And before he knew it, he had a knife company, knife and tool company on his hands. And so during that period of say, I'd put it about 15, 20 years, it was very much driven by innovation. He was working with the US Navy SEALs to develop the SEAL pup, which was one of the most rigorous rigorously tested fixed blade knives ever for the US military. And so there's a lot of user insights and a lot of innovation getting into multi-tools and developing compound leverage and all these other kinds of things. So he did that for quite some time. He got to a place where he couldn't do it all at all of it, you know, on his own in you know basically on his kitchen table.

content: Jonathan Wegner (10:46): So he brought some investors in and they took Know this very premium brand, which Spencer often states that the premium knife market was you know helped along and developed by SOG in the late 80s and early 90s. And they took that very premium brand and offered it at you know lower cost products. So you know, there's still SOG design ethos to it and a lot of the innovation, but you know, people had access. To this interview premium brand at a price point that's far more accessible. So you had your Halo products, your premium products, and you had these sort of more accessible ones. So they they leveraged the brand that way. And then very quickly, the company grew quite rapidly and they sold it to another private equity group, which is the last one that just owned us, who continue that strategy. But the the leadership group that was in place at that time, I think that they overleveraged the brand and went a little bit too hard into Walmart. There was a lot of factors in the market where there wasn't as much of an emphasis on innovation anymore. And things just started to fall apart. So that's sort of the second phase, the what we call the mass market phase. The the really interesting thing that happened then was that SOG went into all these different categories that it had done before. So it went into illumination with dark energy flashlights. It went into backpacks. It went into, I think there was knee pads and belts and all this other kind of stuff at some point. But it showed that there was appetite and there's permission for SOG to try lots of different things. And through that it also grew, you know, very broad brand awareness, which you know was beneficial. But unfortunately the core product of what we make knives and tools just didn't get as much love and attention as it as it used to. That brings us sort of to the third Period. And that is where reorganization and sort of a reinvigoration of going back to the roots of what Spencer actually intended, which was innovation led, user insights led, and using those two as the the key reason for being and differentiation of what we do.

Jonathan Wegner (10:46): So that that's when I entered and I worked with all of the business leaders and key stakeholders to kind of work out. Why does SOG exist? And you know, we we came to this point from the research I was doing as as I just even before I started the with the company, I was working with users to find out why do they like SOG? And is there something something about it that's still interesting? And this is what really convinced me that it's a good opportunity, that there was still a lot of trust for the brand, but everyone said, I wish it was SOG from 10, 15 years ago. So that gave me a lot of hope to to do something interesting with it. And The other thing that was really played out was this of like I think overly tactical aesthetic where everything must be black and everything that must look kind of tactical slash militaristic. And we had people using it for hunting for daily carry and whatever else. And what I introduced was industrial design as a as a key discipline and had that integrated into the way we did things. And what industrial design is about, it's not just about the aesthetics, it's actually understanding who the user is and meeting them. where where they need you the to have the product go and represent, you know, what it is that they need to do. So that way when they pick it up, they fully trust it as an outdoor tool or a daily, you know, something you stick in your pocket as you walk out the door with your keys and wallet and or what else. Or if it really isn't, you know, for law enforcement, military or professional users, we like to group them, that it's absolutely that. So we try to really go in that way where it's very much mission led and user use case led. So it's very much sort of a a design led story that has reinvigorated the brand. So very long answer to your very short question.

Cole Heilborn (17:15): No, that's great. It sounds like so through those three phases, the reputation of the brand has kind of gone through a number of changes as well.

And I think that's it's undeserved because there's lot of great stuff in Walmart. But I think that a knife community is such that there's a there's a a lot of pride that you're buying from a Chris Reeves or Emerson or somewhere it's like you know, small batch kind of maker. And when you look at Walmart, it's kind of like, you do mass manufacture stuff, so that can't be good. But you know, the truth is really comes down to the intent of the design and how well it's been manufactured and the the quality standards and materials and all that kind of stuff. So yeah.

Cole Heilborn (18:04): So why was there a need, or I guess why was there even a conversation about changing the perception of the brand from this Walmart brand to something that getting back to its premium roots? Like why was that a why was that a concern?

Jonathan Wegner (18:18): Money. It always is money. If the if the strategy was working and the you know sales were successful, I don't think that I would be at sold and I don't think that anything would be changing. I mean, generally the thinking within businesses if it ain't broke, don't don't fix it. So there there was year on year decline of like twenty percent in certain certain products and I think revenue and and all those sorts of things. So that was the concern. And the big problem was yeah, relevance was just, you know, in a toilet and people no longer wanted to buy sol or didn't want to be seen as buying sog. and we weren't bringing new customers, whereas there's lots of other brands doing interesting and innovative and relevant things. So yeah, sadly comes down to money, but it's a it's a good motivator to to make changes.

People were seeing it and you know not being activated. It doesn't matter what the call to action was, there wasn't a there wasn't an acceptable level of response from consumers. So then you start looking at what else mm could it be? And one thing was the the website sucked. So you know one way we we tried to measure. Sorry. You did everything you could. the the site was just incredibly difficult to navigate. And after we, after Steve Miller revamped it, you know, and made it far easier to make a transaction to find what you're looking for and find relevant results. you know, sales of even the older product started coming through. But unfortunately, we just had this overarching kind of halo of I don't know, just irrelevance and tired, sort of fatigued brand that may have been great and relevant back, you know, a decade ago. But as we got into sort of the the mid 2010s, it just no longer was was really sort of speaking to the audience through the actual product we made and the way we talked about it. So it was a process of elimination and you know you can only find unfortunately, most of the time you can only find what the problem is by spending some money and seeing whether it changes things or or putting in some sort of level of effort. Money is often the easiest one. Jonathan Wegner (21:58): we had a lot of things hit at once, like in at the beginning of last year when we put in the the new or sorry, implemented the new brand's positioning and product and everything else. everything kind of came out at once, which was January 2020. And it's kind of an unfortunate time if you consider what else was going on then. But if anything, preparedness was front of mind for a lot of people. And that is core to to our brand. I mean, our brand stands for you know providing enhanced capabilities for human potential and survivability and preparedness is all kind of part of that. So it's kind of hard to diagnose exactly what did it, but I think it's that, and I'm gonna sort of you know trumpet about how great the the team is. I think it's that just everyone was really kind of you know, Doing everything they could to re-rehabilitate the brand. And I think all stops were pulled out to just really nail it. And the website is one of those key factors or key tools to be able to communicate what you stand for and where you're going. But also product, I think is also the key thing. It was not only something that people would carry as a marketing vehicle and a marker that things are different from now on. So people would come and look for the new product and see maybe they are 20 to 30 percent higher priced than how what they expected. And they're like, well, you know, SOG is kind of cool. I like what they're doing here, but I might buy some older products because I'm not sure about this more expensive stuff or whatever it might be. So you know, that that reinvigorated. the sale of the older stuff, but also it also reminded people that SOB does more than, you know, I hate to use the example again, but that Walmart knife or whatever it might be.

content:
Cole Heilborn (24:02): When when you're trying to figure out where you wanted SOG to land in its ecosystem of competitors and its positioning, how do you determine or how did you guys think through where do we want this to land? Was that purely based on value conversations about the company or were you considering other competitors and trying to figure out what was a natural spot for SOG to move to?

Jonathan Wegner (24:25): As one considers the position of where you might take the brand, there's a lot of factors that you you take into account. So there's obviously the competitive landscape and see who's doing what at what price point and what sort of feature sets and points of parity, points of difference, all that kind of analysis. But also you're looking at your own capabilities of whether you can do things that are the same or different in-house. So for example, if we had several machines being able to machine, you know, short runs of of different kinds of custom parts. you know, that that would be something that we would use as part of our positioning statement. I there's other brands out there like, I mean, look at Benchmade and Leatherman. Right now, they do a lot of really great custom work that provides something that's that's different. So you know, we also have, I think, a really great innovative hub with our engineering team. So that has created a unique proposition where innovation can continue to be something that helps differentiate us. And also we have a very passionate team about design. And when I talk about design, I'm not talking about design as a aesthetic effect that you wrap something about. It's actually thinking about the end user and then working from that to inform how it functions, feels, looks, you know, all that kind of thing, tastes, if that's your thing. So, you know, we we use a lot of those things to inform us. And then it's looking at our history of where we came from. And you know, also considering of where we as an organization want to go. I mean, brands are not nameless kind of faceless entities. They are made up of the people that that work there. And you know, it was talking to everyone in the business. One of the first things I did was just talk to everyone repeatedly of like where could we go, where shouldn't we go, what's worked, what hasn't, what could work, and pulling all those factors in together and developing multiple different visions for the brand of what it could and should be.

So positioning is a very complex process. It's actually really really fun process as well that I like going through. But yeah, there there was a lot of factors that that came into play. And I wanted to be throughout this process respectful to where the brand had come from because there was a lot of following behind that. But also it was started by an individual who had a vision. So I worked with with Spencer to type conversations about what he'd wanted to do. But we also had to have a vision of like where could this brand be in five, 10 years. So know that that statement that I shared before of you know enhanced capabilities for human potential doesn't say knife in there doesn't say tool it really came from reading the book Sapiens and sort of the idea of you know the things that propel humans forward is our ability to tell stories and continue that storytelling tradition which is actually the passing of information and our ability to create tools and layer on complexity on them. So you know It's the sort of our species sort of key differentiator, if you will, to use that marketing term, against other species is that we can do those two things really well and continue to drive human potential. So our vision is to be really a part of that human story, that you know, what humanity does next, we want to be a part of it, you know, be it pushing the boundaries to climb the highest mountain or go into the deepest part of the ocean, or whether it's off planet. and doing something else. So it it was also inherently a great deal of flexibility in what we could do next, but it was always sort of that that vision, visionary sort of position.

content: Jonathan Wegner (29:12): I mean, it's absolutely necessary to to be able to get to that, you know, really visionary point. you know, you really need understand what tools you have to be able to build up to that. So, you know, we could have said we want flying cars. And you know, if the technology doesn't allow you to get there, you're gonna keep delivering, you know, vaporware for as long as the money, you know, as long as you have the money or until investors get really angry with you. It's coming with pitchforks and torches. But you absolutely need to consider where you're at now and what those incremental steps are. And that's part of the enjoyment I get working with different brands, and especially at SOG, was we try to work out what those incremental steps were going to be to get us there. So the the challenge also you can get sort of stuck in is you get comfortable and you're like, this is what we do really well, and we don't want to disrupt that because that's the money. The the you you want to balance out those incremental updates and steps with you know your your current you know cash flow and capabilities and all those sorts of things. So it's it's a tenuous balance and there's a lot of push and pull. But yeah, you kind of look to the future, but you use the current place that you're at as that platform to build on that. lot of brands will be like, yeah, we want to get there. How are we going to get there? No idea. And that's just you're doing failure. But a lot of the way I work and a lot of the way that my my team works and others that I've found that are you know good at sort of accelerating companies to different sorts of places is considering every layer that you put down now as a platform that's taking you either one direction or another. And if you put those layers even you know every little communication bit, the way your customer service team answers the phone or How easy it is to find their number, for example, be it inside packaging or on the website, or how well trained they are, or anything like that. All these things layer on to create an effect that creates an impression. Because ultimately, where you take a brand, you may have this idea in your mind of where you're at, but ultimately brands are owned by the general publics. And the way they think about you is reality. All you are is a steward to shepherd the brand a certain way, and you can try and influence the way they think. But you know, the way you influence is that is by every little sort of layer they that you put down.

content:
Cole Heilborn (31:45): So thinking about the concept of the value of a brand and how the your customers perceive the value of your brand, what role does pricing each product play in that perception?

Jonathan Wegner (32:00): that's always a fun and tricky one. Whenever we develop a product, Chris may have talked about this. We develop the develop a market research document. That's this document has lots of different names. But the term we'll use is market research document. And it's actually Otto Box's fault where I used to work. That's what they used there. So yeah, anyway, so within that we put some aimpoints of what this product should be, what sort of value it should provide. What kind experience it should provide, some of the materials, some technologies, all that kind of stuff. And you start kind of adding this kind of wish list, if you will. And before you know it, all this stuff kind of adds up, and you have a price range of what it's going to cost to make this product and what it's going to cost or what it could be retail for. And it's always a range. You're looking at competitors, you're looking at you know, the the cost of. goods, things like shipping, steel, steel costs, just raw material costs, you know, all the factors that come into, you know, cost of goods. And you're constantly trying to balance that out. And sometimes you're able to position a product in such a way that it creates a great amount of value because it's very unique. And there's other factors that drive demand to it, but you're able to keep keep the the cost really low. And then there's those sort of like loss leaders that you might call that are you know the margin is much lower, but there's a lot of competition in that space, and you have to, you know, be competitive because people may not pick it up. But price absolutely communicates, you know, what you wanna how you want to be valued. And if you look at iPhone when it was first released. I hate to use Apple as an example because it's just so overused, but it's just so convenient. Everyone knows it. When when Apple launched the iPhone, Steve Barner, the the I think it was the CEO of of Microsoft at the time. Anyway, his fairly head up, just you know, talked so much trash about no one's gonna want to pay this for a for a phone. But Apple wanted to communicate this is something different. And it took a little while for people to use it and work out that it is quite different, that you weren't just paying for a, you know, an Apple logo on it, but it's actually a very different experience. And so they've been able to retain that command. And then when the iPhone Pro Max, is that what they call it? The the the largest one, I can't remember

Jonathan Wegner (34:44): When that was released a couple of years ago, that, you know, hit the thousand dollar mark. And, you know, journalists are all kind of bashing it saying no one's going to pay, you know, any money for that. And now it's one of their most popular selling products. So you know, price communicates a lot. but you know, we try to have a lot of value associated with that. You don't want to just price something at the highest possible price point to see what you can get. I mean, it's a strategy to do that to see what people are willing to pay for it, but it's risky one because logistically then you have to change pricing and then you have to communicate that pricing and then there's price changes that to occur and then all this other kind of stuff that that happens that that is just painful. So you know we we try to determine the pricing quite early on and validate that with our customers. And when I talk about customers, I'm talking about buyers that the retailers and then consumers, which is kind of the ultimate you know validation when they're willing to to pay for it. So when we first launched the the fall 2020 products, which is kind of what we call the the revamp of of SOG, we went up by about a quarter to a third in price because the steel types were you know better grades, the technologies that we included and the mechanism designs were innovative and more complex to to manufacture. And so one, we actually had to raise the price to to you know cover those costs, but also they weren't Initially they weren't as profitable. And there was a lot of there was a lot of pushback from retailers because retailers were like, SOG is this, and you're in this box and you're in this peg range, literally, of like, this is what those pegs should cost. And as soon as you're at this price range, you're going to go under the glass. But we proved that out, you know, now now the retailers don't want the cheaper stuff. They want SOG at this greater price point. So It takes some time. You can't change things overnight. You need to if you're gonna make a change, you have to prove that you're worthy of doing that. So

I think where OXO does really well is the durability often surprises the end user, me in this instance. Of how well it's lasted. So I brought bought a bunch of whisks from William Sonoma, for example, and they're they look, you know, hot. They're really, you nice chrome finish in China, whatever else. But they'll bust up in a year. Whereas my the very first whisk we bought when we moved to the US, you know, 10 years ago, it's still going pretty good. You have your own set of hurdles and challenges every day, and it's always been over the few years of doing the production business, it's always been something that's just in the back of your mind of like, well, how am I going to pay folks this month? How are we going to find our next job? And you slowly start to answer those questions and figure out ways to solve those problems. But pretty early on I discovered this idea and that you just nailed it. The idea that tomorrow I could get a phone call or an email that could completely change this current problem or this perceived problem that I'm dealing with. And knowing that that possibility was out there was it gave me a sense of I didn't have to worry as much because I knew I still had to put in the work, but I also knew that things can just happen that I didn't plan for. Mason Gravely (23:08): It's definitely motivating, especially when times are tough because you'd start digging in anybody's story. Those things seem to be the catalyst for almost anyone remarkable or anyone that's doing something different, even if it's not on a huge scale, it's just like someone you find personally inspiring that you might personally know. A lot of times it is some big break like that that happens along the way because they've been consistent in putting in the work. content: Mason Gravely (24:19): You can. And that's terrifying to think of how many opportunities you potentially have missed. It's like exploring a cave, you know what I mean? The entries are not obvious. It could be a pinhole that could open up to a grand room that you kind of have to be watching for. It's not going to be a doorway necessarily in a natural cave that opens up amazing opportunity to you. It might be something incredibly tiny. And if you talk to anybody that explores caves, that's exactly what it is a lot of the times, and I think life is a lot of times the same way, but you do get better at recognizing opportunity the more you think like that and the more you just be willing to say, yes, my wife and I or my partner, she is way less like that, way less like this. She wants to find her groove, find her purpose and find something she really enjoys and that's it. (25:19): That's what she wants to do the same way every day. Loves it. So thankfully, she's really set up now. She's got jobs she wants and the commute and all that, and she'd be happy if that never changes for the rest of her life, which I find crazy versus me. It's like it's just the way I'm motivated. But if that is your life right now, but you want it to be different, there's a billion opportunities she comes across every day if she chose to look at it that way. And that's all it is, is choosing to look at it that way. Richard Branson has a really good kind of mindset that I like is opportunity is like a bus stop. Don't freak out if you miss that bus because there's going to be another bus coming. There's always another bus. The cadence of the bus might be different depending on where you are and there's ways you can increase it, but find a bus stop and just watch for the bus. (26:19): It's pretty obvious when it comes. A lot of the times they're pretty huge and loud, just get on and you only need to get on one. You know what I mean? You don't have to. So I've definitely learned to not, especially now with kids and things where life just, there's certain things I can't say yes to anymore, at least not as frequently. I get to say yes to a lot of things, still most things, but sometimes I'm like, there's more opportunity out there. I don't need to be obsessive about turning over every rock, but it does keep you on your toes because you never know where life's going to take. And if that excites you, that's definitely the way I enjoy living.

content:
Cole Heilborn (27:02): The more we talk, the more I think about society's pressure or encouragement for people just to go out and chase their dreams and stop at nothing to get to them. I'm realizing what you're saying isn't exactly the opposite of that, but what's your take on this idea of chasing dreams at every cost or no cost?

Mason Gravely (27:25): Yeah, you're helping me formalize my philosophy as we talk about it. I don't know if a lot of people spend their time really thinking through it like this, and I don't know if I ever have to this degree. So I appreciate this opportunity. This is really cool. This is off the cuff. I haven't really thought about this, but just for that question, I work for people and I have know plenty of people that are driven by one single goal. And if you know what that is and you feel strongly about it and you really believe in it, fantastic, absolutely go for it. But I've learned that one size does not fit all with how we live this life. There's a billion different ways set. Well close to 8 billion ways to live this life, and a lot of them are awesome. And so I would say if you are someone that's driven to find one single goal, go for it. (28:26): If you're not like me and you've been frustrated because you felt like you've had to, you've needed to think that way to succeed. Let that go as soon as you can because find out what really does motivate you and what your values are. There's plenty I've learned through my life in the last few years. Wow. It really doesn't matter what I do for a living. It is kind of who it's for and what kind of impact I'm making. And so there are some dreams and goals I've had to let go recently. I'm not going to be that building trails all the time, for instance. But through athletic Bruin, 2% of all our sales goes to building trails. So in a way I am able to make more of an impact with the things I actually do enjoy by focusing on my job. There's all kinds of little things I've learned like that throughout the last few years of, like Seth said, not holding on too tightly to a specific dream, but chasing opportunity as it comes on your way, on your pursuit to that dream in the long run. So yeah, I don't know. I'm also intensely curious person, so all sorts of subjects interest me, but if you have that one single goal, I know plenty of people that do, they are passionate about this thing. I would just be sure that you're not driving yourself crazy or ruining that passion for you by trying to find that path that just isn't there.

content: Mason Gravely (30:33): That's interesting. I feel like I'm thinking about this all the time. I guess I've just never been one to have that long-term goal. When I started playing basketball, for instance, it was like, all right, get to college, make a college team, but beyond. And then I got to college and I'm like, wow, I don't really like this. It's way harder in college than it's like a job now. And so I pursued a different passion, which was biology, and that would clearly lead someone to explore the world. And so when I discovered that, I discovered bike packing and bike packing took over just because of the ability to explore. And then that led to all sorts of things. Now, I guess that's one reason the Adventure Sports podcast is so varied. I've wanted to take sports out of the title for a while and just say the Adventure Stories podcast, because that's all it is. (31:27): It's stories of adventure because that's what I've learned to love the story aspect. So to answer your question about having that pressure to do so, to have some sort of single goal, I do feel at times society does push on us to grow. And I'll be honest, I think I'm fighting back on that a little bit personally this year. Something I try to have an overarch. Now I will say this, I try to have an over overarching theme of the year, something just to keep in a filter, to think every thought through. And I'm writing this on my desk or anything. I probably should, honestly, actually that's a really good thing to do. I should write it right here just to keep it in mind, but I'm not getting a tattoo over anything. Last year it was like literally have fun, have more fun, quit being such a tight, just so uptight all the time. (32:29): The year before that was just gratitude. No, not gratitude, generosity. Just be more generous. I'm a stingy person. Stingy, I'm really cheap. And so my wife was like, you need to just give more money away. And so I really focused on that two years ago and now I feel like it has stuck with me to where it's like, and being at a company, this is not a salesy thing, but we're very generous at athletic and we just give a lot of money away.

content: Mason Gravely (35:08): Go with the flow. If the flow goes to the moon, I'll go to the moon. But I was at a museum by my house, and it's a super small town, nothing major, and it's a very small local museum, and I saw a piece of the moon there. It was in the museum on display. I was like, I don't know much about this, but it feels rare to have a sizable piece of the moon here at our little museum. And it looked like a new display. I was inquiring about it. No one really seemed to, I don't know, think that much of it. I was like, I don't know how rare it is to have a pretty big chunk of the moon that I don't think we have that much of the moon here on earth that we've harvested from the Apollo emissions. But I forgot about it. (35:53): The day goes on. By the time we got home, I just didn't think about it. Two weeks later, I'm listening to a podcast on Moon Rocks and I'm like, this is interesting. And it was talking about how the moon rocks were gifted to all the countries in the EU or the European Union. Everyone got one. All the 50 states got a piece of the moon, but the podcast mentioned the pieces that are the size of a couple grains of rice was the gift size. And that got me thinking again, I'm like, wait, that size, the piece I saw was much larger than that. Not huge, but a pretty big piece. And we only have, I don't know, less, I think less than a thousand pounds of the moon on earth. So obviously tons of it. You need to be used for research and whatnot. Anyway, I started doing some research. (36:41): I'm like, well, why do we have such a big piece? And come to find out, one of the astronauts that landed on the moon, there was 12 over the Apollo missions. One of them lived in this small town, and when he passed away, he didn't originally live here, but his family moved here after he passed away. And with him, they brought a lot of his memorabilia and they were looking for a place to donate it. And so they donated to our museum. So I googled his former wife, his widow is still alive, she's in her eighties, and I just googled her name and I found a phone number and I gave it a call and she answered.

(37:32): She goes, well, we had to rent a tv, first of all to watch him on the moon. And I remember I was cooking dinner, this is the sixties. Things were definitely stereotypical back then and a lot of families. And she goes, I remember getting dinner ready and I had a lot of the family over it, and my kids kept trying to change the channel to cartoons. We never had a TV in our house, we just rented it for the event. And I was like, no, your dad's on the moon. We got to turn it back. And I was like, my mind was blown. And come to find out, she lives like 10 minutes down the road from me, so I'm going to go over her house and she's going to show me all this memorabilia, show me a spacesuit. And she's got more chunks of the moon there. (38:12): And she's like, bring your kids. They'd love it. And I said, how random is that? But it just started with this curiosity about one thing and just putting pieces together. That's all it is. It's being curious and being alert. And that literally, that could be the total end of that story is just having that one conversation with the widower or the, I'm sorry, the widow of one of the moonwalks. But to me that was just a cool thing to talk about and a cool thing to experience. And she was a total hoot, just was making jokes and totally not that old yet. So it was really fun conversation. And so who knows where that leads, but to me that's just really exciting to do things like that. So personally, I'm always trying to do just something like that, or at least just being alert for when things crossover like that. That was a long story, but that was just an example.

Cole Heilborn (39:16): That's an amazing story. I want to hear the follow-up calls and conversations you have with this woman.

Well, it really is just a matter of going over there and recording some stories. So I would love to keep you posted when that happens, but if that's the extent of it, that's the kind of stuff I'm happy doing.

Cole Heilborn (39:44): Lately I've been thinking about the concept of seasons, and here in the northwest we have I'd say maybe two and a half or three seasons. And we're currently, we just got out of, well, we actually had a bunch of snow up here. That's pretty uncommon for us at least in terms of the amount of quantity and how long it lasted. Anyways, I was thinking about seasons when we had this snow and thinking about how the world around us constantly changes. And seasons are such a great example of that. And in different seasons of the year, nature responds a different way. In the wintertime, everything slows down. Life doesn't grow as quickly. Everything kind of hibernates. And I promise this will connect, but I've been thinking about, we were also thinking about our podcast, and as we've jumped into season three with this new year, we've been working on an annual, we put out an episode every Wednesday for the entire year, and we reached a point, I dunno, last fall, where we were like, do we want to be doing this every day for the entire year? Could we adopt more of a seasonality approach? And so I guess my thought process is if the natural world has these cycles of life and growth and slowness, why do we feel the need all the time to be pushing forwards, constantly driving forwards when everything around us ebbs and flows?

content: Mason Gravely (41:14): That's a great question. Yeah, I'm just riffing on this right now, but I love learning from the natural world. I'd say a lot of the principles I live by are natural concepts that you learn just by taking a hike or walking out in the woods or on the beach or whatever. I think there's so much we can gain from the natural world, and I think a lot of our drives now are evolutionarily based, the drive to grow and pursue, and maybe that's an exchange of some sort from the drive to procreate on a constant basis, which obviously isn't socially acceptable anymore to the degree it used to be have tens of thousands of years ago. Or for a dog for instance, my dog or anything, any other animal. So I feel like we do, based on society, have shifted our desires and growth is clearly one that we feel instinctively that we have to. (42:21): I fight against that with the show. I'm talking with the folks, someone that helps me with the podcast and it's like, what if we just didn't worry about growing this year? What if we didn't set goals? What if we just did the show and had fun and enjoyed it? Is that so freaking wrong? It's not like it's making a million dollars anyway. Why not just have a good time? And I think it was a little bit of a realization like, whoa, I guess that is an option, but that feels wrong. I'm not exactly sure why that feels wrong, but I'm also not someone that tries to summit every mountain they see. I really enjoy just sauntering around through the woods and looking at things. And so I would say if you don't feel like setting those big goals and you are content with things being smaller, you have a much higher chance of success. (43:21): I was introduced through the outdoors. I always mention this through hunting and fishing down here in the south where I live. And when I first started doing that, I felt like the only way to experience the outdoors was hunting and fishing, which was you killing something or catching something and releasing it. And at some point I was like, I was terrible at it. My dad was, I love him to death, but we weren't very good at either one.

Cole Heilborn (45:12): And I think everyone comes to the table with their own set of their own world and their own worldly expectations that they have with them, whether they've been brought up with these expectations or just their culture has imposed these expectations. And I think the idea of managing your own expectations is also really interesting. That's what we've been discussing about today, but making your own expectations and owning them for what your values are rather than just accepting whatever expectations are placed on you, I think is easy to say, but very difficult to do.

And don't be afraid of just doing things differently. I'll say that's probably one of the biggest things that's led to any success I have, which probably pretty not necessarily spectacular success, but I'm happy is just being willing to do things a little bit differently, take a few risks and clearly try new things. But if you're the type of person that likes to go with the flow, if you're a type B person in a type A world, there is still place for you and anything you want to do. So just keep going. So I think that's probably the most important thing with anything I tell people is just keep going. Like you said, with your own career, you never know when that break will be. (48:20): If that break never comes, make sure it's a pace that's sustainable for you. Make sure you as a river are flowing at a pace that you can control. There will be times there's rapids and there will be times that you're in a lake trying to make it to the other side. It's very calm. There'll be times where it just flows really well, really nice. And there'll be times crash into a chute to go uphill and it's just not going to work. So you turn around and you go back down and that's fine. Test all that out and you're going to find your path. And that doesn't mean you're not working hard and you're not doing things that you're passionate about, but you just got to keep going. It's our nature to just keep going, so don't fight that and keep going.

Jon Glassberg (05:15): Yeah, so I'm 37 now. I started climbing when I was 11 in Charlottesville, Virginia. That's where I grew up. And I took climbing very seriously through middle school and high school, and then I took a year off after high school. I didn't know what I wanted to do and I kind of just wanted to climb. So I moved to Boone in North Carolina to explore climbing and what that meant, and I didn't really know where it would take me, but I knew that that's all I wanted to do and that's all that mattered. I spent a year in Boone. I was doing all kinds of part-time jobs and just trying to scrape to get by, but to be a climber as much as I could be. And I eventually ended up going to school at App State. I did undergrad and grad school there, and I studied graphic design and business and a little bit of photography and print media actually was my main focus. So I spent a lot of time in that world, various jobs of different types, but nothing very serious and still climbing semi-professionally, professionally throughout that whole time. And then I linked up with a friend in North Carolina and we got really passionate about making climbing films in college. And that was kind of around the time that the DSLR came out. And then suddenly pretty high-end video and video capabilities were available in very inexpensive cameras.

Cole Heilborn (06:53): Was that with the Canon 70 D?

I mean, it was total junk and the videos we were making were horrible, but it was super fun to learn through that process. And I was friends with a lot of climbers and we would travel all over the world kind of documenting what we were doing and turning around those edits within a few days and just kind of cranking out media. I mean, we were making a couple hundred videos every year on different individual boulder problems that we were climbing or sport climbs or trips or whatever it might be. So over the years of doing that with the company louder than 11 that I started, it snowballed and took off and we were kind of on the forefront of internet web free content, basically. (07:50): I mean, we were just content creators basically before we knew what it was. And we were just making tons and tons of climbing films and we didn't care if we got paid for it, we just were pumping 'em out. And we kind of developed our relationships within the industry because of that. And people knew who we were because we were extremely core and we were just creating climbing films all day every day. And eventually as we kind of got better and better at making films, I really was honing my skills as an editor, as a filmmaker, as a director, we started getting more production jobs and we started doing more commercial stuff. And one thing led to another, and that's kind of where we're at now. We do a ton of commercial things, but we also capture lots of documentary and expedition film. And yeah, it's kind of morphing between a DP and a director that connects kind of the outdoor space to a commercial space because that's becoming more and more valuable to people these days, especially with huge films hitting the mainstream about rock climbing and expeditions. (09:04): So it's kind of changed the whole narrative around what the commercial and agency world is comfortable with. So that's kind of taken off, but I still pursue a professional climbing career. I had my best climbing year of my whole life last year. So I mean, certainly haven't slowed down in that regard at all. And I've just gotten smarter about how to position myself as a pro athlete and where my value is in the industry and that kind of thing. But I consider myself to have three jobs, essentially three businesses. One would be louder than 11, my photo and video production company. The second would be my professional climbing career. And the third is this company called Crux Academy that I co-founded with a partner, Jeremy Jensen, who I think you've had on the podcast. Yeah, so that's kind of like the full-time gig is those three jobs. Plus being married and trying to have a life outside of film and photo production. It's a lot.

Cole Heilborn (10:40): You had crafty taking care of you.

Jon Glassberg (10:42): Oh yeah. I mean, we shot in this tiny little LA climbing gym for a few days, and there was probably 150 people on the set. Everybody had their own trailers and stuff. It was everything you would imagine to happen to Brad Pitt or Tom Cruise or something on a movie set, but it was Alex Ho and Tommy Caldwell. They thought it was pretty funny too. So I think overall it was good because we got to hang with our friends and make something about climbing for the mainstream to see, which was pretty cool. But for me, it was exciting. It was like a union job that showed me a lot more of what's in the Hollywood space and how big it is and crazy it is, but also why it works so well. It's like a well-oiled machine and it works for a reason and you get results, which is pretty cool. (11:34): And then we also did a shoot outside. We shot a few days in Red Rock in Las Vegas, and that was pretty hilarious because as you can imagine, the Hollywood scene doesn't really do a lot of location climbing work, so that was very exciting. And I dpd the whole climbing section, so it was very spicy with some of the Hollywood guys cruising around in the desert, getting poked by cactuses, and we were shooting in a hundred degree weather, and it was pretty rugged actually. So they got a good taste of what it's like to be on expedition.

Cole Heilborn (12:11): Those two worlds are a little different, the expedition style adventure filmmaker versus the Hollywood climate controlled studio set. And not that that world is bad, but they are very different when it comes to production work.

And I mean, I think everybody has a unique position that they come to the table with. For me, I am probably in a good way and came to the table with of strong background in rock climbing, and I just had all these connections with climbers, and a lot of those climbers are now 30 and 40 somethings that are in positions at businesses that I work for. So it just kind of became a big networking, long-term lifetime networking thing that kind of paid off in the long run, which is pretty special right place, right time for sure. And being a pro climber and understanding that world and being able to hang with those athletes and also speak that language and be able to know what's cool and what's happening now in the moment kind of set me up to have a pretty cool niche in that space. (14:28): I realized early on as we started making videos about just us and our friends climbing that we're the only ones doing it for free online. There were a few other companies that were providing DVDs and downloads that were paid for in some way, or maybe it was a film festival, kind of like the Real Rock Film festival, but nobody was cranking out the type of media that we on such a consistent level, that was all for free, and that was just expected to get people psyched. We just wanted exposure. We just wanted people to know what we were doing. And I mean, there was maybe one or two other individuals out there that were working on that kind of level. They were pumping out a few things here and there with their climbers that they were associated with, but we were definitely doing probably the biggest and highest volume. (15:18): And it was just, I don't know, it was kind of cool. We were risk takers and we were willing to make terrible videos if it meant that people would talk about it. And we weren't in the business of making commercials yet, or commercial content or brand campaigns or whatever you want to call them these days. But we were just in the business of making things that we thought were cool and documenting our climbing lives. And that niche just carved itself out.

And as right around that time, print was really taking a hit from digital and stuff became more and more online based. And so I just started focusing more on what the web had to offer, and it just exploded. It should have, I mean, it was totally the way forward. And so a lot of that stuff carried through to video, like designing graphics and kind of designing the way that you're presenting the videos that you make and how you're publicizing them and promoting them and stuff like that. So I mean, it all kind of is one and the same if you have a little bit of a graphic design layout mind, you kind of understand a general eye for photography and a general eye for how something will look when you're presenting it and stuff like that. content: Jon Glassberg (18:40): Well, I think as you start out as a freelancer, you're doing everything yourself because you want to save money and you want to make it affordable to get paid to do the work that you do. You don't want to pay for a writer or a graphic designer or an editor or whoever it might be. You kind of do it all yourself and that way you make the most from the project. And maybe you learn a bit about all the different little elements that go into creating something, whether it's a article or a magazine or a film or really good photography or whatever it might be. All of those things have so many layers to pre-production, production and post-production that go into creating something decent. And you start to realize that as a freelancer that you can't just do it all yourself eventually. You have to focus on what you're good at and really kind of dive into that spreading yourself thin. (19:41): You'll be average at all those things all at once when you're trying to pull it off. But if you can focus, you can be really, really good at one specific thing, and that's when you become really valuable in my opinion. And I've kind of realized that over the years. I mean, I've done everything from video editing to producing, to shooting, to assisting literally everything in the photo and video world. And I'm realizing that if I focus and really put my energy all into one of those things, then I can really become good at it and hone my skills. And I think that's slowly becoming directing more and more. And I think directing is also more of a, I think of it also as just kind of a general business manager as well. You might be directing one film and you might be managing that whole production, but I also own a film and photo production company, so there's lots of management that happens there too, and directing of that company. (20:42): So I mean, I think just having that big overarching view on what's happening, whether it's one production or a whole company, you're still directing. So I've slowly become more and more of a director minded person realizing that I can hire really good freelancers that are experts at photography or really good assistants or amazing at lighting, or really good at sound or good editors or whatever it may be that will help elevate a production. But it is something that if I did on my own and I was trying to fill every role, I would be spread super thin and I would just do everything mediocre. And this is a good way to create better products. But I think when you first start, yeah, you're doing it all. So it's really hard to figure out what is your niche, I guess, but also identifying maybe what you have special that's unique to you that no one else really has or maybe other people have, but you're able to really capitalize on it. I think there are plenty of people in the climbing space, adventure expedition, outdoor space that would probably make great film directors and make amazing films, but some people just don't have the mindset or don't have the work ethic or something and they just don't do it. But some do. And when you identify that, then you realize that you have something special.

I don't really know what the right answer to that is. I mean, I think that you find what you're interested in and you pay your dues and you put out as much as you can in, let's use film as an example. If you're interested in outdoor photo and video, you need to be cranking out photos and video projects all the time and not just so that you can get better at your craft so that people just see that you're stuff. (26:45): I know a ton of people that talk about making film projects and talk about how cool this would be if they did that, or they're critical of the outdoor space and why people aren't doing more of this or whatever. And honestly, just go out there and make it. I know that it's hard because you have to have some money to make some projects and you have to kind of be motivated, but I think you can also produce stuff pretty inexpensively that is super inspiring and cool. And people recognize when you put effort towards making stuff, and then that material becomes marketing for your brand down the road. And if you're into film and photo in the outdoor space, people need to know that you're making tons of stuff. Just because you are holding a camera and out there in nature doesn't mean that you're making things. (27:34): People need to actually see the final product. And I often see people with their photo of them on Instagram or Facebook holding a camera and saying that they're a filmmaker or a photographer, but I've never seen anything that they put out, or at least the stuff that they're putting out is not being seen. And I think that that's easy to do with quantity and aligning with people and building relationships with climbers and outdoor enthusiasts that are doing stuff that's interesting. If you make enough stuff, people will see it and will act as its own advertising.

content: Jon Glassberg (30:26): Yeah, I mean, the outdoor industry is not like Hollywood is with mentorship and with understudies and with the kind of ranking and pecking order that kind of helps you guide your way through the industry. If you're interested in, I don't know, being a film director, you're definitely going to start out assisting and shadowing and just getting involved in film production. And the same goes for the outdoor space, but it doesn't have as much structure. I mean, you have to go out and assist as a new photographer or filmmaker, and you have to see how the sausage is made from the bottom of the barrel, really. I mean, you have to understand how things are happening and working before you can jump in and start telling people what to do. So I think that goes back to paying your dues, and I think that's super important. (31:24): But yeah, you really need to learn that process before you can dive in completely and just be willing to take the low paying jobs or the non-paying jobs and build relationships with people and get familiar with your scene. I'm in Colorado, so I mean, if you're in Denver, let's say, and you want to get involved in film production, you need to be out assisting and getting involved in productions, whether it's pre-production or production or post-production, any way you can to see different pieces of the puzzle. But then also, I remember when I was starting, I learned a bunch of stuff that I really wished that had been taught to me earlier. I remember I did a bunch of videos on how to shoot a photo and video from a rope, basically how to jug a rope, how to get in position on a wall and get above a climber and stabilize yourself enough to take video. (32:25): And I always thought back then, in the early two thousands, 2000 tens, we were just trying to share our experience and share our knowledge in the outdoor space so that we could educate people even if they never even use it. People just liked seeing how to jug a rope and get in position to shoot because it was interesting and it was like a niche that had never really been shown.

So I just made a bunch of how-to videos back in the day and talked about how my process worked and maybe mentored some people inadvertently through some videos. (33:22): But I mean, I think putting out information as an expert, like you're saying, is super valuable. People want to learn really badly, and I mean, that's funny. Like why I, I've been involved in this Crux Academy project was it's basically just education about all kinds of different topics in the outdoors. It might be as simple as how to boulder with Nina Williams or whatever, or it could be more in-depth topics. So I think people are really hungry to learn, and especially if there's no traditional way to go through a mentorship or an internship or go through that process, then you need to at least be watching things online and using resources to understand more because that is really how it goes down in the real world.

Cole Heilborn (34:11): So I've heard this before and I have thought this many times, that if you niche yourself too much, then you become pigeonholed and you can't break out of that spot that you have dug yourself into. I guess I'm curious to hear your thoughts on that. Is pigeonholing bad? I know for a lot of people who are just starting out, they're like, if I pigeonhole myself so early, I can't find enough work just to support myself, so I have to spread myself thin, take everything that I can. And so I realized there's the element of time here, which plays a big role in, I think this question, but I don't know you, I mean, have you pigeonholed yourself? Do you feel like you're stuck?

But I mean, it's interesting. I think if you're pigeonholing yourself, you're really becoming an expert at one specific thing. And I mean, I just think about when I hire a sound guy for location work, he's usually a 50 to 60-year-old guy who is really, really good at sound and I hire him because he is going to for sure, and he is going to be awesome at it, but he's also probably not doing a lot of other stuff in production. He is just doing sound work and he's probably not getting a ton of jobs. He's just doing, whenever someone calls, he is ready to go and he is got his kit and he will nail it for sure, but he's an expert and he's pigeonholed a little bit. (35:55): I mean, I think as you get more exposure and as you create more stuff and you just get bigger, your business grows, you will probably start to refine more and more. It would be my guess as as you're freelancing and you're taking any job here and there, you're also working for jobs that aren't paying as much and those jobs don't have as high of expectations of you. And if you're getting 150 bucks to go do sound for a day, no one's expecting you to deliver Hollywood sound all day every day and mix this crazy thing. But you'll learn a lot and you might be able to start to dial in what you love and what you're passionate about, and then that's what you start to seek out more. But yeah, I think you just kind of over time you get more refined.

Cole Heilborn (36:47): So for folks who are just starting out, how important is having a niche or is that something that folks should even be considering? Should they just be focusing on trying things out, feeling out what they like and as they do so they slowly start to become more focused in terms of what they start to call themselves?

I mean, if you're getting into this world, you're probably someone that is pretty self-motivated and you're interested in creating something artistic and fun and exciting, and if you spend your first few years dabbling in all the different types of production and you realize that you're a really good storyteller and maybe you're most motivated as an editor because you get to tell the final story and really tweak and dial in how that story is told, maybe that's what gets you psyched. I mean, ultimately, yeah, any of us could probably buckle down and be one of the different roles in the outdoor industry film world, but if you don't love it, then it's going to be a long career of just going through the paces. So I mean, you're better off finding something that you're actually passionate about, and if you have a niche of any kind, definitely embrace it your foot in the door to at least start to understand if you like something or not. (38:17): And maybe that foot in the door just by being a rock climber gets you involved in rock climbing productions and maybe you realize that you want to get in a narrative film or something like that, totally separate from rock climbing, but you at least got a taste of what it was like to do a production and you kind of see the path from there. I mean, I think any niche just acts as a door opener and as a way to network and a way to just communicate with your scene. And I mean, I've had friends that were passionate rock climbers that were good at video and decided that they wanted to just get into music and shoot music. It was a similar style of shooting competitions. It was kind of like going to a concert and shooting a DJ or shooting a band or whatever. They just found something that was loosely associated to what they originally got their foot in the door with. They honed their skills as filmmakers and then they're like, oh, actually I think music is the next avenue. I'm going to follow that path. I mean, I think you just kind of go with what feels natural and what motivates you because in a creative space, if you're not motivated, it doesn't make sense, I don't think.

You kind of define yourself by what you're most interested in and what you can actually execute on. I mean, you can fake it until you make it only so far. Eventually you're going to have to make something or do something that you may or may not be an expert in. And I mean, I think that's quite challenging when you get to that level where people are paying you a lot of money to do something and you might not be the best at it. I mean, most clients wouldn't care if some of the smaller roles were filled by anyone that could help deliver a final product that they're happy with. But I think that from a director's perspective, you're you're trying to have your finger on the whole process to make sure that you're guiding it for the client to have the confidence in you to achieve it. I mean, if ladder 11 was hired as a production company and they weren't interested in me as the person guiding it, that would be pretty weird, and I would feel like if something went out the door that someone else worked on it, I never saw it. (43:25): That would be weird as well. So you're really, I mean, as a director, I'm involved in everything that we do, even if, I mean it's only me and my wife as full-time employees here and everybody else that we work with is subcontracted, but that's just because one, we don't have the volume that we're overwhelmed that we need to hire a full-time extra staff people or extra staff people to work in. But most of the time we're just flexing up and down for productions. Most companies are, and we just hire individually for the job. So very rarely. I mean, I've had full-time employees in the past, but I don't know that that's necessarily the way forward. I'm still experimenting with it and still learning what's good and bad with having employees and what that means, but that's actually really interesting to me as a business owner is all the really tedious business things that you have to deal with unemployment and health insurance and taxes and tax rates and all the crazy stuff that you just have no idea what to do with when you first get started. (44:39): But that over time you start to learn is super valuable to know. And then being able to serialize that across multiple businesses and use that expertise to quickly develop and run other companies is super awesome. I mean, that's something I was super lucky and fortunate enough to go to grad school and focus on business for that specific reason. I was like, I don't know anything about anything other than climbing and print and graphic design. I need to know how to run a business if that's what I want to do. So I just focused on learning how to do the basics in business and honestly, they could teach you all stuff, all that stuff in business school, but once you actually go and start applying it to a real business that's yours, that actually matters, that'll make or break your financial success is totally different game. So it really changes. I mean, if you're good at QuickBooks and you're organized and you can dial that business side of things in, it just makes your whole life so much easier and you don't run the risk of potentially just imploding and not being able to handle it or burning out and spending all your time trying to punch numbers into a spreadsheet.

Maybe it's just once a week having a conversation with a different freelancer to build relationships and to hear about how they're relating to money. The transparency piece for me is really important. So that's kind of how I can picture the process going from I'm in the hole to, I'm aware that there's a hole. And I think as a freelancer, you assume sometimes that you're just at the mercy of the wind and you take whatever you can because you got to make things work. And some seasons are like that for sure. But as this conversation has, I think alluded to, you do have a lot of control, at least over 50% of the engagement. The other 50 is the client and how you manage that other 50%, you can do it. You don't have to just wait for someone to show up and dangle a carrot in front of you and be like, well, do you want this job or not?

Justine Mulliez (01:21:42): Yeah, absolutely. And it's a very nuanced thing. And we can either continue to lean into that perspective and be passive and kind of be hoping, as you're saying, for the carrot to drop, or you can go create clients and reach out to referrals or reach out to past clients or network. So I think for me, what I always try to leave my clients with is you have the possibility of living creatively in your business, not just in your craft, and thinking creatively and thinking and experimenting and playing and kind of being loose with it for until you get your bearings can be one of the most positive things you can do for your business.

Cole Heilborn (01:22:38): Well, Justine, this conversation could go on for a long time, is it's a never ending topic, and I wouldn't be surprised if we do this again at some point. I think we all deal with this stuff. We're all on our own journey around these different ideas, and I think knowing that we all deal with this stuff as a freelancer, it is tough, but there are ways to work through it as is evident, I think, by what you've shared today.
