content: Cole Heilborn (09:43): Yeah, so I think you hit on the main three buckets that I think about when considering how to charge. There's your typical hourly rates. There's the day rate, which is a little more common in the creative, specifically the film industry. And then there's project rate. And so I think they're all three, and I think every freelancer probably moves through charging three different ways for three different types of projects depending on where they are in their journey. I think hourly is a really easy place to start because you're like, I'm trading an hour of my time for an hour of my services and what I'm going to ultimately deliver this option is great because if there's any overages, if it takes longer to do the job, you're getting compensated for that. One of the biggest challenges of going freelance is quoting projects and calculating time and expenses. (10:40): And if you are off and you have to spend more time, but you're not getting paid more than you're making less money, or in the worst case scenario, are you actually losing money? So charging hourly is a great way to make sure that you're covering your time and you're being compensated. One of the downsides potentially to charging hourly though is that there's, and I'll say this, there's theoretically a limit with how much you could charge hourly if someone were to charge a thousand dollars an hour, people do. I think about attorneys, they charge ridiculous amounts of money per hour. But in the creative world, I think that's much less common, but there's kind of a cap on what you can charge hourly. And so as you get into bigger projects and as maybe your services start to evolve and you're offering more strategy or you're offering different types of value, sometimes hourly, I feel like you outgrow that and what you're providing no longer is best served in an hourly format.

I think day rates makes a lot of sense. If in the film industry it makes a lot of sense because when you're on a production, you're not really thinking about it in the terms of hours, you're thinking about it in the terms of days. And so from a producer standpoint, it's much easier just to think, okay, I have this crew set aside for this amount of day rate per day, and you just kind of total it up in that way. I do think there's a component that a lot of the folks I work with when they work off of day rates as they have an additional gear charge, and that's something to consider as well, is I'm charging for my time, but I'm also charging for my gear. (12:37): And when I say gear, that can include obviously hardware, like cameras and lenses, but that can also include things like your internet and your software and more kind of soft expenses that you have, maybe reoccurring expenses that you have, and maybe you're not going to provide a line item that says Google Suite $15 a month, but those are the type of expenses that you should be considering when you're quoting for your time and however you decide to package that and present it to your client or employer or whoever. It's kind of up to you, but those are things to consider as well.

I think this comes down entirely to your experience and where you are kind of in the game. I say game because it feels like a game, but gosh, I guess to give a little background on how I've done this, I've done tons of free work and I've done tons of low paying jobs where either I lose money or whether I break even my accountant probably wouldn't advise that I keep doing those types of jobs, but I guess my idea is you have to start somewhere. And if you don't have a portfolio, because I believe that chances are you're not going to get hired for something that you haven't done before, and if you can't show that you've done something comparable or similar to a prospective job, chances are unless you have a really good relationship with the client, it's going to be hard for them to hire you because they can't see what you've been able to do. (16:02): I think there comes a point where you just have to build a portfolio of work that you want to do and however you can build that portfolio, I think that's what everyone has to figure out. It is funny, I was looking at my portfolio at our website and most of the projects on there are projects that we have either done at zero cost or have been done entirely for free, which I think is really interesting because most of our paid work is not on our website. And I think that's because I always try to put work out there that I want to get hired for, and more often than not, the things I'm getting paid for aren't always the things that I want to make more of. And I've had to find ways to build projects and make projects that I would like to do more of. (16:56): And so oftentimes that means just taking on a passion project and saying, you know what? I'm going to do this for free. Maybe this other project is going to fund this project or cover my expenses for this month, but I'm going to go out there and try to make it as best I can so that I have an excellent piece on my portfolio that I can then use to sell for the next project. But it comes down to your level of experience. If you're, you're a veteran freelancer and you're in demands and you have plenty of work that reflects the type of work that you want to do, chances are you don't need to do free work. If it's a really strong passion project though, and you believe in it and you have time for it and it feeds your soul, go for it. But if you're a new to the space and you're still trying to figure out where do you fit into the industry and you're trying to build that level of expertise and you don't quite have the portfolio yet, I think you kind of just got to get out there and start making stuff.

And so maybe you yourself are no longer the person out shooting as much, or you aren't the person designing the logo, but maybe you're directing or you're the creative director, or you're taking on more of a producing role and you're hiring people who are hopefully better than you to do the work, and you're providing support in other ways. So I think it was a couple years ago when I kind of reached that point where I had done enough jobs, I had first kind of found what I wanted to do in the film industry, which was produce and direct. (50:53): And I knew, okay, everything else that isn't happy to do it, but I'm not good at it. And I would much rather get better at producing and directing and find other people who can help with those other roles. And then once I found that, once I felt good about that decision for myself, I realized, you know what? I really am interested in trying to build a business beyond just myself. I would love to make this bigger than just me and be able to provide more services and be really selective about how I'm interacting and what I'm doing in the business. content: Maari Casey (08:29): I mean, I think a couple different things, and I think a lot of times I always say when people go from corporate setting or say an agency setting to being an independent business owner or a freelancer, there's a little bit of amnesia that happens on both sides. So vice versa when they go back and you kind of forget what it's like to be internal at a company when you go out to be an independent. And then same thing when you go back from being a freelancer into a company, you forget what it's like to be a freelancer. And what that means is when we get into a situation where a freelancer's frustrated with a client, usually what I'll have them do is say, just remember this person has probably worked 60, 70 hour weeks for the last month. They're probably working multiple jobs, especially right now because such a shortage of talent. (09:11): People are probably worked really, really hard. They're probably managing multiple meetings that shouldn't have been a meeting. They're dealing with all those things that you left to be a freelancer for. And just thinking through a little bit of empathy on what they're experiencing goes a long way. And the same thing for clients. When clients are frustrated with how quickly things are turning or project management or something, I say these people are dealing with multiple clients, you are one of their clients and so understand that they're managing a schedule across the board. So a lot of times I think with just managing a client, it's just really almost thinking proactively for them and understanding where they're coming from. So just assuming they're overworked, they're probably underpaid, they're probably in a bunch of meetings and running back and forth and managing your one vendor of many and then just thinking through how you can help them get ahead a lot of those issues. And that usually goes a long way just because then the conflict does come up. If the client feels like you're kind of in their corner and you're understanding and listening to them and you're not jumping into that panic mode that we've all experienced, then they're usually a lot more forgiving when something does deadlines move or a timeline changes. So just kind of thinking through that part of it.

Maari Casey (10:34): I think all of us have it at some point, depending on the client and how tired we are and stuff like that. I think the key is just to slow down and a lot of times, especially for coming out of agency, agency environments or working with agencies, there's that underlying panic mode vibe that we can get pulled into because of course we're service providers and we want to help them. We want to do a good job. So someone's panic can get you panicked, then everyone's panicking. I think the key is just to take a deep breath, especially when you get in a situation that's maybe getting a little intense, take a deep breath, walk away and get some perspective and say, okay, what do I need to do right now to help us get through this situation or to move the project forward, or how can I reframe this a little differently? And that goes a long way. I think when people jump into the panic mode and it causes more panic, then nobody benefits. At the end of the day, the freelancer is usually pushing work out that they're not happy with and the client's probably stressed out and not seeing all the things. So I think just take a breath, slow down, try to slow everybody down, be that calming presence in the room or on the call.

Cole Heilborn (11:37): Sure. So of all the different freelancers that you guys work with, how common is this challenge of managing clients? Is this prevalent throughout all of the verticals and all of the industries? Are some people really good at it, are some people, how difficult is this to do

Maari Casey (11:58): When you say some people, you're meaning some clients are being better at managing than others.

So it depends a lot of times on your just seniority and how long you've worked because you get used to having those meetings and possibly leading those meetings. If you're coming out of an agency environment as a junior or even a mid-level, sometimes you just haven't had that kind of exposure to run meetings, set expectations, talk through timelines. So if you haven't had that experience, then it's something you almost have to learn as you're going through things. And I see that usually when you have somebody come in who's just starting out as a freelancer, that's usually something we're aware of is like, okay, let's talk through how to set up expectations and how to run meetings and how to get ahead of it. So it really depends a lot of times on the experience they have coming into working independently, but some people are just better inclined to it too. Some people are used to, if they've been in leadership positions, even if it's not in a job, then sometimes they tend to be a little bit better or if they're coming from an account management role or something like that where they're used to leading in project managing.

content: Maari Casey (13:41): Well, okay, so the perfect way, I'm not even say the perfect way to run a project, totally different for everybody, but so I think the main part of it is expectation management, and usually when there is conflict in any kind of project, it's usually because expectations aren't being met and they haven't been really clear. So setting up a really clear SOW, here's the scope, here's the deliverables, here's the timeline, here's the budget, the three legged stool scenario, making sure those are really clear and reading through it again, having somebody look at it and be like, where is the potential confusion? Because it's really easy to miss that. It's really easy to be like, and here's the deliverables. Okay, what has constitute done? Is there a number of rounds that you're agreeing to before? It's a scope creep situation and it can feel a little bit, at least it did for me. (14:32): It can feel a little bit like judgy or non-trusting when you're like, oh, well maybe I'm going to put a kill fee in here, or I'm going to define milestone billing and what that means. But it's honestly, it's important because it's a CYA for you. It's also a CYA for the client. They can go back to that scope and say, you know what? You agreed in the scope to two rounds of revisions and we've only done one round of revision. That means I get another round of revision. So it's really nice to put all those things in paperwork and it feels sometimes a little bit too professional, like I'm being too fancy, but it's important because it will come back to you if you're not outlining those details clearly. So I would say just have a really clear scope of work, a really clear deliverables, really clear timeline because timeline can change the scope. (15:16): We've all been in situations where the timeline was a month and it became three months and then it became four months and it changes things. So being really clear about when timelines are set and then what that estimate and budget includes and where there might be room for a stock fee or an overage if I'm charging for talent or any of that kind of stuff.

This constitutes is the first round of review. Be really clear so that you can look back to your contract and say, remember we did that call. (15:56): That was the first round. The clearer you are, the better you'll be. And there's a Brene Brown quote that is being clear is kind and being unclear is unkind, and there's a reason why It's like when you're not clear, it leaves room for that miscommunication and missed expectations, and then all that icky stuff happens afterwards where you have to be like, no, I meant this. So being as clear as you possibly can be all the way through being really, really transparent with timeline feedback, expectations on the client side. So I'm giving you two days to send me feedback. If it goes longer than two days, it might push the timeline, which might change the overall project scope. So just being really clear where those things are. So a lot of times as creatives, we think we're communicating really clearly, but it's kind of soon as we're communicating in our head or to our friend. So putting it in an email, putting it in a document so you have something to go back to is really essential.

Maari Casey (18:13): Yeah, I think boundaries. I mean, you brought it up with the office hours. Boundaries are so important, and I think especially when we're starting out as independent freelancers, boundaries is one of the last things that we think about because we're just trying to get as much work, and I was like, yes, I will drive by your house and drop off that drive. I don't care if you live 500 miles away, I'll be there. You tend to sacrifice your own time because you don't quite know what it's worth yet. But I think setting boundaries early allows you to really build a business that's successful because it's hard to know how much your time is worth when your time is readily available for free to everybody. So setting up boundaries as far as office hours, response time, super key. Even if some people charge rush fees, if you're asking me to work through the weekend, that's no problem, but it's going to be this. Or if you're asking me to drop what I'm doing and turn something around and 24 hours, it's going to be this. It totally depends on what's important to you and how you want to run your business, but I think setting up boundaries. I don't want to receive text messages on my personal cell phone. You can email me, you can slack or discord me, but I'm not going to respond to a text message. Those types of things I think are really important.

Cole Heilborn (19:19): Interesting. So coupling expectations with scope of work, which are kind of one and the same, but I feel like it's a different type of expectation. You mentioned it earlier, but scope of work is super crucial because that defines what you're going to do and how much you're going to get paid for it. I think a term that everyone's familiar with is this idea of scope creep, but could you define what that is and the problem that many freelancers find themselves in around scope creep?

content: Maari Casey (19:58): I was like, you can be the kill feet, I'll be the scope creep. He was like, no, that's not. Yeah, I mean, scope creep is a real challenge and it's especially tough if you don't know how to handle it because what happens is usually if you've manage expectations clearly, then you're not going to run into that as often, but as you're learning and setting up your contracts, there'll be instances of that and honestly, you'll have clients who you've worked with for years that'll do that just because they're like, oh, Cole's my buddy and he's fine. Slide me some extra deliverables. And I think all you need to do is just be really clear, go up to them. I always say use it as an opportunity to upsell to your clients and say, Hey, I received your email about these additional changes or this additional round can totally do that. (20:45): Here's a timeline to get that done for you. And then now that we're making that change, I can go ahead and amend the contract that we currently have to include that plus the timeline, plus this additional fee, which I'm estimating as blank. Let me know if that sounds good for you. I'll go ahead and send that over for e-sign or whatever. So I would go ahead and just put that all into one thing. This is already happening and here's how I'm going to make it easier for you. I'm going to go ahead and amend our contract, send it over through DocuSign and we can get this rolling as opposed to making it feel like it's an awkward conversation, I would just say expect that they know that and if they push back and they say, oh, I'm sorry, I didn't realize this was a scope group, I need to go and get approval. (21:22): You can say, sounds good. I'll have this contract ready to go amended for whenever I hear back from you. Or if they do push back and they say, well, can we go ahead and do this under this SOW? Then you can say, actually no, this is outside of the scope. And you can see based on what you've done, if you can adjust what you're working on to include that and pull something out, we can adjust the current deliverables list to include this. If this is now a priority, it totally depends again on how much you want to work with the current contract, but I think once you start agreeing to things that aren't covered in the scope, then that's going to be happening more often. So I would just cut it off, no judgment. Again, think about this person's super busy, they don't realize it, they're just trying to get their stuff done and I appreciate people who are trying to get things done. I'm going to make it easier for them and just kind of go in with that attitude and then it won't be weird.

content:
Cole Heilborn (22:11): Gotcha. Is there a way to make a scope of work document that is a hundred percent watertight so that there's no room for misinterpretation or confusion?

Maari Casey (22:26): Probably not, because there's always a few things that are going to come up, but I mean not with scope creep because people will add things on just at the end or I think that the question that always comes up is what constitutes round one, round two, round two didn't really quite deliver all the things, and that's really for you to define as clearly as possible. And then if you feel like it's being pushed, pushed or taken advantage of, then you need to speak up. But I would just, again outlining what's the goal? What is the goal for this project? What does success mean? What is this is done, put it in the can, signed, sealed and delivered, what does that mean? And that's usually a conversation that you should have probably even before you write the SOW, that's your intro call where you're asking about the project, what does success look like for this project for you guys? (23:16): And then clear timing, when is this going to be delivered? When can we expect to review? I would always send over a timeline that's like, here's based on your goal end date, here's my timeline as it works within my schedule. Don't put that off on them. Then they're going to be like, they're going to squish it into three days. Give them a timeline and timeline and based the timeline, here's when check-ins are going to come and we're going to check it on Wednesday. We're going to show you all the work and then we're going to email you over the PDF. We're going to expect feedback by Friday. And then you can say, again, if we don't get feedback by Friday, if it gets pushed in the next week, it could adjust the timeline just to let you know, so timing, budget, rounds of revisions, how many rounds are you going to agree to, and then a clear deliverables list. (24:00): And sometimes you can also include what might constitute a scope change or sometimes you can put in like, okay, if you need extra cuts or something, if you need a couple cutdowns, it's going to be like this per cutdown, like a little la carte menu separately. But I would always put all those things in there and then if you are doing milestone billing, if you're billing up front because you need to cover talent or location or all the things, I would put all of that in the contract and say, here's what I'm going to invoice you. Here's what the invoice constitutes the first 25% or whatever, it's going to be expected upon receipt or net 30, blah blah, blah, blah. So I would put all that stuff in the SOW.

Here's what I've experienced. When I do do a meeting where I'm doing a review, we'll talk about this is the review meeting, number one, here's the expectation. I always set agendas for my meetings just so they know that it's really clear, here's what my role is, here's what your role is, and then that way at the end of the meeting you can say, okay, cool. This is round. This is round one, good to go. And then when you send a follow-up email outline all the stuff that was happening in that meeting, and we'd be like, we're going to go ahead and send the first invoice by first amount looking forward to your feedback. So you're giving them opportunities to say, oh wait, we don't really feel like this is a solid round one or whatever. But hopefully since you've outlined it clearly that it won't be a big issue. If they come back and they're like, well, it's round 1.5, then you can say, well, we don't, no, actually this is round one. That's when you need to push back and just stick to you and say, we've covered all the deliverables for round one. We had a feedback session, we received your feedback, so we're going to move into round two.

Cole Heilborn (26:28): Gotcha. In an instance like that, do you always send a follow-up email recapping a meeting, the CYA email, or do you just leave that up or do you just end the conversation and then not follow up in a written format?

So if I can say, okay, well I'm going to follow up with you, then it's putting me in a driver's seat as opposed to me sitting back on Friday and being like, I wonder when they're going to email me. (32:33): So Zapier is this kind of InBetween tool. I should have my operations talking through this better. It just talks about managing those. There's a great book on negotiations too, and I think that those are really important things to learn how to do. One of the first things I think I would recommend doing, and I still have to remind myself of this, is even though you're possibly a one person business, you need to separate yourself mentally and take a mindset of like, I am Cole. I work for blank. Or I am Murray. I work for company. And separate yourself from the business so that you can make better decisions of what's best for the business. If your goal is to run a business for as long as you want to work, then sometimes you're going to have to make decisions or calls that maybe Mari would feel really uncomfortable making because I'm a nice person and I want everyone to be happy, but it's better for UNY if I make this call. (39:34): So it's good to do that because it allows you to have conflict conversations and negotiations from a point of view that's not emotional. It's like, sorry, this is company's policy is blank. It's not personal, the policy of the business, and I want the business to be successful, so I'm going to back the policies. So it's good to just mentally separate yourself across the board for a lot of things, finances, all that stuff so that you can make decisions independent. It's easier said than done because of course you are your business and your business is you. But when I get into a situation that's a conflict or difficult, I'll sit down and I'll be like, okay, what is the policy that we're following? What is best for this business? Even if it makes me uncomfortable? So that's the first thing I would suggest doing. And then it's really putting everything on the table. (40:21): If you're getting into a situation where you, maybe you're negotiating a scope creep or the client comes back and is unhappy with the work, then I think you need to look at what's the longevity of the client? Is this a client that's relationship that's really worth protecting?

I think there's ways to do it cordially where it's like, okay, well it wasn't a good fit for us and this is just kind of keeping it more one-to-one versus blasting it out on social media and that kind of stuff. I've noticed that you've been frustrated with this type of work. How can we address this? What can I do to fix this? And it sounds like you can kind of, I'll say blame, but you can put things on the company and say, well, this isn't the company's policy. Even if personally I would love to be able to do this for you, if it's, I mean you say policy, it's some written rules somewhere that sounds very fancy. What if I'm in a conversation with a client and I have never come across this circumstance before, but I'm like, I don't know how to respond to this. It feels a little off, but I haven't ever considered this before because I think we find ourselves in those situations frequently or maybe, hopefully not frequently, but inevitably at some point.

Maari Casey (43:30): Yeah, I think it's okay to walk away and think about it. Sometimes the tough part can be feeling the need to respond in the moment and defend, and then you can kind of feel the vibe changing. I think it's okay to say, this is interesting to look at. Let me go back and noodle a bit for a little bit and I'll follow up with you and we can send an email or I'll follow up with another phone call, but give yourself some space to take a step back and look at all those things. Look at the viability of the client, look at the relationship you have, look at the work that's been done. But sometimes you just can't do that in the heat of the moment. I have a public speaking coach, we're talking through breathing. But a lot of times when you get in those situations, conflict situations, you stop breathing because it's like a fight or flight mentality or body takes over and it's like, I must run away and defend. You stop breathing. So it's interesting because your brain actually starts to shut down a little bit, not taking deep breaths. So it's good just to say, you know what? I think this is a good thing for us to look at. Let me take a step back and get back to you in 24, 48 hours with a follow-up. And that's totally fine. That's a good way to get back and actually reflect on it without having to make a quick second decision.

(45:46): We'd love to resolve this project, finish on a high note, whatever it might be. But I would just go direct at the problem. And that's usually the best way to resolve it. It's when you feel uncomfortable. I've learned When you feel uncomfortable, just lean into the uncomfortableness, just be uncomfortable for a little bit and just push through it. And that's usually the best way as opposed to avoiding and emails, and I'm not a fan of emails and text messages to resolve conflict. I think that's super dangerous ground. So I would do a face-to-face or video call or a phone call and just resolve it, which everybody hates because everyone loves just to send it and hopefully it lands, but it's a lot quicker just to get on the phone and be like, Hey, you know what? This just isn't working out and I know you do a good business. I know I run a good business and I want us both to be successful, so let's figure out a way forward so we can finish this up and wrap up a relationship at the end of the day.

That's one of the things I wanted to do with in-company was when we work with contractors and freelancers, we pay everybody net 30 and we manage the back end of chasing down payments and very good pay periods. I was like, as an independent business owner, I still need to pay my mortgage on time and my coworking space lease and all the things. So getting paid regularly, super important. And we should, the few times that this has happened for us and for me, and it's very few because again, you should have a pretty solid understanding of who your client is before you jump into a project with them, you really have to sit down and evaluate a couple other things. You have to evaluate the relationship. (48:51): You have to evaluate the work that's been done. And if you're working with subs, if you're working with other vendors, that can be a problem depending on the scope of what's owed. So you need to look at all those things and evaluate, is my time going after them in small claims court worth? The time I'm going to lose is recouping that money worth spending hours, days, weeks, going back and forth to court, managing documents, pushing them out, legal fees? Is that worth it? And sometimes it is and sometimes it's not. And one of the hardest things is to walk away from a situation where you know that you should be getting paid and you're not, but you're like, you know what? Me spending the next 40 hours of my time to chase down this $10,000 invoice is not going to be worth it at the end of the day. (49:35): And I know I'm going to spend the next 40 days just angry, angry, and mad, and not sleeping well anyway. So sometimes you just have to say it's not worth it and walk away, and that's really hard to do. Make sure you write off that as bad debt on your taxes so that you're getting that off as a tax thing. But hopefully that relationship that whatever you've experienced and learned will help you in your next projects with future clients and being aware and setting expectations again, it hasn't happened very often does happen. Hopefully it's happening less and less as independent. Working becomes bigger, but that's the biggest thing. You just have to evaluate all those things and make a decision and then when you make that decision, don't look back. You're like, you know what? It's not worth my time. This is a bad situation. This is a client I'm not going to work with again. And I will tell my friends, I won't bash them. I'll tell my friends, be cautious working with this person and I'll move on. And I think it's a decision you have to make and like I said, not look back.

They're relatively well known, or they're up and coming within the outdoor industry and they are known. So I do think that a lot of those traditional channels in terms of how are you going to get seen by the right people, LinkedIn is obviously huge. Instagram, having blogs, websites, I am occasionally, especially from a photography perspective, quite blown away at the number of photographers that don't have websites or don't have up-to-date websites. But I think just if you have those channels and you're involved in an industry, I would say there's very few times where we actually get reached out to by somebody and we haven't heard of 'em, especially, I mean, origin is quite core to the ski industry and the travel and tourism industry. John Entwistle (10:51): For sure. Yeah, so I think from when do we work with freelancers perspective, there's really two. And honestly, we work with a ton of freelancers at Origin. So there really are two kind main areas where we would tend to work with freelancers. One is definitely more on the specialized skill side of things. So if there is a specific project or a concept that we come up with that we're looking to execute on, and we just don't have the internal expertise to do that. One of the main examples that comes up quite frequently right now is FPV drones. We are constantly looking for FPV drone operators and skilled FPV camera operators because it is something that is just kind of a hot button topic these days when it comes to marketing. And so yeah, that would definitely be one area is when we have to go outside of just our core service offering and really find a contractor or a freelancer that can fill that gap. (11:53): And then the second piece would be just more of a capacity issue, or not even an issue, but just a capacity opportunity where maybe all of our writers are currently tapped or we have all of our writers assigned to something else, and we will be looking for just really more capacity in one of our core skills. I will say that in that second instance, we do tend to have a pretty trusted pool of freelancers that we will go back to over and over, and we've developed relationships with those people or people over the years. I think even if you go to our website, you'll see that we're always on the search for what we call perm lancers, and they're just, honestly, sometimes they feel like fixtures of the origin family, but they're not on our payroll, they're not salaried employees, and they're much more on that kind of contract to contract basis.

content: John Entwistle (25:01): For sure. So I do think, and again, going back to the agency seeming like this big scary place, we really aren't, and we love beer. We love coffee at agencies, honestly, developing relationships with people within agencies and just a lot of those things are two-way streets. It's like I talked about how we're constantly looking at these feeds and looking at what exists out there and what innovation is happening. And a lot of times, honestly, just sitting down for a coffee with somebody, it can be a great two-way street. So I have a bunch of different peers, and for me, it's interesting because I do play on both sides of that fence. And I think a lot of my photography peers look at me and will call me and ask to go for a beer and just talk about what's going on in the agency world. (25:53): And then I conversely talk to them about what's going on in the photography world. Then we develop just really good two-way relationships. And again, I think that is, so you're never going to get a job from just one of those coffees unless the coffee just happens to be an interview and you aren't aware of it. But it is just that consistency and consistently having those conversations is really what just starts to develop those relationships. You start to become that voice of reason. And so I think definitely from a freelancer perspective, just identifying who the right people to be having those conversations with are, right? If you are a designer or a writer and you're able to have coffee with a creative director and an associate creative director, but it doesn't always have to be at the top levels of an agency either. Oftentimes, if you're a writer and you have a friend who's a writer within an agency and you're just having a conversation about what's going on in an industry, I've seen it before where some of our junior writers have come into brainstorms and said, oh, well my friend was telling me about this recent piece that came out in blah, blah, blah. (27:03): And they bring that to the table and all of a sudden it gets people thinking like, oh, well, who's this friend that recommended this thing? And what skill sets do they have? And would they actually just be the right person for this project? So I do think as much as agencies might seem like these big and scary things, even the hierarchies within agencies, I don't even want to know how many emails some of our creative directors get every day of just, here's my portfolio, check this out. So not being afraid to make those relationships at varying levels within the agency, because that can definitely bring a lot of value that you might not necessarily expect.

Cole Heilborn (27:41): Aside from creative directors, are there other roles within an agency that are kind of those key holders towards those relationships with freelancers that people should be considering?

John Entwistle (27:52): Yeah, I mean I think the creative director is definitely the final decision maker, so that is for sure the ticket. But yeah, like I said, I think really any of those kind of specialist positions where you can be having just those inspirational industry type conversations can be super effective. And then more so if you look at more my realm on the strategy and the account side of things, those conversations and those relationships can for sure be valuable. I would say they're not quite as valuable as they are on the creative side because what we'll end up doing is just making those relationships with people on the creative side. So ultimately the creative side is where you will need to be. But I would say honestly, any kind of door you can get, any kind of relationship you can make can be super valuable. (28:43): And then the one side of things that does exist in agencies is really more the resourcing. And we have people within our agency and our resource directors, our resource managers, and their sole job is to figure out who to put on projects. And they ultimately are the people who are responsible for those contracts, but they don't have a lot of say or weigh in terms of the skill sets that are required in those. So that would be maybe one trap that I would watch out for is just often if you're on LinkedIn and you see resource manager, resource director, you might think, oh, if I can get in front of that person, then maybe somehow I can get put onto a project and they can again route those to the right conversations. But they're definitely not the ones who, and they get inundated with things, with portfolios and with requests and all of that. So yeah, definitely keeping it much more on the what is your path to talking with somebody on the creative team. And yeah, that's for sure where I think the most kind of fruitful relationships can exist.

content:
Cole Heilborn (29:49): Gotcha. Well, I'm sure many folks can relate to receiving LinkedIn spam messages or spam emails. Obviously if you're not on an agency's radar at some point you have to, well, many people reach out to an agency and say, Hey, here's my portfolio as you just described. What are good ways to do that and what are bad ways to do that?

John Entwistle (30:14): Yeah, for sure. I think when you look at if you're a hundred percent right, there is a lot, we just get a lot of volume of requests for these things. And I think really understanding just generally how an agency works and I think specifically to origin, that's how I'll talk because that's kind of where I'm at right now. Not all agencies work exactly the same, but I think generally looking at the outreach to an agency as more of an inquisitive exercise as opposed to an expert or a, I dunno, you could call it bullish, kind of like, I'm going to come in here and I'm going to make an impact. It's such a fine line when you look at freelancers, and this is something that I often struggle with on the photography side of things, is just looking at, okay, if I want to work for me, I tend to work more with brands than I do with agencies. (31:15): I generally only work with Origin. But yeah, I think when you do look at it, it's like, okay, well how much of this approach should I take in terms of trying to figure out what is actually going to be required here as opposed to I know the answers or I have this solution. Because so much of the value that agencies bring is really around the collaboration and just the vetting of ideas, the development of ideas, and it really is a team effort in terms of getting to the final solution. And so a lot of the time we will, or not a lot of the time, but we quite often will have just people who reach out to us with a, I have this solution, I know you work with brand X and this is how you should do this, or this is how I would do this. (32:04): And I would say, it's so rare that you get that right, and it's not because it's not possible to get it right, but it's just because our process is so much more iterative and so much more we want input from a whole bunch of different people on the team to really get to that well-balanced approach. And going back to what we were talking about earlier, that's ultimately how agencies land on these really polished high quality creative pieces is because it has been vetted from a bunch of different angles. We've had copywriters look at it, we've had strategists at it, we've had account people look at it, we've had creative directors look at it, and it really is kind of the input of that broader team that really gets us to that final product. And so I think when we're looking at freelance kind of relationships and when we look at how we want those people to be involved, especially when it's not just on the execution side of things, but when it is in more of that actual creative contribution perspective, we really want to make sure that people are actually going to be valuable and effective players in that space. (33:13): So we do want them to bring their expertise, but we don't necessarily look for people who are just saying, this is exactly what we should do. You might get that right 1% of the time, and honestly congratulations if you do, but realistically, it's just probably going to fall pretty flat because yeah, it's not like we're looking for the right answers. We're looking to collaborate with people on getting to the right answers.

Cole Heilborn (33:39): Okay, that makes sense. Is there a recent example that you could pull from where you got an email or an inquiry from someone and it was very well thought through, very well put together and it cut through some of the volume of emails you had received that week?

John Entwistle (33:59): For sure. I think the best examples that we get really are purpose built portfolio examples. So whether it be a really well curated example or a really well curated set of previous portfolio examples, I'm working right now in really specifically in the social content space. And so we actually just had, and we've just gone through kind of an interview process where we're not sure if we're going to hire a contractor or if we're going to hire a freelancer, or sorry a freelancer or if we're going to hire a full-time employee. But some of the strongest elements that really came forward were these kind of curated profiles of, okay, here's what I've done for previous clients or yeah, it generally is work of here's what I've done for previous clients and here's how I've kind of curated this in a, okay, I did this work for Apple, let's say because it's the most famous brand in the world, and I created this TikTok for them. (35:07): I created these Instagram stories, I created this long form YouTube video or was involved in the creation of these things. And really kind of showing the thought process behind that because I think that's so much what we evaluate for is the thought process and how you're able to think as opposed to the execution of it. And conversely to that, I've seen bad examples where somebody will say, I took your client and I created this suite of social ads for them. And a lot of the time we can start to see the thought process there. But again, it's really that thought process that we're trying to evaluate as opposed to the end result. Because like I said, it is such a team effort to really get to that end result. And then I think too, just looking at the broader portfolio, once you get into specific skills like photography or writing or design, obviously we will want to make sure that this person is competent within those spaces. But again, I think it does go back to that really just showing us that you have the capacity to think within just a process that we'll actually work for or have a thought process that will work with our team as opposed to really just coming straight out of the gun or straight out of the barrel with here's exactly what I think you need.

(38:39): And so I think just trying the right fits for the right projects. And so as a freelancer, if you are trying to just stay top of mind, honestly, finding or sending those things over to us that we will potentially use as inspiration are the things that will make us go, aha, this person sent this piece of inspiration and we're working on this project and this is what we should do. And then there will be the occasional time where we have a project that all of a sudden lands and we're scrambling to get the right people on it. And if you're top of mind, then that's going to be kind of who we're going to. So yeah, I would say definitely focusing on that, kind of reaching out with purpose, not just reaching out with requests or reaching out with any kind of specific, I dunno asks or anything, but more reaching out with relevant pieces. I have seen that overcooked as well. I've definitely seen people who have replied to case studies that we've put out or whatever, and they send us a 16 page essay on what they thought about our case study. Sure, I appreciate it, but it just, it's just not a valuable use of anybody's time. So yeah, I think again, it is about that balance, but reaching out with purpose is for sure a good thing.

So yeah, again, I think it's just that balance of finding the right timing, understanding when some of these things might actually start to come up. If you're pitching us on doing a ski campaign photo shoot in April, chances are we're probably not thinking about that. John Entwistle (42:52): Well, actually maybe in terms of things that are maybe a little bit more old school, definitely the whole idea of a physical portfolio is something that I know that there was a big focus on probably honestly only 10 years ago. And occasionally we will still get a letter in the mail of printed images. And I'm honestly a bit on the fence of that because I do get the allure and the excitement of having something tangible in your hands. But at the same time, when you look at the actual payback or ROI on actually getting some of those things out there, I think there's just definitely a major decline in terms of what that ROI is right now. And so I think just definitely looking at having that strong web presence, having strong social media channels, like I said off the top, I'm blown away sometimes by the lack of just online portfolios that a lot of people have. (43:54): And yeah, I think just the value of really being able to express yourself online in an effective way is just such a valuable skill that I think is not lost on a lot of people, but it's definitely lost from time to time. And I think too, looking at the nature of the work, so much of the work that we do now is digital. So if you're able to actually express the work that you do appropriately through digital mediums, then we're able to actually look at that explicitly against how we would express that work digitally through a client's lens. So yeah, I think just really that kind of honing in on that digital portfolio as opposed to some of the more traditional print elements or in-person, like the art of an email versus the art of the phone call. As sad as that might be, it is just kind of the way that times are going for sure.

And honestly, cold emails are not a bad thing. I would say we definitely get a lot of them as an overall agency. I would say there's massive inconsistencies in terms of who those get addressed to or where they get routed through the agency, but we're pretty good at distributing those internally. And occasionally you'll just get an email that's forwarded from somebody else in the agency that says, Hey, so-and-so reached out. Just take a look through their stuff and feel free to add them to your list if you have it or if you have interest in what they're putting together. (46:08): And so I would say unless you're completely off the mark or you're going in with that really bullish approach like we were talking about earlier, then a cold email can definitely be a good thing. And again, I would make sure that that gets followed up with, can we go for coffee? Should we meet up for a beer? Here are my social channels, here's my email newsletter. What are those kind of areas that you can really open up the doors for those ongoing relationships? Because definitely just a, here's a cold email and I'm expecting work out of it and I'm never going to talk to you again. Those work 0% of the time. So really using that to kind of open up that relationship and that conversation can be valuable for sure.

You have a portfolio, you have a website, okay, how are you actually showing yourself out there? And I think generally in the way that Instagram especially is moving, definitely the feed side of things tends to be a lot more curated. And that's one of the big transitions that I've seen for myself in photography recently, is I used to post to Instagram three times a day and I used to go out and shoot stuff specifically for Instagram, whereas recently I actually went back through and deleted, I dunno, 75% of my Instagram feed and really just left that as a curated overview of what I'm about and who I am. (51:26): And so it really does just kind of sit there as a portfolio piece or a portfolio example. You tag people in stories, they repost your stories, they're happy that you're sharing content. So a lot of the brands that I do work with, that's definitely like, it's who you keep in touch with or it's how you keep in touch with them. A lot of the time's just by tagging them in stories of either imagery and well very candid imagery. It can be me on the skin track or it can be me behind the scenes on a shoot, but yeah, you're tagging whatever company it is that you're working with, and I think a lot of that just kind of more organic and true to yourself, content that exists on Instagram is really interesting.

Kaim York-Feirn (06:07): As the social media coordinator, I work very closely with our marketing and creative teams on our strategy across social media in general. So that includes our blog, our Instagram channel, our Facebook page, and then also looking at new and emerging platforms such as TikTok. Okay,

Cole Heilborn (06:25): Gotcha. So we connected a couple months ago and we started talking about some possible topics and this idea of finding your brand voice or taking the brand voice of a company and figuring out how to present it on social. We're going to kind of dive into the weeds in this topic, but first if you could just set up what is the challenge with this idea that you work on with brands day to day?

Kaim York-Feirn (06:51): Yeah, I think the challenge when defining brand voice is brands often want to put the cart before the horse. And by that I mean deciding to post on a certain platform before they have a strategy for that specific platform and knowing how they would describe their brand to customers. So I think it's really important to come up with adjectives that describe who you are as a brand. Are you adventurous and playful? Do you create high quality products? Are you forward thinking? Then come up with the adjectives that you are not, we're not frilly, we're not serious, we're not elitist, those types of things. And so the biggest challenge that I see is brands trying to get on emerging platforms before they have established who they are internally.

Cole Heilborn (07:43): Gotcha. I guess I'm thinking about Clubhouse as you're talking about emerging platforms, that seems to be a platform that emerged recently. I don't even know if it's still active or not, but it feels like when that popped up, it became all the rage and everyone jumped to it, and I think there was a lot of people, a lot of individual personalities that were on it, maybe more so than brand voices. I'm curious in that instance, did you see any brands trying to figure that out?

Kaim York-Feirn (08:10): I did see quite a few brands on Clubhouse, and it's funny that you bring that up because that's a perfect example of a platform that became all the rage and then kind of died out. So people jumped onto Clubhouse without really knowing or understanding what the platform was and they learned as they went, which is an okay strategy. But I think that when you're talking about platforms that stick around Instagram and TikTok and Facebook, it's very important to have a cohesive posting strategy in terms of what do you want to sound like? Is your audience there and how can we meet them there and create engaging content for that specific platform? So Clubhouse was more of a interaction platform where you got on and you could have discussions with other people about a very specific topic, but you had to be invited. It was also exclusive. I remember getting an invite from someone that worked at our PR agency and I was so excited, but then I got on and I didn't really understand how to use the platform. There wasn't a how to or instructions on how to be invited to a specific room or how to start your own room. And so while I was excited by it and excited to follow the brands that we're posting, I never fully grasped or understood the platform.

Cole Heilborn (09:38): That seems to be a common story, does it not? A platform pops up and it's awesome, and then it just kind of disappears into the ether. Why is that? Why does some catch and stick and change everything and why does some just get us all excited and then we delete it three months later?

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (09:57): I think a lot of it has to do with the way that we interact with each other. It's constantly changing. So when you look at the development of Instagram, it started very much as this platform to post images with inspirational captions. Brands often would use quotes and lots of hashtags. The feed was chronological and it has morphed into more of a storytelling platform where you now have reels and you have video and there was IGTV for a while and now there's still a way to post longer form video content, but you're starting to see the way that people interact with each other change. And so I think that that's a big catalyst for whether a new platform will stick or not. Are you meeting your current audience where they want to interact with your brand?

Cole Heilborn (10:51): Interesting. So I got to imagine if I'm a social media app developer, I could develop something that is either behind the times or too far ahead of where society is at and it's maybe finding that sweet spot that kind of pushes people's imagination and opportunity without going too far or creating something that's kind of a dinosaur.

Kaim York-Feirn (11:16): Yeah, it's funny that you say that about a mix of different concepts because I feel like that's TikTok Vine is another great example of a social media platform that popped up and then kind of died. I don't truly understand why that faded away or why brands never jumped on that, but TikTok has replaced Vine in that sense of creating short form video. And when TikTok first launched, I think the longest that you could post was a 15 second video and now has evolved into up to three minutes worth of content. And so that really speaks to the rise of video and people wanting to watch longer form content and actually sticking around and watching the full thing if it is relatable.

And from that you start to understand who we are, who we aren't. I think a lot of people understand that concept. That's something we've talked about on the show quite a bit, and there's obviously some pretty amazing brands out there that we could all look at and say, yeah, we know who they are and what their voice is. But getting more to your level where how do you take, let's say a brand book and if you're brought in to start to try to understand how are we talking on these platforms? How do you start?

Kaim York-Feirn (12:55): That's a great question, Cole. And to me, there are four main ingredients. The first is defining your brand mission next, your vision, and finally your values, and then finally looking at your audience demographics. So as long as your business has a mission, vision and values from that, you can glean those adjectives that I was referencing earlier and start to define who your brand is, how you want to be perceived by your customers. And then that final piece is looking at where your audience engages most online and meeting them in that space.

Cole Heilborn (13:37): Okay. So can we use Rough Wear as an example? How do you show up on a place like Instagram and how did you get to that conclusion?

I think one key thing to point out before I talk a little bit about rough wear is that it's okay for your brand to have a different voice on different platforms, and I'd love to dig into that a little bit more later. But when it comes to Instagram, I would say that rough wear is very adventurous and playful and forward thinking, but we also create very high quality products. And so we want to display that to our customers, and that comes across in our captions, in the photos that we choose, in the way that we interact in dms. So for example, we are a brand that is okay using emojis in our dms and we are starting to use them a little bit more in our captions. And that's something that's a bit newer strategy, but when you look at our audience demographics, we do tend to relate to a little bit younger audience that is also pretty equally split between male and female, but emojis are huge when you're looking at Gen Z, millennials, et cetera. And so that's a great way to come off as relatable and as somebody who is also knowledgeable, but meeting that customer in their particular space,

Cole Heilborn (15:06): It's wild to think that, I mean, I get it, but it's wild to think that you can spend that much time trying to decide should I use an emoji smiley face and how will that connect or not connect with who we're talking to?

Kaim York-Feirn (15:21): Yeah, and one of the adjectives I would also use to describe us is friendly. And so while we're not necessarily seeking to be your friend per se, we want to relate to people in a way that they would talk to their friends. So we'll use emojis in our responses. We will try to be a little bit less formal and more personal. I think that sometimes there are customer service teams that use very copy and paste responses to questions, and I believe there is a time and a place for that. But when we're talking about Instagram and Instagram dms, that's a place where you can be a lot more personable and treat that person more like a one-on-one conversation.

content:
Cole Heilborn (16:06): Sure. So how did you arrive at those adjectives? If we were to back up? How do those adjectives on Instagram support rough wear's overall brand?

Kaim York-Feirn (16:17): So thinking back to our adjectives, rough Wear is a very adventurous and playful brand because when you think about dogs, you think about those aspects. So they're very dury and goofy and playful, and they are your best friend. They go everywhere with you. You want to take them on lots of adventures. They are your adventure buddy. And so that was pretty easy for us to come up with those adjectives when thinking about Instagram, because we not only want to be relatable, but we also want to show that the outdoors are a space for every person, every dog, every type of adventure

Cole Heilborn (16:55): Sidebar. But do you guys get flooded with user generated content of people and their dogs?

Kaim York-Feirn (17:02): Yes. Our dms are full of people tagging us in stories, people sending us pictures. It's very common as a dog owner to be proud and think your dog is the best dog. They're all good boys and good girls. And so that's one of my favorite jobs or favorite parts about this job is people submitting photos of their dogs doing different things, seeing them go skiing together and go hiking, and maybe it's a puppy going swimming for the first time, or a dog who's sticking its tongue out and just looks super derpy. We get tons of different photos and UGC content submitted.

Cole Heilborn (17:42): As a fellow dog owner, I think my wife and I, yeah, like most dog owners think our dog is the best and is the weirdest, cutest dog out there and no other dog compares. But yeah, I don't know if that trend has become more popular, but I feel like in the last, I dunno, five or 10 years, maybe that's become more of a thing, maybe not. Maybe that's just Instagram has become more of a thing in that time, so we see more of it.

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (18:11): I will 100% agree, Bella, my Bernice Mountain dog is the cutest, dirtiest, best girl, best dog on the planet best. So anytime people want to have a play date, I'm always down. But I think Instagram, like you're saying, is that place where we express that and we share our joy of adventuring with our dogs.

Cole Heilborn (18:34): Yeah. So you mentioned the idea that a brand can have a different flavor of a voice on different platforms. How does that break down for a rough wear?

Kaim York-Feirn (18:44): Sure. So I want to talk about the platforms in general, and I can use a rough wear example when we're talking about it, but Instagram is a much more video oriented platform. It's very story forward, more aspirational. So I would say that rough wear, we'll post more of our video content there. We're looking at doing some more reels and creating user generated content. This is where we really want to relate and share our customer's stories, our customer's journeys, our employees stories. And so I think that when you're talking about social media, you also can't really ignore the conversation about sales. I will say that rough wear is less focused on social media as a sales platform, which I love. And it's much more of an educational platform where you can come to learn about the brand and start your consumer purchase journey. But for us, it's a place where Instagram is the place where we want you to come and be able to see yourself in our content.

Cole Heilborn (19:52): Gotcha.

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (19:53): I guess moving on to Facebook, I would say that that's more of an informational and educational platform. You'll often see brands creating private Facebook groups when you're looking at their updates, they're about products or new blog posts. So thinking about the way that I interact with Facebook as a consumer, I'm looking to learn about a brand's contact information or their hours or look at their product offering. Did they launch a new product yet? I'm in a few private Facebook groups where brands will share exclusive deals and do giveaways and offer discounts. So more educational, less personal and storytelling forward. I'll say that TikTok as one of the newer platforms is a place where we go to watch relatable content. They use popular sounds, music. I think it's way more funny. There's a lot of one-liners. You'll often hear sounds that shoot from the hip. I think that it's a place where brands can let loose a little bit, be a little bit less serious. And then Twitter sadly I think is about to go away RIP, but that's the place where you would share some of your shorter updates, maybe an opinion or two.

Cole Heilborn (21:14): Interesting. Do you think that's on the decline?

Kaim York-Feirn (21:17): I do. I have seen over the last three years that decline in the usage of Twitter, especially in brand strategy. Rough wear has a Twitter account, but I don't think it's been used since 2016 or so. So going back to that concept of meeting your customers where they are and evaluating whether a platform is right for your brand strategy, I think Twitter is a perfect example of that. It's not going to fit into everybody's strategy, especially as we move and evolve into video being the king or queen of content.

Cole Heilborn (21:56): It's funny, I completely forgot that Twitter was a thing. I've never understood it. That's not saying a whole lot, but I always think of it as a platform where the president posts stuff.

Kaim York-Feirn (22:10): Well, it's also kind of like Google Plus. I will hear about Google Plus in some marketing webinar and I'm like, oh my gosh, that did used to be a thing. And when I worked at an agency, we very much had a Google Plus strategy, but that died years ago. And I think Twitter has the same fate.

Cole Heilborn (22:34): Is a place like LinkedIn something that a brand like Rough Wear considers or how does that fit into the equation?

Kaim York-Feirn (22:42): Yes, I'm glad you brought that up. LinkedIn, in the last couple years, I've seen evolve from being more of a personal networking tool to much more of a brand networking tool. And so as Rough Wear's strategy goes, we do post on LinkedIn and we will share some of our blog posts, definitely our job openings and career opportunities and the occasional internal announcement or things that that we're excited about. And I have definitely started to engage more personally with LinkedIn in the last year or so. I think it's a great place to go and read news articles. Ironically, that's where I learned about a lot that's going on in the marketing world or the stocks. That's where I learned about the avocado stuff. So I definitely do think that brands have a place on LinkedIn.

Cole Heilborn (23:42): I think it's become one of my favorite places to go. I think it's the only place that I actively engage or try to my best to keep up with posting something.

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (23:53): I definitely think it's a platform where you can go to get different opinions on things. So I know that one of the big topics right now in marketing is whether to pay ambassadors or if Gear Exchange is still an acceptable way of doing those programs. And so I was reading an article this morning and there were close to 50 comments on it, and I'll say, I didn't know about 80% of the people commenting, but it's really good and interesting to glean information from people's different perspectives. And so you never know who's going to see your posts on LinkedIn. It's not like Facebook where it only gets shown to the people that are following you when you post on LinkedIn. It kind of just goes into more of the vast network. And so again, yeah, I think it's a great place to look and get different perspectives on a particular topic or story.

Cole Heilborn (24:52): So correct me if I'm wrong, but Facebook used to have that sort of an algorithm correct, that LinkedIn has now, and I feel like that's one of the reasons why folks love LinkedIn is because it is let's say more organic. Do you feel like LinkedIn realizes that and they'll hang on to that algorithm or will they go the more Facebook route in the future?

Kaim York-Feirn (25:14): I certainly hope they hang on to the good thing they have going for them right now. The interesting thing about Facebook, I'll agree with what you said, and I think it really changed for them when they went to the pay to play model and you started seeing a lot more brands doing paid advertising and Facebook boosted the types of ads that they were offering. So you went from a single image ad to being able to now do a carousel ad and video ads. And then a couple years ago they introduced Canvas, which I believe is now called the Instant Experience, where you click through what looks like a single image ad, but then it takes you to a landing page, which you can look exactly like your website, which is more experience oriented. So yeah, I'll say that Facebook now is much more of an experience for the customer, whereas LinkedIn is still the more traditional news, chronological traditional way to get your news.

content:
Cole Heilborn (26:21): I mean, all these platforms are constantly changing and evolving. Does that make it tough as a marketer if you're like, okay, LinkedIn today is X and Facebook is X. Well, in a week from now they could be totally different. And if your voice is kind of following the platform and the audience and it's this equation, how do you manage the platforms changing?

Kaim York-Feirn (26:43): Oh my gosh, I am laughing so hard right now. It's a challenge. I don't envy anybody else who's in my position who has a social media manager title. We are constantly subscribed to different newsletters and we're reading about how the algorithms change week to week. Instagram is about to go back to chronological, which I think is a really interesting update for 'em. They also are about to introduce a new style of feed where you can click different buttons to see the people you follow versus explore and other things. So it is constantly evolving. We are constantly reading articles and trying to keep up on what's new. But going back to how we started this conversation, I think that's why it's really important to know who your brand is so that you can evaluate whether a platform is still working for you or if there is a shiny new object, be able to evaluate it with logic and say, yes, this is something that we want to pursue, or this is something we want to keep an eye on and let some other people try it first. I think it's completely okay for a brand to be a late adopter. You don't have to jump on these trends every single time.

Cole Heilborn (28:08): So I feel like that idea goes against maybe the advice that is out there all heard like, oh man, if only you were on the ground floor with Instagram, you could, I don't know, have billions of followers. That seems to be a great motivation to try to jump on something new. But you're suggesting waiting and a pause is okay.

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (28:32): I definitely think a pause is okay. And a possible good example of this is the blue check mark that Instagram has added to what they call verified profiles. So when that feature was first released, it was released to help consumers identify whether a brand was real or if it was a fake account. But as we evolve and time goes on and we all continue posting on these platforms, it has become much less important. I think that Blue check mark was kind of that shiny object for a while where it was like, oh yeah, I want that. How do I get that? It's elusive. We are this real brand, but we can't seem to get this blue check mark. And I remember in my time at Osprey, I spent years trying to get a blue check mark and then was finally able to get it through working with our PR agency, and it seemed like it was almost too easy or too good to be true the way that that happened. (29:38): So now as a consumer, when I look at something like that, I'm like, well, what is the true value of that check mark? Do brands really need to have that? Do consumers really care about that? And so to bring that back to this concept of evaluating whether a platform is good for you or not, I think it's okay to watch and see how an idea evolves because maybe it's not so important to have that blue check mark. Maybe you don't need to be on TikTok. Maybe you're not ready to be on TikTok. And one thing that I have definitely seen is brands who will jump on a platform or jump on a trend too early where they're not ready and they create content and they get hyped about it and they do it for a while, but then you see it die off and you're like, oh, well, what happened to X brand on TikTok? They haven't released a new video in months, and I was really excited about following them. And so then all of a sudden that excitement for the consumer dies out and we move on to the next thing.

Cole Heilborn (30:38): It sounds like playing the long game and maybe being more consistent is more important than jumping on something new.

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (30:47): I would say for brands, consistency is key. I would rather as a social media marketer, be consistent and focus my time on one or two platforms, then try to be on five and have a very inconsistent strategy. So I guess to give you an example earlier, I think podcasting actually is a perfect example. So while it might not necessarily be a brand, I think an individual can also count or where you'll see a show pop up and they give you five or six episodes and then they say, okay, we'll be back for season two on X day. And that day comes and that show isn't back. So I'm a really big True Crime podcast listener, and that happens quite often. There's a show called Up and Vanished that has gone through three seasons and three different iterations. There's a show called Helen Gone, which also is one of those where they got halfway through a season and then stopped posting episodes for a while, and I stopped listening and then all of a sudden six months later, they were like, oh, hey, we're back. But by that time as a consumer, I had lost interest in that story. And so now I'm not going to go all the way back to the beginning and listen and get caught up again, only to in my mind, be disappointed again.

Cole Heilborn (32:16): Yeah, that's a great point. So let's say a brand in this example, this podcast starts off strong, it's awesome, it attracts a bunch of attention and then they don't follow through. And is that a positive or a negative long-term towards the brand or the person that's making the show? Do you come out ahead or behind at the end of the day in an example like that?

content:
Kaim York-Feirn (32:44): Yeah, that's so tough because my brain wants to say behind, but I don't want to feel like I have that negative outlook on things. But when you look at consumer behavior currently, we have a very short attention span. We have all of these distractions, whether that's podcasts and new music, Netflix shows, Facebook ads, Instagram, TikTok. So me as a consumer has to decide where I'm going to spend my time, what platform is most important to me, and I like consistency. I think a lot of consumers also appreciate consistency and they're going to seek out the platforms that fulfill that need for them. So when a brand or an individual posts 10 episodes of a podcast and then that podcast just dies, they're naturally going to move on to the next thing. So we might make it through all 10 episodes, but then in their mind, oh, it's over. (33:47): There's nothing else to listen to. What new podcast can I listen to? And I think about my personal behavior. I love binging a podcast. I think it's challenging for me personally to subscribe to something that comes out every week unless there's a repository of episodes that I can go back and listen to. If I love a show, I want to listen to it all the time when I'm taking my dog for a walk, when I'm driving to the coffee shop, if I'm at the airport. And so in your example, I personally would probably unsubscribe to that particular brand and move on to something that fits my needs a little bit better.

Cole Heilborn (34:32): Interesting. Yeah, so I mean, I can see how that gets translated across various platforms with various initiatives.

Kaim York-Feirn (34:39): When you're talking about consistency, I think that that applies everywhere. If you're not posting consistently on Instagram, you're not going to show up in the algorithm. If you're not posting consistently on TikTok, again, your videos aren't going to show up on the explore page or I'm sorry for you page or an algorithm. I think that also goes for your hashtag strategy. So yeah, you're totally right in that this idea of consistency to me is probably the most important thing when you're talking about a brand strategy.

content:
Cole Heilborn (35:12): So thinking about the cadence of consistency, I know there's the whole algorithm thing, but I guess I kind of want to ignore that is always changing, but you're talking about consistency. Are you saying you need to be posting once a day, once a week? What if a brand only posts once a month, but they're consistent with that? How does that work

Kaim York-Feirn (35:33): When you're talking about Instagram? Once a month is going to be a challenging strategy. Again, I think you have to go back and look at some of the metrics for success that have been set for the individual platforms. Unfortunately, Instagram is one of those where you need to be engaging every week. I think if you're posting two or three times a week, that's great. If you're posting once a week even, I think that that can be an okay strategy for Instagram. But when you're looking at TikTok, I believe that that almost needs to be a daily or every other day strategy. And when you look at some of the bigger brands that are on there like the NFL or some of the news channels or some of the influencers, they are definitely creating new content almost every day. And TikTok specifically is very timely. So when you have a trending sound, you need to use that immediately rather than waiting a couple months because it's not technically trending anymore, and you're not going to get as much traffic as you would if you had jumped on that right away.

Cole Heilborn (36:43): Okay. I don't understand TikTok, what do you mean by a sound?

Kaim York-Feirn (36:49): So the way that TikTok works is you can upload videos and then put a sound over them. So that can either be someone talking, maybe it's like a movie quote that somebody has uploaded or a part of a song that's been uploaded from Spotify or another music platform, or also something that's pretty popular are Siri sounds. So Siri speaking back something that you've typed. And so the great thing about TikTok is you can add a sound to your favorites and then go back and use that later in your own videos. But that's what I mean by sounds.
