So if I'm a brand, and I'll use myself here as an example in TikTok, I look at that and I've never really taken the time to try to understand it or really do anything with it. And I have this cynical perspective of it. If a brand, let's say something like TikTok pops up or the next big thing, and you kind have this like, oh, that seems like it's for teenagers or whatever, is that the wrong attitude to have if I'm a brand?

Kaim York-Feirn (38:03): Not necessarily. So again, to go back to how we started this conversation, I think it's important to look at what your strategy is and does that fit into your goals for your business? So TikTok is a great way to meet Gen Z where they're at and some of the younger demographics, but we are also starting to see millennials or what they're calling elder millennials. There's a trending funny sound going around that's like if you are really old, if you were born in the nineties and there's just people reacting and their hearts just sink and they're like, oh my gosh, I'm old to be on TikTok, and that would totally be true for me. I was born in 88, so I'm in my thirties. And so to be called Ancient on TikTok by the younger generation, you just kind of have to laugh about it. But no, I don't think that that's a cynical way of looking at it necessarily. If it doesn't fit into your business objectives, I actually think that that's a rather smart way of looking at it because maybe your time is better suited, for instance, doing podcasting and posting these to LinkedIn and other places where you're going to get that listenership.

content: Kaim York-Feirn (40:18): It's so funny that you bring up Yeti because they were a bit of the inspiration behind starting that channel. So one thing that was very unique to Osprey I think, was that we worked with a lot of bands, and I didn't realize that when I first started there, but we supported a lot of artists and different bands through partnerships and would send them gear and get to go to concerts, and they would come to our office sometimes and do shows for our employees. And I wanted a way to be able to share that with our audience. And so we started with some Instagram live events and those were fun, but then I thought, not everybody is going to tune into an Instagram live. How can we allow them to take this home and listen whenever they want? And again, going back to this concept of meet your audience where they interact, music is a great way for people to connect to each other regardless of what your profession is, how old you are, anything like that. (41:25): Music is a huge part of our everyday lives. And so that's where the idea was born is if we can create these Spotify playlists, we're not only meeting our customers where they interact with us, we are giving them an inside look into who we are as a brand by creating these playlists by different bands that we work with by different influencers that we work with. And so it kind of sparked a whole idea of, okay, if an influencer writes us a blog, maybe they can also create a playlist that is inspired by their adventure or their trip. It's a way to introduce people to a new side of our brand. Again, it was kind of a fun platform to be on. It fit very well with our vision and values, and very quickly, I think we gained close to 800 followers within the first month of launching it. And so I think you're the perfect example of why it works. In your question, you brought up, oh, take Starbucks home with you and that you found Yeti's playlist. So again, I think that that just kind of validates why a strategy that works

Like, oh, I'm listening to Michaela Schifrin's skiing playlist that she listens to before she races. How cool is that? Or I'm listening to this playlist curated by this band with songs that influence their music. So it's not only a great way for the consumer to discover new music, it's a great marketing tool that again, is not in your face and seems very relatable.

Cole Heilborn (45:27): So when you started the playlist at Osprey, was there any sort of ROI that you were looking for or how did you decide if this was worth pursuing?

Kaim York-Feirn (45:37): That's a great question. ROI, no, I don't think that in our minds Spotify was going to be a revenue generator. The biggest goal for us was to grow our following on a different platform, so increase our audience size and gain new followers or customers in a different space. So for example, or just to clarify, somebody that follows you on Facebook doesn't necessarily follow you on Instagram. Someone that follows you on TikTok also doesn't necessarily follow you on Instagram. So you want to be in as many places as possible or as makes sense for your brand in order to reach the most amount of people.

Cole Heilborn (46:27): So the Spotify playlist, the idea was hopefully to pick up people that maybe don't follow the other accounts and in doing so, maybe they go follow the Osprey Instagram.

Kaim York-Feirn (46:39): Right, exactly.

But one thing that we didn't really touch on is I have a journalism background, and so I am very much a storyteller. The way that I got into social media was because I thought I wanted to be a magazine writer. I graduated during the recession when print advertising and media was starting to decline. And so social media seemed like a natural way for me to still be a storyteller while also growing my career and learning new things about marketing. content:
Kaim York-Feirn (48:37): And my response is twofold. So for a lot of brands, I think it can make sense. It depends on what you're selling and how your audience interacts with your brand or how you've trained them to interact with your brand. So for me personally, I have never purchased a product off of Instagram or Facebook, nor do I see myself ever doing that. I trust a website much more than I trust a social media platform, but then that's kind of a double-edged sword because this is my job, so I kind of have to promote this and work on a strategy that mixes this into what we post. So in my mind, when I'm tagging a product on Instagram, it's more for awareness. If somebody sees an image that has our frontline harness on it, a front range harness on it or a specific leash, I want them to be able to tap that image and say, oh yeah, I want to go check that out and learn more about that. And then they're ultimately going to go to our website and decide if they want to convert or not. But what I'm hoping is that that social media post was more of an educational piece that pushed them to make a purchase down the line.

Cole Heilborn (50:02): Gotcha. Why do you trust a website for a purchase over a brand social media page?

Kaim York-Feirn (50:11): Well, for one, their websites have been around for a long time, and you have platforms like Shopify. Gosh, I'm not super into e-comm, so I know that there are others, but there very trusted sources that manage all of the money and the backend of that and inventory. And I have not had many bad experiences with the purchasing side of a product from a website, whereas selling on social media is a fairly new concept. I'll say that it's come out in the last five to 10 years. So in my consumer brain, it's still fairly new, and I think that there are a lot of kinks to work out. I remember being invited to one of the first iterations of Instagram shopping when I worked at Osprey, and we spent a fair amount of time on the phone with their sales team vetting whether that was something that fit into our strategy or not. And ultimately at the time it did not. (51:20): And so yeah, I think it just kind of goes back to the longevity of it and seeing success with website stuff. I know that it for sure works. I manage some of those metrics and I see that people do purchase from that. The other side of that is that those platforms are very influential with a purchase. So when you see a TikTok person wearing a specific pair of leggings or an outfit, they'll often talk about where they bought it from. Sometimes it's paid for, it's an advertisement, but if I'm scrolling through my feed and I'm like, oh, that's cute, then I'm going to go to the website and follow up.

Cole Heilborn (52:03): Yeah, there's something about having a differentiation between where you're consuming and learning and having fun versus where you're making a decision to purchase something like having a line in the sand or two different Instagram versus an Amazon, it seems more comforting or it seems more like you want to keep those things separated almost.

Kaim York-Feirn (52:31): Yeah, I would agree with that. I like to keep those two concepts very separate.

Kaim York-Feirn (53:17): I think initial gut reaction is Facebook is trying to take over the world. I don't know if that's a good thing or a bad thing. Honestly, I think it was pretty inevitable. When you look at their track record, they purchased Instagram a while back. I also believe they purchased WhatsApp. And so they're buying up platforms that make sense to build this metaverse and try and sort of become a Google of the social media universe. For better or for worse, I mean, Facebook is the giant, when you look at social media strategy, you can't get away with spending money on the internet without giving some of it to Facebook. And so I think they want to continue to be this high power where people come for information and to sell their products. I mean, at the end of the day, meta is going to do what Meta is going to do, and I think we're all just pieces of the puzzle and we have to decide how invested we are in their growth and continue to watch what they do and whether that continues to align with our brand values and whether we want to continue spending money on their platform. (54:39): And I'd say for now, absolutely it makes sense for a lot of brands. I know there were brands during the pandemic like Patagonia that decided to completely pull their advertising budget from Facebook. They can do that because they are a giant when it comes to the outdoor industry, and they get revenue from places that maybe some smaller brands don't. In a sense, I think that that's a little bit unfair that some smaller brands can't get off of Facebook, they just financially cannot afford to because it's a place where they generate a lot of revenue, whereas some of the larger brands can't afford to pull part of their spend or their full spend. So they have created this pay to play environment where it's here to stay, it's not going anywhere. And again, we're all just kind of little pieces in their puzzle.

Cole Heilborn (55:40): Interesting. And I guess we just got to wait and see what happens.

Kaim York-Feirn (55:43): Wait and see what happens. Facebook is going to take over the world someday whether we like it or not.

So part of that is being able to listen to your customers. So Omar will collect all the data of what people are reaching out about so that we know where we're missing things or where we have opportunities. One of the big things when we started, we definitely thought we were more of a millennial product or people that are probably in their thirties, forties, and then younger. But baby boomers is definitely an audience we've heard from. And that was first in customer service because that's not who we see on social media as much Facebook, but not as much our other platforms. And it was impressive without asking any questions, they could do it. And we were like, yeah, we hit this one. It's doing what it's supposed to. It also has a little more streamline form when it's in box, when it's in its box, so it's a lot easier to move around. It's only 20 pounds, so you can pack it in the backpack that it comes in, or it comes with, and I'm sorry, it doesn't come with the backpack, but you can get the pack for it and take it in, hike it into an alpine lake for a full weekend with your super lightweight backpacking gear, just slide your tent and

Jess Anthony (07:28): In. And then we also have, so we kind of split it into two categories, like our rec boats, which are open cockpit. So the inlet is definitely in the rec boat category. If you want to bring a cooler or some gear, bring your dog. That's a good one for that. And then for our performance models, we have the bay and the coast, and those are designed after a lot of really traditional Arctic kayaks that you would see. And if you think about it, comparing it to biking, it's like the models you can just, they move with your body. They're a little sleeker. You can do really tight turns and higher speeds.

Jess Anthony (09:05): Yeah, I think it's having a good story is first and then being able to tell it. Well, the first version of the story you write is never what you put up. So it's a lot of editing, simplifying, and just being able to show it in photos and videos, which actually for our product is a little tricky because when we talk about what is a single still image, we don't really have one because there's the box and there's the boat. So a lot of times video or a photo that shows both kind of gets that point across. But I would say also one of the most important things for a successful Kickstarter launch is getting good content. So hire a photographer or a videographer. If you have budget, it's worth it. And then spend a lot of your time on writing about your products. No one knows it better than you, and then have everybody ask, read it and give you feedback. And then the other thing I would say is hire a PR firm if you can do that. We worked with Purple Orange on our last Kickstarter, which was our most successful, and they really helped us push that forward. They helped us find different awards we could apply for, and we won quite a bit. And that comes with a lot of a attention along the way. So they were just really great to work with as far as getting it in front of more people.

So you can live in an urban city in a small flat and shove it in a closet and then pull it out and be on the water, and that wasn't something that urban dwellers had readily access to.

Jess Anthony (19:28): Yeah, that kind of accessibility is pretty cool. And it actually applies to a lot more people than I would've thought when I was working in customer service. We had folks reach out who had back injuries and had been very active in certain types of sports that weren't able to do them anymore independently. And a lot of people found the Oreo because they were like, oh, it's lightweight. I don't need to be able to put weight above my head. I can pull it out of the back of my SUV or my trunk and get it to the dock and set it up all by myself without anybody having to be around, which is pretty cool to hear that it gives people that independence that you don't need to ask somebody to help you.

Jess Anthony (22:18): Yeah, I think, I mean, I am queer and I feel like I present queer and there's definitely been places where I didn't feel safe. And I think part of being able to get people outdoors is people feeling safe. And if you don't see anyone that looks like you, I think it's very hard to feel like you're welcome somewhere, even if everybody there is like, oh, cool, there's another person. That's fine. So I guess in that respect, representation matters and I think that's something that the outdoors industry can contribute for everybody. And I guess I've been seeing a little bit more of that, but I think it's exciting. I like seeing more of it, and I think it does make a big difference to see yourself represented using a product and just having a good time.

Cole Heilborn (23:09): How does it make you feel when you look at an environment and you see people who are like you and you feel like you can, there's not that awkward barrier of entry. Speaking personally, how do you feel when you see those scenarios,

Jess Anthony (23:27): When you see no awkward barrier

Cole Heilborn (23:31): Or maybe drawing on personal experiences where you have felt that awkward barrier?

Jess Anthony (23:34): Yeah, I think when there's no awkward barrier, you don't feel anything, you're going on your hike or whatever, it feels good. And I think that's what a lot of people, especially people really involved in the outdoors industry feel when they go to most parks. I think when you do feel it, you're just not sure if you feel welcome or if you feel safe. I grew up in Kansas and I've done a lot of road trips all around the country, and I think there have been places where I've felt people look at me and I did not feel necessarily safe or welcome. And usually it's fine for me in every case. It's been fine, but it's just like when you're not sure, you're like, maybe we'll go to the next park. Try it later.

Cole Heilborn (24:20): Yeah. Huh. Yeah. Well, no, that's cool. And I appreciate you sharing your backstory. I think that helps provide context for why you care about the things you do care about. Everyone's story kind of shapes what we do in our future.

That's where everybody likes to go and everyone likes to go in the morning. But I was like, oh, I want to sleep in and I don't want to go where everyone is. So I went to the little far away island and in the afternoon, but apparently there was a three o'clock wind that comes up every day and the boat was really small and there were these massive white caps and I thought we were going to flip over. I had white knuckles the whole way back, and I got back and the guy was like, oh, you went there and you made it back at this time. Nobody does that. I'm surprised I didn't have to come find you. And I was like, oh, okay.

I've come from consumer goods companies where we have to spend a lot of money on making the physical goods on the tech side, they don't. So some of the companies that she's worked for, they have 1230 person marketing groups and agencies so they can test out a lot more ideas and concepts that we just don't have the luxury of doing. I mean, in many ways we're so far behind what tech marketing is doing, and at the same time, I think the consumer goods tends to have a wider audience that understands what we're doing. So I really rely on her to keep me in the loop of what she is working on, and that's made me a much better marketer. But I love to hear what other brands are doing, and I'm a big fan of this podcast here, and I love hearing what other really smart folks are talking about because I really try to be humble as I've gone through my career. What I've learned from some pretty influential folks that I've worked with is that that humility is going to make you smarter and a better, not just a better person, but a better at your everyday job too.

Cole Heilborn (00:03:49): Yeah, interesting. Well, that's a whole nother subject. That's actually not what we're here to talk about, but we're going to have to table that to come back to that idea. Well, Darren, I'd love if you could give us a quick background on nemo, a little introduction to yourself, and just to give folks an idea, we're going to be discussing this idea of building an non-transactional relationship with your customer since you've stepped into the role at nemo. Sounds like there's some pretty exciting projects going on, and I'm really excited to kind of dive into your philosophy behind this idea. But let's start with a little background info.

I was just working as a footwear manager at City Sports in Boston trying to not work the retail floor anymore. I was tired of working weekends and holidays and not having consecutive days off and working retail pre the great recession back in oh eight. I mean, man, what a crazy ride that was. But I am very thankful for the lessons I learned there. I mean, if you can sell shoes and gear to people face to face, I mean I still take those lessons for me everywhere. It was a great foundation in my career. But I had a friend who was by the name of Georgia Shaw, who was a former city sports alum who came back into my store and a busy Saturday morning and said, Hey, you want to interview for a customer service job at brm? (00:05:20): And I was like, yes, please, please get me out of retail. I don't want to do this anymore. And interviewed there and was one of two customer service reps in 2009, right as the five Fingers revolution was taking off. That was a fantastic time to take a lot of the lessons I learned from the running and fitness world coming out of city sports and grow into this awesome new industry to me of the outdoor industry. And that job really started me on a path of being someone who recreates outside. I had a coworker who asked me to go rock climbing. I didn't know what rock climbing was, and I just sounded cool. So I was like, yeah, lemme try it. And we went to a gym two towns away from where I grew up and I was hooked instantaneously. And I remember coming back to the office and going, whoa, all these rock climbing magazines are everywhere. (00:06:19): I just didn't see it. It wasn't until I experienced it, I hadn't seen it and it was all around me and I felt like, how come no one told me about this? I could have been doing this. This is so much fun. And that just led me to my sports today. I mean, I rock climb, I surf, I snowboard, I camp, I hike, and I really thank that first job and my time there working in customer service, sales, operations, logistics.

Thanks man. It's been a ride and I've absolutely loved it. I love the people I work with at every job. So far this has been a very welcoming industry and the sports that I participate in. Same

So I got to imagine the challenge that folks face, and I'm sure you guys face every day, is how to engage your customer without always being there, selling them something. This idea that just because you're interacting with your consumer doesn't mean you have to be pushing product down their throat or expecting something. Where did this idea come from and how has this kind of manifested, at least in terms of the challenges that you see at NEMO compared to some of your past roles?

content: Darren Josey (00:13:24): Gotcha. I go back to being on the shoe floor back at city Sports. I remember talking to different reps and brands and our corporate team understanding the buying process of your core running customer. That customer was coming in every 250 to 300 miles to buy a new pair of shoes. And it was important for everyone in the shoe floor to understand you're going to see that person again. So understand how you're positioning a certain product, understand they're going to come back here to probably get a watch or a pair of shorts. So it was really quick. I mean you could see someone once every four months to maybe eight months, but multiple times a year you'd see the same runners who lived in the area. When I got to NEMO, understanding our products. So I started camping in 2010. Part of my privilege in life is that I was raised by a Puerto Rican mom and a black dad who told me that you're going to enter a lot of spaces in life where you are the only person who looks like you here. So have the courage to go try something even if you're the only one doing it. But do be weary of that. You're walking into maybe that you're the only person like you. So that privilege allowed me when someone gifted me a tent and two sleeping bags when I worked at brm to say, I'm just going to try camping. (00:14:49): That was 2010. I still have that camping gear that is 12-year-old camping gear that I was using up until last year. And so when I came to nemo, I took my running lessons and how often I was talking to that customer and I looked at my own camping experience and said, well, my gear has lasted 12 years. I camped probably three to five times a year. I take really good care of my gear. I also loan it out to friends and family. So if we're looking to talk to our customer owner when they're going to buy something, we're not going to be talking to them that often. So I think just the shrewd business point of view is that NEMO sells durable gear and we need to find other ways to talk to our customer because they're not always going to be looking to buy something that's just not the nature of what we sell. (00:15:36): So I think that's the pure dollars and cents.

content: Darren Josey (00:13:24): The other reason we want to be doing this and creating that non-transactional relationship, I think is understanding or having a wider view on sustainability. So if I go back to my first time camping, being gifted two sleeping bags in a tent, I dragged my, at the time, girlfriend out on a camping trip. We had no idea that you needed a sleeping pad. I just got in the bag and laid down on the rocky Rudy ground and was like, I guess this is camping. That's it, right? I mean, I think I drank enough be I didn't really feel the ground that much, but I'm the kind of person that if I have just a little bit of fun, I'll come back and I'll keep trying to do it again and again. But that's not everybody out there. (00:16:26): And I really try to take my personal experience as well as feedback from other events and interactions I've had with people out there in the outdoor industry. I think there's really three types of people out there and that's why we want to have this non-transactional relationship. I think the first type of person is the person who just hears about an activity and wants to try it. They don't need to see anyone like 'em doing it just that sounds cool, I want to try it. And that's me. I had to learn a lot of hard lessons, not exactly, well, I certainly got hurt bouldering without a pad, something else. I had to learn a hard lesson. But I think that person just needs to see a little bit of spark, a little bit of fun. They're going to keep coming back over and over again. The second group of folks, which I think a lot of people fall into are they need to see someone who looks like them to know this is something our community does and this is safe to do. (00:17:29): I think we want to have resources for these folks as well as that first group so that they keep coming back and have a really positive experience right away to go, okay, this is safe. We can do this, and then let's not let people struggle. I think we as an outdoor industry have maybe taken for granted for too long that we've presented images of a person and an amazing place with some gear and said, you'll just find yourself there. Well, that's just not true.

But there's a lot of people that just won't do that. Or if they have that one bad experience because someone put 'em on something that was too steep or had them go out on a day that was a little bit too big surfing and they almost drowned or felt like they almost drowned, they're not going back. (00:18:22): And so that group, we really want to make sure that we have a lot of resources available to them. And we've done that actually with our adventure resources page, which I can talk about in a bit. And then the last group, that third group are the folks that say, no, we don't do this. And if you do this, you're not one of us. The best way that I could explain that to anyone listening from my own community, I've heard this from both friends and family, is that's some white people. Shit. I still get that to this day. Why are you trying to do these white activities? Well, the best way to address that is to show people of different communities and call them out by name. You can't say only white people do that. If you know me and I'm a person of color and I do this and I'm an outdoor evangelist, I want to bring more people out here. (00:19:15): Now, we don't want to sugarcoat and say, well, racism or sexism or classism doesn't exist in the outdoor world. It absolutely does. It is not nowhere in our society's immune to that. But this is something that is accessible for people of all groups, some easier than others, but this is public land that is made available to the public, and we want to address that group with people of that community and frankly find more leaders of outdoor organizations that can represent and talk directly to that community. And we've tried to set that up with a few of our partnerships this year with NEMO to talk to these groups with representation of that community to them say, Hey, this is a safe space. Here's a place that you can go.

So Cam will proudly tell anyone that NEMO has spent more dollars on sustainability than it has on marketing in the 20 years of this brand existing. That work is really hard to do and it's hard to, our tagline is adventure anywhere, adventure anywhere for anyone forever. And it's hard to adventure anywhere when we don't have a planet to adventure on. So investing in sustainability, it's a long road and dollars spent over the last 20 years have led to really innovative products that improve the performance for people and planet. So that's where NEMO had spent its dollars and time before since hiring me. One of the things I pitched the brand on when I was a contractor was building out these adventure resources to establish that non-transactional relationship. So when you hit our homepage, yes, you see camping gear, but right away you're going to see our adventure resources ribbon. (00:22:16): We want to inspire people, giving them some great videos, recipes, just stories to latch onto and get them stoked. We also want to show some education with these camping by type landing pages. Again, I go back to that my first camping trip, I didn't know you needed a sleeping pad. Showing people with these pages what a campsite can actually look like is really powerful. All the different pieces of kit that you need to create something really beautiful because you never know who you're talking to. You could be potentially, a customer could be looking your site trying to convince a significant other or a friend to go camping. And if all they know is well, when I went camping with my family, or all I've seen is a mildewy table with some cold hot dogs, that's not what I'm interested in. So to show that camping can be super luxurious to show that camping can be simple but still very comfortable, is really important and a good educational aspect of like, whoa, I didn't know it was all these pieces and you don't need all of them.

I'm someone who, I've hired a couple guides in my life and it's been really, really empowering to go outside with someone. The way guides are set up is they want you to be able to do it on your own afterwards. So they're going to show you a great time, but also teach you some things so that you can go out and do it afterwards. And that's really what we as an industry need. And I think a big reason why NEMO was really excited to take on this challenge and build up these adventure resources is that this is a special time in our country's history, right? Anywhere from, if you look at the OIA report, it says over 7 million people have started recreating since the pandemic. (00:24:18): I looked at a K report that said 10 million people. So anywhere between seven to 10 million people started recreating outside. And about a third of those folks said they're not going to do it after the pandemic ends. Well in 2022, it seems like fingers crossed we could be going towards endemic instead of continued pandemic. So this is a special moment for our industry to try to hold on to all of those folks who have newly joined us. But at the same time, for our core audience who's been recreating, I think we've all been recreating more than we ever have before. And so let's inspire these folks to try a new space. So we have, as actually part of our adventure resources, we name the locations of our brand shoots. We worked really closely with the land managers to make sure that these areas were ready, willing, and capable to bring on more traffic. (00:25:09): The A MC was our partner for our backpacking brand shoot, but we're going to continue to build out more potential trips to inspire folks because if you've been doing this for a while, your regular trail, your regular campsites have become busier. So why not try something new, try a gem that you haven't seen before or try camping in a different season?

What I loved about that partnership is that they show black excellence as in camping, and they told us in our initial conversations about 70% of their clientele are first time campers who are coming. content: Darren Josey (00:30:53): Yeah, it's certainly a delicate balance and it runs pretty counter to what I think a lot of folks in the outdoor recreation just for their own personal use, no one wants to see, or most people don't want to see more people at their local surf spot or their local crag. And I've definitely experienced that too. I love for me, well now I do more bouldering as a dad, that's what I have time for. But pre my beautiful daughter, my wife and I spent a lot of time sport climbing at Rumney and parking Lot Wall would be packed, and I'm sure it's been even more packed post pandemic, especially when gyms got closed down. But if we aren't talking about the other amazing climbing areas that are 15 minute hike in a different direction, then we're never going to spread out. But at the same time, we want to make sure we make good stewards of anyone else trying new areas, stay on the trails, really use leave no trace. (00:31:51): Even though leave no trace, folks on their site have kind of changed their stance on geo tagging. So we don't want to be reckless as a brand and say, Hey, here's anywhere that you can go. If we're even going to call an area that could be more ecologically fragile, let's call it out for that and say, Hey, this area needs more resources and work with land management company to get people to either donate time or money to help that area thrive. Because if we don't all spread out, then we're going to lose or not make the most of this moment in time for a lot more people recreating the place. The reason why we as a brand want to do this is that climate change is the crisis of our lifetime, and we have to make real reductions in the carbon that we put out there from producing products and transporting our products. (00:32:45): So that's on us, the brand, but we also want to take this moment to create more stewards of our lands because we really believe that the more people have a good time outside, the more people are going to vote to keep these areas open and accessible. More people are going to spend the time to keep these areas clean and safe and then teach their kids this is how to go into the outdoors. And we don't really want to define what outdoor recreation is, but we do want to show more people the possibilities because I think overwhelmingly people want to experience this in kind of, I guess the word is you don't want to be a Jerry, right? No one wants to go out and kind of fumble around and not know how to get out there. But at the same time, we want to make sure people express themselves as they want to out there. So I hope we're doing it. I mean, we still have a long way to go. It's certainly not perfect, and I really welcome a lot of feedback from others on how we can add more resources and provide more opportunities for people to have a good time and a safe time outside.

What's been the project with the website and what does it look like today?

Darren Josey (00:34:19): Sure. So we just launched it at the start of March. It was a long time coming. We actually, it's pretty crazy because we launched it in about, let's see, I hired my digital director in October and we launched it in March. So pretty quick. It was something that I had been conceptualizing since 2020, but we really wanted to, I looked at a lot of other consumer good sites and when you land on those sites, it's Shop now, buy now, explore these products, pop up in your face, say 15%. We just didn't want to be that brand. And I actually really love the way, I believe it was Al Perkinson said it on your podcast, if you want to be part of the community, you got to contribute to it first. I think he kept saying, buy the beer, pay the band. That's what we wanted to do with our site. (00:35:06): I loved hearing him say it. I was like, that's all we're trying to do with the adventure resources. We want to give something to people so they could have a better time recreating as a way to say, Hey, we're here as a resource. We want you to keep coming back. And so when you hit our homepage, you're going to see only about half the stories or anything to do with buying a product. A lot of it is our sustainability, all sorts of different things from places to recreate and skills to learn. And we really wanted to, I'm excited for next month we have a couple more drops we're going to be doing on expanding out our sustainability page with a really awesome timeline of past, present, and future and what we're doing on sustainability, but also are about us because NEMO is, I think becoming rarer and rarer that a company of our size is majority family owned. (00:35:58): Cam is the CEO, the founder and majority owner, and he's a designer. So NEMO as a brand is product led and values driven. And we really want to make sure we have a website that communicates that because we're, we're a seasonal business and we want someone to be thinking positively about our brand when they pull out their camping gear at the start of the season and to go get timely emails that drive you back to the site to say, Hey, get your gear ready. Here's how to repair something. Here's how to clean it.

Cole Heilborn (00:38:34): So at the very beginning of this podcast, we were talking about the things that the outdoor industry does well and some of the things that maybe we're behind on compared to other industries. This idea of creating a non-transactional relationship, do you feel like as a whole this is, that's something that the industry, how do we perform? Do we do a good job? Do we do a poor job?

Darren Josey (00:38:58): I think we're getting better. There's certainly, I'm seeing more representation in marketing materials and I think some brands do have things built further back on their website that you can really dig to find out. But I think we could be doing a lot better job in making more of these resources, connecting people to others if we have an honest understanding of what we're selling. No one has to do these things. You don't have to go camping, you don't have to go skiing. I think we feel that sometimes I haven't surfed in a month and a half, and I'm right at that point where I really need to get in the water, but I don't have to. And I have other priorities in my life that can come forward and have not allowed me to do that. And if we maintain that perspective that the things that we're selling no one has to do, I think it changes why. (00:39:52): And when we talk to our customer, I mean, I've definitely been part of other friend groups where we're only one friend away. If that person moves away, we're not going to do that trip anymore. And then who's going to bring people together? And then that sort of just crumbles. And I think we have a lot of groups like that in our society where they're one family away if they move, it's kind of done. Or that person was like, yeah, I just had kids and I don't want to prioritize this anymore. I can't do this. And then no one's there to pick up the slack. So I think to one, take advantage of this moment in time where we have so many new people who've come in and to really make sure that, and not take for granted our core customers who've been doing this for a bit. (00:40:34): I mean, we have a really huge opportunity with the boomer generation of a lot of folks who have retired in the last couple of years and they are recreating. And that's actually why, or one of the key reasons why we wanted to show some older folks too in our marketing materials because they're looking to get outside as well. I mean, I definitely know a lot of my own family and friends and their parents who started to recreate outside.

Where should I go camping? And I'm like, ah, see, this is what he needs. (00:41:25): He needs to see someone who looks like himself as well as some other materials to get him outside. He went to a store, he bought the, and then was like, okay, now where do I go? And I think we as an industry need to create more materials for him and his wife. They're looking to get outside and he had basically sat on that camping gear for a year. He didn't know where to go. And I think that's one big area that we can make some pretty quick improvements there for both. I think we spent a lot of time talking about Gen Z, which we should, right? They're the next big age group to come up and start making more purchasing decisions. But let's also not forget about the boomer generation as well as our Gen X folks who maybe grew up with a different interpretation of outdoor adventures. (00:42:15): And we really want to be inclusive. I mean, I've been on a lot of calls where a brand or a group can pivot hard in another direction, and we're nimo really trying to find this balance of we really want to be inclusive. And that's understanding. Some groups need different motivations, different resources, and other groups like our core group, they should still feel like this is a brand they recognize. We don't want to make a hard pivot and have someone who's been an ultralight through hiker with us for a decade and hit our homepage and go, what's this? I don't know this brand. We've certainly seen brands do that over the years, and we really want to truly be inclusive to our core audience as well as newcomers that if you're brand new or you're experience, you hit that homepage and you go, this is the brand I grew up with, or this is the brand that is welcoming to me and my changing taste or my first time, this is welcoming to beginners.

We're still a core backpacking brand and about 25% of the stories we want to always have on our homepage that showcase backpacking. And we want to be more like 15% around car camping. We're still pretty new in the car camping space, but we also want to continue to show about five to 7% of mountaineering. We still want to embrace those epic images from someone on the top of a glaciated peak out there solo doing an incredible trip that's still this brand. We still make great gear for that. We also want to show some of the other activities. I mean, we did a partnership with Firstlight in the hunt and fish space. We still we're actually building out a landing page to talk more about that partnership later this year. But that's something where in the future, we really want to be your home for adventure. (00:44:20): We don't just want to be, or lemme say this, we have an opportunity to bring together the hunt fish crowd and the core outdoor crowd. I think a lot of younger consumers don't necessarily see themselves in those buckets. I'm also an angler. I've never gone hunting in my life, but I love fishing. I don't necessarily consider myself hook and bullet. I guess I consider myself more core, but I do all of those things. I'm equally as excited to take my daughter fishing for the first time as I am to go with my cousin and rent a charter boat and go striper fishing as I am to get back out and lead an awesome sunny sport climb. And I think there's a real opportunity there to bring those two groups together and that's why we want to keep showing some representation of that. So that hardcore outdoor, oh yeah, that's part of this brand as well. And there's other opportunities here that we could all just share this land together because man, when we do that, when we bring those industries together, look out, I think we're really going to be a force for land conservation as well as making sure this plant's around for many more generations to come.

I'm not going to pay you, or maybe I'll give you some gear and that's it. That's just not fair. There is no diversity inclusion without the equity. So when we were putting together our brand shoot last year to be shown this year, the first thing I wanted to do was make sure we found some really good folks that were of underrepresented or marginalized communities. (00:47:26): The second was to make sure that all of them either owned or worked for a company that built pathways to adventure because what we were trying to do was first pay our model's top modeling rate. So I asked a few other folks who were professional photographers in our industry and in others to try to figure out the right model day rate, and we covered all expenses, so transportation, food, lodging, and then we made sure that as part of the contract along with the production company, we have three year rights on that, that the model's rights were also would require to be renewed. So if we want to show them in new materials after three years, just like we'd negotiate with the production company, we would renegotiate with them. And then we want to go to what I was calling exponential equity. So each model has a spot on our adventure resources page where we have a link that we spend our marketing dollars and resources driving our traffic to click to hire them, right? (00:48:28): Because I want to really go beyond, we just cut a check and said, Hey, thanks for your likeness. We're going to throw it on all sorts of stuff and then see you later. We're done with you.

We weren't often talking to consumers as much as I wished, even though we were often trying to glean what we could to represent their thinking and their way of being. So after that 10 year stint and advertising was like, I want to get closer to their thoughts and opinions and their lives and really get in there. (00:07:26): And that's when I switched into doing my own thing and qualitative research. I had a brief stint in Australia, which was really fun, where I actually worked for a qualitative research and consultancy firm to kind of get the nuts and bolts of the business down before I came back and founded the insight in. So I've been doing this for seven years now on my own. And I work for companies that are big and small, everybody from startups to fortune fives and really across categories, which I have some experience in the outdoor realm with some clients like outdoor research and a couple others.

So something that you absolutely positively feel as soon as somebody mentions it or as soon as you hear it out loud, but you may not have put your finger on prior. It's not everybody enjoys spending time with their family. Everybody enjoys spending time with their family except when, and then there's some twist to it. So there's always just a little bit of truth that exists somewhere in your soul or in your heart, and as soon as somebody mentioned it, you go, yeah, you know what? I've always felt that way, or Yeah, I totally feel that way. So I think for me, I don't have a beautiful articulation of it as much as I want that moment where when I say that and I am reading a brief out loud or I'm talking to folks about the way consumers feel or have felt, and people go, oh yeah, I actually totally get that. I am feeling that somewhere in my body or I'm feeling that viscerally. I'm like, yeah, then that was super successful. But yeah, I think there's what I'd hope for and what I think a lot of strategy people and marketing people hope for is that next level down of, okay, and part of that leads into research. I really feel like research is asking the question before the question very often. So if it's like, I want people to activate and do what I want them to do, I need to back out of that and ask the question before that of like, well, what's pushing on them and motivating them? What's making them feel that way? What's driving them? Oh, it's this 20-year-old perception of my category. Oh no, why did that stick with them? (00:11:09): What is it about that that really bugs them? Oh, there's probably an emotion there. Is that feeling like guilt or shame or inadequacy? And then, okay, well, why would someone be feeling that? Well, there's probably a cultural element that's pushing down on them that's telling them that they should feel that way when they get into a situation. So how do we understand at a cultural level what's happening? And so you're really just kind of taking what is and what on the face, and then you're sort of backing multiple questions out of that that involve further wise. And that to me is a really good way to get to an insight. Say you start with something that everybody knows, well then start to interrogate that. And when you go multiple levels deeper, and maybe if you're able to engage with a researcher or you're just able to answer those questions to the best of your ability, I do think you can get to that question before the question kind of format can get you to something real or something deeper or something another level down than just, oh, the behavior we witness is that five out of 10 people enjoy citrus. content: Megan Averell (00:12:45): I think one of the great intersections of research and marketing is the story of the original planner at TBW Shi a day, whose name is now escaping me unfortunately. But the original got mail campaign, which many marketers, at least over a certain age are familiar with. That was really about that moment that you realize that you don't have milk and then you freak out, you need it, right? You're having a giant chocolate chip cookie or whatever it is. And how they got to that campaign was actually through research, because as you might imagine, milk was something that was at that time before the advent of almond milk and before the advent of oat milk and some of those things, it was in everybody's fridge, but no one had a particular affinity towards it. It was hard to articulate what that affinity was. And what I really like about the study that they concocted for that was that it required what I like to call research design, which is you don't just get in there and ask questions. (00:13:46): That's not, I mean, you can, and that's certainly better than nothing, but it doesn't actually get to like, oh, what are we actually trying to find? And then let me backtrack from there and design to get there. And so in this case, it was a very specific problem, which is that upwards of 90% of Americans had milk in the refrigerator at any given time, but no one really gave a crap, right? It was just sort of there. It was very banal. And so if you had loaded a bunch of people into a focus group and said, what do you like about milk? They would've been like, I don't know. It's there. It's kind of creamy, it's kind of good. It's cooling. Sometimes it just would've been a very fruitless conversation. And they realized that. So their research approach was to take it away and they just basically wouldn't allow people to buy milk. (00:14:33): And there's a study named for this, and it's called deprivation study.

content: Megan Averell (00:12:45): And sometimes when there's consumer goods or products that we use all the time, but it's very hard for us to put our finger on what it is about that we care about or why that brand might be different than just X brand or a generic brand or things because it's been a part of our life that actually if you actually remove and take that brand out of people's lives, they may have something new that they stumble on as to why that matters to them. And so sure enough, the actual anecdotes that they used inside the study of eating a bunch of Gabi peanut butter or eating a big chocolate chip cookie and just feeling like that experience wasn't quite what it could be if you had milk, all of those. And then of course there was a very iconic moment where they flipped in the ad, the jug upside down because they were either out or it wasn't in the fridge and it was like got milk. (00:15:26): That was the pin on that campaign. But almost every single one of those scenarios, even though they were made up creatively and ended up looking really cool and had some real creative pizazz to them, they really did come from things. People actually said, oh my gosh, I can't believe I can't have milk with this. I didn't realize what it meant to me. So that's a great example. And I actually have done deprivation studies in my career as well, because sometimes, and we've all can think of some off the top of our head, there are goods and services that are just there, and maybe we use them at a convenience and maybe that's all we could say about them. If you went and asked someone and tapped 'em on the shoulder, oh, well, it's right on the corner. I use it all the time. But if you are able to put people in an artificial situation through research design where they don't have access to that anymore, suddenly they're able to articulate what it is that's really going on, what's really attracting them or repelling them from other brands even, which can get you to differentiation. (00:16:22): So it was a famous example, and I wish I remembered the name of the planner, but it was a really fantastic case study and it's one that's often cited.

Cole Heilborn (00:16:31): Yeah, that's really fascinating. So what would that process look like? Would they bring people into a room and then feed them a cookie but not give them milk? Or how are they reaching this conclusion?

Megan Averell (00:16:44): So they basically just said, okay, you're going to participate in this study and as part of your run of household, you cannot buy milk. You can go to the grocery store and buy everything else, but you can't buy milk. And then they had 'em, I think, keep a journal, and that was back then would've been maybe a physical journal. But now of course we can do those kinds of studies where we're just kind of not necessarily pulling people out of their lives, but we're more like they're touching base with us within their lives. They might log on to now something like a little online discussion board and be like, Hey, here's how I'm feeling on day three of no milk. So without actually, and I think they did some focus groups and things like that, but you're essentially saying just keep living your life and just keep doing what you're doing, but we are going to have this one artificial variable, and then you're going to check in with us about how that is going. (00:17:34): How is that affecting you, if at all? Because sometimes you can't guarantee that it will. I mean, maybe they'll be like, Hey, I found something much better in the interim, and you're like, oh, no. But you kind of have to be open to that journey to find out. But yeah, those are the kinds of studies where you really get into people's lives and you're more flittering above like a drone every once in a while to come in and capture their feedback. But those can be quite longitudinal as well. Sometimes you might do a study like that if it was, for instance, I wanted to know how people buy a car. Well, that's a long research process that they might go through. So I might fl into their lives once a month and check in with them and be like, Hey, how's it going? What's your process right now? What have been some of the twists and turns since we talked last? And you can get a sense of something that's quite a long journey without having to lock people up for 12 months in a focus group facility.

content:
Cole Heilborn (00:18:27): So I'm curious to learn more about your process because we're talking about how these different studies come to be, and there's obvious that there's a lot of work that goes into the preparation and planning of these things. I guess can you explain that? And as a researcher, what is your goal or what are you working towards?

Megan Averell (00:18:47): Yeah, I think that I started my own, this dovetails really well into why I started my own research firm, which is that I think there isn't a lot of care given to research design specifically. I think it's much easier to churn out a list of questions to just sit down and brainstorm and be like, okay, here's our list of 50 questions, and we'll hire sort of a moderately skilled moderator to go in and read those questions and stick to the script, and then we'll issue some kind of PowerPoint that almost even can be bi banal is going question by question to tell you what people said. That is research I have seen out in the world and I am not a fan. And part of the reason I thought I had enough hubris to think, okay, I can start my own research firm was because I knew there had to be a better way. (00:19:41): And I think a lot of that does come down to that research design process of like, okay, well, let's literally start from that objective. What do we need? Research and marketing land is very different than research and academia. We don't have to do a double blind scientific study on how a placebo affects people versus a heavy dose of a medication that requires complete objectivity, and that requires you to really make sure that your questions are not leading in any way and you're not asking about side effects. Oh, are you having a headache? Because people will try to please a researcher. We know because of all of our internal biases to be agreeable and say yes. So they have to be really careful about the way they phrase questions, the way that they conduct themselves. We're in research in the marketing realm, people. This is just the, I call it the beaker approach compared to the bunsen approach. (00:20:40): If you're a Muppets fan that beaker is just kind of a hot mess and half the time he is lighting the lab on fire, that kind of trial and error and just really trying to go for it is really important in research design and marketing. I think that list of questions, when I look at it a lot of times I'm thinking, how do I make this more pointed? How do I make it more focused? How do I make it more interesting for the respondent?

content: Megan Averell (00:18:47): How do I turn this into an activity that they can actually apply some emotive skill sets to not just the sort of frontal lobe of our brain that's going to be very rational when you ask it a rational question, I want someone to play. I want to unleash some playful elements, just like that deprivation study we talked about as one example, right? (00:21:27): Of that's actually not a circumstance many people had encountered in the world. It was an artificial circumstance created to get the result that you needed. You couldn't just list the questions out and call it a day. So that kind of creativity in research design is really what the insight in really strives to do. And that comes from starting, yeah, you might start at that starting point of what do we want to know? But then you've got to think, how can I get there in a way that's really going to create a really evocative experience? Because a lot of times as marketers we're focused on emotion as a strategist in the ad business, I knew that kind of as we talked about earlier, insight was going to be what really mattered to me. So you could come to me and say, oh, I did a bagel study and I came up with seven different reasons that people use bagels. (00:22:18): And 86% of people said that bagels are filling. And this may or may not be an actual example that I've seen a client bring to me as research of 86% of people say bagels are filling. And as sort of the strategist at that time working on marketing and advertising was thinking, well, how do we turn that into something interesting? Where is the material that's going to really scratch under the surface and get people really excited about bagels? And it wasn't going to come from that piece of research. And I kept thinking like, wow, I would've taken that money that they spent on figuring out 86% of people thought bagels were filling and done more of an emotional deep dive into, I don't know what's different about eating a bagel versus eating this. Can you project and tell me how it would feel before, during, and after you are eating a bagel, right? (00:23:07): That's a very different question. That's going to get you a very different outcome.

Megan Averell (00:18:47): And if people start describing, well, before I eat the bagel, I woke up in the morning, well, how are you feeling? Right? You can really get to some more emotional stuff, but you have to ask the question that way. You can't just sort of go like, okay, well list out the three steps of three different attributes you associate with bagels because filling as number one and number two might be something else, but either one of those might be very inconsequential for marketing purposes. The end result needs to be interesting. So what we're doing with consumers needs to be interesting, and that research design needs to be interesting. And sometimes those projective techniques, as we call them, sometimes they work and sometimes they don't. And that's where the creativity and the being beaker and being willing to blow up the lab comes in of like, wow, this personification exercise where I ask people to personify a bagel as if it was a celebrity that is really not working, people are not able to do that, so let's move on. (00:24:08): Let's throw it in the bin and let's start off down a different path. So I think being really heavy on projective techniques being very heavy and more creative ways of asking questions and being really heavy into emotion is what makes a particularly fascinating way of doing marketing, research, design. And of course, none of those things would apply if you were doing academic or the bunston version of research where you had to be much more buttoned up. You can't do that kind of thing, but we can play an experiment and have fun with it and really try to get to that more interesting result.

Cole Heilborn (00:24:44): Yeah. Wow. This research, how is it applicable to marketers? Are there any case studies or projects that you've worked on that you could share some of the insights that you've learned and then some of the decisions that were then made from that insight?

content: Megan Averell (00:25:01): Yeah. I mean, ultimately every single client has different objectives of what they're trying to get out of something. But a lot of times those questions will come from data. So they'll be like, okay, I can see something in my data that's not quite adding up and I don't understand what why is behind that? What's the consumer motivation behind that? So I had a client that came and said, look, our stuff is getting bought at much less of a rate than we think it should be. People aren't converting nearly as much as they should. And what we don't know, is it the page layout? Is it that they're having trouble understanding from an e-comm perspective how to go about things? Is that functional experience broken? Is the product and the way we're displaying the product on this e-commerce website not appealing? Are there questions we're not answering for them about the way that it's made or the way that people, so you can sit and generate that entire exhaustive list of hypothesis, but essentially your problem is you're not converting people at the rate that you should. (00:26:05): And for this particular client, which was an online men's dress apparel company, they had that extra challenge of you couldn't touch and feel the product. And if there are businessmen listening to this podcast, then that touching and feeling a dress shirt is a big part of how you might buy that dress shirt. So how do you do that and convey all of that and get people comfortable with what you're offering in just in e-comm kind of purchase? Well, that became the heart of the question. So actually what we did is I recruited people, this goes back to research design. We recruited people that were in their target market, really high powered sort of male executives who had to dress a certain way for work. So they were looking at men who were wearing dress wear. And then what we did is I talked to them on an online forum where we just kind of talked upfront about what were they looking for in general when they were looking for, this is all the open-ended stuff.

content: Megan Averell (00:25:01): (00:27:01): This is what I call the poll, where you're basically being very open-ended, your hands are completely in the air, and you're just like, tell me how it is to do this. How is it to shop for? What are you looking for? What do you have to feel the men's dress wear? Talk to me about that. And then got all their open-ended feedback. What are some of the great brands that you use? Why do you use those brands? That kind of thing. Then I mailed them product. So we actually took the product and mailed it to them, and during that time, we mailed it to them. The second stage of the research, while this was all happening in behind the scenes was to get them to go to the website. Okay, now site unseen, they were all people that specifically had not heard of this retailer. (00:27:44): That was a key. I wanted them to be very fresh. They came to the website, here's my series of questions about the website up to and including some functional things like put a product in your cart and almost walk through all the way you're going to transact to make sure it wasn't transaction problems. We were kind of checking things off the list, talk to me about the product, how does it feel looking at it, how does it seem to you? That kind of thing. And then of course, meantime, the product was on the way. And the third phase of the research, I actually had them turn on their computer camera and to actually open up the item in front of me to touch it, to feel it. Then I had them go off camera and put it on and come back and talk to me again. (00:28:27): How did it feel to be wearing it? Oh, well, this is interesting, this, I didn't expect this. So what you're getting is you can tell three stages of a full experience. Now, again, this is an artificial experience. There's no way in heck that anyone is ever going to go this exact way through this process. But in diagnosing just everything from their open-ended feedback, what they were currently using to how did they react to the e-comm site as it was to how was it to actually physically put on these things?

So what were the uniting threads that were really important to them, that all the boxes were checked all the way across the way, and then where were the breakdowns of things that were important to them and they weren't getting across? (00:29:12): And then on the negative side, what wasn't working for them about the website, but actually worked for them once they had the product in hand and looking for those disjoints and disconnects as well, what were they phrasing the way that they were the accurate way, or was it a way that consumers were interpreting it that was very different than the way they were presenting themselves on their website? So that's an example of just taking a different approach in research design and pulling it through to something that was really comprehensive. content: Megan Averell (00:30:06): They did almost instantly. I mean, the nice thing about some companies that are on this was on the smaller sort of startup funded end was they were able to make some of those changes immediately. And they did see Lyft over time. In fact, they kind of changed some of not just the day-to-day stuff, which they were able to change right away, but they did change some value proposition stuff. They did change some messaging that was very specifically things that in the game, I like to call it the game of telephone. The things you think you're communicating are often not the thing you're communicating because we use words and phrases for things, and I think any marketer knows that we run into this all the time. Then consumers interpret that. And sometimes that interpretation can go out into left field. It can be like, oh, well you said it's really smooth. (00:30:52): So I think what you mean is that the product is smooth. And it's like, no, I was saying the experience was smooth. You guys missed it. Right? How did you miss that? So what they had found was the way that they were stating their benefit and their unique benefit just wasn't coming across. People just weren't understanding the way that they had phrased it. And so oftentimes it's not like, well, we actually have to overhaul the value proposition. A lot of times it's like, oh, we thought we were getting something across, but when we actually checked in with people, they weren't interpreting it the same way. So if we just tweak the language, they'll be able to come along with us.

content: Megan Averell (00:32:14): Exactly. And there's no lack of hypothesis in a good marketing organization. I mean, that means you're going to sit there and your web team's going to be like, well, when we were designing this, we thought it would be a problem, and now it might be part of the problem. We had a hypothesis that it might be, but then your marketing team is going to be like, actually, I think we might be kind of not getting across this with the way the products look. I mean, some of it just came down to really simple things like they couldn't zoom when they wanted to, so they wanted to click on the product image, and they just wanted to be able to zoom to look at the fabric because of course, if I can't touch the fabric, their nearest best guess was, well, if I can zoom and look at the fabric and the threads and the way they come together, maybe that will help me determine the quality or ascertain the quality. (00:32:58): So it was kind of erroneous. And I think sometimes consumer perception is that, and it kind of sucks because as marketers, we want to live in a place where consumers understand what we understand because that just makes it that much more logical, and it makes it so much more easy to deal with them. But a lot of times they will come up with things like that that you're like, well, of course you can't ascertain by looking at it whether or not the thread count. You're like not an expert. How are your eyeballs really going to tell if this is a quality fabric just by zooming on an image, a static image? That's probably not real, but that is exactly what every single one of these people who'd never met each other and were in private conversation with me one-on-one asked for, right? So there was no influencing of a group. (00:33:45): They were just in private one-on-one, and they were saying, Ooh, I'm having a real frustration where I can't click to zoom to really see it because if I can't touch it, this is basically their proxy now. This is my way of being able to touch it. And that was actually something nobody in the company had thought of. So there was a bunch of hypothesis. Some of them proved to be true about just little problems and issues and things like that. But then there were things like this that consumers just brought out a left field that, okay, well they can't touch it. And the marketers were like, yeah, that's a problem. They can't touch it. But their way of solving that problem was just a little bit off kilter and probably a little different than we would've thought because no one is a site expert on how something's going to feel when you put it on. That's all a little backwards as far as actual logic, but it was their logic. And so a lot of times you have to adjust your framing to that consumer perceptual framing even when it's frustrating, even when you know that it might not. And I guess I keep saying it, it might not be real. I mean, it certainly is very real to them, but it might not have as much basis in fact, as I think a nice clean cut, very straightforward thing would imagine.

content: Megan Averell (00:58:09): Yeah, I think I often hear from folks in the industry that are, other researchers are like, yeah, I'm curious about people. But I also feel like I hear that from marketers a lot. I mean, I don't think people got into marketing so that they could push numbers around an Excel spreadsheet all day long. There is a fundamental truth I think that unites marketing and research, which is we kind of want to know what's driving people, what's up with that? We see things and our first reaction is what's up with that human behavior? It's the same thing that we get from psychologists and things like that too, but in that much more clinical sort of setting. So I think we share that. I don't think that's unique to research. I don't, but I think the intensity of that can be unique to research. I think you really do have to find someone, and if I was looking for a researcher personally, I'd be looking for someone who nerds out hardcore on those elements. It doesn't just say those nice things of like, yes, I really care what people think, but is committed to finding out and is committed to trying different things to get there. (00:59:17): I think a way I just woke up realized, oh my gosh, I want to be a researcher. But I do think the one thing that continually frustrated me that led me into research was that in marketing, we do sit at our desks for most of our day thinking about what people think, but we are not necessarily able to do that with knowledge of actual straight firsthand knowledge of what people think. And that's frustrating is like I've written a million personas in my life. I've written a bazillion customer journeys in my life, and I've written even more value propositions and things like that that have briefs that have a consumer blank in them. But the times I was able to talk to consumers in that 10 years were so fractional that at some point I realized this is made up and we are firmly in fantasy land and I can be very good at what I do and still be very wrong.

I mean, we are in sort of that business of resonance and being compelling. If you are saying stuff, it doesn't matter how factual it is. It doesn't matter if you're 20% better than your competitor. What matters is, is it resonant with them personally? Does it compel them to act? And of course, what we know and what I know as a researcher is that apathy is our biggest motivation. That's our biggest motivation. And so you're having to break through people's biggest motivation in order to get to those next level sets of motivations if you think about it, to get them to change behavior, to try your product or service. (01:01:04): So for me, it was the need I felt a need and a compelling need to know versus just making those assumptions. And now I still do freelance strategy work. I still do consultancy work because I want to keep that saw really sharp, and I want to continue to be someone who does research that can be implemented when I'm over on that side. I feel much better at my job now. I feel much better at the strategy role because I do know where consumers are at almost all the time. And that's a very different feeling than just being like, wow, I got to go to those focus groups one time a year. Or my client actually approved primary research where we got to go out and talk to people in one-on-ones one time a year ago, which is, it was just a glacial pace I felt like for talking to consumers and I couldn't live with that. There was just part of me, it was just like, I just need to bring, even if it's two focus groups, even if it's a minuscule amount of direction, I need to bring some direction to those assumptions, which they very often can be incredibly well, well-formed assumptions really well thought through. But there's still assumptions.

So I think if I could leave everyone on the podcast with anything, it's just that we have these again, really well thought out hypothesis, and a lot of times consumers are basing their opinions on your brands about the most minuscule things you've never thought of. So in one of my articles, I talk about how consumers are often building their brand perceptions from the ground up, and we're building them from the top down. We're going, here's our premise, and then here's everything that falls neatly into beautiful boxes under that premise or pillars or whatever we want to call them. And meanwhile, consumers are just having tangible experiences and so much of what they believe about you actually can ladder quite highly based on a tangible experience. (01:03:09): So for example, consumers have told me that they listen to the ways employees interact with each other when they're on the job. So if I'm a consumer and I'm sitting in a waiting room, or I'm sitting at a checkout stand and I'm watching the way employees treat each other, treat one another, I'm forming impressions about the brand and the way that the brand either trains or treats its people. By the way, my employees are just having what they think might be a private exchange or conversation. And that can be indicative to them of like, well, I bet they're paying them really good wages. They seem really happy, they seem to really love their jobs. And it's like, well, that again, may not be true, but these are examples of the laddering mechanisms. Consumers build from really small, tangible experiences that a lot of times we do not think about. (01:03:55): But companies that do, there's oil change companies where if you go to the fast oil change, I don't know if you've had this experience where you hear them communicating with each other in a really crisp manner, right? One of my friends actually is part of the team, a team working on a particular NFT project, and I won't say which one, but he told me about it and it was a really good chance for me to invest at a very, very low level, pretty risk averse, but I had to set up a crypto account and figure out how to buy crypto and then transfer that to my wallet and then follow this particular NFT project on Twitter, which leads to their Discord community that they've been building out, and then being part of the premin and then the Mint experience. (00:11:00): And I know that there is so much I still don't know, but actually just jumping in and doing it again with very low levels of money involved has been so helpful for me to at least start to get a grasp on this as we work out our North Face strategy and I see what different brands are tackling. I think there's always that element of when anything new comes out. Yeah, it's scary. Sometimes you just want to bury your head in the sand and be like, I cannot learn one more thing. On the flip side, it can be really fun and exciting once you do start to understand it. And yeah, sometimes I think you just have to dive in and do it versus reading about it, if that makes sense.

Cole Heilborn (00:11:44): Sure. Well, and I think in the back of our mind we're all realizing, oh, this could be the next Instagram and therefore maybe I should take this seriously because if I get in on the ground floor, I could really ride this wave. Alternatively, it could become what was that service that Google offered or it was like Google Plus or
