So I'm curious at the North Face in the halls in meetings, what are some of the common technologies that are coming up that are being discussed frequently that you guys are watching or dabbling in?

Bethany Evans (00:12:24): Great question. I guess I do want to acknowledge what you said around the scary elements of it, because it's true, there are already so many frauds and scams coming out. People have been comparing NFTs to Beanie Babies. Are a lot of these projects going to fail? Yes. Are there going to be a lot of learnings and a lot of iterations? Yes. So I think as we talk around the halls, that's part of it. Is this just too scary? Can a big company get into this space? I really see four different buckets for the big brand experience opportunities in the Metaverse, which would be one is customizable avatars and NFTs, this idea of digital and combining the physical and digital worlds, and do you have virtual clothing? I saw a quote and one mom said that her teenage daughter was spending more on virtual clothing for her avatars than on real clothing. (00:13:24): Wow. I mean, that's a shift from when I was a teenager. Second would be virtual and hybrid events as we all went to virtual events over the past two years, and I'm sure our CFOs appreciated the lower travel budgets, but we realized a lot of these conferences, a lot of these industry events, these speaker events, could they be virtual if people don't want to travel or could we at least offer them in a hybrid way where if you're not able to travel, there's also so many issues of accessibility. So I think those are some of the positives that have come out of the pandemic is do we keep the good things and combine them with the old things that we all miss to create something new? So events would be the second one. Third one would be this idea of tokens and brand access tokens and the idea that you might purchase an NFT, which gives you access to a special collaboration or product drop or shopping preview, things like that. (00:14:27): And then the fourth and final one, which I think is more of the OG, is gaming integrations. If we think back to Fortnite and Roblox and all of these games is kind of being on the forefront of this whole idea of the metaverse, which they have been, that is probably the lowest lift in many ways because games already exist.

And there was this idea of future shock that came up, this idea that it can be distressing to have too many rapid accelerations in society and technology happening all at once. And I do think there's that element of that. Exactly as you said, a lot of this can feel scary. It's a lot of new terminology that can feel exclusionary or just very difficult to learn. There's this idea, I think of Crypto Bros and is this something that's accessible to everyone and should it be since the whole idea of Web3 is decentralization? So yes, it's a lot that's being talked about, but I would go back to those four buckets as what seemed to be the initial four ways for brands to think about activating.

Bethany Evans (00:16:28): Is there a word for that? Integration.

content: Bethany Evans (00:16:51): That's a good question too because I think we tend to equate the metaverse with a lot of other things that are adjacent. And I'm certainly guilty of this too. I hear these different terms, and I think we sometimes are using it interchangeably with Web3 point, but that technically those are two different things, and I've heard them described different ways. One that I really like that is really simple is that Web 1.0 was the read web, right? We started to read our newspapers or blogs or there was very tightly controlled content. And Web 1.0 let us access that for the first time in a virtual way. We didn't have to get a physical newspaper anymore or a physical newsletter from our college, for example. And then that Web 2.0 was the read and write web. Now you could start to write maybe you're engaging blogs or forums or social media, but it was kind of that two-way exchange, but still very much with gatekeepers, the Facebooks now the Metas of the world, the different large conglomerates. (00:18:03): And so I think it's interesting that Web3 0.0 then is the read, write and Own web. And I think that piece around ownership is so interesting because the hope is that Web3 0.0 can solve for the idea of ownership over digital things. And it's funny, my husband is an intellectual property attorney, so of course he's already asking and seeing in his world, but wait, how does IP exist in this world? And if there's a claim of fraud, who do you go to if you say, Hey, my NFT was stolen somehow somebody else got the access credentials and now they say they own it. What do you even do about it in that case? So it's this really interesting idea, and it feels like this cultural shift where gaming has paved the way. Going back to your question about metaverse, we're seeing all of the building blocks to get us to that decentralized vision. So whether it's blockchain, crypto and wallets, NFTs, those are all I think building blocks that you would apply to the Metaverse to create the brand experience that you want. Whether that's roadblocks or some of these more sophisticated executions we're starting to see. But yeah, it's so much newness all at once.

It seems like it's maybe a few more years out before we truly are blending the physical and the digital in a more seamless way. Still, it feels pretty clunky if you've tried some of those virtual avatar meeting rooms. I mean, my kids have an Oculus and it's really fun and it's improved so much over how it used to be, but to me it still feels like we have a little ways to go.

Cole Heilborn (00:20:04): Gotcha. So when we're talking about the Metaverse, we're not just talking about how would you define the Metaverse?

Bethany Evans (00:20:15): It's good question. I think to me, the Metaverse is just this idea of a virtual existence that you can opt into the degree that you want, which I think will vary so much person to person. You might have someone who loves living in the virtual world. And again, I think it's so interesting when you go back to the ideas of accessibility, and that's one thing we've been thinking about for the North Face. We're a brand that our tagline is never stop exploring. How does that idea of exploration translate to the Metaverse? You think of something like Ready Player One. Okay, that is a very advanced version of this idea of you could explore in different worlds that have all of these different themes based on pop culture or whatever else. So I don't know that I have a good definition to be honest with you, other than I think it's this virtual idea that Neil Stevenson introduced back in the snow crash. But I think how it actually comes to life and all of this idea of real estate in the metaverse and artificial scarcity, and again, degree of participation that'll probably look very individual, which seems like the whole promise. So yeah, I'm excited by it, but I also have a lot of questions about it.

And maybe just for folks who don't know your affiliation with Vans, because I feel like that seems like a really kind of great case study or example that has provided some insights into some of these things, right?

Bethany Evans (00:22:01): Yes. So I am very lucky to be at the North Face. We're owned by the F Corporation, which owns fans, Timberland Supreme, and a number of other brands. And it's my first time working for a portfolio company. And what I've loved about it is in the past, if I wanted to talk to another company, there were NDAs and all of the paperwork. And with being part of a portfolio company, we can just talk to our sister companies and share information and share projects and data without the need for that level of governance. And so yeah, vans introduced a Van's world within Roblox, which made a ton of sense given their demographic target, which is different from ours. Of course, a huge number of people love Vans. I think everyone from little kids to older adults, so don't mean to say that they do not serve a wide variety of the population, but Roblox, the consumer tends to be on the younger side. I think it's like eight to 12 in there.

Cole Heilborn (00:23:05): And what is Roblox? What is that?

content: Bethany Evans (00:23:08): Yeah, so it's a virtual gaming world, kind of like Minecraft for those who might be familiar with the Minecraft instead of a Roblox. But you have an avatar within Roblox, and there are many different experiences where your avatar can go to participate. So what is really cool about it is a lot of brands have built out their own worlds, worlds within the larger Roblox world. And so Vans is one of them. Last year they very scrappily and quickly, a lot of it was they worked with developers over Slack and they were just trading stuff back and forth all day on Slack is what they shared with us. So I would just say that to say I can't share specifics, but from what they told us, the cost of entry, the development time, it was all much cheaper and much faster than I would've expected. So I think again, sometimes we have in our heads ideas that, oh, only big brands can afford to do X, Y, or Z. (00:24:13): And having worked in both startups earlier in my career and then bigger brands later in my career, I don't think that's true. I think sometimes smaller brands can be incredibly successful doing these so-called bigger activations. You just have to be more choiceful. If you do have a lower overall budget and you have 10 opportunities on the table in front of you, maybe a bigger brand can afford to do eight, and a smaller brand can afford to do two or three, but that doesn't mean they can't do an incredible job at the two or three that they choose. I think again, it's just thinking about product market fit. And for Vans, this made a ton of sense because they had the opportunity to build out, they're so known. Of course, Tony Hawk known for being the skateboarding community is kind of how they originated and grew up. (00:25:06): And so they had the opportunity to build a virtual skateboarding world within Roblox, which is so true to their DNA, and so true to that more younger demographic within their consumers, keeping Vans top of mind. So yes, vans told us about this van's world that they launched and has been very successful. And we said, Ooh, that's really cool. And my colleague Zena worked with them, and we launched a popup North Face store within the Van's world.

Not a lot of development work, not a lot of time or money, but really cool to just test stuff. And I think ultimately that's a way to protect yourself a bit is just testing in different small ways to start. You don't always have to go with this giant fully baked out strategy with all kinds of new technology because what has become very clear to me and my colleagues within marketing as we start to talk about the Metaverse Web3 0.0 is it is not just a marketing conversation within marketing. If we want to throw an event, we can just go through an event. This is so different. (00:27:03): We need to talk to legal, we need to talk to the privacy team, we need to talk to the web development team. Everything in this space touches so many teams that you cannot activate on it in a vacuum. So I think it's very good in a way because it makes you work very cross-functionally internally. The flip side of that, especially at a big company to be candid, is it can be slow, right? And I know you and I talked a little bit about our VF Venture Foundry and kind of the whole idea behind that to try to create some agility even within the framework of a larger company. That's been really encouraging. And they've brought us some partners and some technologies to consider that they've already pre-vetted, pre considered those. So yes, we're working on it.

Cole Heilborn (00:27:53): So with your pop-up store, I could take my avatar to your store and am I purchasing North Face apparel or am I just with in-game credits, or am I just going and browsing through things and throwing them on my avatar? And are these actual products that you guys make or are they designed specifically for the game?

Bethany Evans (00:28:14): These have been 3D versions of actual products that we make. Of course, you can absolutely design online exclusives for virtual worlds, which is something I've already seen a lot of brands start to do, which is really cool. There's even brands that are saying, buy this physical product like this jacket and will also give you the virtual version of it for free is kind of an add-on, which is so interesting. But yes, there is actual, at least with Roblox, there is real money involved. They are purchasing these items using in game credits, which they're spending real money to buy just like you do with so many of these games. And then again, I can't get into the revenue specifics, but for most of these experiences, there's some sort of revenue sharing opportunity that's set up where the brand is actually getting dollars back and they can get those development costs back potentially within a matter of months, and then turn these experiences into a revenue stream, which I think anytime you can speak positively to the bottom line, that's the win. (00:29:28): But for me, especially, it's been so interesting the last couple years with all of the supply chain challenges. I think every retailer has dealt with those products coming in later than you had planned on, or maybe not as much as you had planned on. And how do you deal with that? How do you get stuff to the consumer's hands? How do you adjust all of your forecast? And the idea that you can have virtual goods that aren't dependent on the real world supply chain and are a little bit safer in terms of a projectable revenue stream. That is very interesting too.

content: Bethany Evans (00:30:56): Definitely a big thing we're thinking about is the utility and what is the value exchange? If we're asking consumers to do something like, yeah, technically use their money or their parents' money to buy goods, do those feel like they're actually worth it? And then when you start to think about some of these other things like, Hey, give us your data and we'll give you this NFT or this token or whatever it is. I think with all of these privacy changes that are happening, which need to happen, the idea that in the future people will have crypto wallets which own their digital identity and that they would have more control over how that digital identity gets distributed. I think you have to think about with anything you're planning, and there's some things we're planning I can't talk about yet, but we are really, really thinking about A, what is the infrastructure required to actually build this ourselves versus buy it? There's always that build versus buy consideration. And Nike famously recently bought what was considered the, I heard it described as the Nike of the Metaverse, a company that was pretty advanced in that space, and then Nike bought 'em because Nike can afford to and kudos to them for moving quickly. (00:32:21): But yeah, it's the build versus buy, and then it's that value exchange of one of the things that I manage being our loyalty program. Of course, I see so many applications with all of this within the loyalty space, are we able to better consumer's preferences and cater to those preferences in a whole new way? But then what are we asking them to give up? Are we asking them for more data or different data? And what are we providing in return that makes that feel like a fair value exchange to them? I think we've all been burned, right? Sometimes you join a brand and you feel like you're giving them all this information. Maybe they ask for your birthday, but then they never send you anything on your birthday. So you're like, well, why did you want to know other than for your own database, but what are you giving me back as the consumer if we're giving you that information?

There are some of the early big communities in this space with very active members who it seems like in many cases are willing to embrace or at least give brands a chance when they're trying to activate with these members. As long as it's in a way, going back to what we said about providing value. But that is so interesting to me because I've worked in the influencer space for a long time. When I worked at Southwest, we launched what we called our southwest storyteller program because we felt like the influencer space at that time was so fragmented where you were paying an influencer at a time to do a post and there was no ongoing relationship. (00:36:18): And in some cases, they didn't even know much about your brand. It felt inauthentic, and consumers are not stupid. They pick up on that. And so what we decided to do at Southwest was work with those more micro and medium influencers and launched this program called Southwest Storytellers, where when you were picked to be a southwest storyteller, and we tried to pick a very diverse array of people from different backgrounds and different stories to tell, we would give them tickets for a whole year. So they would spend a whole year traveling around on us, deciding what they wanted to talk about, and then they would roll off into our, what we were calling our storyteller alumni network, where it's like, Hey, we don't want to lose that relationship with you, but we do want to make sure we're always giving new people a chance to participate in this program. (00:37:08): But because it was a year long, we actually built these relationships. We hosted all of these storytellers out at our headquarters, gave them tours, answered their questions, and I think it came across in such a better way because it actually was authentic. So same thing right now that we're talking about these opportunities to maybe co-create with creators in this space who they've already built up a following, they know this space better than we do as brands. Is there a way that we can make something together with them or provide something of value to their community, assuming that their community is maybe a target demographic that we're trying to reach? And again, I think it depends on your brand, but those are some other really interesting executions too. I saw another one that I liked from Levi's. They were letting you win N NFTs, so doing sweepstakes to win an NFT to get your jeans repaired for free. So if you had one of these NFTs, you could bring your old ripped jeans in, and I don't know the exact process, but there was real world value that came attached to this virtual item. So again, those blurred lines, it seems to go both directions.

And so I think there's a lot there. But yes, I would say it all goes back to community. Is this a new way to engage with members or at least a subset of your community?

So right there, you're part of a club. You're one of the only 5,000 holders of whatever this particular NFT might be. And a lot of times within the communities, they have even subsets within that. Okay, within this 5,000 NFT, how rare is yours? And all of us that have this type of rare creation, we're in this little group, but it's all tribes. I think as marketers, we're always just trying to understand what do our consumers care about and how do we give them what they care about in a way that makes sense for our brand? And so much of that has always been around this idea that your consumer isn't one person. It's different tribes of people and very individual people. From a basic demographic perspective, you might look exactly the same, but then you try to dig deeper into those psychographics and those motivations and you realize, oh, they're actually completely different and you should speak to them in completely different ways. You still had a little bit of control in terms of you could kind of, well, you could control, I'll just go back to the old days of Facebook pages, for example. You controlled who was allowed to your page. You could remove followers, you could remove posts that went against your community guidelines that were on your Facebook page. There were sort of some built-in controls for brands. If you're a brand trying to be part of an existing discord community, it's kind of like with Reddit, anytime a brand does an A MA on Reddit, wow, that could go really well or really poorly. It's great, but people say, ask me anything seriously. It's like, are you really prepared to answer anything that they're going to ask? I think there's a little bit, I think a lot of Reddit folks are probably also Web3 folks. I don't know what that Venn diagram looks like, but yeah, just keep it real.

Cole Heilborn (00:42:51): So yeah, you bring up a good point. If a brand is letting go of some of its control in these communities, how does it make sure that it shows up authentically and that it is a showing up in its true self?

Bethany Evans (00:43:07): I think one would be putting culture before technology. We talked a little bit about, there's so much tech behind all of this, but the technology is just an enabler for any of these examples. Who is using the technology? Why and let that drive. I think the decisions versus, oh, here's a new technology capability. Let's use it. Without that decision being driven by, no, no, no, what's the cultural component? Like why and how people are engaging with this. And if you don't know ask. I have gotten much more comfortable over the years at being okay with what I don't know. Again, brands don't know a lot about this, and a lot of people don't know a lot about this. Find the experts, ask them. They tend to be so kind and willing about sharing their knowledge and inviting people into their spaces. I think it's okay to know what you don't know and not be the all-knowing all powerful marketers or brand not.

We've always had this issue as marketers in the 2.0 world of social where you have these walled gardens like Google and Facebook and they don't talk to each other. And how are you finding your customers across these different walled gardens? I think the exact same thing will happen in Web3 0.0, and it will depend on the level of access that people choose to give us now instead of companies in the future. It won't be no, Facebook is saying you can't have that data. The north face, it'll be no coal is saying you can't have that data the north face. So that's a really, really scary but also exciting idea. I always have to sometimes take off my marketing hat and just think of how do I feel as a consumer and what would I be comfortable being shared or known about me? So it's a really interesting idea, even this idea of friendship and less differentiation between digital friends and real world friends. And as a parent, how does that play in? I personally am very hesitant to let my youngest join games like Fortnite because I don't know who he's talking to or what they're talking about or who these people actually are. And so yeah, I think there are a lot of questions about all of this.

content: Bethany Evans (00:48:27): That's the line we're walking. Absolutely. I think there's been really interesting examples like Pokemon Go and the idea of ar where sometimes you can overlay that virtual component on the real world experiences, but you're still encouraging people to get out there and go places and see things. Those are really interesting. Another thing that we're grappling with is the environmental aspect of all of this. NFTs use a lot of energy when they're what's called minted a, a tokenizing a digital file within blockchain, or at least the original blockchain technology. So we're thinking about, okay, sure, there's different offset utilities that exist to make an activation net zero or even negative, like you plant a tree for each NFT purchase, right? There's offset, things like that. Or you can use a lower consumption blockchain. I think polygon would be one or proof of stake, but that's another thing we're considering is we're a brand that very much cares about keeping the outside world beautiful and sustainable. (00:49:39): And we recognize that retail in general has not been kind to the environment. We have certainly been culpable in that, and we've made a lot of changes and are continuing to make a lot of changes to try to make everything we do much more renewable, participate much more in the circular economy where we have different trade-in programs and repair programs and our lifetime warranty program. But yeah, that for us is another huge consideration is like you said, if we're about exploration, what does that exploration look like for the virtual world? And then if that exploration is built on the back of these high energy consumption technologies that are not good for the environment, is there a way we can participate in a better way that doesn't go against our core beliefs? And so yeah, I think those considerations are going to be different for every brand based on what does their brand stand for or care about, but a hundred percent, it's a huge thing to think about. So yeah, I would say we have not rushed in, we are working on all of this, and I've given you a couple little examples, but we have not been one of the earliest movers because there are big questions that we're concerned about and we're trying to take our time and do things the right way. Can't promise, we'll never make any missteps, but I think we don't want to rush in and do things that feel completely antithetical to who we are.

Cole Heilborn (00:51:13): Do you have a way of evaluating what technologies are worth investing in? I don't know if you have a corporate rubric or if you personally have a rubric that you use to try to evaluate some of these things. I dunno, maybe something that people can use to kind of implement in their own scenario if they're trying to validate or understand some of these things.

Bethany Evans (00:51:35): That's such a good one. Yes, we do have different evaluation criteria. I'll say the first thing that we do is we don't act in a vacuum anytime. We're evaluating new technology. We work with our central VF technology partners, and again, this is more specific to portfolio companies, but we try to think about the data flow from the outset, and that is the most unsexy thing ever. But almost all of these technologies, they have some sort of data component where files are being shared, maybe consumer data is being shared, maybe there's APIs. And we are increasingly so protective of consumer data and some of these different metaverse activations that are underway would consider some sort of data exchange. And are these new companies, they're not the legacy companies that already have a lot of this security documentation and privacy documentation in place. So the biggest thing we do to start with is literally just map out the data flows of very simply, what is the use case for this technology? (00:52:48): And that's another thing is trying to separate the use case from the specific provider. Because a lot of times there's multiple providers that could do the same thing and you don't want to get so locked in on one that you're losing side of the forest for the trees. So we try to evaluate to start, not necessarily do we have this one partner in mind that we want to work with, but what are we trying to achieve for our consumer? What does success look like? And then what would need to be true for that success to occur? And a lot of times it is those literal flows and sometimes in those flows discover blockers where it's like, Hey, in order for this to work, we would need a real-time API, but we couldn't do an API or the partner couldn't do an API for X, Y, Z reason. (00:53:35): So it would be really slow and it would be terrible consumer experience. It's those tactical questions that sometimes uncover really, really important things. So yeah, I guess that's my advice is have the big idea. That's awesome, but then get really technical in terms of how that big idea would come to life and be prepared to pivot. I think as marketers, we pivot all the time. You have something in your head and you find out, yes, but or yes. And sometimes it ends up being even better than you initially envisioned, but I think you have to be willing to be flexible, especially in these new worlds where the regulations, the technology, it's all changing by the day.

Is there anyone dabbling in this that you're paying attention to? I know you've mentioned some brands outside the outdoors, but anyone inside the industry,

Bethany Evans (00:54:43): I don't know that I've seen anyone within the industry. Of course, we all pay attention to each other. I haven't seen anyone do a ton in this space yet. And I would imagine it's because a lot of them are asking the same questions that are kind of unique to our industry. So that's great. I think we're all probably taking a similar approach to, cool, let's get into the space, but let's do it carefully. Outside of the outdoor industry, they've been really impressed with Gucci. We've partnered with them on different product collaborations, but I've just always been so impressed with how they're consistently on the forefront of these new technologies pushing the envelope. They also did a ROBLOX execution, but they're one I would just encourage anyone to pay attention to. And also, I think we all have to be honest as marketers and share with each other what are the issues we encounter that we can learn from because there are failures that could easily happen to anyone. (00:55:45): And I think an example of that would be McDonald's. I have a dear friend who recently worked at McDonald's, so this is in no way a knock on them. I think they're an amazing brand, but they famously had an NFT project for their McRibs where some bad actor had embedded racial slurs deep within the blockchain data, and it came out later. And how do you plan for something like that and start to understand even that this is an area of watch out, like, oh, you need to comb through every bit of this blockchain data. And the idea that blockchain is a permanent record, that doesn't go away. I think as marketers, we've gotten used to the ability to update things. Maybe there's an error on our website and we're able to update it and just send consumers a notification that like, Hey, this was wrong. (00:56:38): We fixed it. Here's the new correct information. You can't do that with blockchain. You can send out the apology email, but whatever's on the blockchain is still on the blockchain, at least as far as my understanding. So again, that's not something I would call a failure of McDonald's. That was them experimenting and finding out something that now we're all like, oh, okay, that's something I should watch out for too. And I know we all, as marketers, we have so many different forums. You're providing an awesome forum. We have adage, Adweek, whatever it might be. But I think the more transparent we are with each other about, Hey, here's the potential pitfall, or here's something that I uncovered, it's going to help all of us and help everyone at the C-suite get a little bit more comfortable too, knowing that exchange of information and exchange of best practices is happening just happened in the social space. I mean, I remember when I started in social, there were no best practices, there were no playbooks, there were no industry organizations. And then slowly organizations started coming out, like social media.org that provided a place for marketers to talk to each other and be like, Hey, are you dealing with this too? Or did you see that? And we're going to need the exact same thing for this space.

Bethany Evans (00:58:11): Well, I would say of course I'm excited because a huge sci-fi and fantasy nerd, I grew up watching Star Trek, the Next Generation with my dad. That was our bonding thing. Every week we would watch TNG, and I've always read a ton of science, fantasy, and fiction. So again, going back to Danielle Stevensons of the world and the William Gibson's. So it's kind of amazing that a lot of these ideas I've been reading about for the last 20, 30 years are potentially at least closer than they used to be. And I really, really do love the idea that it could kind of democratize some areas in a new way. I think that is a very powerful thing that could potentially be really good. So I'm very excited about the applications and where all of this could go, but I'm very wary, again, having lived through social, lived through the.com bust. I'm kind of dating myself now, but I'm in my late thirties. I've seen a couple booms and busts, and I think right now it's the new shiny object like we've talked about. Inevitably there will be issues that come out, issues of fraud, money that gets lost, scammers, and how do you address those issues that continue to move forward? And just a really positive, productive way, I think is something we just all need to try to drive as an industry, because then I think, again, there could be so much good that comes out of it.

Cole Heilborn (00:59:44): Yeah, and who knows, maybe in two or three years if the podcast is still going, conversations, this will be happening in a 3D virtual world rather than sitting on Zoom.

Bethany Evans (00:59:56): Exactly. How crazy would that be?

Cole Heilborn (00:59:59): That would be pretty cool. The think about that is pretty wild because I feel like when I think about the use cases of the metaverse, most of my reaction is pretty negative, but that particular interaction seems really cool.

I mean, there's, sure, we've been all getting texts from politicians for years, but as it comes down to brands that really only started less than two years ago, so it's a super insanely new fields. And the cool thing about SMS marketing is that it's been introduced with all these regulations. So email marketing has, when it came to be, it was just kind of really loose and anyone can send emails and this spam and all that stuff. There wasn't really any regulation behind it. But SMS is really being built that you can't just buy a text list and start sending them emails or sending them text messages. If you text someone who you don't have explicit permission to text, you can get fined like $500 depending on the state you're in. And say you send those messages to 500,000 people and all of a sudden 1% of those comes back reporting, you can actually get in a lot of trouble. (11:55): So one, it's cool because there are actual regulations behind it, but two, a couple fun facts about SMS customers are 97% of customers open a text within three minutes of receiving it. Email open rates are typically around 30% at best, so you're really reaching people really well. And so it's just a cool way to get your message across. And it's also really easy to execute. It's a lot easier to write out 140 character text message campaign than it is to design an email and go through that phase. And lastly, it's just a really easy way for customers to interact with you. It's easy to, in a previous role I had, there's a lot of sizing help you needed help with as a dog product. And so people would send back a picture of their dog and be like, how does this look? And it's just thinking about your messaging and understanding that your customers, they might love your brand, but they don't want to be sold to five days a week. They want to be talked to, they want to connect with you, and they're excited about the adventures that they go on with your product, and they want to share that with you. And so the more you give them the opportunity and the channels to share that, you start to see more user generated content. You see these people start to get fomo and they see someone else had that blanket and like, oh my gosh, I want that blanket. And so it's really a positive snowball effect. And I think it can be hard for some brands at first like, okay, well, I send this text on a Friday that just asks people what they're doing this weekend. And obviously very few people are going to buy from that. There's no link in it. There's no call to action. It's just like, Hey, let me know what you're doing this weekend. But building those relationships is retention long play. It makes those customers more loyal down the line when they're thinking about getting a Christmas grif for someone or adding another blanket. They're going to say, blanket Rumble. I love Rumble. They're going to recommend it to friends and family. So this snowball effect there is really amazing.

So my whole basis for reality was what happened in the movies and of course, where was every movie ever filmed, more or less in California. So when I left college, I went to California. I worked in the movie business for a little bit, and I was really, really fortunate. I worked my way into the business, was able to work with a really well-known academy award-winning director by the name of Oliver Stone. I was his story editor. (03:00): I mean what that meant at the time, I don't know, I just kept getting yelled at and I had to make a lot of copies, but I also was able to oversee the story department, the internship department, and I just had to read a lot. The biggest moment sort of in my career, and I still have it, the biggest trophy that I have is when they presented me with an LL Bean tote bag with the name of the production company on it. And that was so that I could carry 20 physical scripts back and forth from the office every night and read 'em and sit in my apartment and just read till I fell asleep and then started all over again. So that was just an amazing experience crash course in storytelling and telling compelling stories and vetting ideas. And then I had a really amazing opportunity to work on some films at Warner Brothers and 20th Century Fox. (03:50): Again, just worked on animation and animation movie from a while back called Osmosis Jones. And that was an incredible experience because the movie lived on the wall for so long. It was like, here's the scene, here are the storyboards. And they just kept refining, refining and refining and kind of what I learned there. Sometimes that's a great thing and sometimes that can be a bad thing to keep kind of whittling away at the movie movie. But ultimately, I also had this really incredible intense desire and passion for the outdoors.

content: Marc Gutman (02:14): I'd always envisioned that I'd lived somewhere out west. And so I moved to Colorado and while I was writing, I was writing a spinoff of Osmosis Jones for Warner Brothers. (04:40): I was writing cartoon episodes and I picked up a job at this tech company in Boulder, Colorado, and it was kind of a predecessor to Zoom. It was a communication collaboration company. They were doing a lot of stuff with mobile phones, and I saw this opportunity, so I spun out of there. I was just super enamored with the startup scene in Colorado. It was kind of booming. It was kind of stereotypical what you might see on the Simpsons or something. It was a little bit of a joke, everybody wearing t-shirts with the name of the company on it and stuff like that. But it was also really, really exciting and a lot of things were happening. And so I started my own company and I was doing that, and at the same time, everyone kept saying, well, you worked in the movie business and you're good at marketing your own company. (05:27): We help us with our story. And I was like, yeah, I can do that. And then we would work together and it would end up in a horrible, awful experiment and nobody was happy. And that was because no one really knew what this word tell our story meant. And it means even to this day, it means so many different things. People say it and they think it means, will you help me with my social media? Will you do a brand film for me? Will you help me with my overall brand? We don't what to say. We have a bad sales pitch. Our value props off. And so it took me a while. I didn't know it that many either, and a lot of failed experimentation, a lot of unhappy people. But I just kept at it because I knew and I believe, and I still believe in my heart that storytelling is the greatest thing that we can bring to a business. (06:14): It's the greatest value that we can bring in communicating and adding value to a business.

And so I just immersed in that and I figured that out and taught myself that. And as you know, having your own business, it's like sometimes the best teacher is hard knocks and real world experience. And I had some failures, but more successes and I finally got better and better at it. And here we are today with Wild Story, which is a brand strategy and design studio. And I like to say that we're here to help brands outmaneuver their competition, but we do that through storytelling. (07:06): And what does outmaneuver your competition mean? It just means I want you to stand out. We want you to be different. We want people to connect and resonate with you so that they choose you. I just really believe that in most instances, people aren't really buying. They're choosing. They've already decided if I want to go buy a mountain bike, I know I want a mountain bike right now. It becomes like I got to go find the one that fits me, and it kind of tells the story and it makes me feel like a cool mountain biker and I'm going to pick that one or whatever. So not just a silly example, but I really do believe that we're more choosing than buying and we really want to help companies do that. So that's what we do here. That's the sort of short, long version. That was a little long of a story, but yeah, we could talk more about it if you'd like. But that's what we're doing to help businesses. And a lot of the businesses we work with are outdoor lifestyle, but we also work with B2B and things like that. We just don't publicize it as much.

And then of course, we're in this really big sort of outdoor lifestyle community, so that's why we end up there.

Cole Heilborn (08:29): Totally. So it sounds like storytelling has taken different shapes over the years, but it's always been something that's been near and dear to your heart. Where does your passion for story and telling a good story come from?

Marc Gutman (08:45): I think a lot, not a lot, but a couple different areas. I kind of alluded to it, but I grew up in Detroit, Michigan. I had a really great childhood, but it was just kind of a boring, everything else always seemed way cooler than Michigan and seemed way more interesting. And it just seemed like something was happening from a very young age. And I credit probably my mother for this. I was just a voracious reader and I would just transport to different places and I had a really ability to have a vivid imagination. But even I remember I used to sit and just read Thrasher magazine and just imagine what those kids in California were like, and I could really kind of feel the sunshine coming off the page. Even then a magazine like Thrasher, it was really sort of this mixed media. It was photography, it was words, it was kind of like street art and stuff like that. (09:45): So when I think of storytelling, I've always been really drawn to these ways of mixed media and composites. I do think that all our senses really are alive. And then the other thing is my dad and I, we just used to love to watch movies. I think that's how we used to really connect. We had a shorthand and he loved movies, and so we'd watch a ton of movies and just laugh together. And I just always loved that world better than the real world, I think. And sometimes that's a superpower and sometimes that's a weakness, that's a kryptonite to live in that world, but I think that's where that comes from.

content: Marc Gutman (10:57): And this is something that we just were talking about, but we work a lot with manifestos manifesto for a business for a person, it's just a rallying cry. It's like what you're about. It's a narrative that you can read and it just embodies what you stand for, who you are, what you believe in. We have somewhere on the internet, it's our most active lead magnet kind of thing, and we have How to Write your own manifesto. And I did a webinar and I talk about it and there's five or six, seven areas that you can just kind of plunk in there. And it's like, who are you? Who are you for? What do you believe? What are your values? Things like that. But then you put it into a narrative and businesses and brands have been using these for 30, 40 years, and it's like, what do you believe? (11:49): It's a rallying cry because even we always talk about values and beliefs, but everyone just kind of throws 'em up on the wall and they're like integrity, right? Everyone's like, what's integrity with a mountain picture? So it really becomes this way that you can get excited, but in its purest form, it's just like what you stand for and what you believe. And so you and I were talking about something that happened to me a few weeks ago, and the short version of that is, so we do brand strategy, but we've been working with a lot of other agencies as well, and they come and they say, Hey, will you work with us? And we're like, sure. And they're like, well, but we have our own process. We have our own format. And going into that, my line was sort of like, Hey, well no problem. (12:42): A lot of things, brand strategies like chicken noodle soup, it's like, hey, everyone has their own sort of special sauce, but at the end of the day, it's basically the same ingredients and the output's basically the same. The only thing really kind of adjusting that output are some of the inputs, which might be budget, which might be time, things like that, size of client. So I went through that process and found that I really struggled and I really had some challenges, and I kind of underestimated how easy it would be to tweak my process into their process.

(13:38): And some of the things are, Hey, we are going to use our process. We're not going to bend on some of these other things because that's how we can be successful. And what happened as well is, and I think anyone who's in the creative space or creating anything in the marketing space can attest to is it was extremely stressful. It was really hard. It was trying to work something that I wasn't familiar with into an output that wasn't familiar. And I think the only way that these businesses really work for us is when we're able to maintain a process and work the familiar. So that was the idea. That's what I was working on. I had written some bullet points, some of which I've just shared here. I've yet to actually write the manifesto. I've actually yet to put that narrative down because just some things got in the way since we've last talked, but it's on my list.

Cole Heilborn (14:36): Were you aware of how important your own process was before this example where you had to adhere to someone else's process?

Marc Gutman (14:47): And this is kind of an interesting nuancey thing, right? I totally abandoned my process. It wasn't like I didn't know my process, but I just thought that the mile markers of my process were enough to hold it all together. And what I realized, and that was a tough thing to learn, was no, that even those little sort of things in the process from output to how you're going to present something to how you're going to go about something really do matter. And so it's not that easy to just plug and play different pieces and things like that. So it was a good lesson to learn.

Cole Heilborn (15:32): So let's take a step back before we dive in a little deeper. Why is process so important for creatives?

content: Marc Gutman (15:41): Well, I mean, I can only give you my thoughts on this, but a couple things. I mean, I think that anytime that we're given parameters, anytime we're given rules, anytime we're given a box that actually sets us free as creatives, I think the hardest thing to do is to have no guidelines and just a blank page. And you're just like, ah. Right. And also at the end of the day, we're here to please clients. I mean, this is not wild story.org. I know your business isn't a non-for-profit. We're in business and we do need to please clients. And so having some constraint that breeds creativity. So I believe that I also, from my own personal experience, creating on a regular basis is really, really, really hard. And so that process gives you steps and steps in the literal word, like stair steps. It gives you the ability to walk up steps one at a time, even when you're not feeling like it. (16:47): I mean, I don't know about you, but I've had so many times where I've just been like, I don't feel creative. I don't feel like doing stuff today actually. And we just mentioned I came off running a marathon over the weekend. I'm kind of feeling down and it's really hard to work today. I need something that I follow step by step to get me going. It also allows you, it allows me in the sales process, I can tell people what to expect. I know what to expect. It helps to control scope of work. And it also helps once in the sales process, I've communicated to a client, my process acts as breadcrumbs and they know exactly where they are in this process, how long it's going to be, where are we, and we can always go back to that and point to that. And then lastly, I think if you want to, and I use this word very, very loosely scale because it's really hard to scale in the creative space, but if you want to add teammates, if you want people to be involved in your business, having a documented process allows them to keep things going and to keep things consistent, and you can bring people on to help you. (18:04): And I guess on that last thing too, you become more efficient as well. So in the story that I just told, I was extremely inefficient, which caused a lot of stress. I was probably, if I look back and I look at the utilization of my time on that project, not good. I probably lost money or didn't make a lot of money, and I was super stressed out. And so we want to avoid all those things as a creative, and that's what for me at least, process does.

content:
Cole Heilborn (18:37): This is kind of a sidebar, but I'm curious if you ever forget your process, and this happens to me frequently, we'll be in the middle of a project, everything's up in the air, we're in the middle of the messy creative stuff, and for whatever reason, I lose sight of what is the next step or what are we working towards? And that's often in that moment there's this sense of, oh, shoot, what are we trying to create? What's our next deliverable? What's our next milestone? And then sometimes I have to remind myself and actually go look at my own documentation and say, oh, that's right. I'm working towards a brief or I'm working on a treatment right now. And then that realigns me and recenters me as I'm working on whatever this thing is.

Marc Gutman (19:22): Yeah, I mean, I don't know if we typically lose sight of the process mid project, but what I will say is I'm a constant process tinkerer and collector, and I'm always like, is someone doing it better? And so I'm always trying to change it up or introduce a new process. And then a lot of times it doesn't go well. And I'm like, why did I do that? Everything's fine. I just can't leave good enough alone. And I think part of that too is when you're working on a creative project, I mean, the way that as creatives, we have fun with these is we explore things. We go off on tangents, we kind of push into different areas and it's like part of our personality, but then that's when we get in trouble when you're like, oh, where am I in this project? Or why? And I start tinkering with the process. I've been trying and trying just to hold our process, but I'm always like, ah, I like the way that person does it better, or I've seen this in a different way, but the steps are typically the same. It's just how we get there that I guess I'm always tinkering with.

Cole Heilborn (20:37): What I'm curious to understand is your process a little bit and what are the important pieces to it that allow wild story to do what it does? Are there any steps that are super critical to what you do that allow the creative engine to flow smoothly and stay organized?

content: Marc Gutman (20:56): Yeah. Well, I mean that's a pretty big question. Absolutely. I mean, everything mean we have sort of operational process, which is just setting up the account in our project management software that we use. We use Notion and getting the shell and everything set up there, making sure that billing's set up appropriately. We have some processes where if you spend a certain amount of money with us as a client, it triggers an automatic welcome gift. So all of those things I think are operational, but super, super important kind of the core things on our process. I'm right now more like I'm putting more and more importance on the front end with the discovery. That used to be something that I think when we started it was just a really quick intake form, and now I'm realizing that everything comes out of that. The challenge is that clients, it's budget. (22:02): And so clients with bigger budget, it's fun because we can take the time to ask questions and really learn and really build. Because what I like to do and what I love about this business in general is I love to come in with a totally empty mind, and I love to come in without expectation and kind of learn. I don't know anything about the industry, even if I do know a little bit. And it takes me down some really interesting paths, and I like to understand how someone might be coming to this for the first time, whatever that might be. And that's going to bring up a lot of questions and hopefully some fresh thinking. And part of that discovery as we get into discovery is I love interviewing people. That's the way I started kind of doing this work, and then I moved away from it. (22:53): It was just so time consuming, but then I was like, you know what? But that's where all the gold is. That's where we really find all the great ideas, all the great insights is interviewing stakeholders, both internally, externally, customers, things like that. So when we think about process, I've been coming way back to, hey, discovery is where it's at. Slowing that down, not budging on that.

Now we can rightsize that, of course, buy size a budget, but that's the really, really big thing. And then also we go through values and beliefs. We go through persona, we go through all this brand stuff. And for the most part, we won't sort of gloss over that. If a client's like, yeah, we just did that six months ago. (23:50): I'm like, great, let's pressure test that. We'll bring in their stuff more often than not. Either I'll just use values, core values or something, and beliefs as an example. They're not still valid or they weren't applicable, or we've just learned something deeper and have gone into a new area that we can really build on those and really take them to the next level. And so clients are rarely unhappy after the fact. But I get it, a lot of this work is tough. You're pulling a lot of leadership teams, a lot of important people off their task for a day, two days, weeks sometimes. And so people are really protective of their time. But I just know, and again, I alluded to it in the beginning of when I was telling you in my story, I've had so many failed client interactions that hurt I care. (24:49): I think probably 99% of all creatives are in this business. They love it. They care about their clients, they want to please them. And nothing hurts more than a client that doesn't get what they want or that's upset and they're just not going to get that if we shortcut the process. And so trying to be better about it, but I'm kind of like everybody too. You get this awesome client on the line and they start making all these exceptions and you've always wanted to work with them. And you start to, all right, I'll change it. But it always goes badly. It always goes badly. And then you have that conversation, why did I do that?

Cole Heilborn (25:28): So understanding, I think I have a much better understanding of to you what process is and why that's important. So jumping back to this story, where part of your process changed, what were some of the big takeaways for you in this example and why did that lead you to start thinking about creating your own personal creative manifesto?

Marc Gutman (25:50): I think that much a brand, much like a company and much like a business, we all kind of do these same things, but the thing that's really, really different is the unique flavor we bring to it. And a lot of businesses I spent, and this is an interesting kind of reflection or realization. I mean, this is what I do for my career. I'm like, your special Cole, you're special, and I hope you find what's special and unique about what you bring to video production, but kind of discounted that has merit, that that's something that's really, really powerful and sticky and our process. So our process is probably similar to a lot of other processes. If you look at it on a board, if you were to every little put a Post-it note and then yours and then someone else's, I mean, we borrow things from other agencies from design thinking, but none of it's like, I don't believe I've invented anything new. (26:53): I don't believe that. But the thing that's really, really unique is how we approach it, how we synthesize it. Some of the things can't even be articulated. It's just the way that we see the lens through which we see that particular process and have comfort with it. And so what I learned is that is so powerful, and I think when these other companies are like, ah, can you just change a process or just kind bring it all together into ours? I think I just discounted that. Now the irony or the thing that's really funny is when I did this, the other agency owner, after I presented everything, he's like, oh man, I was really hoping that you would've done your process, that you would've brought your thing. I wanted to see that. That's what I was really excited about working with you on. And I was just trying to make it easy. I was trying to impress this other agency. I was like, if we do well here, there'll be a ton of other work because blah, blah, blah. It's really big important stuff, and part of that's what makes you different. And we map that out, we figure that out. But sometimes it's a little bit of this, for lack of a better explanation, it's a little bit of this Donald Draper Mad Men pulling sort of this insight out of thin air. Hey, you're this thing or whatever. And so our process helps us to get there. And even then it's a little tough. It's a little stressful. It's like you just don't know. It's never paint by numbers, but when we do different things, then it just becomes like, oh my gosh, are we ever going to even get to where we need to get to? (30:26): Sometimes those positionings, everyone does it a little different. And so then it's like, well, how do we get the output that you want? Everyone does values a little bit different. And the case of the client that I'm referencing, the agency, they just did it different than we did it. I thought they were great. It didn't fit really within their deliverable, and therefore it was just a little bit of a challenge. I think really what people pay us for is our thinking. We need to show that thinking. We need to defend that thinking. And if we don't follow our process, it all kind of becomes patchy and holy and this sort of thinking that doesn't totally make sense because we've been doing it. Cole Heilborn (31:21): Is there a difference? So we've been using the word process and manifesto kind of interchangeably. Is there a difference between the two? Are they the same thing?

Marc Gutman (31:31): I think they're interrelated for sure, because part of the manifesto, part of a brand is how you do what you do. And so how we do it, how we go about it. But I really do think of process is, but a lot of times too, your process is your approach. It's how we see the world. A lot of times your process embodies your values and your beliefs, and so yeah, they're intertwined. And I think that a really strong process is built and supported by your manifesto. It's built and supported by your brand, and it should all be intertwined because really process too, especially for people in a professional services firm, that is your customer experience. That is your product, that is what people will think about you. Yes, they want the output. Yes, they want the end result, but how you interact with your clients, I mean, that becomes your brand. That becomes what people think of you. That becomes, in a way, your manifesto now. It's just like if you were able to sit on the sidelines and watch you go through an entire process, beginning end with a client, and then you were able to put that into a narrative that would be your manifesto.

Cole Heilborn (32:57): So I know you haven't written this down, but it's something that you've been thinking about. If you had to write your own personal creative manifesto, what would be some of the larger components to it? What are some of the critical pieces for you?

Marc Gutman (33:14): I think it's bigger components would be things like who we want to work with. We want to work with forward thinking. Clients that believe in discovery. We want to work with clients that understand that this process of not knowing to knowing that's really the product of what we're selling and that they're patient and that they understand and we want to collaborate. So it's really important to co-create and collaborate. For me personally, I want to collaborate. For me personally, I want to make sure that I have the appropriate amount of support and engagement. A lot of times that comes down to budget because where can we as professional services firms, cut budget for clients, people, our people usually, and we start to pinch there, but yet then that puts more of the load on me personally, and I need the help. I know that I'm at my best when I collaborate with other really smart creatives. And so that's mean. That's one of the biggest ones for me is knowing that. So those are a couple of the things that go into that manifesto of sorts.

Cole Heilborn (34:40): It's funny you mentioned the collaboration piece because after when we first connected, we were talking about some of this, and I think you said, I demand collaboration from clients, from team members, whomever. And I walked away from our last conversation thinking about that idea and this idea of what does it mean to be a creative and kind of create your own rules, create your own manifesto for how you want to work. And I don't think I had ever realized, or I'd put it into words, how much I value that collaboration. I think I'd always assumed it, and I always knew I was at my best when I was working with others, but until I actually realized and actually spoke those words or typed them down, that was really powerful because I was like, oh, I know what I need. I need this. And so thinking about process and manifesto and what do you need as a creative, I kind of feel like every creative has their own manifesto, whether they've written it down or not, that they know they need. It's kind of like the best practices or the rules of engagement for how you operate.

So I know, and I've inherently always known my manifesto, but I've been too afraid to declare it to clients because you're like, I don't want to offend them. I want to get the work. I don't want to tell them how it's going to be. I don't want to tell them where I'm not strong. And part of in my mind, the manifesto is just that. It's like, Hey, this is me, for better or for worse, let's figure out really quick if me and my agency are a good fit, but in a real honest way, in a real, not almost in a really transparent leap of faith and not like, Hey, I'm going to hide some of the warts, or I'm not going to tell you where I'm not strong, or I'm not going to tell you what I'm really, really good at. (36:40): Because I think my tendency, and I don't know if you have the same thing or if you've seen the same thing with other creative agencies, is to be like, yeah, we can do everything great, and we're strong here and we're here to take care of you. And we see the whole landscape. And I don't have any chinks in the marketing armor, but I do. And it's impossible to be great at everything, and I think clients know that. And so while I haven't written it down, I've been very committed to communicating that to clients. And since we've talked, and it's been about a couple of weeks, so this is definitely something that's an experiment, but at least it feels good for me. It feels like I'm not going to be busted or fall down anywhere. And at least it can always be a little bit of, I told you so, right? Hey, I was very clear. This is how we work. But so far that's never come up. But I think a manifesto does that. It kind of sets you free, lets people know, and hopefully people don't engage because of it as well. I mean, if that's the case and if it's polarizing in that way and not super polarizing, I don't want people to not have business, but certainly want anyone that would be a red flag client to be like, we're just not a good fit.

Cole Heilborn (38:00): What has that been like to communicate that manifesto to potential clients over the last couple of weeks?

The work we do with a client, everyone likes the output, but you spend so much time with clients, you interact, and it's how we spend our days as people. It shouldn't be a bad experience, but we really minimize all those sort of areas where the project can go off the rails, where we can have missed expectations because that gap of expectations of missed, that's really neither side's wrong. Neither side's trying to be bad. Neither side's evil. But when we have bad feelings or felt like the value wasn't there, it's because expectations aren't aligned. (40:43): And so this is just another way to really align those expectations between professional service firm and client. And once we start to even minimize, run my video here, but I'm making a motion of closing that gap of bringing it closer, it just increases the odds of success. And at the end of the day, that's all I really, really want. And when we're successful, when we're on time, we're on budget, the client's happy. That's just like a home run. That shouldn't be an exception. That shouldn't be the exception to the rule. That should be the rule. But a lot of times when we are unclear with how we work or process or manifesto or what we believe, then it starts to get out of balance.

Cole Heilborn (41:34): I really like what you said there. Obviously the deliverable is the product, but maybe another thing to consider is that the relationship and how you work with the client is also a product in some form.

And so if we work really hard, if we have good expectations, if we have good process, if we have good shorthanded relationship with the client, just like any other relationship, if we've been honest and transparent about who we are, how we work, where we've made mistakes, they'll also give us a lot of grace in terms of coming back and allowing us to fix that mistake or to realign on the next project or something like that. So it's just good business for us, but it also, it's just good human interaction.

Cole Heilborn (42:34): So distill it all down. What's the takeaway?

Marc Gutman (42:40): Distill it all down. The takeaway is be clear on who you are and who you are not, and then clearly articulate that upfront, loud, and proud to your team, to clients, to vendors. Don't be shy, don't be embarrassed. Don't be scared of who you are. Good things and bad things. Don't be afraid to tell people where you really need help. When I say people, I mean clients like, Hey, this is where we can be really successful and this is where we tend to have problems, or we need to have this component in our process for you. This isn't like a, we're not padding the budget, we're not adding a second camera because we think it's cool. We need that and here's why and just be ready to defend it. But that's the takeaway.

Cole Heilborn (43:30): If folks want to go out and take their ideas and put them into their own manifesto of sorts. Do you have any guidelines or suggestions or first steps for people who are trying to figure out how to put all this onto paper and organize it for themselves?

What's your backstory and what's your vision for the future world? And so those are some areas where you can just go and literally you don't have to write anything grand. You can just do really quick answers, really cool footnotes, and then think about that. The other thing that I talk about in this little manifesto builder package is just go with your phone, put on voice recorder and just go for a walk and just start riffing on these ideas. Transcribe it with a free transcription programmer or something like I use Otter for a couple bucks a month, and you can go and highlight the things that really stood out on your walk and cobble together a manifesto. Super, super easy. And then lastly, you can also employ your team copywriters, things like that. You can really go for it and really think about it. But at its base, it really is about how you feel from the heart and what you believe in. And so smaller business, you have all the answers. If you're a larger business, sometimes you have to involve the team and kind of get some other inputs, but a lot of these things, the process is the same whether you're a bootstrap startup or whether you're a Fortune 100 company.

And I think the Lord has it that he was ski touring and he saw a plane fly over and he was like, man, there's got to be a way that we can get people into the mountains in an easier way. content: Julia LoVecchio (05:16): So we operate, we own and operate 12 individual areas. We've traditionally called them lodges. We now call them destinations because in some instances our operations don't have a lodge actually associated with it, doesn't have accommodation. So yeah, 12 areas within the interior of British Columbia. Our head office is here in Banff in Alberta, but all of our operations exist in bc. We run from early December in the wintertime, early December through to the beginning of May. So it's roughly 22 weeks of operation, which is a very long season. Our guests come from all over the world, predominantly United States and a handful of European countries. And then the rest is sort of the Canada and the rest of the world. Australia is a big feeder for us as well. And then in the summertime, which interestingly enough, we've only been operating our summer, so we've been operating since 1965 in the winter. (06:22): Our summer operation is about 30, 30 ish years old. It was created, we had, there's an organization called TA Tours, and Arthur, the founder of TA Tours, he was a very good friend of Hans Mosers, and he kept on pressuring, he was a guest of ours in the winter, and he kept on pressuring Hans saying, man, you've got these incredible lodges. Why aren't you using them in the summertime? And Hans said, oh, no one wants to, no one wants to come and do that. Everybody hikes in Europe on their own. We don't need this. And Arthur kept on saying, trust me, I can fill your lodges with my guests that I bring to the Canadian Rockies to experience this wonderful landscape. And Hans, it took Arthur several years to convince Hans to actually allow us or to allow him to bring guests. And probably for the first 20 years, 15 and 20 years of us actually having a summer operation for heli access hiking, Arthur was really predominantly our only guest. (07:29): He brought the guests for us and Arthur's guests were a little bit older and maybe a little bit more less experienced in walking around in the mountains and the helicopter, similar to what the helicopter provides us in the winter, it provides us access to places and activities that we wouldn't necessarily be able to do without it. Yeah, I mean, I continue to say it's my greatest career challenge is filling our three operations in the summertime. It's bizarre, but it's the equation of you need this helicopter to get to this place that is so easy for us to make as skiers and snowboarders. It's not the same in the summer.

content:
Cole Heilborn (08:14): I'm curious if mountain biking is something that's ever been questioned or is an offering in the summertime?

Julia LoVecchio (08:22): It's definitely been a question. I think the mountain biking industry is shifting. We are seeing more people travel, spending more of their disposable income on mountain bike experiences. But I would say one of the beauties of our summer experiences right now is there are no trails. When we think about hiking, like traditional hiking, what comes to mind in my little brain is I'm walking in front or behind a group. We're on the single track piece of trail. We're not really talking to each other with the helicopter. What that enables us to do is land somewhere and go for a walk, and we actually do leave a very small, we quote footprint on the landscape helicopter leaves, and we go for a walk and we only have very few people with us. So that, I'd say the intensity of building trails is something that we're not sure at this point that the benefit will be there in the market. There are operators that are doing it, certainly in our world, but yeah, it's not completely off the table, but we're focused on hiking right now and with 80% of the people that go outside to find themselves as a hiker, we think they're still a market for us.

Cole Heilborn (09:51): Yeah, interesting. Well, I'm curious, when did you enter the role of director of marketing with the company?

Julia LoVecchio (09:58): March 15th, 2015. Yeah, so seven years. And I often say that I won the career lottery. I think I have one of the best marketing jobs out there. It's been a real honor to work for such a famous and impressive organization.

What does the future look like? And this idea of aligning the internal and external brand started to be a question that it sounds like you and the team started to ask yourself. So I'm curious, what are those two, the internal and the external brand, and what was this inflection point that you found yourself in?

content:
Julia LoVecchio (11:00): When I think about internal and external brand, I actually personally, and I think we're seeing more and more organizations aligned to this, is that they are not mutually exclusive. You have a brand. Your brand is your brand, and it needs to fulfill the expectations of the customer or the consumers of your products just as much as it needs to fulfill the expectations of the people that work for you, your staff, your employees. And it's almost, there's times when I feel like it's similar to people that say, oh, well, I don't actually accept friend requests or allow my social media feeds to be part of the people that I work with because that's my personal life and my work life is not the same. And I actually believe in a modern world, there's this very gray blending that's happening where the things you do every day, the things you get paid to do every day need to be aligned with the things that you sell. And when they're not, it becomes more difficult for everybody. (12:29): So I mean, I really do think that when we talk about for us at CMH, we talk about our mission is that we guide you through life-changing mountain experiences, and that is, and then our vision is to be recognized as the world leader of guided mountain experiences by our guests, our staff, our partners, our vendors, et cetera. And I think by all of us understanding that not only are we providing these mountain life-changing experiences for our guests, that we ourselves have been transformed by the mountains, it is very, very central to who we are as a company.

Cole Heilborn (13:26): Yeah. So I'm curious, what challenge did you face when you stepped into the role?

content: Julia LoVecchio (13:33): There were a couple key challenges from a marketing standpoint that we saw, certainly that I saw. It is probably two to three years prior to my arrival for every year that our company was growing older, as was the average age of our guests. And we recognized that the loyalty based model that we had survived on and built an extremely successful company on while was very successful. Those loyal guests were aging out and we needed to go and find more guests like them or a new set of guests that were able to spend the next 20 years with us. So we needed to make a shift between from a loyalty based marketing organization to an acquisition based marketing organization. And I would say that prior to my arrival, the pendulum swung very, very, very far to the acquisition side. And it needed to be a mind shift that was happening internally as well. (14:48): But we did it in a way that almost spoke to that everything that we were doing in the past was wrong. And now when I came in, I said, okay, we actually can't go out and find all new guests. That's not going to happen. This is a very niche market. What we need to do is we need to find a balance between how we communicate as an organization that pays an enormous amount of respect to where we came, the guests that helped us build this business, the people that we've been hosting for years who very clearly have become our very, very good friends and almost family. But we also need to stay relevant and be relevant for a new group of people that are going to come in and spend time with us. And there is a fine balance between those things, especially in an environment where you are in the back country at a beautiful lodge sitting in a helicopter with a very small group of people, you need to make sure that you're meeting the expectations of those that have come before while also meeting the expectations of a new group. And it was an excellent revelation for us. But how you do it is ensuring that the team that's focused on whether that is acquiring an email or having a connection, an initial brand interaction with our organization, right through to the people that are going to be rebooking, guest X, that has been filling a particular lodge on a particular week for 15 years, that there similar efforts are going into both.
